stories.Headline: What Does CoreWeave (CRWV) Winning A New AI Training Deal Mean?
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported quarterly results on Tuesday, and the Washington Examiner says the company beat expectations across every metric as it drove rapid utilization of its accelerated computing services. Net income losses continued, primarily because of heavy depreciation and ballooning debt service obligations, which now approach $1 billion in net interest expense. The company rents clusters of advanced chips, typically designed by Nvidia, so customers can train AI models and run them to answer queries, a process known as inference. Nebius, another major NeoCloud, is due to report on Thursday, and analysts expect strong revenues from it as well. Tekedia describes the results as a test of whether the leading neocloud providers can sustain rapid growth while securing the financing needed to buy expensive AI systems and expand data center capacity.

At the end of June, CoreWeave held $5.5 billion in cash against $35 billion in debt, and its debt is yielding 16%, which is consistent with junk status. Yields on some CoreWeave bonds maturing in 2031 rose above 16%, and the spread on its five-year credit default swaps climbed above 1,240 basis points, up about 50% over the past month. Its latest earnings statement showed $1.3 billion outstanding on a financing facility at 15% interest due in March 2028, plus $3.2 billion under a facility due in August 2030 at 11%. In August, the company put its capital spending guidance at $35 billion to $39 billion, against only around $13 billion in 2026 revenue. Analysts surveyed by LSEG expect CoreWeave's latest-quarter revenue to rise about 160% from a year earlier to $3.55 billion, while Nebius is expected to report roughly sixfold growth to about $908 million.

CoreWeave chief executive Mike Intrator said in a LinkedIn post that the company does not anticipate any impact on existing customer commitments or its contracted backlog from shifts in the political landscape. In an October memo to employees, he argued that some companies trying to raise enormous amounts of capital lack the execution, revenue, scale and software solutions that CoreWeave delivers to customers. The Washington Examiner says management must convince the market that it can fund the very wide gap between capital spending and revenue at manageable rates. CoreWeave also has to pay for chips and data center capacity before customers are obligated to start paying for compute capacity. Tekedia reports that the backlog of business is growing, but so is the capital investment needed to deliver it.

Morningstar analyst Luke Yang said CoreWeave appears to have the resources to fulfil its existing contracts and is unlikely to face bankruptcy in the near term, though its five-year growth plans will require more financing. He added that equity issuance is unattractive because the stock has been beaten down, and he wants to hear how management plans to close the financing gap. Paul Meeks of Freedom Capital Markets called the market mood a self-fulfilling doom cycle, and he estimates CoreWeave's revenue could rise from $5 billion in 2025 to $42 billion by 2028 with an EBITDA margin approaching 70%. Anastasia Amoroso of Partners Group said neoclouds will be the most impacted by the deterioration in market conditions, and IREN's Daniel Roberts said capital markets have become more selective, now asking whether contracts can be delivered, financed and run at a profit. IREN has $10 billion in debt, and about 48% of its backlog is tied to Microsoft, although its AI cloud revenue more than doubled and its shares rebounded 20% on Friday.

Several neocloud stocks have lost about half their market value this month, and last Thursday's declines contributed to the Nasdaq's steepest daily fall in 19 months, with Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Micron also hit hard. Democratic candidates won gubernatorial races in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas last week, and voters rejected data center proposals in all but one of 41 related ballot measures across the United States. Anthropic is expected to go public next week at a valuation of around $1.4 trillion, which has dropped by several hundred billion dollars over the past few weeks. Tuesday's higher-than-expected October Consumer Price Index figures led the market to forecast a more aggressive interest rate policy by the Federal Reserve. Unlike Amazon and Microsoft, leading neocloud companies remain unprofitable and rely on a relatively small group of customers, which leaves them more exposed to financing conditions.

The Washington Examiner warns that financial distress at CoreWeave or Nebius could freeze the market for new syndicated debt supporting independent data center builds. A distress event at either company would also trigger contagion across valuations for all alternative infrastructure providers, raising the cost of capital across the AI sector. Funding pressure in the NeoCloud ecosystem could reverberate throughout the economy and arguably lead to a slowdown and a loss of momentum in the race for AI superiority against China. Meanwhile, Britain's Nscale filed for an initial public offering in September but has not published an updated prospectus, SB Energy faces similar uncertainty, and Australia's Firmus abandoned its IPO plans last month. The articles leave open whether CoreWeave can fund the gap between its capital spending and revenue at manageable rates, a question that investors will be watching in Nebius's Thursday report as well.

stories.Headline: Meta is launching its "smallest and most efficient" AI model: Muse Ember.
stories.Summary:
Meta Superintelligence Labs released a new AI model called Muse Ember on Monday, November 9, 2026, describing it as the lab's lightest and most cost-efficient model yet. Meta says Ember was designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day, including tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. The company stressed cost per task, citing Artificial Analysis's composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors such as Anthropic's Haiku and OpenAI's Luna. MarkTechPost describes Ember as a hosted multimodal reasoning model built for the repetitive steps inside agents. Both outlets report that it is the fourth model released under Meta's Muse brand.

Ember costs 10 cents per million input tokens and 50 cents per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.004 per million, according to MarkTechPost. It has a one million token context window and can produce up to 512K output tokens, four times the 128K cap on both rivals. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scores 36, level with Claude Haiku 5.5 at max effort and ahead of GPT-6 Luna at 28. It runs only on Meta's hosted infrastructure, through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, and its weights are private. It natively accepts text, images, audio, and video, so agents can read screenshots, charts, scanned documents, voice memos, and meeting recordings without a separate model.

Meta says Ember is meant to be paired with a larger model such as Muse Wonder inside an agentic harness, summing up the idea as "Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume." TechCrunch gives the example of a customer-support agent, where a heavier model sets the rules for an issue and a lighter model applies them across tens of thousands of cases. Meta also said agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video. According to MarkTechPost, Meta positions Ember below its larger models, with Wonder handling the hardest problems and Muse Spark covering coding and agentic workflows. Ember takes repeatable coding and agent tasks at scale, and it is the first model Meta trained using Muse Wonder Full, its largest model.

TechCrunch notes that at 10 cents per million input tokens Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna, and cost-competitive with open source rivals such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash. MarkTechPost points out that Haiku 5.5 and Luna list the same base rates, so the per-task gap must come from tokens used per task. On Meta's chart, Ember at max effort scores 35.8 at $0.136 per task, while Haiku 5.5 scores 36.2 at $0.411 and Luna's best setting scores 27.8 at $0.152. Artificial Analysis summarized this as matching Haiku at a third of the cost per task. Haiku 5.5 charges $0.50 and $2.50 above 100K prompt tokens, GPT-6 Luna doubles input rates above 272K input tokens, and Meta lists no long-context tier for Ember.

On benchmarks at max reasoning effort, Ember completes 37.8% of tasks on AutomationBench-AA, which uses 657 Zapier business workflows, against 20.2% for Luna and 13.9% for Haiku. It leads Terminal-Bench 4.0 with 40.9 versus Haiku's 39.2 and Luna's 16.4, and leads the AA Coding Agent Index, 46 to 37 to 31. It loses FrontierCode 2.0-AA, scoring 27.2 against Haiku's 34.9, and MarkTechPost lists closed weights and weaker mergeable real-repo code as its weak points. Ember ties Luna on GDP.pdf-AA at 22.8, edges Haiku on OSWorld 2.1 with 69.5 versus 68.9 on partial credit, and scores 80.6 on PerceptionBench with tools. Before Ember came the mid-weight Spark in April, its open source twin Glimmer in August, and the Wonder frontier model in October, and Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna were released October 7 and September 22, 2026.

Meta's flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success, according to TechCrunch. New features such as Spaces and video chat began rolling out earlier this month. Ember's availability is limited to Meta's own hosted services, and the articles say there is no local GPU, laptop, or quantized option. The articles do not say when or whether Ember's weights could be released, or whether a long-context pricing tier might be added. They also give no parameter count for Ember, and none for Haiku 5.5 or Luna either.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA-KAIST Develop 1M Korean AI Training Data
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA and KAIST, the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, are partnering on a research project to build 1 million Korean-language datasets for training artificial intelligence. The articles, both from Chosun Ilbo and dated November 10, 2026, describe the effort as an AI research program worth about 400 billion won. The Korean headline on the second article puts the goal plainly, saying the two sides will create 1 million Korean data items. The pages supplied to us are largely made up of site layout code, so they say little about the project beyond these headline details.

On what the project requires or changes, the headlines give only a few firm figures. The target is 1 million Korean datasets, and the research effort is valued at roughly 400 billion won. The Korean headline names NVIDIA and KAIST as the two partners behind the work. The articles as provided do not give a start date, a timeline for finishing the datasets, or a breakdown of how the money will be divided.

On who is responsible and what they said, the supplied text does not include any statements. No spokesperson, executive or researcher from NVIDIA or KAIST is quoted or paraphrased in the material we have. The second article lists its source as Chosun, a staff-written piece, but gives no byline or named official. As a result, the responsibility for the project rests with the two organizations named in the headlines, and nothing more specific can be attributed to any individual.

As for context and what comes next, the articles as provided do not explain why Korean-language data is being targeted or how the datasets will be used. They also do not say when the work will begin, how long it will take, or when any results might be released. Much of the content that came through is webpage structure and unrelated material, including a separate story about a special counsel investigation of prosecutors. Readers who want further detail on the NVIDIA and KAIST effort will need to wait for fuller reporting from Chosun Ilbo or statements from the two organizations.

stories.Headline: Cisco deploys Mythos 5 in AI Defense to boost AI-focused red team testing
stories.Summary:
Cisco has announced that its AI Defense product will add Anthropic's Claude Mythos to its adaptive AI red teaming framework, and the announcement was published on its blog on November 9, 2026. The company says AI Defense is among the first AI security products to augment its adaptive red teaming framework with the model. Cisco describes the pairing as frontier attacker reasoning combined with responsible controls, so that red team engagements can reflect adversary capability without compromising customer environments. The blog post was written by Amy Chang and Vikram Varakantam, and its headline refers to the model as Claude Mythos while the body at one point calls it Claude Mythos 5. Separately, Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 published research on November 11, 2026 about AI-enabled red teaming tools that attackers are using to run offensive operations autonomously.

Cisco says the model sits inside AI Defense with a fixed job, a registered target, and objectives defined by the human user. The deployment operates only against the target a customer has registered and is authorized to test, and customers get no open interface through which they could prompt the model freely. The controls named are authorization to test only permitted targets, attribution to a named operator, and full auditability. In the adaptive red teaming engine, the model's reasoning produces attack ideas as the engine works to understand a target system and plan tests. When those ideas become concrete payloads, Cisco says the benefit is sharper still, because the capabilities are offered under safeguards built for authorized testing.

Cisco says it pioneered the AI security industry with a number of firsts, starting with the launch of AI Defense, which it calls the first enterprise AI security offering to combine asset visibility, supply chain scanning, algorithmic red teaming, and runtime guardrails in one solution. The company also says it was first to introduce adaptive red teaming and adaptive guardrail capabilities once agents emerged. Cisco regards the Mythos deployment as an early instance of a broader shift, in which frontier security capabilities are made available to defenders under verified, controlled access rather than withheld from everyone. Cisco says customers inform the target and objective while its agentic red teaming framework conducts the engagement within those bounds. Cisco adds that the aim is to augment the system so customers receive an advanced AI red teaming experience.

Michael Moore, Cybersecurity Lead at Anthropic, said enterprises are increasingly building AI agents into their core operations and want to test those agents thoroughly before putting them into production. He said that by bringing Claude Mythos to Cisco AI Defense, Cisco can help security teams red team their agents with advanced reasoning that plans tests and generates attack ideas for each system. Cisco says the timing is consequential because businesses are eager to adopt agentic technologies while security teams work to keep pace. It argues that organizations must now account not only for model behavior but also for how agents behave once connected to a complex system of tools, skills, and sensitive resources. Cisco adds that every environment is different, so security teams need a way to find the risks specific to their own deployments before attackers do.

Cisco explains that AI Defense offers two types of red team testing, standard and adaptive, and that customers have used its red teaming to uncover critical safety and security vulnerabilities in their AI systems. Standard red teaming covers common risks that virtually any agent or AI application would face, such as prompt injection and jailbreaks, sensitive data exposure, and harmful content generation. These tests span thousands of categories, content types, and adversarial techniques and finish in minutes, with a report that maps to Cisco's Integrated AI Security and Safety Framework along with standards from OWASP, MITRE, and NIST. Adaptive testing exists because standard tests cannot cover the risks unique to an organization's application, so users define custom criteria in plain language. The framework then analyzes the target, develops tailored attacks, refines or changes tactics based on the target's responses, evaluates the results, and furnishes a report, while AI Defense recommends follow-up actions and lets customers build custom adaptive guardrails in Policy Studio.

The Cisco post was cut off mid-sentence while describing the design of the deployment, so the rest of the safeguards it lists are not available here. The articles do not say when Claude Mythos will reach customers, whether it carries any extra cost, or how many customers will use it. Unit 42 notes that the ARTEX author recently made the repository closed-source and ceased public development to prevent misuse, and that emerging alternatives are filling the void with new capabilities that threat actors will inevitably co-opt. Unit 42 recommends that defenders remove public attack maps, require authentication on every write endpoint, harden self-service flows, protect federated identities, and replace long-lived cloud keys with role-based access. The articles do not connect the Cisco announcement to the Unit 42 findings, so how the two relate is left open.

stories.Headline: Google AI school policy
stories.Summary:
Google announced this week that it will no longer allow schools to use its search engine unless they opt in to using artificial intelligence, according to both articles. Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, spoke at a virtual briefing on Monday and told The New York Times that search and AI are deeply integrated. The Los Angeles Unified School District said it is reviewing the announcement and what it could mean for schools, educators and students. Google also said that in the coming months, products like Gemini and Google Search would be turned off by default until schools switch them on. Google believes schools should have control over AI in their classrooms, according to the company's own explanation.

Under the plan, Google will block both its integrated AI tool and its search engine for K-12 students starting in January unless a district chooses to turn either feature on. No option will exist for a version of search without AI integration. Phillips said that if a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, it can choose to have Search off entirely. A school that bans AI would see its students lose search access and receive a message from the school saying it is not available. Google said in a blog post on Tuesday that it will make its Guided Learning AI product the default for schools, offering step-by-step help through problems so students do not get quick answers to schoolwork.

A spokesperson for LAUSD said the district believes emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, can enhance teaching and learning when they are introduced thoughtfully, responsibly and with clear safeguards. The district has asked Google for a modification that would allow its AI-generated search summaries to be turned off. Google said it will offer the guided learning tool in its chatbot for student accounts if a school opts in to artificial intelligence. In a post on X on Tuesday, Google clarified that schools can turn off its separate AI products, Gemini and Gemini Notebook, and still use search. However, AI Mode and AI Overview will remain integrated in search, according to that clarification.

Lila Byock, founder of the parent advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, said Google forced its AI products into classrooms and parents fought back. She said Google is now refusing to take no for an answer, and she called the company's ultimatum hostile. She described the decision as an act of bullying and said educational value, not shareholder value, must determine the technology students use. Her group pushed for LAUSD's AI moratorium and for the district's screen time limit, and she called on district leaders to reclaim their authority from corporate interests and divest from Google. The change will force schools to rethink their AI policies in the middle of the school year.

Earlier this school year, LAUSD put in place a moratorium on students using generative AI on district-issued devices. Students in the district can still use Google to search for information, a district spokesperson said, but the AI mode, where students can chat with Gemini, is turned off. Some searches may still show an AI-generated summary or overview, according to the district. Google has long been woven into California students' education, with Search, Chromebooks and Gmail quietly in the background of their daily lives.

Districts across California are debating restrictions on AI and technology use in classrooms, and schools rely on Google's digital workspace for daily lessons and its search engine for research and assignments. LAUSD's Ad Hoc Committee on Generative AI will hold its next meeting on Friday, Nov. 13, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Members of the public can attend at 333 S. Beaudry Ave.

in downtown Los Angeles, and the meeting will also stream online. Interpretation in American Sign Language and Spanish is offered, and community members can request other languages by contacting the Board Secretariat at secretariat@lausd.net or (213) 241-7002. Google's changes are set to begin in January, though the articles do not say how LAUSD will respond. They also do not say whether Google will grant the district's request to turn off AI summaries in search.

stories.Headline: Google Launches Gemini Decisions API With Gemini Decision 1 at $0.10/M Tokens
stories.Summary:
Google has launched the Gemini Decisions API, powered by a new model called Gemini Decision 1 (gemini-decision-1), according to articles published on November 11, 2026. The API does not generate text. Instead, it scores up to 1,000 typed questions against one shared input and returns calibrated probabilities. Google aims it at the small branching calls inside AI agents, such as routing, policy checks, tool selection and grading. It is priced at $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with no output tokens billed.

Each request has three parts: a model ID, a shared input, and a map of questions. The docs define three question types. A yes/no type returns the probability of yes, bounded between 0.01 and 0.99, while a choice type picks one of 2 to 255 options and returns normalized probabilities for each. A score type rates the input on 2 to 255 ordered rubric levels and returns a probability-weighted score. Every answer carries a confidence value from 0 to 1, and Google suggests sending low-confidence cases to a fallback or a human reviewer.

The context window is 262,144 tokens across the shared input and all questions, and the model reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs in one pass. Speed and billing follow from the design, since the model scores candidate options in one forward pass instead of decoding token by token. Google reports median model compute of 50 to 100 ms and 150 to 250 ms end to end, for inputs up to 16K tokens, with latency nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions. The shared input is billed once per request, and each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens. There are no thinking-token, transcription or OCR charges, and the service runs only on Google's hosted API (Gemini Developer API, v1beta), with no open weights or self-hosting.

All benchmark figures are self-reported by Google, which tested the model against TypeSafe Jev 1.14, GPT-6 Luna on OpenAI Decisions, and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. Gemini Decision 1 leads on 7 of 9 accuracy benchmarks, including 92.2% on JevBench versus 90.0% for Jev 1.14. Its weakest result is 58.7% Macro-F1 on Amazon ESCI, and it trails Jev 1.14 on When2Call, 79.9% to 82.0%. Its calibration error of 0.0250 is about half the 0.0494 of Jev 1.14, which matters when setting confidence thresholds for automation. On cost, Google says it is nearly 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite across the shared suite, at $0.88 versus $4.14, though Jev 1.14 is cheaper at $0.68.

stories.Headline: Paras Semiconductors partners with US firm BroadPak for advanced chip packaging in India
stories.Summary:
Paras Semiconductors, a subsidiary of Paras Defence and Space Technologies, has announced a technology partnership with US-based BroadPak Corporation to develop advanced semiconductor packaging capabilities in India. The announcement came in a company release on Monday, November 10, 2026, as reported by PTI and by Electronics For You. Through the tie-up, Paras Semiconductors aims to set up an advanced heterogeneous integration and 3D packaging facility in the country. The proposed facility is an OSAT unit, meaning an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test operation. Electronics For You described the partnership as one that gives Paras Semiconductors access to specialised technology expertise from the American firm.

The proposed unit will focus on 2.5D and 3D packaging, chiplet integration, hybrid bonding, wafer-level and panel-level fan-out packaging, co-packaged optics, and testing and qualification. Paras Semiconductors will gain access to BroadPak's design, manufacturing and integration intellectual property, along with technology transfer and process know-how. The two firms will also explore joint development of packaging platforms for AI and high-performance computing applications. They plan to collaborate on training and skill development programmes for Indian engineers. The planned manufacturing unit will incorporate through-silicon vias, micro-bumping, advanced interposers and redistribution layer technologies, along with wafer-level processing and reliability testing.

Munjal Sharad Shah, Managing Director of Paras Defence and Space Technologies, described the company's entry into the semiconductor sector as a strategic expansion into a technology domain that is increasingly critical. He said it matters for India's AI, data centre and industrial capabilities. He added that the collaboration would help build advanced packaging capabilities that complement the company's existing strengths in optics, optronics and critical electronics. Santosh Kumar, CEO of Paras Semiconductors, said the company intends to build a packaging platform that can meet the performance, connectivity and thermal needs of next-generation applications. He said the collaboration would support capabilities in heterogeneous integration, chiplet architectures, hybrid bonding and advanced system-in-package technologies.

Shah also said the initiative would address India's strategic domestic requirements as well as the wider needs of the semiconductor industry. BroadPak Founder and CEO Farhang Yazdani said India's growing semiconductor ecosystem offers an important opportunity to develop capabilities in heterogeneous integration and system-level packaging. He noted that this opportunity is especially strong as demand for AI and high-performance computing increases. The facility is meant to serve applications in artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, networking, data centres and strategic electronics.

It will also address high-volume manufacturing needs, including devices for optical and optronic systems. Through the partnership, Paras Semiconductors aims to strengthen its presence in India's domestic semiconductor packaging ecosystem and to support emerging computing and strategic electronics applications. BroadPak is headquartered in San Jose, California, and was founded in 2007. According to the release, it brings specialised expertise across advanced packaging design, manufacturing and system integration.

Its capabilities cover 2.5D and 3D IC packaging, heterogeneous integration, multi-die architectures, high-speed interconnects, thermal management and co-packaged optics. Electronics For You said the rising demand for advanced packaging technologies, including chiplets, 2.5D and 3D integration and hybrid bonding, made the decision to collaborate stronger. Paras Semiconductors is a subsidiary of Paras Defence and Space Technologies, whose existing strengths lie in optics, optronics and critical electronics. The articles do not say when the proposed facility will be built or begin operating.

They give no location for it, and they state no investment amount or capacity figure. They also do not say how many engineers will be trained or when the training will start. The two firms have said they will explore joint development of packaging platforms for AI and high-performance computing, so those platforms remain at an early stage. The financial terms of the partnership and any regulatory approvals the facility may need are not stated.

stories.Headline: IBM and Microsoft Launch AI Agent Platform
stories.Summary:
IBM and Microsoft announced Imagine Enterprise on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, an AI agent platform meant to help companies build, run and govern agents that carry out industry-specific business processes. The two companies combined their technologies and expertise to create it, with IBM Consulting supplying the agents and Microsoft supplying the cloud foundation. IBM trades on the New York Stock Exchange and Microsoft on the Nasdaq, and the announcement came from Armonk, New York, and Redmond, Washington. The platform pairs IBM Consulting's collection of more than 6,000 prebuilt AI agents and assets with Microsoft's AI, data, cloud and security technologies. It is aimed at helping banks, insurers and retailers automate business processes, with financial services, insurance and retail named as the initial targets.

The platform draws on agents and assets built through IBM Consulting Advantage, IBM's existing platform for developing and deploying AI applications, and the figure of 6,000 counts agents together with other assets. Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio and GitHub Copilot provide tools for developing and coordinating agents, while Microsoft Fabric connects enterprise data. Microsoft Entra manages identities and access permissions, Purview supports data governance, Defender provides security, and Azure and Microsoft 365 infrastructure supply cloud services. On IBM's side, Process Studio, Context Studio and Advantage Core support the design, deployment and governance of tailored agents. Forward-deployed engineers from both companies will work directly with qualifying customers to integrate agents into existing software and move them from testing into production.

Mohamad Ali, Senior Vice President and Head of IBM Consulting, said clients no longer want AI that simply helps people do the same work a little faster. He said they want to build what he called an agentic business. Ali added that Microsoft and IBM are helping organizations bring human expertise and digital labor together in a way that can scale across the enterprise. In his words, the aim is to turn AI from a productivity aid into a real competitive advantage. The companies describe the platform as designed to connect with existing company systems and to adapt agents to an organization's own information and processes.

SEI, a financial technology, operations and asset management provider, is working with IBM Consulting, supported by Microsoft, to explore emerging and agentic technologies. Its work also involves other technologies from the two companies, with goals that include improving business operations and the experiences of employees and clients. Sneha Shah, SEI's Chief AI Strategist and Head of SEI Next, said the work helps SEI explore how emerging capabilities could support critical processes and be responsibly scaled over time. The announcement does not identify a completed Imagine Enterprise deployment at SEI or give measured results from the new platform. The platform particularly targets regulated industries, where its governance features include controls, observability and AI-compliance support that the companies say help customers manage industry-specific deployments.

The partnership extends Microsoft's efforts to expand AI adoption across its existing base of enterprise software customers. Microsoft has 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats, but fewer than 7% carry paid Copilot licenses, PYMNTS reported in September. Microsoft 365 Copilot costs $30 per user monthly, while newer agent capabilities are billed according to usage. Microsoft has also introduced agents that operate within corporate Microsoft 365 environments, with their own identities, memory and email addresses. The launch comes as businesses raise their AI investments but remain cautious about granting software independent authority.

PYMNTS Intelligence's November report, titled The Agentic Edge Index, found that agentic AI is in use at 89% of large U.S. enterprises. Yet 78% of those companies would restrict agents to read-only access to company directories. Another 18% would allow agents to perform tasks with human approval, while 2% would permit independent execution. The same report found that 51% of executives consider organizational barriers, including staffing, business processes and corporate culture, greater obstacles to AI adoption than technology.

The articles do not say when the platform will be generally available, what it will cost, or which customers qualify for the forward-deployed engineering support. They also do not name any customer that has completed a production deployment of Imagine Enterprise. The text provided from the press release cuts off before the announcement finishes describing how the platform lets organizations avoid starting from scratch or replacing platforms they already depend on. No figures are given for the performance of the agents or for any savings from using them. How many of the 6,000 items are deployable agents rather than other assets is also left unstated.

stories.Headline: Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS) stock price forecast: AI infrastructure growth drives Wall Street's bullish outlook
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group shares rallied sharply on November 11, 2026, ahead of the company's third-quarter earnings release scheduled for November 12. The shares rose 12 to 15 percent in premarket trading, reaching roughly $150 to $154 after closing at $134 on November 10. The rebound followed stronger-than-expected results from CoreWeave, which reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 168 percent. CoreWeave also reported a revenue backlog of approximately $132.5 billion, and its results helped restore confidence in AI infrastructure stocks. Nebius will publish its own quarterly results before the U.S. market opens on November 12.

Wall Street expects Nebius to report third-quarter revenue of approximately $907 million, which would be up 521 percent from $146.1 million in the third quarter of 2025. That figure compares with second-quarter 2026 revenue of $582.3 million, implying expected sequential growth of 56 percent. Analysts anticipate a quarterly loss of roughly $0.60 to $0.70 per share as infrastructure investment accelerates. The expected revenue increase mainly reflects expanding AI computing capacity and growing demand from enterprise customers and hyperscalers. Investment bank price targets for the stock range from $144 to $399, and the broader analyst consensus stands near $297.

The price targets come from several investment banks. Morgan Stanley rates the stock Equal Weight with a $144 target, set in August 2026, while Piper Sandler is Neutral at $185, updated on October 21. Citigroup and Bank of America both rate it Buy, with targets of $265 on November 4 and $310 on October 22. Goldman Sachs also has a Buy at $328, from August 25, and Exane BNP Paribas rates it Outperform at $399, from September 24. Citigroup lowered its target from $324 to $265 in early November, and Piper Sandler cut its target from $237 to $185.

Across 13 analyst ratings, nine are Buy recommendations, three are Holds and one is a Sell. The average 12-month price target is approximately $296.73, although estimates differ between market-data providers. At a premarket share price near $150, that consensus implies about 98 percent potential appreciation over 12 months, which reflects analyst expectations and not a guaranteed return. Wall Street remains predominantly positive on the stock despite its substantial decline from August highs. The Citigroup revision indicates that expectations have become more conservative even among banks that maintain a positive view.

The company has built a significant portfolio of AI infrastructure commitments. In March 2026 it announced a five-year agreement with Meta covering $12 billion of dedicated computing capacity, with deliveries scheduled to begin in early 2027. The arrangement includes commitments for up to $15 billion of additional capacity, bringing the potential total to about $27 billion, and Nebius has indicated it holds more than $40 billion in long-term customer commitments. In October it secured a $3.5 billion senior secured financing facility from Citi, with an initial maturity of 364 days and interest starting at Term SOFR plus 2.75 percent. In August it completed an offering of approximately $5.75 billion in convertible senior notes.

Nebius will publish its results on November 12, and revenue approaching $907 million would confirm rapid business expansion. The market is likely to place greater weight on management's capacity deployment schedule, financing strategy and outlook for 2027. Investors will watch whether data center capacity is coming online on schedule, whether sufficient financing is secured and whether long-term contracts convert into recognized revenue. Left open are the risks around financing, since debt raises interest expenses, convertible securities can dilute shareholders, and elevated U.S. interest rates would make expansion costlier. Reports that Microsoft has increased scrutiny of certain AI infrastructure projects have raised questions about delivery schedules and customer commitments, though this is not confirmation that existing contracts will be terminated.

stories.Headline: AMD or Nvidia: Which AI Chip Stock Would I Buy With $1,000 Today?
stories.Summary:
Two Motley Fool articles, published on November 10 and November 11, 2026, made the case for different AI-related stocks. Harsh Chauhan wrote the first, which compared Advanced Micro Devices and Intel as AI chip investments and concluded that AMD is the better buy. Patrick Sanders wrote the second, which argued that SpaceX could become a $5 trillion company by 2029. Both pieces rely on recent quarterly results and company announcements to support their views. Neither article actually addresses the choice between AMD and Nvidia named in the headline.

In the third quarter, Intel's data center and AI segment grew 78% year over year to $7.3 billion, while AMD's data center segment grew 97% to $8.5 billion. For the current quarter, AMD guides to revenue of $17 billion at the midpoint, a 66% increase, against Intel's guidance of $15.5 billion, about 13% growth. AMD is also projecting revenue growth of more than 80% in 2027. SpaceX, which went public in June, reported third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161%, with net income of $4.4 billion after a $1.1 billion loss a year earlier. Its AI division, which it calls super intelligence, brought in $7.56 billion, ahead of the $5.25 billion from connectivity including Starlink, and capital expenditures reached $19.6 billion.

On the AMD earnings call, CEO Lisa Su said visibility into 2027 keeps strengthening, since customers have expanded their EPYC and Instinct deployment plans and AMD has secured more supply. She said AMD now expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027, with data center AI revenue growing even faster than projected 90 days earlier. Intel's management said on its own call that it expects server CPU industry shipments to rise by more than 30% in both 2026 and 2027. Elon Musk announced in October that SpaceX and Tesla had set up independent committees to explore a possible merger. Musk is not taking part in the negotiations because his ownership stakes in both companies create a conflict of interest.

Chauhan concluded that AMD is the better semiconductor stock to buy, because it is growing much faster than the server CPU market and appears to be taking share from Intel. He noted that AMD trades at 30 times forward earnings, according to Morningstar, against 35 times for Intel. Analysts expect AMD's earnings per share to rise 118% in 2027, compared with 20% for Intel, and they became more bullish on AMD's long-term earnings growth after its latest report. Sanders wrote that he believes a Tesla merger is inevitable and that SpaceX has a realistic chance of reaching $5 trillion by 2029. He also cautioned that the target is aggressive, that a merger is not guaranteed, and that combining two enormous companies would complicate matters for shareholders.

Shareholders of SpaceX and Tesla are the people most directly affected by the possible merger. The Globe and Mail page showed Nvidia down 5.9% on the Toronto exchange the day the SpaceX article appeared. In its Stock Advisor promotion, the Motley Fool said its analysts did not include AMD among their ten best stocks to buy now, even though Chauhan favored it over Intel. The same promotional box said SpaceX was not on that list either. The Motley Fool holds positions in and recommends AMD, Intel, Nvidia, Tesla and SpaceX, while Chauhan says he holds none of the stocks he mentioned and Sanders says he holds Nvidia.

AMD's MI455X graphics cards have begun shipping in volume to customers, and AMD expects them and its Epyc server CPUs to drive stronger data center growth. Intel's Gaudi series of data center GPUs failed to find much favor among customers, and the company seems more inclined toward server CPUs. In June, SpaceX announced an agreement worth up to $6.3 billion with Reflection AI, an open-source model developer, giving it access to Nvidia chips at SpaceX's Colossus data center in Tennessee. That contract includes termination provisions, so its full value is not guaranteed. Nvidia and Apple have already reached $5 trillion in market value, although both have since pulled back, and SpaceX is valued at $1.8 trillion against Tesla's $1.6 trillion.

The articles leave open whether a SpaceX and Tesla merger will happen, and whether it would reach the roughly $3.4 trillion combined value, from which $5 trillion would take about 47% appreciation. Reaching that mark over the next three years is described as ambitious but more achievable than SpaceX nearly tripling its market capitalization alone. Both SpaceX and Tesla are making substantial investments in technologies that have not yet shown their full profit potential, including autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots. AMD's stock has risen 137% in 2026 and Intel's 60%, though both have suffered a brutal recent sell-off in semiconductors. The articles give no comparison of AMD and Nvidia, so the question of how a $1,000 purchase should be split between them remains unanswered.

stories.Headline: #AmazingChina | AI in eyes of global media leaders - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
The 7th World Media Summit took place in Beijing from November 5 to 9, 2026, with media professionals from around the world meeting to examine how artificial intelligence is reshaping the news industry. It was jointly organized by Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing municipal government under the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action." The gathering brought together about 500 representatives from nearly 330 media organizations, think tanks, government bodies and international organizations across 112 countries and regions. Participants explored ways to harness AI to improve news production while avoiding ethical pitfalls that could undermine trust in their content. They stressed that embracing the technology must go hand in hand with upholding journalistic principles, and that international cooperation is essential.

On Saturday the summit released the Global Media Initiative for the Joint Development of AI Application Standards, which Xinhua launched as a concrete step toward cooperation. The initiative brings together major media outlets and other professional organizations to safeguard the authenticity of information, protect data security, and uphold media ethics. Participants plan to work together for about two years to develop a set of standards addressing different media uses of AI, validated by media outlets. The initiative also calls for a global database of AI applications. Separately, two life-sized robot news anchors, described as the world's first bionic humanoid robot news anchors, made their official debut at the summit, greeting the audience in fluent English.

Fu Hua, president of Xinhua News Agency, told the opening ceremony that media professionals should share new technologies and applications, exchange experience in using them, and close gaps in AI research, development and understanding. He said Xinhua is willing to strengthen dialogue with all parties to advance the industry and promote exchanges and cooperation. Fu added that practitioners should make good use of AI while safeguarding the credibility of mainstream media, and that all media professionals should have a fair chance to benefit from it. He said Xinhua looks forward to deeper cooperation with fellow media organizations to promote closer people-to-people ties and advance relations between countries. The Beijing municipal government was the summit's co-organizer, and the articles report no separate statement from it.

Reuters President Paul Bascobert called AI a resource that increases speed, efficiency and scale, but said it must meet journalistic standards, adding that tasks are automated while judgment is not. AFP chief Fabrice Fries described an approach he called "augmented journalism," in which reporters spend less time on routine production and more on meeting people and explaining developments. Toshimitsu Sawai of Japan's Kyodo News called generative AI an assistive tool but warned of copyright infringement, misinformation and cases of out-of-control behavior by models. CNN's Kostas Oikonomou said AI should strengthen reporting rather than replace human judgment, and called collaboration between media companies a strategic necessity. Voices from the Global South, including the Maldives' Aminath Namza, Malaysia's Bernama chairman Wong Chun Wai and Mohammed Alyami of the Union of News Agencies of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, urged that smaller and developing nations share in AI's benefits and in shaping its governing principles.

The articles describe AI as already present at virtually every stage of news production, from story planning and information gathering to fact-checking, proofreading, and the generation of news images and videos. Fries said newsrooms everywhere are under pressure, with audiences expecting faster coverage, more formats, more languages and more explanations. Bascobert noted that news delivery has evolved from carrier pigeons and telegraphs to digital technologies, and that while tools have changed, the principle of getting, checking and reporting facts has not. Tatiana Valovaya, director-general of the United Nations Office at Geneva, warned of synthetic content, information manipulation, privacy threats, algorithmic bias and unequal access to technology. Turkish news platform chief Sumeyra Teymur said she was impressed by earlier AI anchors and saw potential for humanoid robots to cover dangerous events such as earthquakes and conflicts.

The standards initiative is scheduled to run for about two years, during which participants will develop standards for the different ways media use AI and have them validated by outlets. Valovaya named three priorities for media organizations: protecting information integrity and public trust, ensuring AI benefits everyone, and keeping human dignity and responsibility at the center. Alyami said he hopes the initiative becomes a practical avenue for sharing expertise and building capacity, so organizations of different sizes and resources can apply the standards. The articles do not say which outlets beyond the Organization of Islamic Cooperation's news agencies union have joined as participants, nor when the standards or the global AI database will be completed. They also leave open how the standards will be enforced and how the human judgment that speakers stressed will be maintained as the technology advances.

stories.Headline: Texas Paused Data Center Permits Before the Election. Here's Why That Context Matters for AI Investors.
stories.Summary:
Following last week's election, shares of artificial intelligence companies have been falling, which has pulled the S&P 500 lower. Investors fear that new legislation could hinder data center growth and, as a result, slow the development of AI. The market had at first appeared to react positively to the election results on Wednesday, then did a 180 on Thursday as investors digested the implications of a new Congress. Texas had already paused permits on data centers even before the elections took place. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to put a moratorium on building until the government can work with residents to learn what their needs are.

On Thursday, Nvidia and Broadcom fell 8% and 9% respectively in a single day, according to The Motley Fool's report. In that same session the S&P 500 fell more than 4%, while the tech-focused Nasdaq composite dropped 5.5%. Texas accounts for 25% to 30% of the data center capacity planned for development by 2030. In the first few months of 2026 alone, almost 200 data centers asked to be added to the electric grid. About 90% of the large energy consumers requesting massive amounts of power came from data centers, and their requests totaled five times the amount needed to power the whole state at its record-breaking demand.

Hinojosa, the Governor-elect, has said that a moratorium is the only way to give people any assurance of protection until the legislature can meet and pass real protections into law. Texas's current governor has already started an audit of how much energy data centers use and how that affects residents' energy consumption and bills. State lawmakers have questioned, however, whether companies can be compelled to take part in an audit unless a law is passed. The new state government under Hinojosa may pass the laws needed to make such an audit happen. The article's author, Jennifer Saibil of The Motley Fool, says the market did not react to the original Texas pause because it did not know how seriously lawmakers would take the issue.

Georgia and Ohio, the other two states at the center of AI development, also just elected new Democratic governors who plan to halt permits. Investors in Nvidia and Broadcom may be hit hard, since those so-called pick and shovel plays depend on the pace of data center construction. Much of Nvidia's rapid growth story rests on continued building, and the company has reported accelerating growth, including a doubling of revenue in the fiscal 2027 second quarter, which ended July 26. That growth rate will slow if construction slows, and stocks of AI and AI-adjacent companies will be worth less if their growth rates decline. Amazon and Alphabet were seen as better placed because they already have robust platforms, and both rose on Wednesday before dropping again.

Before the election, the market had been worried about AI spending for months, yet it kept climbing and left some of the biggest spenders behind. That spending has pushed many top tech companies into negative free cash flow, which is why investors at first embraced the idea of a slowdown. Nebius Group, which builds full-stack infrastructure for AI workloads in the US, the UK and other international markets, faces its own scrutiny. Regulators and local authorities are reviewing operating permits for several Nebius AI facilities, and some approvals were still pending as of early November 2026. Nebius has a market cap of $35.5 billion and margins of 3.1%, and analysts already tie its story to heavier regulation and environmental rules.

The articles leave open how long the permit pauses and moratoriums in Texas, Georgia and Ohio will last. It is also unclear whether Texas lawmakers will pass the laws needed to compel companies to take part in the energy audit. For Nebius, the timing of its next phase of AI infrastructure expansion could depend on whether its pending approvals come through. The article warns that new governments critical of AI development could cause the AI bubble to pop.

stories.Headline: Cloudflare Jumps 11%, Nebius Surges 9% as AI Cloud Stocks Defy NVIDIA's Slide; CoreWeave Rallies 6% on Wayve Deal
stories.Summary:
On November 9, AI cloud stocks climbed in afternoon trading even as NVIDIA fell, according to reporting by David Moadel for 24/7 Wall St. Cloudflare rose 11% to $297.22, after a third-quarter earnings beat that buyers have kept rewarding. Nebius Group gained 9% to $140.70 as the AI cloud provider headed toward its own quarterly report. CoreWeave rose 6% to $49.18 after signing a multi-year cloud computing deal with British autonomous driving startup Wayve. NVIDIA moved the other way, falling 5% to $177.40, while Oracle gained 3% to $119.16 and IREN rose 2% to $21.98.

The Wayve deal, reported on November 9, has Wayve using CoreWeave's NVIDIA Blackwell-based infrastructure to train and test its driving models. Financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed, and Wayve already uses Weights & Biases, which CoreWeave acquired in 2025. Cloudflare reported its third-quarter 2026 results after the close on November 5, with revenue up 39.2% year over year to $782.51 million. That figure topped the consensus estimate of $738.30 million, and adjusted earnings of $0.38 per share beat the $0.3434 estimate. Management raised the full-year 2026 revenue outlook to between $2.963 billion and $2.964 billion, and guided fourth-quarter revenue to between $845 million and $846 million.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince called the third quarter the best in the company's history. He credited the company's fastest revenue growth in nearly four years, achieved while expanding profitability. Prince also presented Cloudflare on the earnings call as the first agentic cloud, with developers building AI agents on its Workers platform. Management is the source of the raised full-year outlook and the fourth-quarter revenue guidance. Cloudflare's results were published in its own earnings release, which the article cites for the revenue and earnings figures.

Analysts expect Nebius to report revenue of $905 million to $907 million, which would mean growth of more than 500% year over year. They also expect an adjusted loss of between 69 cents and $1.11 per share. Options pricing implies a post-earnings move of 17% or more, and investors are likely to focus on capacity guidance, 2027 run-rate projections and infrastructure spending. The article advises that a conservative investment approach may be warranted until Nebius reports. On the bullish side for Cloudflare, the article points to accelerating revenue, a 17.5% adjusted operating margin and a higher full-year outlook, while on the other side its gross margin fell to 71.2% from 74%.

Cloudflare runs a global edge network that sells security, networking and developer tools on a subscription basis to millions of organizations. Nebius and CoreWeave rent GPU computing capacity to AI labs, hyperscalers and enterprises, and both buy their chips from NVIDIA. CoreWeave reported a revenue backlog of approximately $104 billion as of June 30, while Nebius disclosed $37.5 billion in remaining performance obligations. Oracle pairs its AI cloud with an enterprise software franchise, and IREN owns the land, power and data centers behind its shift from crypto mining. The article says AI shares are drawing buyers back after last week's post-midterm selloff, and that Cloudflare still has $4.4 billion in convertible notes outstanding.

Nebius is expected to report its third-quarter 2026 results before the market opens on November 12. The report could decide whether its run-up holds against high expectations, and the article says investors will watch its capacity guidance, 2027 run-rate projections and infrastructure spending. CoreWeave also has quarterly earnings coming up, though the article gives no date. The next test for Cloudflare is whether its growth can stay near the pace management guided for the fourth quarter. The article leaves open the outcome of the probe into Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, which Yahoo Finance reported on November 9, and it does not say how long NVIDIA's decline will last.

stories.Headline: Chainstack says AI-powered security breach exposed customer data; threat now contained
stories.Summary:
Blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack disclosed that it suffered an AI-powered security breach in late October, which exposed customer names, emails and password hashes. The company published the details in an updated blog post on Tuesday, according to The Block's report of November 12, 2026. Chainstack said the incident has been contained and that its customer-facing services kept operating normally throughout the breach. The attacker reached parts of the company's systems through a third-party component, according to the report's summary of the incident. The Block said it has reached out to Chainstack for further comment.

The attacker first gained access to a development environment on October 26 and reached parts of the production environment on October 29. Chainstack detected the intrusion and cut the access paths on October 31, then finalized its investigation on November 2. Because of the exposure, the company is treating node credentials as exposed and asking customers to rotate them and change their passwords. Self-service rotation for node credentials is currently available in the console, and Chainstack says it works without downtime. The company added that customer nodes, the console and the API were not modified.

Chainstack itself is the source of the account of how the breach unfolded, which it set out in its blog post. The company said the attacker entered through an internet-exposed Grafana instance sitting in a development cluster. That instance had been deployed for testing, with its default administrator credentials and without an additional layer of protection. From there, the attacker obtained machine credentials that reached production and used them to access the database network. Chainstack also said the attacker used the ARTEX AI agent framework to carry out the breach.

Chainstack warned customers to watch for phishing attempts following the incident, saying it will never ask for passwords, tokens or keys. Customers are the group affected, since their names, emails and password hashes were exposed and their node credentials are being treated as exposed. The Block's report places the incident within a wave of cyberattacks and security breaches as AI tools become increasingly capable. The Block reported that, earlier in the same week, the crosschain interoperability protocol Across suffered a domain takeover. Across later restored control of its website and resumed normal operations.

The wider concern about AI-enabled threats also features in a separate opinion piece by Saken Mukan, published by Caspian Post on November 9, 2026. It describes deepfakes, online fraud and extremist propaganda as emerging challenges for Central Asia, and notes that such tools are becoming easier and cheaper to use. On November 6, Astana hosted an Aqaba Process summit on security in the field of artificial intelligence, attended by the presidents of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. King Abdullah II of Jordan, Kyrgyzstan's foreign minister and the speaker of Azerbaijan's parliament also took part. The Aqaba Process was launched by the King of Jordan in 2015 as an initiative aimed at countering terrorism and violent extremism.

The Chainstack articles do not say whether the attacker has been identified, or how many customers were affected by the exposure of their names, emails and password hashes. They also leave open whether any customer node credentials were actually misused, since the company says only that it is treating them as exposed. The Block's request for further comment from Chainstack remains outstanding, so any additional detail from the company is still to come. For now, customers are being asked to rotate their node credentials, change their passwords and stay alert to phishing. In the regional discussion, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev offered to host a regional office of the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism, though that office remains a proposal and has not yet been established.

stories.Headline: [Law Firms Now] Bae, Kim & Lee to Hold Seminar on 'Current Issues and Challenges in AI Regulation' on Nov. 16
stories.Summary:
Bloomberg Law published an essay on November 9, 2026, written by a client who works as in-house counsel and says clients want law firms to use AI, but want more besides. The writer, Patience Bin, is Head of Enterprise AI and Data Governance, Law, and Compliance at Bristol Myers Squibb. She opens with an email from outside counsel marked "Privileged and Confidential," in which the lawyer pasted all seven paragraphs of a chatbot's answer, with quotation marks, instead of giving his own opinion. A separate piece from the ACG Insights site, published on November 10, 2026, argues that private equity's push into law firm management services organizations is really a bet on AI. A third article, published November 11, 2026, in Lawyers Weekly in Australia, says firms can answer clients' appetite for AI with their own branded chatbots offering round-the-clock support in a controlled environment.

The ACG Insights piece describes the structure as a law firm owned and controlled by licensed attorneys, who keep legal judgment and the client relationship, and a separate management company that owns the operating side and can take outside capital. A long-term services agreement binds the two and sets out what the management company does and how it is paid. Illinois went furthest with a law signed in August and effective immediately, which bars MSOs owned or controlled by private equity or hedge funds from charging fees tied to a firm's revenue or profits. Colorado's law took effect in August, bars MSO fees tied to firm or case performance, adds a private right of action, reaches conduct outside its borders, and is set to expire in 2029. California's follow-on law, AB 2305, bars MSOs and other investors from steering litigation decisions, such as which cases to take, how to set fees and when to settle, starting in 2027.

Bin says the minimum clients expect is that lawyers validate, understand and own their output, so that a legal opinion sent to a client is the lawyer's own and can be explained and defended. She says that forwarding unverified AI output transfers the verification work and the risk to the client, who already pays for Claude and can paste a question into it. She wants advice tailored to her company's risk appetite and regulatory environment, plus benchmarking on what other companies in similar situations do, and firsthand experience with regulators. On billing, she says AI should produce savings, and gives the example of advice that once took 40 hours and now takes four. She suggests a well-scoped fixed fee for discrete legal questions, and expects firms to run strong AI and data governance programs and to sign AI riders.

Bin cites a 2026 survey by Axiom in which 59% of legal leaders reported that their law firms had raised fees while promoting AI as a value-add. She says clients will ask which AI tools firms use, how they assess the risks, whether client data can be used for model training, how data is protected against unauthorized access or commingling, and what human oversight exists. She recalls a partner who pitched for work with an AI-generated PowerPoint and could not explain the first box on the first slide, after which the room's attention and respect disappeared. She says clients may already have run a question through AI before calling and may bring its answer along, and that lawyers should not take offense but should challenge it and filter out the noise. The ACG authors, Drew Sacher and Michael Lamm of Corporate Advisory Solutions, say the new laws regulate how an MSO is paid and what it controls rather than outlawing it.

The ACG piece says private equity money is moving into law firms through MSOs faster than most people expected two years ago, as frontier AI labs build products aimed at document-heavy, process-driven work. An MSO makes its money running intake, case management, billing, marketing and the routing of referrals, which is the work AI reaches first. Deal activity sits in personal injury, mass tort, family law, creditors' rights, foreclosure, workers' compensation, immigration, consumer bankruptcy and debt relief, and insurance defense. One law firm advising on these transactions reported 35 closed legal MSO deals through September, and in October a 550-lawyer insurance defense firm took private equity money at a reported value near $700 million. Physician practices have run on versions of the same split for decades, and the new state laws on law firm MSOs borrow heavily from the rules written for healthcare, while nonlawyer ownership of law firms remains off limits in nearly every state.

The authors expect the rules to keep getting more specific rather than shutting the model down, and expect continued M&A in the practice areas built for it. They say lenders are still learning how to underwrite these deals, and that the credit market should deepen as more transactions close. For owners weighing outside capital, they advise a flat or cost-plus fee at fair market value with an outside benchmark, and say noncompetes cannot be had because ethics rules in nearly every state bar lawyers from agreeing not to practice after they leave. The articles leave open how courts and ethics opinions will move the line, since in most states the supreme court regulates the practice of law. They also do not say whether Illinois and Colorado will be followed by other states, how firms will answer clients' demands on pricing and AI riders, or what the headline's November 16 seminar will cover.

stories.Headline: Indian organisations see AI returns but risk readiness declines: Kyndryl
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl released its third annual Readiness Report on November 11, 2026, finding that Indian organisations are seeing stronger returns from artificial intelligence while their readiness to manage the surrounding risks is falling. Sixty per cent of Indian organisations investing in AI and machine learning now report positive returns, which is an increase of three percentage points from 2025. At the same time, the share that consider themselves completely ready to manage external risks dropped by eight percentage points to 27 per cent. The report draws on responses from 3,700 senior business leaders across 21 countries, including 200 leaders in India. Coverage of the findings highlights a growing gap between how widely AI is being adopted and how prepared enterprises are to cope with its risks.

Eighty-five per cent of Indian organisations are now deploying AI in workflows that go beyond pilot projects, according to the report. The proportion of businesses still at the experimentation stage has fallen by 15 percentage points to 56 per cent. Cybersecurity is the leading worry, with 68 per cent of Indian respondents naming cyberattacks as a top external risk, yet only 35 per cent say they are completely prepared to manage them. That readiness figure is a drop of 10 percentage points from the previous year, while globally only 26 per cent of organisations reported complete readiness against cyberattacks. Seventy-one per cent of Indian leaders rated their IT infrastructure as mostly or fully modernised, but 59 per cent said significant re-architecture would still be needed to support AI at scale.

Kyndryl, the technology services company, is the author of the report, and Martin Schroeter, its Chairman and CEO, commented on the findings. He said organisations are increasingly focused on making their early AI returns sustainable. He added that their technology infrastructure, workforce capabilities and governance frameworks are struggling to keep pace with the speed of adoption. The report itself frames the findings around the challenges businesses face as AI moves from experimentation to large-scale deployment. Its summary also points to a distinction between having modern technology infrastructure and having systems that can support enterprise-wide AI deployment.

The surveyed Indian leaders themselves described several difficulties in scaling AI, and these views are what the report records from the people it affects. Seventy per cent of them said their organisations have more AI pilots than they can realistically scale, and 58 per cent said innovation often stalls after the proof-of-concept stage. Half of the surveyed organisations significantly changed their AI strategy over the past year, while 31 per cent reported an AI investment failure. Thirty-seven per cent of respondents experienced disagreements between their chief human resources officer and their chief technology or information officer over AI strategy. Despite the security concerns, three in four leaders said AI was helping their organisations identify threats faster, and the report also raised concerns about AI-driven disruption to established business models.

The report offers some background on how Indian organisations are already putting AI to work. Eighty per cent of them are using AI agents to automate workflows that previously required coordination across multiple teams or systems. This is the third annual edition of the Readiness Report, which gives a basis for comparison, with the 60 per cent returns figure measured against 2025. The proportion of organisations considering themselves completely ready for external risks has fallen by eight percentage points, and the cyberattack readiness figure has fallen by 10 points. Globally, the share of organisations fully prepared for cyberattacks is down by 11 percentage points to 26 per cent.

The articles do not describe any specific actions that Kyndryl or the surveyed organisations plan to take after the release of the report. The only forward-looking element is the statement from Schroeter that organisations are focusing on making their early AI returns sustainable. What the report means for the 59 per cent of leaders who expect significant re-architecture is not spelled out, including how much it would involve or how long it might take. The articles also do not say how organisations plan to close the readiness gap on external risks and cyberattacks. Whether the 70 per cent of leaders with more pilots than they can scale will manage to move those projects forward is left open.

stories.Headline: Google's AI chip expansion opens new doors for Samsung, SK hynix
stories.Summary:
Google is expanding sales of its custom AI chips beyond its own data centers, and that is opening new openings for Samsung Electronics and SK hynix to diversify high-bandwidth memory demand away from Nvidia. The Korea Herald reported on November 11, 2026 that the US tech giant is growing its tensor processing unit, or TPU, business to serve cloud providers and companies building AI infrastructure. On Monday, Google unveiled two new systems, the TPU 8i Max and the TPU 8tx, which expand its eighth-generation lineup to four products. The 8i Max combines two chips in one package, doubling both computing performance and HBM capacity, while the 8tx targets AI workloads that need stronger data security. The wider customer base could give Korean memory makers a broader set of buyers beyond Nvidia's dominant GPU ecosystem.

Google says it now has nearly 100 TPU customers, including companies that run the processors in their own data centers. Oracle plans to offer Google's chips through its cloud platform next year, and Alphabet expects TPU system sales to rise substantially after they contributed to Google Cloud's third-quarter growth. Counterpoint Research forecasts that HBM bit demand for custom AI server chips will grow 35-fold between 2024 and 2028, driven partly by the TPU expansion. Samsung and Broadcom, Google's major TPU development partner, signed a memorandum of understanding in July covering HBM, foundry manufacturing and advanced packaging. Potential cooperation under that agreement is valued at more than $200 billion through 2030, though the estimate spans multiple businesses and includes no confirmed HBM orders.

On the Korean side, SK hynix is seeking a role earlier in chip development, following a February meeting between SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won and Google CEO Sundar Pichai. After that meeting, the memory maker proposed jointly designing customized HBM for future TPUs, and Chey also met Broadcom CEO Hock Tan to discuss next-generation AI chips. Google is working with Taiwan's MediaTek on its TPU 8t, code-named Zebrafish, partly to move away from Broadcom's turnkey model. Under that model, the design partner also handles memory purchases, and Counterpoint estimates it adds a 15 to 20 percent markup to HBM costs. Counterpoint research associate David Wu said that bringing chip design and HBM procurement in-house, starting with Zebrafish, lets Google eliminate the intermediary fee and lower its overall cost.

Counterpoint research director Hwang Min-sung called the shift a major opportunity for memory suppliers to create a high-value business. An industry source said the bigger story is not Google's latest chip specifications, but that Google is turning TPUs into a business serving customers outside its own data centers. With HBM4 and HBM4E, suppliers can tailor memory components to specific AI processors, potentially securing higher-value, longer-term contracts through earlier involvement in chip design. Another industry source cautioned that winning a new customer does not necessarily mean shipping more HBM right away when so much future capacity is already committed. The source added that the real competition is over who gets into the next chip design and secures production slots early enough to turn that relationship into long-term orders.

Capacity is already heavily committed, which makes new orders hard to secure, as SK hynix said in October that agreements with 14 major customers cover volumes equivalent to more than half its total production capacity for 2027 and 2028. That figure includes products beyond HBM. Separately, Seoul Economic Daily reported on November 10 that Samsung Electronics and SK hynix both rose more than 5% in premarket trading on Nextrade. SK hynix traded at 1.213 million won as of 8:12 a.m., up 6.78%, while Samsung stood at 201,000 won, up 5.85%. The rise followed bargain hunting in US chip stocks overnight and a steep drop in oil prices, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose nearly 7% after dropping more than 12% in a single session on the 5th.

Alphabet expects TPU system sales to rise substantially, and Oracle is due to offer Google's chips through its cloud platform next year. Samsung's potential cooperation with Broadcom, valued at more than $200 billion through 2030, includes no confirmed HBM orders, so it remains unclear whether any orders will follow. SK hynix's proposal to jointly design customized HBM for future TPUs has no reported answer from Google, and the articles do not say whether it will be accepted. Whether Google's work with MediaTek on the TPU 8t leads to more direct dealings with memory suppliers also remains open. Analysts at Seoul Economic Daily pointed to the US consumer price index for October due this week, and earnings from AI cloud provider CoreWeave, as possible triggers for a recovery in investor sentiment.
