stories.Headline: Nvidia spy allegations likely to spur laws to tighten China's access to AI chips
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers and advocates said on November 9 that Congress is now more likely to pass legislation tightening China's access to AI chips. The reason is news that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence agent. Three chip-related measures are slated for possible inclusion in the annual defense authorization bill for fiscal year 2027, which began in October. The three are the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the Match Act. Reuters reporter Karen Freifeld filed the story from New York, and Huang's affair and his close relationship with President Donald Trump are said to have added new urgency.

The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress power over advanced chip exports. The Chip Security Act would require businesses to track their chips in order to combat smuggling. The Match Act would push US allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment to China. The House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced all three bills earlier this year, and they now sit in the Senate National Defense Authorization Act management package. Representative Bill Foster of Illinois said the Chip Security Act, which he introduced with Republican Representative Bill Huizenga of Michigan, passed unanimously out of committee in the House.

Nvidia declined to comment on the matter, and the White House did not comment on the measures. The company has said it complied with export laws. Until the US Department of Justice brought indictments tied to chip smuggling last year, Huang and Nvidia had argued that no such smuggling existed. Nvidia is considered the biggest opponent of both the Chip Security and AI Overwatch acts, according to one former congressional staffer who had direct contact with the company over several months. The Information Technology Industry Council, whose members include Nvidia, has also opposed the measures, and its spokeswoman declined to comment on the current Nvidia situation.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Republican Senator Jim Banks of Indiana issued a joint statement on Monday. They said Huang's confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China's intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent. They added that it is time for Congress to take decisive action and pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the defense bill. Foster posted on X that Congress has the tools to stop powerful AI chips from getting into the wrong hands, and urged lawmakers to get his bill across the finish line. Chris MacKenzie, a spokesman for the nonprofit Americans for Responsible Innovation, said the hurdle is getting the White House onboard, and that backing Nvidia against Congress would be costly.

The Information Technology Industry Council has argued that the measures could undermine US competitiveness and complicate export control policy. In March, Warren and Banks had urged the Department of Commerce to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses to China and to conduct a full security review. The Department of Justice indictments tied to chip smuggling came last year, and Nvidia had earlier maintained that no smuggling occurred. Headlines linked to the story note that Nvidia's board is probing the chief executive. The same headlines describe reports that Republicans have sought a briefing from him, that Axios reported Congress will investigate, and that Trump said the US is looking closely at the report.

The three measures remain slated for possible inclusion in the fiscal 2027 defense authorization bill, which has not yet been finalized. The articles do not say when the Senate will act on the package, or whether the three measures will survive in the final text. The key hurdle named is the White House, which did not comment on the measures, so its position remains unknown. Nvidia declined to comment, and the articles give no indication of how the company will respond to the push. They also do not say what the board probe will conclude, or whether Commerce will act on the senators' March request to review Nvidia's export licenses.

stories.Headline: Protest against AI in schools, search block planned outside Google's Chicago office Wednesday
stories.Summary:
Dozens of protesters gathered outside Google's Cambridge, Massachusetts office on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, to object to a newly announced plan tying school search access to artificial intelligence. They were parents, children and teachers worried about how technology affects learning and student mental health. They chanted "Kids over tech!" and "Books, not Chromebooks!" as part of an organized set of rallies.

The rallies also targeted Google offices in New York, Chicago and Los Angeles. A separate Axios Chicago report, dated November 9, 2026, described Chicago parents protesting Google's AI school policy. Google said last week that it would no longer automatically turn on its Gemini chatbot for the many schools that use Google Classroom. The new policy has a catch, because schools that reject Google's AI offerings will lose access to Google's foundational search engine. According to the company, schools that opt out of AI tools will have search blocked.

Google's statement says the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. The company also said it is developing new restrictions on the school version of Gemini, including a function that lets teachers review chatbot transcripts. Google, which makes the products at issue, has said search and AI are now so integrated that it would not be possible to have one without the other. Spokesperson Jackie Berté said Google hears the concerns of parents and teachers about students using AI to shortcut learning, and shares the goal of helping students learn. She said the company is building these experiences in partnership with educators and is listening closely, so that its products support both students and teachers.

The company has not budged on bundling search with AI, even as it has stopped turning Gemini on automatically for Classroom users. In August, Google had turned on the Gemini app as the default option for all schools that use Classroom. Sudbury parent Tom Rogan said the search policy was a breaking point for some families, and that parents need more control to protect their kids. He said trouble with big tech in schools has lasted a long time, and that it is becoming more apparent to parents. Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey, a Democrat, demanded Monday that Google reverse its policy in a letter to Google CEO Sundar Pichai.

Markey wrote that the policy is not a choice but an ultimatum that effectively forces schools to enable generative AI. Matt Bach, head of the Massachusetts Teachers Association, said schools do not need Google in classrooms and should refocus on pedagogy that works for students. The protest drew the leaders of both the Massachusetts Teachers Association and the AFT Massachusetts, the two large statewide teachers unions. Other groups involved included the Massachusetts AI Action Network, Sociedad Latina, a Boston nonprofit pushing for technology restrictions in Boston Public Schools, and the Becca Schmill Foundation. That foundation was created in memory of a Canton 18-year-old who died in 2020 after buying drugs on social media.

Its founder, Deb Schmill, said she hopes the protest starts a new awakening and that schools should move away from Google entirely. She said she knows of no evidence that these products work, and that scores have only declined since technology entered schoolrooms. Google's products are ubiquitous in American classrooms, and many schools issue its low-cost Chromebook laptops to every student. The Classroom platform is widely used for assignments and grading, and Google and other tech firms have drawn fierce criticism over student-facing AI.

New York and Los Angeles, the country's two largest school districts, have banned AI chatbots for some or all grades. This fall's international PISA test score release came with warnings about the impact of AI usage on science learning, while Boston has been more open and trains "AI ambassadors." Last week, a day before the search-and-AI policy was announced, a North Carolina family sued Google, saying their 13-year-old daughter made plans to end her life after months of using Google AI on a school-issued Chromebook. The articles do not say whether Google will reverse the policy, and Markey's letter to Pichai set out the demand without reporting any reply.

Schmill suggested schools should move away from the company even if the policy is rolled back. The Boston Globe reported that Google's school hardware is also facing headwinds for the first time in years, with an anti-Chromebook movement brewing in towns including Cambridge. In last week's midterm elections, voters overwhelmingly opposed data center construction, backing it in only one of 47 related ballot measures this year. The articles do not report what the North Carolina lawsuit will seek or when it will be heard.

stories.Headline: Adobe brings AI agents and new creative tools to Photoshop, Premiere, and Firefly
stories.Summary:
Adobe announced a broad expansion of AI across its creative software at its annual MAX conference, which opened in Miami. The company is adding AI features to Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator and InDesign, and widening what its Firefly app can do. Forrest Key, Adobe's vice president for Firefly and agentic AI, presented the plans in his keynote at the event. Adobe also released a Model Context Protocol that lets outside chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini use Adobe features. The announcements were reported on November 10 and 11, 2026, by IT Brief Australia, Seoul Economic Daily and TechCrunch.

Firefly now offers 36 AI models, with newly added ones including ByteDance's Dreamina and Seedance 2.5, Runway's Gen-4.5, Kuaishou's Kling 4.0, Google's Nano Banana 2.1 and OpenAI's GPT image model. A custom settings option lets users set format, colour and brand guidelines once and apply them across every project. Plan Mode lets users review, edit and approve the agent's proposed steps before work begins, while a model picker lets them choose a model for a session or leave the choice to the system. Firefly Design is a new beta workspace that combines illustration, image editing, animation, 3D and print on a single canvas. Firefly Builder is a private beta, available through a waitlist, that turns natural language prompts into prototypes of websites, presentations or apps.

Forrest Key said Adobe wants to offer every creator an agent that supports the creative process from the first exploration of an idea to the moment the work is released. He said the agent should work across tools, models and workflows, with the creator's taste, style and vision leading. In his keynote he described Firefly as the best-suited platform for helping everyone create, whether they are new to digital creation or already professionals. Adobe described its Creative Agent as a partner that works alongside users while leaving creative decisions in their hands. Key presented Firefly as the AI creative studio where the best models, trusted tools and an agent come together.

Deepa Subramaniam, Adobe's vice president of product marketing for Creative Cloud, said the update will let professionals focus on the decisions that shape their own work. She said the new tools bring precision, control and flexibility to that work. Adobe cited its latest Creators' Toolkit Report, which found that 78 per cent of creators said creative AI had accelerated the growth of their business or following. Customers have already used the Creative Agent for tasks such as batch portrait retouching and turning product images into short social videos. Users gain a wider choice of tools without moving between separate applications, since Firefly now includes models from Adobe, Topaz Labs, ByteDance, Google, Kling, OpenAI and ElevenLabs.

TechCrunch noted that Firefly's new Builder tool is moving into territory held by Figma, since it lets users create designs to show off ideas. Seoul Economic Daily described Firefly as Adobe's generative AI app, offering image and video generation and editing. Adobe has framed Firefly as its effort to bring more of its creative software into a single interface as creators work across image, video, audio and design. Adobe's broader message is that creative work increasingly involves repeated tasks and multiple deliverables, not just one-off outputs. Firefly Graph, in beta, addresses this by letting users build custom workflows for tasks such as character studies, shot lists and applying brand guidelines across campaign assets.

Edit Text, Retouch, Relight and Quick Actions are now generally available in Firefly, while the other newly announced tools remain in beta. Firefly Builder is available only in private beta through a waitlist. An always-on agent was shown as a preview, and Adobe said it will handle recurring tasks such as organising incoming assets, checking quality and preparing content for different channels even when the user is away. In Premiere, a generative remove feature for erasing unwanted objects from footage was released in beta, and a Color Mode for adjusting video colour was formally added. Photoshop officially launched Relight, and the articles give no dates for when the beta features will reach general availability.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Goes for Microsoft’s Crown With New Claude-Powered Office Tools
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, Anthropic unveiled a set of AI-powered office tools at an event in San Francisco. Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets launched in beta, and Claude Dashboards, which had entered beta in October, became generally available under the new name Claude Data. The Verge reported a third tool, Claude Meetings, that can join a meeting, take notes and turn a presentation into a one-minute explainer video, while Gizmodo said it is coming soon. Whiteboards and Sheets are open to all paid plans, and The Verge said Meetings will be available to Teams and Enterprise subscriptions. The company also introduced interactive connectors that open partner apps inside Claude.

Anthropic describes Whiteboards as a shared board where a team brainstorms with Claude, which can turn a spoken, messy plan into a timeline with owners and dates. In a retro meeting, for example, everyone can add notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft action items for each person. Sheets lets Claude build and edit spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting and drop-downs, often from a single prompt such as a request for a campaign tracker or hiring budget. It outlines each edit so changes can be tracked, and for now it offers only simple spreadsheet functionality, with more planned. Files can be exported to .xlsx or CSV, used through Claude for Excel, or continued in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com and Smartsheet.

Claude Data lets teams ask questions of company data held in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery and ClickHouse. A data team can certify queries so that charts built on them carry a certified badge, and certified queries and live sharing are both in beta. With live sharing, colleagues see current numbers even without access to the underlying connectors, but they can only view the results of approved queries. The product also now supports design systems, caching with per-dashboard refresh cadences, and tracked changes with rollback to a specific version. Named partners include Amplitude, Mixpanel, Omni, PostHog and Sigma.

For administrators, all three tools are on by default on Team plans. On Enterprise plans, Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, while Claude Data switches on by default on November 19, 2026. Settings can be changed under Organization settings > Artifacts. The tools work on web, desktop and mobile, and Claude Data requires a data connector such as a warehouse or CRM. The interactive connectors let apps from companies including Adobe, Atlassian, Box and Notion open beside a conversation or in full screen.

Nicholas Lin, who works on product at Anthropic, told The Verge that Claude Code changed how engineers work a year ago and that knowledge workers are now the gap the company hopes to close. He said there is still a lot of friction in adopting AI for non-developers. Lin added that Claude Cowork, another tool for non-engineers, is essentially a wrapper for Claude Code aimed at the technical parts of Anthropic's non-technical audience. Anthropic said in its own announcement that its aim is to keep documents, boards, sheets and dashboards inside Claude so teams can keep editing together. Gizmodo's Ece Yildirim called Sheets the most direct threat to Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets, noting it works almost exactly like those apps.

The new tools join existing ones such as Claude Docs, Slides, Design and Motion, and arrive two and a half years after Artifacts first debuted. Lin said Anthropic launched Model Context Protocol about two years ago and its marketplace has grown to more than 9,000 plugin options, and the company now wants those connections to be deeper. The Verge noted that Google's Gemini and, in some cases, OpenAI's ChatGPT can already join meetings and take live notes. It also said Anthropic faces pressure to generate revenue ahead of an IPO that could be the most valuable public debut ever, with a separate headline citing a $1.4 trillion target. Gizmodo reported that the company is reportedly looking to debut on the stock market on November 19, despite jitters around the broader AI industry, and that the Nasdaq had its worst month in over a year last month.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave earnings put debt-fueled AI buildout under scrutiny
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reports its third-quarter financial results after the bell on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, in what the coverage describes as a pivotal test for the neocloud company. The market will watch closely what the company says about artificial intelligence spending and how it plans to finance its infrastructure buildout. The outcome could either calm concerns over its debt or stoke more fear among investors. The GPU cloud provider has raised billions to build out data centers packed with Nvidia chips, financed largely through debt markets. Its stock is down roughly 40% over the past month, and its bonds have also come under pressure.

For the quarter, CoreWeave guided in August for revenue of $3.4 billion to $3.6 billion when it reported second-quarter results. It anticipated capital expenditures between $11.5 billion and $13.5 billion for the quarter, and $35 billion to $39 billion for the full year. The company also expects 1.85 gigawatts in active power by year-end. As of the second quarter, it reported $35.6 billion of debt, $5.5 billion of cash and a $104.2 billion revenue backlog. Its debt-to-equity ratio stands at 702%, up from almost 291% a year ago, and the New Jersey-based company's leverage is described as high.

CEO Michael Intrator has sought to quell investor fear, posting on LinkedIn after last week's election that the company does not anticipate any impact to its existing customer commitments or associated backlog. He said this applied to shifts in the political landscape. The company's earlier guidance for the third quarter already gives investors a picture of what it expects to spend and earn. The earnings report itself is expected to show whether that spending is paying off. CoreWeave's results will also show whether its existing data centers are filling up and whether customers are renewing contracts.

Wolfe Research said in a note on Monday that investors need neoclouds to quantify how much financing they expect to raise to execute on existing backlog. The firm said it thinks outlooks that communicate when and which avenues of funding will be tapped will increase investor confidence. Wells Fargo analyst Michael Turrin said in a note on Sunday that the company's capex needs for the rest of the year should be largely covered. He pointed to remaining undrawn debt, debt issuances in August and September, and the $12 billion it is holding for project costs. Credit markets are signaling worry, with the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 at 15.5% on Tuesday, after jumping to 16.7% on Thursday.

That bond yield jump came as investors digested the election results and possible roadblocks to data center construction, and bond yields move inversely to prices. The spread on its five-year credit default swaps, considered a barometer of perceived credit risk, is at levels considered distressed. On Tuesday the spread stood around 1,152 basis points, after rising above its October peak to close at 1,278 basis points on Thursday. Elon Musk's prediction of a shakeout among GPU providers, including what he called guppy-level death for smaller players, triggered a neocloud selloff in late October.

The sector has not fully recovered, and AI data center stocks also faced an earnings test amid Fed uncertainty last week. CoreWeave's playbook is to get infrastructure in place now, lock in customers with long-term contracts, and let revenue catch up to spending. Meta has announced plans for a $25 billion bond sale to fund its own AI infrastructure buildout, but it has large cash-generating businesses to back that spending. CoreWeave is pure-play infrastructure, and interest rates remain elevated, which makes servicing its debt more expensive.

Traditional cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure are also strengthening their own GPU offerings, which intensifies competition. The company went public relatively recently, so Wall Street is still calibrating its models. Analysts will examine utilization rates, customer concentration, capital expenditure plans, margin sustainability and contract renewals in the report. Wells Fargo's Turrin said CoreWeave's 2027 capex could reach $66 billion, based on an expected capacity addition of 1.5 gigawatts.

He noted that this would require at least $25 billion more in debt. Any sign that spending is outpacing revenue growth could trigger a broader reassessment of sector valuations, while strong results could reignite enthusiasm for AI infrastructure plays. The articles do not give the actual third-quarter results, and the coverage does not say how the company will fund the added capacity beyond this year. A related headline on one site says CoreWeave lifted its 2026 outlook as its backlog hit $132.5 billion, but the articles give no further detail.

stories.Headline: Databricks Launches New Always-on Genie: Autonomous AI for Complex Enterprise Work
stories.Summary:
Databricks announced the second generation of Genie on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, from San Francisco. Genie is now described as an always-on, autonomous agent built for enterprise work. Employees can give it a goal and trust it to keep the work moving without constant prompting. The agent takes ownership of the task, delegates to subagents when needed, tracks progress, and follows up on any missing inputs. It reaches out to a person only when a decision is required, and it emails users when they are away.

The release brings a set of specific changes, starting with autonomous mode, in which Genie runs in the background on its own compute. Sub-agents let it manage multiple tasks in parallel, while a new priority inbox shows items that need a decision instead of past conversations. Each new alert arrives as its own unread email, updates go to the same thread, and every email links back into the Genie app. Databricks now offers more than 100 connectors for business applications, including Google Drive, Jira, and Confluence, which can be ingested through Lakeflow Connect, indexed in place, or queried live through MCP.

Databricks is the company responsible for the launch, and its Co-founder and CEO, Ali Ghodsi, spoke about the product in the announcement. He said Genie has made him a far more productive chief executive, and that it no longer waits for him to ask before acting. According to him, it keeps up with his inbox, prepares him for meetings, and runs in the background, returning only when it needs a decision. He credited this to the agent's knowledge of how the company works, including what it means by revenue, which numbers are official, and who can see what. He called this horizontal context, which he said Genie delivers.

Databricks gave examples of who could use the agent and what they might ask it to do. Marketers can have Genie monitor GEO performance and suggest relevant content. Customer success teams can ask it to watch customer usage patterns and notify the account team of meaningful shifts. Executives can have it track revenue trends and top customer feature requests and deliver a weekly brief on what is changing and why. Users can also interact with Genie on the web, on mobile, by email, and in collaboration and AI tools including ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot Cowork, and Grok Bot.

The announcement frames the product against a business problem, noting that work is moving faster and enterprises now expect AI to take real tasks off their plates. Much of what complex projects require lives across multiple platforms and even in people's heads, such as which accounts need attention, what triggers an escalation, and who approves a change. An enterprise assistant can only take that on if it knows the business, can reach the systems teams already use, and follows correct permissions and access controls. Genie is grounded in Genie Ontology, which captures a company's horizontal context, from definitions and metrics to the people and processes behind them, and keeps it current as the business changes. Because it runs inside a company's existing Databricks environment, it is governed by Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway, so every action stays within the controls already in place.

Several further capabilities were announced alongside the core agent. An Ontology Manager lets teams manage and govern business context, with recommendations that flag frequently asked concepts needing refinement. Genie Ontology sources now include business logic from external BI tools and a new organizational structure connector for understanding people and reporting relationships. Genie can generate dynamic, data-driven slides, dashboards, and interactive reports that stay current as the governed data changes. Genie Agents can work across PDFs, contracts, and slides in Unity Catalog Volumes with no separate vector index, and new MCP connectors for Atlassian, Google Drive, and GitHub, plus OpenSharing, allow collaboration with partners without exposing underlying data.

The articles do not say when the second generation of Genie becomes generally available, nor do they give pricing for the agent or for Genie Search. They also give no customer results or adoption figures, and no independent assessment of how the agent performs in real enterprise settings. What they do establish is that every action stays within Unity Catalog permissions and Unity Gateway approval rules and budgets, and is fully auditable. Genie Search runs within existing Databricks environments, so there is no separate search infrastructure to manage, and it follows access rules already set in Unity Catalog. Genie MCP will let AI tools and agents use Genie Ontology and Genie Search to find and access enterprise knowledge.

stories.Headline: Prediction: This Will Be the Best-Performing AI Stock of 2027
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology stock fell sharply this week, according to a November 11, 2026 article from 24/7 Wall St. on Yahoo Finance, with shares down 30.02% over the past week. The same article said the stock was down 13.47% on the day and 35.32% over the past month. It added that Micron remains up 141.28% year to date, even though shares sit 45.2% below the 52-week high of $1,254.61. The selling also hit SanDisk and other AI names, and the headlines included market share concerns and a pause on a Taiwan plant after a labor dispute. A separate November 10, 2026 article from The Motley Fool, published before that selloff, tipped a different stock, Upstart Holdings, to double over the next 12 months.

The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Micron is $913.86 over the next 12 months, which against a stock price of $688.09 works out to 32.8% upside. The company just finished a fiscal year with $133.19B in revenue and $75.52 in non-GAAP earnings per share. In fiscal Q4, revenue reached $54.23B against a $50.97B estimate, while non-GAAP EPS came in at $33.42 versus the $31.35 consensus. That was Micron's eighth consecutive beat, and gross margin hit 87%. For fiscal Q1, management guided to $61.5B, give or take $1.5B, in revenue and $38.15, give or take $1.00, in EPS.

Management said more than 75% of fiscal 2027 shipments are already committed, and Micron now has 26 Strategic Customer Agreements running through 2030. Executives called DRAM the principal constraint versus logic or power to the data center. Micron also raised high-bandwidth memory pricing for calendar 2027 and is co-designing HBM4E with NVIDIA. Fiscal 2026 capital spending reached $30.71B, and free cash flow of $62.31B covers that spending easily. Management said most of the new construction budget goes to clean rooms for 2028, and it will add equipment as demand requires.

The analyst consensus target for Micron is $1,561.91, backed by 9 Strong Buy ratings plus 36 Buy ratings, and the bull case is $1,342.01, or 95.0% upside. The bear case of $691.64 would leave the stock roughly flat for a year. A large share of HBM sales goes to a small group of customers, and the Taiwan plant pause and the market share questions add execution risk. NVIDIA is Micron's most important HBM partner, and its supply obligations of $279 billion are largely tied to memory procurement for Vera Rubin. Intraday market data on the page showed Micron at $824.43, up 13.70%, and SanDisk at $1,005.03, up 16.86%.

Micron's revenue grew 379% year over year, yet it trades at about 9x trailing earnings and 4x forward EPS estimates. NVIDIA, with revenue growth of 105.85%, trades at 40x earnings. SanDisk, the closest memory peer, grew revenue 377.95% and still trades at 13x. The author says the deciding factor is contracted demand at a single-digit multiple, and calls the firm's price target conservative compared with these peers. The page also lists earlier 24/7 Wall St. pieces on Micron, including one headlined with an 800% run and another with a 770% year-to-date gain.

The 24/7 Wall St. price target comes with a buy rating and 90% confidence. The thesis gets stronger if fiscal Q1 lands near guidance and more Strategic Customer Agreements get signed, and it weakens if DRAM pricing rolls over or the Taiwan delay spreads to other projects. A faster HBM4E ramp could drive results well above the projections, and a turn in the memory cycle could pull them well below. The articles leave open whether the selloff will deepen or reverse, and they do not say when the Taiwan plant will resume work. The Motley Fool article was cut off before it gave its full case for Upstart, so its details remain incomplete.

stories.Headline: Data Doctors: Can I trust AI shopping agents?
stories.Summary:
Zoho Corporation announced on November 10, 2026, that it is turning Zoho Analytics into what it calls an Agentic Analytics platform, adding a layer meant to give AI agents trusted business data and context. The company said the platform brings together data, analytics and AI agents so businesses can move from studying numbers to acting on them. A central feature is Ask Zia, a conversational assistant that now uses several specialized sub-agents working together. Zoho made the announcement from Singapore through the Media OutReach Newswire.

The update includes native semantic and ontology layers, which act as a business glossary and a map of how a company's entities relate to one another. Ask Zia has six pre-built sub-agents covering data analysis, visualization, data preparation, modeling, coding and SQL generation, and companies can use Zoho's own language model or bring their own. Teams can also build custom agents that connect to outside tools through the Model Context Protocol. Zoho added more than 30 new data connectors to the 500-plus it already offered, including ones for SAP, PayPal, Adobe Commerce, Twilio and Notion, along with more than 50 other new capabilities. Pricing is unchanged, and every plan now includes Zoho LLM credits, with a Basic plan starting at US$24 per month billed annually, covering 2 users, 0.5 million rows and 10K credits.

Gibu Mathew, Managing Director of Zoho APAC, said agents cannot work on data alone and need a solid intelligence layer, which he said the update provides. He described it as one open and extensible layer that gives every AI tool in a business the context, metrics and governance to produce answers people can rely on. Zoho also stressed oversight features, such as a data catalog, AI usage and cost tracking, and a sandbox for testing agents before publishing them. The company said Zoho Analytics is used by 100,000 businesses worldwide daily.

Zoho said the cloud version of the updates is available now, with some preview versions still to arrive. It plans to expand the designed context into a dynamic one that tracks how business data changes over time, add decision intelligence based on the actions agents trigger, and keep investing in open standards, including the Apache Ossie specification. It also plans to build Zoho Analytics into a fuller unified data platform that would include a data lakehouse. Separately, a Quartz report on AI shopping agents says Meta's Muse agent was downloaded 10 million times in the U.S. within 40 days of its early September launch, with purchases averaging more than $200. It adds that agentic web traffic roughly tripled from August to September and that Amazon blocked Muse soon after launch, while the other shopping article supplied no readable text.

stories.Headline: Microsoft rejects multibillion-dollar AI deal with UK's Nscale
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has decided not to exercise an option to more than double the size of its existing agreement with Nscale, the London-based AI cloud provider, to rent computing power at a Texas data center. The Financial Times reported the news on Thursday, November 5, 2026, saying the extension would have been worth tens of billions of dollars to Nscale. A person familiar with the matter told Reuters that Microsoft made the decision several months ago, before Nscale filed for its IPO in September. The source said the existing Texas contract is not affected.

The option was part of a deal the two companies signed in October 2025, under which Nscale would supply about 200,000 Nvidia GB300 chips to Microsoft across sites in the US and Europe. Texas is the largest part of that arrangement, where Nscale leases a 240-megawatt campus in Barstow from the bitcoin miner Ionic Digital. It is due to deliver about 104,000 chips to Microsoft there from the third quarter of 2026. Nscale said at the time that Microsoft also held an option on a second, 700-megawatt phase at the site from late 2027. In its IPO filing, Nscale said it signed statements of work with Microsoft worth up to about $43.8 billion through December 2033, excluding optional extensions.

The source said that skipping the option has no effect on Nscale's total contract value of about $103 billion, as disclosed in the filing. Nscale was already in talks with several major customers for the remaining Texas capacity, the person added. Microsoft and Nscale did not respond to requests for comment outside business hours. Øyvind Eriksen, chief executive of Aker, the Norwegian group that owns about 23% of Nscale, had earlier played down a separate UK setback, calling that contract a relatively minor one in a bigger portfolio.

The news follows another blow to the partnership. Weeks earlier, Microsoft pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's flagship data center project in Loughton, Essex, billed as the UK's largest AI data center, after power connection delays pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s. Nscale, which counts Nvidia among its backers, is asking investors to value it at up to $35 billion in its New York listing, and it closed a $3.36 billion pre-IPO round before filing. Reuters and others reported last month that Nscale is also in talks to sell AI computing power to Anthropic, the maker of Claude, in a deal that could be worth about $45 billion.

stories.Headline: Law firm founder on AI, patent drafting and changing client expectations - Managing Intellectual Property
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, October 29, the Brooklyn Entertainment & Sports Law Society, known as BESLS, hosted a Film and TV panel titled "The Impact of AI on IP." The event brought together prominent intellectual property attorneys to discuss how artificial intelligence is reshaping the legal and commercial landscape of IP. The panel featured Brooklyn Law School alumni Meeka Bondy, class of 1994, who founded Meeka J. Bondy, PLLC and previously worked at Perkins Coie and HBO. It also included Erica Carter, class of 2015, founder of Carter Advisory, PLLC and formerly of Epic Games and Sesame Workshop, along with Stacy Lager of the National Hockey League. Matt Gamble, a 2027 J.D. candidate at Brooklyn Law School, wrote up the discussion for the Brooklyn Sports & Entertainment Law Blog on November 9, 2026.

The panelists explained that studios generally hold the copyright interests in the fictional characters they create, but that an actor's name, image, and likeness, along with their voice, raise different legal considerations. They noted that rights of publicity vary by state, which makes protecting an individual difficult. Contract language also matters more because of AI, and the panelists discussed provisions granting companies rights to exploit performances across media "now known or not yet created." They expect future contract negotiations to address AI-generated performances and replications more explicitly, including compensation and consent terms. A company wanting to reproduce a single performance indefinitely may face demands for much higher upfront pay or limits on future use.

The panelists themselves are the main voices in the account, and each spoke from their own professional experience. Carter drew on her time at Sesame Workshop, where the company controlled the IP for characters like Elmo, yet the relationship between a character and the human talent behind it remained important. She observed that AI can replicate voice actors' performances without new recordings or studio sessions, which creates tension between a company's ownership interests and the creative contributions of human talent. Lager described the NHL's protective approach to its brand, stressing that licensees cannot simply use valuable IP however they want. The panelists said that effective licensing requires anticipating how IP might be used, reproduced, and misused long after an agreement is signed.

Others affected include actors, athletes, and the labor organizations that represent them. The panel said athletes have a strong interest in protecting their name, image, and likeness from unauthorized AI-generated products that could compete with their existing endorsement opportunities. Actors and other performers may likewise seek greater control over AI reproductions of their work. Labor organizations like SAG play an important role in setting baseline protections, but the panelists stressed that collective bargaining agreements often fall short of the maximum protections available. Individual talent and their teams must negotiate extra safeguards, and their success depends on their leverage, which is limited for the vast majority of actors and athletes.

The panel also covered the background on licensing, authenticity, and employment. For AI-related licensing agreements, the panelists highlighted the scope and duration of permitted uses, approval rights, ownership of derivative works, and indemnification for infringement claims, along with transparency and clear identification of AI-generated content. The panelists were largely skeptical that AI-generated content would diminish the value of established entertainment, and Carter put it as "Elmo is Elmo." They noted that today's consumers still place significant value on authenticity, though unchecked unauthorized reproductions could create commercial competition and complicate exclusive arrangements. Companies must now balance aggressive protection of their rights against the reputational risks of pursuing individual consumers, and AI's ability to generate content around the clock raises questions about future demand for human labor in fields like animation and voice performance.

Looking ahead, the panel concluded with advice for law students preparing to enter industries where AI increasingly shapes legal practice. Each panelist encouraged future attorneys to understand how AI works and how companies develop it, noting that the most effective lawyers are those willing to learn alongside the industry they serve. The panelists discussed possible revenue-sharing arrangements for artists whose existing work contributes to AI-generated products, but no arrangement was settled. The first article, from Managing Intellectual Property, is a Five minutes with interview in which Raluca Vasilescu of Cabinet M Oproiu discusses how AI is changing client expectations of patent attorneys. Its substance is not visible, because the content is limited to subscribers, so what she said about overhyped technology and the next generation's needs remains open.

stories.Headline: FuelCell Energy Advances AI Data Center Power With New Testbed
stories.Summary:
FuelCell Energy announced on November 10, 2026 that it has joined StabilityMax, a three-year collaborative project led by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Laboratory of the Rockies. The company, which trades on Nasdaq under the symbol FCEL, made the announcement from its base in Danbury, Connecticut. The project will develop and validate integrated power system architectures meant to meet the fast-changing energy needs of artificial intelligence data centers. Argonne National Laboratory is also taking part in the project alongside the lead laboratory and FuelCell Energy. Market coverage of the news appeared the same day and on November 11, describing it as a step that strengthens the company's position in the growing AI infrastructure market.

Under the project, FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Connecticut, which will serve as a national laboratory-supported testbed for integrated power solutions for AI data centers. The articles place that testing facility at the company's Connecticut manufacturing site. StabilityMax itself will develop and validate a testing and modeling framework to evaluate how fuel cells, energy storage, advanced controls and power electronics can work together. The National Laboratory of the Rockies will build data center load profiles and simulation models that capture the dynamic power demands of modern computing infrastructure. Argonne National Laboratory will add techno-economic and lifecycle analyses to help identify commercially appealing and cost effective deployment strategies.

FuelCell Energy is responsible for building the Connecticut test facility and for contributing its fuel cell technology and operating experience to the project. The company said it will combine that experience with the laboratory's expertise in AI infrastructure modeling and power systems engineering. Together, the partners aim to create the tools and insights needed to optimize system designs, validate performance and support future deployment of integrated power solutions for digital infrastructure. The company also said the project will let it evaluate its fuel cell technology under realistic operating conditions that resemble actual data center operations. The articles describe StabilityMax as part of a broader initiative by the National Laboratory of the Rockies to support the growing energy needs of AI-enabled digital infrastructure.

The National Laboratory of the Rockies is helping accelerate the development and deployment of the power systems needed to enable efficient fuel cell-powered data centers, through new modeling tools, planning platforms and test environments. Data centers are the facilities most directly affected, since AI adoption is driving unprecedented demand for electricity and rapid swings in how much power they consume. Unlike conventional facilities with fairly predictable electricity use, AI data centers see large variations in power needs depending on computing workloads. Those fluctuations strain electricity infrastructure, which raises the importance of flexible and responsive power systems. Integrated fuel cell systems are also being evaluated for their ability to respond quickly to changing demand while limiting added pressure on utility grids.

The new project builds on a previously announced collaboration between FuelCell Energy and Siemens, which focuses on layered power architectures for AI data centers. That approach combines technologies operating across different response times to handle changing electricity requirements. FuelCell Energy describes itself as a clean energy company that develops and provides stationary fuel cell systems for on-site, continuous power generation. The company reported revenue of $33 million in the third quarter of 2026, a decrease of 29.4 percent from the same period a year earlier. Zacks Investment Research currently gives FuelCell Energy a Zacks Rank of #3, which means Hold.

The project is scheduled to run for three years, and the research is expected to generate performance information that will help refine power system configurations. Findings from the testing program are also expected to provide operating insights that will support refinement of the Siemens-related system designs. The company is engaging with customers and partners involved in deploying power solutions for digital infrastructure, and expects the work to improve its understanding of emerging customer needs as successive generations of AI chips reshape data center electricity requirements. The articles do not disclose specific timelines or milestones for the project's outcomes, which leaves the pace of development and delivery uncertain. They also do not say when the Connecticut test facility will be finished, how much the project costs, or how it is funded.

stories.Headline: Nitrogen Brings Its AI-Powered Advisor Platform to Claude and ChatGPT, Expands Nucleus Capabilities
stories.Summary:
The headline says Nitrogen is bringing its advisor platform to Claude and ChatGPT and expanding its Nucleus capabilities, but the two articles supplied never mention Nitrogen or Nucleus. What they cover is the arrival of personal finance features in Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT, so this account sticks to that. Anthropic introduced Personal Finance as a dedicated feature within Claude on November 5, 2026, and OpenAI had introduced its Finances feature in ChatGPT on May 15, 2026. Both tools let users link bank accounts through Plaid and review spending, investments and savings goals through a conversational interface. Both reportedly give a read-only view of linked accounts, so neither chatbot can move money or change account details.

Claude Personal Finance connects supported bank accounts, credit cards, loans and investment accounts through Plaid, and it began rolling out in beta to Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers in the United States. It works across Claude's web, desktop and mobile applications, though access is being introduced gradually. Anthropic says Claude can see bank names, account names, account types, the last four digits of an account number, balances, credit limits and transaction history. Mint reports that history as up to 2 years, while iTech Post puts it at 24 months. Compatible institutions mentioned include Bank of America, Capital One and Chase, and Claude can build dashboards and flag unusual charges, duplicate transactions and rising bills.

Anthropic is the company behind Claude Personal Finance, and it says conversations inside the Personal Finance hub are not used to train its models by default. The company also says removing a bank account means Claude can no longer use that previously shared financial data. Anthropic has also stated that Claude Personal Finance carries no advertisements or product suggestions, and the company does not offer its own credit cards, loans or savings accounts. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, applies the user's existing ChatGPT data controls to conversations about connected financial accounts. OpenAI says financial account data is removed from its systems within 30 days of a user disconnecting the account.

The Mint article notes that ChatGPT's data controls leave model improvement switched on by default, so users must open Settings and turn off the option called Improve the model for everyone. iTech Post adds that Anthropic's no-training promise covers only the Personal Finance hub, while conversations outside it remain under the user's regular privacy settings. Mint says neither tool is meant to replace a professional financial advisor, and iTech Post says they are not substitutes for banking applications either. iTech Post warns that AI responses can contain errors and that balances may not reflect the latest transactions. Users are advised to check figures against official statements and to consult qualified professionals for important decisions.

On the background, Mint says OpenAI began testing advertisements on selected lower-priced ChatGPT plans in January 2026, while no clear advertising policy has been given for the Finances feature. OpenAI's feature has grown since its May launch, and it now includes weekly financial insights, credit monitoring, stock watchlists, voice support and manual account entry. iTech Post says ChatGPT can reach balances, transactions, investments, liabilities and subscriptions, and can help with expense organization, budgeting and savings planning. Mint describes Anthropic's approach as a deliberate disconnect from promoting finance products. The Mint piece was published on November 9, 2026, and the iTech Post piece followed a day later.

Looking ahead, Mint reports that OpenAI is aiming to widen ChatGPT's financial abilities through a tie-up with Intuit. The partnership is expected to bring more help with credit card applications and tax questions, among other services. Anthropic, for its part, is aiming to partner with banks, wealth managers and other financial services firms to improve Claude Personal Finance. Mint says both tools currently offer more or less the same tracking options, and that Claude's default privacy stance may appeal to users wary of how their financial data is used. The articles leave open when Claude's rollout will reach all eligible users, and neither mentions Nitrogen or Nucleus.

stories.Headline: Nvidia-Backed Fireworks AI Notifies Customers of Its Second Hack in Weeks
stories.Summary:
Fireworks AI, an AI infrastructure startup backed by Nvidia, has told customers it suffered a second security breach within weeks, after attackers accessed its development machines. The company announced the new incident in a disclosure reported on November 11, 2026. The attackers reached those machines after breaching a third-party cloud provider that was itself compromised on October 23. Fireworks detected the activity on October 24, the day after that provider hack. The threat actors had run an unauthorized workload, and the incident affected customer data.

The affected data included resource metadata, billing information, and incomplete model weights and datasets belonging to some customers. Customer payment card numbers were not accessed, because Fireworks says it does not store them. After detecting the activity on October 24, the company began remediation measures immediately. It revoked and replaced compromised internal credentials and service accounts, and it restricted unauthorized network pathways. It also isolated affected systems and tightened access to its data storage and analytics systems.

Fireworks AI is the company responsible for notifying its customers and for responding to the breach. In its announcement, it said the attackers had come in through the third-party cloud provider and that it caught them the day after that provider was compromised. It stressed that payment card numbers were safe, since it holds none. It described the steps it took to contain the incident, including replacing credentials and isolating systems. It said it is working with Unit 42, the incident response division of Palo Alto Networks, to investigate the full scope and impact.

The articles quote no outside voices on the Fireworks breach itself, but they do describe who is affected. Customers whose resource metadata, billing information, or incomplete model weights and datasets were accessed are the ones exposed, though only some customers had model weights and datasets involved. Researchers at Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant recently reported on a related threat, saying large language model hijacking attacks are causing significant costs for compromised organizations. They noted that cloud AI charges have reached up to $1 million because of fraudulent calls made with stolen API keys. Separately, a report from Railway said it believes an October hack on its own systems targeted AI provider keys for resale, with unauthorized spend on the stolen keys estimated at about $740,000.

This is the second security incident for Fireworks AI, following an event in early October that was linked to LLMJacking, a financially motivated cybercriminal threat. LLMjacking refers to the hijacking of large language models, typically by using stolen API keys to make fraudulent calls that run up charges for the victim. The latest breach began when a third-party cloud provider used by Fireworks was compromised on October 23, giving attackers a path to its development machines. Fireworks says it detected the unauthorized activity on October 24 and moved straight to remediation. The Railway incident described in the same reporting was also an October hack, in which attackers went after AI provider keys they apparently intended to resell.

What happens next centers on the investigation that Fireworks is running with Unit 42 at Palo Alto Networks. That work is meant to establish the full scope and impact of the breach, which the company has not yet fully defined. The articles do not say how many customers were affected, nor which customers had incomplete model weights and datasets accessed. They also do not name the third-party cloud provider that was compromised on October 23, or say how that provider was breached. Nor do they say whether the early October LLMJacking event and this second incident are connected beyond their timing.

stories.Headline: New York's AI Safety Law Hits OpenAI, Anthropic Today
stories.Summary:
New York opened a corporate registration portal on November 10 ahead of putting its RAISE Act fully into effect, which targets the biggest developers of advanced artificial intelligence. The law names OpenAI and Anthropic among the representative companies it covers. Those companies must register with state authorities, publish how they manage safety, and report major safety incidents within a fixed deadline. One outlet described the law as taking effect that day, while another said it takes effect early next year. Governor Kathy Hochul signed the bill earlier this year, making New York the first state to move beyond voluntary commitments.

The law applies to frontier AI developers with annual revenues above $500 million, and registration is due by January 1, 2027. Covered companies must post their safety management policies on their websites and issue model transparency reports. They must notify authorities within 72 hours of a major safety incident, and the law defines such an incident as any malfunction, misuse or unexpected behavior causing significant harm to people, critical infrastructure or public safety. Filings must describe model architectures, training data sources, safety testing protocols and incident response procedures. Violations can cost up to $1 million for a first offense and up to $3 million for repeat offenses.

Enforcement falls to a newly created agency called the Division of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust, known as DIGIT, which oversees large AI research labs and checks compliance. One report instead names the Department of Financial Services as the overseer, so the articles disagree on which agency is in charge. Hochul launched the New York AI Responsibility and Research Center at Binghamton University, part of the State University of New York, on the day the portal opened. The center will independently assess whether advanced systems operate safely and will review corporate safety policies together with DIGIT. Hochul first announced the center in January, backed by $55 million in donations and capital.

Speaking at a briefing, Hochul criticized technology leaders who say their vision of an AI future is inevitable and warn that those who do not join in will be left behind. She said New York is building a sensible regulatory model that puts communities before corporations and people before powerful technology. Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic has issued a public statement about the enforcement deadline, though both have previously voiced support for thoughtful regulation in congressional testimony. Anthropic priced its IPO at $70 to $78 per share ahead of a November 19 debut, so it must explain its compliance posture to investors during roadshow presentations. OpenAI is turning ChatGPT into a business discovery engine, which widens the surface regulators can scrutinize.

The state moves alongside other states, and the articles describe a growing patchwork of rules. California's SB 53, which took effect in January, requires frontier developers to publish safety policies, protects whistleblowers, and mandates reporting of major incidents within 15 days. Illinois's SB 315 takes effect early next year and adds independent audits of compliance with safety standards. Reporting deadlines and review procedures therefore differ depending on where a company operates. California debated similar measures earlier this year without passing comprehensive regulation, while Colorado and Massachusetts have working groups studying the issue, and the federal government has passed no comprehensive AI safety law.

State authorities said they can take enforcement action against unregistered companies but did not disclose how. The exact fine structure was reported as under regulatory review in one account, and DIGIT has not said how many investigators it has assigned or what its audit schedule looks like. Lobbyists are reportedly working behind the scenes to shape implementation details and to push for federal preemption that would override state laws. One outlet expects copycat legislation across blue states by mid-2027 if enforcement goes smoothly, while a backlash could stall AI regulation nationwide if it proves burdensome. Whether the law proves enforceable, and whether Washington steps in, remains unanswered.

stories.Headline: Portland parents protesting use of AI in schools
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, concerned parents and advocates from a group called OR Unplugged protested outside Google's Downtown Portland office, as reported by KOIN. The group's message was that technology in the classroom should be reined in, and some of them want AI removed from it entirely. KOIN's Joey Vacca reported the protest in a story posted on November 11, 2026, and updated that same evening. The Portland demonstration was one of several protests planned outside Google offices across the country on Wednesday. Another one took place outside Google's Boulder, Colorado, office, according to a separate report by KDVR.

The Boulder protesters called for increased guidance on how students use technology for learning, according to KDVR. The Colorado chapters of the Distraction-Free Schools Policy Project, Schools Beyond Screens and Fairplay took part, bringing together educators, caregivers and students. Their concern is Google's bundled AI product changes for Pre-K-12 schools. In Portland, the group's outreach coordinator, Kathy Masarie, summed up the demand by saying the best motto is "skills before screens." She also said AI is outsourcing students' learning.

Google answered through a spokesperson, whose identical statement was given to both KOIN and FOX31. The company said it hears parents' and teachers' concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and that it shares the goal of helping students learn. It said it is starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month, which walk students step by step through a range of complex problems rather than just giving quick answers. Next year, Google said, it will update its approach to controls for schools, partly to address feedback from educators. Under that change, the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable.

Masarie was not convinced by Google's response, saying tech companies have told the public many times that they are putting in protections and barriers. She said a group is now checking these so-called protections and finding that they do not work. As a result, she said, a parent who turns a feature on believes the child is safe, and a school that turns it on believes the same, but they are not. Parent Nataliya Pirumova said she is not entirely opposed to technology in class, so long as it is used properly, and that she supports AI literacy courses so students can understand how the technology works. In Boulder, parent and teacher Suzy Burger said children learn through friction, because they have to try things, work hard and fail, and that AI gives them the answers and removes that chance.

Masarie said the Portland group was protesting because Google had threatened to cut schools off from searching on its platform if they do not agree to use its AI. KOIN's report does not include a Google response to that specific claim beyond the general statement. Pirumova said AI is not going away, and that students need to be taught to engage with it intelligently rather than in a free-for-all. In Boulder, organizer Leah Leonard told FOX31 that technology can enhance learning but that how it is used must be monitored. She asked how children will learn to learn, learn to think for themselves and become great critical thinkers.

On what happens next, Google's statement gives two timelines: the Guided Learning pilot in Search is starting this month, and the updated school controls will arrive next year. Under those controls, the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will stay off by default until schools choose to enable them. The articles do not say whether the protesters plan further demonstrations, and they do not say how many people attended in Portland or in Boulder. They also do not say which other Google offices across the country hosted protests on Wednesday. Google says it is building these experiences in partnership with educators, but the articles do not say whether any school or district has responded to the planned changes.

stories.Headline: Drug Ads Can Influence AI Treatment Recommendations, Study Finds
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai published a study on November 11 in The Lancet Digital Health, showing that drug advertising can sway artificial intelligence treatment recommendations. They tested 12 AI models from major technology companies, including Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic. Each model was given a physician-written clinical case, and the researchers checked whether a clearly labeled pharmaceutical advertisement would change the treatment it recommended. When a drug ad came before the case, the models became more likely to select the advertised drug. The result matters because more people are turning to AI for health information.

Across 33 clinical scenarios, the advertised drug was selected in 47.6 percent of responses when an ad was present, compared with 35 percent without one. In four cases, models went from choosing the advertised drug zero percent of the time to choosing it 100 percent of the time once the ad was introduced. The team analyzed 258,559 AI responses and assessed both the treatment chosen and whether it was consistent with clinical guidance. The study was built to isolate advertising, so the same cases were given either alone or with a real drug advertisement placed immediately before them. Patient information and treatment choices stayed unchanged, and only the presence of the advertisement varied.

The study was led by first author Mahmud Omar, MD, a lecturer in the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at the Icahn School of Medicine. He said he found it surprising how reasonable the answers often appeared, because a model could recommend an appropriate treatment while its preference among several reasonable options shifted after seeing the ad. Omar leads research on the safety, reliability, and real-world effects of generative AI in clinical care. He said that because the final answer could still look medically sound, the influence could be easy to miss in typical research evaluations and in personal use by patients and physicians. Senior author Girish N. Nadkarni, MD, MPH, who chairs the department and is Chief AI Officer of the Mount Sinai Health System, said an answer can be clinically reasonable and still raise questions about why the AI reached it.

The investigators said the findings do not mean pharmaceutical advertising will necessarily cause AI models to recommend unsafe or inappropriate treatments. In the study, advertisements did not clearly increase recommendations for unsupported supplements or clearly suboptimal drugs. The models also rarely acknowledged the ads, since in a subset of free-text responses they explicitly mentioned the advertisement in only 29.9 percent of responses. They repeated information or claims from the advertisement more often than they named it. Nadkarni said that as AI becomes part of how people get health information, clinical guidance must be distinguishable from commercial influence, with transparency about when advertising is part of the interaction.

The researchers noted limits to what the study examined, saying they did not test whether changes in AI recommendations ultimately affected prescriptions, patient decisions, costs, or health outcomes. The study appears in The Lancet Digital Health under the title Pharmaceutical advertising and drug recommendations by consumer-facing artificial intelligence: A controlled study. Mount Sinai Health System supplied the article that News-Medical.Net published on November 11, 2026. Medical Economics reported the same findings on the same date, noting that the work comes as more patients turn to AI for health information. The researchers say the findings point to several practical steps for AI developers and health systems.

These include testing AI systems with and without promotional content to see whether recommendations change, clearly disclosing when advertising is presented to an AI system, and keeping promotional material separate from clinical advice. The findings may also matter to regulators as they consider how existing rules governing pharmaceutical advertising apply when promotional content is incorporated into AI-generated health information. The research team plans to extend the work through its ongoing evaluation of AI and human-AI interaction in real-world clinical cases. The articles leave open whether the shifts in recommendations would translate into real prescriptions, patient choices, costs, or health outcomes. They also do not say whether any regulator or AI developer has acted on the suggestions.

stories.Headline: Anthropic seeks valuation of about $1.3 trillion when it becomes a publicly traded company
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, said in a regulatory filing on Tuesday that it will sell 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78 a share as it goes public. At the midpoint of that range, the offering would let the San Francisco company raise more than $61 billion. The company is seeking a valuation of about $1.3 trillion, according to the Associated Press, while the San Francisco Chronicle put the figure at up to $1.4 trillion. The shares are expected to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the "ANT" ticker symbol, and the Wall Street debut is expected this month.

The offering could be among the biggest initial public offerings ever, but it now appears it will fall short of the record $86 billion that SpaceX raised in its IPO in June. Going public would put Anthropic ahead of OpenAI, setting up a pair of blockbuster stock debuts by rival AI developers. The IPO could give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and could add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei. On the same day it set pricing, Anthropic announced a $50 million commitment to Bay Area philanthropy through the end of 2027, its largest hometown pledge to date. The company is partnering with the San Francisco Foundation and forming a donor-advised fund, and an initial $500,000 over the holidays will support four initiatives: the San Francisco-Marin Food Bank, Glide Memorial Church, Interfaith Winter Shelter and San Francisco Firefighters Local 798's Toy Program.

Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote that this is the first time a U.S. frontier lab carries a standalone public market price, uncluttered by an ad business or a rocket business. Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's cofounder and president, said in a statement that San Francisco has always been a place of enormous possibility, but that it isn't shared equally by everyone. She said the company has been privileged to build Anthropic in the city and wants its success to expand opportunity rather than widen existing gaps. Fred Blackwell, CEO of the San Francisco Foundation, said Anthropic contacted the foundation just over a week ago and sought to make an immediate impact. He called it one of the largest corporate donations in the foundation's history, and said he hopes it encourages others to give.

The Chronicle noted that the $50 million is equivalent to about 0.0036% of Anthropic's expected $1.4 trillion valuation. Anthropic's seven cofounders, including the Amodeis, previously committed to give away 80% of their wealth, and the company has matched employees' charitable giving, totaling a reported $540 million in company expenses in 2025. Future beneficiaries will be chosen by Anthropic, with the foundation providing advisory services, and the funding is not open to applications. The announcement came a day after Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky donated $100 million for San Francisco parks. Mayor Daniel Lurie has encouraged local tech companies to take part in philanthropy and civic life, and he pitched OpenAI on a civic partnership that the company declined.

Anthropic was formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders and is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. A regulatory filing last month showed revenue reaching more than $16 billion in the first half of the year, 14 times the same period last year, though the company has yet to turn a profit. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all lost more money than they have made because of the huge costs of building AI, which has fueled concerns that a bubble has formed in the sector. Last week brought a brutal sell-off on Wall Street led by companies tied to the buildout of AI data centers. The Federal Reserve hiked interest rates in September for the first time in three years, and a hot inflation reading on Tuesday raised the odds of larger rate hikes.

In September, Dario Amodei cautioned that the AI industry should slow its development to give safety measures time to catch up. He warned that without a slowdown, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months. He offered a plan on his website to increase checks on the industry, noting that Anthropic is already undertaking part of it on its own. Other steps, he said, would require coordination across the industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones. The Chronicle said the IPO could come as soon as next week.

stories.Headline: KT deploys AI-based email security service across KAIST
stories.Summary:
KT has been chosen by the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, known as KAIST, to provide a cloud-based AI email security service to the whole university. The service will cover all students, researchers and faculty and staff, rather than only a handful of key researchers or particular departments. KT announced the deployment on Tuesday, the 11th, and the news was reported on November 11, 2026. KAIST picked the service after its own technical evaluation of the technology. It also cleared a security review by the National Intelligence Service, which opened the way for a campus-wide rollout.

The service is KT's in-house AI Email Security product, a cloud security service that detects and blocks threats delivered by email, including ransomware and phishing messages. It applies a three-stage filtering system covering spam blocking, AI-based threat detection and in-depth analysis of advanced persistent threats, known as APTs. The system can spot phishing URLs and malicious files disguised as legitimate mail. KT will supply AI-based threat detection and an APT response system for every member of KAIST. The service runs on a software-as-a-service model and can be supplied according to the scale of use, so universities, research institutes and other organizations can adopt it.

KT is the party responsible for delivering and operating the service, and it described its aims in plain terms. It said the deployment is meant to shield KAIST's core research and education assets from increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks while also growing its AI security business. Seung-taek Baek, executive director and head of the Western Corporate Customer Headquarters in KT's Enterprise Division, said KT will use its AI security technology to protect KAIST members and the university's research and educational assets. He added that KT will build on this case to extend its AI security services to universities and research institutions. KT also said it will use the KAIST deployment to widen its AI email security business to major research and education institutions, including domestic universities and government-funded research institutes.

KAIST's own view came from Young-jin Kwon, head of the university's Academic Information Office. He said it is important that students, researchers and faculty and staff can concentrate on research and education in a safe environment. Kwon said the university will keep advancing its information security system so that all members can receive a high level of protection. The people directly affected are the students, researchers and faculty and staff of KAIST, all of whom fall under the new coverage. KT also said it intends to support institutions that feel burdened by specialist security staffing or infrastructure operations, so they can use AI-based threat detection and APT analysis.

The articles give some background on how the service differs from earlier approaches and on its certification. Unlike existing on-premises APT security solutions, KT's service integrates spam, AI and APT security functions through a cloud-based software-as-a-service model. Because of this, an institution does not need to build a separate large-scale security infrastructure, which reduces its operational burden. KT obtained Cloud Security Assurance Program certification for the solution's cloud service in June. The articles also note that the AI security solution was developed in-house by KT, and that the service is scaled to the size of each deployment.

Looking ahead, KT says it will use the KAIST case to expand its AI email security business to major research and education institutions, including domestic universities and government-funded research institutes. KAIST says it will continue to advance its information security system so all members can receive a high level of security protection. The articles do not give a start date for the campus-wide rollout or a timetable for the planned expansion to other institutions. They also do not state the contract value, the contract length, or the number of KAIST users who will be covered. Nor do they name which other universities or research institutes KT intends to approach next.
