stories.Headline: Hackers stole AI credentials to get $740,000 in free compute; Railway picked up the bill
stories.Summary:
Hackers exploited Railway, a cloud hosting provider, in an attack that began on October 20 and lasted nearly 26 hours. They first exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway's build infrastructure, evading filesystem isolation protections to obtain an internal credential. Using that credential, they accessed stored build histories and retrieved a copy of Railway's internal source code. They then used a misconfigured trust relationship to reach more of the infrastructure and obtain credentials that decrypt customer environment variables. Railway disclosed the incident on October 22 and posted a follow-up report the week of November 11.

The attackers were fully evicted on October 21, after they had decrypted a subset of roughly 100,000 customer variables, or at most 1.85 percent of workspaces. They generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges, with customers reporting that their keys answered coding questions and performed training-data tasks they never ran. The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to more than 1,850 users, including GitHub and OAuth tokens that Railway reset. Railway worked with GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, SpaceXSI, Stripe and others to revoke potentially compromised keys. Customers were advised to revoke and reapply sensitive environment variables stored on Railway before October 21.

Railway is working to reimburse customers, including for charges that providers decline to refund. The company said it shut down potentially compromised internal tooling and rolled all keys after validating that intruders had been shut out. It moved to a new generation of infrastructure, rebuilt the tooling used to run its infrastructure, and added functionality to mass revoke app permissions after suspicious activity. Railway also said it is moving to short-lived credentials and logging every decryption. The company described the incident as a contest of agent speed, in which both attackers and defenders worked in parallel.

David Shipley of Beauceron Security said AI credentials are becoming the new credit card numbers, and that so-called LLMjacking is expected to displace cryptojacking. Frank Dickson of Dickson Research called Railway's report remarkably candid, noting that it owns its configuration mistake and admits it cannot be sure it found every account the attacker created. Dickson said stolen keys let thieves get cost-free compute while the key owners pay the bill. Customers of Railway, he advised, should treat every stored secret as stolen until rotated. The affected parties are Railway's customers, the 1,850-plus users with linked accounts, and the AI providers whose keys were misused.

AI credentials are cheap to harvest at scale, and attackers can resell access through so-called AI routers that provide models users otherwise could not afford. Such access is valuable for distillation, which transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller one to cut costs. Dickson said training on another model's answers takes millions of questions, and stolen keys spread those questions across thousands of real customers. An investigation by Wiz found that stolen keys were tested within 30 minutes of theft, then flooded with traffic four to seven days later. Wiz also found that a key restricted to a narrow set of model profiles left most of the thief's traffic throttled.

Railway said it cannot yet share the specific details and scale of the exploits because the investigation is ongoing. Dickson advised customers to check AI provider bills and usage logs, rotate cloud, database and payment credentials, and set hard spending caps on every AI key. Customers were also advised to remove public network access to databases, check GitHub audit logs and Dockerhub registry logs, and review all app access. The articles do not say whether Railway has found every account the attacker created, nor whether all reimbursements will be paid. They also leave open whether providers will refund the disputed charges they have declined to reverse.

stories.Headline: AI – Master and Commander: Lessons from graduate student projects and the need for an AI-enriched contract
stories.Summary:
The seminar was held in the spring of 2026 at Goethe University, where 31 master's students used AI to investigate why the EU appears more exposed to international shocks and political, financial and industrial vulnerabilities than before. Students examined defence and security, migration and labour markets, energy and the green transition, strategic autonomy and industrial policy, the Single Market, and monetary policy under uncertainty. The authors describe the seminar as an experiment in how AI might be used in graduate education without displacing students' independent judgement. The question was whether AI could help students without outsourcing the thinking that graduate study is meant to develop. The work ran over six weeks as a graduate seminar, with the authors acknowledging the importance of this challenge in assessment.

The authors note that views on AI range widely, and they cite concerns in the literature about unreliable outputs, including hallucinations and fabricated references. They also describe cognitive offloading, where people delegate tasks to technology, and cognitive surrender, where people stop thinking for themselves. Employers are expected to value people who can reason critically as AI takes over routine tasks. The Guardian reported that 92% of UK students already use AI, and universities were urged to stress-test their assessments. The seminar adopted a pragmatic, optimistic stance in line with UNESCO's human-centred guidance and the OECD's view that assessment should measure learning rather than polished output.

The seminar required each group to submit three elements: a pre-AI outline with a research question, motivation, initial sources and analytical plan, written before any AI use; a core presentation enriched by AI; and a transparency statement listing the tools used, the prompts, and what worked or failed. The authors describe this as an AI-enriched contract designed to keep ownership of ideas with students and to make AI use visible. The final lecture refined research questions and helped students present strategically. The assessment rested on three dimensions set out in a table in the source article. Students were expected to show judgement, not just output, in the final presentations.

Thirteen groups presented, covering defence, migration, energy, industrial policy, the Single Market and monetary policy. Several projects examined how Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the 2022 energy crisis and renewed trade tensions exposed gaps in Europe's architecture, while others assessed whether REPowerEU, the Green Deal and the Critical Raw Materials Act were on track. Methods ranged from policy analysis and surveys to panel regressions, difference-in-differences and text analysis. The authors report that the groups drew the line in the same place, reserving the research question, economic reasoning and final interpretation for themselves while verifying what AI produced. Students and graduate programmes, the authors suggest, face the same tension between speed and understanding.

The authors observed five recurring patterns: AI sped up routine work such as cleaning data, debugging code, formatting charts and translating sources; it helped students use methods they did not previously know; it allowed exploration within a six-week seminar; humans kept judgement, interpretation and fact-checking; and students developed new literacies, including careful prompting and critical checking of sources. The authors conclude that AI behaved as a capable subordinate rather than a master and commander, with students keeping command of questions and conclusions. Each student presented and answered questions for well over 15 minutes on average. The authors note that the phrase master and commander refers to 18th-century Royal Navy officers who captained sloops-of-war.

The authors acknowledge limitations: the cohort was small, self-selected and not random, much evidence came from student reflections, and there was no control group working without AI. Reported gains in speed and ambition therefore cannot be causally attributed to AI or the contract, and durable learning was not measured. Future pilot studies are planned to assess outlines and final outputs separately, require systematic prompt logs, and track whether critical questioning persists. The authors also note that the AI landscape and graduate education are changing continuously. The article is a CEPR/VoxEU piece, and the authors thank Goethe University for financial support and a workshop audience for comments.

stories.Headline: SoftBank swings to first-half loss as AI ambitions face fresh setbacks
stories.Summary:
SoftBank Group reported a first-half net loss on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, after swinging from profit, according to the articles. The company said it faces growing uncertainty over its ambitious artificial intelligence strategy, following political setbacks in the United States and regulatory hurdles in China. One specific setback mentioned is that China blocked SoftBank's $5.4 billion deal to acquire ABB's robotics division. The articles frame the loss as a sign that the company's AI hopes are running into fresh obstacles.

The articles say the setbacks touch several parts of SoftBank's growth plan, including its investments in robotics and data centers. A U.S. election has raised questions about the company's data center plans. The robotics deal, which would have added a major industrial automation business, is now blocked by Beijing. Investors are watching closely to see whether the artificial intelligence strategy can still deliver the growth the company has promised.

The articles identify SoftBank Group as the company responsible for the strategy and the reported loss, with its reporting covered by Nikkei Asia's Tsubasa Suruga. The reporting describes the company's position as one of increasing uncertainty rather than quoting specific executive statements on the outlook. The articles also note that investors are focused on whether the AI growth strategy succeeds. Beyond the blocked robotics deal and the data center questions, the articles do not give further detail on the company's response.

The broader context is that SoftBank has tied much of its recent expansion to artificial intelligence, through stakes in OpenAI and related infrastructure projects. Other recent items in the same coverage include a planned $50 billion AI investment in Malaysia, a planned bond sale to fund OpenAI investment, and the U.S. IPO filing of SB Energy, a SoftBank-backed company. The articles also report that SoftBank's shares fell 11 percent after OpenAI said it would not go public this year. What happens next is not specified in the articles beyond continued investor attention to the strategy.

stories.Headline: Georgia students raise privacy concerns over AI smart glasses
stories.Summary:
Georgia students have voiced concerns about Meta's AI-powered smart glasses, which can record video and take pictures without obvious notice to people nearby. Local reporting by WSB-TV, published November 10, 2026, described growing worry that people are being recorded without their knowledge as the technology spreads. The glasses look like ordinary eyewear but contain built-in cameras, and an LED light is meant to show when recording is underway. Georgia Tech student Gia Pisicchio said she could not tell whether the glasses were recording or switched off, adding that the uncertainty made her uncomfortable.

Georgia Tech student Hufsa Qidwai said unwanted recordings have become a concern on campus, including incidents involving sexual harassment. Earlier this year, University of Georgia police investigated complaints from students who said people wearing smart glasses secretly filmed them on campus. One such interaction involving a student's appearance was later uploaded to social media. Under Georgia and federal law, recording people in public places is generally legal because there is no expectation of privacy there. Recording in private spaces, including restrooms, locker rooms or private homes, can bring criminal or civil consequences.

Meta's smart glasses can translate conversations, send texts, take calls and record video, and Meta says the recording indicator light cannot be turned off or disabled. According to Meta, covering that light with tape stops the camera from working. Meta acknowledges it is exploring facial recognition for the glasses but says no final decision has been made. Kade Crockford, director of the ACLU's Technology and Justice Programs, said people still expect some level of privacy and anonymity in public spaces. Privacy advocates have warned that facial recognition could let wearers covertly identify people around them and store that information.

Students, campus users and bystanders are the people most directly affected by covert recording, and the articles describe young people in particular as targets of misuse. In June, Milton police arrested Christopher Hall on felony eavesdropping and surveillance charges after a mother found smart glasses on top of her car, pointed toward her 13-year-old daughter's bedroom window. Hall's friend told Channel 2's Michael Seiden that he believed there was an innocent explanation, saying Hall may have gotten drunk at a party and left the glasses behind. Georgia Schools Superintendent-elect Dr. Lydia Powell said the technology could create challenges for schools, including students photographing tests or recording others in restrooms.

Smart glasses and other personal electronic devices are banned in Georgia schools under a law that took effect this year. Outside Georgia, this summer in Boston, a registered sex offender was charged with using camera-equipped sunglasses to record children changing at a playground. Privacy concerns about camera-equipped wearables have grown as the technology becomes more common, according to the WSB-TV report. The same reporting noted that the glasses can take calls, send texts and translate conversations alongside their recording function.

Separately, the Times of India reported that the University of Michigan Police Department signed a $127,500 contract with Flock Safety for 15 AI-powered Falcon Flex cameras, which were never installed or put into use. The agreement was signed on February 3, 2025, by Jennifer Carr for the police department and by Mark Smith for Flock Safety. The contract committed the university to $63,750 annually over an initial 24-month period, and it covered FlockOS Essentials software, Vehicle Fingerprint technology and 15 battery packs. Under its terms, camera data would be deleted after 30 days unless archived, and Flock has since reduced its default retention to seven days.

The contract allowed use for any "legitimate public safety and/or business purpose," and Section 5.3 let Flock disclose footage without a warrant on a "good faith belief" that disclosure was legally necessary. Law professor Michael Steinberg said the major issue is that surveillance has moved from investigating suspects to collecting information about everyone. LSA senior Radha Tanner, co-chair of the American Civil Liberties Union at the university, said the problem lies in how the cameras are used and by whom. UMPD deputy chief of police Melissa Overton said the department selected Flock Safety to support public safety and investigative needs, and she confirmed the cameras are not installed or in use.

Overton also said the agreement went through the university's procurement procedures and did not require Board of Regents approval or a separate public approval process. The Michigan Daily reported that the university had, during summer 2025, installed cameras at the entrances of most campus buildings, as well as in the Law Quad and the Diag. In autumn 2025 the university launched the Security Technology Enhancement Project across its three campuses and removed explicit restrictions on surveillance cameras. Lawmakers in Michigan from both parties have called for tighter regulation of Flock cameras, which have faced scrutiny nationally over data sharing and privacy.

stories.Headline: Fed’s Bowman Warns of Stock Correction If AI Bets Don’t Pan Out
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Michelle Bowman warned in written remarks delivered Tuesday local time at the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington. She said U.S. stock valuations could see a "sharp correction" if returns on artificial intelligence investments fail to meet market expectations. She also singled out a sharp rise in private long-term interest rates as another potential trigger. Bowman noted that weaker stock prices could erode consumer spending, while higher borrowing costs would squeeze the housing market and small-business investment. The same day, the U.S. Department of Labor reported that October core consumer price index rose 0.3% month over month, above expectations.

Bowman said she sees persistent inflation pressure and tightening labor market conditions, meaning "there is still work to do" to bring inflation back to the 2% target. She acknowledged that the persistence of inflation has exceeded her earlier assessment, leaving her open to another rate hike at the December meeting. The Fed held rates steady at its October 27-28 meeting, after a 25-basis-point hike in September that was the first since 2023. Bowman said she supported holding rates steady last month to assess economic developments and the effects of the September hike. She also warned that AI-related debt in corporate bonds, private credit and project finance is expected to exceed $800 billion this year.

Bowman described how large technology companies and hyperscalers use their strong credit ratings and off-balance-sheet arrangements to help smaller, higher-risk companies pledge assets to finance data centers and accelerated computing equipment. She noted that cloud giants and chip designers have made equity investments in smaller companies that buy their products, creating the appearance of revolving financing. Bowman warned that once markets come under pressure, this web of capital linkages could amplify risk transmission. Her remarks effectively place the valuation risk of the AI trade on the central bank's radar, affecting investors in technology stocks and companies tied to the data center and chip supply chains.

Governor Christopher Waller argued in a London speech that December should seriously consider a 50-basis-point hike if inflation data remain hot. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who holds a vote this year, said in Houston that the Federal Open Market Committee needs at least two more 25-basis-point hikes. Economists Christopher Hodge of Natixis and Tom Porcelli of Wells Fargo offered differing views on the size of a December move. Christopher Phelan, chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers, publicly opposed a 50-basis-point hike in December. The articles note that U.S. inflation has remained above the 2% target for more than five consecutive years.

Following the remarks and data, the 2-year Treasury yield rose 19 basis points to 4.75% on the day, its largest single-day increase since April 2025. Federal funds futures show investors betting on a 25-basis-point hike in December, another in January and possibly one in April. Before the December meeting, Fed officials will receive one employment report and full inflation data. The articles leave open whether the Fed will opt for a 25- or 50-basis-point move, and whether AI returns will disappoint. More to follow.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Q3 profit up 50%; losses continue
stories.Summary:
OpenAI reported that its quarterly revenue rose about 50 percent to $10 billion in the third quarter, according to the Wall Street Journal, which reported the figures on Tuesday. The ChatGPT maker nonetheless continued to post steep operating losses over the same period. Documents the newspaper viewed showed the company telling investors that its adjusted operating margin improved to -109 percent from -150 percent in the prior quarter. Its operating losses, however, widened to $10.9 billion from $10.1 billion.

The disclosure matters because investors are watching the finances of AI startups closely as they weigh profitability concerns against enthusiasm for the sector. Rival Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is preparing an initial public offering that could value the startup at about $1.4 trillion. Anthropic has started a roadshow for the share sale, which is expected to set a benchmark for the industry. The Reuters report noted that the OpenAI figures underscore strong investor appetite for AI companies despite these concerns.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on the report. The Wall Street Journal was the source of the financial details, which were drawn from documents it viewed. Reuters carried the story and reported that the company had not yet replied when it published. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Mashup Ventures Raises 25.9 Billion Won Fund for AI, Deep Tech Startups
stories.Summary:
Seoul-based early-stage investor Mashup Ventures said on November 11, 2026, that it has closed a 25.9 billion won ($17.6 million) fund, called Mashup First Believer Venture Investment Fund No. 5, without government policy money. The firm will use the fund to back promising startups in artificial intelligence and deep tech. Partners at Mashup Ventures are its largest contributors, and the fund also drew money from successful founders, startups, information technology and manufacturing companies, and financial institutions. The fund has a 10-year life and will focus on pre-seed companies, whose founders are still preparing to launch, and seed-stage companies, which are raising their first outside capital.

Its main investment areas are physical AI, vertical AI tailored to specific industries, energy and aerospace. The firm plans to expand its deep tech investments under Chief Investment Officer Park Eun-woo, who previously led global expansion as chief strategy officer at autonomous drone company Nearthlab. Mashup Ventures was led by Lee Taek-kyung, a co-founder of Daum, and has invested in about 220 companies since 2013, being the first institutional investor in 87% of them. Its portfolio includes Bucketplace, operator of the interior design platform Ohou, as well as MyRealTrip, Remember & Company, Wrtn Technologies and ScatterLab. More recently it has widened its scope to space, advanced materials and energy, with investments in O&B Space, NanoForge AI and Biologen.

The firm has also added specialists to strengthen its capacity to invest in technology startups. This year it recruited AI partner Yang Sung-min, a former engineer who has founded and sold companies, and venture partner Lee Sang-won, a co-founder of Silicon Valley deep tech company Quixo. The two will review the technology of early-stage portfolio companies and support product development and overseas expansion. Lee said the firm believed in founders who jumped into an uncertain market even as the paradigm shifted from the internet to mobile. He added that with AI now moving into robotics, energy and space, the firm intends to be the first investor to back founders before their technology is proven.

Separately, a Proximal Ventures fund was reported on November 10, 2026, by TechCrunch. Its founder, Sahir Raoof, a former SignalFire investor, raised $27.5 million for his first solo VC fund. The firm is betting that AI can automate the tools, infrastructure and services that support drug development, which pharmaceutical companies have historically outsourced. Proximal plans to write checks from $500,000 to $1.5 million to pre-seed and seed-stage startups, and has already backed seven startups.

His practice covers a wide range of fields, including artificial intelligence and machine learning, software and software-as-a-service, semiconductors, robotics, mobility, cleantech, digital health, and infrastructure. He also advises technology companies that sell to federal government customers and that collaborate with government research institutions. stories.Headline: TSMC October revenue hits record $17.81 billion
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, known as TSMC, reported its highest-ever monthly revenue for October, reaching about $17.81 billion. The figure was up 59.7 per cent from a year earlier and rose 14.7 per cent from September. The world's largest contract chipmaker posted consolidated revenue of NT 586.89 billion for the month. October's total beat the company's previous monthly record of $15.63 billion, set in August.

Revenue for January through October totaled $140 billion, a 43.3 per cent increase over the same stretch last year. The company credited the growth to strong demand for advanced semiconductors, particularly chips used in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Its 2-nanometre technology has entered commercial production and is contributing to sales. High-performance computing rose 22 per cent from the previous quarter and now makes up 68 per cent of total revenue, while the 2nm process accounted for 8 per cent of wafer revenue in the third quarter.

TSMC also raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast to about 44 per cent in US dollar terms, up from an earlier projection of slightly above 40 per cent. The company attributed the revision to robust demand for its advanced manufacturing processes during its October earnings conference. For the fourth quarter, it expects consolidated revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion. The company's shares closed 2.24 per cent higher on the Taiwan Stock Exchange on November 10.

The results come as the chipmaker's customers face their own scrutiny. TSMC manufactures chips for several technology companies, including NVIDIA, whose shares fell 4.3 per cent on November 9, wiping out about $190 billion in market value according to Reuters. That drop followed reports of an investigation involving NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with an accused Chinese spy, as well as a proposed shareholder lawsuit. The articles do not say how these developments will affect TSMC's future orders.

stories.Headline: KT Token Factory: Only Seven of 73 AI Models Run on Own Hardware as KT Plans More GPUs
stories.Summary:
KT Corp. said on its third-quarter earnings call on November 10, 2026, that it will expand its own GPU investment to produce more AI tokens for Token Factory, its enterprise AI platform. Token Factory launched on October 30 with 73 models, but only seven of them run as inference services on GPUs in KT's domestic data centers. The other 66 are global models reached through KT's partnership with the US model marketplace OpenRouter. KT did not disclose a GPU count, an investment amount or a capacity figure, which leaves enterprise buyers unable to size the production side of the business.

Park Sang-won, head of KT's AX business division, answered a KB Securities analyst's question about AX costs and Token Factory. He said KT will expand its own GPU investment to strengthen token production and, over the long term, become a domestic hub for producing and distributing tokens. He also said running models on domestically hosted infrastructure carries a significant sovereignty advantage, and that KT will grow self-hosted and brokered models in balance. Management gave no quantitative Token Factory targets on the call, though Park said KT's telecom billing capabilities could create synergy revenue for the platform.

The seven self-hosted models are KT's Midm K 3.0 Pro, Upstage's Solar Pro 4, Motif Technologies' Motif 3, Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra, Google's Gemma 4 31B, Z.ai's GLM 5.3 Flash and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, according to Digital Today. Three come from Korean developers, two from US companies and two from Chinese developers, and KT calls them sovereign AI models in a sense that describes where the model runs, not who built it. KT executive Lee Jin-hyung said the seven were chosen from widely used models in South Korea and the latest models from domestic startups. KT plans to expand the self-hosted lineup to 12 models next year, according to Digital Daily, though SBS reported about 10.

KT says running models in its data centers keeps enterprise data processing in Korea, but that argument covers only the self-hosted tier. The Korea Herald reported that most models supplied through OpenRouter process requests overseas, and KT said it will disclose each model's provider and operating region. KT applies a no-storage, no-training policy to the seven self-hosted models, and AX platform head Won Man-ho said prompts are not stored by default. Customers who need prompts for internal audits can opt in to storage and lookup.

Token Factory bills by usage, and Lee said KT generates a token detail record using a technique modeled on the call detail record that telecom billing relies on. KT applies each model's pricing, issues one consolidated bill and accepts payment in Korean won. KT says its internal testing found about 20% savings from prompt compression and about 5% from automatically switching a request to a cheaper capable model, for a target of up to 25%. KT did not disclose the criteria for those tests, and the reporting reviewed cites no independent benchmark.

KT described a hardware architecture at a September 11 briefing on the government's Modu-ui AI project that splits inference into two phases. Prefill, where the model reads the prompt, runs on GPUs, while decode, where it writes the answer token by token, runs on domestic AI chips. KT says 100 government-supplied GPUs would deliver the work of about 121 through Token Factory and that throughput rises about 31%, with prompt compression cutting input tokens by up to 80%. KT said it would start with 32 domestic AI chips and invest more as their performance improves, and the report cites no independent testing of these figures.

Because Token Factory charges by usage, every token a customer saves is a token KT does not bill. Digital Daily noted that lower token consumption can shrink KT's revenue, which is why KT is betting on margins from producing tokens itself rather than on brokerage fees. Lee said global model intermediaries typically charge about 5% and that KT's main revenue model is not fee-based. KT has named no customers and says it may disclose contracted companies after reviewing usage through December, and it has not disclosed revenue targets or paying-customer numbers.

KT is also discounting the capacity it wants to fill. A 30% promotion on usage fees for the seven self-hosted models runs through November 30 for corporate customers that completed verification and product contracts. The reports reviewed do not say what the promotion costs KT or how much of the self-hosted capacity is in use. Other carriers have chosen differently: STL Partners reports that AT&T treats tokens mainly as a cost to manage, while China Mobile's MoMA gateway offers more than 300 models. That same analysis argues that standalone gateways are hard to differentiate and that operators fare better bundling them with connectivity, compute, security and sovereignty.

stories.Headline: Faculty member addresses artificial intelligence practically and theoretically - The Pennsylvania State University
stories.Summary:
Penn State associate professor Heather Shoenberger, of the Donald P. Bellisario College of Communications, has been working on artificial intelligence both in the classroom and in research. Shoenberger co-created a three-credit undergraduate course, COMM 200N Generative AI for All, with Mehrdad Mahdavi, an associate professor of computer science and engineering. She has taught the course since the fall semester of 2024, and it is cross-listed in the Bellisario College and the College of Engineering, with sections taught in both colleges. The course reaches its enrollment cap each semester.

The course is designed to explain how generative AI works, along with the ethical, sociopolitical and other issues it raises. Shoenberger said the material must be kept current because the technology keeps changing, and she said she prepares well ahead of each class. Her research has produced a published article introducing the human-AI asymmetric relationship theory, or HAART. The article appeared in a special AI-focused issue of the Journal of Advertising, which Shoenberger described as the most prestigious journal in her field. She wrote it with four colleagues from King's College London, CQUniversity, Old Dominion University and the University of Amsterdam.

According to Shoenberger, the theory holds that conversational AI can display relational characteristics, such as simulated emotional responsiveness, commitment, attachment and intimacy, but it cannot experience relational benefits or commitment. Users may perceive a mutual relationship that does not actually exist, which she said could leave consumers vulnerable to dependence, risk and control. She said the framework could eventually encourage more transparency about these interactions and possibly regulation, and that she and her co-authors hope it will aid future advertising research. The articles do not describe any specific next steps beyond that.

Articles.Title: Faculty member addresses artificial intelligence practically and theoretically - The Pennsylvania State University

stories.Headline: Stony Brook FinTech Workshop Explores AI’s Impact on Finance, Announces New Industry Partnership
stories.Summary:
Stony Brook University held its FinTech Workshop on November 6 in the New Computer Science Building, where researchers and industry leaders discussed how artificial intelligence is changing financial analysis, software development and investment decisions. The event was organized by Karina Torres Castro, manager of research and innovation and assistant research professor in mechanical engineering, and it included the announcement of a new AI Innovation Lab in partnership with the financial technology company Broadridge. Students and faculty will work alongside industry experts in the lab to tackle challenges in AI and finance. The workshop included academic research presentations, industry perspectives and a panel discussion, and it was sponsored by the College of Engineering and Applied Sciences, the Long Island Manufacturing Extension Partnership, the Center of Excellence in Wireless and Information Technology and the AI Innovation Institute.

Amy Erickson, executive director of the Long Island Manufacturing Extension Partnership, said AI-driven financial modeling can help small and mid-sized manufacturers reduce waste and make better investment decisions without replacing skilled workers. She described the workshop as the first of several AI-focused programs her organization is rolling out for regional manufacturers. Andrew C. Singer, dean of the college, welcomed participants and introduced keynote speaker Robert J. Frey, research professor and founder of the university's Quantitative Finance Program. Frey, who has held leadership roles at Renaissance Technologies and other financial firms, compared the rise of AI with earlier technological advances that disrupted industries, saying some adjustments can be painful in the short term. He argued that stagnation is not the answer.

At Broadridge, AI is taking on more complex software development tasks, including some once assigned to entry-level employees. Roger Burkhardt, the company's chief technology officer of capital markets and AI, said the career ladder is changing and that new employees may be expected to define problems, evaluate AI-generated code and recognize security vulnerabilities. He encouraged students to experiment with AI development tools while learning to assess their output, and he said critical thinking and communicating with users are lasting skills. Jill Scher, managing director at CBIZ Advisors, began her accounting career in 1994 working with paper ledgers and red pencils, and she now uses AI to analyze financial statements and prepare for client meetings. Frey said that when AI is used properly, students will see it as a force multiplier that increases productivity rather than replacing them.

Pawel Polak, a faculty member in the Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, presented research on an international competition that attracted more than 1,000 registered participants to develop AI agents capable of writing code, forecasting financial trends and simulating markets. Some agents significantly improved the speed of existing software, but others struggled with unfamiliar problems. Teams that incorporated financial knowledge and agents required to explain their predictions generally performed better on new tasks, and Polak said human involvement definitely helps. Lav Varshney, professor of electrical and computer engineering and inaugural director of the AI Innovation Institute, argued that opaque "black box" AI may be less helpful because its inner workings are unknown. He described research using explicit, verifiable rules, with one possible application being financial transactions that fail to settle as expected, a context where traceability matters in regulated industries.

The afternoon panel, moderated by Yvette Wohn, inaugural chair of the Department of Technology, AI and Society, included Polak, Burkhardt, Scher and Melissa Brown, managing director of investment decision research at SimCorp. Brown said her team helps investors understand how unexpected economic developments might affect their portfolios, and she described an exercise considering what could happen if the Federal Reserve lost its independence. She said that work once took hours of searching historical data but now can be done by asking AI to identify similar past circumstances, which "takes five minutes rather than a day." Scher said some clients arrive with AI-generated tax analyses and ask her to confirm them, even when those analyses may overlook changing regulations or individual circumstances. Samir Das, chair of the Department of Computer Science, closed the workshop by announcing the AI Innovation Lab, which he said will focus on experiential learning and on how universities and industry can work together.

stories.Headline: Exploring How Autistic Individuals Interact With Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Stony Brook University and the University of Cincinnati studied how autistic people use ChatGPT, and their findings were published in the Association for Computing Machinery Interactive Health Conference. The study was led by Renkai Ma, an assistant professor at the University of Cincinnati's School of Information Technology, with coauthor Ben Zhang from Stony Brook's Department of Technology, AI and Society. The article is dated November 11, 2026, and it extends earlier research the team published in the proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2026. That earlier study analyzed posts from six major social media platforms about using chatbots for mental health support. The researchers gathered 3,984 posts from Reddit, X and Tumblr, published between January 2023 and September 2025, focusing on firsthand accounts from people who identified as autistic.

The article describes four ways autistic users benefited from ChatGPT, including communication, planning and emotional support. Some users called the chatbot a bi-directional translator between neurodivergent and neurotypical people, helping them adapt messages and interpret replies. Users also relied on it to offload executive tasks such as planning, organizing and getting started. For emotional regulation, some valued expressing difficult feelings without fear of judgment or pressure to mask. The researchers also say these benefits are linked to risks, including automated masking, over-reliance and reinforced beliefs when the chatbot's agreeable responses make them sound credible.

The article attributes its findings to Ma and Zhang, who are quoted describing how autistic users turned to ChatGPT during acute distress and to get unstuck on tasks. Ma said autistic people felt that readers were connecting with ChatGPT rather than with them, and that they had lost the ability to communicate on their own. The authors argue that heavy reliance on chatbots can push autistic users to hide their natural way of communicating. The researchers also recommend that a chatbot separate emotional validation from factual verification, so it can acknowledge distress while checking the facts behind a fear. The article was written with Salomé Davoudiasl listed as its author.

The findings matter to autistic users who turn to chatbots for everyday support, and to the neurotypical people who receive messages drafted or rewritten by them. The article notes that some users worried about losing their own voice when the chatbot wrote for them. Users described messages that sounded less like them after rewriting to fit neurotypical expectations. The article does not give a count of how many users have experienced these effects beyond the 3,984 posts analyzed.

To address these concerns, the authors propose what they call beneficial frictions, such as asking users to set their priorities before the chatbot suggests a plan. They also propose tools that help neurotypical readers interpret direct messages from autistic colleagues. The researchers say these ideas will direct their future research. The article does not say when that research will begin, how the proposed tools would work, or whether any chatbot developer has adopted these recommendations.

Articles.Title: Exploring How Autistic Individuals Interact With Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Ulster County Bans Government Use of AI Surveillance
stories.Summary:
Ulster County Executive Jen Metzger issued an executive order on October 22 banning the use of Flock cameras and other AI-assisted video surveillance technologies in county government. The order, titled "Prohibiting the Use of Flock Cameras and other AI-Assisted Video Surveillance Technologies" and designated Executive Order No. 5, took effect immediately upon its announcement. It bars any department or employee under the county executive's office from buying or deploying such systems, from helping to develop them, and from aiding private individuals or corporations in implementing them. Flock systems, made by Flock Safety, include security cameras, license plate readers and data-sharing networks, many of which use generative AI and machine learning to identify people, track them and build databases.

The ban covers buildings and property under the county executive's authority, including the Ulster County Courthouse, the Sheriff's Office, UCAT public transit facilities, county public works departments and public recreational areas such as rail trails. It does not reach facilities controlled by towns and villages, such as the New Paltz Town Hall, the New Paltz Courthouse or the New Paltz Police Headquarters, and it does not apply to private individuals or businesses. In her order, Metzger argued that protecting public safety and individual rights go hand in hand in a democracy and that the rapid, unregulated growth of the AI sector threatens that balance. She wrote that tech companies dominate AI development without independent oversight, that multiple security breaches have occurred in these companies' systems, and that collected information could be shared outside county government without authorization.

New Paltz Town Supervisor Tim Rogers said he agrees with Metzger's assessment that unregulated AI in security matters can weaken public safety and democratic principles, and he warned that civil liberties could be trampled if for-profit companies are left to operate without limits. He also said the town has no current plan to adopt Flock technology, citing its high cost, and that to his knowledge the New Paltz Police Department does not use it. Rogers acknowledged that surveillance can deliver local benefits, arguing that cameras like those Lowe's operates on Route 299 help deter shoplifting and theft. The New Paltz Oracle reports that the town has three AI surveillance systems in and around its territory, two of them Flock cameras owned by Lowe's facing its parking lot, and that the owner of the third remains undisclosed. Rogers said Lowe's is not required to register these cameras with the town and that no site plan or building review involves Flock cameras, so private companies remain outside local regulation, just as they do at the county level.

Articles.Title: Ulster County Bans Government Use of AI Surveillance - The New Paltz Oracle

stories.Headline: Hands-on experience prepares Wayne State engineers for Michigan’s AI-powered manufacturing future
stories.Summary:
Wayne State University is giving engineering students hands-on work with robots, conveyor systems, machine vision and generative AI, a program reported on November 10, 2026. The work takes place partly in IntelliMake, a new research hub and pilot-scale factory being developed with Kyndryl to advance AI-driven manufacturing. The article says the initiative is already helping graduates land jobs in the field. Students in the James and Patricia Anderson College of Engineering work on experiments that aim to make manufacturing smarter, more flexible and more efficient. The reporting ties the program to the industry's shift toward artificial intelligence.

Michigan's AI and Workforce Plan estimates that 75% of manufacturing jobs will require some form of upskilling as automation spreads. The state estimates responsible AI adoption could generate up to $70 billion in economic impact and support 130,000 jobs. Raj Sohmshetty, co-director of IntelliMake and instructor of IE 6000: Digital Automation, has redesigned that course to combine classroom learning with lab work. Students in the lab work with robots, a conveyor system and a laser engraver, and explore generative AI and AI agents that help robots respond to changing conditions. The course is intended to prepare students to develop systems in which AI agents help machines adapt.

Dr. Ratna Babu Chinnam, professor and chair of industrial and systems engineering and co-director of IntelliMake, said the aim is to create a pipeline of students who can meet the state's urgent workforce need. Sohmshetty is a professor of practice in the Industrial & Systems Engineering Department. Chinnam said computer science students understand AI but may not know how to identify the real need, and that the lab bridges that gap by showing what AI can do. The article presents these comments as the university's account of its program. It does not describe any criticism of the program.

Chinnam said about 10 students spent substantial time in the lab during fall 2025, and several later secured positions with leading companies. Gokula Kumaran Kiruthiga Gopal, a recent graduate of the artificial intelligence master's program, became an AI engineer at Panasonic. She said her IntelliMake experience helped her get the job, and that Panasonic was especially interested in a factory-monitoring system her team developed. Chinnam also said about 70% of students in a recent Digital Automation class were already working engineers or other professionals, including some at automotive companies. Sushant Lingras, an operations manager at PHINA, formerly Delphi Technologies, is pursuing a master's in artificial intelligence there.

Lingras said he developed an AI-powered agent that helps employees quickly access plant information, standard work and operational knowledge. He said the tool eliminated several manual data-entry tasks and reduced the time employees spend searching for information. Derek Stringfellow, an applications analyst at the Great Lakes Water Authority in its Capital Improvement Planning Group, is also pursuing a master's in AI. He said the class shows how such systems are built, how they fail and the role people still play. Stringfellow said he plans to bring these insights to GLWA's IT Group and to technology opportunities in water and wastewater projects.

Chinnam said the IntelliMake facility will expand opportunities for undergraduate and graduate education. The articles state that Wayne State plans to extend the approach to modern quality control, production control, facilities design and operational optimization. The article describes the goal as developing engineers who can turn advances in AI into practical improvements on the factory floor. It notes that testing at a production plant can be impractical, while students at IntelliMake can test ideas in a controlled environment. The articles do not give a timeline or budget for these expansions.

Articles.Title: Hands-on experience prepares Wayne State engineers for Michigan’s AI-powered manufacturing future

stories.Headline: Quectel Wireless Solutions: Quectel SP900BF-AP Smart Module Sets the Pace for Edge AI with 100 TOPS of Computing Power
stories.Summary:
On November 11, 2026, Quectel Wireless Solutions, a global end-to-end IoT solutions provider, announced the SP900BF-AP in Munich, a smart module that lets robots, inspection systems and edge gateways run large AI models on the device itself. The module is built on the Qualcomm Dragonwing IQ-9075 Processor and delivers up to 100 TOPS of on-device AI compute. It allows industrial OEMs to integrate advanced AI directly into their products, which the company says reduces latency, bandwidth costs and data privacy risks tied to cloud-based processing. Processing data locally lets manufacturers support real-time robotics and automated inspection while keeping sensitive production data under their own control. Long-term hardware availability is also meant to meet the extended product lifecycles that industrial customers require.

The module combines an octa-core Qualcomm Kryo CPU running at up to 2.36 GHz with an Adreno 663 GPU, a Hexagon DSP and a dedicated NPU. Memory options reach up to 36 GB of LPDDR5X and 256 GB of UFS storage. Quectel commits to a product lifecycle of up to 10 years, which the company says helps customers reduce inventory, maintenance and upgrade costs. The module is designed to run Ubuntu and Yocto Linux, with support for these still in development. PCIe, USB 3.1, UART, SPI and I²C interfaces let OEMs add 4G/5G or Wi-Fi to suit each deployment.

Raymond Wang, Product Head, Smart at Quectel Wireless Solutions, said the value of AI must be proven on the industrial front line. He said the company is providing a complete, ready-to-use edge intelligence solution that spares customers complex low-level development. The module was developed through close collaboration between Quectel and Qualcomm Technologies, combining modular design with system-level optimisation. Quectel describes the result as stable on-device AI performance in demanding industrial settings. The company presents the module as a way for customers to accelerate their AI-driven transformation.

The module supports autonomous mobile robots with four-camera support, 3D perception and on-device navigation. It also supports production-line inspection that detects defects in real time without moving sensitive data off-site. Edge AI gateways can run large language and vision-language models such as Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma and LLaVA locally. The announcement is the latest from Quectel, which says it has a worldwide team of over 10,000 professionals and offers cellular, GNSS, satellite, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth modules. The company also offers high-performance antennas, value-added services and turnkey offerings including ODM services and system integration.

The SP900BF-AP has completed key technical validation, and engineering samples are now available to selected customers for solution evaluation and joint development. Quectel says attendees at Electronica can find the module and its IoT portfolio on stand C2.601 at the show. The articles do not say when the module will reach general commercial availability or when Ubuntu and Yocto Linux support will be completed. They also do not give pricing or name the customers receiving engineering samples.

stories.Headline: Lafayette City Council rejects proposed new downtown AI bar - KATC
stories.Summary:
Lafayette City Council members voted late on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, to reject a proposed high-tech bar in downtown Lafayette. The decision came amid concerns about safety in the downtown area. The owner had planned to use artificial intelligence bartenders to staff the club. Entrepreneur Quintin Borel had hoped to open a bar called "Plush" in the former "Bliss" cocktail lounge. He said it would use technology to change the patron experience.

Under the plan, bar-goers would scan a barcode and order a drink from their seats. A machine would make the cocktail, and a server would deliver it to the customer. stories.Headline: Kyndryl Report: AI returns rise as enterprise readiness falls
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl, the New York-listed enterprise technology services provider, released its third annual Readiness Report on November 10, 2026. The findings point to a widening divide between the returns organizations are seeing from AI and their readiness to manage the risks that come with it. Some 64% of leaders report positive returns on AI investments, up 10 points from 2025. Average readiness across external risks, however, fell seven points to 24%.

The report draws on the attitudes and actions of 3,700 senior business leaders across 21 countries, including 200 in India. The steepest declines in readiness were for cyber threats and competitive disruption. Just 26% of firms said they were completely ready for cyberattacks, a drop of 11 points, even though three in four leaders say AI helps them identify threats faster. Readiness for competitive disruption from outside leaders' own industries fell 10 points to 23%.

On adoption, 49% of organizations describe themselves as still experimenting, down 13 points from 2025, and 48% substantially changed their AI strategies this year. About a quarter, 24%, saw an AI investment fail, and 21% canceled a major AI initiative. The workforce side lags, with just 27% having formally updated roles and responsibilities around AI and 29% having fully implemented change management. Organizations that have done both are 28 points more likely to be completely ready for their AI implementation and 8 points more likely to report positive returns.

Infrastructure shows a similar gap. Upgrading IT infrastructure was again the top action leaders are taking to mitigate external risks, for the third year running, and 71% rate their estate as mostly or fully modernized. Yet 66% of CIOs believe their technology foundations need significant re-architecture before they can support AI at scale. On digital sovereignty, 68% say solutions offering full operational control are worth a premium of 10% or more, and 60% say greater control is worth slower deployment of advanced capabilities, although leaders in the European Union are slightly less likely than those elsewhere to have taken sovereignty-related actions.

Martin Schroeter, Kyndryl's chairman and CEO, said organizations are now focused on making early AI returns sustainable. He described a new kind of readiness gap, in which AI ambitions are moving faster than the systems needed to support them. He added that the bar for readiness keeps moving as AI becomes more integrated in enterprises. In his view, focusing on people, technology and governance can help organizations win with AI and keep the ability to adapt.

The report gives examples of how AI is pressing on established business models. Retailers are weighing how to benefit from AI shopping assistants without forfeiting direct customer relationships. Software companies face questions about SaaS models as AI rebalances the build-versus-buy equation, and financial institutions are challenged by emerging lending models. These pressures come as AI agents and other new technologies are deployed to erode established industry boundaries.

The Indian findings differ in places from the global picture. There, 60% of leaders report positive returns, up three points, while average readiness fell eight points to 27%. Some 85% of Indian organizations deploy AI in workflows beyond pilots, and 80% use AI agents to automate work that once required coordination across multiple teams or systems. Even so, 70% have more pilots than they can realistically scale, 58% say innovation often stalls after proof of concept, and 31% have experienced an AI investment failure.

Indian leaders reported further organizational friction, with 37% noting disagreement between the CHRO and the CTO or CIO on AI strategy. Complete readiness for cyberattacks stands at 35% among Indian organizations, down 10 points. As elsewhere, upgrading IT infrastructure is their top risk-mitigation action, and 71% rate their infrastructure as mostly or fully modernized. Yet 59% of Indian leaders say significant re-architecture is required to support AI at scale.

stories.Headline: New Report: The Impact of AI on Student Safety and Learning Needs Strong Guardrails and Support for Educators - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
A new Texas 2036 report, titled "In Ctrl of AI in Schools," was released on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, examining how artificial intelligence affects Texas students. The report argues that AI's effects depend on the decisions people make around it, and that its benefits appear when tools include safeguards, operate under clear guidance, and remain under an educator's control in instruction. The findings come as AI use in Texas schools is outpacing the rules governing it. The report was released as Texas lawmakers begin filing legislation for the 2027 session.

A fall 2025 survey of Texas school and district leaders, conducted by the University of Texas at Austin and the Texas Association of School Administrators, found that 86% said teachers were using AI and 61% reported student use. Only 29% of those leaders reported a district policy governing student AI use, and just 20% had one for teachers and staff. The report offers insights meant to help the state give schools and teachers the resources they need to keep pace with AI developments. Its author, Renzo Soto, deputy director of education and workforce policy at Texas 2036, said the early research does not show AI is simply good or bad for students. Soto said that school leaders and teachers being in control of AI is what makes it a resource rather than a risk.

The report reviews mixed research on AI and learning, in which some studies find real gains, others find real harms, and many find both. According to the report, the difference often depends on how tools are designed, how teachers guide their use, and whether students are equipped to think critically and independently. Three laws passed in Texas in 2025 established a foundation for responsible AI governance, including requirements affecting public school districts, but those standards have not yet been turned into consistent, classroom-specific guidance. The report finds that 42 states have issued some form of statewide AI guidance or model policies for schools, while Texas is among the eight that have not.

Building on Texas 2036's recently released legislative agenda, the report sets four priorities for responsible AI use in K–12 education. The first is establishing statewide guidance that gives every school district a common, evidence-based foundation built on laws already enacted by the Legislature. The second is putting student safety first by ensuring AI tools meet appropriate standards for data privacy, security and educational effectiveness before reaching Texas classrooms. The third is equipping teachers with training and resources to recognize AI's risks, understand its limitations, and make informed decisions about its classroom use. The fourth is preparing students through age-appropriate AI literacy that emphasizes critical thinking, responsible use and independent learning.

The report also cites Texas 2036's 10th Texas Voter Poll, in which nearly 85% of Texas voters said protecting student data and privacy is extremely or very important if schools use AI. More than three-quarters prioritized safety and quality standards for AI tools, and 71% said teaching students to use AI responsibly and ethically is important. Mary Lynn Pruneda, director of education and workforce policy at Texas 2036, said parents should be able to trust that classroom technology is safe, protects privacy and helps students learn. She said safety and effectiveness must be the starting point rather than an afterthought. The report does not advocate putting AI in every classroom or banning it entirely, instead calling for a research-based approach that supports teachers' professional judgment.

Soto said AI has not changed what works for students, namely a strong teacher who supports them and builds a solid academic foundation, and that the state has an important role in providing guardrails and resources for teachers. The report is the first installment of Texas 2036's research on AI in K–12 education. A second report will analyze policies, guidance and resources from other states to help Texas build a statewide model policy that prioritizes student safety and learning. The articles do not say when that second report will be released or whether any of the four priorities will become law.

stories.Headline: Meta, TikTok join Google to push back on Indonesia’s planned AI copyright law revisions
stories.Summary:
Meta and TikTok joined Google on Wednesday, November 11, in pushing back against proposed revisions to Indonesia's copyright law at a parliamentary hearing in Jakarta. The revisions would require digital platforms to pay publishers for displaying news content, and they would also set rules for artificial intelligence. If the bill is passed, Indonesia could become the first country in Southeast Asia to incorporate AI in its copyright law. Governments around the world are grappling with the impact of the technology on copyright rules, including the use of human-created work to train AI models. Reuters first reported the planned revisions exclusively in July, citing a draft of the bill, and Stanley Widianto reported this latest development.

The articles describe two requirements in the proposed bill, which would oblige digital platforms to pay publishers for displaying news content and would set rules for AI within copyright law. The pushback from the companies concerns compensation for showing links to news content from publishers, which Google says would harm access. TikTok raised a separate point, saying disclosure requirements should not apply where AI is used only in an assistive capacity. It argued that such disclosure should not cover cases where AI is not used to fully create content. Meta's concern focuses on readership traffic, advertising and subscription revenue, while TikTok asked lawmakers to keep safe-harbour protections in place.

Agung Pamungkas, Google's Indonesia government affairs and public policy manager, told the parliamentary hearing that requiring tech platforms to pay compensation for showing news links would limit Indonesians' access to news. Berni Moestafa, Meta's public policy head in Indonesia, said that requiring platforms to pay compensation meant news publishers could lose readership traffic, along with potential advertising and subscription revenue. Berni added that directing readers to an article is different from reproducing or republishing the article itself. Separately, Noudhy Valdryno, TikTok's head of public policy in Indonesia, told lawmakers that disclosure requirements should not apply where AI is used only in an assistive capacity rather than to fully create content. Noudhy also urged lawmakers to preserve safe-harbour protections, saying platforms cannot reliably determine copyright ownership or licences.

Those who spoke at the hearing were representatives of three large digital platforms, Google, Meta and TikTok, and each addressed a different part of the proposed revisions. Publishers are directly affected, since the bill would require platforms to pay them for displaying news content. Meta warned that publishers themselves could lose readership traffic as well as potential advertising and subscription revenue. Google warned that Indonesians' access to news would be limited if platforms had to pay compensation for showing links to publishers' news content. TikTok's comments touched on how platforms treat content that uses AI only to assist, and on their ability to determine copyright ownership and licences.

The articles supply limited background on the bill, which Reuters learned of in July through a draft it cited when reporting the planned revisions exclusively. The proposed changes to Indonesia's copyright law would require digital platforms to pay publishers for displaying news content and set rules for AI. If passed, the bill would make Indonesia the first country in Southeast Asia to bring AI into its copyright law. This comes as governments globally grapple with how the technology affects copyright rules, including the use of work created by humans to train AI models. Meta's Berni drew a distinction between directing readers to an article and reproducing or republishing it, which frames the argument the companies made on Wednesday.

The articles do not say when, or whether, the parliamentary hearing will lead to a vote on the proposed revisions. What they do establish is that the bill, if passed, could make Indonesia the first country in Southeast Asia to incorporate AI in its copyright law. They give no timetable for lawmakers to finalise the text, and no indication of whether the draft will change in response to the objections raised. It also remains open whether lawmakers will accept TikTok's request to preserve safe-harbour protections or to exempt assistive uses of AI from disclosure requirements. The articles do not say how Indonesian lawmakers or publishers responded to the companies' arguments at the hearing.

stories.Headline: Rackspace and Together AI Announce Strategic Agreement to Support Enterprise AI Inference
stories.Summary:
Rackspace, a company that operates enterprise AI infrastructure, has signed two customer agreements for compute capacity, with the first announced on November 10, 2026. The first agreement is a multi-year AI infrastructure deal with Together AI, which describes itself as an AI Native Cloud. Under it, Rackspace expects to provide and operate dedicated NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 infrastructure connected with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking for Together AI inference workloads. Deployment is planned for 2027, subject to certain conditions. The companies also entered into a separate, non-binding letter of intent to explore a joint go-to-market approach for enterprise-focused AI solutions.

Rackspace will also operate the associated power, liquid cooling, networking and storage for that dedicated infrastructure. The planned deployment will sit in a purpose-built, liquid-cooled facility, supported by NVIDIA networking. The second contract is with Blacksmith, an infrastructure platform for building and testing code, under another multi-year agreement. Rackspace will provide Blacksmith with dedicated compute powered by AMD Epyc CPUs, along with storage, totaling approximately 2MW of capacity in Northern Virginia. Deployment for Blacksmith will begin in early 2027, at a data center Rackspace operates in Ashburn, Virginia.

Gajen Kandiah, CEO of Rackspace, said that enterprise AI requires more than access to compute, and that success depends on bringing compute into production and operating it reliably. He said Rackspace brings more than 25 years of experience operating complex enterprise environments. Vipul Ved Prakash, founder and CEO of Together AI, said that scaling in the enterprise requires infrastructure that can grow with its ambitions. Aditya "JP" Jayaprakash, co-founder and CEO of Blacksmith, said that AI is making it easier to write code, but testing and shipping those changes is becoming the bottleneck. Raj Mirpuri, Vice President of Global AI Clouds and Infrastructure Ecosystem at NVIDIA, said enterprises need infrastructure that turns AI advances into services they can deploy at scale.

Together AI's inference platform will receive the dedicated infrastructure, and Together AI expects to provide the managed cloud platform operating on it. That platform will include access to open source models, inference optimizations and developer tools. Enterprise customers requiring greater control, compliance and data sovereignty are the audience the companies said they intend to explore jointly serving. Blacksmith's developers will receive the dedicated compute for building and testing code. Rackspace's stated goal is to become the operator of the full enterprise AI stack, serving customers in regulated, production environments.

Rackspace, listed on NASDAQ as RXT, has an existing agreement with AMD to deploy 30MW of dedicated AMD compute across its data centers through 2028. Effective November 6, 2026, Rackspace entered into a share purchase agreement with an investor group led by Voss Capital, LP, for an aggregate $66 million private placement of common stock. Rackspace expects to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, working capital, capital expenditures and growth capital, including GPU-related initiatives. Together AI, founded in 2022, says it powers over two million developers. Rackspace's approach aims to align capacity with expected customer demand and the useful life of the hardware.

Rackspace expects to seek separate financing to buy the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems for Together AI and is in active discussions with potential lenders. As of the release date, no definitive GPU financing commitment had been obtained, and there is no assurance one will be obtained on acceptable terms or at all. Rackspace's obligations to proceed with the deployment are subject to a financing condition and other conditions in a definitive agreement. The non-binding letter of intent would require further agreement before any joint offerings are made. The articles do not say how much capacity Rackspace is providing to Together AI or which data center will host it.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave targets 2028 profitability as AI demand surges
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that it expects to become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028. The AI cloud company made the statement as it sought to reassure investors that strong demand and customer commitments can support its debt-fuelled expansion. Shares of the Nvidia-backed company rose about 5 per cent in extended trading after the announcement. The stock had crashed more than 40 per cent in the past month as the firm became the focal point of growing AI bubble fears. Investors were also worried about heavy borrowing for data centres amid rising interest rates and the pace of returns on massive investments.

CoreWeave said it would not tap unsecured debt markets at current yields and had enough cash flow from existing customer commitments to repay current debt and additional borrowing. The company had about US$46.9 billion in total debt as of the end of September, and it expects to raise less than US$5 billion in additional capital through 2027. Its CEO Mike Intrator said the company had US$9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits that will flow in over the next three months. CoreWeave's revenue backlog stood at US$132.5 billion at September-end, up from US$104 billion at the end of June. Its quarterly capital spending rose to US$14.5 billion from US$9.4 billion in the prior quarter.

Intrator said in a statement that customer contracts come first and investment follows, so lenders have something concrete to lend against. He added that customers typically help fund the buildout. CoreWeave said it does not see any material risks to its data-centre buildout from a potential shift in the regulatory landscape after the Democrats' sweeping win in the US midterms. Intrator told Reuters that he expects more scrutiny on how data centres are built and how resources are used. He said he does not think this will materially change how the company builds its infrastructure or distort the costs of the buildout.

Intrator said there will be a pacing issue, as companies need to be more transparent and work through the process with communities, which he expects to be prevalent across the industry. He also said CoreWeave will not ramp up its international expansion plans because of the election results, noting the strategy has been worked on for a year and a half. Public backlash has been growing in the US around data centres' impact on local resources, including water and power. Among CoreWeave's customers are Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic. Earlier on the same day, Anthropic kicked off a roadshow for its share sale at a lower target valuation than earlier estimates.

CoreWeave has never turned a profit, according to data compiled by LSEG, and its shares had also been hit by a broader crisis of confidence in the AI trade. Recent earnings reports from hyperscalers hinted at delays in data-centre projects and a slower ramp in spending. The company said it is largely sold out of capacity through the next year, with about ten times as much demand as available capacity. Its third-quarter revenue surged nearly 170 per cent to US$3.66 billion, beating estimates of US$3.55 billion. Its per-share loss of 95 cents was smaller than the US$1.16 loss analysts had estimated, according to LSEG.

CoreWeave now expects 2026 revenue of between US$13 billion and US$13.3 billion, up from the earlier range of US$12.4 billion to US$13.2 billion. It also raised the lower end of its annual spending target by US$2 billion, now projecting spending of US$37 billion to US$39 billion. The articles do not say when the company will report its results for the coming quarters. They also do not say how the regulatory environment will develop after the midterm elections. Whether the company's expected 2028 profitability will be achieved is not addressed beyond its own projection.

stories.Headline: CoDE: A Patient Cohort-Based Study of Evidence Coverage and Support in Diagnostic Explanations Generated by Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
AI decision models are a newer category of AI systems built to return a bounded, structured answer rather than free-form text. The application supplies an input and a fixed set of permitted answers, and the model returns a selected label, a probability or a score, usually with a confidence value. One example cited in the coverage scores a support ticket against billing, shipping and returns, selecting billing and giving a probability for each option, so the calling code never has to pull a label out of prose. Several of these models compute their scores in a single pass rather than generating output one token at a time, and many accept new questions and answer options at call time.

The articles describe this as a response to the fact that most business processes exist to make judgments rather than produce content, such as deciding whether a claim needs more evidence or whether an application should be approved, reviewed or denied. In September, TypeSafe AI introduced a model called Jev, which it positions as a fast, intuitive System One model. Vercel reported that Jev became the fastest-adopted model in its AI Gateway's history, reaching more than twice as many paid teams in its first 24 hours as any previous launch. Benchmarks cited by Diplo put Jev's response times at 70 to 500 milliseconds, compared with 3 to 329 seconds for frontier large language models in the same tests. Within weeks, AWS, OpenAI, Liquid AI, Cloudflare and Microsoft had also brought decision models to their platforms.

Coforge's Momentuum blue unit compared four decision architectures across customer support routing and insurance underwriting, and in the underwriting benchmark Jev matched all eight rule-derived business outcomes, outperforming the larger frontier models tested. The more telling finding concerned failures: in one scenario a model approved an application despite missing claims history, and only a downstream control caught the error, so auditing intermediate decisions was what exposed the flaw. Coforge concludes that enterprise AI will increasingly divide work among generative models for language, reasoning models for synthesis, decision models for structured choices and governance layers for oversight. Researchers Edona Elshan, Muhammed-Faith Kaya and Dominik Siemon, writing in Group Decision and Negotiation in 2026, trace this trend from early rule-based systems through to today's collaborative architectures.

The articles also flag limits. jnaapti warns that a wrong answer can still be well formed, that a confidence value is not automatically the probability of being correct, and that thresholds should be tested on an organisation's own labelled data rather than copied between providers. Diplo says most AI rules focus on text, image and code generators, leaving no clear category for embedded engines that output only labels and numbers, and it argues that procurement guidance should distinguish conversational AI from decision AI. The articles expect decision models to sit beside large language models rather than replace them, handling high-volume, low-latency judgments while generative systems take on explanation and open-ended reasoning.

stories.Headline: U.S. finalizing rule to block China’s remote AI chip access- The Information
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Commerce Department is preparing to finalize a rule that would stop Chinese artificial intelligence companies from remotely using advanced AI chips through data centers in other countries, according to a report from The Information on Wednesday. The report cited two people familiar with the matter. The rule could be announced this month. It would expand existing semiconductor controls from the department's Bureau of Industry and Security.

The expanded controls would reach seven additional countries, including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. The measure is aimed at blocking remote access and chip smuggling into China. The Commerce Department is consulting with other government agencies before the rule can be finalized. Earlier on Wednesday, Axios reported that President Donald Trump had pushed for tighter export controls to curb illegal chip smuggling, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had opposed the measure.

The rule comes amid a growing controversy over Nvidia's potential links to China after its CEO, Jensen Huang, admitted to an affair with a suspected Beijing spy. Chinese internet companies including Tencent, Alibaba and Bytedance have signed offshore data center agreements that give them access to Nvidia's top chips for training their artificial intelligence models. Those arrangements are drawing more scrutiny both abroad and at home, particularly as Beijing pushes companies to use more domestic chips. Shares of Alibaba and Tencent fell after the report.
