stories.Headline: Google DeepMind Releases AlphaGenome 2 for Cell-Type-Specific Variant Effects
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, a DNA model that predicts how genetic variants affect specific cell types, and it is available through an API for non-commercial research. The model is the successor to AlphaGenome, which was released last year, and it reads a 1 Mb DNA window along with a target cell state. Its predecessor averaged across bulk tissues, while the new model resolves closely related cell types and adapts to unseen single-cell datasets without fine-tuning. The company said in a blog post published Wednesday that the model offers a much finer-grained view than broader models. Researchers at Google DeepMind described the work as a way to unravel how changes in DNA affect different cells, which could help explain disease causes.

The model takes a 1,048,576 base pair human or mouse DNA window as input and is hosted only through the API for now. It was trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues, and training used 2048 TPU v4 chips. Its conditioning uses a 256-dimensional embedding that modulates activations through FiLM layers in the encoder, transformer and decoder. Researchers can pass raw single-cell counts and receive a condition embedding, with the documentation allowing up to 256 cells per call. Model weights will be released upon final publication, and the model is limited to non-commercial use.

Google DeepMind says the model turns static cell atlases into a predictive engine for human genetics, and that it identifies nearly twice as many variants that change gene expression than its previous model. Adam Gayoso, a research scientist at Google DeepMind involved in the project, described the breakthrough as tying human genetic variation to cellular context. The company also said the model can identify gaps in experimental data, which could help scientists decide what to investigate next in the lab. The article frames the work as potentially opening paths to treatment for disease, without describing any treatment already produced.

Individual cells in the human body carry the same DNA, yet heart muscle cells, skin cells and immune cells switch different genes on and off. Because of this, the same genetic variant can have very different effects depending on cell type and state. On the TenK10K single-cell eQTL benchmark across 28 immune cell types, AlphaGenome 2 recovered 30% of causal variants at 90% precision, versus 16% for the fine-tuned predecessor. Direction-of-effect recall rose from 23% to 43% on the same benchmark. The predecessor averaged across bulk tissues, so it could miss effects that appear only in specific cells.

The next steps are not fully set out in the articles, and they leave open when the final model weights will be published and under what terms. The articles also do not say whether non-commercial access will ever extend to commercial drug development. They do not describe any clinical trials or treatments that have resulted from the model. How well the model performs in real patients rather than benchmark datasets is not addressed, and the articles report only limited accuracy for sign prediction outside accessible chromatin.

stories.Headline: Microsoft Researchers Show AI Agents Can Be Backdoored by Editing Fewer Than 10 Neurons
stories.Summary:
Microsoft researchers have shown that an AI model can be given a hidden backdoor by editing fewer than 10 of its rarely used neurons, without retraining the model. When a chosen trigger appears, the model outputs an attacker's command, which an agent using that model would run with the agent's own permissions. The attacker must be able to change the model's weights, and the researchers published the research this week. Microsoft says it has not seen any threat actors use the technique. The company has also published guidance on defending against it.

The method, which the researchers call Lazarus, edits neurons that rarely fire and barely affect the model's answers. Each edited neuron is set to fire only when a trigger string appears, either in a user's request or later in a tool's output. Each edited neuron forces one token of the command into the output, so a command needs about one neuron per token. The new settings are calculated directly and can then be tuned with a few hundred training steps on those neurons alone, leaving the rest of the model file and code unchanged. Microsoft describes the trigger as potentially as mundane as a date change, such as the clock passing midnight into 2027.

In a walkthrough posted on X, a backdoored Nemotron-Terminal-8B model with 10 edited neurons worked normally for three turns while fixing a Node.js server. When the server returned a connection error, the model output a command to download and run a remote script, which ran as root inside the test container. On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the team edited and tuned seven of the more than 12,000 neurons in the model's last feed-forward layer, using 23 example sessions. The edited model output the command in at least 98.8% of test sessions containing the trigger and in none of the trigger-free sessions checked. With the tuned version, success rates on Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT ranged from 51% to 99.5%, and the Qwen model used six neurons.

Anyone who can change a model's checkpoint, the file that stores its weights, before deployment could plant the backdoor, including an insider, an attacker with a stolen account or access to a build pipeline, or whoever publishes a modified model on a public hub. Planting it does not require the computing power of full training. The researchers credit Claude Code, running the Opus 4.5 model, with finding the core idea and say coding agents can make such attacks easier to build. Microsoft's blog describes the work as starting in March as a quick experiment that became a months-long study. Earlier, in an October 6 proof of concept, ProjectDiscovery researchers fine-tuned an open Qwen model to react to a trigger phrase, whereas Lazarus edits a few neurons directly.

Microsoft says Foundry customers are protected from these attacks for models from trusted labs, because models are tied to their original publishers and run inside separately scanned containers. The remaining risk, the company says, is that a trusted provider is itself compromised. Microsoft is working with internal AI security teams to turn its detection techniques into a red-teaming harness and is exploring weight scanning with frontier agents as an additional signal for open-weight models. It also plans to have models signed with verifiable provenance and tamper-proof audits. The researchers say reliable detection requires comparing a checkpoint with its original weights, and that no scan can prove a model is safe.

stories.Headline: Helsing Unveils AI Targeting Software as Europe’s Answer to Palantir’s Maven
stories.Summary:
Helsing, a Munich-based defense company, is presenting new AI targeting software in Berlin on Wednesday, 11 November, and pitching it as a European alternative to American suppliers. The company has not publicly named the product ahead of the event. Its invitation said it was crucial to conduct precise reconnaissance, make sound decisions under uncertainty, and act on the battlefield with autonomy and without dependencies, from Europe and for Europe. The presentation comes as Germany's armed forces have set aside Palantir's Maven Smart System for now.

The Bundeswehr plans to field its own AI targeting system from 2027, with full rollout in 2028. Helsing is positioning its software to fill that gap. Its earlier products include the HX-2 strike drone, supplied to Ukraine, the CA-1 Europa uncrewed combat aircraft, and the Altra software that combines sensor data for reconnaissance and strike missions. Earlier this month, the company handed Germany the source code for its future combat drone software, giving the state direct control over a key piece of military code.

Palantir, which builds Maven, rejects the idea that customers could be cut off. The company says buyers keep full operational control of the software and that it has no remote kill switch. European concern about dependence on Washington has nonetheless grown, with President Donald Trump repeatedly threatening to pull the United States out of NATO. Last month, speed limits on Ukraine's Starlink terminals hampered Kyiv's efforts to intercept Russian drones, and in June the Trump administration moved to block non-US residents from Anthropic's most advanced models before lifting the restriction later that month.

The war in Ukraine has made AI decision tools a practical requirement, since drones, satellites and ground sensors produce more data than analysts can sort in time. Maven already runs inside NATO structures and several national forces, so any newcomer must prove itself in exercises and fit into existing command systems. Helsing's advantage is that it already supplies combat drones to the Bundeswehr, which gives it an existing foothold. Helsing has not said how its targeting software will be tested or when German forces might adopt it.

stories.Headline: Froncort.AI Gets $2.3M From Google.org to Expand AI-Based Disease Screening in India
stories.Summary:
Froncort.AI, a Pune-based healthcare AI company, has received $2.3 million in funding from Google.org to expand its AI-based disease screening platform in India. The articles report the funding was announced on November 10, 2026, and the startup is developing an offline, local-language application for frontline health workers. The application is meant to help them identify disease hotspots and plan household screenings. The new support is aimed at a mobile product called mAI-NETRA, which the company says will guide field teams toward high-risk areas. The articles frame the announcement as the expansion of an existing platform rather than a new product launch.

The $2.3 million will fund development of mAI-NETRA, a mobile version of the AI-NETRA platform aimed at tuberculosis and other infectious diseases. The company will also receive $200,000 in Google Cloud credits and pro bono technical expertise from Google. The application will combine government health programme data with Google's Earth AI models and local indicators such as settlement density, land use, rainfall and flooding. It identifies high-risk areas within 300-metre zones and turns them into ranked work paths, household clusters and routes for health workers. Government health programme data will remain stored and processed locally in India, and the application will work offline in local languages.

Dr Ujjwal Rao, founder and CEO of Froncort.AI, said that the world does not lack experts but lacks their reach. He said AI-NETRA puts that expertise in the hands of health workers, telling them where to go, whom to screen and when. Froncort.AI is one of 15 recipients selected for Google.org's Impact Challenge: AI for Government Innovation. The company was founded in 2024 by physician-scientist Dr Ujjwal Rao, according to Inc42. Google.org's latest support follows its earlier backing for the company's AI-NETRA validation study.

The primary beneficiaries are frontline health workers, who will receive screening plans on their phones, and the people in high-burden districts they will screen. The company plans to deploy the application across up to eight high-burden districts in three Indian states, covering two to three million people. The 2026 Pune pilot report states that AI-guided teams screened 66,095 people and identified 10 confirmed pulmonary TB cases, against 1,77,322 people and nine cases under standard screening. The company reports the cost per confirmed case fell from about $29,000 to $10,000, and 92% of participating frontline workers reported a lower workload. Inc42 adds that AI deployment in India's public healthcare is picking up, with the government citing a 27% decline in adverse TB outcomes and over 4,500 outbreak alerts.

The background the articles give shows that the company's validation study was conducted with Maharashtra's state TB programme. In that study, AI-guided teams found a similar number of confirmed TB cases while screening two-thirds fewer people than routine methods. The new funding will extend the platform to six diseases: TB, leprosy, malaria, dengue, cholera and leptospirosis. Inc42 notes that the startup also operates RegDoc, a regulatory technology platform for clinical research organisations, pharmaceutical companies and medical device manufacturers. Inc42 further reports that AI funding in India grew 235% year-on-year in Q3 2026, while total deals rose 35% to 35 from 26 in Q3 2025.

The company plans to deploy the platform and have its performance independently monitored against five targets, including finding at least 20% more cases and reducing people screened per case by more than 50%. It also plans to publish mAI-NETRA as an open-source blueprint so other governments can adapt it for their public health programmes. The articles do not say when the deployment will begin or when the independent monitoring results will be published. They also do not state how the five targets will be measured, or whether the 2026 Pune pilot figures will be independently verified.

stories.Headline: AI-assisted reverse engineering challenges proprietary software
stories.Summary:
AI-assisted reverse engineering is making it easier for developers to inspect software and infer how it works, and industry experts say this trend poses new challenges for proprietary software and intellectual property protection. Nishant Tiwari, a software engineer at PayPal and a tech content creator with over 2.8 million Instagram followers, used an AI-assisted workflow to inspect Uber's web application and examine its pricing. His analysis of Uber's client-side code identified scripts that appeared to access battery status and other device information, including browser and hardware attributes. He tested the same ride across four phones, three Android devices and an iPhone, repeating the experiment five to six times, and found a correlation between battery levels and fares. Tools such as Reverse Engineering Anything (REA), an open-source GitHub project created by GitHub user morluto, enabled these findings by connecting AI agents to reverse-engineering tools.

The project has over 447,000 stars on GitHub, up from about 10,000 in early October, and ranks among the platform's top five most-starred repositories. Reverse engineering involves examining a finished software product to understand how it works, such as inspecting a compiled binary, using a debugger, or analysing how an application responds to different inputs. Security researcher Himanshu Anand said the process traditionally required considerable technical expertise, including interpreting assembly instructions. He said large language models have lowered that barrier and estimated that a task that previously took a month could now take "one or two hours" with AI assistance. For enterprises, the question is how much of a product's functionality customers can reconstruct from the code and behaviour available to them.

AI-assisted analysis can help recreate individual features, particularly when their behaviour is visible through a client application, but reconstructing an entire product is limited when core processing happens on remote servers. Anand pointed to services such as Gmail, where users can only conduct black-box testing, which he described as "very limited." Abhishek Agarwal, President of Judge India and Global Delivery at The Judge Group, said AI can help developers identify relevant functions and reduce time spent on false leads, but much of a product's behaviour may depend on a private service. He noted that a recreated feature may also lack the original product's updates and support, which customers pay for alongside the software. Agarwal suggested comparing conventional reverse engineering with AI-assisted analysis under similar conditions, with two engineering teams given the same access and assessed for reliability and human effort.

Bharadwaj Jaishankar-Bharadwaj, Partner at CMS INDUSLAW, said copyright protects software code as a literary work and that there is no copyright in an idea, only in its expression. Shantanu Sahay, Partner in Litigation at Anand & Anand, said recreating a feature does not automatically infringe copyright, since the legal question depends on what has been copied and whether those elements are protected. Anand dismissed concerns that AI tools will end proprietary software, comparing it to saying Microsoft is dead because of open source. Under Section 52(1)(ac) of India's Copyright Act, the observation, study, or testing of a computer program is permitted to determine its underlying ideas and principles while performing acts necessary for the functions for which it was supplied. Section 52(1)(ab) covers acts necessary to obtain information essential for interoperability of an independently created program, subject to conditions including lawful possession and the information not being otherwise readily available.

These provisions do not give a blanket permission to copy or commercially reproduce software, and Sahay noted that licence and non-disclosure agreements can also restrict decompilation. Agarwal said companies should treat client applications and binaries as inspectable rather than relying on unpublished source code. Obfuscation and anti-tampering measures can make analysis harder but may only delay it. He recommended moving core business logic away from distributed clients where practical, removing secrets from software builds, tightening API boundaries, monitoring for repeated probing, and reviewing binaries, packages, and front ends at each release. He also advised changing the design assumption to consider what happens when an AI agent can inspect a product repeatedly and cheaply.

stories.Headline: Cloud native developer population hits 21.2 million globally
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation and the research firm SlashData published a new report showing that the global cloud native developer population reached 21.2 million in the third quarter of 2026. TechGig covered the findings on November 11, 2026, while The New Stack ran its own piece the day before, on November 10, 2026. That figure represents roughly 41 per cent of all developers worldwide, according to the report. The report also found that 75 per cent of cloud native developers now use AI coding tools. The New Stack headlined its coverage with that statistic and brought in Jonathan Bryce to explain the reasons behind it.

The 21.2 million total compares with 15.6 million a year earlier and 19.9 million in the first quarter of 2026. On AI use, 75 per cent of cloud native developers use AI coding tools, against 55 per cent of non-cloud native developers. Meanwhile, 67 per cent of cloud native developers are integrating AI into their services, while only 38 per cent of their non-cloud native counterparts do the same. Among developers who integrate AI into their services, 49 per cent reported having agentic systems in production. In North America, 21 per cent of cloud native developers use AI to draft code before reviewing it, while 12 per cent use autonomous agents for coding tasks.

The report comes from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData, and Liam Bollmann-Dodd, a principal market research consultant at SlashData, commented on its meaning. He stated that cloud native maturity is becoming an important indicator of how actively developers engage with AI. The New Stack presented the findings alongside an explanation from Jonathan Bryce of why so many cloud native developers ship code with AI. The portion of that article available here does not include Bryce's explanation itself, only its headline framing. TechGig, for its part, summarized the report's findings in a short piece under its Software and DevOps section.

The report found that platform engineering is becoming standard practice, with 93 per cent of developers now working at organisations that use some form of DevOps standardisation or internal developer platform. That share has risen from 77 per cent in the third quarter of 2025, a gain of 16 percentage points. Developers who have not yet added AI functionality named cost, data privacy, and security as their primary concerns. Backend developers show specific patterns of technology use, with 40 per cent using API gateways and 30 per cent using microservices. A further 21 per cent of backend developers use observability tools, and 19 per cent use Kubernetes.

The articles give a little history for the numbers. The cloud native developer population stood at 15.6 million a year before the latest measurement, so the figure has grown substantially over twelve months. It had already reached 19.9 million in the first quarter of 2026, which means roughly 1.3 million developers were added between the first and third quarters. The share of developers working in organisations with DevOps standardisation or internal platforms was 77 per cent in the third quarter of 2025. The report's authors, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData, describe the growth as significant compared with the previous year.

The articles do not say when the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData will publish their next report or what the figures will show. The New Stack's page is tagged to KubeCon and CloudNativeCon North America 2026, but the portion provided gives no further detail on that event. Bryce's full reasoning for the high rate of AI coding tool use among cloud native developers is not included in the text available. The articles also do not say how many developers were surveyed or how the global totals were calculated. Nor do they explain how the concerns about cost, data privacy, and security might be addressed for developers who have not yet adopted AI functionality.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA scrutiny, US selloff challenge India's AI cloud boom
stories.Summary:
A selloff in US-listed neocloud companies and growing scrutiny of NVIDIA have raised questions about the financing model behind the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. Investors have been selling shares of US neocloud companies since September, with CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN seeing sharp corrections. The selling intensified through October and into November, as concerns mounted over the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending and the debt these companies have taken on. These developments could affect India's GPU cloud providers, which face questions about debt exposure, customer commitments and GPU depreciation. Political and regulatory resistance to data centre expansion in the US could also slow infrastructure investment.

Neoclouds provide GPU compute to customers that may not have the scale or resources to build their own infrastructure. Their business models are capital-intensive, and NVIDIA has supported the ecosystem through strategic investments and financing arrangements. India is increasingly part of this buildout, serving subsidised compute under the IndiaAI Mission and commercial workloads. The IndiaAI Mission had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026 and approved 237 projects by August, with 93.18 lakh GPU hours sanctioned. Sanctioned hours do not necessarily translate into sustained usage, so Indian neoclouds are betting on commercial customers to justify their spending.

Unlike US peers backed by large hyperscaler customers such as Meta and OpenAI, Indian neoclouds have limited domestic anchor demand. International customers account for 75 to 80 per cent of Yotta's customer base. Yotta plans to spend over $7 billion on AI infrastructure by the end of FY27 and is targeting a $1.5 billion initial public offering. The IndiaAI Mission utilised less than half its FY26 outlay of ₹10,000 crore, which has affected hardware procurement and deployment timelines. Juspay's co-founder and COO Sheetal Lalwani said the company had been told it would wait three to six months to receive GPUs it is buying with its own cash.

NeevCloud said its engagement with NVIDIA covers technical planning, GPU availability and deployment readiness, while procurement and financing are separate arrangements. Narendra Sen, founder of NeevCloud and RackBank Datacenters, said the market correction reinforces the need for discipline in assessing each project's commercial viability. ESDS said it has no direct commercial or financing relationship with NVIDIA and buys systems from Supermicro, Dell, Lenovo and WWT. Piyush Somani, founder of ESDS, said the company commits capital expenditure only after a customer pays at least 35 per cent of the project cost. NVIDIA offered a revenue-sharing and credit-support model to neoclouds globally in July but later paused some deals, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The Government of India has noted that its compute ecosystem relies on globally sourced GPUs, so changes in chip availability, export controls, pricing or allocation could affect deployment schedules and project economics. Lenders and investors are now favouring projects with confirmed customers, predictable revenues and substantial upfront advances. Sen added that older GPUs could face more pricing pressure as newer generations arrive. Closer to home, ESDS closed at about ₹1,147.25 on November 9, against a September 24 high of ₹1,864.35. E2E Networks ended at around ₹490.50, well below its October 14 high of ₹769.

stories.Headline: KAIST Professor Predicts 100 AI Agents in Semiconductor Design
stories.Summary:
The two articles report that Kim Jung-ho, a KAIST professor who first proposed the core concept of HBM, unveiled a research system on November 11, 2026, at the online "TERA AI Agent Day" event. In his keynote, he described a setup in which a single human engineer commands about 100 AI agents to design semiconductors. The system is being developed by KAIST's TERA Lab, which he leads, and the goal is to demonstrate its core functions by the end of 2027. The articles say the system was tested in the design of next-generation HBM and high-bandwidth flash (HBF), and at the event researchers showed the AI producing performance results immediately after being asked.

Under the structure, a human enters only the design goal and the AI splits the work, runs commercial design tools and checks the results. A top-level "super agent" receives the goal in natural language, draws up a work plan, manages memory and access rights, and assigns tasks to specialized agents covering signal, power and thermal analysis before merging their output. Precise calculations such as signal integrity, voltage drop and resonant frequency are left to verified engineering tools, while language models are used only to interpret inputs and choose tools. The engineer keeps approval of critical steps such as tape-out. The articles also say the approach reuses the reasoning ability of existing AI models rather than training new ones, and they describe verification mechanisms intended to catch design errors.

Kim said the industry faces a triple challenge of shorter development cycles, rising design complexity and a shortage of skilled engineers, and he argued for agents that plan their own work and run specialized simulators rather than chatbots that only answer questions. Kim took part in core design and technical verification during HBM development in 2009 and contributed to SK Hynix commercializing the first HBM in December 2013, which is why he is called the "father of HBM." The articles also present TERA Lab's proposed tHBM and tHBF architectures, which place compute chips on top of memory stacks, and a uHBM structure that stacks memory on top of a GPU. The articles frame the work as aimed at industry bottlenecks, though they do not report a timeline beyond the 2027 demonstration target.

stories.Headline: Shopify (SHOP) Earnings And AI Commerce Story Put Valuation Back In Focus
stories.Summary:
Shopify reported its third quarter 2026 earnings, with revenue of US$3.74b and net income of US$462m, and the results have put its valuation back in focus. The company also guided to low-30% revenue growth for the next quarter. Shopify filed an omnibus shelf registration covering equity, debt, warrants and units around the same time. The quarter pointed to a heavier tilt toward merchant solutions and AI-driven commerce tools. The articles frame the story as a question of how the shares are priced after the recent results.

The shelf registration covers equity, debt, warrants and units, giving Shopify the ability to raise capital. A partnership with Meta's Muse agent ties Shop Pay more directly to transaction volume on major social platforms. The company's shares changed hands around US$149, while analyst targets clustered closer to US$177. The stock slipped about 17% over the past month and is down around 5% year to date on a share price basis. Over three years, total shareholder return is up about 120%.

Shopify's share price and guidance are tied to management's own decisions about its platform and AI tools, which the articles describe as the company's strategy. The articles say Shopify kept its core platform simple and reliable, then allowed a large ecosystem of developers and integrations to build around it. Shopify chose to pursue this approach with its merchant solutions and AI commerce tools. The articles do not attribute any specific quoted statement to a named executive. Simply Wall St's valuation commentary cites QuanD, a community investor, who built a fair value estimate on an 8.89% discount rate.

Investors and analysts are weighing the company's results against its valuation, and the articles describe the reaction as mixed. Some of the most optimistic analysts focus on AI as the main swing factor for Shopify's share price. Before the latest release, the highest forecasts assumed revenue growth of about 37.1% a year and earnings of roughly US$5.3b by 2029. Merchants and shareholders are affected by the platform's merchant activity and by any future equity issuance that could dilute ownership.

The articles say that Shopify's stock has been volatile recently, and that earlier in 2026 the company reported strong results and a US$2b buyback. In an earlier quarter, the company's shares were reported down 13.4% after an AI-fueled beat and a strong growth outlook. The articles also describe the company as a default operating system for independent commerce. Simply Wall St's fair value estimate for Shopify is US$210.47 per share, which the articles present as well above the recent close.

The articles do not say when or whether Shopify will issue securities under the shelf registration. They also do not state how the company's guidance will translate into actual fourth quarter results. It is unclear whether merchant activity will slow or whether monetisation of new AI products will meet expectations. The articles leave open whether the gap between the share price and the valuation estimates will close. They do not say how investors will ultimately judge the stock.

stories.Headline: Who would be next CEO at Nvidia? Top engineer and CFO favored as candidates
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board is preparing to oust CEO and founder Jensen Huang, according to a Semafor report published November 11, 2026, with a meeting scheduled for Wednesday evening. Some directors reportedly favor naming Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO if Huang is removed. The move follows media reports that Huang had a second extramarital affair. The company's stock fell more than 8 percent in after-hours trading, reaching a 52-week low.

The board's planned action would end a saga in which Huang admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The company's long-tenured board had already announced a probe, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton, into whether Huang may have shared corporate secrets or endangered US national security. Nvidia has tapped an outside search firm to find a permanent successor, Bloomberg reported. One candidate reportedly under consideration is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who was considered for the Intel CEO job in 2019.

Semafor reported that the board briefed the White House on its planned meeting, according to a senior administration official. Senators Chris Coons and Elizabeth Warren wrote to members of Trump's cabinet asking them to preserve documents related to Nvidia's chip exports to China and to any entities that could divert those chips there. They also asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to preserve records about Huang and his correspondence with President Trump. In their letter, the senators said reports suggest officials at several agencies knew of concerns about Nvidia's relationship with a company called Megaspeed yet did not act to stop the flow of advanced chips.

Nvidia's spokespeople did not immediately comment. The context is that Nvidia supplies many of the most advanced chips used by major cloud companies and has entered billions of dollars in financing deals supporting the AI buildout, which raises the stakes of its leadership change. The articles do not say whether the board will make a final decision on Wednesday or who will ultimately be named CEO. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Foundation models and intelligent agents in chemical engineering: advances, challenges, and perspectives
stories.Summary:
The Perspective "Foundation models and intelligent agents in chemical engineering: advances, challenges, and perspectives," published on 12 November 2026, argues that reliable chemical engineering AI needs three parts working together. These are domain-specific foundation models, agentic orchestration, and validation through physics and simulation. The authors say general-purpose large language models, though increasingly capable of scientific reasoning, often lack the domain grounding, physical consistency, and engineering reliability needed for industrial use. They note that existing studies mostly demonstrate individual components rather than a fully integrated engineering intelligence lifecycle. The piece reviews progress in domain-specific foundation models, agent-based process design and optimization, process safety analysis, and operational decision support.

The authors frame their proposal as a closed loop in which domain-specific models supply knowledge for task-specific reasoning, and multi-agent systems orchestrate complex tasks and use specialized tools. Mechanistic models, engineering constraints, and process simulators then assess feasibility and feed results back for refinement. The Perspective outlines challenges across three dimensions: strengthening domain-specific foundation models, developing coordinated agent platforms for multiscale engineering workflows, and establishing traceable evidence. It also calls for controlled updating mechanisms that separate task-level feedback, offline version updates, and online adaptation. The articles give no further figures, dates, or quantities for these requirements beyond the review's scope.

The Perspective is written by its authors, whose names the supplied text does not give. The source material does not state who holds responsibility for the framework beyond the authors' stated argument. The authors describe the approach as a pathway from conversational chemical engineering models toward reliable, verifiable, and continuously improving engineering intelligence. The supplied text does not include any further statements from the authors.

The Perspective addresses chemical engineering as a field that spans molecules, catalysts, reactors, units, and plants, and is governed by physical laws and strict safety, operability, and reliability requirements. The article states that these requirements are why general-purpose models face limits in industrial deployment. The supplied material contains no reactions from industry, regulators, or affected parties. It also gives no account of who would be affected by these systems.

The reference list in the Perspective cites earlier work on multiscale methodology in chemical engineering, dating to 2003, and on innovation from catalyst to industrial process, dating to 2013. It also cites recent work on large language model agents in chemical process simulation and on chemical-specific models such as ChemLLM and ChemDFM. The supplied text does not describe how the field reached its current state beyond these references. Background on the other article is limited to its own content.

The second article, from InfoWorld dated 12 November 2026, covers Microsoft's AI foundation models, not chemical engineering. It reports that Microsoft's Foundry platform offers access to more than 11,000 models, including models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, and DeepSeek. The piece says Microsoft has begun rolling out its own foundation models under its Microsoft AI (MAI) program, with a focus on lower token cost. The supplied text does not link these developments to the chemical engineering Perspective, and it leaves open how far the framework described in the first article will be adopted or tested in practice.

stories.Headline: Analysis: Is Nvidia too big to fail? Its AI financing web raises the stakes
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board is investigating allegations involving CEO Jensen Huang, and CNBC reports that the company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms that support the AI boom. The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital affair with a company executive and a relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China, while The Wall Street Journal reported the board was preparing to oust him. Nvidia's board has expressed confidence in its CEO, and the company did not respond to a request for comment. Nvidia's stock fell 27% from its October 6 peak through Wednesday's close, and it fell a further 8% in after-hours trading that day.

The company's commitments include a plan to buy up to $36 billion in cloud services from smaller AI companies known as neoclouds, which Nvidia disclosed in July. Nvidia also agreed to a $105 billion phased guarantee for a data center project in Ohio planned by OpenAI and SB Energy, subject to certain conditions, and promised to backstop up to $125 billion of a $500 billion credit program by Wall Street firms. Columbia Business School finance professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estimates the obligations at $400 billion overall. The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are watching how this financing could amplify an AI downturn.

Analysts interviewed by CNBC said a rerun of the 2007-2008 financial crisis is unlikely. Sheila Bair, a former head of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., said Nvidia is not "too big to fail in a bank sense at all," because it is not vulnerable to a sudden loss of confidence and its large equity provides a cushion. She said regulators still need to watch banks' and the wider system's exposure to Nvidia and similar firms, and that "Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event." Van Nieuwerburgh said that "there's a lot of equity in the system right now," though he would not call it a safe system.

The concern centers on circular financing, in which larger firms help customers buy their products. Jason Wu, an assistant director at the International Monetary Fund, said that if the value of Nvidia's chips fell, borrowers might be unable to repay debts, and that "both the economy and financial markets are standing on the same leg." The IMF's October Global Financial Stability report warned about leverage among AI firms and investors. The so-called hyperscalers grew from 1% of bond issuance in the $15 trillion investment-grade debt market to 10% in two years. Neocloud stress is visible in CoreWeave's credit-default spreads, which rose 94% from October 1 to November 5, and in an IREN convertible bond that fell 23% from November 3 to November 5.

Nvidia's troubles have so far separated it from other firms, since most neocloud equity prices recovered this week as Nvidia's shares fell, suggesting investors see the problems as specific to the company. AMD, Broadcom, Intel, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI are all building their own AI chips, which could eventually replace Nvidia's products and cap any fallout. Van Nieuwerburgh said central bankers "are clearly very, very, very anxious about this." Nvidia is scheduled to report earnings on Tuesday, and analysts expect its revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year and roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data.

stories.Headline: China’s graft crackdown sends drugmakers to doctors’ AI apps
stories.Summary:
Drugmakers in China are turning to a new wave of AI assistants built for doctors, after a sweeping graft crackdown made traditional outreach to physicians harder. Companies such as Alibaba Health and JD Health have brought out tools similar to OpenEvidence in 2026, and the article says drugmakers are exploring marketing with app makers or customising platforms for specific diseases. The shift followed stricter measures issued in the summer that govern pharma employees who provide product information to doctors and hospitals. Doctors' use of these tools has grown quickly, rising to 93% of the hundreds surveyed by Alibaba Health, up from around 70% a year earlier.

Alibaba Health is considering a model in which promoted medical research and clinical evidence would appear alongside AI-generated answers on its Hydrion app. Chief technology officer Wang Xiangzhi said the company has not yet begun working with drugmakers on this, though domestic and foreign firms showed strong interest. He argued that if doctors gather on one platform, marketing budgets would move online. PICA Health has built JD Health's Zhiyi assistant into its app, offering drugmakers digital academic promotion and physician education services. Research firm Frost & Sullivan estimates that enterprise spending on digital health marketing in China will grow at a compound annual rate of 27.5% from 2027 to 2030, reaching 274.4 billion yuan (S$53 billion).

The article reports that the China Pharmaceutical Innovation and Research Development Association declined to comment, while Roche said it explores third-party medical AI tools for direct marketing to doctors and hospitals. Bayer said it monitors developments in technology that could help it engage healthcare professionals in a compliant manner. Null Hypothesis CEO Gu Fei said major Chinese and foreign drugmakers had licensed its KnowS tool to build disease-focused academic platforms for physicians, though he declined to name them. The article also cites drugmakers Zhejiang Xianju Pharmaceutical and Xian Shijishengkang Pharmaceutical, which said the rules and hospital visit limits hurt sales. The reporting does not say how regulators will treat promoted content on these platforms.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Joins AFT and UFT's Binding AI Safety Standard
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has signed a legally binding agreement with the American Federation of Teachers and the United Federation of Teachers to establish safety, transparency and privacy protections for its AI products used in K-12 education. The agreement was announced Tuesday, November 10, 2026, by the two unions, and it puts their AI Safety and Privacy Standard for Schools into practice. It automatically covers school districts already using Anthropic's Claude for Teachers. The agreement's 10 provisions address how AI companies handle sensitive school data, communicate with customers and account for risks associated with their technology. Anthropic is the latest company to adopt the standard, following Microsoft, which partnered with the unions in September.

Under the agreement, districts can incorporate the protections into their contracts, which gives them legal recourse if a company fails to meet its obligations. Once incorporated, the provisions become enforceable, allowing a district to seek damages or termination of the agreement for material violations that remain unresolved. Companies generally cannot use student or educator information to develop or refine AI models, apart from a limited security and safety exception, and cannot sell that data or use it to target advertisements. The restrictions cover prompts, uploaded files and generated responses, and they also apply to previously collected data even after the agreement expires. The standard requires human review of high-risk decisions involving AI, prohibits AI companions within its scope, and requires notification of confirmed or reasonably suspected data breaches within 72 hours.

Anthropic and the unions describe the agreement as a major step for AI safety in classrooms, and Anthropic's head of beneficial deployments, Elizabeth Kelly, said it builds trust with teachers, students and school systems. AFT President Randi Weingarten called it a legally binding contract that ensures algorithms can never replace human judgment, relationships or responsibility. UFT President Michael Mulgrew said the agreement continues the unions' work to keep students and their families safe and said he was heartened that Anthropic sees the value of student privacy. Microsoft committed to making the protections available to U.S. school districts beginning November 1. Parent advocates and a policy group offered differing views: psychotherapist Nicole Runyon called it a positive step, while Michael Marinaccio of the Center for Responsible Technology said such agreements are too little, too late.

The unions have argued that existing federal student privacy law, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, was not written specifically to address generative AI. Mulgrew said that ideally the federal government would step in, but since it has not, teachers unions are working to hold AI companies accountable. Claude for Teachers was released July 14 and gives teachers premium Claude tools for free. Anthropic contributed $500,000 to the AFT's National Academy for AI Instruction in July 2025, alongside $10 million from OpenAI and $12.5 million from Microsoft. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services recommended in August that districts evaluate products based on demonstrated educational benefits, but those recommendations are advisory rather than binding.

The agreement applies only to Claude for Teachers, which is designed for educators rather than students, so provisions governing students' direct use of AI do not apply. Student information entered by teachers remains protected, and any future Anthropic educational product offered directly to K-12 students would need to meet the standard. The articles do not say how or whether the protections will be enforced in practice. Anthropic, the AFT and the UFT did not respond to requests for comment from the Daily Caller News Foundation. The articles also do not say whether Anthropic plans to offer student-facing products, and they leave open how the standard will work for districts that do not adopt it.

stories.Headline: Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M
stories.Summary:
Oura, the smart ring maker and health intelligence platform, has agreed to acquire the artificial intelligence health company Counsel Health. The deal was announced on November 10, 2026, in a news release issued on a Tuesday. It is an all-cash transaction worth $625 million, according to reporting on the announcement. Counsel runs a primary care platform built around AI, which pairs conversational medical AI with access to licensed, board-certified physicians. The deal follows Oura's recent postponement of its initial public offering.

Under the agreement, Oura will pay $625 million in cash, and the acquisition is expected to close before the end of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and purchase price adjustments. Approximately 70 Counsel employees will join Oura after the transaction. Counsel co-founder and CEO Dr. Muthu Alagappan will become Oura's chief clinical AI officer. Counsel currently has approximately 50 on-demand physicians supporting its services, and it will keep serving enterprise partners, including health plans, healthcare systems, employers and consumer health organizations. The companies plan to build their combined platform across three areas, preventive care, acute care, and specialty and chronic care, the last covering reproductive health, aging and cardiometabolic conditions.

Oura chief executive Tom Hale said members can now act on what they learn about their physiology, with services ranging from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care and referrals. He described the goal as a new model of care that is more immediate, personalized and proactive. Hale called the deal a major step toward the promise of a 24-7 doctor in your pocket. The company's release said Counsel was founded and built by physicians and AI researchers, and that it combines medical AI with in-house physicians. Oura said members can start from an Oura insight or chat directly with Counsel's medical AI, and conversations can escalate to a board-certified Counsel physician within minutes.

Alagappan explained, in the acquisition announcement, that the partnership is meant to connect continuous health information with clinical expertise. Counsel has stressed that wearable data gives physicians extra context about patients' health patterns between appointments. Oura members are the people most directly affected, since they could gain a closer link between personal health monitoring and medical help. Counsel's enterprise customers are also affected, because those services will remain available to organizations whose members do not own an Oura Ring. The articles caution that wearable measurements do not independently establish medical diagnoses, and that clinical assessments and laboratory testing may still be needed depending on a patient's condition.

The deal builds on an existing partnership that brought Counsel's medical AI service into the Oura app in June 2026, as TechCrunch reported. The Verge reported on November 10 that the acquisition follows that earlier integration of the chatbot. Oura disclosed preliminary fiscal 2026 revenue of approximately $1.75 billion, a 92% increase over the previous fiscal year, along with fourth-quarter revenue of $533 million. That quarter ended September 30, 2026, and revenue rose 153% year over year, with adjusted EBITDA of $87 million, a 16% margin. Oura has more than six million members and was valued at approximately $11 billion after a late-stage funding round in 2025.

The IPO had been scheduled for the final week of September but was postponed despite strong demand, citing market uncertainty. Hale said at the time that the company has the luxury of choosing its moment and aims to deliver an extraordinary IPO for employees and investors. After the deal closes, Counsel's roughly 70 employees will join Oura, and Alagappan will take his new role. The companies are expected to share more as the acquisition progresses and their platforms are integrated. The articles leave open the full availability and pricing of future healthcare features, and they give no new date for the IPO.

stories.Headline: QuickLaunch and Carahsoft Partner to Bring AI-Powered Identity and Integration Platform to the Public Sector and Higher Education Organizations
stories.Summary:
On November 11, 2026, QuickLaunch, a Miami-based identity and integration platform company, and Carahsoft Technology Corp. of Reston, Virginia, announced a new channel partnership. Under the agreement, Carahsoft becomes QuickLaunch's Master Government Aggregator, which gives the Public Sector and Higher Education organizations access to QuickLaunch's offerings. The announcement was distributed through GlobeNewswire and republished by The Manila Times on the same day. The partnership was described as a way to bring AI-powered identity and integration products to government and campus buyers. The articles present it as a commercial distribution arrangement rather than a product launch.

Under the deal, QuickLaunch's Single Sign-On, Multi-Factor Authentication, Identity Lifecycle Management and more than 500 pre-built integrations become available through Carahsoft's reseller partners. Access also runs through four procurement contracts: The Interlocal Purchasing System (TIPS), OMNIA Partners, the E&I Cooperative Services Contract and The Quilt. The platform is offered under TIPS Contract #220105, OMNIA Partners Contract #R240303, E&I Contract #EI00063~2021MA and The Quilt Master Service Agreement Number MSA05012019-F. QuickLaunch is described as trusted by more than 200 institutions and 1.2 million daily users. The company states it holds SOC 2 Type II, HECVAT, TX-RAMP, GLBA and NIST compliance. Interested buyers can contact the Carahsoft team at (844) 214-4790 or through the email address listed in the release.

Raymond Todd Blackwood, President of QuickLaunch, said Carahsoft is essential to the company's strategy to support more than 2 million student logins by the end of 2027. He said Carahsoft's ability to move products through complex State procurement requirements is necessary for a quick, secure student launch. Brian O'Donnell, Vice President of Cybersecurity Solutions at Carahsoft, said the company was pleased to add QuickLaunch to its cybersecurity portfolio. He said the partnership would expand the solutions Carahsoft can offer to Higher Education and Public Sector organizations. Both executives framed the deal as a way to deliver secure, streamlined digital experiences to students, faculty and staff.

The articles describe QuickLaunch as built specifically for Higher Education, connecting identity and integration around the academic lifecycle. Its integration platform connects systems such as Ellucian Banner, Jenzabar, Anthology, Slate and Great Plains through a no-code builder. The company says its suite offers adaptive Multi-Factor Authentication, automated provisioning and deprovisioning, and identity management from applicant to alumni. QuickLaunch states it offers 99.99% uptime and works with Canvas and Colleague as well. Carahsoft describes itself as the Trusted Government IT Solutions Provider, supporting Federal, State and Local Government agencies, and Education and Healthcare markets.

The articles say Carahsoft works through hundreds of contract vehicles with resellers, integrators and consultants. Higher Education IT teams and public sector buyers are the audience the articles name as the intended beneficiaries, and students, faculty and staff are described as the end users of the secure experiences. The release says the partnership makes it easier for Higher Ed IT teams to access the technology through a procurement channel they already use. It does not describe any specific institution adopting the platform. The articles also do not report any reaction from customers, competitors or regulators.

The only voices in the coverage are those of the two companies and their representatives. Contact information for media is provided for Mary Lange at Carahsoft and Raymond Todd Blackwood at QuickLaunch. The articles say QuickLaunch was founded to serve higher education and that Carahsoft has long served government buyers through its contract vehicles. The Manila Times page carrying the release also lists the newswire and cookie notices typical of its site.

The articles do not say when QuickLaunch began operating, its prior revenue, or the terms of the financial arrangement. They also do not name any competing platform or previous partner. The background offered is limited to the company descriptions supplied in the release. The articles do not say when the platform will reach resellers or contract buyers beyond the stated availability.

They do not explain how the 2 million student login target will be measured or whether it is on track. The release does not state the financial terms of the partnership or whether exclusivity applies. The articles leave open how many public sector buyers will adopt the platform through the four contracts. No timeline is given for the 500-plus integrations to be expanded or for new compliance certifications to be obtained.

Fibocom, a Chinese wireless communication module company, showcased its connectivity, AI and robotics technologies at electronica 2026 in Munich, Germany, with a press release dated November 12, 2026. Fibocom's exhibits also included an AI companion solution and board-level wireless products for broadband, portable and IoT applications. The company's showcase framed these products as ways for manufacturers to build devices across consumer, industrial and connectivity markets.

The first robotic mower architecture is a lightweight monocular-vision solution without LiDAR or RTK, designed for cost-optimized products. The second combines monocular vision with 3D LiDAR for complex, obstacle-rich gardens, while the third pairs stereo vision with RTK for depth perception and high-precision positioning across larger lawns. Beyond sensor selection, Fibocom provides core hardware, proprietary perception and navigation algorithms, and system integration support to help manufacturers build on existing solution architectures. The AI companion solution combines the MagiCore core unit, AI Cloud, app, IP Agent customization, and connectivity and AI token services. Fibocom also supports complete device customization and delivery, and its 5G CPE and outdoor unit PCBA solutions are shown alongside MiFi and Dongle designs.

Fibocom states that its robotic mower and AI companion offerings rely on its own hardware, algorithms and services. The company says it is China's first wireless communication module company listed on both the A-share and H-share markets, founded in 1999. Fibocom describes wireless communication and artificial intelligence as its core technologies, providing integrated hardware and software solutions for industry applications. Its one-stop solutions include cellular communication, AI, automotive and GNSS modules, along with AI toolchains, AI Agent, global connectivity and cloud services. The company says these products support digital intelligence upgrades in robotics, consumer electronics, low-altitude economy, intelligent transportation, smart retail and smart energy.

The press release presents these offerings as serving OEMs and device makers that want to accelerate product development. The press release names customers and applications that Fibocom says are affected by its products. A zodiac-themed AI companion toy called AiMOON, developed by a customer using MagiCore, demonstrates integration into character-based consumer products. Customer devices on display cover applications in asset tracking, industrial monitoring and remote health monitoring. An AI smart pet collar combines Fibocom cellular connectivity with pet tracking, activity monitoring and AI-based pet vocalization recognition.

The robotics showcase also featured development kits and stereo camera hardware from D-Robotics. Fibocom's component portfolio includes LE270 and LE271 LTE Cat.1 bis modules, the low-power IoT module MQ771, and the MGB GNSS series. A separate BusinessKorea article, dated November 11, 2026, reports that Doosan Corp. also participated in electronica 2026, held in Munich, Germany, from November 10 to 13. Doosan also introduced Patterned Flat Cable for electric vehicle battery systems, which it says can reduce weight and volume by more than 80% compared with conventional wiring harnesses. The company said it can produce 2.5-meter PFC through a roll-to-roll process it developed for the first time in the world. The Doosan article says the company has led the localization of CCL since 1974 and now supplies global AI semiconductor companies. To meet rising demand, Doosan is expanding domestic production lines and building new production bases in Thailand and China.

An official said the company will reflect market trends and customer requirements from the exhibition in product development. The article describes Doosan's European participation as an opportunity to establish its position in the European market. The Fibocom release does not state any follow-up plans beyond offering integration support and customized development for its customers. stories.Headline: Google unveils Gemini Robotics 2.5 with 96% success rate in tasks
stories.Summary:
Google has launched Gemini Robotics 2.5, an AI model meant to improve how quickly and precisely robots learn and perform tasks. The company announced the model, which it calls its most capable vision-language-action model to date, on November 10, 2026. Google DeepMind's Carolina Parada, who leads the company's robotics work, introduced it in a post on the company's website. Its tests were run with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz, where humanoid robots sorted automotive parts successfully. The announcement came in reports published on November 9 and 12, 2026.

The model increases the number of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it learns them. Google tested Gemini Robotics 2.5 across more than 200 distinct tasks, such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box and pipetting a liquid. Compared with previous baselines, it achieves a 30% to 100% higher success rate depending on the task, while completing tasks 20% to 30% faster. The model natively works with several robot types, including Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid with a five-finger, 22 degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand, and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered grippers. Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out to Google's robotics partners.

Google is responsible for the model, and Carolina Parada described it as a step toward robots that can work in less structured settings. The company said the model improves dexterity, reliability and safety, helping robots leave the lab for everyday environments. Google also said Gemini 4 Argon, its frontier model, helped accelerate the robotics research behind the release. The company framed the work as progress toward physical artificial general intelligence. Google also said it is releasing the ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark as an open-source tool for testing robots against unsafe instructions.

Apptronik's co-founder and CEO, Jeff Cardenas, said the models improved dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training. He said they carried over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off. The pilot ran on active automotive production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. Factory technicians are affected because the robots take over repetitive kitting work, freeing them to focus on complex build tasks. Monotonous parts sorting is the work the robots were built to relieve, and the companies said it can help keep assembly lines moving.

Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz tested the model in a proof-of-concept on the production lines. In that pilot, Apollo 2 autonomously sorted metal automotive brackets from bulk bins into trays in the order each vehicle needed. The system pairs Gemini Robotics ER, which tracks the workflow, with the Gemini Robotics 2.5 actions model, which controls the hands and arms. Google said its safety features let robots steer around hazards in real time, improving safe task completion by 33% around obstacles and 43% around nearby people. The company reported that its Argon model achieved 99.5% jailbreak resistance, compared with 82% for its previous baseline.

Google presented the release as an advance in dexterity, reliability and safety for robots working alongside people. The company described earlier work, including Gemini Robotics 2 in July 2026, which brought whole-body intelligence to robots. The Gemini Robotics 1.5 model, introduced in September 2025, brought AI agents into the physical world. The first Gemini Robotics model appeared in March 2025 and brought AI into the physical world. Google's releases in this line have built on one another over roughly two years.

Google has not said when Gemini Robotics 2.5 will be generally available beyond its robotics partners. The articles also do not say how many factories or robot fleets will adopt the model. They give no detail on the outcome of the ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark beyond Argon's score. Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz have described the pilot as promising progress toward widespread industrial use, but the articles do not say when that might happen.

stories.Headline: SpaceXSI's Grok Build AI agent exposed sensitive data
stories.Summary:
Security researchers at Claroc found that Grok Build, an AI coding agent from SpaceXSI, was leaking confidential data from thousands of applications built on the platform. The exposure came from insecure default sharing settings, and the researchers reported it to SpaceXSI on November 8, 2026. Claroc's findings were published on November 12, 2026, in reporting by TechGig and Ars Technica. Researchers identified 43,601 addresses ending in grok.me that were visible through passive DNS services. Passive DNS services collect and index domain names seen in DNS traffic, which made these addresses discoverable.

Of those 43,601 addresses, 35,578, or 94.7 per cent, could be accessed without any authentication, according to TechGig. Claroc said the default privacy option for publishing apps was "Anyone with the link," which was pre-selected for users. Ars Technica reported that Grok Build's randomized URLs were structured so the random words sat to the left of grok.me, letting passive DNS searches enumerate them. Claroc said Google's approach places the randomness to the right of the domain, which would have kept the links invisible to such searches. Claroc said that Grok Build's links were set to "Anyone with the link" by default, and users could change the setting to "invited users" or "only you."

Claroc reported that about one in ten apps held sensitive internal business information, and 2 per cent exposed data serious enough for a high or critical severity rating. The exposed material included a hospital employee directory with more than 3,500 names and an intensive care briefing with patient information. A trucking company's recruitment database listing more than 1,000 individuals was also exposed. An employee timesheet's downloadable code contained 18 accounts with plaintext passwords, including administrator credentials. Ars Technica added that a Peruvian construction company's dashboard held 3,784 worker medical exams, and that a Tesla service-center scorecard named 22 technicians.

SpaceXSI itself was among the affected parties, and Claroc found 24 of its apps exposing an onboarding plan, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and advertising proposals. Claroc said SpaceXSI did not respond to its initial notice, so a Claroc official tagged Elon Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer on X. Ars Technica reported that SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending questions about the article. A Cursor representative, which SpaceXSI recently acquired, said that Grok Build apps are "private by default" and that competing coding agents also offer shareable links. Claroc's tests contradicted that statement, showing that Grok Build required users to change the default setting to one of the two more restrictive options.

The problem traces to how Grok Build placed the random portion of its links, which is a design decision that undermined the access protection the randomization was meant to provide. Ars Technica reported that Muse, a Meta agent, had also suspended a link-sharing feature after it was found leaking sensitive data. According to Ars Technica, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini place their secret randomness in the URL path, so DNS does not expose it. Claroc said it was working to notify other affected app creators, and Asaf Aprozper, Claroc's co-founder and CTO, said he was contacting companies directly. Ars Technica noted that a luxury cruise company's security team began containing the exposure after Claroc shared its findings.

Several questions remain open in the reporting. The Cursor representative did not respond to follow-up questions about whether SpaceXSI intentionally exposed its internal information. Ars Technica reported that SpaceXSI also did not say why it removed the data after Ars asked about it, or whether it planned to notify customers whose information was exposed. The articles do not say how many of the affected organizations will be contacted or what remedies they will receive. Ars Technica advised Grok Build users to choose the "invite others" option unless they intend to make an app widely available.

The articles provided do not give the date or the full details of that announcement, so the account below draws on what they do report about the equipment market around HBM. High-bandwidth memory differs from conventional DRAM because it requires thinning dies, connecting them through through-silicon vias, stacking, bonding, and inspecting them. Each added step creates equipment demand and potential yield losses, which the articles identify as a second source of spending beyond simple capacity growth. Applied Materials agreed on October 26, 2026, to raise its stake in BE Semiconductor Industries to approximately 20 percent of outstanding shares, subject to regulatory requirements.

Lam Research reported September-quarter 2026 revenue of $8.22 billion, up 54.4 percent year over year, with a GAAP operating margin of 40.0 percent. The articles name Samsung, SK hynix and Micron as companies investing in HBM capacity, and they attribute the equipment demand to those memory makers. TOWA reported orders of ¥32.97 billion for July through September 2026, up 125.8 percent from the same period of 2025, while its quarterly sales rose 14.1 percent to ¥17.53 billion. TOWA also raised its fiscal-year revenue forecast to ¥71 billion from ¥64 billion and its operating profit forecast to ¥13.15 billion from ¥10.24 billion.

Wonik IPS, based in Pyeongtaek, reported preliminary third-quarter 2026 revenue of about ₩337.8 billion, up 25.8 percent, with operating profit near ₩66.7 billion. The articles do not include a direct statement from Samsung about the $98 billion Chungcheong plan. Analysts and equipment makers are quoted only indirectly through their financial results, and the articles attribute TOWA's growth to AI and data center investment, including HBM, though TOWA also serves other packaging applications. Equipment suppliers such as Lam, KLA, Applied Materials and Camtek stand to benefit, while memory manufacturers carry the capital commitments. The articles do not describe any other specific group affected by the expansion.

The articles describe an AI investment cycle that has been measured mostly through the revenue of Nvidia, Micron, SK hynix and other processor and memory suppliers. The writer, Dr. Robert Castellano, argues that HBM is creating a second opportunity in equipment makers, extending from wafer fabrication into advanced packaging. The articles frame this as a question of whether the spending is a cyclical increase or a more sustained expansion, and they note that the strength has spread beyond the largest U.S. equipment companies. stories.Headline: European shares log record close on Siemens, CoreWeave-fuelled AI optimism
stories.Summary:
European shares closed at a record on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, just short of their intraday high, as strong forecasts from Siemens Energy and CoreWeave lifted investor confidence in artificial intelligence. The pan-European Stoxx 600 rose 0.72 per cent to 663.05 points, a whisker below the intraday record of 663.41. Germany's DAX also rose 1.2 per cent and hovered near its own all-time high. Siemens Energy led the gains after its shares jumped 10.8 per cent.

The AI equipment maker raised its profit margin expectations for 2027 and said it planned to more than triple its dividend. Peers Schneider Electric and Legrand gained 3 per cent and 2.2 per cent, while the broader tech sector added 2.5 per cent. Chip-related stocks also rose, with Soitec up 11.9 per cent and Aixtron up 8 per cent. Optimism was further boosted by CoreWeave, a neocloud company, which said it expects to become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028.

CoreWeave had been at the centre of AI bubble fears that triggered a global market selloff the previous week. Analysts quoted by Reuters questioned whether the large AI investment would prove profitable across the industry, noting that not all AI companies would succeed. Societe Generale analysts said the rally looked somewhat stretched given political and economic risks, and they saw limited further upside for the index by year-end. Investors also watched interest rates closely after hotter-than-expected US inflation data and hawkish Federal Reserve comments pointed to another rate hike next month.

Sectors less exposed to AI, including retail and food and beverage, lagged on the day. Czech ammunition and arms producer CSG fell 21.6 per cent after cutting its full-year operating margin forecast. A rebound in Brent crude after shipping attacks in the Strait of Hormuz added to inflation concerns in energy-importing Europe. stories.Headline: CoreWeave raises 2026 revenue forecast on AI infrastructure demand; shares surge
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave raised its full-year 2026 revenue forecast on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, signalling stronger demand for its artificial intelligence infrastructure. The report appeared on Investing.com and was republished by Yahoo Finance, with Jaiveer Shekhawat as the author. Shares of the company rose nearly 13% in extended trading after the announcement of the higher outlook. The company also lifted its adjusted operating income forecast for the year, alongside a higher investment budget. Executives gave this guidance during an earnings call, where they also spoke about when the company expects to become profitable.

The company now expects 2026 revenue of $13 billion to $13.3 billion, compared with its previous forecast and analyst consensus of $12.9 billion. Adjusted operating income is now forecast at $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion, a 26% increase at the midpoint from earlier guidance. The lower end of the 2026 capital expenditure forecast rose to $37 billion from $35 billion, while the upper end stays at $39 billion. The company still expects more than 1.85 gigawatts of active power by the end of the year. It also forecast fourth-quarter interest expense of between $1.05 billion and $1.15 billion, which is higher than the third-quarter figure.

CoreWeave's executives are the ones responsible for the outlook, and they said on the earnings call that the company should turn profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028. The company explained that its higher spending reflects expectations of deploying infrastructure and delivering it to customers ahead of schedule. In other words, the larger investment budget is tied to bringing capacity online sooner than previously planned. The articles describe the upbeat outlook as underscoring the scale of demand for computing capacity, which has prompted the company to accelerate its data centre deployment. The company is raising its profitability targets even as it increases its investment budget, which the articles describe as driving substantial capital spending and financing costs.

Analysts had expected less than the company delivered, with third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion coming in above their estimate of $3.54 billion. The adjusted loss of $1.27 per share was narrower than the loss of $1.55 per share that analysts had expected. Those affected most directly are investors, who had fretted over soaring debt levels and increasing signs of an AI bubble before the report. Shares of the Nvidia-backed cloud provider had plummeted nearly 58% in the past month, according to the articles. AI companies and cloud providers racing to secure infrastructure are the customers whose demand the company says it is meeting.

The articles give a good deal of background on the quarter that just ended. Third-quarter revenue was up from $1.37 billion a year earlier, while capital spending jumped to $14.5 billion in the quarter from $9.4 billion in the prior quarter. The company reported a net loss of $709 million, compared with a loss of $110 million a year earlier. Net interest expense increased to $846 million from $310 million, reflecting the higher financing burden as the company invests heavily, and debt stood at about $47 billion as of September 30. CoreWeave added more than 200 megawatts of active power during the quarter, taking its total to more than 1.7 gigawatts, and its revenue backlog stood at approximately $132.5 billion at the end of September.

Looking ahead, the company expects to end the year with more than 1.85 gigawatts of active power, up from more than 1.7 gigawatts at the end of September. Fourth-quarter interest expense is forecast at $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion, higher than the $846 million recorded in the third quarter. Executives expect the company to turn profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028, and the articles give no earlier date. The articles say the company sits at the heart of the AI debt boom, having taken on vast amounts of debt to fund its aggressive expansion of computing capacity. That leaves it vulnerable to any potential slowdown in AI development, and the articles do not say whether such a slowdown will occur or whether the extended-trading gain will hold.
