stories.Headline: ‘Children are not a pilot programme’: Lucy Calkins on use of AI in schools
stories.Summary:
Lucy Calkins, a Columbia University professor who created the reading and writing curriculum Units of Study, spoke with The Hindu about the use of AI in schools, and her interview was published on November 11, 2026. Calkins had given a lecture at Shiv Nadar School in Gurugram on October 31, 2026, and the piece carries a photo credit to a special arrangement. Her curriculum is used in thousands of schools across the United States. The article's central concern is that the literacy crisis has grown especially urgent in both India and America.

In the interview, Calkins argues that developing deep reading and writing skills in children matters more than ever now that AI can generate text in seconds. She is quoted saying that by the time children reach middle school, they can let AI take over their reading lives entirely. Her remark frames the problem as one of habit and skill formation rather than access to technology. The article presents her view as a warning to educators and families rather than a list of prescribed policy changes. The excerpt does not spell out specific measures schools should adopt.

Calkins is the person whose views the article reports, and the interview was conducted by Nivedita S. for The Hindu. The piece is labeled as an interview under the education category, and it appears in the paper's education coverage. The article does not report any formal response from school authorities or government bodies. Calkins's central point, as the headline makes clear, is that children should not be treated as subjects of an experiment with AI tools. The text available does not describe further developments or follow-up actions.

stories.Headline: AI in Practice: AI Helped DHL Save More Than $1 Million in Outside Counsel Fees in One Year
stories.Summary:
The article is a feature profile published by Law.com on November 10, 2026, written by Trudy Knockless, about DHL Supply's general counsel Mark Smolik and his department's use of artificial intelligence. The piece opens with Smolik's early work organizing DHL's legal files nearly two decades ago, which he initially saw as a filing task rather than the foundation for later AI work. That groundwork eventually supported an initiative that let the legal department bring employment-related legal work in-house. The result, according to the headline, was savings of more than $1 million in outside counsel fees in a single year.

The article's full body is behind a subscription wall, so the visible text offers only the opening of the story. From what is shown, the change is a shift of employment-related legal work from outside firms to DHL's own lawyers, enabled by AI tools built on the earlier document organization. The savings figure is stated as more than $1 million in one year, and the period is described as a single year without a specific date range in the visible text. The visible excerpt does not describe which AI tools were used, how many matters moved in-house, or what staffing changes were made.

Smolik is the general counsel of DHL Supply and is the person the article centers on, and the excerpt quotes no statements from him. The visible text also does not give his specific comments on the savings or the AI program. Two related Law.com pieces appear in the page navigation: a November 9, 2026 article by Tony Thompson on research from WorldCC, Deloitte and Ironclad about the gap between individual AI productivity gains and organization-level results, and a November 6, 2026 article by Brendan Pierson on copyright suits over AI training against Meta. Neither is about DHL, and the visible text does not connect them to this story. The visible material does not say what comes next for DHL's program.

Articles.Title: AI in Practice: AI Helped DHL Save More Than $1 Million in Outside Counsel Fees in One Year

stories.Headline: Blue J Announces $176 Million Series E to Put AI Agents to Work for Tax Professionals
stories.Summary:
Blue J, a tax research and advisory platform, announced on November 10, 2026 that it has raised $176 million in Series E funding. The round was led by JMI Equity, a growth equity investment firm, and existing investors Oak HC/FT and Sapphire Ventures also took part, along with Intrepid Growth Partners. The raise values the company at more than $700 million, or more than $1 billion Canadian. Blue J says the capital will help it scale Workflows, its agentic AI for tax work, and expand in the United Kingdom and internationally.

Workflows builds on the research engine that has answered more than 14 million tax questions, and lets tax professionals hand over tasks such as reviewing returns before filing, preparing responses to IRS notices, analyzing partnership, LLC and trust agreements, assessing multistate nexus and drafting client communications. The output is meant to be ready for a partner's review, with supporting sources and workflow steps available for inspection. Practitioners still review the work and make the final judgment calls. Blue J's chief executive and co-founder, Benjamin Alarie, described the goal as giving every tax professional a team of AI agents that can carry work from a client's first question to a finished deliverable under the professional's direction. JMI Principal Jack Duane said JMI believes Blue J has built the best research platform in the market, and Duane will join Blue J's board as part of the investment.

The round follows rapid growth, with annual recurring revenue up 165% in the 15 months after the company's Series D round. More than 6,500 organizations now use Blue J, including Big Four firms and Fortune 100 companies. The company has doubled its team over the past year and expects to exceed 200 employees by year-end. In October, Blue J partnered with Legora to bring its tax research into Legora's agentic operating system for legal work, which is used by more than 140,000 legal professionals.

Articles.Title: Blue J Announces $176 Million Series E to Put AI Agents to Work for Tax Professionals - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Fish Audio Releases Live 3, a Full-Duplex Voice Model That Reacts in 186 ms
stories.Summary:
Fish Audio has released Live 3, a full-duplex voice model designed for real-time voice agents that can keep listening while it speaks. According to the article, the model lets a caller pause, interject with a phrase like "mm-hmm," or change direction without breaking the call. Fish Audio says Live 3 can decide to respond in as little as 186 milliseconds for short reactions such as quick acknowledgements. The article was published on November 11, 2026, by MarkTechPost.

The company's central argument is that turn-taking, meaning knowing when to speak and when to wait, should be handled inside the speech model rather than through hand-tuned pipeline rules. Most voice agents split recognition, reasoning, speech generation and timing across separate stages, but Fish Audio says Live 3 was trained on real human conversations to learn when to acknowledge, wait, respond or stop. A separate reasoning layer still holds the agent's instructions and tools. Live 3 is available through the Fish Agent Platform, the Fish Audio API, and on-premises for enterprises, with the Agents platform in public beta. A $0.035 per minute rate, half the $0.07 list price, applies until December 31, 2026, and phone calls add $0.01 per minute.

Fish Audio is responsible for the release and its claims, and the article reports that the company has shown behavior demos but published no benchmark scores. The 186 millisecond figure applies to short reactions, not to the time until a full reply begins, and the company has not published a latency distribution. The article also notes that the third-party tracker OrcaRouter reported no Artificial Analysis score for Live 3 as of November 11. The piece situates Live 3 among competing full-duplex and realtime voice models, though the details of those comparisons are not fully covered in the excerpt provided.

Articles.Title: Fish Audio Releases Live 3, a Full-Duplex Voice Model That Reacts in 186 ms

stories.Headline: Artifact AI Names Rafael Casas Head of Deployment
stories.Summary:
Artifact AI has named Rafael Casas as its head of deployment, a role announced on November 10, 2026, in which he will help accounting firms put the company's intelligence and orchestration capabilities into practice. His job is to connect each firm's methods and client knowledge with the work its teams deliver. The appointment supports Artifact's stated focus on helping firms build on their own expertise to deepen client relationships and develop specialized services. The company says human judgment stays at the center of that effort.

The platform learns at two levels, the firm's approach to client service and the context and requirements of each client, and it uses that knowledge to inform how its agents prepare work. Teams can see and change what the system has learned, so they can shape the work around their practice. Accounting and the month-end close are described as a practical starting point, where recurring work and professional review refine the record of how a firm serves each client. Once a firm's methods sit in one place, its people can build agents for a single client or for a specialized service without writing code. Casas will work with firms to tie those opportunities to outcomes their teams want to reach.

Ariel Harmoko, co-founder and CEO of Artifact AI, said the company's conversations with firms keep returning to how AI can reflect the way their people work and the needs of each client. Harmoko described the goal as an intelligence layer that firms can see, change, and build on, with their expertise guiding the work. Harmoko said Casas understands the profession and the realities of adoption, and will bring firm experience back into product development. Casas said in his own statement that his role is to help firms apply the technology in ways that support their teams and strengthen client relationships. He described the job as being a partner to the profession as well as a technology provider.

Casas brings roughly two decades of experience in accounting technology, consulting, and strategic partnerships, with a background that spans Workday, Sage, Oracle NetSuite, and QuickFee. He serves on CalCPA's CAS Advisory Council and YEP State Committee and is an instructor and author for the AICPA Business Learning Institute. The article places his appointment within Artifact's broader push to make accounting firms' knowledge more accessible across a practice. It does not give details on the timing of specific deployments or on pricing.

Articles.Title: Artifact AI Names Rafael Casas Head of Deployment - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: When AI Falls Short, Only 8% Blame the Technology, Latch Research Finds
stories.Summary:
Latch, a Seattle company, released its State of AI Automation at Work 2026 survey on November 10, 2026, along with a new accounting automation platform. The survey covered 742 U.S. working professionals and found that AI projects that fell short were most often stalled by missing context rather than weak technology. Among those whose projects fell short, 57% blamed missing context such as bad data or a system that did not understand how the work is done, while only 8% said the technology was not capable enough. The same survey found that 73% of respondents say AI output needs a person to step in at least sometimes, a share that rises to 84% among finance and accounting professionals.

The findings point to gaps in how work is recorded and passed along. Respondents estimated that only 41% of recurring work is documented well enough to hand off, and 83% said their regular work involves judgment calls that written instructions do not cover. Another 61% said their organization had rehired a former employee for institutional knowledge. Latch's platform is designed to address this by watching a person perform a task while asking questions about exceptions and reasoning, then building an automated "sidekick" that runs the work and stops to ask when a decision needs a human. Latch's own finance team reported that a month-end Xero-to-Google Sheets workflow, once turned into a scheduled sidekick, dropped from more than 200 clicks to about a dozen and saved 15 minutes per run.

Stefan Kalb, cofounder and CEO of Latch, said AI lacks the knowledge that experienced accountants carry, such as which variance to ignore or which vendor always needs a second approval. He argued that accountants can teach that knowledge once so that repetitive steps are handed off and staff can focus on judgment and advisory work. Kalb also said that implementing AI securely across a team can be difficult and costly, particularly when it requires significant IT involvement. He described the platform as one that understands natural language and video and asks questions the way a human teammate would.

The release also includes an offer for accounting and finance teams. Teams that email Kalb at stefan@latch.ai by November 30, 2026, will receive 1,000 free Latch credits. The company says the captured knowledge is available to any AI agent over MCP. Latch was founded by Stefan Kalb and Jared Kofron and is backed by Fuse, Soma Capital, Garry Tan, Liquid 2 Ventures and Pioneer Fund. More information is available at latch.ai.

Articles.Title: When AI Falls Short, Only 8% Blame the Technology, Latch Research Finds - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Billionaire venture capitalist Vinod Khosla says judge AI by usage, not stock prices
stories.Summary:
Billionaire venture capitalist Vinod Khosla said on Tuesday that AI should be judged by how much it is used rather than by stock prices. He made the remark on Yahoo Finance's Deirdre Bosa Live, where he said, "It's not prices, it's actual usage." Khosla, a Sun Microsystems co-founder and early backer of OpenAI, measures usage in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process. The article notes that Wall Street has been asking whether AI is a bubble, with most of the worry focused on who is paying for it. Khosla's view was presented as a response to that debate.

The companies leading the AI build-out are spending faster than their businesses bring in cash. Combined free cash flow for Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle fell to about minus $31 billion in the third quarter, according to Goldman Sachs. That compares with positive $37 billion to $62 billion a quarter through 2025. Much of that spending goes into computing power that AI labs rent to run their chatbots. OpenAI's quarterly revenue jumped nearly 50% to $10 billion.

Khosla pointed to internet history to support his case. He noted that the share of Americans online kept climbing through the dot-com crash, rising from about 43% in 2000 to 59% in 2002, even as the Nasdaq Composite lost 78%. The article's source for these figures is the World Bank and the International Telecommunication Union. Kai Wu, founder of Sparkline Capital, argued that usage was never the problem and that overbuilding was. He cited research showing telecoms spent more than $500 billion laying fiber, with 85% of it sitting unused, and that the cost of bandwidth then fell 90%.

Corning, which made the glass for that fiber, fell 99% from 2000 to 2002 and did not top its dot-com high until February of this year. The article reports that the company signed a deal worth up to $6 billion to supply fiber for Meta's AI data centers that month. Its stock more than doubled by late June and has since given back more than half, closing Tuesday near its 2000 peak. Wu said cheap bandwidth benefited later users, noting that Netflix and Meta "came around and started using it." Alphabet, Meta, and Netflix have since added more than $5 trillion in market value since their first trades, per the article's account of company filings.

The article says the bandwidth pattern is already showing up in AI. OpenAI cut the price of its Luna model 80% after launch, and CFO Sarah Friar said use rose almost tenfold. Khosla said there will be a silicon shortage for a couple of years, while Wu noted that chips wear out over years rather than decades. John Chambers, who ran Cisco through the dot-com boom and bust, told Yahoo Finance's Sozzi Unleashed this month that he expects "major train wrecks" this time as well. The article does not report any further schedule for these developments.

Articles.Title: Billionaire venture capitalist Vinod Khosla says judge AI by usage, not stock prices

stories.Headline: With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips
stories.Summary:
Fractile, a British startup building AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C round backed by Britain's Sovereign AI Fund, announced on November 11, 2026. The company said the investment aims to ensure the United Kingdom has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy. The round was led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Redpoint. Fractile is now one of the best-funded players in the race to build purpose-built AI chips, alongside Axelera, Etched and OLIX.

The funding matters because these chips are one way to lower the cost of inference, which means running increasingly demanding AI models in production. Fractile is pursuing a full-stack approach that pairs its hardware with a machine learning compiler meant to speed up how large language models run on its chips. The company describes itself as a frontier AI company, and the British government said the valuation was over £5 billion, a figure that could be around $7 billion according to reports from the Financial Times and a Reuters source. After a pivot, its design stacks DRAM, the most common type of memory, directly on top of each chip in a way the company hopes will avoid the usual tradeoff between memory and capacity. That tradeoff has grown more painful with agentic AI, where companies want long chains of tasks run on large models without losing speed.

Fractile's chief executive, Walter Goodwin, wrote in a LinkedIn post that the company still has a lot of work ahead. He said the new funding will let the startup ship its first chips and systems next year. The British government has framed the investment as a step toward a stronger national role in AI hardware. The company's leadership has presented the round as the next phase of that effort rather than a finished milestone.

Fractile's progress will now depend on whether it delivers working chips and systems next year as planned. The articles do not say how the chips will perform against competitors or when they will reach customers. Fractile's approach to memory is still unproven in production, and the available reporting does not describe any customers or orders. For now, the round gives the company resources to attempt that delivery.

Articles.Title: With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips

stories.Headline: AI could eliminate up to 70% of manual risk tasks in banks, free capacity for strategic roles - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
A McKinsey report published on November 10, 2026, says artificial intelligence could eliminate 60 to 70 percent of manual operational tasks in banks' risk functions. The estimate, which ANI reported through ET CIO, depends on the process and how far it is automated. The report says the freed capacity could let lenders focus on deeper risk analysis, strategic decisions and AI development. It describes this as a shift that is already underway rather than a distant possibility.

The report names the routine work that AI could take over, including data gathering, documentation, compliance checks and monitoring. Human staff would still oversee complex assessments and important decisions. McKinsey says banks could reinvest half of the released capacity in stronger analytical skills, strategic risk advice and faster portfolio decisions. The rest could go to specialised AI engineering, data governance and platform development. Selected risk workflows could achieve structural efficiency gains of 30 to 60 percent after human validation is accounted for.

McKinsey is the source of these findings, and the report is the basis for the figures. It notes that some leading banks are aiming for productivity gains above 30 percent across their risk functions over the next two to three years, compared with the 5 to 10 percent annual targets common under traditional approaches. Early uses in areas such as credit assessment, financial crime monitoring and regulatory compliance have produced productivity gains of 30 to 50 percent in wholesale lending. The same work reported output quality rates of about 95 percent. The technology can also flag borrower stress earlier by monitoring financial information, credit ratings and sector developments.

McKinsey warns that scaling AI will require changes in workforce planning, technology systems and governance. Banks would need staff who understand both risk management and AI, along with clear rules for checking the accuracy and reliability of AI outputs. The report says scattered AI projects may fail to deliver wider benefits unless banks build shared platforms and common governance standards. McKinsey concludes that the question for banks is not whether to move to an AI-enabled risk model but when and by whom, and that early adopters could gain cost and productivity advantages.

Articles.Title: AI could eliminate up to 70% of manual risk tasks in banks, free capacity for strategic roles - ET CIO

stories.Headline: SEC Wins 5.8 Billion Won HBM Inspection Order From Micron
stories.Summary:
SEC, a company known for its electron beam technology, said on November 10, 2026 that it had signed a contract worth 5.8 billion won with Micron's Singapore subsidiary. Under the deal, SEC will supply X-ray inspection equipment for Micron's high-bandwidth memory production. The order covers SEC's NF120 series of manual X-ray inspection systems, which will be installed on a mass-production line. The deal is expected to help SEC move further into the semiconductor market, beyond its existing businesses in electronic components, batteries and defense. SEC first began working with Micron in 2023, and the new contract strengthens that relationship.

Micron is investing $7 billion in HBM and advanced packaging facilities in Singapore, with operations scheduled to begin in 2027. The articles say that as Micron keeps spending on HBM and DRAM, SEC could win further orders for inspection equipment. SEC is also moving from manual systems toward automated inline inspection equipment. In October it won an order for its Semi-scan Wafer system, to be used on a wafer-level packaging mass-production line run by a global outsourced semiconductor assembly and test company.

The company is also seeking to enter the market for inline HBM inspection equipment. An SEC official said the Micron order shows how important X-ray inspection has become in HBM manufacturing. The official expects demand for inspection equipment to keep rising as global chipmakers expand HBM production capacity and capital investment. The articles identify the official only by role and do not name them.

Articles.Title: SEC Wins 5.8 Billion Won HBM Inspection Order From Micron - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

stories.Headline: CoreWeave turns to customer prepayments, shorter contracts to fund AI growth
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, a company that rents out the computing power behind AI, disclosed in its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday that it is changing how it pays for its growth. The neocloud said it is asking customers to pay up front more often, borrowing against specific contracts, and pursuing short-term deals that can carry higher prices. The company reported $3.66 billion in revenue, up 168% from a year earlier, but it also posted a $709 million net loss and $846 million in quarterly interest expense. CEO Michael Intrator told analysts on the earnings call that the company will not use the unsecured debt market at current yields.

Instead, CoreWeave plans to rely on loans backed by specific customer contracts, drawing funds as needed to build infrastructure for a backlog of $132.5 billion. The company expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months, including more than $3 billion tied to signing new contracts for capacity it has already built. Rivals Nebius and IREN have also relied on large Microsoft prepayments, which suggests the industry is moving toward having big technology customers pay for buildouts. The approach eases immediate borrowing needs, but it also commits CoreWeave to providing services at prices that may look less attractive later if demand changes.

Intrator said prices rose about 25% in July and another 10% later in the quarter, and that prices were still climbing in a way that more than offsets cost increases. He also said the company is allocating more capacity to short-term deals where pricing justifies it, selling at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for four- and five-year contracts on new infrastructure is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt. In August, CoreWeave closed a $2.6 billion loan called DDTL 5.5, its first built specifically for shorter-term customer contracts, which lets it borrow in installments. The article notes that lenders tend to favor longer contracts because they offer more predictable cash flow, so short-term deals involve a tradeoff.

Wall Street responded positively to the earnings, but bond investors have been more cautious, with yields on some of CoreWeave's bonds rising above 15% last month. That reaction suggests concern about the debt needed to build data centers before those investments produce returns. The article describes CoreWeave's strategy as a way to expand without relying on unsecured debt, one that could boost profits while adding risk around contract renewals and pricing. It also shows how much the AI infrastructure boom depends on demand that has yet to be proven over time. TechCrunch said it had reached out to CoreWeave for more information about its loan facility.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave turns to customer prepayments, shorter contracts to fund AI growth

stories.Headline: Getty Images faces London AI firm in court
stories.Summary:
Getty Images is challenging a ruling at the Court of Appeal after the High Court dismissed its core legal argument in a case against Stability AI, a London-based AI firm. Getty alleges that Stability unlawfully copied and processed millions of copyrighted images to train its Stable Diffusion image-generation model. The High Court mostly sided with Stability in a judgment handed down last November. The appeal was heard on Wednesday and Thursday.

At the centre of the appeal is a narrow question about secondary copyright infringement. Getty asks the court to decide whether an AI model trained overseas on copyrighted images can be classed as an "infringing copy" when imported into the UK, even if the model stores no copies of the images. Getty's barrister told the court that the company's photo database is highly valuable for training AI models. She argued that Stability does not believe it should have to pay for that content. Stability's written case focused on the fact that the images were downloaded and stored in data centres outside the UK, where UK copyright law does not apply.

The case was heard at the High Court in June 2025 before Mrs Justice Joanna Smith. Getty dropped one of its primary copyright infringement claims just two weeks into that trial. The claims that remained were secondary infringement, trademark infringement and passing off. The court found that Getty succeeded in part on its trademark claim, but only for older models and on isolated examples. Getty declined to comment, and Stability AI was approached for comment.

The dispute comes as Getty Images moves through a wider corporate restructuring. The company filed for US bankruptcy last month as it pursues plans to go private. It also abandoned a planned $3.7bn merger with rival Shutterstock in July, after scrutiny from the UK's Competition and Markets Authority. Stability AI's directors include the filmmaker James Cameron, known for the Avatar film series. The Court of Appeal's ruling on the secondary infringement question has not yet been reported.

Articles.Title: Getty Images faces London AI firm in court - City AM

stories.Headline: 'No permanent friends': Nvidia’s two-track play may reduce Korean chipmakers to subcontractors
stories.Summary:
Nvidia is reportedly pushing Taiwan's TSMC into the memory business while keeping Korean memory chipmakers close, a two-track approach that experts warn could leave Samsung Electronics and SK hynix as mere subcontractors. Samsung and SK hynix supply the high bandwidth memory that powers Nvidia's AI chips, but industry sources worry control over memory design and production could tilt toward Nvidia and TSMC. The Information reported on Friday that TSMC has begun drawing up plans, at Nvidia's request, to produce 3-D dynamic random-access memory. TSMC is weighing whether to build a new plant or convert an existing one for that work. Unlike conventional DRAM, which lays memory cells on a single layer, 3-D DRAM stacks them vertically to pack more capacity into the same footprint.

TSMC said the next day that it remains focused on contract chipmaking, its core business, echoing its founding principle that it never competes with its customers. SK hynix relies on TSMC to make the base dies for its HBM4 chips, and a base die links the memory layers above it to the processor. Nvidia unveiled its own custom HBM, called NVHBM, in August, moving the memory controller into the base die for a more compact design. Last month Nvidia reportedly asked Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to have their NVHBM base dies made on TSMC's 3-nanometer process. Nvidia's push is driven by a memory shortage, as HBM supply has failed to keep up with AI demand and prices keep climbing.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's company has said designing its own memory structures and interfaces would let it boost performance and rely less on any single supplier. TSMC needs HBM to finish Nvidia's GPUs, so more say over memory production could cut GPU shipment delays and win TSMC a bigger share of the AI chip supply chain. Kwon Seok-joon, a chemical engineering professor at Sungkyunkwan University, said TSMC could claim the most lucrative parts of the memory business without building a DRAM plant. He outlined four routes: making more base dies, leading chip stacking through hybrid bonding, teaming up with Taiwanese DRAM makers, or producing the peripheral circuits that run 3-D DRAM. Kwon said Korean companies need to become co-designers of the base die and secure hybrid bonding mass production before TSMC does.

A former SK hynix executive warned that if Korea's two memory giants fail to lead in base dies, bonding and heat treatment as HBM moves to 20 layers or more, they could be reduced to subcontractors supplying only DRAM cells. Hybrid bonding is expected to become essential once HBM stacks reach around 20 layers. Nvidia is also courting Korean partners beyond memory, signing a memorandum of understanding with SK Telecom and the AI chip startup Rebellions at Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026 at Coex in Gangnam District on Monday. The deal followed talks with the Ministry of Science and ICT on linking homegrown neural processing units to Nvidia systems through NVLink Fusion. Nvidia has also invested in Point2 Technology, and plans more investment in Motif Technologies, RLWRLD and Upstage.

Kim Yong-seok, head of Gachon University's semiconductor education center, said that in business there are no permanent friends or allies. He urged academia to pursue forward-looking research on 2.5-D and 3-D packaging, HBM interfaces and high-performance memory system design. He also said the government should help train engineers who can design logic and memory together and expand related infrastructure. The article does not say how long the TSMC plans will take or whether either the new plant or the conversion has been chosen. It also does not say whether Samsung, SK hynix or Micron have agreed to Nvidia's request on base dies.

Articles.Title: 'No permanent friends': Nvidia’s two-track play may reduce Korean chipmakers to subcontractors - Korea JoongAng Daily

stories.Headline: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model
stories.Summary:
BotPsy is a 0.8B-parameter model that Tether AI Research introduced on November 11, 2026, for function calling and agentic workflows. The model is built on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is suited to on-device deployment. Tether describes it as a personal assistant that uses tools to handle simple tasks in domains such as web search, travel, commerce, device control, files, calendars and email. Because of its small size, the company says it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. Tether states that BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use.

BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic performance of its base model on key benchmarks. BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5. Against Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5 times its size, BotPsy scores higher on five of six benchmarks, including BFCL v4 at 44.0 versus 37.7. On safety, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time in automated red-teaming, compared with 36% for its base model. The model is to be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license, in bf16, Q8 and Q4 precisions, as safetensors and as GGUF files.

Tether AI Research, operated by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V., is responsible for the model. The company says it aims to be at the forefront of performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models, arguing that frontier cloud LLMs carry high and unpredictable costs. It also contends that third-party providers can modify, deny or deprecate access at any time. The company further argues that proprietary models offer limited customization and pose risks to privacy, data control and transparency. Tether says that many routine workloads can be processed efficiently on-device.

BotPsy is aimed at users who want personal assistant tasks handled locally, with personal data kept on local hardware. The company says the model keeps user data private and provides instruction-following reliability on secure on-device workflows. Developers and researchers who use the open weights and the QVAC SDK or llama.cpp are also a target audience. The articles do not report any reactions from outside the company or from competing developers.

Tether's training used four sequential stages: supervised fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and two rounds of reinforcement learning. Three Qwen3.5-4B specialist teachers, trained for tool use, general reasoning and instruction following, guided the distillation stage. The company says supervised fine-tuning boosted tool use but lowered knowledge and instruction following below the base model. Distillation and the later reinforcement learning stages restored and improved those capabilities, according to the company's figures.

The articles describe planned future work by Tether that would extend on-device agentic capabilities, strengthen peer-to-peer search, and optimize local fine-tuning through QVAC Fabric. They say future versions would let smartphones delegate heavy tasks to home PCs or trusted P2P nodes. The articles do not give release dates for the open weights or for any of the planned features. They also do not report independent evaluations of BotPsy beyond Tether's own benchmark results.

Articles.Title: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

stories.Headline: Cogent and OpenAI build cyber defense factories for enterprises
stories.Summary:
Cogent, a North American startup, has built Cyber Defense Factories for enterprises with OpenAI models, announced on November 10, 2026. The systems are designed to find security vulnerabilities and fix them automatically, moving at machine speed as attackers exploit flaws more quickly. Cogent says the hardest part of security work has become fixing vulnerabilities rather than finding them, because remediation spans several teams and requires knowing how an attacker could exploit a flaw. The company's AI agents combine GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 with each customer's context and controls to carry work from investigation through verified remediation.

Each customer gets a Context Engine that maintains an enterprise knowledge graph of assets, vulnerabilities, identities, ownership, and dependencies, which background agents keep current across security tools. GPT-6 Astra handles upfront planning and complex reasoning, and Cogent's co-founder and CTO, Geng Sng, calls this a memory harness for the enterprise. Agent Policies define the changes each enterprise permits and which need approval, and a policy engine called TRACE checks tool calls against those policies before they run. An Agent Gateway independently checks authorization, and higher-risk work can run in isolated sandboxes. Customers can choose to delegate investigation, require approval for changes, or allow bounded autonomous remediation.

Cogent describes the work as its own, with Geng Sng quoted saying that OpenAI models can sustain long-running tasks so agents can carry work from investigation through verified remediation. The company says customers used its factories after critical PHP2Shell flaws were disclosed in PHP, a language used to run websites. Cogent reports that a Fortune 1000 automotive customer cut its mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities by 75%, and a Fortune 500 IT services customer reached 5 times vulnerability-triage throughput. Vijay Bala, Global CISO at trading platform MarketAxess, says Cogent helps the firm focus fixes on the greatest risks and the paths an adversary could use. Geng Sng says OpenAI models are more cost-efficient than other providers, which matters for large agent swarms.

Cogent plans to expand autonomous remediation, moving from simple configuration changes to multi-step fixes across enterprise systems, and is developing autonomous discovery and validation in a closed-loop system. Through Trusted Access for Cyber and Daybreak, the company receives support for internal red-teaming and attack-path research, including access to Daybreak Red for authorized offensive research. Geng Sng says good defense requires good offense, and that this research helps the team decide which defensive capabilities to build next. The article does not give pricing, availability dates, or the number of customers using the factories.

Articles.Title: Cogent and OpenAI build cyber defense factories for enterprises

stories.Headline: How Conversational AI Is Moving Hotel Linen Management From Reactive to Proactive
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion piece by Mike Rispoli, VP of Product Management at Laundris, published on Hospitality Net on November 11, 2026, arguing that conversational AI can move hotel linen management from reactive to proactive. Rispoli says that for years linen management has been reactive, with operators counting stock, discovering shortages, reordering when inventory runs low, and investigating losses only after they become expensive. He writes that AI, combined with real-time RFID inventory data and historical usage patterns, offers a way to flip that model. He describes the goal as helping operators understand what needs attention now and, increasingly, what may need attention next.

Rispoli says hotel operators want housekeeping teams to spend less time searching for linen and more time servicing rooms. They also want to avoid emergency orders without stockpiling unneeded inventory, and to find where linen is being lost before replacement costs build up. He argues that conversational AI helps by letting an operator ask a question in plain language instead of learning another reporting system or digging through dashboards. The answer can come in seconds, which he presents as a relatively simple change in how people interact with technology.

He describes manual linen counts as a weak point, since staff often count at the end of a shift, when they are rushing, and stacks may be estimated rather than counted or carts and closets may be missed. When operators lack confidence in their inventory, he writes, they either over-order to avoid running out or discover shortages too late and place emergency orders. Employees also spend hours searching for linen and recounting stock, and losses that cannot be separated from normal wear and tear keep replacement costs rising. Rispoli says he sees this primarily as an operational efficiency problem rather than a data problem.

Rispoli describes RFID as a major step forward that removed much of the manual work of tracking inventory by letting hotels automatically track individual items. He says dashboards still require users to know which report to open, which graph to read, and which filters to apply. He presents Laundris Assistant as the product that puts this idea into practice, working with inventory data already captured in the Laundris platform so operators can ask about stock, locations, loss trends, and inventory needs. Laundris, he notes, is a technology company modernizing commercial laundry and linen services through RFID tracking and AI-powered analytics.

Rispoli argues that combining real-time inventory data with historical usage patterns lets operators act earlier, identifying trends that suggest a shortage is coming and unusual loss patterns before they become significant expenses. He says this moves linen management from figuring out what happened to understanding what needs attention next. He also says that without accurate information, the safe answer is often to order extra of everything, and better visibility lets operators buy what the property actually needs. He adds that faster access to information gives hotel teams time back, which he says is where he believes conversational AI can have its greatest impact.

Articles.Title: How Conversational AI Is Moving Hotel Linen Management From Reactive to Proactive

stories.Headline: Micron Technology (MU) Commits $1 Billion To Landmark AI Infrastructure IPO
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology, listed as MU on the NasdaqGS, is committing US$1 billion to Anthropic's private placement as part of the AI lab's upcoming initial public offering. The article reports this on November 11, 2026, in a piece by Bailey Pemberton published by Yahoo Finance. Anthropic is targeting more than US$90 billion from a public share sale and a US$26 billion private placement, according to the deal outline. The transaction places Micron alongside major chip, cloud, and data firms that are financing Anthropic's AI infrastructure build-out. Micron supplies memory and storage semiconductors to data centers, AI developers, and device makers across the US, Asia, Japan, Europe, and other regions.

The article says the commitment ties those core products directly to one of the highest-profile AI infrastructure builds currently in progress. It also says the stake is intended to hard-wire Micron into the AI infrastructure stack alongside Nvidia and AMD, as a funding partner rather than only a component vendor. The move is framed as treating future memory demand as contract-backed rather than purely cyclical. The article attributes the analysis to Simply Wall St, which says the story was produced with the assistance of AI automation based on its data and analyst forecasts. That analysis states that the deal sharpens an existing concern about high capital intensity and execution risk in new fabs.

It says tying more capital to a single AI customer adds concentration and timing questions that only future contract disclosures and cash generation will settle. The article also notes that Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned. The page carries several earlier headlines about the Anthropic partnership, with items dated four and five months before publication. Those items describe Micron's Anthropic arrangement as a collaboration to scale next-generation AI infrastructure and a supply deal, and some reference Micron's June 24 earnings report. The page also shows Micron's share movement and other market figures on the day of publication, but the article itself does not say what happens next beyond the timing of the Anthropic IPO.

Articles.Title: Micron Technology (MU) Commits $1 Billion To Landmark AI Infrastructure IPO

stories.Headline: CrowdWorks Joins Government Manufacturing AI Project
stories.Summary:
CrowdWorks, an artificial intelligence technology company, has partnered with agentic AI company Enhans to take part as an official partner in the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources' 2026 AI Model Development Project Based on Manufacturing Tacit Knowledge. The announcement was published by The Elec on November 10, 2026. The project's goal is to turn large volumes of unstructured field data, which hold the experience and intuition of highly skilled manufacturing experts, into high-quality training datasets. It also aims to build an ontology-based AI guidance model to help frontline workers.

Within the project, Enhans will lead the development of an ontology and guidance AI model drawn from the tacit knowledge of experts in the refining and petrochemical industries. CrowdWorks will handle preprocessing of the unstructured field data and will use its Alpy Knowledge Compiler, which relies on automated document parsing to convert tables, images, performance curves, graphs and mathematical formulas into text that AI can be trained on. The company plans to build infrastructure able to process up to 7.5 million pages over the project period. CrowdWorks described the work as its full-scale entry into the emerging market for manufacturing tacit knowledge.

The article attributes the announcement to CrowdWorks, which said the project marks its entry into this market and that it expects to play a leading role in the manufacturing industry's AI transformation data market. The article does not include a direct statement from the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources or from Enhans. It does report that the ministry plans to raise its budget for AI solutions using manufacturing tacit knowledge from 48 billion won this year to 290 billion won next year. The article does not say what outcomes the project will be judged against or when the guidance model is expected to reach frontline use.

Articles.Title: CrowdWorks Joins Government Manufacturing AI Project - www.thelec.net

stories.Headline: A New Committee Will Spend a Year Weighing AI's Impact on City Life
stories.Summary:
A three-member council committee in Riverside began a 13-month review of artificial intelligence on Thursday, Nov. 5, and the first meeting drew residents who urged caution about data centers. The Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Policy Ad Hoc Committee will study how AI affects city services, privacy, jobs, utility costs and infrastructure. Its recommendations are due to the City Council by November 2027, though chair Steven Robillard said that date is a guideline rather than an absolute deadline. The review is advisory, and the committee will hear from outside experts, study other cities and gather public input before sending its findings to the full council.

Speakers at the public comment period raised concerns about the strain data centers could place on local resources. April Glatzel questioned whether the city could support such facilities given residents' efforts to conserve water, and she said she would accept less convenience rather than risk those resources. Tinka Friend welcomed the committee but asked members to weigh the consequences carefully before decisions reached them. Robillard said no data center proposal was before the committee, and Chief Innovation Officer George Khalil said he knew of no current project. Councilmember Philip Falcone said he opposes data centers while supporting the broader review.

The proposed work plan goes beyond data centers to examine how residents interact with City Hall, including multilingual translation, 311 assistance and permit help, along with the AI tools staff use for drafting and research. Riverside's administrative AI policy, effective July 2024, requires human review of AI-generated material, verification of facts, disclosure of AI use and an option to reach a human. The schedule moves from city services to infrastructure and land use, then to workforce, economic opportunity, privacy, cybersecurity and vendor accountability. The infrastructure review will consider electricity demand, water use, zoning, noise and who would pay for utility expansion, with computing loads of 20, 50 and more than 100 megawatts under consideration.

The committee's members include Robillard, Councilmember Steve Hemenway and Councilmember Philip Falcone, and Hemenway asked that the review capture both positive and negative social and economic effects. Khalil said protecting resident information and keeping access to city employees remain priorities. Robillard said members want perspectives beyond city staff and that hearings will feature experts answering committee questions. The committee's schedule could change, and additional meetings may be needed as the review proceeds.

Articles.Title: A New Committee Will Spend a Year Weighing AI's Impact on City Life - The Raincross Gazette

stories.Headline: Databricks' new Genie tool is the latest sign of the AI industry's full court press for knowledge workers
stories.Summary:
Databricks, a San Francisco data and AI company, announced on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, a second generation of its Genie assistant that operates as an always-on, autonomous agent for enterprise work. Users can give Genie a goal, and it takes ownership of the work, delegates to subagents, tracks progress, follows up on missing inputs, and reaches out when a person needs to make a decision. A new priority inbox highlights items needing attention, and Genie emails users when they are away. The launch came a day after Anthropic released its own set of AI productivity tools aimed at corporate users. Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi said the agents run in the background at all times.

The new Genie is grounded in Genie Ontology, which captures a company's horizontal context, including definitions, metrics, people and processes, and keeps it current as the business changes. Genie Search expands to more than 100 enterprise data sources, including Google Drive, Jira and Confluence, and indexes content in place without moving or copying it. Genie runs within a company's existing Databricks environment and is governed by Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway, so every action stays within existing controls. Genie now runs in autonomous mode on its own compute, and every action is fully auditable. Ontology Manager, a new feature, lets teams manage and govern business context.

Ghodsi, who co-founded and leads Databricks, said Genie has made him a "10x more productive CEO" and that he uses it every hour of the day. He said it can work because it knows how the company operates, including what counts as revenue and which numbers are official. Ghodsi also said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is an amazing CEO and should remain in that role after the revelation of Huang's extramarital affair with a woman U.S. officials believe to be a spy for China. Ghodsi said he thinks the industry will weather the storm. Databricks, still privately held, raised $5 billion at a $190 billion valuation in August.

The industry is pushing harder into corporate work because AI has transformed software programming but remains experimental in other business functions where returns are less clear. Anthropic's prospectus for its initial public offering said the work of knowledge workers represented more than $40 trillion in economic value globally in 2025. Anthropic's IPO, expected the following week, could value the company at $1.4 trillion, and many in the industry are watching it closely. Anthropic's tools include a spreadsheet application that competes with Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets, and a feature that lets Claude join video calls. Some believe recent advances in AI agents and model capabilities may let the technology capture a broader part of the market.

Articles.Title: Databricks' new Genie tool is the latest sign of the AI industry's full court press for knowledge workers
