VerticalScope signed its first two data agreements with frontier AI labs in October, without naming them. One is a non-exclusive license to train models on a selection of communities, with fees tied to the volume of content delivered. The other pays VerticalScope when its content contributes to an AI-generated answer, and it began in November with a subset of communities. Goodridge said AI companies, AI search engines and AI agents made 115 million attempts to access the communities over the past 30 days, and that VerticalScope blocks any company that tries without an agreement.

The shift comes as Reddit faces similar pressure, with its search referrals reportedly falling by more than 1 million a week on average in October. Reddit began testing an AI shopping experience in February that places product carousels with prices and purchase links in its search results. A PYMNTS Intelligence survey cited in the coverage found about 61 million U.S. consumers, or 23%, now start online retail research with AI, but Amazon closed 60% of respondents' most recent AI-assisted purchases. The articles do not say how VerticalScope's model will perform as its AI licensing revenue begins, which the company expects in the fourth quarter.

Articles.Title: VerticalScope Turns 2 Billion Forum Posts Into AI Shopping Revenue

stories.Headline: Most large firms plan higher open-weight AI use to cap bills, study shows
stories.Summary:
Nearly six in ten senior executives at large companies plan to increase their use of cheaper open-weight AI models over the next year, according to a study by Capgemini released on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The survey found that the shift is driven by AI bills overshooting budgets. Fifty-nine percent of the surveyed executives said their AI spending over the past year had been significantly above their expectations or budgets, by 24 percent on average. Fifty-three percent said they were worried about AI costs, up from 45 percent last year. Capgemini said open-weight models handled 72 percent of traffic on OpenRouter, a multi-AI provider, in September, yet accounted for just 27 percent of AI spending.

The consulting firm reported that open-weight tokens were on average 87 percent cheaper than closed ones. Open-weight models, such as those from DeepSeek or Mistral, can be downloaded and run anywhere, while closed options like Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini are only accessible from the cloud. Closed models still have a place, since half the respondents said they would keep them where the complexity of a task justified the extra cost. The study was conducted by Capgemini, an IT consulting firm that helps companies embed AI into their existing platforms. It surveyed 500 executives at enterprises with annual revenue above $1 billion across 10 countries.

The article presents the findings as the company's own research rather than attributing a policy or requirement to any single party. The trend echoes moves by other large players. SAP's finance chief said last month that the company was replacing some of its costliest AI models with cheaper ones where performance held up. Anthropic, which launched its IPO roadshow this week, also warned in its prospectus that customers may shift to cheaper options, including open-weight models.

Articles.Title: Most large firms plan higher open-weight AI use to cap bills, study shows

stories.Headline: The Pensions Regulator Sets Out Seven Principles for Trustees' Use of AI
stories.Summary:
The Pensions Regulator (TPR) has published guidance on how trustees of pension schemes should use artificial intelligence, dated 10 November 2026. The guidance does not create new legal requirements or change trustees' existing duties. It explains how those duties apply when AI is used by the trustee board or by the scheme's advisers and service providers. It sets out seven principles that TPR expects trustees to follow.

The first principle is to start with the problem rather than the technology, using AI only to solve real problems and improve member outcomes, efficiency and value for money. The second principle keeps human responsibility central, since trustees remain accountable for everything done for the scheme, including outsourced work. For each significant use of AI, trustees should be able to say what it is used for, what data it uses, who is accountable, how its decisions can be challenged by a person, and what happens if it fails. Where AI significantly influences a decision, trustees should be able to explain what service was used, what human checks were made and who made the decision. The guidance also notes that data protection law restricts decisions with significant effects that are made solely by automated means.

The third principle treats governance as ongoing, with AI risks built into the scheme's risk management framework and kept under regular review, with oversight proportionate to the risk. The fourth principle asks trustees to plan for disruption, so that business continuity plans cover AI failing or becoming unavailable. The fifth principle stresses data quality, since AI magnifies the effect of poor data, and warns against "shadow AI", meaning use of unapproved public AI services. The sixth principle covers transparency, noting there is no general duty to tell members about every use of AI, but trustees should consider what members need to understand where AI directly affects them. The seventh principle asks trustees to test outcomes for unfair bias across groups and to consider vulnerable and digitally excluded members.

TPR has also published separate guidance on identifying and managing hidden AI-related investment exposure, prompted by concern that the growing influence of AI companies on global markets could create concentration risks that leave investors more vulnerable in a downturn. That guidance asks trustees to understand their scheme's aggregate exposure and test whether diversification will hold under stressed conditions. The article, written by lawyers at Mayer Brown, advises trustees to review the guidance and check whether their current arrangements for AI meet TPR's expectations, and to act where gaps exist. The article does not describe any enforcement action or deadline.

Articles.Title: The Pensions Regulator Sets Out Seven Principles for Trustees' Use of AI - Mayer Brown

stories.Headline: Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) Is Pouring Billions Into AI: Could Massive Spending Weigh on Future Returns?
stories.Summary:
Moon Capital Management, an investment firm, released its third-quarter 2026 investor letter, which focused largely on the heavy spending on artificial intelligence by major technology companies. The letter reported that the firm's equity portfolio gained about 4% in the first nine months of 2026, compared with roughly 12% for the S&P 500 over the same period. It noted that market gains had been narrow, with nearly half of S&P 500 constituents declining and the median stock rising only about 4%. The firm also said it had avoided direct AI investments because it is unsure which companies will ultimately capture the economic benefits.

The letter says the major hyperscalers are expected to spend about $1.2 trillion on capital expenditures in 2027 and another $1.4 trillion in 2028. Semiconductor demand has been strong, with the S&P Global Semiconductor Index rising about 95% through September. Moon Capital questioned whether these infrastructure investments would generate adequate returns. The firm said it remains focused on businesses whose economics it can assess with confidence and whose shares trade at meaningful discounts to estimated intrinsic value.

The letter named Microsoft Corporation, which develops software, cloud services, personal computing products, and enterprise solutions, as one of the holdings it highlighted. Microsoft's stock closed at about $545.18 per share on November 9, 2026, giving it a market capitalization of $3.96 trillion. Its one-month return was 1.9%, and its shares traded between $352.83 and $555.80 over the past 52 weeks. In the letter, Moon Capital said that while AI-related investment accounts for a large share of U.S. GDP and S&P 500 earnings growth, it remains to be seen whether the eventual returns will justify the capital committed.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) Is Pouring Billions Into AI: Could Massive Spending Weigh on Future Returns?

stories.Headline: Governor's 2027 preview touches Alexandria's asks on housing, solar, and AI, but not transit or school funding
stories.Summary:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger released the first preview of her 2027 legislative agenda on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at the State Capitol in Richmond. The preview, called "Moving Virginia Forward," was outlined alongside House and Senate Democratic leaders and touches several of Alexandria's requests for the General Assembly, including housing near transit, solar energy, and artificial intelligence. It does not mention transit funding, the state's school funding formula, or immigration enforcement, all of which appear in the city's draft legislative package. The preview landed hours before City Council was scheduled to receive that draft at its Tuesday night meeting.

The release and a two-page summary describe the agenda as a set of select proposals rather than the full program. Spanberger and legislators are expected to travel the state in the coming weeks to announce more. Council plans to hold a public hearing and adopt Alexandria's package on Saturday, November 14. The General Assembly session begins January 13, 2027.

Together, these dates set the timeline for how the city's requests will be weighed against the governor's priorities. The governor's office issued the release, and Spanberger and the Democratic leaders of the House and Senate presented the agenda in person. The Alexandria Brief, a local outlet, reported on the preview and on the city's pending package, which is the document Council will consider. The articles do not describe any response from city officials to the omissions on transit and school funding.

Alexandria's requests on housing, solar, and AI have been met in part by the governor's preview, while transit and school funding remain unaddressed in it. The articles do not say whether those omitted issues will appear in the later announcements. Council's vote on Saturday will determine what the city formally asks the General Assembly to consider. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Governor's 2027 preview touches Alexandria's asks on housing, solar, and AI, but not transit or school funding - The Alexandria Brief

stories.Headline: OpenAI's Q3 results and Nvidia's scandal impact on the AI ecosystem
stories.Summary:
OpenAI reported third-quarter revenue of $10 billion, up from about $6.7 billion, a growth rate near 50 percent quarter over quarter, according to new figures reported in a Yahoo Finance video dated November 10, 2026. The same figures show Anthropic reported $17 billion in third-quarter revenue, growth of 47 percent quarter over quarter. OpenAI's growth had been 18 percent in the second quarter, while Anthropic had grown 144 percent in that quarter. Anthropic is about to go public, with its IPO expected the following week. Investor Vinod Khosla, one of OpenAI's earliest backers, said he invested only in OpenAI and not in Anthropic.

Khosla said OpenAI was valued at $1 billion when his firm first invested in it. He argued that investing in one company gives deeper insight into the field than investing in both, since neither company shares that information with investors in both. He said revenue was less important to him than token usage, and that OpenAI had chosen to price its tokens lower, increasing its share of tokens. He argued that open-source models are not cheaper to run because of the premium Nvidia charges on its silicon. He said OpenAI's own silicon would lower its cost per million tokens as more of its inference moves onto that hardware.

Khosla said he regularly has dinners with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, and that these conversations give him insight into where AI is going. Khosla also said that a silicon shortage would keep Nvidia and Google chips priced at a premium for a couple of years. The discussion also touched on Nvidia's scandal, which the headline and show description reference, though the articles give no details of it. Anthropic investors who hold only that company's stake, Khosla suggested, would get more insight than investors spread across both firms.

Khosla's view on OpenAI's pricing and silicon was challenged on air by host Deidre Bosa, who noted that third-party serving firms such as Fireworks and Base 10 are making open-weight models easier to run. Bosa also noted that Google's TPUs had started to be sold to outside customers. Khosla replied that neo clouds buy Nvidia chips at premium prices and must sell at high prices, and that cost per hour of a chip had risen over the last couple of years. The articles do not say how the Nvidia scandal affects the broader AI ecosystem, and they end before the outcome of Anthropic's IPO or of OpenAI's enterprise and "dots" rollouts is known.

Articles.Title: OpenAI's Q3 results and Nvidia's scandal impact on the AI ecosystem

stories.Headline: Digital Health and AI: Key Regulatory, Reimbursement and Policy Developments
stories.Summary:
Last week, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services finalized its 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System rule and its Medicare Physician Fee Schedule rule, both of which address digital health and artificial intelligence. In the outpatient rule, CMS coined the term "Software as a Medical Service" for software that supports clinical decisions through algorithmic analysis. CMS also created an interim payment pathway, assigning qualifying services to New Technology Ambulatory Payment Classifications and establishing a new status indicator, O1. The policy does not guarantee separate payment for every AI-enabled tool, since payment still depends on service and coding requirements. CMS also finalized separate payment for certain stand-alone algorithmic analyses of previously completed laboratory data, including secondary analyses of genomic sequencing results.

The physician fee schedule rule did not create an AI-specific payment pathway, but it signals growing attention to how technology affects physician work and quality measurement. CMS issued a Request for Information seeking industry input on technology-enabled primary care and on how Medicare payment might account for clinical AI. The rule cites an estimated 25 percent penetration of AI documentation tools, such as ambient scribes, among U.S. physicians. CMS also said more than 40 percent of U.S. physicians had self-reported using OpenEvidence, an AI application that answers clinical questions from peer-reviewed sources. Many commenters expressed skepticism and urged CMS to ensure that any Medicare-paid AI demonstrates proven clinical value.

CMS said it would consider that feedback in future rulemaking. CMS addressed AI in the Medicare Annual Wellness Visit, stressing that a physician or other health professional must still perform the visit and that clinicians must retain responsibility for clinical decisions. The agency said AI may support components such as administering the Health Risk Assessment, reconciling medications for clinician verification, and drafting a personalized prevention plan for clinician review. CMS said it was not aware of how AI could conduct a cognitive assessment under the current standard.

Beneficiary-facing software used to implement a prevention plan must not constitute the practice of medicine or replace the beneficiary-clinician relationship, and it must comply with fraud and abuse laws, including the Anti-Kickback Statute. CMS may issue further guidance in future rulemaking. CMS also tightened oversight of remote patient monitoring and remote therapeutic monitoring after findings by the Office of the Inspector General about potential fraud, waste and abuse. The rule extends the established-patient requirement to remote therapeutic monitoring, so practitioners must furnish a separately reportable initiating face-to-face visit, in person or via telehealth, before monitoring begins.

CMS also finalized a requirement that clinical staff performing these services be directly employed by the billing practitioner or practice, subject to incident-to requirements. That requirement may materially affect digital health companies that provide outsourced monitoring services. CMS delayed its implementation until Jan. 1, 2029, giving providers and vendors more time to adjust their operating models. Separately, the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology streamlined portions of the federal health IT certification framework, and the American Medical Association released a clinical AI liability framework.

The AMA framework would allocate responsibility among clinicians, AI developers and deploying healthcare organizations based on each party's authority, access to information and ability to control or mitigate risk. It rejects the assumption that keeping a physician "in the loop" automatically shifts responsibility away from developers or health systems. Congress has also extended several Medicare telehealth flexibilities through Dec. 31, 2027, including audio-only telehealth and access from beneficiaries' homes. Pending legislation, including the PATIENT AI Act and Doctors Not AI Act, reflects continued congressional attention to AI reimbursement, oversight and privacy.

Articles.Title: Digital Health and AI: Key Regulatory, Reimbursement and Policy Developments - JD Supra

stories.Headline: Armanino builds an AI App Factory on Microsoft Foundry, cutting production time 89%
stories.Summary:
Armanino, an accounting, consulting, and technology firm in San Ramon, California, built an AI App Factory on Microsoft Foundry and GitHub Copilot, according to a Microsoft customer story dated November 11, 2026. The firm set out to grow by meeting rising customer demand for AI solutions without proportionally increasing its resources. Its production time for new AI applications fell by 89 percent. Consultants now turn a two-hour client session into finished requirements in 30 minutes. The firm also builds solutions it once found too costly to attempt.

The App Factory is a standardized four-phase delivery pipeline covering discovery, design, engineering, and launch, running end to end on one Microsoft stack. Discovery uses Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot, and design uses Microsoft Copilot Studio to build a client-facing agent prototype. Engineering runs on GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Azure DevOps, while launch adds automated test coverage through Playwright. Foundry serves as the landing zone for all factory output, carrying model orchestration, prompt management, evaluation pipelines, and production deployment. Armanino also moved from Claude and ChatGPT to GitHub Copilot for engineering, with the back end now entirely Microsoft.

Carmel Wynkoop, Partner, Artificial Intelligence Solutions at Armanino, said the firm had to reengineer its delivery workflows to be AI-native rather than simply adopt AI tools. Drew Armanino, Lead, Artificial Intelligence Solutions, said the firm's small core developer team had to produce output for a large business, and that constraint became the catalyst. Talbot Harty, Artificial Intelligence Delivery and Product Lead, said that after switching tooling to GitHub the team revved an enterprise application update in four hours. The article does not name a separate party responsible for the story beyond Armanino and Microsoft's own customer-story format.

Armanino's clients, many of which already operate in the Microsoft ecosystem, are affected by the change in how solutions are delivered and governed. Casey Williams, Director, Dynamics 365 Finance & Supply Chain at Armanino, said Requirements Miner has let the firm expedite FitGap reviews and bring in milestones sooner. Chris Hood, Director, Sales at Armanino, said the tool halves the time for discovery-to-solution discussions and product demonstrations. Drew Armanino said the firm's ability to engineer solutions has increased tenfold, and that many current projects would not have been attempted before because they were time and cost prohibitive. Wynkoop said the most consistent client reaction is surprise at seeing a working prototype instead of a strategy deck.

Before the factory, Armanino ran Claude for intake to functional spec and ChatGPT for use case intake, with standalone services in between that consumed engineering time on handoffs. Each new build restarted from zero on identity, security, deployment, and monitoring, and the firm's growth ambitions were limited by its developer headcount. The firm's Cloud Sync service, an Azure-native integration and analytics offering used by multiple customers, runs on Azure Functions, Azure SQL Database, Azure API Management, Azure App Service, and Microsoft Entra ID. The App Factory has produced a technical accounting memo drafter for ASC 606 revenue recognition analysis, Requirements Miner, a request-for-proposal generator, and an agentic application that replaced the marketing department's tooling. Armanino's listed industry is accounting and tax services, and it has 1,000 to 9,999 employees.

The article says Armanino is adding Microsoft Fabric as the governed data layer beneath the App Factory. It also says the factory pattern is moving into healthcare and adjacent industries, and that each shipped application is being productized for resale to mid-market clients. The articles do not give a timeline for either effort, the number of clients that have deployed factory-built applications, or the commercial terms of any resale. They also do not report how the 89 percent and 90 percent figures were measured beyond the firm's own statements.

Articles.Title: Armanino builds an AI App Factory on Microsoft Foundry, cutting production time 89%

stories.Headline: London-based AI chip startup Fractile raised $720M from Thrive, Founders Fund, and others, sources say at a $7B post-money valuation, up from ~$1.1B in May (George Hammond/Financial Times)
stories.Summary:
London-based AI chip startup Fractile has reportedly raised $720 million from investors including Thrive and Founders Fund, according to people familiar with the deal. The funding round, reported by the Financial Times on November 11, 2026, values the company at $7 billion after the investment. That figure is a sharp increase from the roughly $1.1 billion valuation the company was said to have in May. The articles available describe the round only through this headline and the sourcing behind it, and they do not name the other investors.

The reporting says the valuation has grown about sixfold in roughly six months, from about $1.1 billion in May to $7 billion now. The sums and dates in the report come from sources rather than from a company announcement. The available text does not explain how the capital will be used or what product milestones it is meant to fund. The Financial Times attributes the information to unnamed sources and credits George Hammond as the reporter on the story.

The articles do not include any statement from Fractile, Thrive or Founders Fund confirming the terms. Because the details rest on people close to the deal, the figures should be treated as reported rather than confirmed. The available articles give no further context about Fractile's technology, customers or competitors, and they say nothing about next steps such as a formal announcement or closing of the round. More to follow.

Articles.Title: London-based AI chip startup Fractile raised $720M from Thrive, Founders Fund, and others, sources say at a $7B post-money valuation, up from ~$1.1B in May (George Hammond/Financial Times)

stories.Headline: Why an ex-Cohere leader doesn’t want you to call his new law firm “AI-native”
stories.Summary:
Blackletter, a law firm founded by former Cohere and Blue J leaders, announced on Tuesday that it has raised $6 million USD in seed funding. The company was started by Jonathan Rosenbluth and David Stewart, both ex-Cohere product and engineering leaders, along with former Blue J COO Avi Brudner. Its goal is to run a law firm on top of its own AI legaltech platform. The firm is based in Toronto and New York City and uses fixed-fee, outcome-based pricing instead of the hourly billing common in the industry. It says it can deliver quality legal work faster and at lower cost than traditional firms.

The seed round is meant to help the company hire more lawyers and engineers. Blackletter is building tools for its own lawyers to use fully, which Rosenbluth says contrasts with vendors selling software to firms whose lawyers have little incentive to use it. The round was led by Lerer Hippeau, a New York City venture capital firm, with participation from Seven Stars, Maple VC, Garage Capital, and Ripple Ventures. Cohere co-founders Aidan Gomez, Ivan Zhang, and Nick Frosst also took part, as did TwelveLabs CEO Jae Lee and Adaption CEO Sara Hooker. Rosenbluth said the company has worked with 75 clients since emerging from stealth in June.

Rosenbluth rejects the description of Blackletter as an "AI-native law firm." He told BetaKit that calling it that suggests cheap and fast service, and that the firm is simply hiring strong lawyers. He compared the label to calling a firm Microsoft-native because it uses Microsoft Word. Clients named by the company include TwelveLabs, Fanatics, and Toronto-based Ada, though Rosenbluth declined to say whether Blackletter helped with Ada's recent $600 million CAD merger with Dialpad.

He said the idea for Blackletter came to him while at Cohere, when it became clear that AI should be improving legal services but he was not seeing that benefit as a client. Rosenbluth believes building the firm in both Canada and the United States will help make top-tier legal services more widely available. He expects the company to push the rest of the legal sector to innovate. The article does not describe any further timeline or plans beyond the seed funding and hiring.

Articles.Title: Why an ex-Cohere leader doesn’t want you to call his new law firm “AI-native”

stories.Headline: Elon Musk wants to build a s $24 billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Texas company town
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk's SpaceX wants to build a $24 billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Starbase, Texas, a city that hosts SpaceX's Starship rocket program. The city has posted a notice of a public hearing on a gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility within its corporate limits. The project has an initial cost of $24 billion and will apparently be owned by SpaceX. The site is described as a massive 10 gigawatt facility that goes up for approval in December. Starbase is essentially a company town, since it mostly sits on land owned by SpaceX and its population mostly comprises company employees.

The articles describe the project as part of SpaceX's push to build 10 gigawatts of compute in 2027 alone. The $24 billion budget covers only the initial phases, and the company's announcement says the project could include future expansions. The facility could be one of the biggest and most expensive data center projects focused on a single site. The project might face less local opposition than the company's Memphis facilities. Gas turbines would power the facility, as they do at the company's other data centers.

Bloomberg reports that the project could face resistance from incoming Texas governor Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned against approving new data centers. Hinojosa has pledged to hold off on such approvals until the state legislature enacts stronger protections against potential harms from those projects. The articles say her arrival in the governor's office could override the local climate that might otherwise favor the project. The articles do not say how Hinojosa will act on the proposal itself.

Musk's company, which the articles also call SpaceXSI, has been building its Colossus I and Colossus II data centers near the Mississippi-Tennessee border. Those projects have faced backlash, including a lawsuit from area residents seeking to curb pollutants from the large number of gas turbines required to power them. Area residents are the people most directly affected by those pollutants, according to the lawsuit. The articles note that data center measures lost badly in the recent U.S. midterm elections. Musk has since written on X that data centers in space look appealing right now.

Beyond Starbase, SpaceX is working on launching data centers into space, and Musk has outlined a first-generation AI1 compute satellite with a 150kW peak compute payload. The company has also submitted a proposal to the FCC for a 1-million-satellite Orbital Data Center System. The articles say this space work could accelerate after the midterm results. The articles leave open whether the Starbase project will be approved in December. They also leave open whether Hinojosa will move to block it, and whether the company will expand the facility beyond its initial phases.

Articles.Title: Elon Musk wants to build a s $24 billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Texas company town

stories.Headline: Our AI Problem Isn’t Too Little Regulation. It’s Too Much.
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion essay rather than a news report, so there is no discrete event to write up as a news story. Published on November 10, 2026, on the Learn Liberty website and co-written by Alex Tokarev, an associate professor of economics and philosophy at Northwood University, and Kristin Tokarev, a producer for Stossel TV, the piece argues that the United States faces too much AI regulation rather than too little. The authors say that lawmakers respond to new technology with alarm, hearings, and calls for restrictions, and they claim that America led in AI because entrepreneurs, investors, and engineers were free to act without government direction. They note that 13 of the top 15 AI applications are American, with the most successful Chinese ones ranked fourth and tenth.

The authors contend that China is investing across the AI ecosystem, including semiconductors, cloud computing, autonomous systems, and energy infrastructure, with the aim of controlling the technology stack. They argue that Washington should not answer with more central planning, pointing to the Soviet Union's failure to match Silicon Valley as evidence. Their main example of regulatory harm is Defense Department procurement, which they say buys software as though it were aircraft carriers, so that contracts can take years to clear reviews and the technology is outdated by delivery. They say that compliance burdens favor large companies able to employ armies of compliance officers, and they urge a risk-based approach, arguing that software predicting helicopter engine failures should not face the same scrutiny as software used in lethal targeting. They also say that cybersecurity standards, accountability, and human supervision for autonomous weapons are appropriate, while maintaining that not every application carries the same risk.

The essay does not identify any specific pending bill, rule, or agency action, and it does not name a particular lawmaker whose proposal it opposes. It concludes that America's advantage has come from free enterprise rather than central planning, and that the AI contest is about whether free societies can out-innovate authoritarian ones. The article itself says it expresses only the authors' opinion and not the position of Students For Liberty, the organization that hosts it. It also promotes the group's Local Coordinator Program and invites readers to join. The piece does not describe any subsequent developments, so what happens next is not reported.

Articles.Title: Our AI Problem Isn’t Too Little Regulation. It’s Too Much.

stories.Headline: Softbank loses $3.7 billion on canceled AI data center gas turbine orders days after denying Elon Musk’s claim it was defaulting
stories.Summary:
SoftBank has taken a $3.7 billion loss after canceling reservations for gas turbines meant to power AI data centers, according to a report from the Wall Street Journal published around November 11, 2026. The Japanese investment firm had reserved more than 13 gigawatts of power-producing turbines, citing unnamed people familiar with the orders. The company's CFO had recently rejected a claim by Elon Musk that SoftBank had defaulted on turbine contracts. SoftBank has now canceled its remaining reservations with GE Vernova, its turbine supplier, and unwound contracts for orders that were too far gone. The reserved capacity amounts to more than six Hoover Dams' worth of power.

SoftBank had planned a 9.2-gigawatt power plant in Ohio, with construction scheduled for early 2027 and a cost of $33 billion. That plant would supply power to a neighboring eight-gigawatt data center. The data center is to be leased to OpenAI, and Nvidia had entered discussions about guaranteeing around $250 billion of financing for the project. Turbine manufacturers regularly charge customers tens of millions of dollars per gigawatt. Orders for turbines must be placed years before they are needed, and SoftBank had placed large orders expecting demand to outstrip supply.

SoftBank's chief executive, Masayoshi Son, believed the turbines would be vital to the company's earning potential. The company told investors on a recent earnings call that the orders had been placed to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortages. SoftBank says the cancellations were voluntary and that it did not default on its orders. Chief Financial Officer Yoshimitsu Goto said the claim that it had defaulted was simply not correct at all. Musk had made the default claim in a post on his X social network.

The turbines convert natural gas into the electricity used by data centers. The reserved turbines were intended for AI data centers, the sector the reservations were meant to serve. Musk, who is the chief executive of xAI, is the source of the default allegation that SoftBank rejects. The articles do not describe who else might be affected by the cancellations.

The reservations were made after SoftBank initially planned to use the turbines for future gas-powered plants, before the company changed direction. By early 2026, SoftBank had reserved more power generation capacity than the entire state of Connecticut. The articles say the company cornered a large share of global gas turbine production capacity. The cancellation followed SoftBank's denial of Musk's claim that it had defaulted on turbine blade contracts.

The articles do not say what SoftBank will do with the Ohio plant or the OpenAI-leased data center after the cancellations. They also do not state whether GE Vernova or other parties will take further action, or what the remaining effects on SoftBank's earnings will be. Whether Nvidia's financing discussions will continue is not addressed. More details on the company's next steps are not given in the articles.

Articles.Title: Softbank loses $3.7 billion on canceled AI data center gas turbine orders days after denying Elon Musk’s claim it was defaulting

stories.Headline: Elvis AI Voice Lawsuit, Olivia Rodrigo’s ‘Take Me Home,’ BTS Song Case & More Top Music Law News
stories.Summary:
Elvis Presley Enterprises, which owns the late singer's intellectual property, sued Suno, the AI music firm, in a lawsuit filed last week. The suit accuses Suno of stealing Presley's likeness by allowing users to clone his singing voice. The complaint calls Presley's voice "unmistakable and iconic" and says the identity behind it was stolen and stored on Suno's servers. The case is described as a follow-up to an earlier Presley lawsuit against Anthropic filed two weeks before. The article is part of Billboard's weekly Legal Beat newsletter dated November 10, 2026.

The new case differs from the earlier Anthropic suit and from many others against Suno, which center on copyrighted material used to train AI models. Instead, it invokes likeness rights, state-level protections covering a person's name, image and voice from commercial exploitation. The article cites the ELVIS Act as part of the claim. It also notes that Suno may raise counter-arguments, which the full Billboard story discusses. Presley's estate is the party bringing the suit against the company.

The article gives no further statement from Elvis Presley Enterprises beyond the lawsuit's language quoted above. It also gives no direct response from Suno to the new claims. The article attributes the lawsuit's accusations to the complaint itself. Those accusations concern the cloning of the singer's voice and the commercial use of his identity.

Beyond the Presley case, the newsletter lists other music law stories from the same week. A lawsuit against HYBE over the BTS song "Swim" was dropped by its accusers less than four months after filing. Days before the Presley suit, Suno asked a judge to dismiss a case brought by Jason Isbell and other artists over similar name-and-likeness claims. Other legal items in the newsletter include a copyright case over Dua Lipa's "Levitating," which she settled.

The article does not say how the Presley lawsuit will proceed, what court it was filed in, or what damages the estate seeks. It does not report any ruling on the new complaint. The newsletter also reports that the Presley case, the Isbell case and other suits against Suno are pending, and it does not give their outcomes. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Elvis AI Voice Lawsuit, Olivia Rodrigo’s ‘Take Me Home,’ BTS Song Case & More Top Music Law News

stories.Headline: Scott Wiener was the AI-safety world’s congressional pick. Can the freshman find his voice on Capitol Hill?
stories.Summary:
Scott Wiener, a San Francisco Democrat and congressman-elect, won his race to replace Nancy Pelosi on November 6, 2026, and is now a freshman in Congress. He authored the country's first major state AI safety law, and his move to Washington, D.C. comes as Democrats take control of the House. Democrats appear ready to pursue comprehensive national regulation of artificial intelligence for the first time. The main open question is whether President Donald Trump would sign such legislation. Rookie members rarely receive the most coveted committee assignments on Capitol Hill, which makes Wiener's regulatory role uncertain.

Lofgren, the ranking member on the House Committee on Science, Space and Tech, said the midterms showed Americans want responsible action on AI. The House Committee on Energy and Commerce has been a main venue for AI-safety fights, but experts doubt Wiener will get a seat there. The Science, Space and Tech committee is open to first-timers, and House Democrats have been considering a new select committee on AI. Wiener told MIT Technology Review he would be eager to serve on that select committee if it is created, but he declined to comment for this story.

Lofgren told Mission Local she welcomes all excitement about joining her committee and is eager to speak with prospective members. An AI safety lobbyist in D.C., who spoke anonymously, said he would be surprised if Wiener did not land on the Science, Space and Tech committee. The day after Wiener's win, an outside evaluation team from Model Evaluation and Threat Research, or METR, released a report on Nov. 5 about Anthropic's use of AI. The Berkeley, California-based nonprofit said Anthropic's AI had sped up the company's research, but Anthropic redacted major portions of the evidence reviewed.

METR said AI is not yet able to make "highly significant and fully autonomous contributions" to the most important parts of model training. Some observers read the report as evidence that Anthropic's AI systems are improving themselves recursively, a risk for those worried about models refining themselves faster than humans can understand. Jake Mendel of Coefficient Giving said he needed to call his family, while Dane Sherburn, a former OpenAI preparedness team member, said he felt sick. George Mason University economist Robin Hanson was skeptical, calling it more like a one-time speedup than continuous acceleration.

Last year Wiener authored successful state legislation setting transparency and reporting requirements for AI models, and he has opposed more hardline stances such as a moratorium on data centers. His campaign received millions of dollars in support from Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed AI safety nonprofit, along with direct contributions from Anthropic and OpenAI employees. Wiener has said there was "no Anthropic money in this race," and Anthropic said it earmarked its giving for non-political purposes. Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, said Energy and Commerce will likely handle the biggest AI issues, though it is highly competitive.

Democrats in power have not settled how they will handle AI regulation, and the unnamed D.C. lobbyist said progressives may favor oversight investigations while moderates may focus on repairing the party's relationship with big tech. The federal question of preemption could void state laws such as Wiener's legislation, which have appeared in the absence of a comprehensive federal law. Haworth said AI touches so many areas that legislation could come from less obvious panels, such as the Veterans Affairs committee, which could act on AI scams. The articles do not say which committee Wiener will be assigned to, whether a select committee will be created, or whether any AI bill will reach the president's desk.

Articles.Title: Scott Wiener was the AI-safety world’s congressional pick. Can the freshman find his voice on Capitol Hill?

stories.Headline: Chinese banks have been using artificial intelligence (AI) for their work in earnest, from simple ta..
stories.Summary:
Chinese banks have been putting artificial intelligence to work in earnest, moving from simple task automation toward systems that accelerate research and handle complex jobs. According to a report by the Chinese outlet Caixin on the 11th, Jiangsu Bank replaced 1.2 million cumulative business hours through AI-related applications. Shanghai Pudong Development Bank handled a workload equivalent to more than 2,500 internal digital workers per year. The Bank of China's AI system has reached the ability to identify 305 types of documents across 3,800 business scenarios. Overall, the strongest results so far come in tasks that involve repetitive, regular, large-scale information processing.

Those tasks include document processing, customer response, payment fraud detection, and preliminary credit ratings. Jiangsu Bank cut the time needed for credit approval for small and medium-sized enterprises by 30 percent after introducing AI. Investment research is still being tested, since AI can shorten basic work such as collecting information, analyzing financial statements, selecting items, and drafting reports. However, the article says this does not mean AI can make reliable investment decisions. Reports generated by AI serve as reference material or a starting point, and they are hard to apply to external publications or decisions carrying large financial risk.

When information is incomplete or conflicting, humans still interpret results, verify evidence, and make the final call. The next step is expected to be "AI agents" that carry out several connected tasks. Jungshin Securities has developed its own AI for exchange-traded fund screening, stock analysis, and financial statement analysis. Major institutions such as the China Commercial Bank and the China International Finance Corporation have introduced financial AI solutions, including Kimi from the startup Moonshot.

The article notes that the reliability of such agents depends on the quality and currency of the information available to them. Financial institutions must therefore supply accurate, up-to-date data and define the access rights and scope of their AI agents. Cost and integration remain obstacles, and the article describes them in detail. An official at Tencent's Workbuddy platform said self-built AI projects alone cost millions to tens of millions of yuan, roughly tens of billions of won, with maintenance costs on top.

Self-built systems also take about three months to update, while Software as a Service can be updated in two days, though it brings security and data risks. Fragmented data and a gap between business and technology staff also limit what AI can do. Cybersecurity is another concern, as the Bank for International Settlements estimated that simple cyberattack costs fell from $50 to $100 per case and sophisticated attacks from $5,000 to $10,000. Fan Yuan, chairman of the cybersecurity company Anheng Information, argued that the financial industry should review its security governance for the AI era.

Articles.Title: Chinese banks have been using artificial intelligence (AI) for their work in earnest, from simple ta..

stories.Headline: Canopy Coworker AI System Now Available to All Firms
stories.Summary:
Canopy has made its Coworker AI system available to all firms on its Standard, Plus, and Premium plans, announcing the release on November 10, 2026. Coworker is offered as an Experimental Feature, which Canopy describes as an early-access program similar to an open beta. The system is an AI teammate built into Canopy that can operate inside the platform for a firm, taking on tasks such as chasing missing documents, building custom reports, and recommending next steps. Canopy says it is meant to improve productivity and profitability for firms.

Hanna Bjornn, SVP of Product at Canopy, said that much of the work draining accounting firms is the chasing, checking, reminding, and cleaning up rather than the accounting itself. According to Bjornn, Coworker works in three steps: the firm sets an objective, the system carries out the workflow across the whole client base, and it flags only the exceptions that need professional review. To help firms test it on real work, Canopy is adding bonus credits on top of what each plan already includes through April 2027. Because Coworker sits inside Canopy, it already knows each firm's clients, team, workflows, and permissions and can begin acting on them right away.

Firms that used Coworker during early access described several uses. One team had it locate clients with heavily billed bookkeeping hours but no monthly contract, producing upsell leads from a single request. Another firm had it fix 338 bookkeeping tasks missing tax-year tags without anyone editing them one by one. Coworker also compared client-sent documents against prior-year records to find missing items and draft follow-ups, which the article says was among the most-used capabilities in early access. Canopy further reports that Coworker can prepare client briefs, run weekly data quality checks, and identify multi-office staff with capacity for a batch of returns.

Canopy states that Coworker runs entirely inside its secure platform, so client data is never passed to outside AI tools. It follows each firm's user and role permissions, logs every action, and asks for approval wherever the firm requires it, with more independence possible as trust builds. Coworker arrives one week after Canopy released Tax Workflow Automation, which handles intake, preparation, and delivery for each return, while Coworker monitors all returns at once and drafts follow-ups for blocked or missing items. Canopy presents the two together as steps toward an autonomous firm where routine work runs on its own.

Articles.Title: Canopy Coworker AI System Now Available to All Firms - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Anthropic agrees to strict AI privacy rules in schools
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company, has agreed to a set of strict privacy rules for schools that use its tools, according to a report published November 11, 2026, by District Administration. The standards apply automatically to schools that use Claude for Teachers, the article says. They ban AI providers from training their models on data belonging to students and staff. The agreement was reached with the American Federation of Teachers and the United Federation of Teachers, the two unions named in the report.

The article gives no further figures, dates for when the rules take effect, or penalties for violations, so those details cannot be reported here. What the report does establish is the core change: schools using the product are protected from having student and staff information used to train the company's models. The rules cover the schools that use Claude for Teachers rather than all AI tools in education. Beyond that, the report offers only the headline terms of the deal.

The article names Anthropic and the two teachers' unions as the parties to the agreement, and it does not include direct statements from any of them. Micah Ward is listed as the reporter. The piece appears alongside related coverage on AI in schools, including a separate story about Google restricting its search engine in schools that ban AI, but those stories are not part of this agreement. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Anthropic agrees to strict AI privacy rules in schools - District Administration

stories.Headline: How CUBE Is Transforming Global Regulatory Compliance with AI
stories.Summary:
CUBE, a regulatory technology company, is extending its AI software by placing its regulatory intelligence directly inside the platforms businesses already use. Its Powered By technology lets software providers access CUBE's regulatory data and AI agents without having to collect, organise or maintain the underlying information themselves. The latest example is Thomson Reuters, which has integrated CUBE's technology into CoCounsel Legal. The article says the integration gives corporate legal teams and international law firms access to regulatory information across more than 150 countries and could reach up to one million legal professionals.

Through this integration, CoCounsel Legal users can research laws, rules, guidance and regulatory developments alongside Westlaw, Practical Law and Reuters content. CUBE has also published internal benchmark findings comparing its regulatory intelligence agents with two leading AI models. The evaluation, conducted in August 2026, involved 13 regulatory queries covering the UK, Spain and the UAE. According to CUBE, its agents identified three to four times more essential regulatory material than the competing models, and six to 17 times more regulatory guidance, codes and supervisory material, depending on the model. The article notes these results come from CUBE's own evaluation rather than independent testing.

Ben Richmond, Founder and CEO of CUBE, said the company aims to be the regulatory data infrastructure that the world can trust and that delivering regulatory intelligence at the point of need is the future of the industry. Thomson Reuters said its subject matter experts assessed how CUBE's content would complement its existing resources before the integration. Its representatives said that global coverage and quality were both essential to them and that CUBE met both requirements. The article also says CUBE has spent 15 years building a database covering more than 12,000 issuing bodies across 750 jurisdictions, validated by 250 subject matter experts and processing more than ten million data points each year. CUBE adds that 24 of the world's 29 Global Systemically Important Banks already use its regulatory intelligence.

Articles.Title: How CUBE Is Transforming Global Regulatory Compliance with AI

stories.Headline: Gilbert + Tobin rethinks the business of law with AI
stories.Summary:
Gilbert + Tobin, one of Australia's leading corporate law firms, has been rethinking how it works with AI, according to an OpenAI interview with its Partner and Chief Executive Officer, Sam Nickless, published on November 11, 2026. The firm began by encouraging its people to experiment with AI, while barring the entry of client data or confidential information. It then introduced ChatGPT Enterprise in a controlled setting, and later ChatGPT Work and Codex to support defined, multistep workflows. Throughout, people remain responsible for reviewing and approving the output. The article describes the arrangement as built around secure handling and governance, not cost cutting.

Australian data residency, contractual protections, role-based access and administrative controls were cited as the basis for scaling up use while meeting the firm's and its clients' requirements. Nickless said the main value so far lies in freeing staff to spend more time on client meetings, coaching their teams and mentoring future leaders. He also said the firm did not set usage targets, and that 87% of enabled ChatGPT users were active, more than twice the rate the firm typically sees for other tools. Nickless attributes the adoption largely to leaders using the technology themselves, which he says sets the tone for others. The firm's business transformation team demonstrated workflows tailored to different functions, and videos, showcases, challenges and an early AI bounty drew ideas from across the organisation.

Nickless also described a personal "digital twin," a custom GPT built from his writing and feedback, which his direct reports use to test their thinking before meeting him. He said the tool does not make decisions or speak for him. In one example, Nickless said the firm used ChatGPT Work in a confidential annual review involving its 120 partners, completing file updates and PDF bundling in minutes at a cost he put at about $62. He advised other chief executives to use the technology themselves, pair that with clear governance, and keep people accountable for results. The article is a promotional case study published by OpenAI, and it does not describe any further steps or timelines for the firm's rollout.

Articles.Title: Gilbert + Tobin rethinks the business of law with AI

stories.Headline: K Altman Law Highlights School Artificial Intelligence Controls and Questions for Families
stories.Summary:
Google said on November 3 that it plans to turn off access to the Gemini application, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search for kindergarten through twelfth-grade student accounts until school administrators explicitly enable them. The company described these changes in an announcement about administrator controls and new learning features in products used by schools. It said it would provide schools with further details in the coming months, before the changes roll out. The announcement also described learning features in Search and Classroom, along with the timing of the proposed updates.

K Altman Law, a firm led by Keith Altman, has highlighted questions for families and schools as artificial intelligence tools become more common in educational technology. The firm says that artificial intelligence features may appear in standalone applications, classroom products, or search experiences, and that disabling one product does not automatically disable every such feature in another. Availability and controls can depend on the product, the school's configuration, the account, and the timing of any changes. The firm suggests that a clear school technology policy can explain which tools are available and how students are expected to use them.

Altman said that families should have understandable information about the technology students can access through school accounts. He said schools and parents can support informed use by discussing available controls, privacy expectations, and the appropriate ways for students to seek help from trusted adults. The release does not name any official responsible for enforcing these changes beyond Google's own announcement. Google's plans were described as proposed, and the release does not say how those plans will apply to any particular school district.

The firm recommends that families ask schools which artificial intelligence tools and search features are available through a student's account and device. It also suggests requesting the school's current technology-use, privacy, monitoring, and parent-notification policies, including any anticipated changes. Families are advised to ask whether separate controls apply to standalone applications, classroom tools, and search, and when changes are expected locally. The release notes that students who use accessibility tools or receive disability-related services should ask how any technology changes will affect their access. The release is general information, not legal advice, and laws and procedures vary by jurisdiction.

Articles.Title: K Altman Law Highlights School Artificial Intelligence Controls and Questions for Families

stories.Headline: OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit over $30 billion AI data center
stories.Summary:
Residents of Effingham County, Georgia, have filed a RICO lawsuit against county commissioners, county officials, OpenAI and its affiliates over the company's "Project Camellia" data center. The lawsuit alleges that the defendants conspired to get the project approved through closed-door negotiations and confidential agreements. The plaintiffs are Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr. and Raymond Carver, who are seeking civil damages. They say the project has harmed their property values, and that purchase offers for nearby homes have dropped or been withdrawn since the data center was announced.

The lawsuit names all Effingham County Commissioners as defendants, including Chairperson Damon Rahn, Forrest Floyd, Roger Burdette, Jamie DeLoach, Elizabeth Helmly and Phil Kieffer. It also names County Manager Tim Callanan, Industrial Development Authority CEO Brandt Herndon, the Authority itself, OpenAI, Octans GA LLC and Savannah Industrial Development LLC. The project is expected to cost between $20 billion and $30 billion and be built across five phases, with a planned compute capacity of 3.2 gigawatts. OpenAI has promised that it will pay the full cost of its required infrastructure upgrades and that the site will use a closed-loop water system with minimal water use.

The plaintiffs allege fraud and concealment through non-disclosure agreements and misleading public statements, which they say kept residents uninformed about the project. They also allege a civil conspiracy to advance the project through confidential negotiations and closed-door decisions. The complaint further claims improper land transactions, zoning violations and civil racketeering. The articles do not record a response from the named defendants.

Opponents say the county tried to secure the land, tax incentives and zoning approvals without informing residents until key decisions were final and contracts signed. The lawsuit's allegations are based on those claims, and the articles say the project's supporters have made the promises about utility costs and water use. The plaintiffs' claims about property values rest on the withdrawn purchase offers for nearby residential properties. Residents of the county are the group the lawsuit says is affected.

The RICO Act was originally designed to counter organized crime, and Georgia's version is less strict than the federal law. Georgia has used its version in the 2023 election racketeering case against Donald Trump and 18 others over the 2020 presidential election results, and in Young Thug's trial over YSL Records. Georgia State University criminal justice professor Volkan Topalli has said the state's version is too broad. Separately, developers have faced complaints for using non-disclosure agreements in data center negotiations, and West Feliciana Parish in Louisiana closed a data center deal without one.

Articles.Title: OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit over $30 billion AI data center

stories.Headline: 6 Members of Congress Set for 'Broadband and AI' as Reps. Pramila Jayapal and Jennifer McClellan Join Keynote Lineup
stories.Summary:
Broadband Breakfast announced that two House Democrats who are writing artificial intelligence legislation, Reps. Pramila Jayapal of Washington and Jennifer McClellan of Virginia, will deliver keynotes at its Broadband and AI in the Next Congress conference. Their additions raise the number of members of Congress on the program to six. Rep. Greg Landsman of Ohio will take part in a fireside chat with the outlet's editor and publisher, Drew Clark. Sen. Ed Markey, Rep. Buddy Carter and Rep. Nanette Barragán were announced earlier as keynote speakers.

The announcement was published on November 10, 2026. The conference is set for Tuesday, December 1, at the National Press Club in Washington. Registration for in-person attendance costs $245, and Breakfast Club members receive an additional $100 off. The program begins at 9 a.m., with doors opening no later than 8:30 a.m., in the Grand Ballroom.

Comcast and Broadband Nation Expo are gold sponsors, and INCOMPAS is a silver sponsor. Full program details and registration are available on the event page. Jayapal has represented Washington's Seventh District, which includes most of Seattle, since 2017, and she co-leads the House version of the AI Civil Rights Act. That bill would bar companies from using biased algorithms in high-stakes decisions and require testing before and after deployment.

In October 2026 she released a framework for a national AI charter that would require AI companies to meet public-benefit conditions. McClellan has represented Virginia's Fourth District, which includes Richmond, since 2023, and in March 2026 she introduced the bipartisan AI-Ready Networks Act with Rep. Jay Obernolte. That bill, H.R. 7783, would direct the National Telecommunications and Information Administration to report on how AI is being adopted in U.S. commercial telecommunications networks. Landsman has written legislation requiring data centers to cover the full cost of their energy and infrastructure needs, while Barragán introduced the Artificial Intelligence Environmental Impacts Act with Rep. Don Beyer.

Markey, who authored the Telecommunications Act of 1996 in the House, released an AI Accountability Agenda in July 2026. Carter is the lead sponsor of the American Broadband Deployment Act, H.R. 2289. The conference is organized around four panels covering catastrophic AI risk, permitting reform, data center power and ratepayer protection, and federal preemption versus state AI rules. Additional speakers are still to be announced.

Articles.Title: 6 Members of Congress Set for 'Broadband and AI' as Reps. Pramila Jayapal and Jennifer McClellan Join Keynote Lineup

stories.Headline: Litera Brings Document Comparison and Firm AI Search to Microsoft Copilot for Legal - LawSites
stories.Summary:
Litera announced on November 10, 2026, in Chicago, that its Litera Compare and Firm AI Search tools are now available inside Microsoft Copilot for legal through plugins. The announcement describes Litera as a Legal AI platform provider that unifies the practice and business of law. Litera also said it has adopted Microsoft 365 E7, the Frontier Suite, which the company says gives it access to the most advanced tier of Microsoft's enterprise AI stack. The company frames the integration as a follow-on to its recent announcement as a Microsoft Copilot for legal launch partner. The articles describe the launch as bringing 30 years of deterministic document comparison accuracy into the environment where lawyers work.

Through the plugins, lawyers can ask Copilot in plain language to compare documents, and Copilot calls Litera's comparison engine to generate a legal-grade redline. Litera Compare works across Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files, and the company says its proprietary algorithm is more accurate than general-purpose LLMs. Firm AI Search connects matter databases, CRM platforms, expertise profiles and experience records into one conversational interface. Its answers are cited and respect ethical walls and access permissions. A sample query asks which firm lawyers have handled cross-border M&A work for pharmaceutical companies in Germany, and the search draws on Litera Foundation, matter systems and expertise databases.

Joey Benedek, Senior Vice President of Product Management at Litera, said law firms and corporate legal departments are increasingly making Copilot their productivity standard. Benedek said the integration brings legal intelligence into that environment and that Compare delivers the deterministic accuracy high-stakes legal work demands. Carina Negreanu, Partner Director, Science & Verticals at Microsoft, said Copilot is designed to be the AI layer where legal professionals work. Negreanu said Litera's integration is a strong example of how partners with deep industry expertise can extend Copilot's value for legal professionals. The articles identify Litera's own leaders and Microsoft's representative as the sources of these statements.

Law firms and corporate legal departments are the groups the articles name as the users who depend on these capabilities. Benedek said the E7 adoption is meant to speed how quickly new capabilities reach firms and in-house teams. The articles say Litera serves more than 15,000 global customers and over 1 million daily users, including 99% of the Am Law 100. Litera is integrated directly into Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace across devices, according to the company. The articles present these figures as Litera's own description of its reach and do not report any independent assessment of the tools' performance.

Litera's own description places the company's roots in 30 years of legal expertise, and the articles say it combines legal technology with Lito, its award-winning Legal AI agent. The articles report that Litera offers AI solutions spanning legal drafting, document comparison, contract review, knowledge management and business development. The articles were published by LawSites on November 11, 2026, with author Robert Ambrogi. Press contacts listed in the release are Jared Albert of Litera and Tracy Wemett of BroadPR. The articles do not describe any pricing, availability dates beyond the announcement, or customer deployments.

Articles.Title: Litera Brings Document Comparison and Firm AI Search to Microsoft Copilot for Legal - LawSites

stories.Headline: SEA AI funding rises 121 percent to $4.2 billion in 9M 2026 - Tracxn
stories.Summary:
Southeast Asian artificial intelligence companies raised $4.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, according to a statement from Tracxn released on Thursday, November 12, 2026. That total is up 121 percent from $1.9 billion in the same period of 2025 and 453 percent above the $768 million raised in the first nine months of 2024. The funding came across 28 rounds, which is down 12 percent from 32 a year earlier. The firm said the total was concentrated in a small number of very large rounds, with the ten largest accounting for 98 percent of all funding.

The single biggest deal was Kling AI's $2.8 billion Series D in July 2026, backed by BlueFive Capital, CPE and Guofang Capital among others, which alone equaled 66 percent of the total. Sharpa followed with a $670 million Series D in August 2026, backed by Alibaba, Meituan and Tencent among others, and Zelostech raised a $300 million Series C in February 2026. The average round rose to $152 million from $60 million in the first nine months of 2025. Late stage companies took $3.8 billion, or 89 percent of the total, while early stage funding fell 25 percent to $444 million and seed funding rose 28 percent to $33.8 million.

Tracxn's figures show the enterprise applications segment raised $3.1 billion, about 16 times the amount it drew a year earlier, and Singapore-based companies accounted for essentially all of the capital. The number of investors backing the sector fell to 56 from 69, and 39 of them were investing in Southeast Asian AI for the first time. Exits were limited to one acquisition and one public listing, with MiniMax listing in January 2026 at a market capitalization of $6.5 billion and Manus being acquired by US-based Meta in April 2026 for an undisclosed sum. No new unicorns emerged during the period, the same as in the first nine months of 2025.

Articles.Title: SEA AI funding rises 121 percent to $4.2 billion in 9M 2026 - Tracxn

stories.Headline: Mercedes Lawyer Joins AI Native Compound Law
stories.Summary:
Compound Law, an AI-native law firm based in Berlin, has hired Marc Schuba, a former White & Case lawyer who most recently served as Legal Counsel at Mercedes-Benz, and Philipp Brandt, a business lawyer with more than 20 years of experience, who joins as a partner. The firm was co-founded by the former General Counsel of Zenjob, Julian Jantze, who is now its Chief Legal Officer. The article reports the hires on November 11, 2026. The move is notable because it involves an experienced in-house lawyer from a major corporation joining a firm built around a model that avoids the billable hour and puts AI at the centre of its work. The firm runs on two linked companies: a regulated law firm that advises clients and is responsible for the legal work, and a technology company that builds Compound OS, its AI platform.

Compound OS uses AI agents to prepare research, carry out analysis and draft documents, after which a lawyer reviews every result and is accountable for the final output to the client. Work is billed at fixed prices agreed up front rather than at hourly rates. The new hires will cover IT and AI law, data protection and intellectual property. The firm's focus is Germany and the EU, where, according to the article, the top 100 German law firms billed more than €10bn last year, and it plans to extend into further markets as it grows. Schuba told the publication that the traditional law firm model is out of date because it sells the same judgment repeatedly by the hour.

He argued that good legal judgment can be captured, refined and applied at scale, so that the firm codifies it once, lets its agents apply it, and improves it with each matter, which he said makes competitive fixed pricing possible. Jantze said that both new partners have long built their own software and online tools, and that clients with questions on software contracts, the EU AI Act, trademarks or a crisis will be routed directly to a partner with years of experience in the field. The article places the hires within a wider pattern in which experienced lawyers leave traditional firms to work in firms that do not bill by the hour, and it notes that these so-called NewMod firms are increasingly taking on complex, high-value work rather than only startup contracts or bulk review. The author suggests that large commercial firms are still using AI within a billing model that often works against its wider adoption, and expects more AI-native firms to appear. The article does not say what further steps Compound Law will take or when it will enter new markets.

Articles.Title: Mercedes Lawyer Joins AI Native Compound Law - Artificial Lawyer

stories.Headline: OCC Gives Bank Examiners a New Playbook for Reviewing AI
stories.Summary:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency released a new guide on November 4 called the "OCC Supervisory Framework on Bank Use of Super Intelligence," which is meant to help its examiners review how banks use artificial intelligence. The guide focuses on generative AI, which creates text and other content, and agentic AI, which can act without a person stepping in each time. The agency used the term super intelligence because the executive branch adopted it in place of artificial intelligence, following a September 29 executive order signed by President Donald Trump. Some AI tools now handle credit decisions, customer service and fraud detection, which prompted the agency to set out how examiners should check them. The article frames the release as a response to the growing amount of work banks are handing to these systems.

The guide does not create new rules for banks, according to an analysis from the law firm Ballard Spahr, and it works as a resource for examiners instead. Banks will not treat AI as a separate risk category, and examiners will instead look at how AI changes risks banks already manage, including fraud, privacy, cybersecurity and work with outside vendors. The OCC built the guide around six areas, asking what an AI system is allowed to do, what happens when it makes a mistake, what guardrails exist, who is watching, how a bank recovers from failure, and whether safety checks keep working over time. The guide also ties risk to how much freedom a system has, and it lays out four risk levels, with autonomous payment bots and instant credit decisions at the top and internal tools that never touch customer data at the bottom. The OCC warned that a person who simply clicks approve does not provide real oversight, and reviewers need the skills, facts and power to reject or stop what the AI does.

The OCC's position is that banks remain responsible for their AI systems, and a bank is still on the hook if its AI breaks the law, the analysis said. The agency pointed to customer harm from chatbots that give wrong answers about fees, interest rates or account balances, which could lead to legal trouble. Because many banks buy their AI from outside companies, vendors face extra scrutiny, and the guide asks whether contracts spell out who pays when an AI tool causes harm. It also asks whether vendors must warn banks before changing how their AI works, since a vendor could add new AI features to an old product without the bank noticing the new risks. In a bulletin released with the guide, the OCC said the document sets no binding standards and banks are not expected to use it to grade their own AI programs.

Even without binding force, the analysis said banks should not ignore the guide, which offers a clear preview of what examiners may ask in future bank exams. Banks are encouraged to study it and check whether current risk and compliance programs already cover the issues the OCC raised. Institutions that find gaps now may have an easier time when examiners arrive, the analysis suggested. The article does not say whether the OCC plans further guidance or enforcement actions tied to AI, so those details remain unclear.

Articles.Title: OCC Gives Bank Examiners a New Playbook for Reviewing AI - PYMNTS.com

stories.Headline: Pactum: Procurement’s Execution Layer for the Agentic AI Age
stories.Summary:
Pactum, a procurement technology company, has been developing AI agents that carry out procurement tasks themselves rather than only supporting human staff, according to an interview published on November 12, 2026 by Procurement Magazine. The interview features Paige Wei-Cox, the company's Chief Product Officer, who has more than 25 years of enterprise technology experience, including two decades at SAP where she led SAP Business Network. The company started by letting enterprises negotiate with thousands of suppliers at scale, and it has since widened its aim toward a connected AI layer for indirect procurement. That layer rests on four capabilities: Intake, Alignment, Negotiation and Sourcing.

The newly launched Intake Agent applies procurement policies and category strategies to purchasing requests, decides how goods or services should be bought, and prepares aligned, compliant requisitions. The Alignment capability checks requests against relevant policies and contracts, and Pactum's work with AstraZeneca is cited as an example. There, the Alignment Agent has reportedly cut requisition and contract reviews from days to less than a minute, with 100% requisition coverage. Negotiation lets AI agents engage suppliers at a scale that would be hard for human teams to match, aiming for the best overall commercial outcome rather than only the lowest price. Sourcing extends these activities so that commercial intelligence can be turned into action.

Wei-Cox argues that the main challenge is not proving that AI can perform a task but establishing the trust, governance and operational reliability needed to delegate meaningful work at scale. Enterprises must decide which tasks agents can perform independently, where human approval is required and when decisions should be escalated. She contends that human control need not mean reviewing every action, since policies, commercial objectives and escalation thresholds can set the boundaries within which agents operate. Pactum is designed to work alongside established platforms, with integrations involving Coupa, SAP Ariba and Microsoft Teams. The company also lets suppliers negotiate over email, avoiding the need to register on another portal.

The article presents this as part of a broader move in enterprise software from supporting human decisions toward carrying out defined work autonomously. Wei-Cox says the company hopes to help enterprises manage more spend, improve compliance and secure stronger commercial outcomes without scaling operational effort at the same rate. As the connected AI workforce develops, she believes the focus will increasingly shift from what AI can recommend to the work organisations can confidently hand over to it. The article is a premium interview and does not report any regulatory requirement, deadline or formal change beyond the product launch described.

Articles.Title: Pactum: Procurement’s Execution Layer for the Agentic AI Age

stories.Headline: Judge rules Novig's sports event contracts are not swaps, letting New York enforce its gambling law
stories.Summary:
A federal judge in Manhattan has denied sports prediction market Novig's request for a preliminary injunction that would have stopped New York from enforcing its gambling laws against it. In a filing dated November 10, U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon of the Southern District of New York ruled that Novig's sports event contracts are not swaps under the Commodity Exchange Act, according to The Block. Because the contracts fall outside that definition, she concluded, federal commodities law does not preempt New York's gambling and sports-wagering rules. The ruling was reported on November 11, 2026. The practical effect is that New York can now require Novig to obtain a state gambling license or stop listing and trading the contracts.

McMahon wrote that the contracts "bear more than a passing resemblance to sports betting," and she reasoned that they do not depend on events with a financial, economic or commercial consequence, which is the test for a swap. Novig, whose legal entity is Ludlow Exchange LLC, had sued New York Attorney General Letitia James and state Gaming Commission officials on August 5, arguing that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has exclusive jurisdiction over event contracts. The CFTC had designated Ludlow as a contract market in June, and Novig began offering sports contracts to New York customers in August. The ruling is narrower than it might first appear, though it goes further than an earlier decision against Kalshi. In July, Judge Analisa Torres of the same court denied Kalshi a preliminary injunction while assuming, without deciding, that its sports contracts were swaps.
