A finding that such contracts are not swaps at all would undercut the starting point of the preemption argument that Kalshi, Polymarket and others rely on. Lawyer Daniel Wallach told The Block that federal courts in the Second Circuit have now issued 10 rulings in sports prediction-market litigation, all favoring the states. The ruling does not end Novig's lawsuit, and the company is litigating the same issue in several other states. The Block said it had asked Novig for comment.

Articles.Title: Judge rules Novig's sports event contracts are not swaps, letting New York enforce its gambling law - MLQ.ai

stories.Headline: Courts’ budget request, AI ethics guidance, veterans’ honors lead Florida Bar News Briefs
stories.Summary:
The Florida Bar's weekly podcast, Florida Bar News Briefs, released an episode on November 10, 2026, covering three developments in the legal profession. The episode reports on the judicial branch's latest budget request, which seeks a new courthouse in Lakeland for the Sixth District Court of Appeal, higher salaries for judges, and case management technology for the trial courts. It also reports that former Florida Attorney General Bill McCollum and Duval County Judge Mose L. Floyd, both Florida Bar members, are being inducted into the Florida Veterans' Hall of Fame. A third item covers a proposed advisory opinion from a Florida Bar committee on whether artificial intelligence can generate suggestions for attorneys.

The budget request is the centerpiece of the first story, and the articles give no dollar figures, dates for construction, or timelines for the salary increases or technology upgrades. The advisory opinion under consideration would address how lawyers may use artificial intelligence when it produces suggestions in their work. The committee's proposal reflects input from a handful of attorneys, most of whom, according to the briefing, want more guidance on the subject. The articles do not describe the opinion's specific provisions or whether it has been adopted.

The Florida Bar's Journal and News Department produces the podcast, which is part of its multimedia network. The articles do not include direct statements from McCollum, Floyd, the judicial branch, or the committee members, so no quotations or positions from them can be reported here. The articles also do not say when the Hall of Fame induction will take place or when the committee will vote on its proposed opinion. Beyond the episode itself, the coverage offers no further context or next steps.

Articles.Title: Courts’ budget request, AI ethics guidance, veterans’ honors lead Florida Bar News Briefs - The Florida Bar

stories.Headline: Validating GPU Platforms with Runtime AI Inventory via the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's developer blog published a post on November 11, 2026, describing how its AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) now includes a qualified AI bill of materials component built on the open source k8s-aibom project. The integration tracks AI workloads running on Kubernetes, and it was announced as part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform. AICR is an open source modular component of that platform, and k8s-aibom is an open source project created by Google. Two stock recipes, h100-gke-cos-inference and h100-gke-cos-inference-dynamo, select k8s-aibom by default. Other GKE recipes can opt in during generation using the --runtime-inventory flag, and recipes that select it can opt out with --runtime-inventory disabled.

AICR generates version-locked recipes and reproducible deployment bundles, with checksums and optional signing through aicr bundle --attest. The integration was validated with AICR v1.2.0, which pins k8s-aibom 1.6.2, and the k8s-aibom controller emits CycloneDX 1.6 AIBOM records for supported workloads. During steady-state observation, the tested setup showed about four API-server requests per minute, 2.2 millicores average CPU, and a 28 to 34 MiB controller memory working set. The article names NVIDIA as the author of the AICR component and Google as the creator of k8s-aibom, and it describes the two projects as addressing opposite sides of the same problem. AICR works at the runtime deployment layer, covering drivers, operators, kernels, and Kubernetes components, while k8s-aibom watches workload and pod APIs higher in the stack.

The authors state that neither view is sufficient for AI governance on its own. The article describes the work as aimed at platform teams and application teams that deploy AI workloads with tools such as NVIDIA Dynamo, Kubeflow, or Slurm. The stated audience includes teams that need to find unregistered or shadow AI workloads, identify models and inference runtimes, track external AI APIs and vector databases, detect drift in AI dependencies, and support security reviews and compliance audits. Mutable image tags such as :latest are described as a risk, because two nodes can run different code under identical tags. The article also notes that k8s-aibom inventory is opt-in per namespace, and that no sink and no secret access are configured by default.

Organizations running GKE clusters with H100 GPU nodes are the affected group the article describes. Background given in the article is limited to the motivation: application teams update AI workloads independently of platform recipes, so a reproducible deployment bundle alone cannot establish which workload artifacts run on each node. The article explains that AICR records qualified deployment intent and evaluates it against a cluster at a point in time, while k8s-aibom records what it observed and how confidently it determined each attribute. It also states that the pairing is meant to close a gap between the platform configuration and the workloads actually running.

The article leaves open how the integration will perform beyond the tested configuration, and it does not say when AICR or k8s-aibom will ship further updates. It notes that Helmfile, Terraform, and Fleet require a documented manual CRD update in some transitions, and that AIBOM records can appear before pods are running. The article ends with links to the AICR and k8s-aibom repositories as next steps. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Validating GPU Platforms with Runtime AI Inventory via the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory | NVIDIA Technical Blog

stories.Headline: Kenosha County man faces 12 felony counts under new Wisconsin AI law
stories.Summary:
A Kenosha County man, Tristan Preuss, 23, faces 12 felony counts after allegedly using AI to manipulate photos of his ex-girlfriend to make her appear nude and posting them online. According to a criminal complaint, he created four fake social media accounts posing as her, beginning in August 2025. The charges are brought under Act 34, a Wisconsin law passed last October that makes it a crime to post a synthetic intimate representation of an identifiable person. Authorities described this as one of the first times the charge has been prosecuted in the state. Preuss is expected in court on Dec. 2 for an initial appearance.

The complaint alleges that in some of the posts, Preuss demanded money in exchange for the images, directing payment to a phone number that belonged to him. When police questioned him, he reportedly said he had no ill intent, that the images were for his own satisfaction, and that he was sorry. He also told police he did not know the conduct was illegal, a claim tied to how new these charges are. Local attorney Jonathan LaVoy, of Kim and LaVoy S.C., said the public distribution of the photos is a key factor in the case. The evidence against Preuss appears fairly strong, LaVoy said, though the statute itself may face legal challenges on appeal.

LaVoy also described the broader issue, saying AI brings both benefits and harms and that the law is trying to catch up with the technology. The article notes that the case is one of the early tests of this new Wisconsin statute and that its legal footing could be examined by the state's appellate courts. The information came from the Kenosha County criminal complaint, the state court records system, and LaVoy. The story also notes that portions of the article were produced with AI assistance and reviewed by a FOX6 journalist and an editor before publication.

Articles.Title: Kenosha County man faces 12 felony counts under new Wisconsin AI law

stories.Headline: Law in the age of AI: Law Faculty’s International Research Conference
stories.Summary:
The Law Faculty of the University of Colombo will hold its annual International Research Conference on 13 and 14 November 2026, under the theme "Law in the Age of Artificial Intelligence (AI): Advancing Equality, Sustainability and Innovation." The conference is designed to bring together legal experts, academics, researchers and practitioners from Sri Lanka and abroad. Its purpose is to examine the legal challenges and opportunities that arise as AI becomes more widespread. Organisers say the event will focus on how the law can respond to these developments in a fair and forward-looking way.

The programme includes thematic sessions on commercial law, private and comparative law, and public and international law, each viewed through the lens of AI. Participants are expected to take part in scholarly discussion, interdisciplinary research and new legal approaches to the problems AI poses. The aim is to encourage dialogue across disciplines rather than within a single field of law. The event is intended to produce ideas that address how AI affects equality, sustainability and innovation.

Justice Rohantha Abeysooriya, President's Counsel and President of the Court of Appeal, will attend as Chief Guest. The University's Vice Chancellor, Prof Indika Karunathilake, will be Guest of Honour. Prof M. Sakthivel, Dean of Research at the Tamil Nadu National Law University in India, will deliver the keynote address. The conference is being steered by Conference Chair Dr Udapadie Liyanage, working under the guidance of the Faculty's Dean, Prof Sampath Punchihewa.

The conference is an annual event, and this year's edition is set to concentrate on AI, a subject that the articles describe as producing emerging legal challenges. The articles do not report any specific outcomes, recommendations or follow-up measures from the gathering. They also do not say what material will be published afterward. Further details about the sessions and proceedings are not available in the reporting.

Articles.Title: Law in the age of AI: Law Faculty’s International Research Conference

stories.Headline: Energy crisis and AI rise reshape economic decisions, CBC Governor says
stories.Summary:
The Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus and member of the ECB Governing Council, Christodoulos Patsalides, said on Wednesday, 11 November 2026, that the energy crisis and the rise of artificial intelligence are reshaping economic decisions. He made the remarks in his opening speech at an MNI Connect Video Conference with economists, investors and financial market participants. He called for readiness to adjust assessments as the evidence evolves. Patsalides focused on the persistence of the energy shock and the growth of AI, which he said shape today's economic landscape. He said the blockade at the Strait of Hormuz had altered the course of history through the energy inflation channel.

Patsalides said supply shocks differ in magnitude, duration, systemic interactions and the political landscape in which they unfold. He said the ECB Governing Council must understand how the energy shock spreads through the economy and act to meet its 2% inflation target in the medium term. He said policy credibility depends on disciplined use of a robust, data-based analytical framework. He stressed a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach as essential under heightened uncertainty. At the October meeting, the Council kept key interest rates unchanged because inflation expectations remained well anchored and monetary transmission remained effective.

Patsalides said the ECB estimates that around 90% of the rise in energy inflation reflects adverse energy-supply developments linked to the Middle East conflict, rather than excessive domestic demand. He warned that this should not lead to complacency, and that monetary policy must keep inflation stabilising at the medium-term target. He said a key question is how far higher energy prices are becoming embedded in broader inflation dynamics. He noted slight upward pressure in food-price and services inflation, while core inflation remained unchanged. He said crude prices had recently retreated substantially, though their forward path requires ongoing observation.

Patsalides said that, although long-term inflation expectations are firmly anchored, short-term inflation expectations remain persistently higher and require heightened vigilance. He described AI as disrupting lives and being here to stay, and said both energy and AI are global and disruptive, with implications for growth, inflation, financing conditions and financial stability. He said AI has become a significant contributor to euro area growth through spending on AI adoption and European firms' participation in the global AI supply chain. He cited research suggesting AI-related investment could reach as much as $9 trillion between 2025 and 2032. He said technology and hardware firms issued around $350 billion in bonds this year, roughly double the amount issued a year earlier.

Patsalides said that, with capital expenditure rising faster than cash generation, financing is increasingly pursued through bond markets, private credit and interlinked circular funding arrangements, which make underlying risks harder to assess. He said total outstanding hyperscaler bonds stand at around $570 billion, of which €39 billion has been issued in euros. He said European investors participate in euro-denominated issues, mainly by allocating less to US Treasury bonds. He said increased supply, credit risk and uncertainty are widening credit spreads in both the debt and CDS markets, although investor absorption has been smooth so far. He added that there is little evidence AI financing has materially crowded out funding for other sectors.

Patsalides concluded that the energy crisis erodes purchasing power and constrains production, while AI promises higher productivity and growth. He said both call for rigorous examination of evidence and careful assessment of uncertainty. For energy, he said, this means further study of the granular networks of price dynamics. For AI, he said, it means greater visibility into opaque funding structures and closer scrutiny of the assumptions behind projections. He said sound policy must look beneath aggregate developments and identify how disruption spreads through the economy.

Articles.Title: Energy crisis and AI rise reshape economic decisions, CBC Governor says

stories.Headline: The AI Debt Bill Is Coming Due, But Biotech Has Revenue to Show for the Boom
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4% on November 5, 2026, its worst session since 2020, after the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped more than 12%. The sell-off followed Democratic midterm wins in key data-center states, which raised the odds of tougher AI regulation. The article describes the pressure as falling on the AI buildout itself, including its debt, permits, power and politics. Companies that buy compute rather than build data centers carry none of that financing risk. Tempus AI and Recursion Pharmaceuticals are the biotech examples the article offers for that role.

Debt is the weak point in the builder story, according to Ross Givens, market strategist at Traders Agency. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave carry expensive borrowing, and hyperscalers are issuing stock and bonds to fund capital expenditures on AI capacity. Givens argues that as compute costs fall, builders could be left servicing heavy debt against shrinking prices. He compares the shift to Netflix replacing the trip to Blockbuster, noting that the winner did not build the pipes. The article says money is moving from the companies making AI to the ones using it.

Givens is quoted as saying he is not calling the end of AI, and the article notes that drug developers hold large datasets that AI helps them use to test and design treatments faster. Tempus AI, which tests tumors and builds a library of results, is described as earning revenue from both doctors and drug companies. Recursion Pharmaceuticals is described as the earlier, riskier position, with robots running cell experiments while AI selects compounds. The article says Givens treats $3 to $4 as the band where Recursion's idea stays in play, and that its shares could lose most of their value on a failed trial.

Tempus AI reported third-quarter revenue of $411.5 million, up 23%, with adjusted EBITDA of $25.6 million and raised full-year guidance above $1.60 billion. Recursion's runway was extended after an October offering of 61.54 million shares at $3.25 raised roughly $187.2 million. The iShares Biotechnology ETF, which holds 248 companies led by Gilead Sciences, Amgen and Vertex, is presented as a broader way to hold biotech without single-trial risk. The article says it set a record closing high above $221 in early November before falling a few percentage points in the sell-off.

The article's background is that many railroad builders went bankrupt under debt while grain traders profited from the rails, and that dot-com fiber builders failed while Alphabet, Amazon and Meta turned bandwidth into empires. It notes that the 10-year Treasury yield is near 4.9% with a December rate hike back on the table, which the article says pressures unprofitable, long-dated stocks most. Givens is described as walking through entries, stops and chart setups weekly through his Black Ops Trading Club. The article states that AI adoption must keep spreading for biotech to remain a leadership group.

The article leaves open whether biotech will keep attracting capital on days when chip stocks fall, and whether the rotation has lasting strength or was a single week of fear. It does not say how the debt-funded builders will fare as compute costs fall, or what tougher AI regulation would look like. It also leaves open whether Recursion's cash runway will hold through its trials, and how the new Tempus collaborations will affect its results. The articles give no further timetable beyond the December 1 date in MarketBeat's stock preview.

Articles.Title: The AI Debt Bill Is Coming Due, But Biotech Has Revenue to Show for the Boom

stories.Headline: Dentons conference examines employment law changes and workplace AI
stories.Summary:
The Dentons Elevate Scotland conference, held in Glasgow, examined the sweeping changes in the Employment Rights Act 2025 and the effect of artificial intelligence on the workplace. The event was designed to help in-house lawyers and human resource professionals keep pace with developments driven by legislation and technology. Alison Weatherhead, partner and head of employment and pensions at Dentons, led a session on the Act that covered trade union access and unfair dismissal. She said Dentons has a practical toolkit and other resources to help companies work through the changes.

Weatherhead explained that trade unions can request formal physical or digital access to a workplace, and that businesses with 21 or more workers are now within scope. Employers may refuse such a request, but the Act creates a statutory presumption that access should be granted. Timing is tight, with 15 working days to respond to a request and 25 working days to negotiate terms. She also warned that penalties can rise quickly, with fines of up to £75,000 for a first breach of an agreement, £150,000 for a second, and £500,000 for any further breaches.

Other sessions covered building a personal brand, time management, competition law in the workplace, and the EU Pay Transparency Directive. Sarah Jackman, counsel at Dentons, spoke with regulatory colleague Katy MacAskill about the Financial Conduct Authority's guidance on non-financial misconduct. Jackman said the guidance marks a new era for employers, who must consider exits, investigations, references, conduct in private lives and manager accountability. Weatherhead chaired a panel on AI in employment that included Elouisa Crichton, Rowena Rix and Nicola Hamilton of Edrington.

The panel explored how organisations are moving from AI experimentation to practical implementation. Rix argued that AI should be built into actual workflows rather than merely made available, and that governance should not become a department of no. Crichton examined how AI affecting people and employment decisions raises questions of fairness, discrimination, transparency, privacy, accountability and where human judgement must sit. She stressed that trust and engagement are vital and that organisational messaging should not drift away from lived experience. The article does not report any further steps or outcomes from the conference.

Articles.Title: Dentons conference examines employment law changes and workplace AI

stories.Headline: Voluntary buyouts: Big Tech pays staff to walk away as the AI bill comes due
stories.Summary:
On October 26, Microsoft opened a Voluntary Exit Offer to about 60,000 employees, roughly 27% of its global workforce. Google later extended its voluntary exit programme to staff in Canada, France, Germany, Japan and Switzerland. Meta is finalising a voluntary departure scheme in France that could see up to a third of its roughly 300 French staff leave. On November 4, Canva told 1,271 employees, or 22% of its workforce, that their jobs would end, change or move. Canva's package is not strictly voluntary, but it has drawn wide attention.

A voluntary buyout is an offer of money and benefits to employees who agree to resign, and unlike a layoff, nobody is forced out. Microsoft's October offer covers participating teams in the US, UK, Canada and India at internal level 70 and below, with no age or tenure test. Employees must decide by early December and leave on December 31. Canva's departing staff receive at least six months' salary, 12 months of continued healthcare where provided, and a chance to apply for a USD 10,000 grant. Google's Swiss staff received one month's salary per year of service, capped at 12 months.

Microsoft, Google, Meta and Canva have not framed these exits solely as cost cutting, and the articles do not give a direct statement on their motives beyond what follows. Meta's chief people officer, Janelle Gale, told staff the April cuts were meant to run the company more efficiently and offset its other investments. Canva tied its slower growth directly to AI computing costs. Microsoft's chief people officer, Amy Coleman, said the turnout for its spring scheme reduced the size of the July layoffs, when the company cut 4,800 jobs.

Supporters say buyouts let people leave on their own terms with real support, and about 30% of those eligible for Microsoft's spring scheme accepted. Critics argue that buyouts may not guarantee the right people leave, since Microsoft's spring scheme targeted long-serving staff who hold knowledge about systems the company still depends on. Employees who decline offers may wonder whether they are next, given Google's record of following voluntary offers with layoffs in at least one division. Alphabet's workforce grew to 204,757 at the end of September from 194,668 in March.

Alphabet expects to spend between USD 195 billion and USD 205 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, more than double its 2025 figure of USD 91.4 billion. Meta has narrowed its 2026 range to between USD 135 billion and USD 145 billion, and Microsoft expects about USD 170 billion for the fiscal year to June 2027. Canva cut its 2026 revenue growth forecast from 30% to 20% in August, and investors Blackbird and Airtree later marked its value down from USD 42 billion to USD 34.9 billion. The articles leave open whether the buyouts will meaningfully reduce headcount or payroll costs against these capital budgets.

Articles.Title: Voluntary buyouts: Big Tech pays staff to walk away as the AI bill comes due

stories.Headline: EU Unveils DFA Bill to Regulate AI-Driven Personalized Pricing and Purchase Nudges [Global AI Briefing]
stories.Summary:
The European Commission formally adopted and unveiled the Digital Fairness Act bill on November 11, 2026, local time, aiming to rein in online companies that use artificial intelligence to steer consumers toward purchases or charge different prices to different people. The article notes that AI now analyzes consumer preferences and purchasing power to recommend products and ads, and can even buy on a shopper's behalf. The EU wants new consumer-protection rules for this digital marketplace. The bill has not yet become law, since it must still be deliberated and approved by the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. It is meant to sit alongside the Digital Services Act and the Digital Network Act, giving the EU a three-pillar framework for AI and digital industries.

The bill would target practices that pressure consumers into buying, such as labeling an item as the "last one" when stock is not low or showing a fake sale countdown. Subscription services that are easy to join but hard to cancel would also be regulated. For AI-driven personalized advertising and pricing, the bill would bar companies from using sensitive personal information to exploit consumer vulnerabilities and would require more transparency about how prices are set when they vary with demand. Rules could also reach gaming and content businesses, including repeated payment prompts aimed at minors and influencer promotions not clearly marked as advertising. The article says the law would extend consumer protection beyond false advertising and data leaks to cover how AI influences buying decisions, including guaranteeing freedom of choice when AI agents buy for consumers.

The European Commission is the body that unveiled the bill, and the article reports its aims in its own words without attributing new quotes to officials. Its stated core aim is to stop online platforms and e-commerce companies from misleading consumers and to strengthen consumer rights in the digital environment. The article also cites experts who advise South Korean platforms, gaming firms, and e-commerce companies operating in Europe to review their recommendations, personalized advertising, and subscription-cancellation procedures. It adds that calls are growing to review consumer-protection principles in South Korea's own market, where AI-powered pricing and purchasing-agent services are spreading. The report is a translated Korean news piece and does not indicate a timetable for the bill's passage.

Articles.Title: EU Unveils DFA Bill to Regulate AI-Driven Personalized Pricing and Purchase Nudges [Global AI Briefing]

stories.Headline: Bill Gates Says Next Four Years Are Critical for AI Safety, Calls for Urgent Regulation
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates warned that the next four years will be a critical window for ensuring artificial intelligence safety, according to a report published on November 11, 2026, by Bloomingbit. The report cited Cointelegraph, which said Gates made the comments that day. Gates pointed to rising risks, including cyberattacks, bioterrorism and threats to critical infrastructure. He described these as major risk factors that grow as AI technology advances. Gates said AI could surpass human intelligence by 2030, and that it may replace human jobs across a range of industries.

He called for swift regulation of AI to address these threats. He also urged cooperation between the United States and China to respond to them. The articles do not describe any specific rule, law or deadline that has been proposed. Gates, a co-founder of Microsoft, is the person who made these remarks, and the articles present them as his own warning rather than a formal government position.

The Bloomingbit piece was written by reporter JH Kim and includes an AI-generated summary that the outlet says is for reference only. Its tags link the story to AI safety and crypto regulation. The articles do not say whether any government or company has responded to Gates's call. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Bill Gates Says Next Four Years Are Critical for AI Safety, Calls for Urgent Regulation

stories.Headline: Inside Greece's new AI Act framework
stories.Summary:
Greece has set up its national framework for enforcing the EU AI Act through Law 5321/2026, which took effect on its 20 July publication date unless a provision says otherwise. The law spreads oversight across existing sectoral regulators instead of creating a new standalone AI authority. Its publication came about two weeks before the European Commission and national authorities began enforcing the AI Act on 2 August, when new transparency rules took effect. The bill moved quickly, opening for public consultation on 21 June, with the text finalized and enacted within two weeks after consultation closed on 6 July.

The Hellenic Data Protection Authority has been designated as the market surveillance authority for prohibited AI practices, Annex III high-risk systems and Article 50 transparency obligations. It also serves as Greece's single point of contact with the Commission and other member states. As a result, enforcement of the AI Act and the EU General Data Protection Regulation sits with the same regulator. Legal commentators have pointed out that many AI systems covered by Annex III process personal data or directly affect fundamental rights, which gives the authority's existing data protection expertise direct relevance to its new role.

The article was written by Aspasia Xirou, a data privacy risk specialist at the International Monetary Fund, and it was published by the IAPP. The author's analysis describes the structure of the law and its timing rather than attributing new decisions to any particular official. The Greek Ministry of Digital Governance handled the bill's public consultation and its passage. The article does not report any direct statements from ministry officials or from the data protection authority about how they plan to carry out the new duties.

The move reflects a broader choice available to EU member states, which have discretion over how to organize the national authorities that the AI Act relies on. Greece chose to build on an existing regulator rather than create a new body, and the article presents this as a distributed model in contrast to other approaches. The article does not describe specific enforcement actions, penalties, or a timetable for further guidance beyond the dates already noted. Further developments on how the framework operates in practice are not covered in the article.

Articles.Title: Inside Greece's new AI Act framework - IAPP

stories.Headline: AI in Corporate Law and M&A: Where Technology Meets Judgment - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
On November 11, 2026, The National Law Review published a commentary by Michael Weis of Weis & Burney titled "AI in Corporate Law and M&A: Where Technology Meets Judgment." The article is an opinion piece, and the author says it does not necessarily reflect the position of the publication. Weis writes that he is frequently asked about artificial intelligence, including its impact on legal practice and on mergers and acquisitions. He says the broader question of AI's impact on business is too wide for one article, so he focuses on the first two questions. The piece is dated Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

Weis compares AI in legal work to medical symptom-checking websites, which can suggest possible diagnoses but do not replace a physician. He argues that AI can help attorneys with routine matters, document review, legal research, identifying relevant forms or precedents, and researching jurisdictional requirements. He notes that lawyers have long relied on form files, case research services, treatises and written analyses, and that AI lets these resources be accessed and analyzed faster. He says experienced counsel must still know what questions to ask, what information matters, what authority applies, and how the law applies to a client's facts. He stresses that AI is a valuable tool but not a substitute for legal judgment.

The article lists areas where AI is relevant to evaluating a business in an M&A transaction: accounting and financial analysis, valuation, operations, human resources and employee benefits, intellectual property, tax, technology and cybersecurity, and market analysis. Weis says buyers can use a target's AI use to assess operations, competitive position, efficiency and future prospects, while sellers can position their business with the same considerations in mind. He argues that a company's AI readiness can affect its value, since effective use may bring efficiency, productivity, better customer service and growth. He adds that a company that has fallen behind may face investment needs or competitive challenges that buyers must weigh. He suggests diligence should ask how technology is used, whether it fits the business, and what infrastructure and expertise support it.

Weis points to heavy investment in AI infrastructure, which he says is creating demand across many industries, including data center construction, real estate, energy, equipment, logistics, chips and networking. He identifies environmental, infrastructure and community concerns, particularly around data center development and energy consumption, as legitimate issues. He says these competing interests must be balanced, and that the balance will influence investment and development decisions. The article does not name specific companies or transactions, and it does not give figures on investment amounts or energy use. Weis writes from his position as a practitioner, and his observations are presented as opinion rather than as findings from a study.

Weis describes the impact of AI on business and transactions as still evolving, and he calls the challenge for corporate lawyers one of using AI while preserving professional judgment and client-specific analysis. For buyers and sellers, he says technology strategy can affect operational performance, competitive position, risk and business value. He concludes that AI is unlikely to be a discrete issue addressed once and set aside, and that it is becoming part of the broader environment in which companies operate. The article offers no new deadlines, regulatory changes or pending decisions. It also leaves open how buyers should price AI readiness in a deal, and how the balance between data center development and community or environmental concerns will be struck.

Articles.Title: AI in Corporate Law and M&A: Where Technology Meets Judgment - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Google Will Offer Vermont Schools Two Ways to Keep Search for Students. Both Include AI
stories.Summary:
Starting early next year, Google Search will be off on Vermont students' school accounts unless their district turns it on. Google announced the change on November 3, and it says any district that enables Search will get one of two versions, both with artificial intelligence built in. Four Google services will also start off by default in early 2027, including the Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and the AI tools inside Google's assignment app. A district can turn on Search without turning on the Gemini chatbot, but it cannot turn on Search without its AI features, such as AI Overviews and AI Mode. Students in a district that leaves Search off will see a message that it isn't available.

The two versions differ in how they respond to students. The standard version works like the one adults use, offering AI summaries and chat, while the Guided Learning version runs through a student version of Gemini and is designed to walk students through problems step by step rather than give answers. Vermont's Agency of Education has already advised schools to keep chatbots away from pre-K through grade 2 students and to limit AI in grades 3 to 5 to subject-specific tools that stick to the lesson. The agency's January guidance is advice rather than a rule, and it said all Vermont schools were using Google for Education, so the change could reach every public school system in the state. Compass asked the agency whether either option fits its recommendations for elementary grades, and the agency has not yet said.

Google says the change gives schools more choice, not less, and it argues that the guided version will keep students from getting quick answers to schoolwork. Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, has said that search and AI are deeply integrated, which is why the two cannot be separated. Critics are not persuaded, and when a Times reporter tested the public version of Guided Learning, it wrote a detailed essay for an Advanced Placement history assignment. Common Sense Media rated AI Overviews and AI Mode an unacceptable risk for young users in July. On November 9, Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey wrote to Google's CEO asking the company to reverse the change by November 30, and the agency said it is facing considerable pressure from educators to give districts more control over which AI features are enabled.

Google has not set an exact date for the change and says schools will get details in the coming months. The Agency of Education says it will keep watching and share recommendations as more information emerges. Parents who want to know what their district plans can ask whether Google Search will be turned on for students and in which grades, which version would be used, and what students would use for research if it stays off. They can also look for their district's AI policy and review the state's grade-by-grade guidance in the Vermont AI Guidance for Education.

Articles.Title: Google Will Offer Vermont Schools Two Ways to Keep Search for Students. Both Include AI - Compass Vermont

stories.Headline: US-Canadian AI-powered law firm start-up Blackletter raises $6m in seed funding round
stories.Summary:
US-Canadian legal technology start-up Blackletter has raised $6m in a seed funding round, according to The Global Legal Post, which reported the news on 11 November 2026. The round was led by early-stage investor Lerer Hippeau, with legal funding specialists Seven Stars taking part alongside Maple VC, Garage Capital and Ripple Ventures. Several AI founders also joined the round, including Aidan Gomez, Ivan Zhang and Nick Frosst of Cohere, Jae Lee of Twelve Labs and Sara Hooker of Adaption Labs. The firm says it will use the money to expand its platform and to grow its bench of lawyers and engineers.

Blackletter describes itself as a firm that pairs experienced lawyers with its own AI software to deliver legal work faster and at lower cost. Its current practice areas are corporate, commercial, financing, M&A and employment. The firm has built a proprietary platform, Blackletter OS, which stores knowledge about each client and manages legal matters from start to finish. It charges fixed fees instead of traditional hourly rates, and says AI reduces the time its lawyers spend on each case.

Jonathan Rosenbluth, the firm's co-founder and CEO, argued that the traditional law firm model is built to benefit the firm and its senior partners rather than clients or many of its lawyers. He said Blackletter was designed the other way around, so that its technology and structure let it act as a strategic partner to clients. Graham Brown, managing partner at Lerer Hippeau, said the legal industry is ready for structural change and praised the team's mix of AI experience and expertise in scaling legal operations. Since emerging from stealth mode in June, the firm says it has signed more than 75 early-stage and growth-stage companies and investors as clients, including Ada, Antidote, Fanatics Betting & Gaming and Twelve Labs.

The New York and Toronto-based firm was co-founded by Rosenbluth, Avi Brudner and David Stewart. The article notes that Rosenbluth and Stewart previously worked together at software developer Oumi for eight months before starting Blackletter. The report places the round within a wave of investment in legal technology this year, pointing to Athena, a US AI-powered hybrid corporate law firm that secured $2.5m in pre-seed funding the previous week. The article does not say what further funding or growth milestones Blackletter expects to reach.

Articles.Title: US-Canadian AI-powered law firm start-up Blackletter raises $6m in seed funding round

stories.Headline: Sen. Elizabeth Warren Said to Take Senate Banking Gavel in January, Push Tougher Crypto, AI Rules
stories.Summary:
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, is said to be set to take over as chair of the Senate Banking Committee in January. According to reporting cited in the articles, she plans to pursue tighter oversight of financial and technology companies, including rules for cryptocurrencies and prediction markets. Cointelegraph reported on November 9 that she also intends to tighten export controls on artificial intelligence chips sent to China. The report frames this as part of a broader push to strengthen scrutiny of Wall Street firms and major technology companies.

Her financial and housing priorities are also outlined in the coverage. They include a cap on credit-card interest rates, an expansion of the affordable housing supply and a reduction in consumer debt. Crypto businesses tied to President Donald Trump's family are expected to be a key focus of her oversight. The articles describe these as areas where she would seek to use committee authority, though they do not spell out the specific bills or steps she would take.

Those points, however, rest on reports that have not been fully confirmed. The articles state that her assumption of the chairmanship has not been separately verified, and neither has the timeline for any specific legislative effort. The coverage is based on a November 9, 2026 report, and the articles do not describe any formal announcement from Warren or the committee. Readers should treat the plans as reported intentions rather than settled policy.

Articles.Title: Sen. Elizabeth Warren Said to Take Senate Banking Gavel in January, Push Tougher Crypto, AI Rules - bloomingbit

stories.Headline: Vanta Buys Pillar to Tie AI Governance to Real-Time Controls
stories.Summary:
Vanta, a San Francisco-based trust platform, plans to buy Pillar Security, a Tel Aviv, Israel-based startup led by a former Aqua Security product manager, to link AI governance with real-time security enforcement. The deal was reported by Calcalist on November 9, 2026, and Vanta's proposed acquisition was covered by GovInfoSecurity on November 11, 2026. Calcalist reported that the deal is valued at approximately $150 million and consists of a combination of cash and shares. Vanta's GRC Senior Director, Khush Kashyap, said the purchase will help organizations discover AI assets, apply policy-based guardrails, block unsafe actions and produce audit-ready evidence. Pillar was founded in 2023 and, according to its own counts, employs 33 people, while Calcalist puts its staff at more than 20.

The transaction would combine Vanta's governance and evidence tools with Pillar's agent discovery, monitoring, red-teaming and enforcement capabilities. Following completion, Pillar would become Vanta's research and development center in Israel, and its team would join the U.S. company. Pillar's technology would be integrated into Vanta's platform, which serves more than 20,000 customers. Kashyap said the combined product would let customers turn written AI policies into automated controls that block unauthorized agent actions at runtime. Vanta's CEO and co-founder, Christina Cacioppo, said customers and regulators want proof that a company's AI does what it claims, and that a policy document alone does not provide that.

Vanta says the deal responds to a gap between knowing what policies require and seeing whether AI agents follow them. Kashyap described enforcement without governance context as producing alerts, and governance without enforcement as producing a paper trail. Pillar's CEO, Ziv Karliner, said the acquisition gives the company access to Vanta's security and governance context and a way to serve a larger customer base. Calcalist reported that Pillar's founders, Ziv Karliner and Dor Sarig, will remain with the company to lead its AI security business. Customers affected include Vanta's more than 20,000 customers and Pillar's customers, which include Fortune 500 companies as well as technology and financial firms.

Kashyap said Vanta's AI governance early-access program is the most requested in the company's history and is six times oversubscribed. She also said daily Vanta agent users have grown 253% over the last three quarters. Vanta's own research, cited by Calcalist, found that 65% of IT and business leaders say their use of agentic AI is outpacing their understanding of it, and that fewer than half have a framework for granting or limiting AI autonomy. Calcalist reported that Pillar raised $9 million since its founding in 2023, with its seed round announced in April 2025 led by Shield Capital, with participation from Golden Ventures and Ground Up Ventures. Karliner previously spent more than four years at Aqua Security, including two-and-a-half years as a product manager.

The articles do not confirm the purchase price, since a Vanta spokesperson disputed the $150 million figure reported by Calcalist and declined to disclose the price. The articles also do not say when the acquisition is expected to close or whether regulators must approve it. Vanta launched its AI governance product in July 2026, according to Calcalist, and its governance tools are used by companies, with auditors at more than 20,000 companies accepting its evidence. Calcalist said Vanta's platform serves more than 20,000 customers, and Kashyap said auditors at more than 20,000 companies accept its evidence. The articles leave open how the combined product will be priced and how Pillar's products will be packaged after integration.

stories.Headline: A.I.Matics' AIM-T1 Named CES Innovation Awards® 2027 Honoree in Two Categories
stories.Summary:
A.I.Matics, a South Korean Vision AI company, announced from Seoul that its AIM-T1 AI vision inspection platform has been named a CES 2027 Innovation Awards Honoree. The recognition covers two categories, Artificial Intelligence and Construction & Industrial Tech. The announcement went out by PR Newswire on Nov. 9 or 10, 2026, depending on which published version is used. The Manila Times carried it with a Nov. 10 date line, while the PR Newswire release itself carries Nov. 9. AIM-T1 is described as a platform that helps electronics manufacturers identify defects and adapt their inspections to new products.

AIM-T1 is designed for quality, process and manufacturing engineers who work with products such as camera modules, semiconductor packages and printed circuit board assemblies. It combines modular imaging hardware with software-defined inspection so that teams can adapt their inspection workflows on a single common platform. The system uses reference samples of acceptable products to set inspection criteria and to flag deviations that may indicate defects. Its optical system pairs liquid lens technology with electronic focus stacking, capturing images at multiple focal planes without any mechanical Z-axis movement. Camera resolution, lens magnification, lighting and inspection configurations can all be adjusted, and operators use a dedicated software interface to configure criteria, review results and refine inspection models.

A.I.Matics is the company responsible for AIM-T1, and it is a subsidiary of Dreamtech. In its release, the company says the platform addresses a recurring challenge in electronics production, which is keeping inspection consistent as product designs and manufacturing requirements change. It says the platform incorporates world model technology and in-context learning. A.I.Matics states that the platform is designed to reduce reliance on specialized expertise at each product changeover by making inspection knowledge easier to reuse. The company also plans to showcase AIM-T1 at CES 2027, where it intends to meet manufacturers, automation equipment integrators and potential distribution partners.

The release identifies electronics manufacturers as the group most affected, especially those running facilities with frequent product changeovers. It notes that introducing a new product can require collecting defect images, revising inspection criteria and adjusting imaging equipment. Those tasks, it says, place additional demands on experienced inspectors and AI engineers. For manufacturers reshoring production or adding regional capacity, the release says that transferring inspection expertise is an important part of bringing new facilities online.

A separate article from The Elec reports that Sapiens, a company with no connection to A.I.Matics, also said on Nov. 10 that its VIORA AI smart glasses, still under development, won CES 2027 Innovation Awards in two categories. The CES Innovation Awards program is organized by the Consumer Technology Association, which describes it as recognizing outstanding design and engineering in consumer technology products. A footnote to the release adds that the awards are based on descriptive materials submitted to the judges. It also says the association did not verify the accuracy of any submission or any claims made, and did not test the item that received the award.

A.I.Matics describes itself as a Vision AI company that began as an in-house venture at Hyundai Motor Company in 2000 and was incorporated in 2003. It built its expertise in automotive vision recognition by supplying lane departure warning systems to automakers, and it now develops industry-specific AI solutions for transportation, logistics and manufacturing. Its proprietary AI engine, aimNet, is combined with imaging technology and application software, and its portfolio also includes AI-powered driver safety cameras, the aid fleet management platform, intelligent process and operations management solutions, and AI chatbots for logistics call centers. CES 2027 will take place Jan. 6-9 in Las Vegas, and A.I.Matics plans to exhibit AIM-T1 there.

Booth and meeting details will be announced once they are confirmed, so the company's location at the show is not yet known. The articles do not give a price, a commercial launch date or the names of any customers or distribution partners for AIM-T1. Further product information is available at vision.aimatics.ai. In the same coverage, Sapiens says it is working with the Fast.B platform to commercialize VIORA, with a launch targeted for the first half of 2027.

stories.Headline: Quantum could solve AI energy drain, says tech founder
stories.Summary:
Australian startup Diraq is running what it describes as the first field test worldwide of a small quantum computer built on a silicon chip inside a commercial data centre in Sydney. The company's founder, Andrew Dzurak, says quantum computing could help curb the large energy demands of artificial intelligence, and the test is reported in articles published on November 9 and 10, 2026. The test is taking place at a Sydney facility operated by Equinix, where Diraq's computer currently has eight quantum bits, or qubits, on a silicon chip. Diraq plans to gradually upgrade that to 150,000 qubits by 2029, and to build a system with two million qubits that reaches the definition set by the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency by 2031, two years ahead of the deadline. The system is self-contained and draws less than 20 kilowatts of power while running alongside a computer at room temperature.

The energy problem Dzurak points to is the gigawatt-scale demand of large data centres, which the articles describe as warehouse-like buildings full of servers used to train or run AI tools. That demand either requires new power plants or adds pressure on electrical grids, and it has sparked community backlash. Dzurak argues that quantum machines, which usually need extremely cold cryogenic temperatures, are moving out of university labs and could ease that burden in data centres within five years. He told AFP that the next generations of AI are looking to consume so much power because many of the problems they solve are better suited to quantum calculations. Beyond AI, he listed uses such as calculating the behaviour of molecules for pharmaceuticals, lighter batteries and the chemical industry.

Dzurak is the founder of Diraq, and the articles quote him at length on the company's plans and the economics of the technology. The company estimates that using quantum computing for drug trials could raise success rates by 10 percent and cut the cost of bringing a new medicine to market by a third, provided it runs for under $100 million per year. Dzurak said this will only happen if quantum computers can be built cost-effectively. Cathy Foley, president of the Australian Academy of Technological Sciences and Engineering, said Australia has more than 50 quantum-related businesses but that commercialisation is among its biggest challenges. Dzurak credited AUKUS, the defence technology partnership between Australia, Britain and the United States, with reducing security barriers to sharing quantum technology, which he called essential for Diraq's work across Australia and its offices in the larger US market.

The articles place Diraq among six global companies at the third stage of the DARPA quantum benchmarking initiative, which will test whether any quantum computer can solve real problems at a cost that delivers value by 2033. Another Australian startup, PsiQuantum, is also on the DARPA list and is backed by an Australian government investment of Au$1 billion to build a different model of quantum computer in Queensland, with construction starting in June. Dzurak said the country is experiencing a Silicon Valley moment in quantum. The articles also note that Michelle Simmons' startup Silicon Quantum Computing was named by Time magazine as having one of the best inventions of 2026, a quantum-enhanced AI chip.

stories.Headline: Zum Introduces Zoe, A Conversational AI Assistant Built for Student Mobility
stories.Summary:
Zūm, a student mobility company, introduced Zoe, a conversational AI assistant built into Zum CMX, in a release datelined Redwood City, California, on November 10, 2026. Zoe is designed for transportation teams, operators and administrators, and it turns each district's own data into clear answers and next steps. The company says the aim is to help teams solve problems faster so every student starts the day on time and is ready to learn. The release says that in the 2024-25 school year more than one in five students were chronically absent, and that seven in ten school districts surveyed faced driver shortages. Zum CMX connects every aspect of student mobility in one platform, and Zoe draws on a single source of real-time data across the operation.

Zoe reads routes, runs and timesheets together, and it is built to help close gaps caused by information spread across separate screens. It assesses overall on-time performance, separates isolated incidents from recurring patterns, and recommends fixes for recurring route and timing issues. It identifies routes that routinely need cover drivers or are frequently split, and it can compare a route or run with a prior version and summarize the changes. It flags unusual paid-hour patterns, drills into repeated extra stops or unexplained dwell time using historical telematics, and gives teams step-by-step product guidance. The release states that Zoe operates under Zum's existing data privacy and security commitments and was designed with privacy, security and human oversight at its core.

Ritu Narayan, Founder and CEO of Zum, said that AI is only as powerful as the system and data behind it. She said student mobility has long relied on outdated, disconnected systems, and that Zum CMX was built to change that. She described Zoe as AI embedded directly into the operating system rather than layered onto outdated technology. Tomas Beccar Varela, Interim Executive Director of Transportation at San Francisco Unified School District, said that in student transportation every minute matters. He said his district sees promise in tools like Zoe that make transportation data easier to access, interpret and analyze.

The tool affects transportation teams, operators and administrators who make hundreds of decisions each morning, often with incomplete information, and through them the students and families who depend on bus service. The release says more than 7,500 schools in 19 states rely on Zum CMX. Zum describes itself as redefining mass mobility with Zum Connected Mobility Experience (CMX), and it is also advancing the transition to electric mobility by turning school buses into mobile energy assets that can support a cleaner, more resilient grid. The release notes that Zum CMX expanded across Los Angeles Unified School District this school year, and that Zum recently announced an update to its driver training for National School Bus Safety Week.

Zum says new capabilities will continue to make the system smarter, and that Zoe can help districts anticipate issues, understand their impact and act before they disrupt service. The release does not say when additional capabilities will arrive or how Zoe's recommendations will be measured against results. It also does not state the price of Zoe, whether districts must adopt it, or how many districts currently use it. The articles provide no independent evaluation of its performance.

stories.Headline: SAP Expands Collaboration with AstraZeneca to Adopt RISE with SAP and Business AI - Engineering / Artificial Intelligence - SAP | KXEN
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, SAP SE announced that AstraZeneca, a global biopharmaceutical company, is migrating to SAP Cloud ERP Private through the RISE with SAP journey. The announcement was made from Walldorf in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, and it extends a relationship between the two companies that spans 20 years. The move is described as a full-estate migration that extends one of the largest SAP footprints in life sciences. The release was distributed by NewswireToday with SAP as the stated source.

The migration simplifies and standardizes AstraZeneca's technology landscape, which the release says helps create a more agile and resilient digital foundation. Through its Axial Business Transformation Programme, AstraZeneca is moving from legacy environments in SAP ERP Central Component to SAP Cloud ERP Private. The shift is intended to support more standardized ways of working, harmonized data and connected processes across the enterprise. AstraZeneca is also exploring business AI capabilities from SAP, including the Industry AI portfolio, the Joule solution and agentic use cases across finance, supply chain and manufacturing. The SAP Business Data Cloud solution can support AstraZeneca in building a clean data core, and the SAP Green Ledger solution can connect sustainability and business data across its value chain.

AstraZeneca's Chief Information Officer, Chris Taylor, said SAP has been a key part of how the company runs its operations for more than two decades. Taylor said the next chapter of the partnership is about more than modernizing technology, and that through Axial the company is simplifying how it operates. He added that the goal is to move faster and unlock greater value from AI, so that insight can be turned into action more quickly. Thomas Saueressig, Chief Customer Officer and Member of the Executive Board of SAP SE, said companies across life sciences and healthcare are rethinking how technology can help them manage complexity. He said the Axial programme shows how cloud, data and AI can create a stronger foundation for innovation at scale.

The release describes AstraZeneca as a science-led company focused on the discovery, development and commercialization of prescription medicines. Its therapeutic areas named in the release include oncology, rare disease, cardiovascular, renal and metabolism, respiratory and immunology. The release states that the business AI capabilities have the potential to enhance productivity, strengthen data quality and governance, and enable faster decision-making. The release also says that the SAP Business Data Cloud solution can bring together disparate data sets to create a trusted foundation for future AI adoption. Media contacts named in the release are Lawrie Benfield and Sonya Domanski, both at SAP.

The articles do not say when the migration will be completed or what it will cost. They do not report any results from the migration, and they give no timeline for the AI capabilities AstraZeneca is exploring. The releases state that the content was created with the assistance of artificial intelligence and reviewed by an editorial team, and they carry forward-looking-statement warnings about risks that could cause outcomes to differ. The articles also do not say which AI capabilities AstraZeneca will ultimately adopt.

stories.Headline: Investors worry the AI trade needs Nvidia's Huang and its largesse
stories.Summary:
Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy linked to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, pitched a multimillion-dollar AI infrastructure project to investors, according to a Financial Times report. The pitch claimed she could secure Nvidia's advanced chips and cited Chinese technology giant Alibaba as a prospective client. Huang and her business partner Kang Wei sought investment in early 2025 for a Southeast Asian data-centre project. The proposal was estimated to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars, according to the FT, which cited two investors who were approached. During the pitch, the pair said they had no problem securing Nvidia graphics processing units.

The proposed project raises questions about how advanced Nvidia chips could reach Chinese businesses through infrastructure located outside mainland China. US export controls restrict Chinese companies from owning certain advanced AI chips. Chinese businesses can, however, lease computing capacity from overseas data centres, subject to applicable restrictions. Documents reviewed by the FT showed that Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, through subsidiaries in 2024. People familiar with the company described Alibaba as Megaspeed's anchor customer and largest client.

Alice Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, and allegations say she was recruited by Chinese intelligence to build a relationship with Jensen Huang. The allegations say she was meant to influence his position on US restrictions on advanced chip exports to China. The allegations have not been independently established. Beijing has rejected the espionage claims, while Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing related to chip smuggling. Jensen Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair and apologized to his wife and family.

US intelligence officials reportedly believe Alice Huang was connected to a Chinese espionage effort targeting Jensen Huang. The alleged aim was to gather information about the Nvidia chief and sway his efforts to persuade Washington to ease AI chip export restrictions. Nvidia's independent directors have launched an investigation into whether he was targeted in a foreign intelligence operation. The company has said it has no reason to believe its national security interests or confidential information were compromised. The allegations have renewed attention to Nvidia's business dealings in China and the security of its global AI chip supply chain.

The FT report and the allegations leave open whether the proposed data-centre project was ever funded or built. They also leave open the outcome of Nvidia's investigation into whether Jensen Huang was targeted. Whether Alibaba's ties to Megaspeed breach any restrictions has not been addressed in the articles. The articles do not say whether Washington will change its chip export policy.

stories.Headline: Op-ed: When local government adopts AI, who is accountable?
stories.Summary:
Vista Irrigation District's board adopted an artificial intelligence policy on September 9, according to an October 14 report in The Coast News, while noting that the district had not yet used AI in its operations. The district's director of administration, Shallako Goodrick, said that employees might still use freely available writing tools. She named confidentiality, discrimination, staff training, and vendor use among the agency's main concerns. The article presents the policy as a sensible first step toward governing AI before it is widely deployed.

The op-ed argues that a policy alone does not show that AI is being used responsibly. Its central question is whether employees can spot an error, challenge it, and stay accountable for decisions made on the public's behalf. The author, Glenn Broder, uses the example of an employee relying on an AI summary of a customer complaint that misses an applicable rule, with a supervisor approving the draft because it sounds reasonable. In that case, he says, responsibility rests with the employee and the agency, not the software. Oversight, he adds, must mean more than clicking approve.

Broder recommends five steps for local agencies. They should define where AI is allowed and where it is not, with stronger independent review for higher-stakes decisions such as service, payment, or eligibility. They should protect confidential information and write vendor contracts that spell out what data is processed, where it goes, and who can access it. Staff should be trained to test AI output by checking claims against evidence, and they need a clear path to escalate when evidence is missing. Finally, agencies should publicly explain how AI is used, which decisions stay human, and how errors are corrected.

Broder also notes that AI may reach agency services through third-party vendors even when an agency never buys an AI system itself. He draws a firm line between adopting a policy and proving it works, since proof requires evidence that training is effective, vendors comply, and errors are caught before they reach residents. He credits Vista Irrigation District for acting before deployment, and he urges North County agencies to make their oversight visible and verifiable. His closing principle is that AI should assist public servants and never excuse them from exercising public judgment. The articles do not describe any specific incident or further schedule of action beyond this.

stories.Headline: DEPDev backs EO to create National AI Council
stories.Summary:
The Philippine government plans to create a National Artificial Intelligence Council this November, after its AI governance framework was approved, according to the Department of Economy, Planning and Development. Undersecretary Rosemarie Edillon confirmed to reporters that the National Innovation Council has already approved the long-awaited framework, which the department first announced in late April. The next step is an executive order that the department hopes President Marcos will issue within two weeks. Edillon spoke on the sidelines of the third-quarter economic performance briefing, held on a Monday. The department's secretary, Arsenio Balisacan, cited the framework as one of the government's policy priorities for steering the economy toward recovery.

The proposed council would oversee the implementation of the framework and make sure its strategies and policies are carried out in a coherent manner. Each of the framework's six pillars would have its own technical working group, with at least one private sector representative joining each group. The six pillars are enabling resources, research and development and data, capabilities, building expertise in AI, infrastructure support, and demand generation. The private sector would also play a role in implementing standards and assurance mechanisms, with third-party certification given as an example. The framework will serve as the government's formal policy on AI and adopts a human-centered and rights-based approach.

The Department of Economy, Planning and Development, through Undersecretary Edillon, is responsible for proposing the council and the executive order that would create it. Edillon said the council's role is to make sure the framework's strategies and policies are put in place, and that organizations comply with ethics and principles. Balisacan said in his speech that the framework provides a basis for innovation that advances transparency, security, human-centered development, and responsible AI use. He added that technology must strengthen people's capabilities and livelihoods. Edillon also stressed that the department does not yet know how the final executive order will be written.

The framework is intended to guide the work of agencies across sectors, including education, health and agriculture. The Department of Science and Technology and the Department of Information and Communications Technology will continue implementing AI programs in those areas. Balisacan linked the framework to a disappointing economic growth rate of 2.1 percent in the third quarter, which he said called for steering the economy back toward recovery. Balisacan also said that foundational learning, nutrition, and health remain essential so Filipino workers can adapt, thrive, and lead. President Marcos has separately told government agencies to use AI to improve services.

The articles do not say when the executive order will actually be signed or how its final terms will read, and Edillon said the department does not yet know how it will come out. They also do not say who will chair the council or when the technical working groups will be formed. The reports do not describe the private sector representatives who will join the working groups or the specific standards they will set. Whether the council will be established within the November timeframe the department hoped for remains unconfirmed in the articles.

stories.Headline: Nvidia, SK Telecom, Rebellions forge AI chip alliance
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, SK Telecom and the Korean chipmaker Rebellions signed a memorandum of understanding on Monday, November 9, 2026, at Nvidia's AI Day Seoul event at Coex in Seoul. The agreement aims to bring locally developed AI processors into Nvidia data center systems. The Ministry of Science and ICT announced the deal, and the three companies later issued a joint press release on the same day. The signing was held in Seoul, where Rebellions chief executive Park Sung-hyun, Chung Suk-geun, chief technology officer and head of the AI CIC at SK Telecom, and Ashish Karandikar, vice president of NVLink Fusion at Nvidia, took part.

Under the memorandum, the firms will use Nvidia's NVLink Fusion technology to link Rebellions' neural processing units with Nvidia GPUs while SK Telecom develops AI data center infrastructure. NVLink Fusion lets third-party chipmakers integrate their processors into Nvidia's rack-scale computing architecture, so different types of accelerators can run within a shared infrastructure. Rebellions will connect its Rebel R200 neural processing units to Nvidia's platform and use the Nvidia MGX rack architecture for rack-scale system development. SK Telecom plans to deploy these systems in its AI data center, drawing on its proprietary models and services. Rebellions' R200 systems are expected to be ready for deployment in 2028.

Jensen Huang, founder and chief executive of Nvidia, said Korea has the talent, technology and industrial ambition to become a world leader in AI, and that NVLink Fusion lets Korean chipmakers connect custom processors to Nvidia's AI factory platform. Sunghyun Park, cofounder and chief executive of Rebellions, described the announcement as a turning point for sovereign AI and said the company would deliver low-latency, energy-efficient inference for frontier models at scale. Jung Jai-hun, president and chief executive of SK Telecom, said the collaboration validates next-generation sovereign AI infrastructure that combines global AI technology with Korean AI semiconductors. Bae Kyung-hoon, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT, said the government will actively support the collaboration and further cooperation with Nvidia on physical AI and securing GPU supply.

The collaboration is expected to affect Korean chip designers, who gain a way to test their processors within Nvidia's data center architecture and pursue customers overseas, according to the ministry. Data centers may also benefit, since the ministry said combining neural processing units and GPUs could help them balance performance and power use. The companies plan to split AI inference between the two processor types, with Nvidia GPUs handling prefill and Rebellions NPUs handling decode. The partnership is also intended to support AI services tailored to Korea's language and industries, including public-facing services under the government's AI for All project. Rebellions gains access to an established supply chain of original design manufacturers and component suppliers through the MGX ecosystem.

Background from the articles: the arrangement comes as demand for AI inference, which uses trained models to generate responses, drives interest in specialized chips that lower operating costs. Rebellions develops inference accelerators, and its flagship Rebel100 is built specifically for inference, with a chiplet architecture and open-source software. The company is backed by Aramco, Arm, Kindred Ventures, KT, Mirae Asset Group, Samsung, SK Hynix and SK Telecom. SK Telecom has been a telecommunications leader since 1984 and has a long-standing collaboration with Nvidia on AI development. The ministry has also pursued similar links with AMD to give Korean chip designers access to multiple global computing platforms.

Separately on Monday, the ministry and Nvidia held an AI startup partnership forum that brought together 22 Korean companies, including Upstage, Twelve Labs, FuriosaAI, DeepX and Rebellions. Nvidia executives Deepu Talla and Jonathan Cohen attended. Lee Do-kyu, deputy minister for ICT policy, said the forum aimed to help Korean companies find cooperation opportunities with Nvidia and expand into global markets. The ministry pledged support for follow-up work, including joint research, commercialization and eventual overseas sales. The articles do not say how the ministry plans to extend the partnership model to other domestic NPU makers beyond stating that it wants to do so.

stories.Headline: North Carolina artificial intelligence experts weigh in on our AI anxieties
stories.Summary:
The North Carolina Department of Information Technology, known as NCDIT, is seeking artificial intelligence vendors to help integrate and implement generative AI within state government agencies, according to a Spectrum News report published November 9, 2026. The state is exploring how AI could play a larger role in everything from online state services to the tools government employees use behind the scenes. Proposals from potential vendors are due November 30. The effort is meant to give agencies a simpler route to AI tools that are secure and trusted, while providing employee training and security safeguards.

The plan is built around protecting personal information, making sure people can understand how the state reaches its decisions, and keeping humans accountable when something goes wrong. State Director of Cybersecurity Laura Rodgers described AI as a tool rather than a replacement for existing services, and she said the state's approach differs from some industry practices where workers are pressed to use AI or face dismissal. NCDIT Secretary and State Chief Information Officer Nate Denny said in a statement that the aim is to deliver government services to residents better and faster and to free employees to spend more time serving the public. Rodgers argued that the deliberate, guardrails-first approach should make residents feel safe, though she said public trust will remain critical.

A separate WUNC News broadcast from November 11, 2026, approached public worry about AI from another angle. Host Jeff Tiberii, who co-hosts the station's "Due South" program, convened a panel to separate fearmongering from real anxieties and to discuss how AI is shaping society and individuals. The guests were Lee Rainie, director of the Imagining the Digital Future Center at Elon University, Emmy Martin, a technology reporter for the New York Times and a UNC alumna, and Saif Khairat, chief AI officer and vice provost for AI at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, who is also a professor in the School of Nursing. The program, which runs about 50 minutes, was published with a description noting that headlines about AI tend to frighten audiences. Taken together, the two reports show state officials promoting cautious adoption while public discussion focuses on separating real risks from exaggerated fears.
