stories.Headline: Governor Hochul Declares NY Will Lead the Nation in AI Science and Safety; Launches New Research Institute
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research, based at State University of New York's Binghamton University, to advance AI science and safety. The announcement was made on November 10, 2026, and the Center is meant to bring together academic expertise to advance AI safety research, accelerate scientific discovery, and independently test advanced AI systems for safety and security. The Center will convene more than 80 leading scientists from colleges and research institutions across New York State who have expertise in AI safety, security and computer science. It is supported by Empire AI, Governor Hochul's $500 million public-private initiative to drive AI research for public good.

Greg Morrisett of Cornell Tech and Jeannette Wing of Columbia University will serve as interim co-directors of the Center. The Center's work will include independent testing of frontier AI systems, foundational scientific research, and the training of a new generation of AI safety experts. One of its first objectives is a national recruiting effort for experts in areas such as formal methods and verification, interpretability and alignment, and biosecurity. The Center will also give state officials objective evidence to inform policy decisions about AI safety and accountability. Separately, the state's Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) opened an online portal for large frontier AI developers to register by January 1, 2027.

Governor Hochul said that while the federal government fails to act, New York is leading the way on AI safety and holding big tech accountable. Tom Secunda, Empire AI Board Chair, said independent testing will help researchers understand what increasingly powerful systems can do and how to use them safely. SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. said SUNY would help ensure New York State is a national and global leader in advancing AI safety and security. Binghamton University President Anne D'Alleva thanked Governor Hochul and Secunda, a Binghamton alumnus and Bloomberg LP co-founder, for their support. The New York State Department of Financial Services Acting Superintendent, Kaitlin Asrow, said DFS is leading implementation of the RAISE Act through the DIGIT Office.

The RAISE Act requires large frontier AI developers to register with the state and meet strict safety, transparency and reporting standards. New York's requirement to report any critical safety incident within 72 hours is the strongest in the nation, according to the state. Beginning in January, large frontier developers must publish safety frameworks on their websites, and all frontier developers must report critical safety incidents and publish model transparency reports. The Center was first announced in January with a $30 million philanthropic gift from a group of donors led by Tom Secunda, along with a $25 million research investment from SUNY and operating capital from New York State. The announcement builds on Governor Hochul's broader AI safety agenda, which includes implementation of the RAISE Act.

At the state's request, the Center will be able to provide expertise, assessments and evidence to help inform state policymaking and oversight of frontier AI developers. The Center will coordinate with DIGIT to begin reviewing developers' published safety frameworks and recommending ways to strengthen requirements. Governor Hochul said that in the coming months she will continue exploring ways to build on the RAISE Act. SUNY describes itself as the largest comprehensive system of higher education in the United States, with 64 colleges and universities. The system's research expenditures were nearly $1.5 billion in fiscal year 2025.

stories.Headline: Nvidia spy scandal revives push to write China chip export limits into the defense bill
stories.Summary:
Reports that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman U.S. officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence have given Washington's chip hawks a fresh argument, and they are pressing it in this year's defense bill. Lawmakers and advocates told Reuters that Congress is now more likely to pass limits on China's access to AI chips, with three measures possibly headed into the National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal 2027. On Monday, Nov. 9, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he strongly supports chip restrictions in the final bill, after a classified briefing for congressional leaders. The woman is Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's big Southeast Asian customers, and she has not been charged. Huang has admitted being unfaithful to his wife, and Nvidia's board has opened an investigation into whether he was targeted by foreign intelligence.

The three measures already sit in the Senate's manager's package for the defense bill, after the House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced all of them earlier this year. The AI Overwatch Act would treat AI chip sales to adversary nations much like arms sales: Commerce would have to notify two congressional committees at least 30 days before licensing chips such as Nvidia's H200, and Congress could block a sale by joint resolution. Blackwell-class chips would face mandatory denial, and the House text would end existing licenses for covered exports. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track their chips to fight smuggling, and its House version passed committee unanimously.

The MATCH Act would push U.S. allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment sales to China. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks said in a joint statement that Huang's relationship with a suspected spy makes the national security concerns even more urgent, and they urged Congress to pass the AI Overwatch Act. Nvidia declined to comment and says it follows export laws, while its board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. China's foreign ministry calls the spying allegation unsubstantiated.

The White House did not comment on the bills, though The Information reported that its officials shared feedback with congressional staff in late October. President Donald Trump has backed Huang, calling him an amazing guy and saying Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy. Congress has been here before: a similar Senate provision, the GAIN AI Act, was dropped from last year's final defense bill after lobbying by the White House and Nvidia. A former congressional staffer told Reuters that Nvidia is the biggest opponent of the Chip Security and AI Overwatch Acts, and an industry group that counts Nvidia as a member also opposes them.

If the provisions are dropped again, they would return to a Congress run by Democrats from Jan. 3, with chip hawks such as Chris Coons and Warren in line for key chairmanships. Nvidia's licensed H200 sales to China were under 1% of data center revenue last quarter, so a congressional veto would mainly cap future sales. Huang was asked to give House Republican chairmen a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18, and Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Nov. 17. Nvidia shares fell about 5% on Monday, more than 20% below their peak a month earlier.

stories.Headline: GoodRx Launches MCP Integration with Google Cloud Gemini for Healthcare: Real-Time Prescription Pricing at the Point of Care
stories.Summary:
GoodRx announced that it is a launch partner for Google Cloud's Gemini for healthcare, debuting an integration built on the Model Context Protocol, known as MCP. The integration connects GoodRx's real-time prescription pricing, discount cards and savings directories to the generative AI foundation models that Google Cloud has tailored for healthcare. The announcement was reported on Nov. 10, 2026. Google Cloud itself introduced Gemini for healthcare as an agentic AI solution for healthcare operations, according to a press release issued that Tuesday. The partnership marks the first enterprise deployment of GoodRx's MCP server.

Through the integration, clinical care teams, health system navigators and operations staff can ask for brand and generic prescription prices in natural language without leaving their AI workflows. The platform checks the prescribed medication, dosage, quantity and patient ZIP code against local pharmacy networks. It returns comparative retail prices along with coupons and digital discount cards that patients show at the dispensing counter. The integration also indexes and surfaces manufacturer-sponsored self-pay and patient-assistance programs, so providers can see financial assistance criteria early in the clinical decision. It operates inside Google Cloud's healthcare-tailored environment within HIPAA-compliant parameters, preserving patient data privacy controls and enterprise administrative governance.

Nitin Shingate, GoodRx's Chief Technology Officer, said AI is changing how people find and access healthcare. He said bringing trusted pricing and savings capabilities into AI-powered workflows puts affordability information in front of people when healthcare decisions are made. He described the standards-based MCP integration, which starts with Google Cloud, as a scalable foundation for extending GoodRx capabilities across the wider AI ecosystem. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian spoke about the broader Gemini for healthcare launch. He said the core challenge in healthcare is not a lack of information but the friction of making data actionable across a highly regulated ecosystem, and that the platform was built with healthcare customers to resolve chronic bottlenecks.

Gemini for healthcare is built on top of the universal Gemini agent and is meant to unify clinical, operational and administrative systems involved in healthcare delivery and health plan operations. It brings together information from electronic health records, billing platforms, clinical guidelines and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services datasets. According to the release, the context providers and payers need, such as patient history, coverage guidelines and administrative data, is rarely kept in one place. The effort to bridge those gaps falls heavily on the people delivering care and running operations. That includes clinicians who spend more than a full day each week on clinical documentation and administrative requirements.

GoodRx's announcement also describes how earlier approaches to linking external pricing data with large language models relied on brittle custom REST API wrappers or static retrieval-augmented generation vector embeddings that quickly decayed. By adopting the open Model Context Protocol, GoodRx offers a standardized layer that lets Gemini for healthcare call GoodRx endpoints as a specialized external tool whenever a pricing or affordability question comes up. The American Hospital Association has estimated that administrative costs account for 25% to 35% of total healthcare spending in the United States. Separately, Superscript CEO and Co-Founder Rahul Naidoo told PYMNTS that most medical providers see patient default rates of 20% to 40%, because patients often do not pay bills that arrive six weeks later. Superscript's approach is to give practices an accurate, patient-specific price before care, collect it at the point of care and attach payment options.

stories.Headline: Sino-US AI cooperation necessary for the common good of humanity: China Daily editorial
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, China's National People's Congress Standing Committee approved the agreement establishing the World AI Cooperation Organization, making China the first of its 38 founding members to do so. The decision was taken at the 25th session of the committee's 14th term. China proposed the organization, which it hosts, and its president unveiled it at a July event held alongside the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference. Thirty-eight countries joined as founding members, and the organization's stated aim is to help countries share in the opportunities AI brings. Preparations are still underway before full operations begin, and more countries are invited to join.

The articles say Beijing has named cooperation and support for developing AI capabilities in the Global South as priorities. According to the reporting, the organization should encourage consultation and shared contributions among members, support AI for the public good, and promote a governance framework that is fair and reasonable. The report on China's approval sits alongside an editorial from China Daily dated November 11, 2026, which argues for Sino-US AI cooperation. That editorial urges both countries to prioritize cooperation while keeping competition within reasonable limits. It also calls for multilateral platforms such as APEC to help bridge gaps on AI governance.

The editorial describes remarks by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent at the National Committee on US-China Relations in New York on Tuesday. Bessent called for a constructive relationship based on balance and reciprocity and hoped the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen this month would advance a new bilateral AI dialogue. He said the dialogue aims to guard against shared risks and prevent misunderstandings between the two systems. According to the editorial, Bessent said both sides expect to exchange best practices for testing advanced models before release and have agreed to set up a direct channel for alerting each other to serious incidents.

The China Daily editorial also criticizes Washington's current restrictions on Chinese technology. It says Microsoft and other companies and trade groups have reportedly urged the administration to reconsider a planned ban on imports of a crucial component used in AI data centers, arguing the ban would hurt US competitiveness. It further notes that Washington has been weighing bans on new Chinese optical transceivers over claims of data theft or malware risk that the editorial says have never been substantiated. The editorial concludes that AI risks cross borders and that Washington would benefit from moving beyond zero-sum thinking and heeding the business sector.

stories.Summary:
Only one article was supplied, and it is a report from the Institute for Family Studies rather than a news story about a single event, so the facts available are a survey and background rather than a breaking development. The report, by Jared Hayden, Ken Burchfiel and Michael Toscano and dated November 2026, asks what parents want for AI in K-12 classrooms. It finds that 56% of parents want AI fully blocked in schools, 26% want less AI than is currently required or allowed, 13% want more, and 6% want as much as possible. It also reports that 75% of Republican parents and 72% of Democratic parents support pausing AI in schools.

On timing, the report says parents favor later introduction: only 3% want AI in kindergarten and 9% want it in elementary school, while 20% want it in 12th grade or later and 22% want it never. It says 77% of parents believe AI will undermine learning, 79% that it will enable malicious student behavior, and 73% that it will expose children to serious risks. The most popular positive case, that it prepares children for the future workforce, was endorsed by 51%. Among the report's other findings, 38% of parents want AI used only in computer labs, while 25% want books and handwriting only.

The report places these attitudes against a background it describes in detail. It says nearly 4 in 10 American students attend schools where AI use is explicitly allowed or required, 15% attend schools where it is blocked, and 45% attend schools where no official action has been taken. It notes that 88% of public schools issued one-to-one devices in the 2024-2025 school year, and that US PISA reading and math scores have declined. It also cites the paused AI use in New York City and Los Angeles schools and a Nevada law protecting person-to-person school counseling. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Plurai raises $13 million for AI agent simulation platform
stories.Summary:
Plurai, a startup, announced on Wednesday that it had raised $13 million in seed funding to improve the reliability of AI agents. The round was led by Team8, with participation from U&I, Velocity, and Mercer. The company, which uses simulation techniques with synthetic data, was publicized in an article published on November 11, 2026, by TechGig. Spines, a publisher that calls itself a hybrid publisher, also announced funding that week, reporting that it had secured $64 million for its AI-powered book publishing platform. Fortune published that report on November 9, 2026, and Spines said the funding was announced on Monday.

Plurai builds a digital twin of a company's electronic systems, including its knowledge bases and tools, so its models can be prepared for difficult edge cases. The platform integrates with existing agentic tools such as Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and Cursor. Tests run in cooperation with Nvidia and Nebius showed Plurai's models outperforming mid-tier frontier models at a lower cost. Spines' $64 million comprises a $29 million Series A-1 equity round led by Zeev Ventures, with participation from Aleph, NordStar, M-Fund, LionTree, and angel investor Dan Senor. It also includes $35 million in a non-dilutive growth financing facility from Twelve, a credit-focused investment management firm.

Co-founders Ilan Kadar and Elad Levi previously worked for Nexar, an autonomous driving technology company, and Kadar also worked with Waymo to simulate and evaluate its end-to-end deep learning driving software. Ilan Kadar told TechCrunch that building an AI agent demo is easy, but achieving reliable and cost-effective operation is hard, and that Plurai seeks to build a simulation layer to address this. Yehuda Niv, the founder and CEO of Spines, said the company was founded in 2021 as an "operating system for authors." Niv said he founded Spines after concluding that AI would eventually make traditional publishing companies irrelevant, and he had earlier bootstrapped Niv Publishing.

Reah Miyara, a Google DeepMind researcher, supported Plurai as an angel investor and stated that Plurai's advantage comes from understanding production failure modes and generating synthetic data to tune models. Oren Zeev, founding partner of Zeev Ventures, said in a statement that Spines has all the ingredients to become the category leader in the next generation of publishing. Niv said Spines only publishes books "100% written by humans" and uses software to try to weed out AI-generated manuscripts. He said the company exists to "empower" human writers rather than replace them. The company has roughly 350 employees, about 50 of whom work in R&D.

Spines has offices in Israel and New York and works largely with authors who cannot obtain a traditional publishing deal or who want more control. Hybrid publishers take an upfront fee and a cut of royalties, but provide more service than self-publishing. Spines reports a $50 million annual revenue run rate, representing 400% year-over-year growth, and says it has published more than 8,000 authors and about 12,000 titles. Roughly 400 new writers sign up each month, and Spines recently raised author royalty shares from 70% to 80% of net royalties. Copyright questions arise around AI-designed covers, since U.S. courts and the Copyright Office have held that wholly AI-made images cannot be copyrighted, a point Niv disputed by describing Spines' licensing approach.

Plurai's funding will go toward building its simulation platform, and the articles do not say what milestones the seed round is expected to reach. Spines plans to use the debt facility to fund growth and the equity to build out its product and expand into the U.K., Canada, and Australia. Niv said he is aiming for 200% to 300% annual growth and that Spines is in early talks with one of the Big Five U.S. publishers about a partnership. The articles do not say whether that partnership will be finalized, nor do they give Spines' valuation, which the company declined to disclose.

stories.Headline: AutoSwift secures close to A$10 million from Singapore's X Star Technology to scale AI WINGMAN
stories.Summary:
AutoSwift, an Australian developer of automotive AI, secured close to A$10 million in strategic investment from Singapore-headquartered X Star Technology, announced on 10 November 2026. The platform in question is AI WINGMAN by AutoSwift, and the funds are meant to accelerate its development and growth. The investment is described as a vote of confidence from international investors in Australian automotive AI. The announcement followed the platform's showcases at the AADA Convention & Expo in Sydney in July and at AIMCONNECT 2026 in Singapore in October. AI WINGMAN is an agentic customer engagement platform that works alongside dealer sales and servicing teams.

AI WINGMAN handles enquiries across web chat, SMS, WhatsApp and telephone, and it helps dealerships respond to customers and identify sales opportunities. It uses dealerships' own customer and operational data to help sales teams win repeat purchases from existing customers. The platform is already used by franchised dealers of BYD, Zeekr, Land Rover and Kia. The investment is intended to support the platform's growth across the Australian automotive retail industry and the wider region. AutoSwift itself is described as an Australian fintech venture that provides AI-powered solutions for buying and financing vehicles.

Lei Shen, Director of AI WINGMAN, said the investment reflects growing recognition of purpose-built AI solutions that transform how dealerships engage customers across the ownership lifecycle. He said dealerships face more intense competition and complex market conditions, and that many sales opportunities are lost through neglected or delayed engagement. Shen said the platform was developed to turn untapped dealership data into actionable insights. Shawn Yang, CEO of X Star Technology, said in a separate statement that the investment reflects the company's focus on AI designed for automotive customer engagement. Yang said the company looks forward to working with AutoSwift to bring the next generation of automotive AI to more dealers.

X Star Technology is a Singapore-headquartered automotive finance technology company with operations across Asia Pacific, Latin America and the Middle East. It is wholly owned by Hong Kong-listed Yixin Group (HKEX: 2858) and serves more than 2,000 automotive dealers, manufacturers and financial institutions worldwide. AIMCONNECT 2026, organised by X Star and held on 11 October in Singapore, brought together over 250 industry leaders from 11 countries. Those attendees included representatives of more than 100 automotive organisations, over 60 financial institutions and around 20 technology companies. Alan Crookes, a former CEO of BMW Group Financial Services for Asia Pacific and a panellist at the event, called backing from X Star a strong signal for Australian innovation.

Dealerships, customers and the automotive retail industry are the parties most directly affected by the platform, since it is designed to change how they handle enquiries and sales. The articles give no figures on how many dealerships or customers currently use AI WINGMAN beyond the named brands. The reports describe the investment as a strategic milestone without giving a timetable or specific targets for growth. The articles do not state what share of AutoSwift the investment represents or what terms were agreed. They also do not say when the new capital will be deployed or which new markets AI WINGMAN will enter.

stories.Headline: Nvidia Board Probes Leak Claims as Jensen Huang Admits Affair
stories.Summary:
Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an ethnic Chinese businesswoman under investigation on suspicion of spying for China. The board has launched an independent investigation into allegations that confidential information was leaked from the company. The board said there is no basis to conclude that national security or company secrets were compromised so far. The episode has drawn attention in Seoul, where Samsung Electronics and SK hynix signaled caution about possible tighter export controls on AI chips. Huang has said he intends to remain in his post as the investigation proceeds.

The U.S. House Select Committee on China, the Foreign Affairs Committee and the Intelligence Committee have requested a closed-door appearance on the 18th. Nvidia has a market capitalization of $4.5 trillion, equal to 6,081 trillion won, and 42,000 employees. Roughly 60 executives have reported directly to Huang under a structure centered on one person. The company has no formal succession plan in place, according to the articles. Investors in the Korean market are watching how the probe affects the governance structure built around a single leader.

The articles state that Huang admitted the affair, while the board, not Huang, ordered the independent review into the leak claims. The board has said it is examining whether confidential information reached outside parties. Huang has said he plans to stay on as chief executive despite the scandal. The articles do not attribute further statements on the investigation to any other named official. The board's findings have not yet been published in the articles reviewed.

Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, both major suppliers of memory chips, signaled caution over the possibility of tighter export controls. Analysts quoted in the coverage said a governance shock at a leading chip designer could affect the wider AI supply chain. U.S. lawmakers have pressed for information from Nvidia, affecting the company and its executives directly. Korean investors holding Nvidia exposure through funds and local chipmakers face uncertainty about regulatory outcomes. The articles do not give further detail on the number of investors or institutions affected.

Nvidia has grown into one of the most valuable companies in the world, and its leadership has long been closely tied to Huang personally. The articles note that the company's governance structure places a large number of executives under one person. Earlier reports cited by the coverage described a U.S. intelligence suspicion that the businesswoman was spying for China. The articles also mention that Huang's personal relationship came to light through reporting in the U.S. press. The background provided does not extend beyond these facts.

The U.S. House committees are expected to hear from the company at the closed-door session scheduled for the 18th. The board's independent investigation is ongoing, and its scope and timeline are not set out in the articles. It remains unclear whether the probe will find any compromise of national security or company secrets. The articles do not say whether a formal succession plan will be created or when. Whether U.S. export controls on AI chips will tighten, and how Korean chipmakers would respond, is left open.

stories.Headline: BigBear.ai Expands Gross Margin by 878 Bps: What Drives the Gains?
stories.Summary:
BigBear.ai reported a sharp profitability improvement in the third quarter of 2026, with its gross margin rising 878 basis points year over year to 31.2% from 22.4%. The company attributed the gain mainly to a growing contribution from its generative AI platform, which it acquired through the Ask Sage transaction in December 2025. Stronger revenue performance also helped lift results during the quarter. Quarterly revenue grew 31% year over year to $43.6 million, the company's third consecutive quarter of organic revenue growth. Gross profit climbed roughly 83% to $13.6 million from $7.4 million, signaling improving operating economics.

The generative AI platform lets government agencies and critical industries securely access advanced AI models, build agentic workflows and process sensitive information in secure environments. Adoption across federal agencies, including the FBI, NASA, the U.S. Coast Guard and the Department of Energy, supports its expansion. The company secured more than 25 contracts worth over $225 million in value since the second quarter. Its backlog rose 22% sequentially to $330 million, improving visibility into future revenue. Management also raised its 2026 revenue guidance to $150 to $165 million.

The articles do not name a single executive who spoke on the results, but the company's management raised 2026 revenue guidance to $150 to $165 million. Management's outlook ties future profitability to sustained generative AI adoption, a favorable revenue mix and effective cost management. The articles frame those factors as necessary for turning gross margin gains into stronger operating profitability. The company's stated view is that the platform and contract wins support its revenue visibility and growth.

Analysts and data providers cited in the articles, including Zacks Investment Research, emphasized the margin trend and valuation. Shares gained 6.5% over the past month, outperforming the Zacks Computers - IT Services industry. BigBear.ai trades at a forward 12-month price-to-sales ratio of 6.98, a discount to industry peers. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for the 2026 and 2027 loss per share widened to 41 cents and 25 cents over the past 30 days. Its Zacks Rank is #4 (Sell).

BigBear.ai's shareholders and investors are directly affected by these figures, as the articles report adjusted EBITDA remained negative at $9.1 million and selling, general and administrative expenses rose to $31.3 million. Government agencies using the platform are also affected by its expanding adoption. The articles note competition from Palantir Technologies and C3.ai in enterprise and government AI markets. Palantir reported third-quarter 2026 revenue up 96% year over year to $2.31 billion, with a gross margin of about 83.4%. C3.ai reported a fiscal 2026 GAAP gross margin of 31%.

The articles describe BigBear.ai's generative AI platform as an emerging growth and margin catalyst within its business. The Ask Sage transaction in December 2025 brought this platform into the company. Its quarterly revenue has grown organically for three consecutive quarters. Earlier in the articles, the company is described as operating in a market for enterprise and government-focused artificial intelligence solutions. The platform's focus on specialized, mission-ready AI solutions is presented as supporting its differentiation in security and defense markets.

The articles leave open whether the margin expansion will be sustained, since they say profitability challenges persist. They do not state when BigBear.ai expects to reach positive adjusted EBITDA. Future revenue depends on converting its backlog and contract wins, but the articles give no timeline for that. Whether Palantir's scalable software model will widen its advantage over BigBear.ai also remains unaddressed. The articles give no further guidance or outcomes beyond the 2026 revenue range and the consensus loss estimates.

stories.Headline: Leaked documents: OpenAI's adjusted operating margin improved from -150% to -109% from Q2 to Q3 (Berber Jin/Wall Street Journal)
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, PBC launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering of Class A common stock on November 10, 2026. The company and its shareholders plan to sell 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 each, with the shares listing on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Of those shares, 801.35 million are being sold by the company and 23.65 million by existing holders. At the top of the price range, the offering could raise up to $64.35 billion. Anthropic filed an amended Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, and the registration statement has not yet become effective.

The filing estimates a fully diluted valuation of roughly $1.24 trillion to $1.38 trillion, below earlier expectations of around $1.5 trillion. CNBC reported that the filing puts the top valuation at up to $1.405 trillion, compared with the $965 billion valuation during the $65 billion Series H announced in May. Anthropic also said it has approximately $81 billion in annualized revenue run rate as of October 31, 2026, up $10 billion, or 14.1%, from September. Patrick Moorhead wrote that a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price includes $10 billion each from Google and Nvidia, $2.5 billion from AMD, and additional investment from others. The shares are expected to price next Wednesday and begin trading on Thursday, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Leslie Picker.

Anthropic, which is led by Dario Amodei and six cofounders, is the company responsible for the filing and the roadshow. In an updated S-1, the company confirmed that it has determined that the Autonomy 2 capability threshold has been met, based on what it described as a dramatic acceleration of overall AI research and development progress. Anthropic's filing also describes a governance structure in which a single founder share and a single trustee share effectively control the company, according to Keith Porcaro's LinkedIn post. The company's own marketing for the IPO began with the roadshow launch.

Investors and commentators reacted to the offering in varied ways. Mohamed El-Erian pointed to the company's revenue growth for the nine months ending in September, and Jim Cramer said the growth could justify a record-breaking IPO. Judith Lynne wrote that the offering could shift Anthropic's finances onto the public, while Ricardo argued that buyers would have little ability to influence the company's decisions. Michael Kramer noted that up to 316 million shares could become tradable on the first trading day after the prospectus date, and that a deal of 825 million shares seemed large.

The people who buy the shares, and the public that holds them, are most directly affected by these terms. Anthropic's IPO follows a period of market volatility, and a Wall Street Journal headline described the company as preparing to push ahead despite market jitters. Reports noted that AI infrastructure stocks fell by 50% in October, and Anthropic's valuation target is lower than earlier expectations. The company's Series H in May valued it at $965 billion.

The filing also reports that Anthropic has generated $42 million in legal fees for the IPO, according to a Bloomberg Law report. The shares are expected to begin trading on Nasdaq after pricing next Wednesday, though the registration statement has not yet become effective. The articles do not say where the final price will settle within the $70 to $78 range, how much of the 20% retail allocation will be filled, or whether the institutional demand will hold. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI Opportunity Fund Expands AI Skills Training Across Asia Pacific with 28 Phase Three Local Implementing Partners
stories.Summary:
AVPN, Asia's largest platform for social impact, announced on November 11, 2026 the 28 organisations selected as local implementing partners for phase three of the AI Opportunity Fund: Asia-Pacific, supported by Google.org and the Asian Development Bank. The new cohort extends the Fund's AI skills training into schools, universities and workplaces across 19 markets, including through organisations taking part in AI Ready ASEAN, led by ASEAN Foundation. Most of the new partners will work directly with K-12 teachers, university students and faculty, reaching the educators who shape the next generation of workers. Other partners will reach healthcare workers, agricultural and service-sector workers, and employees of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. The same day, AVPN also launched the AI Opportunity Learning Platform.

The platform gives learners access to localised AI training and recommended learning pathways in 16 languages, with a pathway suggested after a short assessment. Certification is available on completion of training. A Gemini-powered assistant helps users navigate the platform and provides guided learning. For phase three, AVPN brought on two new strategic partners: the Raspberry Pi Foundation, which will help local partners localise its Experience AI content, and the Ayala Foundation, which will give educators and students in the Philippines access to Google AI learning resources and support local partners there. Among the funded organisations, Pratham Education Foundation in India will train teachers to use AI critically, JA Korea will pair Google's AI training with formal certification for public school educators, and AI Edu Corp in Vietnam will support embedding AI literacy into national teacher standards.

AVPN chief executive Naina Subberwal Batra said that AI tools are already entering classrooms and workplaces across the region, and that the challenge is helping people use them well and know when not to rely on them too heavily. She said local organisations understand the languages and communities they serve and can adapt training in ways a regional programme alone cannot. Marija Ralic, head of Google.org APAC, said access to AI skills depends on whether people can find relevant training in a language and setting that works for them, and that the platform brings training and local partners together in one place. The Fund was launched in 2024 with a USD 15 million commitment, received a further USD 10 million in phase two in May 2025 and another USD 10 million in phase three in May 2026, bringing Google.org's total commitment to USD 35 million. To date, the Fund has trained more than 850,000 workers and 63,000 small businesses through almost 60 local implementing partner organisations, delivering programmes in more than 30 local languages.

stories.Headline: Caine Prize clears Zimbabwean author of AI writing allegations and adds new rules
stories.Summary:
The Caine Prize for African Writing has cleared Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza of using artificial intelligence to write his award-winning story, while also announcing new rules to guard against generative AI in future submissions. The allegations were raised in an article by The Atlantic magazine and sparked debate on social media about whether Black authors face unfair AI-related accusations. The prize organizers said an internal review found the evidence clear, so Kundizeza's award stands. Kundizeza said he felt relieved that the allegations had been dismissed and that he was happy to move on. The Caine Prize plans to introduce AI declarations and an AI use policy for entrants.

The organization said it will also require writers to disclose any use of generative AI in their submissions. The rules are meant to address concerns about how such tools may be used in the competition's entries going forward. The prize did not say in the available reporting how the new measures will be enforced. Kundizeza's response was delivered after the prize announced its findings on Wednesday, and he spoke to reporters on Thursday. He said he was grateful for the review and that he hoped the matter would now be closed.

Responsibility for the review and the new policy rests with the Caine Prize organizers, who said the evidence did not support the claims made about his story. Commentators quoted in the reporting described the accusations as having been fueled by broader assumptions about African writing. The matter comes amid wider discussion about how literary prizes and publishers should handle AI-generated writing. The articles do not describe any further steps in the case or any legal action. The Caine Prize's new AI measures are expected to apply to future competitions, and the articles give no date for when they take effect.

stories.Headline: AI hoaxes are deceiving 911 dispatchers, and they're only getting harder to detect
stories.Summary:
In August, a caller made a bomb threat to Wheatland Union High School in Yuba County, California, and the voice on the call was generated by artificial intelligence. Police responded overnight and classes at the school were canceled, though there was no bomb and no one was hurt. Authorities said the call was part of a series of hoax calls, also called swatting, made to schools across the country over the summer. The Yuba County incident stood out because it was an example of a new and growing challenge for emergency responders. Swatting calls can go to 911 or to police departments, with callers reporting a bomb threat, a mass shooting or another life-threatening emergency in order to trigger a massive response, according to the FBI.

Swatting calls made with AI-generated voices or background sounds are making these hoaxes sound more realistic, which makes it harder to tell what is real. Companies such as ElevenLabs, which creates synthetic voice software, offer AI tools that are incredibly cheap and readily available. APCO and the Public Safety Threat Alliance, an information-sharing and cybersecurity group, studied how common swatting is at 911 call centers and published their findings in June. Their report was based on 766 responses from public safety communications professionals, and about 14% of dispatchers said they had been targeted using AI tools. Mel Maier says he thinks that figure will keep rising as the tools become more advanced.

Mel Maier is the CEO and executive director of APCO International, the Association of Public Safety Communication Officials, and he says swatting voices used to be easy to recognize. He says that now they sound natural, can insert pauses, and can use filler words such as "uh" or "um." Maier also notes that people have been killed and injured in swatting attacks. April Heinze, NENA's vice president and chief of 911 operations, says there are hallmarks of a swatting call, including that most swatters do not dial 911 directly. She explains that 911 provides location, a callback number and the name of the phone's owner, and that it is really impossible to spoof your location on 911.

Brandon May, an assistant professor of forensic psychology at the Florida Institute of Technology, says he can clone his own voice on ElevenLabs for less than $20. He says he can change the intonation, the depth or pitch of the voice, and the pauses. May says it is no longer simple to look at an image or hear a voice and tell that it is AI, and that people are duped by this all the time. He adds that elaborate fraud callers using AI chatbots are even tricking people into handing over their life savings. May says the increasingly sophisticated fake voices and sound effects make it especially hard for dispatchers to judge what is real on what he calls high-stakes, high-consequence calls, and he says detection will be nearly impossible.

Swatting calls usually trigger a big, chaotic police response, which redirects public safety resources away from real emergencies. The goal of such calls is to harass or retaliate against their targets, such as a public official. APCO and NENA: The 9-1-1 Association, which both represent 911 dispatchers, say incidents like the one in Yuba County reflect their growing worries about how bad actors could use AI. Heinze says swatting calls are usually made to police departments or courthouses, and the callers are then ultimately transferred into 911 centers. She says trying to trace those calls is impossible, and that the long-running swatting problem now includes this AI element.

APCO and NENA are developing ways to train their members to deal with these new threats, despite the difficulty. Both Heinze and Maier decline to describe the specifics of the training, saying more public information would make it easier to train AI to fool dispatchers. Maier does note that APCO is working on training criteria for caller interrogation, in which dispatchers ask specific questions at such a granular level that an AI cannot take the answers from a public database or a social media post, or guess them. Both Maier and Heinze emphasize that dispatchers will always assume calls reporting a life-threatening situation are real and will keep sending emergency resources to any call for help. Heinze says public safety will have a very strong response even when there are indicators of swatting, because a life-or-death situation means you can never take chances, and the articles do not say when the training will be ready.

stories.Headline: Intel and Altera Simplify Sensor Integration for Edge and Physical AI
stories.Summary:
Intel and Altera announced on November 11, 2026, that they will collaborate on a flexible, real-time sensor bridge for edge and physical AI systems. The announcement came from Santa Clara, California, and combines Intel compute, connectivity and software with Altera FPGAs. The companies say the work aims to help equipment makers connect and act on data from increasingly sensor-rich environments. The partnership targets healthcare, aerospace and defense, and robotics applications. The collaboration centers on modular reference solutions that pair programmable hardware with a consistent Intel compute and software foundation.

The articles say these designs are meant to handle sensor data that must be merged while meeting requirements for timing, performance, power and cost. Some applications need very high bandwidth or flexible form factors that place input and output away from the compute board. In those cases, sensor data must be streamed rapidly into memory for the host Intel processor to use. The companies say this approach should let manufacturers adapt as applications and sensors change and move more efficiently from prototype to deployment. Dan Rodriguez, corporate vice president and general manager of Intel's Edge Computing Group, said customers need a simpler way to turn real-world data into timely action as sensors multiply.

Farhad Shafai, head of business solutions and marketing at Altera, said physical AI systems must sense, decide and act in real time, and that Altera FPGAs supply the connectivity, data processing and deterministic control needed for that. Shafai added that the FPGAs remain programmable as sensors and AI models evolve. Both executives framed the combined offering as a flexible foundation that manufacturers can tailor to their needs. The companies plan to apply the work in three areas. In healthcare, they are jointly developing a reference solution aimed at the strict latency and real-time requirements of advanced equipment.

In aerospace and defense, they are working on reference solutions for next-generation mission systems with a focus on size, weight and power for converged AI and signal-processing workloads. In robotics, they plan to combine Intel compute, connectivity and robotics software with Altera FPGA technology to address complex sensing and timing needs. Developers will reach these capabilities through Intel's Open Edge Platform SDK and an Altera SDK. The articles do not give timelines for when the reference solutions will be released.

stories.Headline: Veterans tour Washington war memorials using AI glasses
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, a group of veterans from across the country toured Washington's war memorials using special sets of AI glasses to help them locate fallen service members. The trip was an honor flight sponsored by Meta, and the veterans spent three days in the capital. Many of them were blind or visually impaired, so each received a pair of Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses to help them move through the memorials built in their honor. The glasses use built-in cameras, microphones and AI to sense the wearer's surroundings and describe them aloud.

The glasses could be used to read details about the memorials and to explain what the wearers were facing. Meta has committed to donating 130,000 pairs to visually impaired and blinded veterans nationwide. According to John Bockstanz, an Innovation Policy Manager at Meta, the glasses are already helping users regain independence in places like busy airports, restaurants and clothing stores. He described the effort as an ongoing, year-round commitment rather than a single flight.

John Bockstanz, who is also an Iraq War veteran, said the company worked with the veterans so they could ask the glasses what they were seeing and get more information about each memorial. Victor Dunham, a Vietnam veteran from Texas, used his pair to research a friend named Anthony, known as Tony, who died while serving beside him. The glasses helped him locate Anthony's name on the Vietnam Memorial wall. Dunham said the experience closed a loop he had carried for decades.

The trip also gave Dunham a chance to share the experience with his son Mark, an Iraq War veteran who came along. Dunham called the visit wonderful and said he appreciated it beyond belief. He described it as the most meaningful thing he had ever done with the company. The articles do not describe any further plans for the trip beyond the three days in Washington.

stories.Headline: Coframe, which uses AI to make websites that test and personalize themselves for each visitor, raised a $25M Series A, bringing its total funding to $35M (Ben Bergman/Business Insider)
stories.Summary:
Graphon, a San Francisco startup, raised $35 million in a Series A round led by RRE Ventures, announced November 10, 2026. The company builds software that helps AI agents store and retrieve information over time, addressing what Business Insider describes as agent "amnesia." Founder and CEO Arbaaz Khan said the company uses a mathematical framework he used during his Ph.D. research into coordinating swarms of robots, which gave the company its name. Graphon has raised the funding to further build and sell its technology. The round follows a roughly $8 million seed round the company closed earlier this year.

Rather than treating documents, videos, and images as isolated snippets, Graphon maps the connections among them, including where information came from and when it changed. Khan compared common AI search systems to tearing pages out of a book, crumpling them, and tossing them into a bin. The product is compatible with off-the-shelf agents such as Claude or GPT, and Khan said users can push in any amount of data. Graphon targets two groups: individual developers and companies with large stores of technical and operational data, such as industrial businesses, financial services, and healthcare companies. The company says its software is already used by the San Francisco 49ers and HP.

Khan is the company's founder and CEO, and he described the problem directly to Business Insider. He said that in common AI search systems, each piece of information lives on its own, so the information is effectively lost when agents search for pieces to answer a question. Graphon instead creates what Khan called a connected "fabric" of information. The article attributes these comments to Khan in his own words, and it does not describe any other party as responsible for the technology or the funding.

Besides RRE Ventures, the Series A included participation from Energy Impact Partners, Hitachi Ventures, Gaia VC, and HP. The article notes that HP is both an investor in the round and a company that uses Graphon's software. Graphon has 20 employees and plans to use the new cash primarily to hire engineers and researchers, along with some sales and go-to-market staff. Khan said the company expects to remain focused on enterprise customers before moving further into personal devices and consumer products. The article does not describe other reactions or effects beyond these statements.

The article's background is limited to Graphon's own history and its funding. The company's name comes from "graphons," a mathematical framework Khan used during his doctoral research. The seed round of roughly $8 million was closed earlier in 2026, and the Series A brings the company's total funding to about $43 million. The article is an exclusive by reporter Shubhangi Goel, who covers AI and startups for Business Insider's Singapore bureau. The article provides no further history of the company or of the wider market.

The article does not say when Graphon will release a broader product, what pricing or revenue the company has, or how many customers it has beyond the 49ers and HP. It also leaves open the timing of any expansion into personal devices and consumer products, which Khan said will follow the enterprise focus. Graphon plans to hire engineers, researchers, and sales staff, but the article gives no specific hiring targets or dates. Whether the connected approach will outperform other AI memory systems is not addressed in the article.

Anthropic launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering of Class A common stock, which the company and its shareholders plan to sell at $70 to $78 per share. Anthropic's executives, led by CEO Dario Amodei, are presenting the offering to investors, and the filing names seven founders and five trustees who would control the company through a single founder share and a single trustee share. Current shareholders and public market buyers are the groups most directly affected, since the sale will be open to institutional and retail investors. The filing also includes a lock-up schedule under which up to 316 million Class A shares could become tradable on the first trading day after the prospectus date. Coverage also notes the offering would rival SpaceX's record IPO. Anthropic's previous valuation and fundraising history are cited in the filings as context for the range now being offered to the public. stories.Headline: Alphabet Kicks Off Asia Bond Sale as AI Firms Face Scrutiny
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, the parent company of Google, began marketing its first Hong Kong dollar and Singapore dollar bond sale, according to Bloomberg, which reported the move on November 11, 2026. The company is testing investor appetite at a time when companies focused on artificial intelligence face growing market volatility. Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter, that Alphabet set initial price guidance for proposed 2-year, 5-year and 10-year Hong Kong dollar bonds at around 4.6%, 5% and 5.5%. It is also marketing 2-year, 5-year, 10-year and 30-year Singapore dollar notes, with guidance around 2.75%, 3.25%, 3.65% and 4%. The proceeds are earmarked for general corporate purposes, which may include repaying outstanding debt, and the bonds could be priced as early as Thursday.

The offering arrives during a difficult stretch for technology borrowers. Bloomberg said investors have grown more cautious toward AI-linked assets after a broad market selloff the previous week, driven by worries that a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections could bring tougher scrutiny of data center development and AI infrastructure spending. Turmoil at Nvidia, the leading AI chipmaker, has also weighed on the sector, with the company reportedly working with an outside firm to find potential replacements for chief executive Jensen Huang. Alphabet's deal is part of a wider push by large technology firms to tap new debt markets for AI projects. This year the company has sold bonds in Australian dollars, Swiss francs, British pounds, Canadian dollars and Japanese yen, and earlier this month it raised €6 billion, or $6.7 billion, in a multi-tranche euro sale.

Bloomberg noted that Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta have been borrowing at a record pace while committing tens of billions of dollars to build out their AI capabilities. The report said Alphabet paid materially higher borrowing costs on its most recent euro deal than on its inaugural euro offering in May, as concerns about the pace of AI spending grew. The source article does not say how much the company ultimately plans to raise in the Asian currencies, beyond a related market report of up to $3 billion, nor what final pricing will be. Further details on demand and final terms are likely to emerge once the bonds are priced.

stories.Headline: HUMAIN Partners with VUZ to Advance a New Generation of Immersive AI Streaming and Learning by Launching HUMAIN Plus
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, HUMAIN, a PIF company delivering full-stack artificial intelligence capabilities globally, announced a strategic partnership with VUZ in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The two companies will develop immersive AI learning experiences through HUMAIN+, a new initiative focused on equipping leaders, professionals, faculty, and future innovators with practical AI capabilities. The partnership debuted publicly with the first showcase of HUMAIN+, a flagship immersive learning experience. The partnership combines HUMAIN's vision for streaming and applied AI education with VUZ's immersive video technology to create a new approach to streaming and learning. HUMAIN+ is a world-class immersive streaming and learning platform that the companies describe as a new model for AI education, available in the next few months.

Through immersive digital experiences and AI-driven sessions, delivered both virtually and in person, participants will engage with AI in more interactive, contextual, and experiential ways. The companies are designing and delivering educational experiences that move beyond traditional online learning. Participants will experience AI concepts, demonstrations, and real-world applications in environments designed to increase engagement and practical understanding. The attendees at the showcase received an early look at this model. The platform is intended to support the development of talent, leadership, and workforce capabilities across Saudi Arabia and globally.

HUMAIN's chief executive, Tareq Amin, said that AI should fundamentally change how the world learns. He said HUMAIN+ was created to build a new generation of AI talent through practical, immersive streaming and learning experiences. Amin said the partnership with VUZ brings together AI and immersive technology to make learning more engaging, more accessible, and more connected to how people will work. VUZ's founder and chief executive, Khaled Zaatarah, said immersive technology and video streaming can transform industries, including education. He said the partnership lets VUZ apply its latest technology to AI streaming and education to help learners build practical knowledge.

The learners who will use these experiences include leaders, professionals, faculty, and future innovators, and the partnership is aimed at accelerating AI adoption across Saudi Arabia and globally. HUMAIN serves both public and private sector organizations, unlocking value across industries and driving digital transformation through human–AI collaboration. VUZ is a global immersive technology company that delivers immersive video across education, entertainment, sports, government, and digital infrastructure. VUZ holds two USPTO-granted patents in immersive capture, streaming, and playback, and serves partners and users in 23 markets. Headquartered in Riyadh, VUZ aims to contribute to the growth of Saudi Arabia's digital economy, develop local talent, and export Saudi-built technology to the world.

HUMAIN describes itself as a global artificial intelligence company with a growing portfolio of sector-specific AI products, and it focuses on intellectual property development and global talent leadership. Its four core areas include next-generation data centers, hyper-performance infrastructure and cloud platforms, advanced AI models including Arabic large language models developed in the Arab world, and transformative AI solutions. The press release states that the partnership's forward-looking statements may differ materially due to risks and uncertainties. HUMAIN has said it undertakes no obligation to update those statements. The articles do not give further detail on the timing, cost, or participants of the first HUMAIN+ sessions beyond the availability window.

stories.Headline: Kazakhstan-linked hackers used AI to steal Tajik government documents, researchers say
stories.Summary:
A hacking group linked to Kazakhstan used artificial intelligence to steal more than 2,000 national security-related documents from neighboring Tajikistan, according to a report published on Wednesday by the Singapore-based cybersecurity company CloudSek. The company said it caught the group, which it said was nicknamed "Silent Lynx," after the hackers accidentally left a server exposed to the internet. The attackers used Hermes, an open-source framework for autonomous AI agents, to carry out the intrusion. CloudSek said the activity was tied to the group's espionage work.

CloudSek's data indicated that the hackers began reconnaissance using Hermes around mid-August and broke into Tajikistan's electronic document system a couple of weeks later. The AI agent then reportedly wrote a custom program to download the files, organize them, and split them into chunks to steal them more efficiently. Exposed data also showed the instructions the hackers gave the agent, which described it as an elite offensive security specialist and red teamer. The company said this shows that instead of typing commands by hand, the attacker told the AI what to do and the AI planned, executed, and documented the attacks. Reuters noted that cybercriminals had previously been assigning break-ins to autonomous AI agents.

Kazakh and Tajik government officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and efforts to reach Silent Lynx were unsuccessful. CloudSek said it found evidence the hackers spoke Russian, worked Kazakh business hours, and often accessed the exposed server through a residential Kazakh internet connection. Other researchers have previously tied the Silent Lynx group to Kazakhstan. The report's findings are based on the data CloudSek recovered from the exposed server, and the article does not describe any further steps by authorities.

stories.Headline: An analysis of the tech job market in late 2026: product managers seem to be benefiting most in the AI era, demand for engineers is plateauing, and more (Lenny Rachitsky/Lenny's Newsletter)
stories.Summary:
Lenny Rachitsky published his second job market report of 2026 in his newsletter on November 10, 2026, calling it the most surprising and interesting of the five he has done over the past few years. Its headline finding is that product managers appear to be benefiting most in the AI era, while demand for engineers has stalled. He said open product manager roles are at their highest in nearly four years, up 75% from the March 2023 low. He also found that actual hiring for every core product role has been flat or in decline over the past few years. The report is the paid version of the newsletter, and the full seventh takeaway was reserved for paid subscribers.

The analysis rests on two proprietary datasets, the first being TrueUp, which powers Lenny's Jobs and tracks global job openings at more than 9,000 tech companies. The second comes from Live Data Technologies, which tracks hires, departures and promotions for 124 million professionals, and its hiring numbers in the report are specifically for the United States. Product manager openings have grown faster than any other core tech role since the start of 2023, rising 56% compared with 43% for engineering. Product manager hiring has held up the best of the five core roles, and its share of hiring grew from 16% in 2021 to 21% today. There are now 3.8 open product manager roles for every open design role, up from 2.6 earlier this year and 1.9 in early 2023.

Hiring data shows U.S. employers hired about 2.9 product managers for every designer over the past 12 months, up from 1.9 in 2022. Rachitsky is responsible for the analysis, and he thanked Amit Taylor and Alex Hamilton for sharing the data with his readers. He read the gap between growing product manager openings and flat or falling hiring as a sign that demand is growing while landing great product managers is getting harder. He said the same is true for engineers, since openings are up 44% since January 2024 while hiring is down 17%. He pointed to demand for tech recruiters as a bright spot, with open recruiter roles up nearly 300% since mid-2023, and suggested this may be a leading indicator of a reacceleration in engineering hiring.

On design, he said he is hopeful the trend turns around as companies recognize that great design can be a differentiator in an increasingly noisy market. He also offered theories for the decline in user research, including the faster pace of product development and better tooling that lets non-researchers run their own studies. Engineering openings have stalled for the first time in the history of the report, growing 29% through 2024, 15% through 2025 and just 2.5% this past year. U.S. companies hired about 113,000 software engineers from May 2025 to April 2026, less than half the 2022 peak of 239,000, and the number has dropped every year since 2022. Engineering is still the largest category of tech hiring by far, with over 120,000 engineers hired in the U.S. in 2025 and more than 65,000 jobs currently open.

Designers are hurting, with about 1,900 open product design roles globally, the lowest since tracking began and down 28% from a year ago. U.S. companies hired about 12,600 product designers over the past 12 months, against 27,600 in 2022, and about 1,800 user researchers, down 66% from 5,300 in 2022. Meta and Google together made about one in eight of all U.S. user research hires in 2025, and only 108 user research jobs are currently open globally. On the background the report gives, the most mentioned skills in product manager job descriptions two years ago were SQL, Jira, AWS and Python, whereas today LLM is the most mentioned, with Claude third and Cursor, OpenAI and MCP in the top eight. For engineers, Python remains the most mentioned skill and LLM has just passed Java in postings, while Kubernetes has proved durable.

For designers, Figma remains the leading skill and demand for it has grown over the past three years, but Claude became the second most mentioned skill this spring, crossing CSS, and Cursor has also edged past CSS. Forward deployed engineer openings are up 4.6 times in the past year, to around 1,500 from only a few dozen globally in the past, mostly at Palantir, though some growth may reflect rebranding of titles such as sales engineer. Security engineering is among the fastest-growing specialties, while demand for mobile and front-end engineers has nearly halved in the past year, which Rachitsky ties to AI letting smaller teams own more. Bay Area roles now make up a record 15% of open tech roles, with openings there up 43% from a year ago, and one in four product manager and design roles and one in five engineering roles are there. Remote roles have fallen to a record low of 14% of open tech roles, down from 21% in late 2022, with remote engineering at 14% from 25% and remote design at 19% from 34%.

Product management is the exception, holding steady at about 21% for the past two years. Sometime last year, open product, engineering and design roles based in the Bay Area came to outnumber remote roles globally, where remote once led almost two to one. The report says Rachitsky will be watching the recruiter trend closely as a possible sign that engineering hiring will reaccelerate. He saved his seventh takeaway for last, saying the tech job market is growing fast but mostly outside of software, and the full details sit behind the paywall. The articles do not say whether the product manager advantage will last or what the design and user research figures will look like in his next report.

stories.Headline: Tester joins AI, data and surveillance company with MAGA ties
stories.Summary:
Former Montana U.S. Senator Jon Tester has taken a job as a senior advisor at Palantir Technologies, an artificial intelligence, surveillance and data analytics company with ties to the GOP and the Trump administration. The Chronicle reported the move on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, after the opportunity reached Tester's desk in July. Tester's role is limited to advising on real-world uses for AI and on increasing efficiency and ease of use. He said he talked one-on-one with people at the company, including CEO Alex Karp, before accepting. The articles give no further terms of the position, such as pay or length of contract.

Palantir's software is used by U.S. immigration enforcement and the Israeli military. The company was co-founded by billionaire conservative Trump ally Peter Thiel. Its work has drawn scrutiny from the American Civil Liberties Union, a nonprofit advocacy organization. The articles say Tester's advisory work is separate from data centers, though he described the two as connected. He said he is not working on data center issues for the company.

Tester said he does not believe data centers are inherently wrong, but he called them "screwed up big time" because they can overload energy grids. He said communities should be "driving the bus" and that operators need "absolutely 100% transparency." Tester said AI hearings, accountability and oversight will come in Congress and that talking across the aisle is important. He said he hopes to use his experience as a third-generation organic grain and crop farmer to streamline administrative work in food production. He said he is "not the most technologically gifted person in the world."

Tester said AI could let the U.S. Department of Agriculture and crop insurers interact without overlapping paperwork, easing the load on farmers. He said shared medical records between Veterans Affairs facilities and the private sector could work better with AI. He said he respects Palantir's stated commitment to civil liberties and privacy. Tester said Montanans tend to share a libertarian tilt and dislike "big brother telling us what to do." Karp has said only vocational or technical workers and neurodivergent individuals with out-of-the-box problem-solving skills can thrive in an AI-driven world, and that AI could disrupt white-collar jobs.

The articles report that the newly elected majority in Congress could soon use subpoenas to compel major tech executives to testify under oath about AI. On July 23, Democratic California representative Ted Lieu and Texas Republican Nathaniel Moran introduced the AI Kill Switch Act, which could authorize slowdowns or shutdowns of AI systems that cause catastrophic harm. That bill remains in limbo. No federal rule currently requires AI developers to be able to intervene if a system behaves dangerously. A poll by The AI Policy Institute found that 86% of voters support a guaranteed shutdown capability.

Tester endorsed Democratic Representative-elect Sam Forstag, who proposed a kill switch on AI during an Oct. 26 visit to Montana State University before Election Day. Tester said he has not compared notes with Forstag on AI but likes him a lot, and that Forstag may have information Tester lacks. Tester said he does not know whether a kill switch is realistic. The articles end with Tester saying Congress should bring in people who know the industry, ask tough questions and pass something that works. They do not say whether Tester will testify, whether any subpoenas will be issued, or whether the kill switch bill will advance.

stories.Headline: Not funny: US comedians say 'sexualized' AI personas steal jokes
stories.Summary:
Several American stand-up comedians say AI-generated social media personas are copying their jokes, according to an Agence France-Presse report published on November 11, 2026. Julia Jasunas, a Los Angeles-based comedian, said an account called "Aylen Skye" lifted a joke about kissing a roommate that she had spent years developing. AFP found several similar sexualized AI personalities on Instagram and TikTok that were reusing material from real comedians, and it was unclear who was running them. Some of the accounts appeared to drive traffic to subscription services that host pornography.

The Aylen Skye account gathered more than 230,000 Instagram followers and a Meta verified checkmark before it was removed, while the TikTok version still exists and links to Fanvue, a subscription platform with adult content from AI models. New York comedian Olivia Carter said a copycat video used her joke about asking out a personal trainer, a bit she once performed on Jimmy Fallon's show, and she has stopped posting new material online. California comedian George Brett Olson said an account called "Tiffany Sloane," with over 370,000 followers, copied his joke, his outfit and his stage setup. Experts quoted in the report describe the problem as part of a wider pattern in which AI systems take creative work from painters, musicians and others without payment or credit.

The comedians said platform owners should do more to stop this, and Jasunas argued that companies with the money and technology have a duty to tighten their rules. Meta did not immediately comment, while a TikTok spokesperson pointed to community guidelines that bar sharing content that violates another user's intellectual property rights. Meta's head, Adam Mosseri, responded to Olson's complaint by saying that banning AI was not practical but that the company wanted to direct more traffic to original creators. He added that Meta should work out what it could do about wholesale copying, though he said he was not sure what that would be. Olson called the response a "big nothing-burger."

Carnegie Mellon University professor Michael Smith told AFP that comedians once policed one another's jokes informally, but large language models scraping the internet have made that difficult to enforce. Smith warned that the accounts siphon clicks and money from artists who rely on social media to build audiences and win bookings, which could weaken the early stages of comedy careers. Olson said he sees the issue as a choice made by the companies rather than something that cannot be avoided. The report does not say whether any platform has announced new measures in response.

stories.Headline: IBM report finds 94% of surveyed enterprises faced a sovereignty challenge, with AI the most common
stories.Summary:
The IBM report, Proof, Not Promises: The Digital Sovereignty Index, was released on November 11, 2026, and it finds that 94% of the enterprises it surveyed faced at least one sovereignty challenge over the previous three years. Those challenges included AI-provider failures, regulatory conflicts, critical vendor disruption, government restrictions such as export controls, and data-access problems. Of the organizations affected, 81% had to supply formal evidence of control to regulators, customers, auditors or internal stakeholders. IBM describes the gap it has found as an "overconfidence gap," in which leaders believe they can prove sovereign control but the evidence often falls short of the Index's highest standards.

The report measures whether an organization can retain and prove control over its critical AI, technology, operations and data, especially when conditions change or dependencies come under pressure. It assesses six areas: responsibility, which asks whether the organization can prove who was accountable; trace, which asks whether it can show exactly what happened; constraint, which asks whether it can prove its controls were working; intervention, which asks whether it can show how it responded and recovered; legitimacy, which asks whether it can explain and justify decisions under scrutiny; and exit, which asks whether it can prove it could change provider or recover operations if needed. The findings suggest that the difficulty is less about control itself than about sovereignty efforts not being built to answer these questions smoothly under pressure. Only a third of respondents, 33%, test their ability to demonstrate sovereignty continuously or as part of regular governance and assurance processes.

IBM's Senior Vice President and Chief Global Affairs Officer, Jonathan Adashek, said that sovereignty should expand future choices rather than restrict them, and that boards need to show how they can adapt, change strategy or change critical provider. He added that the next step is stronger evidence that governance works, including testing exit capabilities, understanding critical dependencies and focusing on where a loss of control would have the greatest impact. Emmanuel Frenehard, Chief Digital Officer at Sanofi, said that digital sovereignty is a business reality rather than a compliance checkbox, and that it is a matter of business continuity as AI becomes embedded across the enterprise. The report itself does not say which organizations or regulators, beyond these two executives, took any position on the findings.

AI emerged as the most common sovereignty problem, with AI-related issues, including incorrect outputs, explainability problems, model or provider failures and governance concerns, cited by 44% of respondents. That figure was ahead of significant provider changes at 35%, formal audit or regulatory events at 38%, data-access or transfer issues at 33%, and government restrictions such as export controls or sanctions at 30%. An average of 82% of respondents said they were very or extremely confident they could provide evidence of sovereign control. However, only 26% of enterprises reached the Index's Leading Digital Sovereignty tier, and enterprises in that tier were more than twice as likely to resolve their most testing challenge without material disruption, at 52% compared with 22% of establishing enterprises.

The research behind the Index combined a review of 27 sources, including legislation, standards, governance frameworks and academic research, with 25 interviews with policymakers, regulators, public-sector officials and policy experts, and perspectives from 17 senior customer leaders across five countries. Its quantitative survey covered 2,003 senior decision-makers at large enterprises in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France, Saudi Arabia, India and Japan. Among the barriers that respondents reported to proving sovereignty were manual or time-consuming evidence collection, cited by 56%, and fragmented evidence across teams and systems, dependence on third parties for records, and legacy systems or inconsistent standards, each cited by 53%. Half of respondents, 50%, pointed to untested controls, recovery or exit arrangements. The report does not describe any specific steps that organizations are scheduled to take next.
