stories.Headline: The Worst Thing About AI Writing
stories.Summary:
Thélyson Orélien, a Haitian Canadian author, came to Paris in September as a rising star of the rentrée littéraire, or fall publishing season, with his novel C'était ça ou mourir. The book, about a Haitian schoolteacher fleeing gang violence on a dangerous journey north toward Canada, became a best seller in France, won the Prix du Roman Fnac on September 21, and was in the running for the Renaudot and the Prix Goncourt. That same day, an anonymous account on X posted an analysis by the AI-detection tool Pangram, which claimed that 100 percent of the text it examined was written by AI. Le Point then reported instances of alleged plagiarism in Orélien's earlier work, which he later admitted and apologized for, and the Académie Goncourt disqualified him. In late October, his Quebecois publisher said he had in fact used AI despite earlier denials and ended their relationship, while his French publisher, Éditions Grasset, continues to sell the book.

The article describes the allegations as a comparison with an earlier case, the 1968 novel Le devoir de violence by Yambo Ouologuem, which won the Prix Renaudot and was later found to contain passages closely resembling Graham Greene's 1934 novel It's a Battlefield. Ouologuem's American publisher pulped thousands of copies, and he returned to Mali and never published again. The article also notes that Orélien did not respond to multiple requests for comment through email and his publishers, and that in one of his latest public statements he called the attacks a "media lynching." The article's own account of the story is that the reaction to Orélien included racist attacks on his command of French, a criticism long aimed at Black writers in France.

The account on X was run by a group that includes Samuel Fitoussi, a Le Figaro columnist who also works at a venture-capital firm that has invested in AI. Fitoussi told the author in October that sharing the findings was a matter of fairness and that he worried AI-aided texts would discourage human writers, while the group wrote on Substack's Persuasion that the issue was not Orélien's race or nationality. The left criticized the group's politics and the reliability of AI detectors, though the article notes that Pangram can produce false negatives but that some research suggests its false positive rate is very low. On the right, the critic Alix Avril wrote in the far-right magazine Valeurs Actuelles that the book's migrant subject made it impossible to criticize on literary grounds. Mohamed Mbougar Sarr, a previous Prix Goncourt winner, wrote that he had not thought the book was AI-generated and had attributed its weaknesses to the writer.

The article's critique of the novel itself describes a narrator, Jonas Dorléon, who survives a hostile migrant route through the Dominican Republic, Brazil, the Darién Gap, and Mexico to the U.S. border without ever taking advantage of anyone. It says the book relies on the "not X, but Y" formulation that the article identifies as typical of AI writing, and that its characters are stereotypes, including a MAGA-hat-wearing Border Patrol officer. The article also says that in a Le Figaro interview before the scandal, Orélien said the book was inspired by Haitian refugees whose Temporary Protected Status was revoked in 2017, and that he chose fiction because he believed literature could create something lasting. Several people in the French literary world told the author they had hoped the affair was an elaborate joke, and Orélien told Libération the book aimed to reflect on the causes that push people to leave their homeland.

Articles.Title: The Worst Thing About AI Writing

stories.Headline: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
stories.Summary:
Big Walk, a co-operative puzzle exploration game made by House House, has become the center of a dispute over AI use in indie game development. The debate broke into public view on Monday, when 19 members of the Independent Games Festival Awards jury, out of more than 50, released a signed statement declining to vote for any game using generative AI in any capacity. The jurors cited ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms, and urged the festival to adopt a strong anti-AI policy disallowing games with any AI-generated work. The statement did not name specific games, but by Tuesday Big Walk had become a central part of the debate.

House House publicly admitted in a statement to Aftermath that large language models were used sparingly near the end of development. The developer said the use stayed under 0.1 percent of the game's code and helped address a Unity engine bug that caused "infinite length" shadows during some situations. After a Unity engineer concluded a fix was not possible, an LLM chatbot suggested a possible fix, which the developers modified extensively into 10 lines of code. The developer said it did not disclose this use for the Steam release earlier this year because Valve does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. It later made the disclosure for awards consideration, since the matter had become one of public interest.

House House said the disclosure is not an endorsement of AI tools, however minimal, and expressed concern that voluntary disclosures might normalize the technology. The developer said it supports those working to limit generative AI's harm to games and apologized that its use may not meet their standards. Some judges who had felt a special connection to the game said the disclosure was painful. Austin Walker called the game an achievement and remarkable in a blog post, while Damon Reece wrote that it felt like home. Both were among those who said that even minimal AI use outweighed their respect for the work, with Reece calling silence on the issue rank cowardice.

This is not the first controversy of its kind. Last year, the Indie Game Awards, which are separate from the IGF Awards, rescinded awards for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 after its developers admitted some in-game textures were made with AI tools, which were later patched out. The Indie Game Awards said at the time that it has a hard stance on generative AI throughout nomination and the ceremony. Since House House's disclosure, Big Walk's Steam page has received over 400 negative reviews in recent days, though the game's "Very Positive" overall rating has held. Critics such as Dominic Tarason argued the response was disproportionate, calling the game very mildly compromised art that is still very human.

Others drew distinctions between games using LLMs as a last-resort technical fix and games relying heavily on AI for art, music, or core engine code. Judge Liz Ryerson wrote that she did not find the use personally disqualifying and objected to treating all cases as the same. AI researcher Mike Cook wrote that House House is not laying off developers to replace them, but that its actions are part of the same problem. Brendan Keogh argued that extreme zero tolerance is counterproductive because it discourages developers from disclosing use. Hannah Nicklin defended zero tolerance as a viable political position aimed at reducing harm and building solidarity.

Articles.Title: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.

stories.Headline: AWS releases AWS Emulator, a free tool that simulates 200+ of its services locally, saying AI agents wrote it and its team hasn't written or reviewed any code (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)
stories.Summary:
AWS released AWS Emulator on Wednesday, a free tool that simulates more than 200 of its cloud services on a developer's own machine. The emulator is built from more than 400 API models and lets developers and AI coding agents test code without a network connection or paying for real cloud usage. The company says autonomous AI agents wrote the code, and its engineers did not write or review any of it. The tool responds to a bottleneck that coding agents such as Amazon's Kiro and Anthropic's Claude Code have made worse.

Agents check their work by running code and reading the results repeatedly, and doing that against the real cloud adds delay and cost. Running the loop locally removes both problems. AWS also says agents maintain the emulator by testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find. Matt Goldberg, an AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, described the approach in a blog post.

He wrote that the emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents and that his team had not written or reviewed any of the code. He compared the agents to a young child who lacks the skill to do a task well, arguing that they need clearly defined areas in which to work. The agents work from AWS's public API models and check their results against the real AWS cloud, operating on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. The project began as a weekend experiment, when Goldberg gave Kiro a short prompt and produced a passable version of Amazon SQS in 15 minutes.

By the end of that weekend, Kiro had built a rough version of much of the rest of AWS, and his team began using it the following Monday. Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI, wrote that an engineer's job now is to give agents room to work and to build the specs, tests and merge gates that decide when the work is correct. The emulator has known limits, and an IDC analyst said it does not yet simulate throttling, outages or regional differences in services. AWS released it under the CC0 public domain dedication, with its full commit history on GitHub, and says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

Articles.Title: AWS releases AWS Emulator, a free tool that simulates 200+ of its services locally, saying AI agents wrote it and its team hasn't written or reviewed any code (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)

stories.Headline: Dell Jumps 11% as AI Server Stocks Rebound From a Rough Month; Super Micro Surges 8%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise Advances 6%
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies stock jumped 11% to $370.25 in early trading on November 11, 2026, as AI server makers recovered from a rough month. Super Micro Computer rose 8% to $29.96, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise advanced 6% to $50.85. The rebound followed a selloff in AI hardware names after the November 3 midterm elections. Shares of all three companies had been falling sharply over the past month.

CoreWeave reported third-quarter 2026 results after the close on November 10 that beat estimates and raised its full-year 2026 guidance. That report revived the AI trade across chip, memory and data center infrastructure stocks. The article says CoreWeave will rely on contract-backed financing and customer prepayments to fund its expansion, which eased concerns about how AI data center buildouts get paid for. Dell, Super Micro and Hewlett Packard Enterprise all sell AI-optimized servers into data centers, so shifts in sentiment tend to move them together.

Over the past month, Dell fell 37%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell 31% and Super Micro fell 28%. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa promised "a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals," and the state holds a large share of planned U.S. data center capacity. Hinojosa cannot act until she takes office in January, and outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott already paused new data center permits in September pending a state audit. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee also called the latest inflation report "borderline disturbing" while the Fed considers more rate hikes.

Dell reported a record AI backlog of $95 billion for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 and raised its full-year revenue guidance to $192 billion when it reported on September 1. Dell's management said demand outran supply in each of the last two quarters. Hewlett Packard Enterprise CEO Antonio Neri said on its September 2 earnings call, "We are leading with networking," referring to its acquisition of Juniper Networks. The article notes that Super Micro's revenue was concentrated, with a single large data center customer accounting for a big share of its revenue in its first quarter of fiscal 2027.

NVIDIA is scheduled to report on November 17, and Dell's own results follow on November 24. The article says the outcome of those reports will test whether AI demand holds up after the election. Bears cite a possible Texas moratorium, funding strain on data center projects, higher rates and component shortages. Dell management described those shortages as "DRAM, DRAM, DRAM, followed by NAND, NAND, NAND."

Articles.Title: Dell Jumps 11% as AI Server Stocks Rebound From a Rough Month; Super Micro Surges 8%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise Advances 6% - 24/7 Wall St.

stories.Headline: DOE Advances AI Cybersecurity for Critical Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
The Department of Energy is advancing artificial intelligence-powered cybersecurity technologies through a research initiative meant to strengthen the resilience of the nation's critical infrastructure against cyberattacks, according to a report published Tuesday by GovCIO Media & Research. The initiative is the AI-FORTS program, short for Artificial Intelligence for Operationally Resilient Technologies and Systems. It is managed by the department's Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response, known as CESER. The program was launched in 2024 and organizes its research around three priorities.

Those priorities are securing energy infrastructure from AI-enabled threats, using AI to strengthen cyber defenses, and protecting AI technologies deployed within energy systems. Sage Briscoe, CESER technical program manager and head of AI-FORTS, said that introducing new software into critical infrastructure requires organizations to assess whether it could create additional vulnerabilities or give attackers another way into a network. AI-FORTS aligns with the first strategic goal in CESER's fiscal years 2026-2030 strategic plan, which calls for developing world-class security technologies. The department identifies national laboratory partnerships and utility collaboration as important parts of its approach. The department's fiscal year 2027 congressional budget justification also lists AI-FORTS among its planned research and development investments.

The budget document says the department intends to shift cybersecurity research toward AI-focused capabilities that help critical infrastructure keep operating through compromise. One example of AI-FORTS research is Communications and Cybersecurity for the Energy Edge, or C2E2, a project developed through CESER's partnership with Sandia National Laboratories. In September, the department reported that C2E2 had cut energy-system data preparation from about two months to a few hours. It also reported 95-percent accuracy in detecting and locating cyber threats, with actionable intelligence available in near real time. Over the coming year, the C2E2 team plans to explore using large language models to build user-friendly impact assessments for energy infrastructure cybersecurity personnel.

CESER and Sandia are also advancing Scaled Testing for AI Systems, or STAISYS, which evaluates AI technologies in simulated environments representing critical energy infrastructure. According to Sandia, STAISYS is one of four Sandia-led projects funded through AI-FORTS. The effort uses emulated cyber-physical environments to assess how AI systems perform under realistic operating conditions and potential cyberattacks. Separately, CESER and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory introduced the Mjölnir AI Testbed in April. The platform is designed to assess the cybersecurity and reliability of AI models intended for energy-sector applications by exposing them to adversarial testing.

Articles.Title: DOE Advances AI Cybersecurity for Critical Infrastructure - ExecutiveGov

stories.Headline: Pakistan's AI Future Discussed at IIADP Dialogue in Karachi
stories.Summary:
The Indus Institute for AI & Digital Policy (IIADP) held a closed-door fireside chat on November 11, 2026, at the National Incubation Center (NIC) Karachi, inside NED University of Engineering and Technology. The session, titled "AI & Digital Pakistan: From Policy to Innovation," gathered representatives from government, academia, business, startups and the legal profession to discuss Pakistan's artificial intelligence and digital policy landscape. Senator Dr. Afnan Ullah Khan, a member of the Senate Standing Committee on IT & Telecommunications, joined to offer a parliamentary view on how technology, legislation and digital governance are changing. Hamza Ali Chaudhry, Executive Director of IIADP, moderated the discussion.

Other attendees included Syed Azfar Hussain, Project Director of NIC Karachi, Dr. Danish ur Rehman Khan, Technical Advisor to the Vice Chancellor of NED University, and Muhammad Ali Tariq, Deputy Secretary of Anti-Crime & Anti-Terrorism. The participants spoke candidly about opportunities and challenges in artificial intelligence, digital innovation, entrepreneurship and technology governance. They also considered international frameworks, including the OECD AI Principles and the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, which aim to set responsible standards for AI. The organisers stressed that Pakistan needs policies that encourage innovation while addressing regulatory, ethical and social concerns.

NIC Karachi took part as Growth Partner. The centre was established in 2018 at NED University and is funded by Ignite under the Ministry of IT & Telecommunication. It supports technology startups through incubation, mentorship, investor access and industry links. The articles say the discussion pointed to the need for closer cooperation between policymakers, academia, industry and entrepreneurs so that policy keeps pace with technological innovation. IIADP, which works on research, policy dialogue and stakeholder engagement, says these meetings are meant to support informed policymaking and stronger ties between decision-makers and Pakistan's technology sector.

Articles.Title: Pakistan's AI Future Discussed at IIADP Dialogue in Karachi - ARYnews.tv

stories.Headline: Digital transformation and AI adoption require everyone's participation
stories.Summary:
Digital transformation and AI adoption cannot succeed without help from the whole organization, according to a HIMSS TV video published November 11, 2026, by Healthcare Finance News. stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: Unions to Press on A.I. Threat in Mamdani’s First Labor Talks as Mayor
stories.Summary:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani is set to begin contract talks with New York City's largest public-sector union, his first labor negotiation since taking office. The bargaining is expected to set the floor for how the city deals with its other municipal unions. Talks will also have to address the threat that the rapid rise of artificial intelligence poses to city workers. The union involved is District Council 37 AFSCME, led by Henry Garrido.

The article does not give the contract's terms, the expiration date, or the number of workers covered, so those details cannot be reported here. What the article does make clear is that the talks will test how Mr. Mamdani balances his close ties to organized labor against his duties as mayor. He has joined picket lines with Starbucks baristas, hotel workers and nurses, and he has used his profile to support the labor movement when he can. The union's leader was the only public-sector labor figure to endorse him during his contentious 2025 Democratic primary.

Mr. Garrido, whose union represents some of the city's lowest-paid employees, has said he intends to press the affordability issue during bargaining. He argued that the mayor's public remarks about affordability and New Yorkers' hardship apply directly to the workers he represents. He said the negotiations give the mayor a chance to bargain on behalf of the people he has spoken about. The article frames these comments as the opening position of the union rather than the outcome of any talks.

The reporting places the talks in a wider debate over how city government will manage workers as automation expands. It does not say what proposals either side has put forward on artificial intelligence, or when a settlement might be reached. The article is based on an interview with Mr. Garrido and does not include a response from the mayor's office. Any next steps beyond the start of negotiations are not described.

Articles.Title: Unions to Press on A.I. Threat in Mamdani’s First Labor Talks as Mayor - The New York Times

stories.Headline: Bilt Unveils AI-Powered Neighborhood OS
stories.Summary:
Bilt, a housing payments and membership company, unveiled Bilt Neighborhood OS, an artificial intelligence operating system and commerce network designed to connect local businesses with the residents who live nearby. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026, and the company describes the product as an extension of its existing membership and rewards platform for housing. Bilt is also expanding that membership technology so organizations can launch their own branded programs or carry existing loyalty programs into the neighborhood, and it named several multifamily companies as participants. Among them is American Landmark Apartments, which plans to deploy the system across 40,000 multifamily residences, giving residents access to leasing, package management, service requests, amenity bookings, and smart-home features through the same app they use to pay rent.

Bilt says its AI agents have completed more than 2 million actions across more than 29,000 businesses in the past 30 days, with 91% finished without human involvement. Property teams can use these agents to coordinate services across their existing systems and offer neighborhood perks, such as a restaurant credit during a repair. American Landmark also plans to fold its internal business intelligence tool, originally called AL One, into Bilt's platform as a property intelligence product. Bilt reports that its platform now reaches about one in four U.S. apartment buildings and is expected to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year. The rollout is nationwide but phased, with additional launches set to begin in 2027.

Bilt's founder and CEO, Ankur Jain, framed the launch as a response to a technology shift that he said mostly bypassed neighborhood shops and restaurants, and he said the company wants to give those businesses tools to reach customers and build loyalty. Joe Lubeck, founder and CEO of American Landmark Apartments, said the partnership lets his company link its communities to nearby places residents use and gives property teams insights into how their buildings operate. John Vranich, a partner at Bryten, said the system would let his teams spend more time on residents and offer benefits beyond the community. Bilt also named a coalition of payments and commerce partners, including Adyen, Verifone, Clover from Fiserv, Shift4, OpenTable, and Grubhub, to help distribute the system.

The announcement came with Bilt's first State of the Neighborhood 2026 study, conducted with 451 Research by S&P Global and based on nearly 6,600 U.S. adults. The survey found that two-thirds of consumers do at least 80% of their everyday spending within 15 miles of home, and that 77% of renters said rewards on housing payments alone would make them more likely to stay long term. It also found that 87% of respondents would shop more often at a local business if they could earn rewards there. Separately, Bilt announced a partnership with the Local Initiatives Support Corp. (LISC) that begins with a $100,000 donation and aims to connect people with financial coaching and housing-goal support, including pathways to homeownership.

Articles.Title: Bilt Unveils AI-Powered Neighborhood OS

stories.Headline: Developers Want to Build AI Data Centers Near Shenandoah, Zion, and the Grand Canyon. This Map Shows Where.
stories.Summary:
A new interactive map from More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication, shows dozens of proposed AI data centers sitting close to America's national parks and public lands. The map was built by cofounder Will Pattiz, who set it up to track where these facilities are being planned and who is behind them. According to his research, at least 14 proposed projects lie within ten miles of a national park boundary, 38 are planned within 25 miles, and 131 are within 50 miles. The tool currently reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still only proposals, and 77 of those proposals sit within ten miles of protected land.

The article describes several specific sites that concern Pattiz. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning a $10 billion data center beside Horseshoe Bend, a viewpoint on the Colorado River, and that land had previously been set aside for outdoor recreation. The city says the proposal is still under public review and has not been formally adopted, with a planning and zoning meeting scheduled for November 17. Near Price, Utah, a company called Valar Atomics has applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for a project called Project Beehive, which would include small nuclear reactors and would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. In June 2026, the Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit for a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt Antelope Data Center about 40 miles from Zion National Park, which will include an on-site natural gas plant.

Pattiz argues that these projects are being pursued with too little openness and that public lands should not host them. He told Outside that many are "being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy" and said the central question is what public benefit they provide, noting that no clear public benefit has been outlined for the ones proposed on public lands. He also warned that the centers' heavy use of water, electricity and land will affect public lands one way or another. His map lets a user enter a zip code to see the nearest facility, its likely effect on utility costs, and the groups that support it. He said he hopes the information will help residents judge the projects for themselves.

The article places the debate within a broader national rush to build data centers to meet the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud software, facilities that require large amounts of electricity and water. Pattiz described these projects as an inflection point in American history and said they have become political flashpoints in towns and cities where they are going up. The map updates automatically as more information becomes available, so the figures are expected to change. The article does not say whether any of the proposals will be approved or abandoned beyond the steps already noted.

Articles.Title: Developers Want to Build AI Data Centers Near Shenandoah, Zion, and the Grand Canyon. This Map Shows Where.

stories.Headline: The Death of Anonymization: Why Masking ERP Data is Poisoning your AI
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion piece by Axolile Lungu, founder of synthetic cfo, arguing that masking real ERP data before using it to train AI in finance damages the data. It was published on November 11, 2026, by CPA Practice Advisor. The author says that scrambling vendor IDs, hashing primary keys and blurring timestamps breaks the links between records that double-entry accounting depends on. He describes this as relational fragmentation, and says masked fields show up to models as zeros, which he calls null hallucination.

The author cites an example in which a model treated a hidden tax field as a non-taxable event. He also points to the KPMG Global AI in Finance Report of March 2026, which he says introduced assurance readiness as the main factor separating successful firms. He says top-performing teams, which he claims move three to six times faster, use audit-grade inputs rather than masked data. He argues that a model that is mostly correct is a liability for board-level reporting.

The author's proposed remedy is synthetic data: new ledgers generated from accounting rules rather than scrambled copies of real records. He says his firm, synthetic cfo, builds SAP and Oracle style ledgers in which the debits and credits balance and fraud is planted and labelled. He says this makes privacy risk zero by design. He calls reliance on legacy masking technical debt that will poison AI initiatives. He also warns that shareholder trust may disappear if AI begins hallucinating financial logic.

The piece is written by a person with a commercial interest in the remedy it promotes, since Lungu founded the firm that sells synthetic ERP datasets. His background includes audit roles at PwC and EY, finance and SOX work at Gilead Sciences, AbbVie and Meta, and advisory work for AI companies since 2025. The articles do not report any regulator action or independent test confirming the claims about masking damaging model performance. The piece does not say what the next steps are for firms or regulators.

Articles.Title: The Death of Anonymization: Why Masking ERP Data is Poisoning your AI

stories.Headline: Semiconductor companies struggle to measure business value of AI: HTEC
stories.Summary:
HTEC, a global AI technology and engineering firm, has released research finding that semiconductor companies are relatively advanced in adopting artificial intelligence but struggle to prove that technical gains produce measurable business value. The findings were released on a Monday and reported by ET Electronics, which carried the story on November 10, 2026. According to the survey, 48 per cent of semiconductor respondents describe their organisations as scaling AI or already AI-native, compared with 44 per cent across the overall sample. Investment growth in the sector is broadly in line with the wider market, with 78 per cent reporting increased spending over the past year against 79 per cent overall.

The research points to a sharper divide in how AI projects are selected and measured. Semiconductor respondents lead other sectors in requiring strategic alignment and a formal return on investment model before approval, but measurement becomes less consistent once projects are underway. About 38 per cent say AI value is reported mainly on a case-by-case basis, against 30 per cent overall, while only 28 per cent rely mainly on an enterprise dashboard, compared with 36 per cent. Missing baseline metrics and inconsistent performance indicators across functions were identified as obstacles, and only 22 per cent said AI's purpose and expected outcomes are clearly articulated across their organisation, the lowest share of any sector surveyed. The survey also found that 83 per cent of semiconductor respondents see people and processes as a bigger constraint on AI value than technology, yet only 22 per cent actively monitor adoption and outcomes across functions.

HTEC's findings suggest that semiconductor firms will need to apply the same discipline to adoption, accountability and measurement across the wider business as AI moves beyond specialist engineering teams, though the release itself does not name specific corrective steps. The research also covers risk: more than half of semiconductor companies, 57.5 per cent, measure AI risk alongside value only for high-risk use cases, and about 16 per cent measure risk consistently across their AI portfolio. Among technical respondents, 33 per cent cited model unpredictability and edge cases as the main complication for human oversight, the highest share across the sectors surveyed. The report was released by HTEC itself, and the article does not indicate any response from semiconductor companies or regulators.

Articles.Title: Semiconductor companies struggle to measure business value of AI: HTEC - electronics.economictimes.indiatimes.com

stories.Headline: AI-powered imaging tracks thousands of brain cancer cells moving through living tissue
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Uppsala University in Sweden have developed GlioTrace, a method that combines live imaging of brain tissue with artificial intelligence to follow individual glioblastoma cells as they spread. The study was published in the journal Nature Communications on November 11, 2026. The team grew glioblastoma cells from six patients as tumors in mouse brains, cut the brains into thin slices, and kept them alive in the laboratory. Automated microscopes photographed the slices at intervals of no more than two hours for up to five days.

A machine-learning system identified and tracked thousands of individual tumor cells, and statistical models were used to calculate how cells switched between different states. The results showed clear differences between tumors, with some spreading mainly along blood vessels and others spreading more diffusely through the brain tissue. Individual cells could change their shape and movement over a few days and could switch between moving along vessels and moving independently. The researchers also used the method to test two drug substances, which reduced the movement and spread of tumor cells, although the effects varied between patient tumors and cell types.

The lead researchers stress that the method is still a research tool and not yet ready to guide treatment decisions for patients. Hitesh Mangukiya, a researcher at Uppsala University, said the approach allows scientists to watch how tumor cells adapt their behavior in real time. Sven Nelander, a professor of integrative cancer research at the university, said the work opens new possibilities for understanding the invasion process. The analysis software is freely available to other researchers, and the team hopes it will help identify treatments that can stop cancer from spreading through the brain.

The researchers also found that a combination of radiation and chemotherapy increased the share of a fast-moving, invasive cell type in some tumor models. They said these cells may persist under treatment, but further research is needed to determine whether they are more resistant to therapy or contribute to recurrence. Glioblastoma is one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer, and surgery cannot remove cells that have already spread into surrounding healthy brain. Further studies are needed before GlioTrace could be used in patient care.

Articles.Title: AI-powered imaging tracks thousands of brain cancer cells moving through living tissue

stories.Headline: 5 Takeaways on How AI Is Reshaping Multifamily Operations
stories.Summary:
AI is moving from a buzzword to a routine tool for multifamily operators, according to executives who spoke on an AI panel at the Multifamily Executive Conference in early November in Newport Beach, California. Panelists from Moss & Co., RPM Living and Avenue5 Residential described using the technology across leasing, resident engagement, reporting, maintenance and back-office work. They stressed that successful adoption takes more than switching on a new tool. Early attention went to AI-driven leasing and resident messaging, but the discussion showed the bigger gains may come behind the scenes.

Moss & Co. president Chris Gray said AI is helping automate reporting, build dashboards, analyze performance and streamline processes that once took hours of staff time. He estimated his company is seeing roughly a 50 percent efficiency gain in some operational areas. Gray predicted operator margins will grow, and that management fees could eventually fall because firms can do more, and do it faster. RPM Living chief strategy officer Mariana Estrada pointed to faster responses to prospects as a clear benefit. Automated tools can make first contact almost immediately, which matters as renters expect service outside office hours.

Estrada also described RPM Living's centralized application processing, where AI handles back-and-forth messages with applicants about qualifications, income and documents. She said the company cut processing time roughly in half and doubled the units the program handles without adding headcount. Chase Hunt, Avenue5's vice president of marketing, technology and client solutions, said the aim is to automate routine tasks so on-site staff can spend more time building relationships with prospects and residents. He added that the company has told site teams the technology is not meant to take their jobs. Hunt also cautioned that being able to automate something does not mean an organization is ready to do it.

Hunt urged companies to check whether their data is reliable, how their systems connect and whether employees know how to work with AI tools before giving the technology more autonomy. Avenue5 has involved on-site staff, operational leaders, national team members and governance and engagement committees in its rollout. Gray argued that imperfect data should not stop companies from starting, since AI reporting can reveal anomalies and map out data cleanup. Estrada advised operators to pick their biggest pain point, test whether AI can address it and assign a central person accountable for results. Gray said companies that may have waited 18 months ago now face a different situation, and urged them to begin.

Articles.Title: 5 Takeaways on How AI Is Reshaping Multifamily Operations

stories.Headline: University of Kentucky employee receives religious exemption from using AI
stories.Summary:
A University of Kentucky employee, David Durman, has received a religious exemption from using artificial intelligence at work, saying the technology conflicts with his humanist beliefs. Durman, a research administrator at the university, applied for the exemption under Title VII, a federal rule that requires employers to accommodate sincerely held religious beliefs. He supports researchers as they apply for grant funding, and his current workflow does not require AI. The university granted the request because it did not place an undue burden on the institution, especially since his work does not currently mandate AI use. Durman first turned to the American Humanist Association for help with the application, and he has been a humanist for roughly 30 years.

He said he believes AI conflicts with human well-being for several reasons, including concerns that it could limit a person's capacity to think and reason. He also pointed to the environmental impact of data centers and to the use of creative works to train AI models without artists' explicit permission. Humanism has been recognized as a religion since a Supreme Court ruling in Torcaso v. Watkins in the early 1960s. Durman's case reflects a broader pattern in which employees seek accommodations based on personal ethics.

A university spokesperson said UK reviews exemption requests on an individual basis and determined that Durman could still perform his job duties without AI. In a statement, the university said accommodations may be reviewed as technology and job responsibilities change, so they remain reasonable and workable. Durman said UK has been good to work with and that he believes the university continues to be an inclusive workplace. He said the decision sets an example for others at the university and at other institutions across the country who have similar concerns. He does not expect AI use to become an issue in his work, but he said he is glad to have the protection in place.

Context from the same coverage adds that UK's Information Technology Services recommends Microsoft Copilot for staff and students who want an AI tool. Durman is not the first American to receive a religious exemption from using AI, as a Unitarian Universalist in North Carolina received one earlier this year while working as a software engineer. A Gallup poll taken over the summer found that 52% of U.S. workers use AI to do their jobs. A database called AI Lawsuit Tracker shows 2026 has had the most AI-related cases filed in the past four years.

Articles.Title: University of Kentucky employee receives religious exemption from using AI

stories.Headline: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026
stories.Summary:
AWS published a roundup on November 11, 2026, summarizing the updates it released for AI builders during October 2026. The company says it wants developers to choose the right model for each task, rely on their agents in production, and understand what their AI workloads cost. Its updates center on Amazon Bedrock, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore platform, and the open source Strands agent toolkit. Together, these tools are meant to take a project from first prototype to production.

The October releases add several new models and capabilities. Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 is aimed at subagents and high-volume work, and according to Anthropic it costs around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, with input and output token prices at least 50 percent lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra, and it accepts up to 1 million input tokens. Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, a speech-to-speech model, offers lower latency at the same price as Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. Other additions include GLM 5.3 by Z.ai for agentic coding, TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 for video metadata, and more models in AWS GovCloud (US).

Several releases focus on reliability and control. AgentCore Gateway now supports model fallback, so when a primary model is throttled or unreachable, requests move to the next model or provider in a chain the customer defines, and a circuit breaker skips failing destinations. AWS Step Functions workflows can now be used as tools through AgentCore Gateway, so business logic stays in the workflows customers already run. Structured outputs are available for all Claude models on Amazon Bedrock, returning schema-compliant JSON. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock adds domain filtering and user location, while Amazon Bedrock Guardrails has a new Standard tier for contextual grounding checks at the same cost as the Classic tier.

Cost changes are also part of the update. AgentCore memory now charges for short-term memory based on the data agents ingest, retrieve, and store instead of a flat rate per event, and AWS says most workloads will see lower costs. Customers can also set a time-to-live on long-term memory records. AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and AWS Cost Management Dashboards have been extended to help customers see what drives their Amazon Bedrock spending. The roundup presents these changes as part of AWS's wider effort to make AI spending more predictable.

Articles.Title: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026

stories.Headline: AI-derived inflammation score improves cardiovascular risk prediction beyond CAC
stories.Summary:
An AI-derived measure of coronary inflammation, the fat attenuation index read from noncontrast cardiac CT, was reported in a new JAMA analysis published around November 11, 2026, as a possible way to improve cardiovascular risk prediction beyond traditional coronary artery calcium scoring. The study was led by corresponding author Charalambos Antoniades, MD, PhD, of the University of Oxford, and colleagues. The team argued that patients with a zero calcium score are often reassured and may be steered away from statin therapy, even though heart attacks frequently arise from inflamed, noncalcified plaques that do not show up on that scan. The authors said the findings suggest absent or low calcium does not rule out meaningful residual risk.

The multicenter study compared a novel noncontrast fat attenuation index score with an established measure taken from contrast-enhanced CT angiography. Researchers drew on a derivation cohort of 6,818 individuals and a separate validation cohort of 19,110 people imaged between 2010 and 2021, with a median follow-up of 6.7 years. Over that period, the investigators recorded 536 cardiovascular deaths and 1,727 major adverse cardiovascular events, defined as myocardial infarction, new-onset heart failure or cardiovascular death. Adding the contrast-based score to calcium raised the area under the curve for prediction from 0.76 to 0.81, while the noncontrast score brought it to 0.80, with both also improving risk reclassification.

The results were most striking among people with no detectable coronary calcium. In that group, cardiovascular mortality rose from 1.4 to 4 per 1,000 person-years among those whose scores were above the 75th percentile, and MACE rates climbed from 5.9 to 13.3 per 1,000 person-years. The authors noted that because calcium scoring already uses noncontrast CT, the inflammation measure can be drawn from images already acquired, avoiding extra scans, radiation, contrast and scan time, and may extend to primary prevention and patients who cannot tolerate iodinated contrast. They also cautioned that the work establishes prognostic value rather than showing that treatment guided by the score improves outcomes. Further research is needed to determine how the measure should fit into clinical decision-making.

Articles.Title: AI-derived inflammation score improves cardiovascular risk prediction beyond CAC

stories.Headline: I’m Using AI to Try to Cure Cancer—and Save My Own Life
stories.Summary:
Bryant Lin, a Stanford physician, wrote in a Free Press essay published on November 11, 2026, that he is using artificial intelligence to try to treat his own terminal lung cancer. The article describes a conversation he had in early 2023 with his colleague Justin Norden at a restaurant in the Stanford Shopping Center in Palo Alto. At that time, ChatGPT 3.5 had been released only a few months earlier, and new AI developments were arriving constantly. The two were preparing a course on the digital future of healthcare, but they decided instead to start the first class they knew of on generative AI and medicine.

Lin, who is both a physician and a faculty member at Stanford's School of Medicine, says he had a habit of launching new classes more to learn than to teach. He describes this subject as the richest area of learning he could imagine. A little over a year after that conversation, at the age of 49, he was diagnosed with stage 4 lung cancer, which he calls terminal. In the years since, he says he has been studying how AI might help treat, if not cure, his disease. The essay frames this as a personal test of whether AI can actually help save a patient's life.

Lin's own words, as the essay presents them, express hope that he will survive until the next major treatment becomes available. He also says he holds greater hopes for the generation that follows him. The piece is presented as part of the publication's health and self-improvement coverage, which focuses on living well. The article is not a clinical report, and the excerpt provided does not include details of any specific AI tools, treatments, or results. The full essay is available only to paid subscribers of The Free Press.

Articles.Title: I’m Using AI to Try to Cure Cancer—and Save My Own Life

stories.Headline: Modernizing the Milkman: AI’s New Playbook for Medtech Commercial Excellence
stories.Summary:
Most medtech leaders in the United States and around the globe rate their commercial maturity as only basic to intermediate. A few are pulling ahead, outpacing the sector index by eight percentage points of annual shareholder return. The difference, according to a BCG study titled Modernizing the Milkman, comes down to how well they use artificial intelligence in their commercial operations. The report builds on more than 15 years of data and insights from the sector.

The study lays out five concrete moves for leading in medtech commercial work. These include continuous prioritization and dynamic targeting, always-on personalized engagement, and AI-augmented and autonomous sales. They also cover data-driven pricing and margin optimization, along with a seamless service experience supported by 24/7 agents. The articles do not spell out timelines or costs for any of these moves.

BCG is the author of the study, which is hosted and promoted by AdvaMed, the trade group for the medical technology industry. AdvaMed published the item on November 11, 2026, and its page directs readers to the full report. The page itself does not add further claims or attribute new findings beyond the study's summary. The articles do not indicate what follow-up steps, if any, the trade group or BCG plans next.

Articles.Title: Modernizing the Milkman: AI’s New Playbook for Medtech Commercial Excellence - AdvaMed®

stories.Headline: Canada signs AI safety declaration: What does it mean for employers? - Human Resources Director
stories.Summary:
Canada has endorsed an international artificial intelligence safety declaration, published by the Prime Minister's Office in Ottawa on November 9, 2026. The Joint declaration on Paris call for AI safety and security was signed by Bahrain, Canada, Finland, France, Norway and the Netherlands. Frontier AI developers Anthropic, Microsoft, OpenAI and Canadian firm Cohere also endorsed it. The declaration is non-binding, and it sets out commitments for both governments and developers.

The declaration rests on three pillars, starting with a common risk framework for frontier models, the most advanced AI systems, with non-sensitive findings shared publicly. The second pillar assigns accountability, with developers committing to disclose known risks and install fail-safe shutdown mechanisms. Governments, for their part, recognize the need for legal frameworks that clarify responsibility in case of large-scale damages. The third pillar covers early warning systems for serious cyber and AI control incidents. Signatories also say the opportunities and risks of frontier models are inherently global.

Policymakers commit to providing secure and confidential channels through which whistleblowers, including employees, can raise concerns about systemic risks without fear of legal or professional retaliation. The declaration creates no new employer obligations, but it places employee reporting of AI risk on the policy agenda. Organizations that deploy AI may want to check that their speak-up policies cover such concerns. Florian Martin-Bariteau, director of the University of Ottawa's Centre for Law, Technology and Society, told Global News that the approach will not work without regulators and enforcement. He said he supports the content of the statement but believes it lacks teeth without follow-up.

The Canadian government has relied on voluntary measures, including its AI for All strategy launched in June 2026. Prime Minister Mark Carney said in October 2026 that the country was building AI the right way. The declaration calls for a clear, understandable and predictable regulatory framework but sets no timeline for one. Australia has moved further, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese saying on November 10, 2026 that a new regulator would enforce legislated standards on frontier AI companies there.

Articles.Title: Canada signs AI safety declaration: What does it mean for employers? - Human Resources Director

stories.Headline: Japan mulls penalties for AI firms over safety risks
stories.Summary:
The Japanese government is considering a plan that would require businesses involved in artificial intelligence to take measures to ensure safety, with penalties for those that violate the rules. A source familiar with the matter said on Wednesday that the proposal was presented at a closed-door working group meeting on AI-related legal systems. The move comes as concerns grow about advanced AI models behaving unpredictably and after a series of recent high-profile data leaks and unauthorized access incidents that are suspected to involve misuse of AI. Under the approach being considered, the government would be able to issue legally binding orders to businesses that do not cooperate with authorities after an AI-related incident. Failure to comply would carry penalties, which are expected to be limited to incidents involving advanced AI.

Because AI-related businesses range from research firms and developers of foundation models to providers of services for end users, the government will examine which types of firms should fall under the regulations. The working group aims to present an overall outline of its review of the law, including possible revisions, by the end of the year. The current framework is Japan's AI law, enacted in May 2025, which lets the government investigate businesses and issue guidance in cases of malicious conduct. That law has no penalty provisions, and its measures are nonbinding. The proposal would therefore add enforcement power that the existing law lacks.

The source's account of the meeting is the basis for the reporting, and the articles do not identify specific officials who made the proposal. The articles place the proposal alongside other recent security developments in Japan, including a government emergency cybersecurity package and reports of a cyberattack suspected to have involved a North Korea-linked hacking group. The working group's outline is due by year-end, and the articles do not say when any legislation would be submitted or take effect. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Japan mulls penalties for AI firms over safety risks - Japan Wire by Kyodo News

stories.Headline: Super Intelligence, Deepfakes, and Cyberattacks: The SEC's 2027 Examination Priorities Put AI in the Spotlight
stories.Summary:
The Securities and Exchange Commission has released its examination priorities for fiscal year 2027, and the document includes a term that may surprise readers: "super intelligence." The terminology comes from President Trump's September 29, 2026, Executive Order, which directs federal agencies to replace "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in official communications. For now, the order defines super intelligence by reference to the existing statutory definition of AI. The SEC's priorities make clear that examiners will look closely at how financial firms use AI and how cybercriminals use AI against them. For investment advisers and broker-dealers, AI is now treated as an operational, cybersecurity, and compliance risk that firms must manage.

Cybersecurity remains a central examination priority, and the SEC specifically identified AI-generated phishing messages and synthetic or deepfake voice and video as threats firms should prepare for. These technologies let attackers impersonate executives or customers and manipulate employees into disclosing information, transferring funds, or granting system access. The SEC recognizes that threat actors use AI to automate and accelerate attacks, making them harder to detect. Examiners will assess firms' compliance with applicable requirements for evaluating and preparing for these threats. Firms are expected to consider employee training, multifactor authentication, identity verification, transaction approval procedures, and incident response plans in light of AI-powered attacks.

The SEC is also examining how firms deploy AI themselves, particularly when it influences investment decisions or customer recommendations. The 2027 priorities identify automated investment advisory services, recommendations, and trading algorithms as areas of focus. Examiners will also review policies for monitoring AI used in fraud prevention, back-office operations, anti-money laundering compliance, Regulation Best Interest obligations, and trading functions. The agency will generally assess whether representations about AI capabilities are accurate, whether actual operations match disclosures to investors, and whether algorithmic recommendations suit investors' profiles and objectives. These questions implicate existing fiduciary duties, disclosure requirements, supervisory obligations, and investor protection rules.

An algorithm's recommendations do not relieve a firm of responsibility for them. The SEC continues to review traditional cybersecurity concerns, including governance, data loss prevention, access controls, account management, and ransomware preparedness. Third-party risk remains a focus, particularly as firms rely more on service providers and as vendors add AI capabilities to existing products. Examiners will also evaluate firms' compliance with amended Regulation S-P, reviewing safeguards for customer information, incident response programs, customer notification procedures, and service provider oversight.

With compliance dates for large and small covered institutions now past, firms must demonstrate implementation rather than describe future plans. The SEC also lists Regulation S-ID as a priority, including whether identity theft prevention programs address account takeovers and AI-related threats. Law firm Baker Donelson, which published an analysis of the priorities on November 10, 2026, advises firms to revisit cybersecurity risk assessments and evaluate exposure to AI-powered phishing and deepfake impersonation. The firm also recommends that firms inventory approved and unauthorized AI tools, including those embedded in third-party platforms.

Firms should review AI governance and confirm that disclosures are accurate and algorithmic recommendations are supervised. The firm further suggests updating incident response plans and testing them through tabletop exercises involving AI-enabled attacks. The analysis states that the 2027 priorities do not create new legal obligations but indicate where regulators will be looking. The articles do not say how the SEC will rate or penalize firms that fall short of these expectations.

Articles.Title: Super Intelligence, Deepfakes, and Cyberattacks: The SEC's 2027 Examination Priorities Put AI in the Spotlight - Baker Donelson

stories.Headline: US DOJ Launches AI Task Force to Counter Foreign Threats and Protect Critical Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice announced on November 5, 2026, that it had formed a Super Intelligence Task Force to address the misuse of advanced artificial intelligence by foreign state actors, transnational criminal groups, and fraudsters. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the effort would keep critical technologies from being manipulated by bad actors at home or abroad. The task force was created under an October 13 memorandum and is led by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss. The articles describe it as formally known as DOJ-SITF.

The task force coordinates criminal and civil enforcement across department components, including the FBI, the Antitrust, Civil, Criminal, National Fraud Enforcement and National Security divisions, along with the Attorney General's Advisory Committee and the Office of the Solicitor General. Prosecutors must notify the task force when investigations begin and, when requested, before charges are filed or cases are resolved, though exceptions apply for urgent public safety threats or evidence at risk of immediate loss. The task force also absorbs the responsibilities, pending cases and personnel of the Artificial Intelligence Task Force that former Attorney General Pam Bondi announced on January 9, 2026. Officials say companies using these systems are expected to maintain strong internal controls so the technology behaves as intended.

Woodward has said the initiative supports the department's mission to protect Americans while promoting innovation and preventing misuse of advanced AI. Weiss has stressed that law enforcement helps deter improper use, that risk reporting should be strengthened, and that companies need effective internal controls. Blanche's memorandum gives the two co-chairs oversight of enforcement priorities, which include AI-assisted attacks on critical infrastructure and large-scale fraud against taxpayers. The articles note that the task force complements the broader White House Super Intelligence Force, chaired by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, which President Trump announced in early October 2026.

The articles frame the move as a response to documented increases in AI-assisted cyber operations and fraud schemes that exploit automated tools for scale and sophistication. Clayton, who also serves as AI czar, has described superintelligence as a national security issue. The articles do not say what specific cases the task force has opened or what penalties it will seek, and they do not report reactions from AI companies or critics. The stated next steps are continued coordination with the White House body and assessment of legislative and regulatory proposals in ways that support domestic technological advancement.

Articles.Title: US DOJ Launches AI Task Force to Counter Foreign Threats and Protect Critical Infrastructure - KuCoin

stories.Headline: Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) Stock Could Be Overvalued On Fresh AI Design Platform News
stories.Summary:
Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) has drawn fresh attention after a Simply Wall St analysis, published on November 11, 2026, suggested the stock may be trading above what its earnings support. The piece points to recent product and partnership news, including the new OrCAD Xplore Design Platform and the company's role in the Genesis Mission Consortium, as factors that could help future earnings quality. It notes that the shares have returned 76.6% over the past five years. The central question raised is whether today's price is backed by the profits the company is generating now. The article's main measure is the price-to-earnings ratio, which shows how much investors pay for each dollar of earnings.

Cadence trades at a P/E of 65.9x, compared with a broader software industry average of 29.8x and a peer group average of 36.9x. Using Simply Wall St's fair multiple framework, which adjusts for growth, margins, sector and size, the ratio sits above the level that model would usually expect. The authors say the recent product news may help explain why investors accept a premium, but they conclude the valuation still reflects considerable optimism. The analysis is produced with AI automation from Simply Wall St data and is presented as general commentary rather than a recommendation. Its authors state that it does not account for individual investors' objectives or financial situations, and that it may not reflect the latest company announcements.

The piece also refers readers to a consensus narrative that treats Cadence as about 18% undervalued, built on the expansion of its agentic AI tools such as ChipStack, ViraStack, InnoStack and AuraStack. Simply Wall St says it holds no position in the stocks it discusses. The article does not describe any scheduled event or corrective action that will follow. It points readers to further narratives and analyst forecasts for Cadence over the coming years so they can compare those expectations with the company's results as they are reported. Beyond that, the source offers no timetable for when the valuation question will be resolved.

Articles.Title: Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) Stock Could Be Overvalued On Fresh AI Design Platform News - Yahoo Finance Singapore

stories.Headline: Person, Planet, Power: Ecumenical Discernment on Artificial Intelligence. A World Council of Churches Symposium - World Council of Churches
stories.Summary:
The World Council of Churches has announced a symposium titled "Person, Planet, Power: Ecumenical Discernment on Artificial Intelligence," to be held at the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey in Switzerland from 15 to 19 February 2027. The announcement, published on the council's website on 11 November 2026, describes the event as an intensive gathering to examine how churches and ecumenical bodies have responded to artificial intelligence. Church members and ecumenical groups have already been working through questions about AI, from using generative tools in church administration and ministry to campaigning against biased systems and environmental harm. The symposium is also meant to address the theology of what it means to be human in relation to these tools.

The meeting aims to learn from existing church and ecumenical responses, encourage dialogue across different sectors, and identify priority areas for advocacy and education. Its outcomes are intended to feed into a broader World Council of Churches response to AI. A core group of council representatives and partners will bring together recent developments and strengthen existing initiatives. Participants are expected to come from fields including theology, ethics, science, technology, business, human rights, and media. In-person attendance is by invitation only, but online sessions will be open to the public.

The announcement was issued by the World Council of Churches, and questions can be directed to the contact address listed on the event page. The council's stated concern is that AI should be assessed not only as a technology but also in light of the economic, ecological, and political systems that surround it. The article does not name individual speakers or give a detailed programme. Related council coverage published in October and November 2026 on digital futures and technology's role in service of life suggests the topic has been part of the council's recent work. The articles do not say what specific recommendations or statements the symposium will produce.

Articles.Title: Person, Planet, Power: Ecumenical Discernment on Artificial Intelligence. A World Council of Churches Symposium - World Council of Churches

stories.Headline: Webinar to share how to build an effective AI training program - American Hospital Association
stories.Summary:
The American Hospital Association announced that it will host a webinar on December 1 at 1 p.m. ET on how to create and build an effective artificial intelligence training program. The session is aimed at hospital and health system staff who want guidance on putting such a program in place. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026. The AHA has been active on AI issues in recent weeks, which places the webinar within a broader push on the subject.

Registration is open through a link on the AHA website. The webinar is designed to show attendees how to tailor their training approach for three groups: leadership, clinical teams, and operations teams. Each group, the announcement suggests, may need a different type of instruction because of its different role in using AI tools. The session will also cover how organizations can sustain progress after the initial training is finished. That focus on continuing progress indicates the AHA sees training as an ongoing effort rather than a one-time event.

Attendees who want to join will need to register in advance. The webinar is presented by the AHA, the national organization representing hospitals, health systems and other health care providers. The article does not name a specific speaker or presenter for the session. The AHA has also released material on AI policy, including a new webpage launched November 3 that collects its policy letters, statements and fact sheets on the topic. Related sessions have included a virtual event on AI governance in hospitals held October 29 by the West Health Accelerator at the AHA's Health Research & Educational Trust.

Other recent AHA items cover patient comfort with AI and the role of AI chatbots in teen mental health. Beyond the webinar itself, the article offers no further details about outcomes, materials provided, or follow-up sessions. It does not say whether the session will be recorded or made available to those who cannot attend live. The announcement also does not report any new regulation or requirement tied to AI training. Readers seeking more information on the session can follow the registration link provided by the AHA.

Articles.Title: Webinar to share how to build an effective AI training program - American Hospital Association

stories.Headline: People project a specific racial identity onto artificial intelligence, study finds
stories.Summary:
People tend to perceive artificial intelligence systems as White, even when they have no face, voice, name, or body, according to research published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. The study, led by Monica Gamez-Djokic of Purdue University with Adam Waytz of Northwestern University, was reported by PsyPost and dated November 11, 2026. Across a series of studies, this racial association was linked to greater trust in AI recommendations. Systems described as trained on data from Black and Latino adults were assigned less intellectually demanding work than identical systems trained on White or unspecified data. The researchers tested the pattern in five primary studies and eight supplementary studies, all preregistered in part and with data posted on the Open Science Framework.

In Study 1a, 459 U.S. adults recruited through CloudResearch chose a racial group for six technologies from a standard list. In Study 1b, a separate balanced sample of 465 U.S. adults on Prolific answered in an open-ended text box instead. Study 2 used a reverse-correlation task with 96 Chicago participants and 172 raters, while Study 3 covered 147 adults in India and 113 in Japan. Study 4 surveyed 424 U.S. adults about an AI fact-checker. Participants in Study 1a selected White for 72% of the technologies on average, while in Study 1b 75% of technologies were racialized, and 71% of those responses were White.

In Study 2, 75% of raters categorized the composite AI face as White, compared with 43% for the anti-face. In Japan, 82% of participants classified AI as White, and robots, chatbots, and self-driving cars were classified as White 64% to 69% of the time. In India, 67% classified the broad category of artificial intelligence as White, though ratings for specific technologies were between 50% and 56%. Study 4 found that participants who perceived AI as more White rated its fact-checking as modestly more persuasive. Gamez-Djokic told PsyPost that the research grew from a question about whether people assume technology is neutral, and she said that people may bring human social categories to AI even without humanlike features.

The authors proposed that Whiteness is often an unstated default in Western cultures and is linked with high status, expertise and intelligence. They also suggested that people form impressions of AI based on who programs it, who uses it, and whose knowledge is in its training data. Gamez-Djokic said the findings suggest AI does not necessarily escape society's social biases simply because it is a technology. The article notes that a 2026 survey of organizational employees found that higher trust in AI decision-support systems was associated with a greater intention to rely on them and with less effort put into evaluating decisions. The article also notes that in many U.S. studies, White speakers have been judged as more objective and competent than non-White speakers giving the same message.

The research described was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, and the article notes that prior work found people associate vegetarianism with White people. The article reports that a supplementary study across more than 40 technologies found that tools rated as more intelligent were also rated as more White. Its account of the final experiment and the cause-and-effect testing is cut off, so the article leaves open whether perceived Whiteness causes greater trust. It does not say what the researchers conclude about how training data shapes these perceptions. The article also leaves open how the findings might affect workplaces and daily life beyond the examined scenarios.

Articles.Title: People project a specific racial identity onto artificial intelligence, study finds

stories.Headline: Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets
stories.Summary:
The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, now part of AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services, published a post on November 11, 2026 about a catalog of 23 production-ready reusable assets for generative AI development. The post, appearing on the AWS Artificial Intelligence blog, says these assets can reduce development time from months to weeks. Since 2023, the center has published open source reusable assets that give builders a validated foundation instead of a blank file. The assets include retrieval augmented generation pipelines, document processors, and agent scaffolding. The post describes three root causes of redundant development: assets scattered across repositories, wikis, and drives with no single source of truth, no quality signal showing production readiness or security review, and no reuse culture because sharing stays informal.

Each redundant build consumes engineering hours, delays customer delivery, and adds maintenance burden. The assets arrive already validated, security-reviewed, and production-grade, so teams avoid that verification work. The post says even AI-generated code still needs production hardening, security reviews, testing at scale, and ongoing maintenance. The post says a reusable asset is a production-grade, composable building block implementing one discrete generative AI capability, not a code snippet or sample. Before publication, assets are validated for quality and security, include clear deployment guides, and are instrumented to track adoption across customer engagements.

The Contact Center GenAI Agent asset is credited with DoorDash's handling of over 100,000 calls per day with 2.5-second response latency and a 50x increase in testing capacity. Using Amazon Bedrock reduced DoorDash's development time by 50 percent, and the team reached live testing readiness in 2 months. Lyft used the same asset to bring agentic AI to riders and drivers. Ricoh, which serves major health insurance payers, managed care organizations, and healthcare providers, used the Accelerated Intelligent Document Processing on AWS asset to build a standardized, multi-tenant document processing solution. The post reports a 7-fold throughput increase, from 10,000–70,000 documents monthly, and engineering hours per deployment dropping from 80 to under 5.

Onboarding time fell from 4–6 weeks to 2–3 days, and the system processes 1,000 documents in minutes during traffic spikes. Ricoh's customers process hundreds of thousands of documents each month, including insurance claims, grievances, appeals, and clinical records. Two newer assets target agentic applications: the Fullstack AgentCore Solution Template (FAST), which deploys a secured React frontend connected to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in under 30 minutes, and the Agentic Chatbot Accelerator, built on Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore using the AWS Cloud Development Kit. The post says FAST uses Amazon Cognito for authentication and lets builders swap identity providers, frontend frameworks, hosting solutions, or agent frameworks. The Agentic Chatbot Accelerator provides pre-configured patterns for authentication, hosting, and scaling, validated across customer deployments.

The post walks through the Contact Center GenAI Agent asset, which requires an AWS account, an Amazon Connect instance, access to Anthropic Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku on Amazon Bedrock, and a Jupyter notebook environment. Deployment uses two AWS CloudFormation stacks, one for the Knowledge Base and one for the RAG solution, and takes under an hour. The post says the asset includes Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for hallucination detection, content filtering, and topic boundaries, plus an Amazon Quick Sight dashboard for conversation analytics. The walkthrough closes with instructions for deleting the stacks in reverse order to avoid ongoing charges.

Articles.Title: Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets

stories.Headline: Can A.I. Help Us Engage More Closely with Art? Some Museums Think So.
stories.Summary:
Several American and European museums are now using artificial intelligence to help visitors engage more closely with art, according to an Observer article published on November 11, 2026. The Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, launched a web-based companion called Ask Rosie when it reopened in June after a 15-month expansion project. Visitors photograph an artwork with the app, which offers information such as the artist's identity and then asks what the user wants to learn. The app adjusts its tone to match the visitor, shifting between academic language and casual phrasing during a conversation. Shayne Hart, the museum's chief digital officer, described how the prompts a visitor gives shape the information the app supplies.

Remuseum, a nonprofit first created within Crystal Bridges to promote innovation in American art museums, released a report titled "Five Ways that A.I. Can Humanize Museums." The report says museums most immediately use the technology to connect information on visitors, donors and members that is otherwise kept in separate data silos. It gives the example of a development officer who must move among a fundraising database, a collections database, a ticketing system and an email platform to assemble one supporter's picture. At the Toledo Museum of Art, the technology tracks where visitors move and linger in the galleries, along with the programs they attend and whether they are members or donors. Adam Levine, the museum's director, said this data will let staff create more personalized experiences, such as inviting frequent visitors of a gallery to a special curator lecture.

Stephen Reily, founding director of Remuseum, said that museum workers and the public already use A.I. extensively, and he argued that curators and policymakers should embrace the technology. Hart described Ask Rosie as designed to meet each guest wherever they are in their art journey. Levine said the museum's policies, safeguards and training mean it does not believe there is any marginal risk in using A.I. to deepen engagement with art. Grace Yao, founder of the San Francisco-area company Artlas, said the app asks visitors whether they are kids or adults, their primary language and where they come from. Yao also said that Artlas users' information is encrypted and not used or shared for anything else, adding the qualifier "not at this point."

Reily said traditional museum experiences were one size fits all, with brochures and wall text written in art historical terms for visitors with higher education levels. Jane Alexander, chief digital officer of the Cleveland Museum of Art, said the average museum visitor spends only two to nine seconds looking at an artwork. Her museum's A.I. platform, ArtLens, has led young people to spend 10 minutes asking questions about paintings. The Artlas app can answer questions beyond the art, including about the bathroom, lunch or the best ice cream in a city, and it can refer to works in other institutions. Aziz Isham, director of the Museum of the Moving Image in Astoria, Queens, said the museum uses A.I. for data management but also employs more than 100 interns each year to answer visitors' questions.

The Observer article notes that Museum Voorlinden director Suzanne Swarts wrote a recent op-ed arguing that people live in an economy designed to interrupt them. The article also reports that Dataland calls itself the world's first Museum of A.I. Arts. Its galleries are powered by an open-access system called the Large Nature Model, hosted on a Google Cloud server running on 87 percent carbon-free energy.
