Carahsoft offers AI-focused events, webinars and training resources to support agencies at each stage of adoption. The healthcare summit panel, titled AI Governance and the Role of Policy Expertise, will examine what responsible AI looks like as these tools move into payment, oversight and enforcement decisions. The article does not say how many agencies have moved from pilots to full operational use. It also gives no figures on the cost of agency AI programs or the results achieved so far.

Articles.Title: Carahsoft’s Mike Adams on Turning Government AI Pilots Into Mission Outcomes

stories.Headline: Databricks’ new AI agent tells CEO Ali Ghodsi the unvarnished truth
stories.Summary:
Databricks on Wednesday unveiled an updated version of its AI agent Genie, which can now carry out multi-step jobs that take extended work to finish. The agent works through an ontology that Databricks built to give it context from the information customers store on the Databricks platform. The company says corporate leaders can assign it a wide range of tasks, and it will complete them without supervision. To demonstrate, CEO Ali Ghodsi showed TechCrunch how he uses the agent internally, walking through his actual recent chats and charts rather than a scripted product demo.

Ghodsi showed how the agent analyzed the parts of an employee satisfaction survey where the company scored poorly, and how it helped him rate and discard fixes that some executives had proposed. He also showed how it summarized a large sales pitch to a prospect that went badly, including the features the prospect said it needed before buying. In addition, the agent reviewed his past podcast appearances to develop likely interview questions. During the conversation, he even had it suggest what he should say to the reporter, and its advice was not bad.

The article describes Ghodsi using Genie to surface the information he is now unlikely to hear as a senior leader, a source of candid feedback about what was going wrong. He pointed to Dunbar's number, the theoretical limit of about 150 people with whom humans can maintain stable relationships. In a small startup, a CEO knows everyone and employees feel safe delivering bad news directly. With roughly 12,000 employees, Ghodsi acknowledged he cannot know everyone, so a salesperson may not confess a failed call and an HR manager may not admit a satisfaction idea will likely fail. He said that companies with more than 150 employees could get value from this kind of agent.

Databricks is now pitching Genie as an always-on agent for business leaders, in part because Ghodsi uses it internally and in his personal life, which the company calls dogfooding. He believes the tool can do for business work what AI agents and harnesses are doing for programmers. On cost concerns, he said spending can be controlled through Databricks' Unity Gateway product, which lets companies set usage limits and swap in less expensive open-weight models. The article notes that the company's approach is framed around these controls as agents take on more work.

Articles.Title: Databricks’ new AI agent tells CEO Ali Ghodsi the unvarnished truth

stories.Headline: "We're building the organization of the future, where AI agents will talk to one another."
stories.Summary:
Nir Korczak, chief marketing officer of Playtika, told the Gaming Conference hosted by Calcalist, Google, and Playtika on November 11, 2026, that the company is building an organization where AI agents communicate with one another and carry out tasks on their own. He described the shift as moving toward an ecosystem in which agents talk to each other, rather than employees using AI tools in isolation. According to Korczak, Playtika reached a new milestone in recent weeks in this effort. The change reaches into daily marketing work.

One system analyzes campaign performance and recommends ways to improve results, and although employees still approve some recommendations, the goal is to expand automation over time. Playtika has linked its internal marketing system, called "Samurai," to other systems so that decisions are documented and new capabilities can be added to the workflow. A second tool, an AI agent named "Corey" that acts as an organizational analyst, connects to agents and data sources across the company and is built into Microsoft Teams, where staff and executives can ask it complex business questions. Korczak said Corey is, for all intents and purposes, an employee.

Korczak also said the creative process is being transformed. He said that this year, with a smaller workforce, the company produced three times as much output, and that tasks that once required substantial video production budgets can now be handled by marketing staff with the click of a button. He stressed, however, that quantity alone is not the goal, so the company still employs creative professionals to develop original ideas that set it apart from competitors. In his view, AI is no longer limited to producing advertising content and is changing nearly every role in the marketing department.

Korczak framed these changes against a competitive backdrop in which barriers to game development are falling and the number of publishers is growing by about 30 percent a year, raising the cost of advertising and user acquisition. Other entertainment segments, led by short-form drama series, are competing for the same ad inventory and users. He also described a broader shift in which consumers increasingly rely on AI agents, so that brands may eventually communicate agent to agent with consumers. He concluded that if companies learn to use AI capabilities and build agent-based organizations, they will be able to construct the new marketing system for 2027.

Articles.Title: "We're building the organization of the future, where AI agents will talk to one another."

stories.Headline: Study evaluates AI tools for making medical documents easier to read
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers from the Universidad Carlos III de Madrid evaluated several artificial intelligence language models for simplifying medical reports into clearer language for non-expert readers. The work was published in the journal Scientific Reports. The researchers said many people struggle to understand their own medical documents, which affects how well they can manage their health. Their approach uses language models to produce one version of a report for clinicians and another for patients, explaining abbreviations and complex phrasing. The study is one of several efforts aimed at improving communication between doctors and patients.

The timing matters because Royal Decree 707/2026 takes effect on January 2, 2027. It was published in the Official State Gazette on September 3 and sets the first rules on basic cognitive accessibility conditions. The decree requires documents, administrative procedures and services to be easier for citizens to understand. It applies to public administrations in areas including justice, healthcare, employment, digital services and transport. The researchers describe plain language as a structured method that makes information easy to find, understand and use, rather than just shortening sentences.

The team tested 50 medical reports drawn from clinical cases supplied by the Andalusian Society of Family and Community Medicine. Each report had three adaptations written by cognitive accessibility experts following the international standard ISO 24495-1:2023, producing 150 adapted texts. The researchers compared four model families, including Llama 3.2 at 1B and 3B, Salamandra at 2B and 7B, RigoChat-v2 at 7B and Medical-mT5 at 3B, across simplification, accuracy, readability and environmental impact. They found no single model performed best in every area. Llama-3.2-3B gave the most balanced results, while RigoChat-v2-7B scored highest on output quality and readability.

The researchers also identified three recurring errors across all model families: oversimplification that removes clinical details patients need, invented or altered data, and incoherent sentences. Paloma Martínez, a co-author, said human oversight remains essential in healthcare because of these errors. The team has released its models, dataset and prompts as open-source material on GitHub and Zenodo so others can reproduce and extend the work. The research was carried out under the HumanAI project, funded through Spain's State Plan for Scientific, Technical and Innovation Research.

Articles.Title: Study evaluates AI tools for making medical documents easier to read

stories.Headline: J. Crew debuts new AI shopping tool that’s designed to think like a stylist
stories.Summary:
J. Crew on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, debuted Style Advisor, a consumer-facing AI shopping tool built to think like a stylist. The tool runs on a collection of Anthropic's models and was announced by the retailer that day. Its design reflects the company's history, which began as a catalog and grew into a physical and omnichannel retailer. Style Advisor is trained on data from thousands of outfit pairings from J. Crew's photo shoots, along with its styling principles and accessory pairings. The tool will first appear on J. Crew's desktop website and is expected to later be added to its mobile app.

J. Crew says Style Advisor asks questions to understand a shopper's intent, such as a wedding outfit in Miami that is not too formal. In the future, the tool will also pull in data from a consumer's past purchase history to make more personalized recommendations. Style Advisor uses Claude's Fable 5.1 for complex and ambiguous judgment, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 4.5 for speed and back-and-forth responses, and Opus 5.5 to build a working prototype. J. Crew also built a back-end observation layer that lets the retailer closely monitor costs. The company says that layer helps keep the tool scalable.

Danielle Schmelkin, chief information officer at J. Crew, said the tool aims to recommend more than the single item a shopper picked up. Lauren Collett, Anthropic's enterprise go-to-market leader, said the company must decide what experience it wants for shoppers and map the right models to deliver it. Schmelkin also said the retailer wants to keep refining how it uses the models, both for customer outputs and for efficiency. She credited her push for employees to build AI habits and find their own "a-ha moment."

The tool was conceptualized by a J. Crew digital product designer, who built a working prototype before engineers joined the project. It was not mandated from the top of the C-suite. Shoppers are the group most directly affected, since the tool changes how they receive styling advice online. J. Crew's employees are also affected by its internal AI fluency program, which starts with basics and advances to vibe coding. The company's internal AI lab, "Second Thread," began with the tech team and has widened to all corporate employees.

J. Crew has run a two-day tech summit for four years, featuring workshops, hackathons, guest speakers, and vendor presentations. The summit was first open only to the tech team but has more recently been opened more broadly. The company's history includes preppy staples such as cashmere cardigans and tweed jackets, and high-profile fans including Michelle Obama, Demi Moore, and Meghan Markle. The articles say that for decades those styling decisions were made by humans, and that this changed with the introduction of AI. Adoption of retailer AI assistants also lags general chatbots, per McKinsey.

The articles do not say how Style Advisor will perform with shoppers or how much revenue it will generate. They also do not give a date for the mobile app launch, beyond saying it is expected later. Details on future purchase-history features and their timing are not provided either. Whether the back-end cost monitoring will change pricing or scale plans is not stated. The articles leave open how J. Crew will measure the tool's success.

Articles.Title: J. Crew debuts new AI shopping tool that’s designed to think like a stylist

stories.Headline: Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Aids Healthcare Simulation Debriefing as Supportive Adjunct
stories.Summary:
Researchers Aseelah Alnazawi and Mohammed Almarhabi published a scoping review in Advances in Simulation finding that artificial intelligence currently supports human instructors during healthcare simulation debriefing rather than replacing them. The review mapped international literature on computational debriefing tools used in clinical training. It covered seven eligible studies published between 2023 and 2026, which applied artificial intelligence through automated speech tracking, structured summary reports, and learner dialogue interfaces. The authors concluded that the research is preliminary, exploratory, and mostly limited to single-institution pilot trials. Few of the studies showed objective gains in learner performance, clinical competency, or patient outcomes, so the tools are treated as complementary aids rather than substitutes for facilitators.

Simulation is an established teaching method that lets learners practice clinical reasoning, technical skills, and teamwork without risk to patients. Debriefing, a structured facilitator-led reflective session, is treated as its core component, helping participants analyze their actions and team dynamics. The review noted that traditional debriefing depends heavily on facilitator memory and observation, which strain under complex team dynamics and dense performance data. The authors applied Arksey and O'Malley's framework, with refinements by Levac and colleagues and Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, and followed the PRISMA-ScR checklist. Searches of MEDLINE via Ovid, Scopus, Web of Science, and CINAHL, plus grey literature, identified 46 initial records.

After removing 25 duplicates and excluding 14 of 21 screened citations, seven full-text articles were included. The authors and included studies describe the included work as heterogeneous in design, with three studies conducted in the United States, two in Switzerland, one in Chile, and one in South Korea. Three functional domains emerged: communication and performance analytics, generative systems that assist facilitators with preparation and feedback, and learner-facing reflective dialogue systems. In the analytics domain, Brutschi and colleagues showed speaker diarisation could distinguish individual speakers in debriefing audio, while Armijo-Rivera and colleagues found novice instructors spoke for an average of 56.09 percent of debriefing time. Tscholl and colleagues' automated teamwork reports drew criticism from simulation experts for speaker misattribution, inaccurate behavior categorization, and missing non-verbal cues.

Gonzalez and Nagendran found no statistically significant correlation between student course grades and debriefing duration in screen-based virtual nursing simulations. The review emphasized that human oversight remains essential, and the authors stressed that educators must keep ultimate responsibility for interpreting computational analytics. Because these tools capture audio, transcripts, and performance metrics, the authors raised concerns about data privacy, informed consent, algorithmic bias, and output transparency. They also warned that debriefing depends on psychological safety, so automated systems must not produce punitive or inaccurate evaluations that damage the learning climate. Technical problems reported across studies included poor audio quality, transcription errors, speaker misidentification, and an inability to register non-verbal interactions or emotional subtleties.

Jang and colleagues' nursing study reported improvements in student clinical confidence and domain knowledge, but the authors noted those cohorts were small, single-institution, and lacked control groups. Students, nursing and medical trainees, instructors, and clinical teams in simulation-based education are the populations the review addresses, and the authors call for rigorous evaluation before wider use. The articles do not state how quickly such tools will move into routine practice. They also leave open whether the reported learner gains will hold in larger, multi-institution studies with comparison groups and long-term behavioral follow-up. The articles do not specify which privacy safeguards or consent standards institutions should adopt.

Articles.Title: Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Aids Healthcare Simulation Debriefing as Supportive Adjunct

stories.Headline: AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets
stories.Summary:
Arctic Wolf Labs has disclosed a campaign in which an emerging agentic penetration testing platform called AntiFox was used to steal Amazon Web Services credentials and move laterally into compromised environments. The report was shared with The Hacker News, and the story was published on November 11, 2026. In several recent intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and their related AWS environments. The activity chained web exploitation and web shell deployment to enable configuration discovery, credential validation, cloud-service enumeration, secret access, and storage operations. AntiFox is available for download from GitHub and is described as an artificial intelligence-driven autonomous penetration testing platform.

Some of the initial access was tied to a compromised internet-facing Internet Information Services application, which was used to create an ASPX web shell through the IIS worker process, w3wp.exe. On that server, commands identified the execution context with whoami, enumerated the application directory, checked permissions with icacls, and tested whether files could be written into the web root. The attackers also attempted to connect to an internal production database using a credential extracted from the application configuration. In other attacks, the actor started with a valid AWS credential and abused valid IAM identities to validate it and enumerate dozens of services. Those services included IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock.

Arctic Wolf Labs is the source of the findings, and it said the Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with the confirmed malicious actions. The company observed that most of the authenticated cross-service API requests ended in an AccessDenied error. Some of the discovery and secret-access operations did succeed, according to the firm. In at least some instances, the activity progressed beyond Secrets Manager enumeration to a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Elsewhere, a valid AWS identity was used for S3 discovery and object operations through API calls, and Arctic Wolf warned that agentic frameworks make penetration testing techniques more accessible to threat actors.

Arctic Wolf added that these frameworks increase the speed and consistency with which the techniques can be applied in live attacks. Check Point Research said a cybercriminal with limited technical skills can task AI agents with investigating many targets in parallel and exploiting them with less manual effort. CERT-EU said the relevance of such tools lies in their scale, speed and persistence, since they can work through long attack chains without the fatigue that limits manual testing. It added that complex payload crafting often goes untested in manual assessments because the effort can exceed what the severity of the finding justifies.

GitGuardian said each of these frameworks has public source code and wires a model into a loop that runs tools and acts on their output. AntiFox has been forked 251 times and starred 474 times as of writing, and its description says a planner, worker and main-agent system runs the full engagement over a dual-graph core. The project says it focuses on delivery, turning what the AI finds into a report that an engineer can understand, reproduce, back with evidence, and hand to the client. The disclosure comes as threat actors increasingly weaponize AI-powered penetration testing tools such as ARTEX to automate stages of an intrusion with minimal human intervention.

Censys counted 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026, mostly in the U.S., Hong Kong, China, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea, though not every instance is necessarily malicious. Check Point Research identified 2,557 systems hosting ARTEX, including 10 misconfigured instances that exposed their full databases, and the Apple code-signing campaign harvested more than 300 certificates, of which three passed full validation. AntiFox and ARTEX belong to about 45 open-source agentic attack frameworks, which include PentAGI, RedAmon, and DarkMoon for network kill chains, and research prototypes such as Incalmo, hackingBuddyGPT, VulnBot, HackSynth, AutoPT, and Ares. The articles do not identify the precise vulnerability that gave the attackers code execution on the IIS server.

They also leave undetermined how the threat actor obtained the valid AWS credential used in the other attacks. No victims are named, and the articles do not say how many environments were compromised or which production secret was retrieved. Nothing is said about whether Alibaba Cloud or AWS has taken any action in response to the findings. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets

stories.Headline: HP, EdgeRunner AI Partner on Domain-Specific AI for Defense, Federal Agencies
stories.Summary:
HP and EdgeRunner AI have announced a collaboration to bring EdgeRunner's domain-specific artificial intelligence software and agents to HP's AI personal computers and workstations used by the military, federal agencies and other critical industries. The announcement came from EdgeRunner AI, which said the effort was revealed on Tuesday. The companies are working to adapt EdgeRunner's software to run on HP hardware and to link it with systems that warfighters already use. The reporting is dated November 11, 2026.

The work covers EdgeRunner's specialized AI models, agents and edge harness, which are meant for compatible HP AI PCs and HP Z Workstations. The software is designed to handle conversational AI, language translation, document analysis and agent-based workflows. HP and EdgeRunner are still deciding which systems, configurations and use cases to validate. The companies plan to announce specific features, purchasing options and availability once that validation is complete.

Tyler Saltsman, co-founder and CEO of EdgeRunner AI, said demand is rising for AI that understands how specialized users work and can run wherever they are. He said the company's military-tuned models center on defense use cases and local execution, and that the HP partnership gives it a way to bring those capabilities to high-performance computing platforms. Todd Gustafson, president of HP Federal and head of U.S. public sector at HP, described the effort as a way to move high-performance, domain-specific AI closer to the edge for critical industries. He said the goal is to identify validated configurations that can support local AI workloads in demanding customer environments.

The collaboration builds on HP's earlier federal work, including its June 2024 acquisition of CyberCore Technologies, a Maryland company, for an undisclosed sum. Matt Barry, chief operating officer at HP Federal, has stressed endpoint security by design for government and contractor systems and has pointed to HP Wolf Security and HP Sure Admin as tools to reduce attack surfaces. EdgeRunner AI has its own government record, including a 2025 agreement with Carahsoft to offer its Athena platform to agencies. This year the company released WarClaw, won a Space Force contract to develop AI agents for acquisition modernization, and teamed with the Army's Artificial Intelligence Integration Center on an Army-specific model. The Navy also granted EdgeRunner OS an Impact Level 6 Authority to Operate.

Articles.Title: HP, EdgeRunner AI Partner on Domain-Specific AI for Defense, Federal Agencies

stories.Headline: ByteDance Builds Assistant to Take on US AI Labs
stories.Summary:
ByteDance, the Chinese technology company, is reportedly developing an artificial intelligence agent similar to Meta's Muse, according to a Bloomberg report published Wednesday, November 11. The effort could help ByteDance narrow its gap with AI labs in the United States in the coming years. The report cites unnamed sources saying that ByteDance co-founder Zhang Yiming described the plan to the company's AI team at a meeting. He reportedly said ByteDance can compete with Anthropic and OpenAI, though he thinks that will take until at least 2029 or 2030.

The new agent would serve a function similar to Muse, which Meta debuted in September and which the report describes as a success for its creator. Meta has begun adding Muse to hardware such as its smart glasses, and it plans an upcoming device called Muse Charm built around the agent. The report says it is unclear whether ByteDance also intends to pair its agent with hardware. Zhang reportedly focuses on data, and the report notes that ByteDance's Seed AI models are pre-trained on datasets smaller than those used by its frontier competitors.

Meta's own push has been significant, as PYMNTS reported on October 21 that Muse had become a new centerpiece of the company's AI ambitions. Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg pointed to the assistant on the company's third-quarter earnings call as evidence that the strategy was working. More than 10 million people in the United States and Canada set up Muse within six weeks of its launch, and about 25% use it daily. The broader competitive picture shows that these assistants are gaining traction with users, which raises the stakes for newcomers like ByteDance.

Consumer attitudes toward AI agents also set limits on what such products can do, according to a PYMNTS Intelligence report released in October. That report found that 63% of consumers would let an AI agent help with credit by comparing offers, but only 49% would let it complete and submit an application. It also found that 79% said it is very important or essential for an agent to explain in plain language why it chose a particular offer or action. The articles do not say how or when ByteDance's agent will be released, or whether it will address these concerns.

Articles.Title: ByteDance Builds Assistant to Take on US AI Labs

stories.Headline: AI-native applications need distributed cloud, not just GPUs
stories.Summary:
Vultr, a cloud provider operating under the legal name The Constant Company LLC, has been arguing that enterprises building AI-native applications need more than raw GPU capacity. The position was laid out by Kevin Cochrane, chief marketing officer of Vultr, in an interview recorded at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA and broadcast on theCUBE, with John Furrier and Rebecca Knight of theCUBE Research. The article is dated November 11, 2026. Vultr sponsored the segment, a disclosure the article states plainly.

Cochrane said the early wave of so-called neoclouds focused on building large GPU clusters for a small set of buyers, often reselling that capacity to hyperscalers. In his view, the sector lost sight of the fact that companies still need a full cloud to run their workloads. He said the architecture has drifted back toward centralized systems and that the longer direction of computing is toward decentralized, distributed systems built on open standards and open source. The article also says distributed inference is a focus, with Vultr working with partners such as Vast Data Inc. on a global namespace that shares KV cache across nodes. Cochrane argued that networking between data centers, including private networks isolated from other tenants, is the main obstacle to enterprises adopting GPUs from newer cloud providers.

Vultr is also backing the open-source community, according to the article. The company has joined the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a platinum member and highlighted its Open Source Credits Program, which provides infrastructure to maintainers of new CNCF projects. Cochrane said maintainers cannot be expected to fund compute themselves, and asked how a major CNCF project can be built without it. The article notes that the views are Cochrane's and that neither Vultr nor other sponsors have editorial control over theCUBE content.

Articles.Title: AI-native applications need distributed cloud, not just GPUs

stories.Headline: Agent substrate: how Kubernetes became the foundation for AI
stories.Summary:
Kubernetes, the container orchestrator, has grown into what enterprises now rely on to run artificial intelligence agents, according to a SiliconANGLE report published on November 11, 2026. The article frames this as a shift in which Kubernetes acts as the agent substrate, a change that revives older security ideas such as the network perimeter. It also raises the importance of moving workloads smoothly between clouds. The story centers on remarks made at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, where Broadcom unveiled two open-source initiatives.

Broadcom is pushing two main efforts to make the platform simpler to deploy and safer to run. The company's approach is security in depth, which uses its vDefend firewall at the network perimeter and deeper inside the system to cut off network access when rogue agents appear. Broadcom also isolates agents inside compute boundaries called vSphere Pods, which are micro virtual machines that create a secure runtime. On the portability side, the company is co-chairing a new working group on Kubernetes workload conformance, which aims to end separate validations for each distribution.

Dilpreet Bindra, senior director of engineering in the VCF Division at Broadcom, is the main voice in the report. He said that KubeCon blew open the doors on a project that some had considered stable and less active, because Kubernetes has become the foundation for AI. Bindra also said Broadcom wants Kubernetes to work the same way wherever it runs, so that users do not need separate validations for VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service and other distributions. He described the company's contribution of its VM API project to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a way to bring virtual machines into Kubernetes as first-class citizens.

The article places this discussion within a wider debate about how agents change cloud infrastructure, and it notes that the interview was sponsored by Broadcom, which had no editorial control over the content. The report does not describe specific timelines for when the working group will produce results or when the VM API project will reach a particular milestone. It likewise does not say how widely the security approach has been adopted by customers. The piece appears as part of SiliconANGLE and theCUBE's coverage of the conference, with the full video interview included.

Articles.Title: Agent substrate: how Kubernetes became the foundation for AI

stories.Headline: Don’t just prompt AI — architect it: Introducing the Professional Agentic Architect Certification
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud has announced a new certification called the Professional Agentic Architect, aimed at proving skill in building production-ready AI agents. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026, by Gary Eimerman, managing director of Google Cloud Learning. The certification is the latest step in the company's Gemini Agent Ready initiative, which nearly one million developers are already using to learn about agents. It was first used internally, where Google trained thousands of forward deployed engineers and strategic partners over the past four months, and is now being opened to the wider developer community and partner ecosystem.

The certification uses a hybrid format rather than a traditional multiple choice test. The first part is a proctored multiple choice exam that tests system design choices, architectural standards, cost optimization, and security governance. The second part is a set of hands-on labs on Google Skills, where candidates build, test, and debug live agentic workflows in an active cloud environment. The curriculum covers building agents with low-code tools, using coding agents for application development, developing custom agents on the Gemini platform with open source frameworks, evaluating and deploying agentic workflows, and securing and governing them. Candidates who pass both parts receive a digital badge.

The announcement was written by Gary Eimerman, who presents the program as a response to enterprise demand for agentic workloads, which the article says has skyrocketed. Google says its forward deployed engineers and partners work directly with customers worldwide, and that standardizing training ensures its own teams follow the same standards it recommends. The article also cites research with Ipsos, reporting that 82% of learners using Google Skills say listing Google Cloud certifications on a resume draws more recruiter responses, and that 90% of cloud professionals say such credentials give them verified know-how for in-demand roles. Ravi, the vice president who manages Google's forward deployed engineers, is also named as a contributor to the program's rollout.

Developers can get started by registering for Gemini Agent Ready, which offers 35 free monthly learning credits on Google Skills. Google Cloud customers can join a no-cost, cohort-based guided certification journey called Get Certified, while partners can register for Partner Certification Kickstart. Candidates are directed to review the exam guide, learning path, and sample questions, complete the hands-on preparation modules, then take the multiple choice exam and the lab requirements. The article does not state the exam fee, pass thresholds, or the number of participants who have completed the certification so far.

Articles.Title: Don’t just prompt AI — architect it: Introducing the Professional Agentic Architect Certification

stories.Headline: Plurai wants to help AI agents work better using the same approach that helped get self-driving cars to roads
stories.Summary:
Plurai, a startup, has raised $13 million in seed funding to build simulation tools that aim to make AI agents more reliable. The round was led by Team8, with participation from U&I, Velocity and Mercer, and the announcement came on Wednesday. Co-founders Ilan Kadar and Elad Levi previously worked at Nexar, which develops autonomous driving technology. Kadar had worked with Waymo to simulate and evaluate its end-to-end deep learning driving software.

The company's approach creates a digital twin of a business's electronic systems, including the knowledge base and tools an agent will use in production. It maps the possible flows an agent could take and uses that map to prepare the model for edge cases. The platform works alongside existing agentic tools such as Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and Cursor. Plurai also uses the data it gathers to post-train small, open-weight models tailored to individual customers.

Kadar described the core problem as the gap between a demo and a product that is both reliable and cost effective. Tests done with Nvidia and Nebius showed Plurai's models outperforming mid-tier frontier models at lower cost, according to the article. Reah Miyara, a Google DeepMind researcher who backed the company as an angel investor, said its edge comes from understanding failure modes in production and generating synthetic data to tune models. Kadar argued that general models will not know a particular business's policies.

The article gives background on agent reliability, citing LiveBench 2.0, where Claude Fable 5.2 and ChatGPT-6 Astra succeeded on 82.9 and 75.6 out of 100 tasks. A test by the AI infrastructure company EON in a simulated corporate environment found the top model, Claude Opus 4.8, reached 76.8% accuracy. The article notes that agents booking travel can ignore spending policies, and that combining data from multiple sources or long customer conversations can cause errors. It also compares this to the simulation methods used to bring self-driving cars to roads.

Meta's Muse agent, launched in early September, drew 10 million downloads in the U.S. within 40 days, with buying as its most popular task and average purchases above $200. OpenAI followed with its own always-on agent, Dots, a few weeks later. Amazon blocked Muse almost immediately and had already spent a year in court fighting Perplexity's shopping agent. Walmart announced a system giving each agent its own profile with purchase approval or spending limits, while JPMorgan said it would not let outside agents into customer accounts.

Articles.Title: Plurai wants to help AI agents work better using the same approach that helped get self-driving cars to roads

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s I.P.O. and the Clubby Business of A.I.
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company, has begun the roadshow for its initial public offering, a move that has drawn major attention in the A.I. industry. Investor demand for the stock offering is reported to be robust so far. The company's latest I.P.O. prospectus disclosed a $26 billion private share sale, which has drawn scrutiny for what it reveals about how money moves through the sector. The figures in the filing also showed which investors stand to gain the most if the listing succeeds.

The $26 billion private share sale is worth close attention because it highlights circular financing, a pattern in which money flows among companies that also depend on one another as customers or backers. Reporting on the filing suggests this kind of arrangement underpins much of the A.I. economy. The story was reported by Sri Muppidi, and the newsletter that carried it framed the offering as among the biggest recent stories in artificial intelligence. Earlier in the same coverage, attention had been on the scrutiny facing Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, before the Anthropic roadshow took center stage.

The articles do not identify any individual or executive held responsible for the financing structure, and they do not supply direct statements from the company on the circular financing point. The newsletter is written by a team of DealBook reporters and editors, led in this edition by Andrew Ross Sorkin. Beyond the roadshow and the prospectus, the material leaves open how the offering will price and how the investors named in the filing will be affected. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Anthropic’s I.P.O. and the Clubby Business of A.I.

stories.Headline: "AI has caused an insane inflation in the number of games; it’s becoming harder to capture a player's attention."
stories.Summary:
Anat Horvitz, a director at Google Israel, told a panel at the Gaming Conference hosted by Calcalist, Google, and Playtika that there is an insane inflation in the number of games. The panel, held on November 11, 2026, was moderated by Meir Orbach of Calcalist. Horvitz said it is harder than ever to capture players' attention. Eitan Reisel, managing partner at the investment fund vgames, joined the discussion about how artificial intelligence is changing the gaming industry. Their remarks were published by Calcalist on November 11, 2026.

Over the past year, game downloads fell 11 percent, according to Horvitz. Revenue nevertheless grew for a third consecutive year, rising 1.5 percent this year. Horvitz projected that 136,000 new games will be released in 2026, a massive increase compared with 2025. Only 6 percent of total playtime goes to games released within the past year. Reisel said that with a $5 million seed investment he now expects a casual-game developer to launch 12 games, up from two.

vgames has raised $500 million, with backing from The Phoenix and in partnership with General Catalyst. Horvitz and Reisel did not describe a regulatory requirement or legal change; their remarks concern the industry's economics. Reisel said that games can now be released much faster but still need significant capital. Horvitz said the bottleneck has shifted from production to attention, and that winning it requires AI, creative strategy, and in-depth data analysis. Reisel said that automated media-buying systems have shifted the advantage to those who can generate ideas and creative concepts.

The vgames financing model covers user acquisition costs, with the fund repaid from revenue generated by the users it helps acquire. Reisel, speaking as an investor at vgames, described the model in which the fund finances expenses rather than taking equity. He said that if a company needs $10 million, he can provide $8 million, acting as a kind of bank for the gaming industry. Horvitz described Google's role by pointing to tools that let even small studios produce games in a matter of days. Reisel said that his portfolio company generates 800 creative assets a week, and he said he has invested $800 million.

Horvitz said that Israeli companies have expertise in monetization and data analytics and think globally from day one. Smaller studios and founders are the groups the speakers described as most affected, since financing terms and launch competition now shape their options. Horvitz said that many studios now launch 12 or more games and want to determine quickly whether a game's economics work. Reisel said that the ability of competitors to clone games has reached an insane level. Horvitz said the industry is seeing a wave of mergers and acquisitions, with companies acquiring existing titles instead of developing every game themselves.

The article notes that Israel's gaming industry employs 14,000 workers and makes up 2 percent of GDP. Calcalist's report places the panel in the context of a gaming industry that Horvitz said is undergoing a transformation driven by artificial intelligence. Reisel said that AI has made game development faster and cheaper while intensifying competition for players' attention. The article states that the gaming industry needs capital, but the terms of investment have changed. Reisel noted that running a gaming company has not become easier, because companies must constantly create new content and invest large sums in marketing.

Horvitz said the industry's bottleneck has moved from game production to competition for players. Calcalist's article does not say what will happen next for the vgames financing model or for the 136,000 games projected for 2026. The panelists offered no timeline for the expected shift toward acquisitions. The article gives no outcome for the competition among studios to retain players, and it does not say how the industry's revenue trend will develop beyond this year.

Articles.Title: "AI has caused an insane inflation in the number of games; it’s becoming harder to capture a player's attention."

stories.Headline: The AI industry's week from hell
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced on Tuesday, November 11, 2026, that it plans to raise as much as $64.4 billion in an IPO that targets a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion. The offering fell short of earlier expectations, as the valuation sits roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago. Slowing revenue growth, soaring infrastructure costs and a sharp market selloff all contributed to the lower target. The article describes the move as one of the largest IPOs in history, and the timing added to a difficult week for the wider AI industry.

The reset came after a series of setbacks for AI companies that began with last week's midterm results. Voters in 40 of 41 local ballot measures nationwide favored restrictions on data-center development. Congress will also gain AI-skeptical Democrats who may use subpoena power to look into the industry's safety record and political influence. Nvidia has shed more than $1 trillion in market value since New York Times reports on October 29 linked CEO Jensen Huang to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, and the FBI, the company's board and Congress are investigating. The Nasdaq also lost $2.5 trillion in value on Thursday, its worst session since April 2025.

Anthropic's own figures show the strain. Its annualized revenue reached $81 billion in October, but its long-term commitments to chips, data centers and computing infrastructure have climbed to nearly $901 billion. Other financial warning signs appeared as OpenAI scaled back its fundraising ambitions and SoftBank reported a $3.7 billion write-down on U.S. data-center equipment. The article also notes that lenders are growing wary of financing the industry's infrastructure spending. Still, Google, Nvidia and other technology giants have committed another $26 billion in private investment alongside the public offering.

The article suggests the outcome will depend on whether Anthropic can post a strong debut and keep its share price up after trading begins. It points to SpaceX, whose stock surged after its record June IPO but later fell below its offering price within weeks. If Anthropic completes the offering, the company could bring in roughly $85 billion in net new capital. The article argues that even a valuation of $1 trillion or $1.5 trillion may not reassure investors who expected as much as $2 trillion only weeks ago.

Articles.Title: The AI industry's week from hell

stories.Headline: Former Chinese Ambassador Cui Tiankai on China-US Relations and AI Governance
stories.Summary:
Former Chinese Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs and Ambassador to the United States Cui Tiankai spoke on November 7 at the "APEC China Year · Greater Bay Area Academic Roundtable" in Shenzhen. He shared his views on China-US relations and artificial intelligence governance. The event was part of the lead-up to the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, which is due to be held in Shenzhen in about ten days. The article reports the remarks as a keynote speech followed by a conversation with Professor Li Cheng of Hong Kong University. The Shenzhen Hetao Institute and the Centre on Contemporary China and the World at the University of Hong Kong invited him to take part.

On China-US relations, Cui called for a relationship of "constructive strategic stability," with cooperation as the priority and competition kept within reasonable bounds. He said China's development has never aimed to replace or challenge the United States. He argued that competition between the two countries should not become a zero-sum game, since cooperation benefits both and confrontation harms both. On AI, he said the two countries have the capability and responsibility to keep the technology under human control and serve the public good. He proposed three steps for an Asia-Pacific framework: establishing AI for good as a guiding principle, building on APEC's cooperation record, and promoting inclusive development and integration.

Cui said the political, economic and social challenges facing the United States have deep structural causes and cannot be blamed on any single leader. He said domestic political developments in the US should not undermine bilateral relations. He criticised Washington for broadening the concept of national security and for politicising scientific, educational and people-to-people exchanges. He called on the US to remove unnecessary barriers to these exchanges and restore normal cooperation, saying even modest progress through dialogue would be worthwhile. On AI, he rejected an approach driven by fear and suspicion toward China's technological progress, saying zero-sum thinking is especially inappropriate in so advanced a field.

The remarks reach people across the Asia-Pacific region, which Cui said is home to nearly 40% of the world's population. He said the region accounts for more than 60% of global economic output and almost half of global trade, with internet penetration approaching 90%. He argued that AI development in such a region carries enormous significance for the world. He said countries at different stages of development should all have opportunities to take part in AI governance and benefit from technological progress. He also stressed that different technological pathways should be allowed to compete fairly, while the guiding principles must be set from the outset.

The speech builds on a July 2026 position set out at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance in Shanghai. At that event, a Chinese national leader called for a people-centred approach and AI for good, and for a fair and equitable global AI governance system. Cui cited that address and its questions about how humanity should coexist with machines and how the benefits of AI can be shared. He drew on APEC's history, noting that the region has weathered natural disasters, financial crises and a global pandemic over more than three decades since the forum was established. He also invoked a classical Chinese passage on understanding and transforming the world.

The articles do not say how the US government has responded to these remarks, and they do not describe any specific policy the US has adopted on exchanges or AI. They also do not set out concrete measures that would result from the Shenzhen roundtable or the APEC meeting. The articles do not say which barriers Cui had in mind, or what form any AI cooperation between the two countries would take. It is also unclear how the other APEC members will respond to the proposals, and whether the three suggestions will appear in the leaders' meeting outcome.

Articles.Title: Former Chinese Ambassador Cui Tiankai on China-US Relations and AI Governance

stories.Headline: Dartmouth provost resigns over undisclosed AI use
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth Provost Santiago Schnell has resigned and is leaving the university after a faculty-led committee found he used artificial intelligence in his writing without properly disclosing it. President Sian Leah Beilock announced the resignation on Oct. 28 in an email to the campus community. She wrote that the decision was Schnell's own and was made out of respect for his colleagues and the institution. Beilock had formed the committee on Sept. 25 after news reports questioned his AI use, including an August Semafor article about AI-written opinion pieces that named his Washington Post column.

The committee's report, dated Oct. 27, concluded that Schnell used AI in ways that broke at least one publication's disclosure rules and that he was not forthcoming about it. It did not use AI detection tools, relying instead on his logs from Dartmouth's enterprise tool, Claude, and his emails. In one journal paper, it found he used Claude to substantially edit a manuscript, troubleshoot code and generate figures without the disclosure the journal required. Schnell told Semafor he used ChatGPT to refine arguments and check grammar in a Post submission, which the committee called a clear violation of the paper's policy. The report also said he did not provide logs of his personal AI accounts when asked, though he did hand over his Dartmouth laptop.

The committee was led by former provost David Kotz and included Hany Farid, Peter Orner, Lindsay Whaley and Odette Harris. It said it was not recommending any disciplinary action. Schnell did not respond to a request for comment, and Dartmouth's media relations director did not immediately reply. Beilock wrote that leaders must model the transparency and human judgment expected of students and scholars. History professor Matthew Delmont will serve as interim provost through June 2028.

Articles.Title: Dartmouth provost resigns over undisclosed AI use

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence and Dual Tracers Tackle PSMA Heterogeneity in Prostate Cancer
stories.Summary:
The article reports that a scientific review, published in Frontiers in Oncology, examines how variable target expression complicates diagnosis and treatment of castration-resistant prostate cancer. Its authors are Surilige, Jiacheng Liang, and Ruimin Ren of the Third Hospital of Shanxi Medical University. The review was carried in a November 11, 2026 article on bioengineer.org. It assesses dual-tracer imaging, downstream pathway inhibitors, and artificial intelligence as ways to address target heterogeneity. The article describes this work as a synthesis of existing research rather than a new trial.

The review centers on prostate-specific membrane antigen, a glycoprotein abundant on prostate cancer cells and metastatic deposits. Prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography detects malignant deposits using radioisotope-labeled ligands. Pairing these tracers with fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose captures metabolically aggressive lesions that lack ligand uptake. The article also cites gallium-68 PSFA-01, a heterobivalent tracer targeting both the glycoprotein and fibroblast activation protein, which showed higher lesion detection than monospecific tracers in preliminary human evaluations. Lutetium-177 vipivotide tetraxetan was approved following the VISION and PSMAfore phase III trials, with PSMAfore showing 9.3 months versus 5.6 months of radiographic progression-free survival.

The authors attribute this variability to clonal evolution, epigenetic changes, and lineage plasticity that can drive tumors toward neuroendocrine phenotypes with reduced target expression. They say the review was written by the three named researchers, who evaluate these barriers in the disease. The article does not give a direct quotation from them in the portion provided. It notes that current guidelines, including those from the Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, rely on visual criteria without standardized quantitative thresholds for uptake adequacy. Patients with advanced, aggressive disease, especially those with TP53 and RB1 inactivation, are described as most affected by these diagnostic blind spots.

The article describes preclinical and clinical work on PI3K/AKT and MAPK pathway inhibitors, including phase III trials such as IPATential150 and CAPItello-281 that showed radiographic progression-free survival benefits in biomarker-selected cohorts. It also notes that none of these investigational combinations is currently approved to reverse target heterogeneity. On the artificial intelligence side, the article cites automated segmentation reaching a mean Dice coefficient of about 0.89 and reducing contouring time from 30 to 45 minutes to about 15 seconds. It reports an 82 percent sensitivity for automated metastasis detection with about 1.8 false positives per patient, and an area under the curve of 0.98 for distinguishing malignant hotspots across 72 patients.

The authors caution that most models rely on retrospective, single-center datasets with small samples and lack rigorous external validation across scanners and radiopharmaceuticals. They note that high technical accuracy does not prove improved survival or clinical utility. The article states that large-scale prospective multicenter trials with harmonized protocols remain essential. It does not specify when such trials will begin, which combination regimens will advance, or whether the artificial intelligence tools will reach routine clinical use.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence and Dual Tracers Tackle PSMA Heterogeneity in Prostate Cancer

stories.Headline: U.S.-China Engagement Ahead of the Trump-Xi APEC Summit,AI DIalogue
stories.Summary:
The United States and China held a video call on November 6, 2026, with Vice Premier He Lifeng, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, days before the APEC leaders' meeting in China. The call, announced by both sides, centered on carrying out understandings reached by the two presidents in Beijing and Washington. Chinese and U.S. readouts of the call differed in emphasis. A separate phone call between Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Secretary of State Marco Rubio took place on November 11.

Beijing expressed serious concerns about recent U.S. economic and trade restrictions against China. Washington stressed that China must fully and immediately meet its commitments, particularly on agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals. The U.S. said it would closely assess China's implementation of the Busan arrangement. GE Aerospace announced more than $12.9 billion in agreements on November 6 at the China International Import Expo, including an order from China Eastern Airlines for 202 LEAP-1A engines.

Bessent is responsible for the U.S. statements, which he framed as protecting American workers, farmers and businesses. Foreign Minister Wang Yi described the Rubio call as positive and constructive, while China's readout did not say what Rubio had said. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun dismissed espionage claims linked to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as groundless speculation and malicious smears. Taiwan Affairs Office spokeswoman Zhang Han said cross-Strait semiconductor cooperation serves both sides.

Bessent disclosed the new AI arrangements in remarks on November 11 at the National Committee on US-China Relations' annual dinner. He said the U.S. had set up a dialogue with China on superintelligence, at President Trump's direction, to guard against shared risks. Both countries also expect to exchange best practices for testing advanced AI models before release, and to keep human judgment in command of the technology. A direct channel will let either side promptly alert the other to serious incidents involving its superintelligence models.

Bessent credited Henry Kissinger, who died at 100 and had met Xi in Beijing on his last trip, with raising concerns about superintelligence as a new class of strategic danger. China has already set up several pre-release AI safety mechanisms, including security assessments and regulatory filings for generative AI services. These include red-teaming, adversarial testing and third-party evaluations, under the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said China and the United States remained in communication about leader interactions later this year.

It remains unconfirmed whether the two presidents will hold a meeting at APEC or whether the Jensen Huang affair will be discussed there. The articles also do not say whether China will meet the agricultural and rare earth commitments the U.S. demanded. Details of the AI dialogue's first meeting and its schedule are not given. Neither country has confirmed a date or format for the planned leader-level exchanges.

Articles.Title: U.S.-China Engagement Ahead of the Trump-Xi APEC Summit,AI DIalogue

stories.Headline: QSAN and JetStor to Showcase 3U60 NVMe All-Flash Storage for On-Prem AI at SC26
stories.Summary:
QSAN Technology Inc. and its U.S. distribution partner JetStor will showcase QSAN's 3U60 NVMe All-Flash Array at SC26 in Chicago, Illinois. The announcement was dated November 11, 2026, from Taipei, Taiwan. SC26, also known as Supercomputing 2026, runs from November 15 to 20 at McCormick Place. The companies are presenting the array as part of their push for on-premises AI infrastructure.

The 3U60 array holds up to 60 NVMe SSDs within a compact 3U chassis. It uses an innovative OCP card-based design that QSAN says delivers high flash density and infrastructure efficiency. The platform is positioned for low-latency, high-throughput data access for AI pipelines, large datasets and HPC work. QSAN also says selected NVMe platforms support NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage for more efficient data movement to GPUs.

QSAN describes its enterprise NVMe portfolio as supporting the full AI data lifecycle, from ingestion and preparation through training, inference and long-term retention. The company says it is combining its in-house hardware and software engineering with JetStor's established U.S. market presence. Steven Lin, General Manager of QSAN Technology Inc., said storage must evolve to deliver greater density, performance and efficiency as enterprises bring AI workloads in house. Lin said the companies look forward to showing how the storage can help organizations accelerate enterprise AI adoption.

QSAN invites enterprise AI infrastructure architects, HPC professionals, system integrators, AI solution providers and IT decision-makers to explore the technologies at SC26. Visitors are encouraged to schedule one-on-one meetings with QSAN representatives to discuss their on-premises AI, HPC and storage requirements. The articles describe JetStor as a U.S.-based provider of enterprise storage serving organizations with demanding capacity, performance and reliability needs. They say the collaboration brings QSAN's technologies to customers across the United States.

QSAN describes itself as committed to building AI-ready enterprise IT infrastructure. The company says it aims to help organizations protect, deploy, scale and manage mission-critical data and applications. SC26 is described as the largest international HPC conference, attracting more than 18,000 attendees from around the world. A separate Women in HPC workshop and networking reception is also scheduled at SC26 in Chicago on November 16, 2026.

Articles.Title: QSAN and JetStor to Showcase 3U60 NVMe All-Flash Storage for On-Prem AI at SC26

stories.Headline: Anthropic says a key AI safety alarm has been triggered, days before its IPO
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, in an amended prospectus filed alongside the price range for its record-setting IPO, Anthropic said it has met a key safety threshold. A week earlier, the company had told would-be investors that AI speeding up its own research might "imminently" trigger this alarm. The filing says Anthropic made the determination based on what it expects from future models and its overall rate of progress, not on what it has observed from current models. The threshold sits in the company's Responsible Scaling Policy, its rulebook for adding tougher safety measures as its AI becomes more powerful.

The threshold is triggered when AI is doing enough of Anthropic's research to roughly double how fast its models improve. The policy says that pace would pack two years' worth of AI progress, at its 2018-2024 rate, into a single year. Anthropic set its IPO price range at $70 to $78 per share on Tuesday as it began its roadshow, the round of investor meetings before pricing. That values the company at as much as about $1.4 trillion, counting every share that could exist, and trading could start as soon as Nov. 19, according to reports. Nvidia and Google are each buying $10 billion of Anthropic stock at the IPO price, part of a $26 billion private placement that also includes AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and Taiwan Semiconductor.

Anthropic says crossing the threshold means more safeguards, not a shutdown, and that humans stay in charge. The filing says the company does not expect to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding. It says it is weighing policy changes to keep humans in control, and that AI has already been accelerating its research and development. Anthropic said it is still weighing what crossing the threshold means and will release further reports. The filing also warns that, as Claude speeds up work inside the company, the organization may lose visibility across certain processes in a way that may become difficult for any individual or group of humans to understand and control.

METR, an independent nonprofit that tests AI systems, estimated last week that Anthropic's models have been improving nearly twice as fast since October 2025. In a separate review, METR called Anthropic's August argument that it was still below the threshold "overstated" and said it was "plausible" the line was crossed by mid-July. Constellation Research founder Ray Wang said ahead of a Yahoo Finance live show appearance last month that in all S-1 filings the risks are deliberately overstated. For investors, the filing's risk factors warn that after a catastrophic AI incident, no single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have the capacity to cover the damage. Amazon and Google already own big stakes in the company.

The fear behind the threshold is that AI will improve itself faster than people can check it. In 2023, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei joined other AI leaders in warning that the "risk of extinction from AI" should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war. The same filing swapped in "super intelligence" for "AI" in places, citing President Trump's Sept. 29 executive order telling federal agencies to use the term. Mentions of "AI" fell by about a quarter from the Nov. 2 version, by Yahoo Finance's count, though the filing treats the terms as interchangeable. The change came two weeks after Trump criticized the Wall Street Journal on Truth Social for sticking with the phrase "artificial intelligence."

Anthropic's roadshow is now under way, and trading could begin as soon as Nov. 19, according to reports. The company has said it will release further reports on what crossing the safety threshold means for its safeguards. The articles do not say which additional safeguards Anthropic will adopt or when they would take effect. They also do not say which policy changes the company is weighing to keep humans in control, or whether the IPO timeline could shift. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Anthropic says a key AI safety alarm has been triggered, days before its IPO

stories.Headline: Applied Digital And Harwood: A Teaching Moment For AI Data Centers?
stories.Summary:
Tech giants are reportedly set to spend about $9 trillion on the U.S. artificial intelligence buildout over the next six years, and that spending is now running into resistance at the local level. On Nov. 3, more than 250,000 voters across 10 states cast ballots on local measures that would restrict or allow data centers. The article reports that a strong 73% of the voters weighing in took part in these decisions. The piece frames these votes as a possible teaching moment for the companies building AI data centers.

The article's central point is that data center developers can no longer treat local opposition as a minor hurdle to clear. Governors facing reelection have been putting obstacles in the way, and voters have now weighed in directly on whether these facilities should be restricted or permitted. The measures on the ballot covered a wide range of communities, showing that the question of where data centers go is becoming a matter of public decision. The source text is cut off before it lays out the specific rules or limits each measure would impose.

The article does not name a single party responsible for the ballot measures, and it does not attribute specific statements to the companies or officials involved. Its framing points to the large technology firms driving the buildout as the parties that now face the pressure. Beyond the overall trend, the piece describes voters and governors as the forces pushing back. The available text does not provide direct quotes from any of them.

The context offered is a broader shift in which AI infrastructure is moving from a purely corporate and financial question into one shaped by local politics. The article's headline and summary suggest that developers will need to respond to these voter signals as they plan future projects. The text provided does not say what concrete steps companies or regulators will take next, so further developments remain unclear. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Applied Digital And Harwood: A Teaching Moment For AI Data Centers?

stories.Headline: Google SWE points 48 AI agents at NASA Lidar, finds unmapped Maya pyramid in 72h
stories.Summary:
An independent researcher says he used 48 AI agents to scan public NASA lidar data of Mexico's Maya lowlands and flagged a previously unrecorded archaeological site in about 72 hours. The lidar strips cover roughly 1,200 square kilometres of jungle, and the agents examined them image by image, looking for pyramids, platforms and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes and roads. The researcher then wrote a report with the site's details and sent it to Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History, known as INAH. In a written reply, INAH said its records showed no registered archaeological site at the location he gave.

The site, as the author describes it, includes a levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least 8 to 12 metres tall, a raised courtyard attached to it and a flat-bottomed hollow that may have been a water reservoir. The researcher checked the raw point cloud to confirm the shapes sat on the ground rather than in the tree canopy. He also reports that a later update, dated 11 November, says the same site had already been mapped in a 2025 study by Estrada-Belli and colleagues, which the agents missed while searching the literature. In that case the find is a rediscovery rather than a new one, though the site was not yet in INAH's register. The author notes that none of this is official yet.

The researcher, who says he is not an archaeologist, presents the work as evidence that agentic AI can contribute to scientific fields beyond coding, mathematics and physics. He describes the origin of the project as an idea he had while travelling in Peru, prompted by the story of Hiram Bingham and Machu Picchu. He also reports that he consulted several AI tools during planning and that he translated his report into Spanish with their help. He says he offered INAH help with a field check, and notes that under Mexican federal law any fieldwork at an archaeological site requires INAH's authorisation. The decision on whether to send a team rests with the local INAH centre, and the author says he will post an update if one goes.

The author's own interpretation is speculative: he suggests the site may be a small Classic-period Maya civic centre dating roughly from AD 250 to 900, with the pyramid as a temple and the courtyard as a possible residence for a local ruler. He acknowledges this is conjecture drawn from a long conversation with the agents. For further context, the author points to earlier lidar work in the region, including a 2024 discovery of a Maya city in Mexico by Auld-Thomas and colleagues and a 2025 study by Estrada-Belli and colleagues estimating population in the Maya lowlands. Whether the site is confirmed, and whether INAH sends a team to verify it, are still open questions the articles do not answer.

Articles.Title: Google SWE points 48 AI agents at NASA Lidar, finds unmapped Maya pyramid in 72h

stories.Headline: Suno AI Music Review 2026: Can Artificial Intelligence Create Professional Songs and Music Videos?
stories.Summary:
Suno, a platform that generates complete songs from written prompts, has been reviewed in an article published on November 11, 2026, by Rebellion Research. The piece asks whether artificial intelligence can create professional songs and music videos. It describes Suno as one of the most recognizable platforms for this purpose. Unlike earlier systems that produced only instrumental loops or short samples, Suno can generate structured compositions with vocals, lyrics, melodies and instrumental arrangements. The article frames the question as one about whether these tools can replace traditional workflows or simply add new creative options.

Users describe a genre, mood, instrumentation, vocal style or lyrical theme, and the platform generates audio from those instructions. The article's examples include an atmospheric electronic piece with piano and synthesizers, and an energetic rock song with distorted guitars. The technology learns statistical relationships among musical structures, vocal traits and audio patterns, so users guide results through text and revisions rather than arranging instruments by hand. The article says this lowers technical barriers that traditionally required musicians, studio equipment, mixing software and production experience. It also cautions that accessibility does not guarantee artistic consistency, since outputs can have repetitive lyrics, unnatural phrasing or weak vocal delivery.

The article credits Suno with making complete compositions accessible to a broader audience, and says it can speed experimentation for independent creators. It lists strengths such as generating songs from descriptions, producing vocals and lyrics, supporting many styles and offering alternative arrangements. Limitations include the need for repeated revisions and unpredictable links between prompts and output. The article also notes unresolved questions about copyright, training data, licensing and commercial rights, which matter to creators who plan to earn money from their work. It adds that a technically impressive song differs from a commercially successful musical identity.

Finally, the article says that Suno's commercial rights and licensing terms are matters creators should check, rather than assume. Music distribution increasingly depends on visual presentation on platforms such as YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, according to the article. It says a song paired with a static image may struggle for attention against content with movement or narrative. Traditional videos require locations, cameras, performers, editing software and sizable budgets, while generative video systems can create visual sequences from text prompts and reference images. The article notes that building a coherent music video is harder than producing isolated clips, because it requires visual continuity, consistent characters, synchronization with song structure and a complementary aesthetic.

It describes Enkio as a platform designed for that purpose. Enkio's workflow, as described, lets users supply an existing audio track, including a Suno track, and build a video with reference images, visual prompts and scene-level review. According to the article, Enkio's actual output quality, rendering consistency, pricing and reliability require independent testing before performance claims can be established. The article also states that compatibility with Suno audio should not be taken as evidence of an official commercial partnership. It identifies character consistency, synchronization and long-form narrative coherence as the main technical challenges for AI video.

The article argues generative AI could cut costs for independent musicians and digital creators, and that human creative direction remains important. It points to record labels, advertising agencies, social media companies and digital content businesses as parties with incentives to reduce production costs. The article warns that cheaper production may intensify competition for attention, making distribution, originality, branding and intellectual property management more important. The article's final assessment is that Suno is a compelling option for experimenting with AI music, while creators seeking full multimedia productions may need additional tools for visuals, editing and distribution. It says Enkio illustrates how specialized video tools could complement AI music generators, though their comparative capabilities should be tested directly.

It concludes that the key development is the emergence of interconnected AI production workflows. The article leaves open the outcomes of copyright and licensing disputes, the sustainability of revenue for these companies, and how audiences will respond to abundant AI-generated content. It also leaves open how well Enkio and similar tools will perform in practice. Sources cited include the U.S. Copyright Office, the Recording Industry Association of America, YouTube and the companies' own websites.

Articles.Title: Suno AI Music Review 2026: Can Artificial Intelligence Create Professional Songs and Music Videos?

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Cellular Immunotherapies Across Diverse Autoimmune Disease Models
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is being applied to cell-based immunotherapies for autoimmune disease, according to a comprehensive review of computational engineering and cellular immunology published on bioengineer.org on November 11, 2026. The review covers systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and inflammatory bowel disease, which all arise from a breakdown in immune tolerance. Conventional drugs, including broad immunosuppressives, systemic corticosteroids, and biological agents, control acute symptoms but often fail to restore lasting balance between protective and autoreactive immune pathways. They also cause systemic toxicities and leave patients more vulnerable to opportunistic infections. Therapists seek longer remissions by recalibrating immune tolerance while preserving protection against microbial pathogens.

The review describes machine learning as a way to decode cellular heterogeneity, streamline clinical manufacturing, and guide personalized treatment across autoimmune conditions. It identifies three functional roles for artificial intelligence in regenerative immunotherapy, linking molecular observations to clinical delivery. Algorithms first detect subtle cell states and pathogenic subsets that manual classification misses. Computational pipelines then optimize the expansion, characterization, and quality validation of cell products such as mesenchymal stem cells, engineered regulatory T cells, and induced pluripotent stem cell derivatives. Predictive models finally assess donor potency, estimate flare-up risk, and anticipate therapy-induced immune toxicities.

The review's authors are not named in the material provided, and it does not attribute specific statements to individual researchers. The article presents the framework as a systematic, data-driven replacement for empirical therapeutic selection. It frames these tools as a way to tailor interventions to each patient's immune profile across different autoimmune pathologies. The material does not quote any researcher or describe any response from clinicians, regulators, or patients. Patients with the listed autoimmune diseases are the population the review addresses, along with clinicians and manufacturers of cell-based products.

The review describes CD19-directed CAR-T cells as having induced sustained remissions in fifteen patients with severe systemic lupus erythematosus, idiopathic inflammatory myositis, and systemic sclerosis. Complete B-cell aplasia in those patients lasted an average of 112 days after a single infusion. A separate small series of five patients with treatment-resistant systemic lupus erythematosus showed persistent improvement and autoantibody clearance. The article notes that remission persisted even after naive B cells returned. The review explains that artificial intelligence was adopted in these fields because of known problems with cell therapy.

Persistent antigen exposure in inflamed tissue can exhaust T cells, and cytokine release syndrome poses clinical risk. Mesenchymal stem cells face donor heterogeneity, batch-to-batch variability, and replicative senescence during expansion.
