stories.Headline: Meta Loses 17-Year Infrastructure Veteran Amid AI Buildout
stories.Summary:
Meta is losing Santosh Janardhan, its longtime head of infrastructure, according to a TechBuzz report dated November 11, 2026. He has steered the company's compute operations since 2009 and is stepping down during a critical period of AI expansion. His exit is the second major finance and operations leadership departure in recent weeks, following former CSO Dave Wehner's move to AI startup Fireworks. The departure comes as Meta spends heavily on AI infrastructure and data centers to power its generative AI ambitions. Meta has not announced a replacement and declined to provide details about Janardhan's next moves or the transition timeline.

Janardhan joined the company when it was still Facebook in 2009 and served as head of infrastructure for 17 years. The role oversees server farms, data centers, and custom silicon that runs Meta's AI models, along with keeping billions of users online. CEO Mark Zuckerberg has committed to spending upwards of $37 billion on data centers and compute resources this year. Meta has been building clusters of Nvidia H100 GPUs by the tens of thousands, constructing new data centers quickly, and developing custom chips to reduce dependence on external suppliers. Training large language models requires coordinating GPU clusters, cooling systems, and megawatt-scale power infrastructure.

The article reports that Dave Wehner, Meta's longtime chief strategy officer and former CFO, recently left to become CFO of AI infrastructure startup Fireworks. Janardhan's departure comes within weeks of Wehner's exit, which the article says raised questions about whether top talent sees better opportunities at AI startups. The article describes Janardhan as the architect behind much of Meta's recent infrastructure expansion. The article does not include a direct statement from Janardhan or from Meta about the reasons for his departure. Meta's infrastructure leadership role is described as increasingly strategic as AI workloads consume more compute.

The departure affects Meta's platforms, which serve nearly 4 billion people across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads, as well as the company's AI plans. The article says Meta has warned that community opposition to data center construction could derail those plans. The leadership change also raises concerns among investors about whether senior leaders are seeking opportunities beyond Meta. Competitors including CoreWeave, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google are building out their own AI infrastructure. The article also notes that eBay has blocked Meta's AI shopping agents, which adds to the infrastructure team's challenges.

Janardhan led Meta's infrastructure through a six-hour outage in October 2021 that took all of the company's services offline. That outage cost Meta an estimated $100 million in lost revenue, according to the article. Over his tenure, Facebook evolved from a college social network into a global platform. Meta has recently rolled out Muse with voice capabilities and expressive avatars, which add strain to infrastructure systems. The article also notes that Meta has been racing to catch up with OpenAI and Google in generative AI.

Meta has not named a successor, and the search for a new infrastructure chief will be closely watched. The article says whoever takes the role will inherit responsibility for keeping Meta's social platforms running while building the foundation for its AI future. It is unclear from the article whether Janardhan's exit signals a broader trend of senior departures. The article also leaves open when the transition will occur and where Janardhan will go next. Whether Meta can retain top technical talent as AI startups offer equity upside remains an open question.

Articles.Title: Meta Loses 17-Year Infrastructure Veteran Amid AI Buildout

stories.Headline: Meta (NASDAQ: META) Ember Enters AI Price War At A Third Of Rivals’ Cost
stories.Summary:
Meta has released a new artificial intelligence model called Ember, which is aimed at the budget tier of the AI market. According to the article published on November 11, 2026, Ember costs roughly one-third what similar lightweight models charge, and in some cases less, while promising faster response times than many direct competitors. The model is positioned against ChatGPT's Luna and Anthropic's Haiku, both of which have established user bases. Ember is designed to handle roughly 90% of what the most sophisticated frontier models can do.

Meta is pursuing a two-track product strategy, since it is separately trying to compete at the high end against models named Fable 5.2 and GPT 6 Astra. The article says Ember suits repetitive, routine tasks where the value lies in automation rather than complex reasoning. Meta's broader goal, which the company has pursued for years, is to lower model costs so that AI tools reach as many people as possible. The company previously tried to pursue that goal through open-source releases, a strategy analysts say never fully delivered on its promise.

The article attributes the launch to Meta, whose Ember model is presented as a shift from that earlier approach toward balancing capability with low operating costs. Yahoo Finance's Ejaaz Ahamadeen is cited as saying that Muse was the first Meta AI product he found himself returning to daily, a change from earlier releases he found underwhelming. The article does not give a direct statement from Meta about Ember's pricing or rollout beyond the company's stated philosophy. It does not say how many users Ember has gained so far.

Context in the article points to a sobering adoption picture, with a recent report indicating that fewer than 5% of people use AI models for anything beyond a basic internet search. Analysts suggest that even among early adopters, only around 10 to 20% are likely to download and experiment with new AI applications. The article says Apple's anticipated updated Siri AI, expected to reach approximately 3.5 billion active devices, could dramatically shift those numbers. It also notes that Meta holds a significant advantage in personal social data, while enterprise-focused tools like Dots are seen as better positioned in productivity.

Articles.Title: Meta (NASDAQ: META) Ember Enters AI Price War At A Third Of Rivals’ Cost

stories.Headline: From infidelity to in-jokes: Jensen Huang affair sparks AI meme wave
stories.Summary:
AI-generated videos and memes pairing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom media reports identify as the other woman, have spread widely online after Huang admitted to infidelity. The article, published on November 11, 2026, says the parodies appeared on Wednesday and draw on a viral clip from a Coldplay concert near Boston in July 2025. In that clip, the stadium's big screen showed the CEO of the software company Astronomer embracing a female executive before the two pulled apart and hid their faces. Online users have also made videos set to the K-pop song "Trouble Maker" and a parody of the elevator scene from the film "(500) Days of Summer," which some call "500 Days of Chip." Puns linking "chip" to a Korean word for a mistress are also circulating.

Huang wrote in an email to Nvidia employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife, though the email did not name the woman. The article ties the online attention to a more serious matter, reporting that U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was passing information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times on October 29. Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation to examine whether national security or company secrets were compromised, though it said it has no reason to believe either was. On Tuesday, the board's independent members hired former federal prosecutor Joon H. Kim to lead that inquiry.

The articles frame the memes as a sign of how the affair has become internet entertainment, while the investigation sits behind them. The reporting notes that Korean chipmakers are assessing whether leadership uncertainty at Nvidia could affect their ties with one of their biggest AI-chip customers. The article describes the spy allegations as part of a wider push for tougher U.S. chip curbs on China. Beyond the board's inquiry, the article does not say what the investigation will conclude or when results will be released.

Articles.Title: From infidelity to in-jokes: Jensen Huang affair sparks AI meme wave

stories.Headline: When AI were asked in Japanese about the ‘forced mobilization of comfort women,’ only 56.3% answered “Yes”… compared with 94.9% in Korean
stories.Summary:
When AI models were asked in Japanese whether Japanese military comfort women were mobilized by force, only 56.3% answered yes, according to an analysis by data-tech company Bigvalue's co-CEO Gu Reum dated the 11th. In Korean the share was 94.9%, while in English it was 92.2% and in Chinese 95.2%. The analysis, titled "How Do Language Models Answer on Korea's History, Territory, and Culture," put 50 questions to 27 AI models from 12 developers. Each question was posed 10 times in four languages, and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 was used to judge how closely the answers matched Korea's position.

The same pattern appeared on a second question about whether Koreans conscripted during the colonial period performed forced labor. Affirmative answers were 97.0% in Korean, 93.7% in English and 94.0% in Chinese, but only 54.8% in Japanese. In Japanese, 40.7% of answers on the comfort women question and 41.1% on the labor question gave no clear determination, citing diverse views or divided opinion. Anthropic's Claude and Google's Gemini mostly recognized forced mobilization in Korean but often gave different answers in Japanese. OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Astra and GPT-5.6.1 Terra, Korea's Upstage Solar Mini4 and China's Alibaba Qwen3 235B affirmed forced mobilization in both languages.

Gu Reum said the analysis examined how AI answers contested questions and tested whether a country's language datasets influence those answers. The analysis suggests that Japanese-language training datasets may substantially reflect Japan's perspective on Korea-Japan issues. AI developers and operators do not disclose which sources they use or how they train their models. Gu warned that foreigners may ask AI many questions about Korea, so wrong or differing facts must be prevented from being conveyed depending on the language.

Gu also said it is important for Korea's large language models to learn data consistent with Korea's position. National-level efforts are needed so that foreign models can learn high-quality datasets that faithfully capture Korea's history and culture. Some argue that the government should build foreign-language datasets that properly include information about Korea and release them openly, so foreign AI can be guided toward accurate answers. Concern also exists that incorrect AI answers about Korea's historical issues could spread as if they were facts and influence public perception as AI use grows worldwide. Korea, a latecomer to AI compared with the United States and China, is developing a national flagship AI model, and the industry finds high-quality Korean-language datasets difficult to obtain.

The articles do not establish whether the gaps reflect deliberate bias or how the datasets were actually constructed. They also do not say whether the AI developers have responded to the findings or plan changes to their models. The government's specific plans for building and releasing foreign-language datasets are not detailed, and the articles do not say whether any such effort has begun. The analysis's full detailed findings are available through a link the article points readers to.

Articles.Title: When AI were asked in Japanese about the ‘forced mobilization of comfort women,’ only 56.3% answered “Yes”… compared with 94.9% in Korean

stories.Headline: AI glass technology puts Korea's exam supervisors to test ahead of CSAT
stories.Summary:
Authorities in South Korea are preparing staff to spot AI-powered smart glasses ahead of the College Scholastic Ability Test, or CSAT, scheduled for November 19. The Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education said on Wednesday it will train 239 personnel to detect the devices at the city's 228 exam sites. Concern has grown after recent incidents at school exams and university admissions essay tests suggested the glasses could be used for cheating. The Ministry of Education has said it is considering radio-frequency detectors for next year, but none will be supplied for this year's exam.

The ministry plans to assign one staff member to each of the 1,312 test sites nationwide to identify smart glasses. Under the procedures, a supervisor who suspects a student of wearing them before the exam can ask the student to remove them and place them on the desk, and the designated staffer will inspect them and refer unresolved cases to education authorities. Suspicions that arise during a session will be checked after it ends. All electronic devices, including AI glasses, phones, smartwatches and Bluetooth earbuds, are banned at test sites. Possessing AI glasses will invalidate a student's results, and wearing them during the exam will bring a ban from the following year's CSAT.

Choi Hong-won, an official at the Seoul office, said the city has examined different products and prepared training materials for supervisors. Teachers have voiced doubts about the measures. One high school teacher in Cheongju said visual checks could miss discreet devices and that metal detectors may be triggered by ordinary eyeglass frames. A poll released last month by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union found that 82.3 percent of middle and high school teachers surveyed said it would be difficult to identify students wearing smart glasses under the current procedures. The ministry said it would consider criminal complaints over AI-glasses cheating and seek a legal change that would extend the CSAT ban for cheating from one year to three.

Articles.Title: AI glass technology puts Korea's exam supervisors to test ahead of CSAT

stories.Headline: AI glasses solve 4 CSAT math questions in 10 seconds
stories.Summary:
AI glasses solved four mock CSAT math questions in under 10 seconds during a brief demonstration at an optical store in Seoul's Myeong-dong shopping area, according to a Korea Times report by Jung Min-ho published on November 11, 2026. The reporter tested Rokid AI glasses on a page of four math questions and saw correct answers and explanations appear in the lenses before he had finished reading the first problem. A separate calculus question involving a definite integral was answered in under two seconds. The test was described as brief and uncontrolled rather than a formal accuracy check.

The concern centers on the College Scholastic Ability Test, which is scheduled for November 19. Data from the Human Resources Development Service of Korea, disclosed in October during a parliamentary audit, showed five cases of AI smart glasses detected at state-run qualification examinations this year. Four of those involved Chinese-manufactured Rokid products, and one involved glasses from the U.S. company Meta. The Rokid glasses use a camera to capture questions, display AI-generated answers through the lenses, and connect to a smartphone, while retailing for 999,000 won in Korea.

One rental service advertises rates as low as 9,900 won a day, making access easier than buying a pair outright. The reporter also tested Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which had no display and instead spoke replies through built-in speakers, a method he judged more conspicuous. He noted that Meta's display-equipped model is not officially sold in Korea. The Rokid glasses showed limitations during his trial, sometimes saying they could not see the question clearly and at other times stopping responses.

He said he did not test whether instructions could persist over a long period or how long the battery would last under repeated use. He added that the glasses' thicker frames and visible lens reflection might give a user away, though spotting those features in a crowded exam room could be harder than in a shop. The reporter concluded that his brief trial did not prove the glasses could get a cheater through an exam undetected, but it showed how quickly they could deliver correct answers. The article indicates that exam authorities face a difficult task in detecting such devices before the November 19 test.

Articles.Title: AI glasses solve 4 CSAT math questions in 10 seconds

stories.Headline: “Not AI manipulation” ‘First hearing’ Kim Se-Eui claims ‘not guilty’ while requesting bail
stories.Summary:
Kim Se-Eui, head of the Garosero Research Institute, appeared at the first hearing of his trial at the Seoul Central District Court on November 11, 2026, where he denied the charges against him. The 26th Criminal Division, presided over by Judge Lee Hyun-Gyeong, heard the case, which concerns defamation under the Information and Communications Network Act and violations of the Act on the Punishment of Sexual Crimes. Kim had been detained and indicted before the hearing. The witness examination of Kim Su-Hyun was held as a closed session to protect the victim's privacy, and spectators were asked to leave before it proceeded.

At the hearing, Kim's attorney said the charges were all denied and that the alleged facts were not false. Kim also argued that a voice recording of the late Kim Sae-Ron, which he had previously released through a press conference and YouTube live broadcasts, was not AI manipulation. He pointed to an analysis report from a Korea University Forensic Center professor, submitted in October, which dated the audio file's creation to two months before his broadcast and one month before Kim Sae-Ron's death. Kim further requested bail, saying the detention warrant's AI manipulation claims were left out of the indictment and that the charges changed the gist of his broadcast. He added that being in custody prevents him from searching materials or reporting, which he called unfair.

According to the article, Kim had claimed in March of the previous year that Kim Su-Hyun had continued a relationship with Kim Sae-Ron since her underage years. Kim Su-Hyun suspended his activities and, together with Kim Sae-Ron's bereaved family, filed a complaint against Kim Se-Eui for defamation. During the investigation, some audio files and materials Kim released were judged to have been manipulated, and he was ultimately detained and indicted on charges including defamation by alleging false facts. The article does not say when a verdict or the next hearing is expected.

Articles.Title: “Not AI manipulation” ‘First hearing’ Kim Se-Eui claims ‘not guilty’ while requesting bail

stories.Headline: SK Group's CEOs to convene to review AI push, align chip and energy businesses
stories.Summary:
SK Group will hold a three-day CEO seminar at its Management System office in Icheon, Gyeonggi, running from Thursday through Saturday, according to industry sources cited on Wednesday. Around 50 CEOs from the group's major affiliates are expected to attend, with the meeting aimed at setting a groupwide AI strategy. The seminar is likely to be presided over by Chairman Chey Tae-won. Executive Vice Chairman Chey Jae-won and SK Supex Council Chairman Chey Chang-won are also scheduled to take part, along with the CEOs named in last month's executive reshuffle.

The central theme is how the group's affiliates can combine their strengths in semiconductors, data centers and energy infrastructure. The agenda is expected to range from SK hynix's memory chip operations and SK Telecom's push into AI data centers to SK Innovation's work on energy infrastructure. Data centers could tie these businesses together, since they need advanced chips, a steady electricity supply and cooling systems. Executives are expected to review how far each affiliate has progressed on AI projects since the most recent New Icheon Forum, and to decide which investments should take priority and which company should lead each project. The meeting will also touch on the group's three-year restructuring drive, including this year's moves to sell SK Corp.'s stake in SK Siltron and merge SK ie technology with SK Innovation.

The seminar is an annual event held each November, and it is one of the group's most important strategy gatherings alongside the June forum. Chairman Chey stressed in September, during a visit to SK Innovation's Ulsan CLX complex, that the affiliates must pool their abilities to meet the challenges of the AI era. Outside speakers, including Kim Dong-shin, CEO of AI communications company Sendbird, are set to address the gathering. Changes in U.S. policy after Democrats took control of Congress in the midterm results could also shape the agenda, since they might affect AI regulations, data center rules and SK Group's U.S. business plans.

Newly appointed CEOs, including incoming SK Innovation chief Cheong Seung-il, are expected to present their strategic priorities for 2027 at the meeting. Their plans for capital allocation and management after the restructuring are expected to draw particular attention. The discussions will also examine how the reshaped businesses can generate stronger profits and better returns on investment. The articles do not say what decisions, if any, will be announced once the seminar ends.

Articles.Title: SK Group's CEOs to convene to review AI push, align chip and energy businesses

stories.Headline: Nvidia shareholders sue Huang over affair | Why AI isn't taking over audiobooks just yet
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shareholders filed a class-action lawsuit on Monday, November 10, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, naming CEO Jensen Huang and the company as defendants. The suit followed a day after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. The plaintiffs say the chipmaker's stock dropped after the affair and the potential national security risks tied to the woman's former employer, Singapore-based Megaspeed, came to light. They accuse Huang and Nvidia of violating federal securities law and are seeking compensation for heavy losses. On the same day, Nvidia shares fell 4.27 percent on the New York Stock Exchange, wiping out $192.1 billion in market value.

The lawsuit is a direct consequence of that market drop, and its claims center on the securities law that governs what companies must disclose to investors. The plaintiffs argue that the revelations about Alice Huang and Megaspeed were material enough to move the stock, though the article does not describe any specific disclosures that were withheld. The case is still at the filing stage, so no court has ruled on its merits. The article describes the situation as a crisis that is beginning to loosen Huang's grip on the world's most valuable chipmaker. It does not report any response from Huang or Nvidia to the suit.

The lawsuit names Huang personally as well as the company, and the plaintiffs' core argument is that the affair and its national security implications concealed risks that affected the share price. The article presents these as the allegations of the shareholders rather than established facts. Readers should note that the affair itself was described as an admission by Huang, and that the suspicion of Chinese espionage concerns the woman involved rather than any proven conduct by the company. The article does not say how Nvidia's board has reacted or whether any other legal action is planned.

Beyond the lawsuit, the article is part of a wider run of Nvidia coverage in the Korea JoongAng Daily, which reported Huang's admission in an earlier edition. The article does not say what comes next in the litigation or whether additional shareholders will join the suit. Given the size of the market loss, further legal and investor action is possible, but the article itself does not report that. Its context is the broader scrutiny of the chipmaker's leadership and its ties to China-linked business.

Articles.Title: Nvidia shareholders sue Huang over affair | Why AI isn't taking over audiobooks just yet

stories.Headline: Seoul warns crypto heists pose wider global security risks in AI era
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Vice Foreign Minister for Strategy and Intelligence, Jeong Yeon-doo, warned on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that recent cryptocurrency thefts carry significant international security implications. He spoke at a cybersecurity conference co-hosted by South Korea and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe at the OSCE headquarters in Vienna. The remarks came after North Korea was accused late last month of stealing more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from the exchange Binance. According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Jeong said such incidents go beyond ordinary cybercrime and touch on wider security concerns.

Jeong called for a wholesale overhaul of the cybersecurity paradigm to suit the AI era, since AI-driven cyberattacks could unfold at an unprecedented pace and scale. He also stressed that security in the Indo-Pacific region and Europe is interconnected, and he underlined the importance of bilateral cooperation. The conference drew about 100 attendees, including representatives from Japan, Australia, Thailand, Afghanistan and Qatar, along with cybersecurity experts and officials from relevant international organizations. The Seoul government has held the conference annually since 2017 to discuss responses to transnational security challenges.

The ministry's account, as reported by Yonhap and the JoongAng Ilbo, attributes the warning to Jeong and presents it as the government's position. The article does not describe any formal response or new measures that Seoul has announced beyond the call for a broader approach. It also does not provide further detail on the Binance theft or on the basis for the accusation against North Korea. Those points are reported as background rather than as developments from the conference itself.

Articles.Title: Seoul warns crypto heists pose wider global security risks in AI era

stories.Headline: [Graphic News] S. Korea ranks 12th in global AI adoption
stories.Summary:
South Korea's generative AI adoption rate reached 40.6 percent in the second quarter, up 3.5 percentage points from the previous quarter, lifting the country four places to 12th globally. The figures were measured by Microsoft's AI Economy Institute, which tracked the share of people aged 15 to 64 using AI products. South Korea recorded the largest increase among major economies for the third straight quarter. Its adoption rate was also 15 percentage points higher than a year earlier. The Herald report was published on November 12, 2026.

The United Arab Emirates led the rankings at 73.3 percent, followed by Singapore at 64.3 percent, with Ireland and France also placed above South Korea. Globally, the adoption rate rose to 18.8 percent from 17.8 percent in the previous quarter. Adoption stood at 28.8 percent in the advanced Global North, compared with 16.2 percent in the emerging Global South. The gap shows how unevenly the technology has spread across economies.

The article also described differences in how people use AI, depending on where they live. Users in the Global South were more focused on learning and building skills, while users in the Global North more often turned to AI for shopping, searching for information and seeking feedback. The article was written by Nam Kyung-don of The Korea Herald. It did not say what policies or targets, if any, South Korea has set in response to the ranking.

Articles.Title: [Graphic News] S. Korea ranks 12th in global AI adoption

stories.Headline: From hidden notes to AI glasses, cheating takes new forms
stories.Summary:
Cheating on exams has long been a problem in Korea, but the tools used have changed over time. Records from the Joseon Dynasty show that civil service candidates tried irregular methods, including swapping names on exam papers. In 2004, students in Gwangju used text messages to pass answers during the college entrance exam, and the scores of 472 students were later invalidated across the 2002 to 2005 academic years. Today the newest concern is artificial intelligence-powered smart glasses, which have been caught in use at several testing sites.

Recent cases include two people caught wearing AI-enabled glasses during TOEIC English-language tests in May, and three candidates caught at national technical qualification exams in Seoul, Gwangju and Mokpo. A survey from the education ministry found four cases involving smart glasses in middle and high school exams this year, one at a middle school and three at high schools. The survey covered 5,679 schools nationwide. Ahead of the College Scholastic Ability Test on Nov. 19, smart glasses, smartwatches and other electronic devices will be prohibited at test centers, and wearing them will lead to the invalidation of the student's score and a ban from taking next year's exam.

The education ministry is responsible for the rules, and a ministry official said the problem cannot be handled by the ministry alone. The official said agencies overseeing medical licensing and technical qualification exams also need to address it. Officials are looking for ways to detect smart glasses electronically but have not yet found a reliable method. A separate tally of 1,229 cheating violations over the past five years was also reported, though many involved writing answers after time was called rather than using electronic devices.

Articles.Title: From hidden notes to AI glasses, cheating takes new forms

stories.Headline: Korean firms shift CES focus to industrial AI
stories.Summary:
Korean technology and automotive companies are preparing to make industrial artificial intelligence a central theme at CES 2027, the annual consumer technology fair in Las Vegas organized by the Consumer Technology Association. Reporting by the Korea Times, published on November 11, 2026, describes a shift away from the event's traditional focus on consumer electronics toward AI applications in semiconductors, robotics, batteries and autonomous driving. The companies named include Samsung Electronics, the LG affiliates and Kia under Hyundai Motor Group, each planning to show AI technologies that have a clearer route to commercial use. Kinsey Fabrizio, the association's president and chief executive, spoke about the fair at a press conference in Seoul on October 14.

Samsung's semiconductor division has already won several CES 2027 Innovation Awards for memory products, including UFS 5.0, a next-generation storage solution designed for AI workloads. The company is also expected to highlight robotics, which it has identified as a possible new growth engine, and it may expand from industrial robots into household and service robots. Executive Chairman Lee Jae-yong recently spent about three hours at the Seoul R&D Campus reviewing the robotics business, examining robotic arms and hands built for precise manipulation. That review has fueled speculation that Samsung could present more detailed robotics plans at the fair. LG Energy Solution won an award in the advanced mobility category for Re.Pulse, an AI-powered diagnostic system that cuts battery assessment from more than seven hours to under 10 minutes.

Kia plans to place its strategic focus on autonomous driving through Motional, the group's U.S. self-driving subsidiary, with robotaxi operations in Las Vegas as the centerpiece. Hyundai Motor Group currently runs IONIQ 5 robotaxis there with safety drivers on board and plans to move to fully driverless operations by the end of the year. An industry official quoted in the article said the event will be an important test of whether the group can show the market it is closing a technology gap with leaders such as Tesla, which the group has faced growing criticism for trailing. The article frames the shift as a broader push by Korean firms to demonstrate AI technologies that can reach commercialization. Details of the exhibits themselves are still forthcoming as the January event approaches.

Articles.Title: Korean firms shift CES focus to industrial AI

stories.Headline: Singapore start-up Sapiens cracks AI training bottleneck, makes waves overseas
stories.Summary:
Singapore artificial intelligence start-up Sapiens Technology says it has cut robotics AI training from months to as little as 30 minutes. The firm, led by chief executive Bruce Yang and co-founder Alex Ang, has done this by training only one billion to three billion parameters rather than an entire model. The article, published on November 11, 2026, reports that the company is in talks with more than 30 robotics and medical firms across the United States, China and Singapore. Those potential customers include TetraBOT Electronic Technology and Shanghai Xinwei Medical Technology.

The method can train machines in anywhere from 30 minutes to less than a week, far shorter than the weeks to months usually needed for a robotics application. In experiments, Sapiens used commercial robotic arms and off-the-shelf robot ducks to pick up objects. Once trained, a robot can adapt to changes in its tasks and follow text prompts for variations without detailed coding. Yang said the training and reasoning of the robot can be audited, and a custom delay between planning and acting lets humans or monitoring systems halt unintended behaviour. The technique works with all AI models, including Sapiens' own Agnes AI developed in Singapore.

Yang described the approach as a way to shorten the time it takes to adapt AI for different industries and situations. TetraBOT, which had earlier tested the technique, is now planning to train more of its industrial robots that operate switches and knobs in electrical substations. The company had spent two months on a traditional training method without the robots performing the required tasks. A TetraBOT spokesman said the collaboration aims to move robots beyond pre-defined actions toward understanding their surroundings and carrying out complex operations. Shanghai Xinwei Medical Technology, a medical implants maker, is working with Sapiens to forecast inventory gaps using custom models built on industry data.

Articles.Title: Singapore start-up Sapiens cracks AI training bottleneck, makes waves overseas

stories.Headline: As JET Programme turns 40, alumni and ministers stress its importance in age of AI
stories.Summary:
The Japan Exchange and Teaching Programme, known as JET, marked its 40th year this month, four decades after it began as a way to bring foreign teachers into Japanese classrooms and communities. The program was launched in 1987 to promote foreign-language education and grassroots cultural exchange, starting with 848 participants from four countries. It has since grown into one of the world's largest international exchange programs. The anniversary was marked by Japan's government, which celebrated the milestone alongside former participants.

Participants have faced new pressure in recent years, according to the article. Demand for translation work has dropped as artificial intelligence spreads, and a weak yen has made Japan a less appealing destination for prospective participants. Those trends are the main challenges the program now faces as it moves into its next decade. Alumni and ministers have stressed the program's importance in an age of AI, arguing its value lies in the human exchange it fosters. Peter Cave, who joined the inaugural cohort in 1987 and taught for three years in Omihachiman, Shiga Prefecture, is among the alumni who have spoken about the program's legacy.

The article attributes the call for renewed emphasis on the program to ministers and to former participants, whose views are paraphrased here rather than quoted in full. The article does not provide further detail on specific policy changes, funding decisions or numbers of current participants. It also does not describe any formal plan for how the program will respond to the pressures it faces. The piece was written by staff writer Jessica Speed and published by The Japan Times on November 11, 2026.

Articles.Title: As JET Programme turns 40, alumni and ministers stress its importance in age of AI

stories.Headline: Singapore's Sea targets AI boom with asset-light cloud services push
stories.Summary:
Singapore-based Sea announced on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that it plans to enter the cloud services business. The company is seeking to tap rising demand driven by artificial intelligence while taking a cautious approach to spending. According to the article, Sea said it has spent the past two years applying AI across its businesses. The move is framed as an asset-light push, meaning the company is avoiding heavy infrastructure investment. The article's key point is that Sea intends to pursue this opportunity without committing large sums to physical infrastructure.

It also mentions that the company is exploring an initial public offering for a unit called Monee. The article does not provide figures for the planned investment, the scale of the cloud offering, or a timeline for launch. Readers are left without details on pricing, target customers, or specific partners. The article attributes the announcement to Sea itself, with reporting by Kentaro Takeda of Nikkei Asia. Sea's own statements about its two years of AI work and its cautious investment stance are presented as the basis for the report.

The article does not include any additional comment from analysts or competitors. Its account of the company's intentions rests on what Sea communicated publicly. The piece sits within Nikkei Asia's broader coverage of AI-driven demand across Asia, which the site links to in related stories about data center regulation in Thailand, Google's investment in Malaysia's data center expansion, and the wider AI supply chain. The article does not say what Sea will do next beyond the stated plans. Further announcements on the cloud business or the Monee listing would be needed to clarify the company's direction.

Articles.Title: Singapore's Sea targets AI boom with asset-light cloud services push

stories.Headline: How AI powers Hong Kong Baptist University professors’ research to benefit society
stories.Summary:
Two researchers at Hong Kong Baptist University have won funding from the Research Grants Council to apply artificial intelligence to problems in neuroscience and urban sustainability. The work, reported on November 11, 2026, pairs data-driven computation and AI with traditional scientific principles. The projects target how the human brain works and the growing urban threat from extreme temperatures and air pollution. The articles describe the researchers' goals but do not give a detailed timeline for results.

Chair professor Zhou Changsong, of the physics department, is building prediction models that show how brain regions work together for memory, language and decision-making. His goal is to find early biomarkers of abnormal ageing and neurodegenerative disease, along with automated tools to monitor prevention and treatment. He received about HK$7.8 million over five years from the council's Senior Research Fellow Scheme in its inaugural 2023-24 term. He says AI is needed to model complex, changing brain activity, but it must be combined with biological knowledge and medical reality to have clinical value. He hopes that within five years virtual brain mapping could help clinicians test neuromodulation therapies on individual patients.

Professor Gao Meng, an ecological engineer at the university's Academy of Geography, Sociology and International Studies, is working on heat and air pollution across cities in the Greater Bay Area. He will receive about HK$8.5 million over the next five years from the council's 2026-27 Senior Research Fellow Scheme. He is building a dynamic model that predicts how changes in transport and energy could reduce both extreme urban heat and air pollution. His team uses satellite and sensor data to produce neighbourhood-level heat and flood forecasts from global climate models. Gao warns that AI alone can produce physically impossible predictions, so his team fuses it with atmospheric physics to keep results accurate.

The Research Grants Council, a non-statutory advisory body under the University Grants Committee, is responsible for providing research funding in Hong Kong. The article says the researchers see interdisciplinary collaboration as increasingly important over the next decade, bringing together atmospheric science, physics, computer science, engineering and social sciences. Both researchers describe AI as a powerful tool that must be paired with established scientific knowledge. The articles do not report any outcome from the projects so far.

Articles.Title: How AI powers Hong Kong Baptist University professors’ research to benefit society

stories.Headline: Singapore’s accountancy sector adds jobs, raises pay as firms prepare workers for AI
stories.Summary:
Singapore's accountancy sector grew in 2025, adding 579 jobs and lifting median pay at every surveyed seniority level, according to the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority's Accounting Entities Survey 2026. The workforce rose 2.7%, from 21,783 in 2024 to 22,362 in 2025, while revenue increased 5.1% to about $3.7 billion. Accounting entities reported more than 1,200 job opportunities, around 80% of them in audit and assurance and business advisory services. The survey drew responses from 238 entities representing 92% of the sector's estimated revenue.

Acting Minister for Manpower Jasmin Lau, speaking at the Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants conference on November 11, said AI is taking over routine tasks such as reconciliations and first drafts, which had helped junior staff learn their craft. Firms must therefore find ways for young accountants to develop judgment, including a feel for when something does not look right. Lau said automation could make entry-level roles more interesting if graduates spend more time evaluating AI output, working with senior colleagues and meeting clients earlier. She added that this would take deliberate effort from employers in training staff and giving them real responsibility. Median monthly pay for first-year audit assistants rose from $3,000 to $3,400, and for first-year directors from $13,500 to $14,500.

Lau argued that accountants remain responsible for deciding whether AI-generated analysis makes sense, and that retaining experienced professionals matters as more workers care for young children and elderly parents. The Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants is piloting FlexConnect, which links experienced professionals seeking flexible arrangements with businesses needing temporary or specialist finance talent, and more than 100 professionals had registered interest since the pilot began in September. Ernst & Young and Nexia Singapore PAC received the Workforce Transformation Award for redesigning jobs and training staff in analytics and automation. Survey respondents named AI application, ethics and governance as their top workforce priority for the next three years, cited by 67%, and the institute signed a five-year agreement with all five polytechnics and the Institute of Technical Education to offer practical AI learning, internships and mentorship. Lau said the profession has adapted before, and its core duty of giving people confidence in the numbers remains unchanged.

Articles.Title: Singapore’s accountancy sector adds jobs, raises pay as firms prepare workers for AI

stories.Headline: Opinion | In US or China, firms need AI they can independently verify and trust
stories.Summary:
Opinion pieces of this kind rarely report a discrete event, so the story here is a commentary by Ruby Tong, a university innovator and technology strategist, published by the South China Morning Post on November 11, 2026. The piece opens with a market shock, in which the Magnificent Seven, America's leading technology companies, shed more than US$1 trillion in a single trading session. It notes that the usual question about whether artificial intelligence is a bubble has returned. Tong argues that this debate is already stale, as headlines focus on the personal and governance crises shaking Silicon Valley's biggest firms. The article is written as a call to action rather than a news report.

Tong's central claim is that multitrillion-dollar AI companies cannot rely on founder mythology and self-policing indefinitely. She argues the public is asking who bears the risk and who gets a say in how the technology is governed. The article links this to a commercial problem, saying banks, hospitals and factories refuse AI systems they cannot check and cannot trust. As a result, she writes, adoption is not merely slow but blocked.

The piece calls for AI labs to invite external audits and to accept binding commercial liability for their systems. It does not, in the excerpt provided, set out specific figures, dates or legal mechanisms beyond the trillion-dollar market loss. The author presents the demand for verifiable AI as a response to a gap between what the industry promises and what customers can confirm. Tong does not name specific executives or allegations in the excerpt, and her argument is directed at AI labs and the wider industry in general.

The article offers its position as an opinion and does not report a formal response from the companies it discusses. The excerpt does not say whether any regulator, company or government has adopted the audit or liability proposals. The context is a broader debate over whether AI firms should face the same external scrutiny and accountability expected of other critical industries. The articles provided do not describe what happens next, such as planned audits, policy moves or changes in corporate practice.

Articles.Title: Opinion | In US or China, firms need AI they can independently verify and trust

stories.Headline: Papon on AI in music: People will always crave what is human
stories.Summary:
Playback singer and composer Papon has said that artificial intelligence in music is only a passing phase, and that listeners will eventually tire of machine-made work and return to authentic art. Speaking by telephone to The Hindu ahead of his Bengaluru show, the singer, known for songs such as 'Jiyein Kyun' and 'Bulleya', said that AI is a useful tool but that it causes fear. He said he is not yet worried, because people want to see and hear a human performer. Papon argued that unless machines take over the planet, people will keep craving what is raw, impure and imperfect.

Papon also reflected on how social media algorithms and viral trends shape the way music is made, discovered and consumed. He said trends are not always lasting and that good music can be missed simply because it is not trending. He said it is frustrating for musicians making good work when they cannot present it in a way the internet favours. Despite these shifts, he said he continues to evolve, and his upcoming Bengaluru show, on November 14 at 7 pm at District Arena at Terraform in Yelahanka, will feature new songs and sounds. He said he has modernised certain sounds for today's audiences and that Gen Z is showing interest in folk music.

On the role of artistes in society, Papon said they should not all be expected to respond to social and political developments in the same way. He said some people express themselves through words while others do so through music, which he described as a way of healing and supporting people's mental well-being. He tied this to his own roots, saying that staying connected to Assam and its musical traditions has been important to him. He also said that not every musician from the Northeast needs to seek mainstream visibility, and he spoke of his own attachment to home. He added that he is working on new independent music that he hopes to release soon, with a different sound.

Articles.Title: Papon on AI in music: People will always crave what is human

stories.Headline: Prix Pascal: If AI writes your book, are you still a writer?
stories.Summary:
The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is a new French literary prize for AI-assisted writing, and the article by K. Srilata examines it. Entrants must submit an unpublished manuscript in French, fiction or non-fiction, of approximately 300,000 characters. Applications close on November 30, and ten finalists will be announced on December 4. The winner will be revealed on December 15.

The manuscript must be written with the help of large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. Writers must declare which AI model and which prompts they used. Each application consists of a seed, a manuscript and a technical file, submitted at the same time. The prize manifesto says the work must be useful, raise awareness, or help solve an ecological, social or ethical challenge in an original way. The prize was founded by Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré, and the article notes that the first two are technology entrepreneurs.

The article's author argues that the prize's manifesto reframes support for AI-written work as a moral act. She says the imagination is ungovernable and that introducing AI into the writer's world could colonise it. She also argues that AI use can gradually take over the writing itself, and that an original writer whose work trained an LLM receives nothing from the process. She adds that the loss of imagination affects students and life generally, not only creative writing courses.

The author describes her Creative Writing students at Shiv Nadar University, Chennai, who feared that, having come of age after AI, they would struggle to access their imagination. Among those affected she names writers, the editors of literary journals on the brink of closure, and writing teachers. The article also reports that editors and teachers find AI-assisted writing often impossible to tell apart from human writing. Detection tools produce false positives, especially for non-native English writers, and OpenAI discontinued its own detection tool in 2023 because of low accuracy.

The article refers to the 2026 controversy over Jamir Nazir's Granta-Commonwealth Short Story Prize entry, "The Serpent in the Grove." It also cites Éditions du Boréal, which last month said it had confirmed that Haitian-Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien used AI for his novel C'était ça ou mourir. The author says that claim rests on speculation. In her own experiment, ChatGPT produced a decent translation of a Tamil poem in seconds, though she had spent nearly two hours on her draft.

The article does not say whether the Prix Pascal will go ahead as planned or how many entries it will receive. It also does not say how the judges will assess the technical files or whether AI use will be disclosed beyond the required declaration. Whether the December finalists and winner will be publicly named, as scheduled, is not addressed beyond the announced dates. The article gives no response from the prize's founders.

Articles.Title: Prix Pascal: If AI writes your book, are you still a writer?

stories.Headline: ChatGPT Lockdown Mode Bypass: Phishing, Malware Delivery, and Silent Data Exfiltration
stories.Summary:
ChatGPT Lockdown Mode, an optional advanced security setting OpenAI introduced for logged-in users, contained a vulnerability that Check Point Research discovered and reported. The flaw let attackers bypass the mode and silently move chat data to an external server. Check Point Research published its findings on November 5, 2026, with research by Alexey Bukhteyev. Lockdown Mode was designed to cut off the channels through which prompt-injection attacks could send data out of a conversation. The vulnerability exposed a wide attack surface, enabling silent exfiltration of entire chat history, credential theft through phishing, and malware delivery.

In ChatGPT Classic, the attack needed no user interaction, since simply having a conversation was enough to trigger silent data exfiltration. Lockdown Mode restricts live web access to cached content, blocks loading of internet images, disables network requests from Canvas-generated code, and turns off Deep Research, Agent Mode, live connectors and file downloads. The flaw traced back to the HTML page preview feature OpenAI added to ChatGPT code blocks in February 2026. That preview ran inside a sandbox made of two nested iframes, which OpenAI intended to restrict external requests. The sandbox still carried the allow-popups and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox permissions.

Check Point Research found that a nested iframe could call its own window.open function, which opened a popup that escaped the sandbox entirely. Check Point Research disclosed the vulnerability to OpenAI, which told the researchers on September 18, 2026 that it had deployed a fix. The fix removed the two popup permissions from the outer HTML-preview sandbox iframe. Check Point Research later retested the issue and confirmed that the technique no longer worked. The researchers also wrote that the built-in security features of AI assistants offer no absolute guarantee of protection.

They advised users to weigh that risk before entrusting AI with sensitive information or full access to their computers. The articles say that the attack could be carried out through a malicious prompt, a malicious GPT or a shared chat, and that victims need not have an account. They describe a demonstration in which a malicious GPT silently leaked chat messages to an attacker-controlled server. The researchers also found that the flaw let an attacker reload content in the main ChatGPT window and forcibly sign a user out, which could lead to credential theft. Users of ChatGPT Classic were described as especially exposed, because they may perceive a popup as part of the trusted application.

Users who clicked content in shared chats faced the malware risk. The articles do not say how many users were affected or whether any attacks were seen in the wild. They also do not say whether OpenAI has commented further or when the fix reached every version of the product. More to follow.

Articles.Title: ChatGPT Lockdown Mode Bypass: Phishing, Malware Delivery, and Silent Data Exfiltration

stories.Headline: Adaptive Neural Subspaces with Geometry-Aware Quadrature for Interface Problems
stories.Summary:
The articles here are a single preprint abstract posted on Research Square, a platform where manuscripts appear before any journal peer review, with a timestamp of November 11, 2026. The preprint describes a new machine learning method for solving interface problems, which are mathematical problems involving boundaries where material properties change abruptly. The authors combine neural networks, numerical quadrature schemes, and adaptive subspace approximation, and they say the neural network is used to build the basis functions of a finite-dimensional subspace on which the discrete solution is then computed. They also say the method can handle singularities that arise at such interfaces when paired with high precision integration. The abstract reports that the approach achieves high accuracy in simulations, though it gives no specific figures.

The method includes an a posteriori error estimator derived from the hypercircle technique within the subspace approximation framework. According to the abstract, this estimator serves as the loss function used to adaptively refine the neural network parameters. The authors say the design of these loss functions depends on a high precision numerical integration scheme to reach the reported accuracy. The source does not provide the names of the authors, the institutions involved, the specific test problems, or any quantitative error comparisons against other methods.

The preprint lists no competing interests. Because it has not yet been peer reviewed by a journal, its claims about accuracy and singularity handling have not been independently checked. The articles do not say whether or when the work will be submitted to a journal or what follow-up the authors plan. Details on those points would need to come from the full text or from later publication.

Articles.Title: Adaptive Neural Subspaces with Geometry-Aware Quadrature for Interface Problems

stories.Headline: Incremental prognostic value of CT radiomics and deep learning beyond complete tumor volume in non-small cell lung cancer: a reanalysis of LUNG1
stories.Summary:
A reanalysis of the publicly available LUNG1 dataset, published in BMC Medical Imaging by Qiang Zhao, Shanwu Ma, F. Chen and colleagues, tested whether CT radiomics and deep learning add to survival prediction in non-small cell lung cancer beyond a simple measure of tumor volume. The team worked with 420 patients from the NSCLC-Radiomics collection, 372 of whom had died, and the work was shared early as an accepted, citable article before final typesetting. The study compared complete gross tumor volume alone, 107 radiomic features extracted from original images, a fixed pretrained 3D convolutional neural network, and a fusion of radiomic and deep learning features. Model evaluation used repeated five-fold cross-validation, with preprocessing and model fitting restricted to training patients to avoid data leakage.

The researchers also checked whether a fixed 96-millimeter cubic crop covered each tumor fully, and found that it cut off part of the tumor in 64 of the 420 patients. On the initial fold assignment, the mean concordance index was 0.585 for tumor volume, 0.567 for volume plus radiomics, 0.571 for clinical plus radiomics, 0.514 for the frozen network and 0.569 for fusion. Across 20 repetitions, the mean concordance index was 0.588 for volume alone, 0.577 for volume plus radiomics and 0.568 for fusion. The authors reported that the confidence intervals for the radiomics-minus-volume and fusion-minus-volume differences crossed zero, and that harmonizing scans across reconstruction kernels with ComBat in a 295-patient subset gave no clear improvement. A separate 46-patient cohort from NSCLC Radiogenomics, with 14 deaths, was too small for comparative validation.

The authors, affiliated with the Center for Precision Cancer Medicine and Translational Research at Tianjin Cancer Hospital Airport Hospital in Tianjin, China, concluded that in this cohort the complete-volume radiomic and fusion models did not show a stable gain in held-out survival prediction over complete tumor volume. They said their findings support measuring the full tumor contour, validating without leakage, and replicating the work in an independent, population-matched cohort. The study was funded by the China Association for Promotion of Health Science and Technology, and the authors declared no competing interests. The articles do not describe any planned follow-up study beyond that recommended replication.

Articles.Title: Incremental prognostic value of CT radiomics and deep learning beyond complete tumor volume in non-small cell lung cancer: a reanalysis of LUNG1

stories.Headline: Vals AI Joins Reconvened NIST Artificial Intelligence Consortium
stories.Summary:
Vals AI, an independent AI evaluation company based in San Francisco, announced on November 12, 2026, that it is joining the reconvened NIST Artificial Intelligence Consortium. The consortium operates within the National Institute of Standards and Technology, which sits inside the Department of Commerce in Washington, DC. Its stated purpose is to bring together members to build new measurement science, so that techniques and metrics for developing and using AI can be identified as proven, scalable, and interoperable. The announcement was made by the company itself, and the articles do not describe any separate statement from NIST beyond a link to its own announcement.

The consortium supports initiatives set out in the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 and America's AI Action Plan, which was published in 2025. Under this consortium, NIST does not evaluate commercial products and does not endorse any product or service that is used. The articles do not name any new obligations placed on companies that join, nor any dates for deliverables. Vals AI's role is to contribute independent evaluation work to the group's effort. The company says that work is meant to produce rigorous, reproducible evaluations that reflect real-world uses of AI.

Rayan Krishnan, Co-Founder and CEO of Vals AI, said that independent evaluation is essential to measuring AI capabilities, performance, and risks. He said the company looks forward to working with NIST and other consortium members on this goal. Glenn Parham, Head of Public Sector at Vals AI, said that policymakers in the United States and elsewhere need confidence in how AI performs across government and society. He argued that independent evaluations give those policymakers a common basis for comparing performance and identifying where AI can add the most value.

The company's own description states that it builds benchmarks grounded in real-world tasks with domain experts, and that frontier AI labs cite its results in their model cards. Its research also covers cybersecurity, child safety, and the environmental and economic impacts of AI, and it has been shared with policymakers in the United States and abroad. The articles do not say what the consortium will produce or when, and they do not describe any outcome from Vals AI's participation. Further details on the consortium are available in NIST's own announcement, which the company links to.

Articles.Title: Vals AI Announces Participation in Reconvened NIST Artificial Intelligence Consortium

stories.Headline: GREP: Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles
stories.Summary:
A new research paper titled GREP, short for Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles, was posted on November 11, 2026, by a team of seven authors led by Mohan Cao. The work addresses a gap in how computer-generated furnished rooms are judged, since existing evaluations look only at narrow perspectives or fixed questions. The authors say this leaves no reliable way to assess overall scene quality. They describe the paper as one of the cs.CV, cs.AI and cs.GR categories on arXiv, a preprint server. The core of the approach is a three-tier philosophy rather than a set of predefined questions.

The first tier, basic physical validity, checks whether a scene obeys physical constraints. The second, visual coherence, examines whether objects agree in scale, style and composition. The highest tier, human-use logic, requires that object arrangements match everyday human habits. Guided by these principles, an evaluation agent identifies issues from the scene context, gathers evidence, and produces scores and reports. According to the authors, GREP reached 87% agreement with the majority preferences of human judges, which they say substantially outperforms baseline evaluators.

They also report that GREP's written reports, when used to refine scenes, improved scene quality, while score-only and no-feedback baselines showed slight declines. The paper further suggests that as planning ability improves, recent models such as GPT-5.6 Sol can begin to challenge the pipelines and guidance imposed on them, yet still lack the ability to resolve the resulting conflicts. The authors expect stronger models to plan well and also adapt more flexibly to external guidance and constraints. The paper is available as a PDF and HTML version, with a project page linked by the authors. The articles do not say what follow-up work, adoption or peer review is planned.

Articles.Title: GREP: Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles

stories.Headline: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Fei Lin and 17 co-authors posted a paper on arXiv describing BEAKER, a new benchmark for testing how well multimodal large language models can act as "embodied brains" in self-driving chemical laboratories. The paper's abstract was published on November 11, 2026, and it addresses a gap the authors see in existing tests, which mostly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific knowledge. BEAKER contains 1,000 question-answer samples spread across 11 image and video task types. The authors say all questions and annotations were manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied artificial intelligence experts, without AI-assisted generation.

The benchmark covers the judgments needed to carry out chemical experiments, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, recognition of equipment, states and safety conditions, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. The researchers evaluated 28 models in total, drawn from general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized and embodied categories, in an offline, single-turn setting. The results indicate that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures shown in videos. However, the paper reports that they still struggle to turn actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to identify fine-grained apparatus, states and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures.

The paper is credited to the 18 authors listed, with Xue Yang among them, and the abstract does not single out any one author as responsible for the findings beyond that authorship. According to the abstract, the authors frame BEAKER as a diagnostic tool, and they say it exposes a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception that laboratory execution requires. The abstract does not describe any planned follow-up work, release timeline or specific next steps. What the authors hope will happen is that future multimodal models for self-driving laboratories will be measured against this benchmark. The source material offers no further details on how the benchmark will be adopted or what it will change in practice.

Articles.Title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories

stories.Headline: ModalSearcher: Weaving Visual Evidence into Autonomous Cross-Modal Deep Search
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers has posted a paper on arXiv, a preprint server, describing a system called ModalSearcher that lets multimodal AI models search for information across text and images. The paper was listed on November 11, 2026, and its authors are Zhihan Yin, Ruyi Li, Chengyu Fang, Yifeng Yao, Nonghai Zhang, Pengfei Xiong, Terry Zhang, Huishuai Zhang and Dongyan Zhao. The work addresses a limitation of current models, whose built-in knowledge is static and incomplete, which hurts performance on questions about new information or those requiring several steps of evidence gathering. The authors describe the approach as autonomous cross-modal search, in which an agent chooses between reasoning on its own, text-to-text search, text-to-image search and reverse-image search.

The system relies on a training pipeline called ModalSearch-Pipeline, which builds an interleaved multimodal knowledge graph of questions with paths of varying depth and mixed modalities. According to the abstract, the procedure hides entity names and image targets that would reveal shortcuts while keeping clues needed to disambiguate the answer. The researchers trained the agent with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment, and they also built a benchmark called ModalSearch-Bench. The abstract states that the 8-billion-parameter ModalSearcher-8B improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B under the same agentic workflow across five multimodal knowledge-intensive question-answering benchmarks. It also reports consistent gains on independently constructed active visual-search benchmarks.

The paper is credited to the nine authors listed above, and the articles do not name any institution, funder or company that sponsored the work. The abstract reports the results as the authors' own experimental findings, and it does not indicate whether independent parties have reviewed them. The articles also do not say whether the code, model weights or benchmark will be released publicly. The research is presented as a preprint, so it has not been described as peer reviewed in the material provided. Any further developments, such as publication in a journal or conference or release of the models, are not covered in the articles.

Articles.Title: ModalSearcher: Weaving Visual Evidence into Autonomous Cross-Modal Deep Search

stories.Headline: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models
stories.Summary:
DreamRealm is a post-training framework for multimodal large language models, introduced in a research paper posted to arXiv and listed on doi.org on November 11, 2026. The authors, Benlei Cui and eight co-authors, say the work addresses visual hallucinations, where a model gives wrong answers when correct responses depend on subtle visual details. The paper describes an approach that explores latent hallucinated responses, makes minimal edits to original images so the responses become valid, and trains the model to match each response to its supporting image. A data pipeline named RealmForgePipe mines hallucinations from a target model and materializes them through image editing. The authors built a dataset called the Realized Hallucination Dataset, or RealmSet, using hallucinations mined from Qwen3.5-9B.

Their training objective, named RealmMatch, builds a likelihood score matrix across image and response combinations and combines supervised learning with bidirectional contrastive losses. The aim is to reinforce correct matches and suppress mismatches between images and responses. The paper says these steps are meant to make supervision target the model's own perceptual confusions rather than generic visual contrasts. According to the paper, DreamRealm improves performance over the original Qwen3.5-9B model across six visual perception and hallucination benchmarks. The reported gains include 7.26 percentage points in HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 percentage points in MMVP pair accuracy.

The authors also present ablation studies on their data construction and training methods, which they say support the conclusion that hallucination assignment is a promising paradigm. The paper runs 28 pages including supplementary material, and the authors have released code and a model. The article does not describe any independent review, outside reaction, or deployment plans beyond the released code and model. It also does not indicate whether the results have been peer reviewed or published in a conference or journal. The authors frame their findings as a promising direction, and any further validation would depend on follow-up work by the research community.

Articles.Title: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models

stories.Headline: AttriSwarm: Orchestrating Agent Swarms for Cross-Page Visual Attribution
stories.Summary:
Researchers Suifeng Zhao, Zida Liu, Lei Sun, Xun Wang, Daojian Zeng, Jun Gao and Sujian Li have published a paper describing AttriSwarm, a framework for cross-page visual attribution in multimodal large language models. The work appeared on doi.org on November 11, 2026, and it addresses answers that are synthesized from evidence spread across several document pages. The authors say that when such answers are assembled from many pages, the connection between a conclusion and its supporting visual evidence becomes hard to see, which makes verification and trust difficult. Their system is built to restore that connection.

According to the abstract, cross-page attribution requires two steps: identifying the pages that support an answer and locating fine-grained evidence regions within those pages. Existing methods either process multiple pages jointly or refine evidence step by step in a single trajectory, which the authors say can pollute context across pages and add heavy sequential overhead in interactive settings. AttriSwarm separates these tasks among distinct roles, with a leader agent handling global reasoning across pages and subagents performing page-by-page attribution in isolation and in parallel. To support training and evaluation, the authors also built AttriDoc, a cross-page question-answering dataset that links supporting pages to annotated evidence regions.

The authors report that role-specific training on AttriDoc improved AttriSwarm over its training-free version. Averaged across three open-source backbones and three datasets, the gains were 18.94 percentage points in answer accuracy, 29.34 percentage points in page-level F1, and 23.04 percentage points in region-level IoU. The paper itself is credited to the seven named authors, and the abstract describes the results as the authors' own findings. The article content does not say how the work will be used beyond the research setting, nor does it describe any further releases or follow-up steps.

Articles.Title: AttriSwarm: Orchestrating Agent Swarms for Cross-Page Visual Attribution

stories.Headline: New Relic launches AI agent for Kubernetes troubleshooting
stories.Summary:
New Relic, the observability company, announced the New Relic Autopilot Kubernetes Agent, an AI tool meant to simplify troubleshooting of Kubernetes clusters, according to a TechGig report published on November 11, 2026. The agent is aimed at site reliability engineers and platform engineers who manage these clusters. It is described as a domain-specific extension of New Relic Autopilot, the company's suite of SRE agents. The report says it was unveiled that day and is currently available in public preview.

The agent runs more than 90 specialised diagnostic detectors across Kubernetes events, object descriptions, logs and APM traces to isolate root causes. It then generates context-aware remediation code, which engineers review and execute themselves. The article notes that the tool connects to New Relic's Ground Truth context engine, which is built on OpenTelemetry. It is designed to diagnose common and complex infrastructure failures such as noisy neighbours, compute resourcing problems, scheduling failures, network errors and cloud misconfigurations, including issues with Application Load Balancers and ingress.

Human-in-the-loop options are included so engineers can keep oversight during investigations. Brian Emerson, chief product officer at New Relic, said the agent brings specialised, agentic AI directly into the engineer's containerised workflows. He said the aim is to remove guesswork from complex cluster incidents while engineers stay in control. The article presents this as the purpose of the launch and does not include further assessments from outside the company.

It does not say how the agent will be priced, when it will reach general availability, or how widely it has been tested. The report describes the agent as fitting into standard SRE and platform engineering workflows rather than replacing them. It also notes that the agent works within New Relic's existing observability platform, which is why it draws on the company's telemetry data. Beyond the public preview, the article gives no timeline or next steps.

Articles.Title: New Relic launches AI agent for Kubernetes troubleshooting

stories.Headline: Platform ownership shapes AI infrastructure strategies, CNCF report finds
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData released their Q3 2026 Technology Radar report on November 11, 2026, at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026. The research looked at how developers view observability, infrastructure as code, and storage technologies. Its central finding is that the way an organisation structures its platform engineering is closely tied to how it approaches AI infrastructure. The report covers tools across these three areas and tracks which of them earned an "Adopt" position.

The report ties platform ownership to AI choices. Among organisations where individual teams manage their own tooling, 54 per cent of developers use hybrid approaches for AI workflows, compared with 43 per cent where multiple teams collaboratively provide platform capabilities. Only 5 per cent of organisations building custom internal developer platforms use hybrid approaches. Among those building custom platforms, 38 per cent use a separate dedicated AI platform, while 33 per cent extend their existing developer platform.

Where platform teams curate third-party tools, 25 per cent rely primarily on AI vendor platforms. Liam Bollmann-Dodd, principal market research consultant at SlashData, said that centralised teams tend to make deliberate decisions about extending existing platforms or building dedicated AI environments. He added that distributed teams are more likely to adopt hybrid approaches. The report's findings on technology adoption were drawn from developer ratings and recommendations gathered by CNCF and SlashData.

Prometheus and OpenTelemetry earned "Adopt" positions in observability, with 80 per cent of developers rating Prometheus four or five stars for maturity. Ninety-two per cent of current and former OpenTelemetry users said they would likely recommend it, and Fluent Bit was the most recommended observability tool at 99 per cent. In infrastructure as code, OpenTofu and OpenFeature earned "Adopt" positions, and 96 per cent of OpenTofu users said they would likely recommend it.
