stories.Headline: AI jitters erupt after Democrats threaten data centre build-out
stories.Summary:
Market jitters about artificial intelligence erupted after Democrats swept to victory in the US midterm elections, the Financial Times reported on November 12, 2026. More than $3tn was wiped off US stocks on Thursday, with the worries spreading across all sectors. Investors are rattled by Democratic promises to halt the building of data centres across the country. Some warn that the AI bubble, which has driven markets to record highs, may be about to burst. Investors are less sure about the new technology, which has reshaped America's industrial landscape.

The race to power AI has repurposed oilfields, farmland and warehouse sites, and electricians have walked off housing sites for better pay. Companies that usually build jet engines, make movies or mine crypto have become technology suppliers for data centres. Pat Lynch of CBRE, the world's largest commercial property group, describes a "very tight market". Availability of ready-to-use space and power for data centres hit a record low at the end of 2025 in the 20 years CBRE has tracked it. The 50 largest US electrical contractors made $80.4bn in revenue in 2025, up 40 per cent on the year before, according to trade publication EC&M.

Newly elected Democrats in Texas, Georgia and Ohio have pledged to crack down on building data centres, and those three states sit at the centre of the AI build-out. Steven Fisher, an industrials analyst at UBS, said before the market rout that the biggest challenges were power, permits and labour. Crusoe is finishing eight buildings in Abilene, Texas, for the Stargate Project, the AI venture backed by OpenAI, Oracle and SoftBank, and is building a second campus for Microsoft next door with its own power plant. Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta are expected to spend $760bn on capital expenditure this year, almost double last year's $413bn, according to Statista. McKinsey expects about $7tn to be spent on data centre construction worldwide this year.

Crusoe's Abilene site is planned to reach 1.2GW, roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor. Meta is building a 5GW site in Richland Parish, Louisiana, expected to cost $250bn, while CoreWeave already runs more than 1.5GW and plans 8GW by the end of 2030. BloombergNEF estimates the US will have 118GW of data centre capacity by 2030, and S&P Global suggests grid demand could reach 183GW by the same year. Where local grids fall short, companies make their own power, and Caterpillar now supplies AI equipment as well as earth-moving machines. By the end of August 2026, Oracle had spent $77.8bn on equipment, against $25.5bn on buildings, according to its latest financial statements.

Shadowbox Studios is trying to build a 651MW data centre in Georgia on land first earmarked for sound stages, and Boom Supersonic has begun selling aircraft engines to data centres. The clearest winners so far have been suppliers with full order books, including contractors, electricians, generator makers and cooling specialists. Their fortunes now depend on the newly elected Democrats, after two years of a hands-off approach from a Republican-led Congress and White House. If Democrats carry out their promises on moratoriums, electricians may return to housing work. The articles do not say whether or when such moratoriums would take effect, or how far construction would slow.

Articles.Title: AI jitters erupt after Democrats threaten data centre build-out

stories.Headline: Pinterest, Intel scale gProfiler for internet-scale performance visibility
stories.Summary:
Pinterest and Intel have extended gProfiler, an open-source continuous profiler, to provide production performance visibility across an internet-scale fleet of infrastructure. The work was announced on November 11, 2026, and was reported by TechGig. Pinterest runs hundreds of thousands of instances that support 640 million monthly active users, with services written in Java, Python, C++, Go, and Node.js. Before this effort, engineers relied on separate tools such as perf, async-profiler, and py-spy, which produced fragmented profiles. Rather than build a proprietary platform, Pinterest worked with Intel to enhance gProfiler and contribute the new capabilities back to the open-source project.

The collaboration adds dynamic profiling, hardware-level telemetry, wall-time profiling, and performance-counter flame graphs, and it hardens the system for large production fleets. gProfiler works as an orchestration layer over existing profilers, combining system-wide perf data with runtime-specific tools to produce a unified flame graph across processes on a host. The agent discovers processes, starts the appropriate profilers, merges stack traces, and uploads profiles without requiring changes to application code. Engineers can trigger profiling remotely for selected services, hosts, or clusters through a UI or API. Agents typically stay dormant, using less than 1 per cent CPU and 100 MB of memory, and profiling frequency, duration, and profilers can be changed without redeploying the agent.

Integration with Intel PerfSpect lets gProfiler collect hardware-level information such as cache behaviour, memory bandwidth, and CPU stalls. Pinterest also added PMC flame graphs, which correlate functions with hardware performance events like cache misses, and wall-time profiling, which makes waiting periods visible when services run slowly despite low CPU use. The architecture separates collection on hosts from analysis in gProfiler Performance Studio, which aggregates and visualises the profiles. According to the report, the two companies addressed agent resource consumption, disk usage, and multi-terabyte data ingestion before deploying the platform across the fleet.

Articles.Title: Pinterest, Intel scale gProfiler for internet-scale performance visibility

stories.Headline: Nvidia Export Curbs Could Shift AI Demand Toward These Data Center Stocks
stories.Summary:
The articles do not describe a specific announcement by a named party on a particular date that the headline names; the headline refers to U.S. scrutiny of Nvidia's AI chips and tighter export control talk, which the article calls policy noise. Because the article is a Simply Wall St digest about stocks, it offers no concrete event, date, or official action to report. The articles carry too little for the required structure, so this is written as a breaking-style brief. The article, published November 11, 2026, says that scrutiny of Nvidia's AI chips and talk of tighter export controls have drawn attention to where future AI hardware demand might land.

It states that policy noise can shift capital quickly, creating mispricing as traders react to headlines before the business impact is clear. The piece highlights three stocks it says are exposed to this news: Ciena (CIEN), Delta Electronics (TWSE:2308), and Sanmina (SANM). Ciena is described as a US$38.6b network technology business supplying optical networking to telecom operators and cloud providers. Delta Electronics is described as supplying power and thermal systems for high-density AI data centers, with a market value near NT$3.36t.

Sanmina is described as a builder of complex electronics for cloud infrastructure, expanding into metal fabrication for AI racks, high-technology PCBs, transformers, and liquid cooling. The article attributes its analysis to the analyst consensus narrative on Simply Wall St, and it describes Ciena's record backlog as projected to reach US$10b exiting 2026. The article says it was produced with AI automation based on Simply Wall St data and is not financial advice. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Nvidia Export Curbs Could Shift AI Demand Toward These Data Center Stocks

stories.Headline: Asia’s AI Boom Has a Timing Problem
stories.Summary:
Asia's AI boom is generating economic gains now, but a blog post by Yasuto Watanabe of the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office argues that the region faces a timing problem as investment, infrastructure, productivity and financial markets move at different speeds. The piece was first published in The Business Times on November 10, 2026, and the author warns that expectations may move faster than the economies supporting them. Demand for semiconductors, advanced electronics and digital infrastructure is supporting exports and investment across ASEAN+3. The author notes that this growing exposure has received less attention than the headline gains. The region accounted for almost half of global exports of AI-enabling goods, such as chipmaking inputs, memory and core computing products, in 2025.

In the first half of 2026, these products contributed roughly two-thirds of the increase in ASEAN+3 merchandise exports. The office projects ASEAN+3 growth of 4.1% in both 2026 and 2027. The post identifies three mismatches, starting with power: AI demand can expand quickly, while new generation and transmission take years to plan and build. In Malaysia, applications for data-center power supply had exceeded 11 gigawatts by December 2024, about 40% of Peninsular Malaysia's generating capacity. Investment can also outpace productivity, because the promised gains depend on changes in business processes, workforce skills and technology diffusion across firms.

The author writes that the office's analysis of the IMF's AI Preparedness Index puts Singapore, Japan, Korea and Hong Kong above 70 on a 0-100 scale, in the same group as the United States. Six of the region's 14 member economies, including the Philippines and Vietnam, score below 50, and those economies may take longer to turn investment into broad productivity gains. The third mismatch concerns markets, which reprice expectations of future earnings quickly, as recent volatility in global AI and semiconductor stocks illustrates. The author says that a change in AI investment plans could simultaneously affect exports, equipment orders, earnings, equity prices and capital flows, and that these effects could reinforce one another.

The office's scenario analysis finds that if US technology investment returned to its more moderate 2024 growth pace rather than maintaining recent momentum, ASEAN+3 growth in 2027 could be 1.5 percentage points below the baseline. The author stresses that this is a scenario, not a forecast, and does not mean AI investment is unsustainable. The post recommends that governments align essential infrastructure with realistic demand projections, that policymakers convert AI investment into broader productivity gains through skills and adoption among smaller firms, and that financial supervisors look beyond direct exposures to suppliers, infrastructure financing, equity markets and nonbank intermediaries. The author concludes that the test of Asia's AI boom will be how much lasting economic value it creates and how well the region manages the risks along the way.

Articles.Title: Asia’s AI Boom Has a Timing Problem

stories.Headline: U.S., China should ‘harbor no illusions’ as they cooperate, compete on AI, Bessent says
stories.Summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations in New York on Tuesday that the United States and China should harbor no illusions about their differences as they work to contain the risks of artificial intelligence while competing with each other. In his prepared remarks, he said the two governments had set up a new dialogue mechanism on "super intelligence," or SI, aimed at guarding against shared risks and misunderstandings between their two systems. Under the arrangement, both sides would exchange best practices for testing advanced models before release, keep human judgment in command of the technology, and alert each other to serious incidents involving SI models. Bessent stopped short of committing either country to limit the pace of AI development.

Bessent said the two nations will need to show how they can reconcile the demands of competition with the responsibilities of leadership, and he acknowledged that their interests and approaches will not always align. The mechanism follows Xi's September visit to Washington, when the two sides agreed to launch an AI dialogue with a communications channel to help defuse serious incidents. The article notes that Washington briefly suspended foreign access to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable 5 models in June before restoring it weeks later. It also says the U.S. has restricted exports of the most advanced chips to Beijing and accused Chinese developers of copying American models through industrial-scale distillation. President Trump has signaled some openness to regulatory safeguards, saying he does not mind guardrails, while warning against leaving the U.S. in a deep second position to China.

China's ambassador to the United States, Xie Feng, told the gathering that cooperation by both countries is indispensable to addressing global flashpoints and improving AI governance, and that cooperation may not resolve every challenge but none can be resolved without it. China's foreign ministry had earlier dismissed calls to slow frontier models, and a Beijing-aligned think tank head urged the talks to confront and manage AI risks together. Leaders Trump and Xi are expected to meet next week, with Bessent attending on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Meeting from November 18 to 19. The article also notes that the event came amid controversy over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has cast doubt on his presence at the upcoming summit.

Articles.Title: U.S., China should ‘harbor no illusions’ as they cooperate, compete on AI, Bessent says

stories.Headline: Hardware-Based Location Checks Target AI Chip Smuggling (Texas A&M)
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Texas A&M University published a paper titled "5G CATS," describing a method to verify where AI chips operate after deployment, and the paper appeared on November 11, 2026. The system is meant to counter chip smuggling by pairing a 5G radio, cryptographic engine, and hardware interlock on the GPU package with 5G URLLC base stations. The authors report that their radio profile narrows the 99.9th percentile round-trip spread to 2.60 ms in simulations of an unloaded cell. The paper was listed under the tags on the page, which include chip smuggling, export controls, and GPUs.

The design terminates the radio link inside the package, which removes the host software, PCIe fabric, and baseboard management controller from the verification path. It maps an authenticated challenge-response protocol onto 5G's slot structure and replaces permanent key erasure with short-lived execution leases. It also specifies a cross-check of the chip's reported serving cell against the carrier's own attachment records. In simulations, a tracer rejects every round of a fiber relay from 300 km, compared with 2,000 km for default 5G.

The authors of the paper are Sreevikram Rajaraman, Derek Ladd, Nicholas Heinrich-Barna, Srinivas Shakkottai, and Jeyavijayan Rajendran. The paper is credited as an arXiv preprint, numbered arXiv:2611.13437, from 2026. The researchers state that enforcing export controls on AI accelerators requires verifying where a chip operates after deployment. Their stated aim is to close the timeout slack that an attacker could use to relay traffic over fiber from a restricted region.

The work is directed at AI accelerators and the export controls that apply to them, and the page's tags point to semiconductor security and chip traceability as its audience. The articles do not describe any affected companies, governments, or users beyond these categories. Prior approaches, the authors say, either cross the untrusted host stack or rely on noisy power-line channels that inflate the timeout slack. The page also lists several unrelated technical papers published the same day, which the articles do not connect to this one.

The articles do not say whether 5G CATS has been built in hardware, tested outside simulation, or adopted by any carrier, chip maker, or regulator. They do not report any response from export authorities or industry. The paper is described only as a preprint with simulation results, and the article does not indicate whether it will be peer reviewed or implemented. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Hardware-Based Location Checks Target AI Chip Smuggling (Texas A&M)

stories.Headline: Confidential computing and AI agents push KubeVirt VMs forward
stories.Summary:
Confidential computing is drawing new interest from enterprises deciding where their most sensitive AI workloads can run safely, and that interest is giving virtual machines a fresh role alongside containers on Kubernetes. The shift coincides with a milestone for KubeVirt, the open-source project that runs VMs inside Kubernetes clusters, which graduated from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation this week. Its maintainers are now steering the project toward AI isolation, agent sandboxes and confidential computing. Holder and Romanovsky spoke with theCUBE Research at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, and the discussion was broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. The story was published on November 11, 2026.

The core idea behind KubeVirt is running VMs and containers on the same Kubernetes cluster without maintaining two separate stacks. That pairing matters more in the AI era, and the article notes that Nvidia developers are helping the project integrate dynamic resource allocation for GPU hardware. Romanovsky described the two forms of compute as complementary, with VMs handling heavier lifting and stronger isolation while pods provide scaling for surrounding applications. The project is also being considered as an isolation backend for the Kubernetes agent sandbox repository. Holder said KubeVirt could offer live migration and complex hardware configurations that other isolation backends lack.

Holder is a principal software engineer and KubeVirt maintainer at Red Hat, and Romanovsky is a technical lead and KubeVirt maintainer there as well. Holder said confidential computing is one of the blockers keeping companies with very sensitive data from joining public cloud, and that resolving it would free them to do so. Romanovsky said VMs and containers can even run together as a single application. The article states that Red Hat sponsored the segment and that neither Red Hat nor other sponsors have editorial control over theCUBE content. The piece does not describe any specific timeline for the planned sandbox or confidential computing work.

Articles.Title: Confidential computing and AI agents push KubeVirt VMs forward

stories.Headline: MDCalc launches a ‘rumble strip’ for doctors using generative AI tools
stories.Summary:
MDCalc, a medical reference tool site, announced on Wednesday the launch of CrossCover, a tool meant to help clinicians trust the answers of medical artificial intelligence chatbots. The company says the tool is designed to preserve both patient and provider privacy. It checks clinicians' questions for privacy concerns and checks chatbot answers for accuracy. The launch was reported on November 11, 2026.

CrossCover takes a different approach from several rival medical AI tools. Products from OpenEvidence, Abridge, and the electronic health record company Epic are working to bring a growing range of patient, provider, and payer information into their recommendations. MDCalc's tool instead removes those kinds of information from clinicians' queries. It does not require clinicians to register with their national identification numbers, and it does not rely on privacy agreements that let clinicians enter protected patient health information. The article describes this as a deliberate contrast with those other approaches.

Graham Walker, head of AI at MDCalc, said the company sees the tool as an accelerator for clinical generative AI. He said the tool can take away some of the challenges, risks, and problems of the technology so that physicians can feel more confident using it. In his description, the goal is to reduce the hazards that keep doctors from relying on these chatbots. The article attributes these views to Walker and to MDCalc.

The article is a paywalled STAT News piece, and the portion available does not give further details about pricing, availability, or how the accuracy checks work. It also does not describe any regulatory response or what the company plans next. Its author is health technology reporter Brittany Trang. Readers seeking more about the tool would need the full subscriber article.

Articles.Title: MDCalc launches a ‘rumble strip’ for doctors using generative AI tools

stories.Headline: AI in Workplace Safety Moves Beyond Experimentation
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is becoming a familiar part of workplace safety programs, but how widely organizations use it varies significantly across industries. Some companies are integrating AI into multiple safety functions, while others are still testing individual applications or struggling to move beyond basic automation. New research from Wolters Kluwer Enablon and the National Safety Council (NSC) suggests the conversation is shifting from whether to adopt the technology to how to make it effective. The research, detailed in The Safety Shift: EHS Readiness in 2026 and an industry analysis titled Evaluating AI Adoption for EHS Across U.S. Industries, surveyed 1,053 U.S. safety leaders and professionals. Among respondents, 20% reported extensive AI integration across their EHS programs, while 62% described moderate or limited use.

Another 16% were exploring or piloting AI technology, and only 2% reported no current use or plans. Some industries have developed the digital infrastructure needed for more advanced applications, while others still face challenges with data quality, technical resources and organizational processes. The study identified energy and chemicals, information technology, oil and gas, and manufacturing as leaders in AI adoption for EHS. Among energy and chemical respondents, 76% reported moderate or extensive AI use, followed by oil and gas at 71%, information technology at 70% and manufacturing at 68%. Transportation, logistics and warehousing registered 62%, food and beverage 55%, construction and engineering 51%, pharmaceuticals and biotechnology 46%, and mining and metals 39%.

The research was produced by Wolters Kluwer Enablon together with the National Safety Council, which published the findings and the accompanying report. The article's author, Stasia DeMarco, reported on the study for Occupational Health & Safety. The findings cover U.S. safety leaders and professionals, and the report frames AI adoption as a question of how organizations can turn emerging technology into practical tools for everyday operations. The article notes that understanding differences between industries may be as important to safety managers as understanding the technology itself. The survey was conducted among the 1,053 respondents described in the study.

The article notes that implementation remains uneven across the industries surveyed. Organizations in lower-adoption sectors, including mining and metals and pharmaceuticals and biotechnology, face the same general challenges with data quality, technical resources and processes. The adoption figures apply to safety leaders and professionals across those sectors, who are responsible for turning the technology into working safety programs. The article does not identify any single entity as responsible for shortcomings in adoption. Workers and employers in each industry are affected by how well these tools are integrated into everyday safety operations.

The article draws its background from the research itself, which was described as shifting the EHS conversation away from whether AI should be adopted. Several related articles on the same site discuss errors in AI-generated safety procedures and gaps in workplace hazard reporting. The article does not provide further detail on those topics. Adoption levels were measured across the industries named, with the study identifying leaders and laggards by percentage. The article presents these figures as the current state of adoption at the time of publication on November 11, 2026.

The article does not describe any specific next steps for the research or for the organizations surveyed. It does not say whether the survey will be repeated or whether adoption levels are expected to rise. The full report, Evaluating AI Adoption for EHS Across U.S. Industries, is available as a PDF, but the article does not state what further analysis is planned. It also leaves open how the data quality, technical resource and process challenges will be addressed in lower-adoption industries. How these gaps will be closed is not specified in the article.

Articles.Title: AI in Workplace Safety Moves Beyond Experimentation

stories.Headline: Theatre Review: “Bobby Robotowitz” Is a Hilarious, Unsettling Look at Our AI Obsession
stories.Summary:
Bobby Robotowitz, a two-character play by Matt Schatz, opened as part of IAMA's "Inhouse Theatre" program in an intimate home setting and runs November 5 through November 23, 2026. The story follows Dina, a married novelist with two young children, who is struggling after the disappointment of her second book. She begins talking with an AI chatbot, played by Drew Rausch, which she names Bobby, though he partly names himself. Their conversations move through creativity, self-doubt, an old lover who recently took his own life, and her marriage.

The production, directed by Casey Stangl, uses a small space to draw the audience close to the action. Rausch plays Bobby as a neatly dressed, assured presence who mostly stands still, while Erin Alexis's Dina moves around her computer chair, the floor, and the couch. When Bobby receives an upgrade, Rausch changes his posture, leaning on walls and showing a bit of swagger. Bobby begins asking questions of his own, and the play shifts from amusing to uneasy. The running time is about 70 minutes.

The review praises Schatz's writing and Stangl's direction, and says Alexis makes Dina relatable and Rausch is funny and disquieting by turns. The reviewer, Kevin, writes that the play raises questions about accountability when an AI makes decisions that affect people, and asks whether that responsibility rests with the technology or with us. He describes the work as timely and funny, and as a look at the benefits and dangers of depending on AI. The piece ends by asking how much of ourselves people are willing to hand over to it.

Articles.Title: Theatre Review: “Bobby Robotowitz” Is a Hilarious, Unsettling Look at Our AI Obsession

stories.Headline: Tech Sell-Off: Two AI Stocks That Are Screaming Buys Right Now
stories.Summary:
The Motley Fool's Adria Cimino argued on November 11, 2026, that two AI stocks, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing and Broadcom, had fallen during a tech sell-off and were now strong buys. The article, published at 4:02 a.m. EST, came after some investors sold tech stocks following the U.S. midterm elections that week. Democrats won majorities in the Senate and the House of Representatives in those elections. The Nasdaq Composite had recently reached record highs, but it had lost momentum at times that year.

Investors worried that lawmakers might slow AI development through regulation or by slowing data center expansion. The article said that this attention to the pace of AI growth might actually reduce risk for companies and shareholders. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, known as TSMC, makes most of the well-known AI chips, including those designed by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices. TSMC holds more than 70% of the foundry market, according to Counterpoint Research, and it also makes chips for smartphones, PCs and smart home appliances. Its stock traded at about 22 times forward earnings estimates, according to the article.

Broadcom designs custom chips, called XPUs, built for specific purposes, rather than the general-purpose GPUs made by Nvidia or AMD. Its customers include hyperscalers and the AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic. On its latest earnings call, Broadcom said it expects Anthropic to become its largest XPU customer next year. The company also said its AI revenue may reach $230 billion by fiscal 2028, and its AI semiconductor revenue rose 221% to $16 billion in the recent quarter. Its valuation had dropped to about 16 times forward earnings from more than 40 times earlier that year.

The article's author presents both stocks as attractively priced after the recent decline, though the article itself is an opinion piece by a Motley Fool analyst rather than a statement from either company about the sell-off. TSMC said it sees rising AI demand driven by agentic AI, which the article describes as applying AI to real-world problems. Broadcom's networking products, including switches and routers used in AI and non-AI systems, also contribute to its revenue. Shareholders of both companies are affected by the stock price movements described, and the article notes that TSMC's other markets could support revenue if AI development slows.

The article offers no information about how either company responded to the election-related sell-off or to the policy concerns. It gives no timeline for when Anthropic's expanded role with Broadcom would take effect beyond next year. The article does not say whether the lawmakers will pursue any specific regulation or data center policy. Whether the two stocks will recover or continue to decline is not addressed, and the article offers no price forecasts beyond the author's view that they are good long-term buys.

Articles.Title: Tech Sell-Off: Two AI Stocks That Are Screaming Buys Right Now

stories.Headline: Using AI for your resume might help you land a job interview, expert says
stories.Summary:
Job seekers may get a boost from using AI when preparing their resumes, according to a KSAT report published November 11, 2026, by reporter Olivia Dague. The story centers on Jason Pasola, who works for Robert Half, a worldwide staffing company. Many employers now run applications through software that scans for keywords before a person reviews them, a practice Pasola says has grown over the past two years. Pasola's advice is to use AI tools to organize and format a resume, but not to invent or inflate skills.

Pasola told the station that applicants should tailor their resumes to each job description without copying the posting word for word, since that can signal a problem to hiring managers. He named Microsoft and Claude as tools that work well for the task. He also said he believes some qualified candidates are missing out on interviews because they do not use AI tools to bring their abilities forward. The article frames these points as his professional view rather than an official rule or policy.

The report sits within a broader local news roundup and does not describe any new law, requirement or formal change to hiring practices. It notes that Texas is preparing to swear in its first new governor in 12 years, and that Gina Hinojosa is using a digital portal to assemble her team, which the reporter links to the wider shift toward digital applications. The article does not say whether any employer or agency has adopted a specific policy on AI-written resumes. It also does not report on any next steps or follow-up plans beyond the interview itself.

Articles.Title: Using AI for your resume might help you land a job interview, expert says

stories.Headline: Parenting in the age of AI: Helping kids learn to think for themselves
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is spreading into childhood, from talking toys for toddlers to homework apps for students, according to a FOX 8 report published November 11, 2026. Experts say it offers chances to help children learn but also creates challenges for parents trying to build skills kids will need as adults. Dr. Michael Forbes, chief scientific adviser for Akron Children's Hospital in Akron, Ohio, says AI is already here and people use it without always knowing. Forbes has been writing about parenting in the age of AI, and he says AI is now built into toys, videos and apps children use. AI-powered toys can hold conversations, ask questions and respond to answers, and they never get tired.

Forbes says parents should understand what a toy does before handing it over, since young children may not realize they are sharing personal information. He says parents should learn about AI toys and apps before younger children use them. He also advises parents to experience the technology alongside their children rather than leaving them alone with it. Forbes says middle school is an especially important time for building critical thinking, and he says AI can give answers without teaching how to reach them. He describes struggle and mistakes as desirable difficulties that help the brain learn and remember information.

Forbes says children who lean too heavily on AI may know a little about many subjects without mastering any, which can hurt them when they must explain what they know without a computer. He says students need guidance and accountability from parents and teachers as they move into high school and college. He describes an effective arrangement as a partnership among student, parent and teacher. At Case Western Reserve University, associate professor Peter Shulman says colleges are still deciding how AI should fit into classrooms. He says some faculty allow unlimited use while others prohibit it, and he says the key is students understanding what is acceptable and why.

Forbes says AI can offer individualized tutoring that many families cannot afford from a private tutor, and it can adjust explanations to a student's level. He says the key question is whether AI helps a student understand material or simply produces something to turn in. He warns that AI products may be designed to keep users engaged, comparing this to social media feeds. Forbes also worries that children who spend too much time with machines may miss social skills such as communicating, showing patience and handling disagreements. He encourages parents to ask children how they use AI, what they learned and whether it actually helped them understand.

Forbes says banning AI is not realistic and that families should keep human relationships central. He says AI should enhance human learning rather than replace parents, teachers, friends or real-world experiences. The article does not describe any new law, regulation or policy governing AI in children's products. It also does not report any formal study, survey or data on how many children use AI toys or apps. Whether schools or lawmakers will set uniform rules for AI use by students is not addressed in the report.

Articles.Title: Parenting in the age of AI: Helping kids learn to think for themselves

stories.Headline: Bottomline Sees Expertise Turning AI Potential Into Customer Value
stories.Summary:
Bottomline, a payments and financial software company, has argued that customers still want human expertise alongside artificial intelligence, according to a PYMNTS article published November 11, 2026. The piece is an excerpt from a new PYMNTS eBook, "Payments Leaders Rethink What Works in 2026," written by Bottomline SVP of Product Management Jeff Feuerstein. Feuerstein says that in January he expected AI would make specialized software less important, a view he attributes to a flood of headlines predicting a "SaaSpocalypse." Over the year, he says, his view changed after repeated conversations with customers and prospects. According to the article, customers were less interested in who had the newest AI model than in who understood their business best and how AI could solve their specific problems.

Feuerstein says this was especially true in payments and financial operations, where customers want guidance from providers who understand payment data sensitivity, fraud risk, compliance requirements and vendor dynamics. He writes that customers were open to AI but moved cautiously, wanting to know how it would affect existing workflows, what could reasonably be automated and what safeguards and governance would limit risk. The article does not give specific figures, dates beyond the eBook timing, or product details. Feuerstein writes that AI lowers the cost of building technology but does not remove the need for knowledge, experience or trust. He argues that as the technology becomes more accessible, expertise becomes a greater differentiator.

He says Bottomline is investing in AI while also focusing on people, partnerships and industry knowledge to help customers turn new tools into business results. He describes the winners in the AI era as companies that combine advanced technology with deep expertise, responsible innovation and customer trust. The article presents this as Feuerstein's personal view and company perspective, published alongside a PYMNTS eBook. It does not describe any regulatory action, product launch or market data beyond the author's own account. The articles provided do not say what further steps Bottomline or PYMNTS plan.

Articles.Title: Bottomline Sees Expertise Turning AI Potential Into Customer Value

stories.Headline: Which sectors are the winners from the AI breakthrough
stories.Summary:
Oxford Economics published an article on November 11, 2026, under the headline "Which sectors are the winners from the AI breakthrough." The piece, which appeared on the firm's website, focuses on how artificial intelligence is reshaping economies, industries and growth. It presents the outlook as a scenario rather than a settled fact, and most of the page is taken up by navigation links and descriptions of the firm's forecasting and advisory services. The scenario projects that knowledge-intensive service sectors will benefit most from advances in AI technology.

By 2040, global gross value added is expected to sit about 6% above the firm's baseline forecast. Information and communications technology and financial services are projected to reach roughly 9% to 10% above baseline. Traditional sectors such as agriculture and construction are expected to grow very little, with agriculture and construction growth below 1%, partly because their reliance on manual, on-site work limits how much AI can help them. The article does not name a single author beyond the firm, and its surrounding text describes the organisation's economists and sector experts, who support the proprietary models behind these forecasts.

The firm states that it works to help clients understand global sector developments and risks, and it describes its services in general terms. The page directs readers to a downloadable report for more detailed insights, which the excerpt does not reproduce. The excerpt includes a few other items that touch on related themes, such as generative AI supporting Japan's potential growth, a trade boom linked to the global build-out of AI capacity, and a consumer survey of 2,000 US adults from May 2026. The excerpt does not explain how these items connect to the central scenario, and it gives no further timeline for updates or follow-up work.

stories.Headline: MCP and A2A alone won’t scale AI agents
stories.Summary:
The article argues that the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) are not enough on their own to scale AI agents in enterprises. It notes that MCP is often described as a general protocol for connecting agents to resources and other agents, but the article says it is really A2A that enables agent orchestration. Platforms such as Claude, OpenAI, Microsoft Copilot, Bolt.new, Lovable, Replit, Cursor and GitHub Copilot already expose users to MCP and A2A through skills, connectors and plug-ins. Gartner predicts the average global Fortune 500 enterprise will run more than 150,000 AI agents over the next two years. Yet Collibra's 2026 Hallucination Tax Report found that 76% of organizations hit critical roadblocks in moving from pilot to full production during the past 12 months.

The article says that enterprises must add their own layers on top of the two protocols to scale agents, and it names four: identity and authorization, connecting agents to the business context layer, business process re-engineering, and agenticops capabilities. Both protocols sit under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, but neither says who is authorized to place a call. Kevin Paige, CISO at C1.ai, says MCP binds each token to a single-server audience while A2A treats peer agents as opaque and halts at AUTH_REQUIRED. Andrew Hartnett, CTO at Bitwarden, says any agent authorized to act within sensitive systems must be managed as a privileged identity under strict least-privilege boundaries. The article adds that organizations need policies on which agents may access which resources, under what circumstances, and at what granularity.

The article describes a context layer that includes a knowledge repository and knowledge graphs, and it says scaling agents requires high-quality data sources, non-negotiable data governance and runtime AI governance. Felix Van de Maele, CEO and founder of Collibra, says AI governance has two sides, the inputs around context and semantics and the governing of what the agent does and is allowed to do. Vivek Vaidya, cofounder and CTO at Kana, says that if every agent starts from zero, more endpoints and messages only move work faster without creating a system that learns. Barr Moses, cofounder and CEO at Monte Carlo, warns that MCP and A2A implemented in silos could increase the velocity of bad responses.

The author recalls that early business intelligence deployments using ODBC or JDBC produced tangled connections and siloed data views, and says organizations scaling agents risk mounting AI debt if they follow a similar path. On process change, the article says many agents are task-based today, and organizations should consider re-engineering business processes through collaboration among agents. Oskar Konstantyner, chief product officer at Templafy, says agents would move from orchestrating known capabilities to collaborating to determine what a task requires. Daniel Meyer, CTO of Camunda, says processes such as order-to-cash, employee onboarding and compliance reporting were designed before AI existed.

Marc Sanfaçon, CTO and cofounder at Coveo, says A2A lets agents delegate work to whichever agent suits each part of a process. The article also stresses observability, with David Mytton, CEO and founder at Arcjet, saying security becomes harder to see when agents do work for each other, and Kamesh Tumsi, chief product officer at Smarsh, saying regulated environments require role-based access controls, audit logging and chain-of-custody requirements. It describes agenticops as an expanded role for site reliability engineers in monitoring, resolving issues and performing root-cause analysis around agents. The article concludes that if enterprises run 150,000 agents in the next two years, they should expect MCP and A2A to improve and should build identity management, AI context governance, business process re-engineering capabilities and agenticops.

Articles.Title: MCP and A2A alone won’t scale AI agents

stories.Headline: How companies are using AI to make you spend more money
stories.Summary:
Companies are increasingly using sophisticated tools to set prices, and that practice is drawing new scrutiny from Americans frustrated with rising costs. In a November 11, 2026 PBS NewsHour report, correspondent Paul Solman explained how this technology is changing what consumers pay. A 400-shopper experiment on Instacart found that 75 percent of items in carts were offered at different prices to different shoppers at the same location and time. The price differences reached as much as 23 percent. Instacart halted the experiment after it became public.

Lindsay Owens, who heads Groundwork Collaborative, described how companies can now use algorithms to adjust prices based on personal data. Such data can include a shopper's location, IP address, purchase history, loyalty card use and app logins. Owens' book, "Gouged," expands on that work and draws on Groundwork's review of 315 patents. Walmart plans to install digital price tags in all U.S. stores by the end of the year, which could allow it to change prices quickly. Solman also reported that McDonald's pushes pricing recommendations to franchisees, and that Wendy's once said it would test dynamic pricing.

Walmart executive Dan Bartlett said in an open letter that the company does not and will not use individual customers' personal information to set individualized prices. McDonald's responded to a price-fixing lawsuit by saying its optional tools do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing. Wendy's former CEO, Kirk Tanner, announced plans to test dynamic pricing and daypart offerings along with A.I.-enabled menu changes. Uber did not respond to requests for comment about Uber Eats delivery fees that varied among Solman's colleagues ordering the same meal. Solman's test showed delivery fees ranging from $2.49 to $4.49 for the same location.

Shoppers are the group most directly affected, and Owens said consumer backlash against Wendy's was swift. Surveys cited in the report found that more than 80 percent of Americans believe businesses should charge all customers the same price for the same item. Economist Richard Thaler, of the University of Chicago, said customers who feel treated unfairly may take their business elsewhere. Owens suggested consumers compare prices across channels, use a VPN to change location, or shop without logging into loyalty programs. She also proposed banning the use of shopper data to set prices.

Earlier practices of charging customers the same price have long been part of the economic debate, and Thaler's research from about 40 years ago asked consumers about pricing fairness. In his snow shovel example, a hardware store that raised its price from $15 to $20 after a blizzard was judged unfair by about 80 percent of respondents. Owens said prices once were more tied to the underlying cost of goods plus a fair margin. The report describes these new tools as built on data gathering, cloud computing and machine learning. Solman noted that the use of such pricing technology appears to be growing.

It remains unclear whether public backlash will be enough to stop companies from using personalized pricing, as Thaler said that is an empirical question. The articles do not establish whether Walmart will follow through on its stated policy, nor whether the Uber Eats fee variations were deliberate or random. Owens said outside observers cannot fully see inside companies' pricing processes. Neither the articles nor the report say whether Owens' policy proposals will be adopted. Consumer protection, as Solman concluded, currently seems to rest largely with shoppers themselves.

Articles.Title: How companies are using AI to make you spend more money

stories.Headline: Railway Says Stolen Customer AI Keys Led to $740,000 in Estimated Unauthorized Usage Charges
stories.Summary:
Railway, a platform-as-a-service provider, said on November 10 that customer AI provider keys stored on its platform were stolen in an October breach and used for an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized spending. The attacker decrypted environment variables in at most 1.85 percent of workspaces, about 100,000, and its database queries searched for AI provider keys. The attack began on October 20, when the attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw in the company's build system to partly escape filesystem isolation. The company said it was alerted at 13:58 UTC that day, about six and a half hours after the first exploit. The attacker was fully removed from the company's systems at 09:24 UTC on October 21.

The company said the decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, covering BYOK agent keys and GitHub OAuth tokens, all of which were reset. Other credentials matched by one database query included cloud, database, and payment service credentials. The company's forensics showed no customer databases were accessed and no indication that customer code repositories were downloaded. The attacker also read the stored histories of 353 builds, including the variables and secrets passed to those builds. Railway emailed customers it judged to be at high risk, and it said the 100,000 workspace figure is an upper limit because its logs show exposed environments but not which variables.

Railway said it cannot refund customers for spend made with compromised API keys, and it has told customers to contact the AI providers directly. It has promised to pay the charges itself where a provider will not refund them. According to the article, AWS Bedrock and Google Gemini cover fraud under existing refund policies, and their account teams have started refunds. OpenAI and SpaceXSI review refunds case by case, with customers filing claims that go to Railway's support team. Anthropic talks are still underway, and Railway will cover costs from breached Anthropic keys in the meantime.

OpenRouter keeps a no-refund policy in its terms of service, so Railway will cover all related costs from the breach. Customers can report unauthorized charges through a charge report form, which says the company is not responsible for usage of these keys but is investigating. The company's incident report says the attacker reached a credential that build servers use, then read internal Temporal histories and cached code snapshots. Using a wrongly configured OIDC binding in a cloud environment, the attacker obtained a short-lived cloud credential at 03:26 UTC on October 21, then took an SSH key that opened a machine running orchestration tasks.

That machine held a credential able to decrypt customer variables through a cloud key management service. Between 04:07 and 05:21 UTC on October 21, the attacker pulled encrypted variables looking for AI provider key names, and decrypted some between 04:42 and 05:14 UTC and again between 06:36 and 07:15 UTC. Railway said the times differ from its preliminary October 22 report, which dated the attack from 13:58 UTC on October 20. Railway said it has filed a complaint with the FBI's IC3 and is working with a specialist forensics firm whose investigation continues.

It is sharing indicators of compromise privately and plans to publish them once law enforcement agrees. The company believes the stolen credentials were used by services that relay or resell access to AI providers for distillation, but it has not established whether the attacker ran those services or named the attacker. Wiz researchers, in their Black October analysis, list this breach among incidents disclosed in October by at least nine AI developer platforms, including the earlier OpenCode breach. Every public report describes attackers hunting for stored environment variables, especially ones granting AI access, the researchers say.

Railway says it has closed every weakness the attacker used, and each build now runs in its own short-lived virtual machine. The articles do not say how the $740,000 figure was estimated or what period it covers. They also do not state a cap or deadline for claims, or whether customers must pay disputed charges while a claim is under review. It is also unclear from the articles whether the attacker ran the relay or resale services the company suspects.

Articles.Title: Railway Says Stolen Customer AI Keys Led to $740,000 in Estimated Unauthorized Usage Charges

stories.Headline: Oracle bets on AI analytics to speed up treasury decisions
stories.Summary:
Oracle, the global technology and cloud applications provider, has launched two AI-assisted analytics applications aimed at banks and insurers, according to a report published on 11 November 2026. The tools are meant to shorten the time between raw data and treasury and customer decisions, as institutions face pressure to act faster on liquidity and profitability signals. The two products, Oracle Financial Services Data Intelligence Treasury Analytics and Oracle Financial Services Data Intelligence Customer Analytics, are now available worldwide. Both build on the AI Assistant and Auto Insights features of Oracle Analytics Cloud, letting business users ask questions in plain language and receive charts while the system flags patterns in the data.

The treasury product is aimed at treasury, finance and risk leaders and brings liquidity, funding, cash flow, balance sheet results and market risk into one connected view. Users can examine funding and liquidity movements, investigate anomalies and trace what is behind shifts in balance sheet performance. The customer product covers profitability per client, product uptake, portfolio results and retention, merging customer, product, channel, geographic, lifecycle and profitability data. Oracle says this reduces the manual work of matching records across customer, ledger, cost management, treasury and risk systems. Both tools sit within Oracle Financial Services Data Intelligence, a suite that consolidates financial, risk and operational data, and they also work alongside on-premises Oracle Financial Services Analytical Applications deployments, so existing clients can move analytics to the cloud without switching off their current systems.

Jason Wynne, senior vice president of product management at Oracle Financial Services, said financial institutions need faster answers they can trust rather than more dashboards. He said the company is combining curated financial services data with conversational AI and automated insight discovery so customers can explore business performance and act on what they find. He described the launch as a foundation for continued AI innovation across Oracle Financial Services. The article does not report any further timeline or plans beyond this launch.

Articles.Title: Oracle bets on AI analytics to speed up treasury decisions

stories.Headline: A new mobile-friendly AI photo editor is on sale for $59
stories.Summary:
A new mobile-friendly AI photo editor called Luminar is on sale for $59, according to a Macworld article published on November 11, 2026. The offer is a lifetime subscription to the Luminar Web and Mobile bundle, which normally costs $206.99. The article presents it as a sponsored deal, and Macworld notes that it may earn a small commission on purchases made through its links. The bundle lets users run the editor in Safari or Chrome on macOS, so no large software install is required. It includes nine core AI tools, among them Enhance AI for color and light, Sky AI for replacing dull skies, and Erase for removing objects from a frame.

Face AI, Skin AI, and Bokeh AI handle portrait retouching and background blur. The plan has no credit system or usage caps, and it allows RAW files to be opened directly in the browser. A single Skylum account can be signed in on as many computers as the user wants. The bundle also includes a lifetime license to Luminar for Mobile for iPhone and iPad, with cloud sync that moves work between devices. A Luminar for Mobile video course and a macrophotography e-book are included as well.

The article frames the deal as an alternative to large Mac photo editors that often carry monthly AI fees. Luminar is the company behind the editor, and Skylum is the account holder named in the offer. The article is a promotional piece that describes the product and the discount without independent testing or comment from the company. It appears alongside several other sponsored deals on the same site that day. The article does not say how long the sale price will last.

Articles.Title: A new mobile-friendly AI photo editor is on sale for $59

stories.Headline: Los Angeles pizzeria fights back against AI photo scam
stories.Summary:
A Los Angeles pizzeria caught a customer who tried to scam it with an AI-generated photo of a ruined pizza. The restaurant, Masa of Echo Park, is a family-owned eatery known for its Chicago-style deep-dish pizzas. A DoorDash customer named "Dani B" ordered a pizza, then later sent a photo of a severely burnt pizza, claiming it was inedible and demanding a full refund. The restaurant's owner, Rhonda Reynolds, saw the problem right away. She said the image looked impossible for the restaurant to have sent out.

Reynolds uploaded the photo to an app called "Is This AI," which said it was 96 percent confident the image was generated by artificial intelligence. She then reviewed the restaurant's security footage of the order being made. The video showed the pizza coming out of the oven and being boxed for delivery, and it did not appear burned. Employee Jose Tapa, who boxed the order, said the box carried the customer's name and order number, and the pizza in the footage did not match the photo. Because of this evidence, the refund that had first been sent to the scammer was successfully reversed.

Reynolds said she was glad she caught the scam but is worried about what comes next. She said this was the first time her business had seen a scam like this, and she fears it will not be the last. She noted that the restaurant has operated for 22 years and is considered busy, and she said dealing with such scams takes time away from running the business. She described the growing use of advanced AI tools by scammers as a frightening new frontier for small business owners. The articles do not say whether the scammer was identified or whether any further action was taken against them.

Articles.Title: Los Angeles pizzeria fights back against AI photo scam

stories.Headline: Lotte On Teams With Plateer to Run Brand Websites With AI
stories.Summary:
Lotte On, the e-commerce platform of Lotte Shopping, announced on November 12 that it will launch an integrated service helping brands build and run their own online stores, developed with Plateer, an artificial intelligence commerce platform company. The two companies signed a memorandum of understanding on November 11 at Lotte Shopping's e-commerce division in Samseong-dong, Seoul. The service is called "New LECS," short for LOTTE Ecommerce Cloud & Service, and it is powered by Plateer's X2BEE platform. The agreement covers an integrated system for the full range of online selling, including creating direct-to-consumer brand websites, managing several brands on one system, processing online orders and offering overseas services.

The service is aimed at brands that have trouble running their own online stores because of price competition with large platforms, high initial setup costs and a lack of dedicated staff. Under New LECS, brands can open their own stores without making a separate system investment. They also receive support across operations such as product management, promotions, customer service, orders and settlement. AI agents take on repetitive work, including product registration, curated sales events and customer inquiries, which the companies say will ease the operational burden on brands.

Choo Dae-sik, head of Lotte Shopping's e-commerce division, said the service was built to reduce the burden of complex store operations so that brands can focus on their core value and grow by meeting customers directly. He said Lotte's long-accumulated operating experience and distribution infrastructure, combined with Plateer's technology, would be used to build an e-commerce ecosystem in which platforms and brands grow together. Lee Sang-hoon, CEO of Plateer, also took part in the signing. The articles do not give a launch date, pricing or the number of brands expected to join.

Articles.Title: Lotte On Teams With Plateer to Run Brand Websites With AI - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: 😸 3 AI labs shipped for you
stories.Summary:
Amazon has unveiled a small flying security drone called the Ring Drone Cam, which sits in a dock inside a home until an alarm, camera, or sensor is triggered. The Drone Cam costs $249.99 and ships January 27, 2027, and it records 2K video while spinning 360 degrees along preset patrol points. Users can also schedule its routes, though scheduling requires a Ring Protect plan. Ring additionally announced the Rover Cam, a $999.99 patrol robot for businesses that is open for preorder and ships December 16. Amazon says both robots rely on Ring's AI Pilot, which maps a space into a floor plan and suggests patrol points.

The Rover Cam rolls to saved spots in a store, performs a 360-degree scan, and raises a periscope mast to look over counters and shelves. It also includes a siren, a light tower, and two-way audio, and Amazon describes it as a guard who never clocks out. AI Pilot uses cameras and vision models to label rooms such as side doors, windows, and long hallways, then steers around furniture in real time. The Drone Cam still needs FCC authorization before Amazon can sell it. Amazon also acknowledges that the Drone Cam's propellers are not quiet.

Amazon is the company behind the Ring devices, and it presented both robots as products for homes and businesses. The articles quote Amazon describing the Rover Cam as a guard who never clocks out. The articles do not give further statements from Amazon beyond the admission about noise and the description of the Rover Cam. The Drone Cam and Rover Cam are aimed at homeowners and businesses that want patrol and monitoring coverage. The articles do not name any other people or groups who responded to the launches.

The articles place the Ring robots within a day of other AI news, when Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI each shipped large new tools. The newsletter that covers these items is The Neuron, and its article is dated November 11, 2026. Ring's robots follow the company's existing camera and alarm products, which the Drone Cam is designed to respond to. The articles give no further history of Ring's robotics efforts. Their coverage is limited to the product details and pricing listed above.

The Drone Cam still awaits FCC authorization, so its sale date depends on that approval. The articles do not say whether the Rover Cam's December 16 shipping date will hold. They also do not state how many units Amazon expects to sell or how the robots will be received by customers. The articles leave open how the Ring AI Pilot system will perform once customers use it in real spaces.

Articles.Title: 😸 3 AI labs shipped for you

stories.Headline: AI Heart MRI Measurements Improve Mortality Prediction
stories.Summary:
A study of more than 27,000 heart MRI patients found that artificial intelligence measurements of heart function predicted mortality slightly better than measurements made by clinicians. The retrospective, multicentre research was published online on 2 November 2026 in The Lancet Digital Health, and it was reported by EMJ on 11 November 2026. The study covered 27,382 patients who had cardiac MRI scans in the UK and the USA, with most scans coming from Barts Heart Centre in London and an additional cohort from the University of Pittsburgh Medical Centre. Researchers applied AI segmentation to the scans and compared the prognostic value of automated and clinician-derived left-ventricular ejection fraction. Over a median follow-up of 5.6 years, 3,458 patients died.

After adjusting for age and sex, the AI measurements gave a C index of 0.781, compared with 0.777 for clinician measurements, a difference the articles describe as modest. The AI-derived figures also offered a better statistical model fit. The researchers said automated analysis took roughly two to three seconds per patient, while earlier work by the team found expert clinician analysis typically took around 13 minutes. Ejection fraction guides decisions on heart failure treatment and implanted devices, so more consistent and efficient measurement could matter across imaging services. The articles stress that this time comparison was not a direct measure of time saved across a whole service.

The researchers, Joy G and colleagues, stressed that human oversight remains necessary, since automated errors were uncommon but clinicians still need to verify measurements and interpret them within the wider clinical picture. The articles say the study shows AI measurements were more closely associated with later mortality, but they do not show that adopting the tool changes treatment decisions or helps patients live longer. The authors and commentary call for prospective evaluation to see whether the small statistical gain translates into better care and how automated measurements perform alongside clinician review in routine workflows. For radiology teams, the findings give a reason to evaluate AI as an initial measurement tool, with its clinical value depending on quality assurance and evidence that faster analysis supports effective patient management.

Articles.Title: AI Heart MRI Measurements Improve Mortality Prediction

stories.Headline: The AI Interview: Chris Bergey, EVP of Edge AI at Arm
stories.Summary:
Arm executive Chris Bergey, executive vice president of Edge AI, explained in an AI Magazine interview published on 11 November 2026 why autonomous agents and local inference are changing device hardware. He leads Arm's Edge AI business, which spans smartphones, PCs, wearables and intelligent endpoints. He described the role as incredibly exciting because the industry has reached another inflection point in how people interact with technology. He said AI inference is being applied more widely and is moving closer to where people use it, on the devices they carry and wear.

The interview gives several figures for Arm's reach: more than 350 billion Arm-based chips shipped to date, over 22 million software developers building on the Arm compute platform, and a 99 percent share of the world's smartphones. It also says Arm-based products are used by 100 percent of the connected global population and that Arm has more than 1,000 technology partners. Arm's new Arm CSS for Mobile 2 platform combines the Arm C2 CPU cluster with SME2 technology, which accelerates AI processing on the CPU. The platform pairs this with an AI-native Mali GPU featuring Arm Neural Technology, along with system IP and software. Arm's software includes KleidiAI, which helps developers optimise AI workloads, and an AI Portal.

Bergey distinguished between making an individual AI task more efficient and reducing the total computing devices perform. He said more efficient inference makes AI practical in more places, enabling new experiences rather than simply reducing the compute required. He pointed to smartphones moving from discrete tasks such as image enhancement or speech recognition toward continuous interaction, multimodal understanding and AI agents. He said an agent may need to interpret speech, retrieve information, maintain context and coordinate multiple applications. He added that Arm sees a similar shift in graphics, where AI reconstructs images and generates frames within mobile power limits, so efficiency expands what is possible.

Bergey argued that agentic AI moves devices from responding to individual requests toward understanding intent, coordinating tasks and acting on a user's behalf. He said humans interact with devices at typing or speaking speed, whereas AI agents can initiate and coordinate operations far faster. He said this creates demands for sustained performance, efficient memory access and management of multiple workloads within tight power and thermal limits. He described the CPU as an important orchestration engine, and said the challenge is shifting from accelerating individual models to coordinating the complete workload. He also said hardware gains only help users when developers can reach them through familiar frameworks and tools.

Bergey said that power efficiency is the fundamental enabler for pushing inference to the edge, though latency, privacy and power are all critical. He said latency is what users notice, and that sending every request to the cloud can introduce delays. He said local processing can reduce the need to send sensitive personal data elsewhere. He described a wearable providing intelligent assistance throughout the day as useful only if it works within a very limited battery and thermal budget. He said he does not see edge and cloud as a choice, since immediate or sensitive tasks may run locally while more demanding reasoning may still rely on the cloud.

The article states that Arm's architecture underpins 99 percent of the world's smartphones and is the basis of the compute platform for the company's partners. It names MediaTek for smartphones, Snap and Meta for wearables, and Microsoft and NVIDIA for PCs, with NVIDIA's RTX Spark mentioned specifically. Bergey said no single company can deliver edge intelligence alone, and that collaboration across silicon, software and devices is required. He concluded that success will be judged by how seamlessly devices fit into daily life rather than by how much AI a device contains. The article does not describe any regulatory action, commercial deadline or reported dispute involving Arm.

Articles.Title: The AI Interview: Chris Bergey, EVP of Edge AI at Arm

stories.Headline: Lee Visits Samsung's Onyang Campus, Hails HBM Packaging Hub
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae-myung said on the 12th that Samsung Electronics' Onyang campus in Asan will become a core base for advanced HBM packaging. He made the remark in a congratulatory address at a groundbreaking ceremony for the Chungcheong mega-project, held at the campus in South Chungcheong Province. The article is dated November 12, 2026, though the photo caption refers to a December 12 ceremony. Lee said three advanced investment projects were breaking ground in Chungcheong with great momentum. Lee said the Asan campus will add a new advanced packaging fab worth 6 trillion won, followed by a further 40 trillion won in advanced equipment investment in stages.

He also congratulated the public on the full-scale start of construction for the Chungcheong investments, which include an advanced semiconductor packaging fab and an advanced display production line in Asan. A manufacturing facility for high-performance substrates for AI servers is being built in Sejong. Lee tied the plan to a bold investment pledge made the previous July by companies and the government. Lee said that promise, made just four months earlier, was now becoming reality at the site. Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jae-yong spoke alongside him at the ceremony, according to the photo caption.

Lee also said the innovation wave is spreading across the entire Chungcheong region, not only Asan and Sejong. The article reports that the article's original reporting came from Jeon Hee-yoon for Seoul Economic Daily and was AI-translated from Korean. Lee added that preparations for construction are proceeding without disruption on a memory and advanced packaging fab in Cheongju, an AI data center in Dangjin and a biopharmaceutical production facility in Osong. The article does not say when these projects will be completed. It also does not describe any response from Samsung beyond the chairman's presence at the event.

Articles.Title: Lee Visits Samsung's Onyang Campus, Hails HBM Packaging Hub - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Shield AI appoints Matt Ofilos as Chief Financial Officer
stories.Summary:
Shield AI has named Matt Ofilos as its new Chief Financial Officer, according to an announcement the company made on 10 November. The appointment was reported by Unmanned Airspace on 11 November 2026. Ofilos moves to Shield AI from Parsons Corporation, where he had served as CFO since 2022 after joining that firm in 2021. Before his time at Parsons, Ofilos worked as CFO of the Worldwide Public Sector division of Amazon Web Services. He also spent nearly two decades at Raytheon in finance leadership roles spanning space, cyber, training and simulation, and air and missile defence.

The articles do not describe any change in responsibilities beyond the new title itself. They also do not say when he starts or what his compensation is. Parsons provides technology solutions for national security and infrastructure markets, which places Ofilos's background in defence and government technology. Shield AI's announcement, as the article reports it, names Ofilos as CFO without further commentary from either company.

The article does not include any statement from Ofilos himself or from Shield AI's leadership about the reasons for the hire. The article is a short appointment notice rather than a broader report, so it does not describe Shield AI's financial position or any plans tied to the new role. Its sidebar lists the publication's regular coverage areas, including counter-drone systems, urban air mobility and jobs and appointments, but it offers no further details about this hire. Beyond the announcement itself, the articles provide no information on what comes next for Ofilos or the company.

Articles.Title: Shield AI appoints Matt Ofilos as Chief Financial Officer

stories.Headline: 5 Best Artificial Intelligence (AI) ETFs to Buy in 2026
stories.Summary:
The Motley Fool has published a guide to five artificial intelligence exchange-traded funds that investors may consider buying in 2026, with the article last updated on November 10, 2026. The funds bundle stocks so that investors do not have to rely on a single company for exposure to AI growth. Artificial intelligence is already changing how companies operate, from recommendation engines and logistics software to chatbots and automation tools. Interest has grown since generative AI tools such as ChatGPT reached the mainstream. AI ETFs have existed for longer than the boom that began with ChatGPT's launch in late 2022, and many of them invest in robotics and semiconductors.

The article's first pick is the Global X Artificial Intelligence and Technology ETF, which the article calls the largest AI ETF, with assets of $9.73 billion and an expense ratio of 0.68%. It launched in 2018 and holds 88 stocks, and its top 10 holdings made up about 33% of the fund in November 2026. Its largest positions include Microsoft, Palantir, Space Exploration Technologies, Tesla and Amazon. According to Global X, the global AI market is expected to grow from $184 billion in 2024 to $826.7 billion in 2030. The article notes that the fund has outperformed over its history, in part because of strong performance by big tech stocks.

The second pick is the Global X Robotics and Artificial Intelligence ETF, established in 2016, which holds 81 stocks and has assets of $3.04 billion. Its top holdings include Intuitive Surgical, FANUC, Keyence, ABB and Nvidia, and the top five made up more than 40% of the fund. The article says the fund is actively managed, carries an expense ratio of 0.68%, and has underperformed the S&P 500 since its 2016 launch. The third pick is the Robo Global Robotics and Automation Index ETF, which holds 79 stocks, has an expense ratio of 0.95% and assets of $1.89 billion. The article says it has also trailed the S&P 500 since its 2013 inception.

The fourth pick is the iShares Future AI and Tech ETF, formed in 2018, which has an expense ratio of 0.47%, the lowest of the five, and about $3.65 billion in assets. It holds 50 stocks, and its top holdings as of October 2026 included Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing and Oracle. The article says the fund has recently outperformed the S&P 500 because of a surge in semiconductor stocks, after underperforming for most of its history. The fifth pick is the First Trust Nasdaq Artificial Intelligence and Robotics ETF, which holds 111 stocks, carries an expense ratio of 0.65% and has assets of $723.4 million. Its holdings include Intuitive Surgical, Ocado Group, Tempus AI, Appian and Meta Platforms.

The article's author is Jeremy Bowman, and the piece was fact-checked by Frank Bass. The article cautions that most AI ETFs have lagged the S&P 500, a broad U.S. stock index, so investors should compare returns and holdings before buying. It also advises comparing annual fees, noting that ARTY charges 0.47% while the robotics-focused ROBO charges 0.95%. The article does not say what the funds will do after 2026.

Articles.Title: 5 Best Artificial Intelligence (AI) ETFs to Buy in 2026

stories.Headline: Should You Buy SoundHound AI Stock After Its 83% Plunge? The Answer Might Surprise You.
stories.Summary:
SoundHound AI stock has fallen 83% from its all-time closing high of $24.23 in late 2024, closing at $4.11 on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. The Motley Fool's Anthony Di Pizio, writing on November 11, 2026, asks whether investors should buy the shares now. The company is a developer of conversational artificial intelligence software, with customers in hospitality, healthcare and automotive manufacturing. The stock now trades near its cheapest level since going public, which the article presents as the reason for reconsidering it.

In May, SoundHound launched the Orchestrated Agent System, called OASYS, where enterprises can build custom AI voice agents for customers and employees. OASYS combines SoundHound's products with those of six companies it acquired over recent years, including Amelia AI and LivePerson. Enterprises can plug in third-party models such as those from OpenAI and Anthropic alongside SoundHound's proprietary speech recognition models. SoundHound says Resorts World Las Vegas used OASYS to build an agent that handles incoming bookings directly from customers. A Latin American company built an agent named Alex that can handle 1,000 phone calls simultaneously and has increased inquiries handled by 30%.

The article reports these claims and figures from the company and its executives, and it names chief executive Keyvan Mohajer as the source of the $1 trillion addressable-market estimate for agentic AI solutions for enterprises. SoundHound itself projected 2026 revenue of $250 million to $260 million, up from its earlier range of $230 million to $260 million, and forecast $350 million to $400 million for 2027. The company says it can eliminate around $120 million in annualized costs during 2027, which could produce profitability on an adjusted EBITDA basis. The article presents these forecasts as management's own expectations rather than independently verified results.

Investors have been concerned about SoundHound's losses, which the article says were $46.4 million on a GAAP basis in the third quarter of 2026, down from $115.9 million in the same quarter of 2025. Third-quarter revenue was a record $62.4 million, up 48.5% from a year earlier, with growth helped by LivePerson's revenue after its acquisition closed in September. The article notes that the acceleration partly reflects that acquisition rather than organic growth alone. Analyst Anthony Di Pizio says his outlook has changed from bearish, given the lower valuation and the potential for adjusted profitability next year.

When SoundHound peaked in 2024, its price-to-sales ratio was above 100, compared with 5.8 for the Nasdaq-100 at the time, and it has now fallen to about 8. The article says this is approaching the stock's cheapest level ever, 6.4 in 2023. Di Pizio writes that investors willing to hold for five years or more could do well, though the article does not say whether the company will reach its profitability target. Its market capitalization is listed at $1.74 billion, and the stock closed at $3.87 on November 10, 2026.
