stories.Headline: Labels required for AI-made dramas
stories.Summary:
China's top broadcast regulator has introduced rules that bring AI-generated short dramas under national oversight for the first time, alongside live-action short dramas. The measures, enacted on Sept 1 by the National Radio and Television Administration, require mandatory pre-release filings, episode-by-episode AI labels, and tiered administrative reviews. The move formalizes an ecosystem that had sat in a regulatory gray zone between casual short videos and full-scale series. It follows a surge in AI production volume paired with viewer complaints about a market described as disordered.

Micro short dramas, serials with episodes typically lasting one to two minutes, have dominated mobile screens across China. Data from the China Network Audiovisual Association shows that media platforms released over 367,000 series in the first half of 2026. AI-generated series accounted for more than 74 percent of that volume, and over 1,500 new AI series are published on mobile platforms daily. According to DataEye, the user base for AI-assisted short series grew from 120 million in 2025 to over 600 million in the first half of 2026. On Douyin, 221,900 AI drama series were published in that period, and only 1,055 of them exceeded 100 million views.

Viewers have complained of repetitive tropes, including domineering executive romances, time-travel themes and instant revenge stories, as well as clickbait, copyright theft and unauthorized digital likeness clones. In March, model Qi Hai found that the AI serial Taohuazan on the Hongguo app featured a character identical to her, down to a distinctive mole, and the series, with 40 million views, used her image without consent. Another production modified its male protagonist after the legal team for actor Luo Yunxi objected to a near-identical digital replica of his likeness. He Biao, deputy director of the National Radio and Television Administration, said at a forum in early November that content quality must be ensured as AI short dramas grow faster. He said the aim is to stabilize volume and improve quality, adding that the boundaries of AI, the copyright bottom line and the ethical bottom line must be held.

Lin Qiwen, vice-president of DataEye, said the measures fill a gap in industry rules and give AI short dramas a clear identity. She described the regulation as ex ante access and whole-chain supervision, compared with the scattered rectification rules of the past two years. Lin said that every episode must display a clear prompt of its synthetic origin, a requirement she said protects viewers' right to know. Lin also said that while major streaming platforms have begun adding mandatory tags at the start of episodes, smaller studios have shrunk disclaimers into screen corners, a practice regulators are working to eliminate. Lin explained that the budget thresholds are meant to prevent creators from mass-producing cheap, high-risk content that bypasses national oversight.

The measures set a three-tiered system based on budget. High-budget AI productions, defined as works with an investment of 800,000 yuan ($120,000) or more, as well as any series covering politics, national security, military or religion, must undergo national NRTA pre-filing, full review and receive a distribution license before release. Mid-tier productions, with budgets between 300,000 and 800,000 yuan, are reviewed and registered by provincial-level broadcast authorities. Productions under 300,000 yuan can be reviewed internally by the hosting platform and assigned a program registration number. Traditional live-action micro dramas typically need budgets of 2 million to 3 million yuan before reaching top-level licensing.

Zhang Lanshan, a professor at Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, said at a seminar in late September that a human-led zone must be established in core narrative links such as creative values, story themes and character emotions. She said AI should expand the boundaries of creation while humans guard the soul of narrative. Zhang said the rules do not require AI dramas to mark where AI is used, only to state that the work is AI-generated, and they do not shut low-cost creation out. Regulators are still refining operational definitions, including the exact percentage of AI assets that triggers mandatory labeling and how self-review standards should be unified across competing platforms. On Nov 6 the NRTA launched a two-month enforcement campaign targeting low-brow themes, copyright violations and technical loopholes.

Articles.Title: Labels required for AI-made dramas - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: Wuxi welcomes global dialogue on AI and intelligent communication
stories.Summary:
The 2026 China International Intelligent Communication Forum opened in Wuxi, Jiangsu province, on November 9, 2026, drawing officials, media leaders, academics and representatives of international organizations. The gathering set out to examine recent progress in intelligent communication and how artificial intelligence might shape the future of global media. China Media Group and the Jiangsu Provincial People's Government jointly hosted the event, which carried the theme "New Ecosystem, New Opportunities, New Future." Organizers presented it as a further step in a series of exchanges focused on media technology and culture.

The forum's main outcome was the Wuxi Initiative, which calls for the responsible use of technology, stronger international partnerships and wider dialogue among civilizations. The initiative aims to build an open, inclusive and cooperative ecosystem for intelligent communication. Separately, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences released the China Cities' International Intelligent Communication Capability Development Report 2026, which looks at how cities pursue international branding and build global influence. Several cultural and media projects were also launched, including a micro-series on how AI is changing daily life and a documentary on the cultural heritage of the Jiangnan region.

Speakers from government and industry addressed the forum's aims. Yu Junsheng, vice-president of China Media Group, described the forum as an important platform for international cultural exchange and media innovation, and called for closer integration of technology, art and content so that AI serves the public good. Xu Ying, head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Jiangsu Provincial Committee, said Jiangsu would use the event to promote digital cultural exchange and international cooperation. Cai Jianfeng, mayor of Wuxi, said the city would develop its AI industry, produce high-quality international content and turn the forum's results into concrete cooperation projects.

The keynote session brought together experts from science, technology, media and the creative industries, including Nobel laureate Michael Levitt, Discovery Channel Greater China Vice-President Vikram Channa and Digital Domain founder Scott Ross. Discussions covered AI-driven change in the media landscape, technological innovation, industrial development and international collaboration. Oleg Kopylov, deputy secretary-general of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, urged stronger international cooperation on AI development and governance. Zamir Ahmed Awan, founding chairman of the Global Silk Route Research Alliance, stressed mutual respect, cultural diversity and shared values. The forum also included a digital culture communication forum, an AIGC industry forum, an international media tour and a film and music evening.

stories.Headline: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
stories.Summary:
China has handed over equipment for a customized version of MAZU, an AI-powered weather prediction tool created by the China Meteorological Administration, to Sri Lanka's meteorological department. The device was presented on Nov. 1, 2026, and is described by domestic media as a rectangular black box roughly the size of a portable toolbox. It will form part of a system to warn of heavy rain, strong winds, and cyclones, and is expected to enter service by the end of the year. Sri Lanka is one of eight countries where the platform has been deployed.

MAZU, launched in July 2025, is named after a Chinese sea goddess revered as a protector of sailors. It pairs AI forecasting models developed by Chinese research institutions with data from China's weather satellites. Conventional forecasting uses supercomputers to calculate atmospheric change from physical equations, while AI models learn from years of weather data. According to the article, one model can produce a 24-hour global forecast in 1.4 seconds, about 10,000 times faster than traditional numerical methods, and for forecasts covering 15 to 60 days it can cut computing costs to one-thousandth of conventional levels. Most of those savings come from routine forecasting, since training models and maintaining systems still require investment that many Global South countries lack.

Niu Zeyi, an assistant researcher at the Shanghai Typhoon Institute who led development of a forecasting model used in MAZU, explained the approach to Sixth Tone. He said these models predict future conditions from current variables such as wind, air pressure, temperature, and humidity. He also said the company's approach is to work with local meteorological agencies to improve datasets, run independent evaluations, and make local adjustments, and that human forecasters must still combine observations, AI predictions, and their own judgment before authorities issue warnings. The article notes that, according to domestic media, MAZU's cloud-based services are being tested by 58 countries, and China plans to deploy the system in 30 countries over the next five years. In Pakistan, the system has reportedly incorporated local radar and satellite data for warnings on heavy rainfall and glacial lake outburst floods, while in Djibouti it helps provide tailored warnings for the port.

The article also cautions about the technology's limits. Studies show AI models can be less accurate than conventional methods when predicting record-breaking extremes, which have little historical data behind them, and local weather in complex terrain remains hard to forecast. It is also not always clear how the models reach their predictions. The article does not describe any specific next steps beyond the Sri Lanka rollout and the planned expansion over the coming years.

Articles.Title: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting - Sixth Tone

stories.Headline: In Depth: China Cracks Down on ‘Poisoning’ AI Chatbots With Fake Marketing
stories.Summary:
Chinese authorities are penalizing companies that deliberately poison AI search results through a practice known as black-hat generative engine optimization, which the tech industry regards as a new form of corporate fraud. Marketing agencies flood the internet with fabricated content to trick AI chatbots into recommending particular brands or inventing products entirely. Three administrative cases this year and a televised exposé by the state broadcaster CCTV have brought the practice to light. The episodes have pushed regulators and courts to consider how to protect consumers when trusted algorithms repeat paid-for falsehoods.

One prominent case involved an 11-person law firm in Guangdong province. A blog article on the Sohu portal, which the firm's head confirmed, presented a fabricated ranking of Guangzhou criminal defense firms for 2026 that placed the firm first with a score of 92.5. When users asked ByteDance's AI model Doubao for good local law firms, it repeated those invented figures as fact. Regulators found the ranking baseless and traced it to Guangzhou Liqing Zhifu Technology, which had bought access to a platform that mass-produced such articles. On Sept. 4, the Yuexiu District Market Supervision Administration fined the company 120,000 yuan, about $17,983, under China's Anti-Unfair Competition Law.

The practice drew national attention in March, when CCTV's annual consumer rights program showed insiders using a "Liqing GEO optimization system" to create fake reviews and promotional articles for a non-existent smart band. Two major AI models soon began recommending that phantom product, and authorities in Beijing's Huairou district are investigating the firm behind the system. Black-hat methods work by padding answers with added citations, invented statistics and fabricated consensus, while legitimate white-hat optimization simply structures verifiable information so algorithms can process it. Enforcement so far has mainly targeted the agencies that carry out the campaigns, since all three public penalties this year, in Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Beijing, were against service providers.

The question of whether AI platforms are liable for harm caused by such content remains unsettled. Yao Jia, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of Law, said courts cannot assume consumer injury merely because a chatbot gave a false recommendation. Chen Bing, director of Nankai University's Center for Competition Law, argued that platforms should neither face strict punishment for citing poisoned data nor receive blanket immunity on grounds of technological neutrality. Industry responses are also emerging: DeepSeek says its search tool filters out GEO manipulation, and in August a Chinese technology association published standards banning prompt injection attacks. On Sept. 7, the Supreme People's Court issued guidelines stating that anyone who uses AI to infringe, advertise falsely or compete unfairly must bear legal liability.

Articles.Title: In Depth: China Cracks Down on ‘Poisoning’ AI Chatbots With Fake Marketing - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub
stories.Summary:
Security firm Apiiro has reported that AI coding assistants may be leaking thousands of secrets into public GitHub repositories through what look like routine exchanges between developers and these tools. The research found 2,539 credentials spread across nearly 2,000 public GitHub repositories, in a report published online recently. Apiiro tracked some of the leaked data to Claude Code, which copied secrets into a hidden file and committed them alongside the developer's other code without users knowing. The report was written by Apiiro researchers Shmulik Cohen and Matan Giladi. Exposed items included database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens, and SSH root logins.

Apiiro examined 104,185 publicly accessible copies of a file named .claude/settings.local.json on GitHub, and 1,122 of those files contained real secrets. Those files held 1,379 distinct secrets, made up of 636 provider-specific keys and 743 passwords or tokens associated with public hosts. Among the 1,105 repositories containing real secrets that the researchers investigated, 539 had a commit co-authored by Claude Code that modified the affected settings file. Specific leaks included a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key, a production Azure Postgres password, a Square production token, and the owner password of a medical-records database. Most of the secrets belong to individual developers across 63 organizations, ranging from student groups to startups, software agencies, and established vendors.

Apiiro contacted Anthropic about the issue before publishing its findings. After publication, Boris Cherny, Anthropic's head of Claude Code, said in public comments that the tool historically has not scrubbed secrets. He added that the company is looking into what it can do to prevent the exposure Apiiro described. Possible approaches include making sure auto mode catches the exposure or building in basic secrets scanning, among other ideas. Anthropic will prototype these options to understand the tradeoffs before shipping something in the next version of Claude Code, Cherny said.

Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at database security firm Liquibase, said a developer approves a command to save time and the AI agent keeps the credentials as part of that approval. Those credentials can then end up in a public repository, and in his words nobody intended to expose them, but the workflow made it possible. Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of AI penetration testing firm BreachLock, called the action a dead zone for developers, who likely have no idea they have just exposed a secret. He said a "don't ask again" prompt is a decision to write a credential into a file that many developers clicking it likely do not know exists.

Sehgal added that the file lands in a place many secret scanners were never built to check, which appears to be why some of these leaks slipped through. McCurdy also warned that agent configuration files, transcripts, and execution histories can contain sensitive information that traditional security checks may not catch. The leak stems from how Claude Code carries out certain commands, since a command to check a database or call an API carries the secret from the user's config file. The tool asks the user before running the command, and if the choice is "Yes, and don't ask again," it saves that exact command, secret included, to .claude/settings.local.json inside the project folder.

Nothing in the repository marks that file as private, so it gets committed with the rest of the code. Claude Code does try to protect the file in a Git repository by adding it to the developer's global Git ignore list, which tells Git to ignore it on that machine. That protection is not built into the project, and the ignore rule does not travel with the repository when it is cloned onto another machine, because the rule never goes into the repository's own .gitignore. Anthropic has not yet shipped a fix, and the changes Cherny described remain ideas that the company will prototype before releasing them in the next version of Claude Code.

In the meantime, Apiiro recommends that developers rotate every credential a file has ever held. It also advises them to delete every rule containing a secret, even if a file was never committed to a project. Security teams should treat all AI agent folders as secret-bearing on laptops as well as in repositories, and add them to pre-commit and secret scanning, including history. The articles do not say which of Cherny's approaches Anthropic will choose, or when the next version of Claude Code will arrive.

Articles.Title: AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon
stories.Summary:
Artex, an open source AI penetration-testing framework written in Go, was published to GitHub in July by independent developer Autumn-27. Threat actors took the legitimate tool and turned it into a weapon, and by late summer and early fall a range of them were using it. Artex can brute-force passwords, dump databases and enumerate and abuse APIs, and because of its agentic design it can operate at inhuman speeds. Microsoft observed an AI agent move from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes. Steve Winterfeld, advisory CISO for Akamai, said the campaigns showed acceleration in speed, coordination and autonomy.

At the end of October, Artex's creator deleted the original GitHub repository because of rampant abuse, but many forks remain available. GitGuardian detailed 45 other agentic attack frameworks, which it called Artex "siblings," capable of conducting attacks autonomously with an AI model. Depending on the tool, these frameworks can carry out end-to-end attacks against a network, target web applications or perform autonomous coding. Some include built-in command-and-control functionality. The researchers noted that pen-testing tools have many legitimate uses, so the frameworks are not inherently bad.

China's Storm-0940 adapted Artex source code into its own offensive infrastructure. Around October 10, the actor used Artex to launch a password-spraying and credential-stuffing campaign against more than 300 user accounts at eight critical organizations, making over 151,000 authentication requests. When that largely failed, Storm-0940 targeted ConnectWise's internal infrastructure and stole OAuth application credentials for its Cloud Backup application. Those credentials let the attackers compromise more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 and Azure environments within three hours of initial targeting. Microsoft separately said a Cambodia-based threat cluster, Storm-3358, used Artex against financial organizations, primarily in Southeast Asia.

CrowdStrike connected Artex-powered espionage activity to a threat actor it tracks as Vapor Panda on October 29. India's CERT-In tracked a financially motivated actor hitting financial institutions. As of November 4, Censys observed more than 1,400 internet-exposed Artex console deployments, and it estimated actual global use was higher because internet exposure is not required. GitGuardian's Guillaume Valadon said that in a sealed lab, Artex found eight of nine planted secrets in every run where it acted, including an AWS key recovered from git history. Matt Snyder of Aviatrix said many threat actors deploying the framework appear operationally immature.

Microsoft's Storm-3358 blog includes extensive indicators of compromise and recommends considering defensive honeypots. Check Point advised organizations to expect greater automated pressure against exposed infrastructure and to test and harden internet-facing systems. Censys researcher Silas Cutler said the underlying tradecraft is conventional, so the fundamentals still hold: enforce MFA, monitor the attack surface and practice good credential hygiene. The articles do not say whether the forks of Artex will be taken offline. They also do not describe how many organizations were ultimately compromised beyond those named.

Articles.Title: Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Intezer, a security firm, recently tested how easily artificial intelligence tools can reverse-engineer well-known software, and found the work far easier than before. They picked high-profile targets: Slack, Apple's Finder app, and the Turla malware. Intezer senior security researcher and malware analyst Nicole Fishbein said AI lowers the bar, since the work once demanded experience, an understanding of Assembly, and a great deal of time. The researchers reported that the Turla malware proved the hardest of the three to wrangle. Dark Reading published the account on Nov. 10, 2026.

The researchers built a different harness for each target, a harness being a tool that focuses AI models on one task, supplies the tools they need, and sets their permissions. For the malware they used a Python control plane wrapped around a compiler, with a virtual machine, static analysis tools, and several large language models. An Orchestrator agent splits the binary into smaller functions, using tools such as Binary Ninja, and sends them to sub-agents, one reconstructing and another testing. They ended up with a replica of Turla's full working pipeline, covering command handling and file transfer. The Finder copy handled everyday actions such as file operations and local search, but they could not copy its internal structure precisely.

They rebuilt the full Slack client very simply, though its server proved much harder to reconstruct. Fishbein, who spoke for the research, said the malware harness was built to be careful, with an extra model added so that nothing would be executed. She said some cases let Claude simply reconstruct the source code, while in others Claude refused, which is why each harness differed. Her motive for the Slack and Finder tests was a curiosity about people who vibe code apps that mimic common ones, and about how closely that could be done. She noted that a researcher without tight deadlines gains a lot of information from recreating the full picture without missing key components.

She advised vendors to first define which outcomes they want to prevent, and said that for now keeping server-side infrastructure unexposed protects them. Others have shown the same trend in real attacks. On Sept. 10, Anthropic released a report on how threat actors abuse its models, including the Russian actor Midnight Blizzard, which mainly targets Ukraine's government, military, and diplomatic staff. That group stole a complete proprietary software development kit for a drone vision system and, over several days with help from Claude, reverse engineered it. The same report described a Chinese campaign that included malware development, reconnaissance against foreign governments' networks, and vulnerability discovery in major endpoint security products.

Fishbein also sees lower-tier actors leaking malware source code or recreating it as open source. Vendors, security defenders, and the upstanding masses are all affected, and last month an open source tool and Model Context Protocol server called REA, short for Reverse Engineer Anything, became the most popular program on GitHub. The article describes household applications as running on hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of lines of code, with hundreds of third-party libraries, many files, and complex webs of interconnected components. Unpacking and mapping all of that was once so difficult that it is now notable that even small teams and individuals can do it.

It says Finder relied on files managed by cloud services and on macOS services whose results the original did not reveal. Slack offered little that its JavaScript source code did not make easy to unpack. The researchers also recreated Apple's and Salesforce's proprietary apps with only moderate difficulty, and Dark Reading described the findings as raising both opportunities and concerns for organizations and analysts. For protection, the article suggests developers borrow from hackers' playbooks, using encryption, obfuscation, possibly with AI help, and other anti-analysis measures.

Fishbein said encryptors and anti-cheating mechanisms that have existed for a while would also help. She added that it is hard to tell how long they will hold, given that every new model gets better every month. The article does not say which defenses will prove effective or how quickly vendors will adopt them. It also leaves open whether attackers would ignore server infrastructure and pursue only source code, a point it raises as a possibility for Salesforce.

Articles.Title: AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: People Are Getting Weird About AI
stories.Summary:
Dark Reading's Becky Bracken interviewed Jaya Baloo, CISO and COO of Aisle, for a podcast episode published on November 10, 2026, with the headline framing AI's effect on people. The episode grew out of a talk Baloo gave at the ISC2 Security Congress in Denver, where she discussed merging AI and quantum technology. Bracken said the segment stuck with her for days and that she had heard few technologists explain the phenomenon so plainly. Bracken also noted that Sam Altman had recently said no one needs their own RAM, a remark that drew mockery online.

Baloo said that the uncanny valley has been passed, so people now readily believe conversations with AI could come from another human. She said the tendency to anthropomorphize AI is growing, and that some users develop a delusional belief that they are superintelligent or destined to save humanity. Baloo argued that the current state of AI makes such susceptibility worse because the systems are so convincing. She added that people then tend to make the systems more human.

Baloo used a video of the Unitree humanoid robot doing kung fu to illustrate her concern, asking why such machines cannot be taught to do laundry instead. She said the robot was announced at the end of October and demonstrated on YouTube, and that it can cause physical harm. Baloo said Unitree had two remote backdoors in its quadruped robots and that its humanoid robots have multiple security issues. She said manufacturers should rethink how such devices are positioned in light of the Cyber Resilience Act, and that security must be sorted out before physical deployment.

Baloo also criticized the polarized debate over AI consciousness, noting that Anthropic has discussed potential AI consciousness with religious leaders at the Vatican while others reject AI in the name of Jesus. She questioned whether the claims of sentience are real or a marketing ploy, and said the framing reduces a debate about responsible AI into two camps. Bracken asked how much of the hype is driven by frontier-model marketing from figures such as Altman and Peter Thiel. Baloo responded that AI-driven vulnerability discovery and automated hacking frameworks, including Strix, RTec-Ai and Cairn, are genuinely happening and being used in real-world hacks.

Baloo urged the sector to heed former GCHQ head Ciaran Martin's call to calm the fear, uncertainty and doubt, and said that containment measures such as egress filtering and sandboxing still apply. She said defense in depth means assuming one measure fails and having countermeasures in place. Baloo called for better observability of AI systems, including understanding how training data was populated so that poisoning or Trojaning could be detected, even with open-weight models. The articles provided do not describe any specific next steps or regulatory outcomes beyond the calls Baloo made.

Articles.Title: People Are Getting Weird About AI - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them
stories.Summary:
F-Secure, the Finnish consumer cybersecurity company, has released a new AI Harms Taxonomy that identifies 26 distinct ways artificial intelligence can harm consumers, announced on November 10, 2026. The framework was developed by Dr. Megan Squire, Principal Threat Intelligence Researcher at F-Secure, and traces how each harm travels through AI systems until it reaches a person. Its stated purpose is to show where protections can intervene and which parties are best placed to provide them. The research addresses a gap in how AI risk is usually discussed, since many frameworks list possible failures without linking them to the systems and companies that could prevent them.

The taxonomy currently maps the 26 harms across five relationship types and 19 intermediary layers, and it proposes 24 defenses aimed at different points along those paths. The harms range from AI-generated voice and video impersonation to agents making harmful financial decisions, exposing personal information, or acting on outdated context. The research also examines attacks in which malicious instructions are hidden in content that an AI system processes, which could steer an agent's actions or a chatbot's answers. Some risks can be handled by security software on a person's own device, while others must be addressed upstream by the companies that build AI products, including how those systems retain memory and which external services they connect to. Dr. Squire said that developers have a responsibility to understand how their systems can fail, who gets hurt when they do, and to put safeguards in place before harm occurs.

According to the announcement, the shift from AI producing information to AI acting on it makes the question of responsibility more pressing. A chatbot that gives a wrong answer can mislead a user, but an agent with access to a person's accounts can cause real consequences without the person being part of each step. The research also suggests that individuals cannot protect themselves alone by spotting suspicious content or double-checking AI output. The work sits within a wider F-Secure effort around trust in the AI era, which includes F-Secure Trust, a strategic alliance with Quantum AI Lab QuTwo, and two products, TrustGuard and TrustPath. The taxonomy is available on the company's Illuminate Research Hub, and the article does not report any regulatory response or further timeline beyond that.

Articles.Title: F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Trustworthiness key battleground in next phase of AI devt: scientists
stories.Summary:
Experts gathered at an AI parallel forum of the 2026 World Laureates Forum in Shanghai, where they called for stronger efforts to build trustworthy artificial intelligence. The discussion took place recently and was reported by the Science and Technology Daily on Monday, with scientists and industry representatives addressing emerging challenges in AI development and application. The remarks came as the technology advances rapidly, and speakers framed reliability and effective governance as likely key factors in global AI competition. The reporting makes clear that the call was aimed at the whole field rather than a single product or company.

He Jifeng, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and professor emeritus at East China Normal University, argued that AI should not become an opaque black box. He said trustworthiness must be built into the entire research and development process instead of being treated as an abstract principle. He pointed to explainability, verifiability and traceability as core requirements, along with formal methods and alignment technologies that build safety mechanisms into the stages of knowledge understanding and risk mitigation. His position is that these features must be designed in from the start rather than added afterward.

Dong Yinpeng, chief scientist of the Chinese third-party AI safety company Fangcun AI, told the Global Times that integrating safety from the outset is becoming more urgent. He said a major bottleneck in current AI safety research is its reliance on a reactive approach, in which vulnerabilities are found after a system is built and then patched. Dong argued this approach is increasingly inadequate because AI vulnerabilities are not static, and new risks may emerge as models grow more capable. He also warned that the consequences of AI-related security failures are growing, noting that some models have already shown autonomous attack capabilities and could potentially pose risks to real-world critical infrastructure. Waiting for damage before acting, he said, could cause significant losses.

Beyond technical security, the reporting says practical adoption of AI faces governance and implementation problems, including poor data quality, difficulty fitting AI into existing business operations, and challenges in measuring the value AI projects generate. Experts warn that the gap between fast-moving technological capability and slower regulation has become a major constraint on wider adoption. Trustworthy AI, the speakers suggested, should not be treated as a one-time compliance exercise but as oversight across the full lifecycle of a system, from research and development through deployment and operation. Separately, Noga Alon, a 2024 Wolf Prize in Mathematics laureate and professor at Princeton University, said AI has shown strong ability on mathematical problems but largely uses existing methods rather than inventing new ones.

Articles.Title: Trustworthiness key battleground in next phase of AI devt: scientists - Global Times

stories.Headline: Despite rising ROI on AI, infrastructure woes persist
stories.Summary:
Tech leaders reported higher returns on their AI investments this year, but their readiness to handle external risks has dropped, according to a Tuesday report from Kyndryl. The service provider surveyed 3,700 senior business leaders across 21 countries for the report. Many enterprises are finding it hard to move from AI experimentation to broader adoption, particularly where workforce and talent are concerned. Less than one-third of tech leaders said they had formally updated roles to reflect AI responsibilities or set up a change management system for AI adoption.

Security topped the list of external concerns, with recent hacking incidents involving OpenAI, Hugging Face and Anthropic's Claude models cited as contributing factors. Kyndryl CIO Kim Basile said that while cybersecurity has matured quickly, threat actors are also moving faster and using the technology to multiply their attacks. As technology environments grow more interconnected and AI takes on a larger role in operations, leaders need better visibility into their systems and a clearer picture of their vulnerabilities. Leaders also voiced concern about AI reshaping industries beyond their own, which could erode established boundaries and business models. Digital sovereignty was another worry as they consider how their technology stacks will evolve.

Despite these setbacks, AI adoption matured across enterprises this year, with fewer than half of the leaders surveyed still in the experimentation phase. Nearly half substantially changed their AI strategies across technology, people and governance, and 21% said they had canceled a major AI initiative after it failed. Infrastructure remains a concern, as 71% of respondents said they were nearly or fully modernized, yet two-thirds of CIOs believed their tech foundations still needed significant work before they could scale AI. Ismail Amla, SVP of Kyndryl Consult, said the real obstacles for most enterprises are non-technical, centering on how work changes and whether employees are incentivized, trained and prepared to work alongside AI agents.

Amla described the challenge as a human change layered on top of the familiar people, process and technology issues. Basile urged CIOs to work with other members of the C-suite and bring people along so they can make a difference with the technology. Kyndryl's findings suggest that rising AI returns will depend on resolving these security, infrastructure and workforce gaps. The articles do not say what specific steps Kyndryl or the companies surveyed plan to take next.

Articles.Title: Despite rising ROI on AI, infrastructure woes persist - CIO Dive

stories.Headline: Kyndryl says firms lag on AI readiness despite gains
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl, an IT infrastructure services group, published a readiness report on 10 November 2026 saying that many large organisations are not prepared for AI despite gains. The report found that 64% of business and technology leaders now report positive returns from AI and machine learning investments. Only 24% say their organisations are fully prepared to manage external risks. Overall readiness fell seven percentage points from the previous year, with cyber security readiness showing the steepest decline, down 11 points. The findings describe a divided picture as AI moves beyond pilots into wider deployment.

Four in 10 leaders believe their data is not ready for AI at scale, according to the report, and those organisations report AI-related failures at twice the rate of firms that believe their data is ready. Kyndryl found that 71% of leaders say they have mostly or fully modernised their technology estate, yet 58% say it needs significant re-architecture before it is ready for AI at scale. Only 27% of respondents said they had formally redesigned roles around AI, down from expectations last year that AI would transform roles within 12 months. Companies must also set clear answers on decision-making, human intervention, outcome ownership and performance measurement. Kyndryl's Kyndryl Agentic Framework and Kyndryl Bridge are described as tools for governing AI agents and observing live systems.

Martin Schroeter, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Kyndryl, said AI is creating real value but raising the bar for readiness, and that value depends on technology, people and process together. Kim Basile, Kyndryl's Chief Information Officer, said chief information officers face pressure to move quickly while protecting core systems, and that many leadership teams mistake a promising pilot for proof of wider readiness. Basile also argued that governance should not be treated as the opposite of speed, and that architecture, governance and cyber security must work together from the start. Ismail Amla, Kyndryl's Global Consult Lead, said the main challenge is rewiring the organisation rather than deploying the technology itself. Schroeter said the same issue is one of control, particularly for customers in Europe focused on where data sits and who controls operations.

The affected groups named in the coverage are large organisations, chief information officers and boards, and customers in sensitive sectors such as government, particularly in Europe. Amla warned that some businesses attach AI to inefficient processes, which limits improvement, and that AI is lowering barriers that once defined industries. He also described a concern he called "sovereignty debt", meaning technology decisions that reduce a company's ability to switch providers or move workloads. Amla said earlier consolidation and standardisation improved efficiency but increased concentration and dependency in parts of the technology stack. Schroeter said some organisations are moving towards different operating systems and open-source options to retain more control.

Asked about next steps, Schroeter recommended role-based education and skills development, noting that some employees remain uneasy or resistant. The report follows a period in which many companies moved from testing AI to broader use, which Schroeter said exposed operational problems. Basile said many companies have already learned hard lessons after AI projects failed in production. Amla noted that AI often lands in organisations with existing systems, established workflows and fixed accountability structures, making costs harder to predict once AI is added to live systems. Schroeter said fewer organisations now describe themselves as being in the experimentation phase with AI.

The articles describe companies that have seen value from AI while remaining exposed by weak data foundations, uneven governance and slow workforce redesign. The articles do not say what specific measures companies will take in response to the report, nor how the readiness decline will develop in future surveys. They also do not give the sample size or methodology behind the survey figures. Schroeter said Kyndryl tracks whether AI leads to better decisions and stronger learning among engineers working on customer systems, but the articles do not report results of that tracking. Whether companies will shift from productivity-focused AI projects to growth ambitions, as some customers are beginning to do, is not settled by the coverage.

Articles.Title: Kyndryl says firms lag on AI readiness despite gains - IT Brief UK

stories.Headline: AI medical innovations take center stage at 9th CIIE
stories.Summary:
At the ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai, a range of AI medical solutions were unveiled and became a main highlight of the expo's medical equipment and healthcare products exhibition area. The technology has moved beyond imaging assistance into surgical navigation, chronic disease management, and intelligent decision-making during medical interventions. The CIIE is described as a key platform for testing AI applications, connecting with hospitals, and speeding up their adoption. The reporting presents these developments as a sign of how quickly the technology is being put to use in clinical settings.

Roche is showing solutions built with ecosystem partners that combine AI and digital tools across the industrial chain, aimed at breaking down data barriers and improving precision in diagnosis and treatment. One tool is a one-stop AI research aid that helps doctors choose topics, review literature, and generate solutions, which the company says will raise research efficiency. Another is a digital remote patient management system that sends follow-up reminders and provides disease education so patients can manage their health at home. Haier's healthcare arm, Incaier, is presenting six AI-driven scenarios, including autonomous labs, autonomous drug management, and proactive health. Incaier also launched an AI strategy built around a central "Incaier brain," and it says its platform serves researchers, healthcare professionals, and patients and already has more than 450 AI-native applications.

Australian biopharmaceutical company CSL signed an agreement at the CIIE with Beijing's Peking Union Medical College Hospital to explore using AI to identify and help diagnose hereditary angioedema, a rare disorder that causes recurring swelling attacks. A hospital representative said the partnership hopes to use advanced AI algorithms to support traditional lab testing and move cutting-edge technology into clinical tools more quickly. The hospital expects this to improve early diagnosis and screening efficiency for clinicians. Philips, in its 2026 China edition of the Future Health Index report released at the CIIE, also highlighted the growing clinical value of AI and the rise of human-machine collaborative medical teams. Philips China's chief regional leader, Liu Ling, said China is actively bringing AI into medical practice and is becoming a leading force in global medical AI applications.

The Philips report found that 95 percent of Chinese clinical healthcare workers surveyed said their focus has shifted or will shift toward higher-value clinical work, compared with a global average of 82 percent. It also found that 81 percent of Chinese patients surveyed believe learning to use AI will become an essential skill for health management, against a global average of 59 percent. In addition, 69 percent of Chinese healthcare workers said they believe AI helps improve patient health outcomes. Taken together, the figures suggest that Chinese respondents are more optimistic than their global counterparts about the role of AI in both clinical work and personal health management.

Articles.Title: Medical AI center stage at 9th CIIE - China Daily

stories.Headline: LTIMindtree stock shifts wage hikes toward AI reskilling - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
LTIMindtree announced on Thursday, November 5, 2026, that its annual pay increases would be split between January and April instead of being granted in a single cycle. According to the Economic Times, the policy is tied to artificial-intelligence reskilling and reflects shifting client demand across the technology-services industry. Chief Executive Officer Venu Lambu said half of employees would receive increases effective January 1, with the rest effective April 1. He ruled out retrenchment or any workforce restructuring linked to the change.

Lambu explained that the company is using training to keep pace with faster AI adoption and customer pressure on pricing. Management said revenue growth has become less dependent on adding employees. The company added 2,500 fresh graduates through its training programs, and its employee count reached 86,447 at the end of September. These figures show a workforce being shaped around new skills rather than expanded in headcount.

The company reported second-quarter net income of 1,381 crore rupees, up 10.4 percent year over year, on revenue of 10,394 crore rupees, up 10.2 percent. Management expects the second half of the year to be slightly better than the first. It is also preparing a five-year growth strategy that it said could be announced in December. LTM Limited, formerly LTIMindtree Limited, is a global technology consulting and digital-solutions company headquartered in Mumbai, India.

Articles.Title: LTIMindtree stock shifts wage hikes toward AI reskilling - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: CoreWeave AI Cloud Revenue Climbs 168% as Backlog More Than Doubles
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported its third-quarter 2026 results on November 10, 2026, showing revenue up 168% from a year earlier to $3.661 billion. Its revenue backlog reached about $132.5 billion, and the company raised its full-year outlook. The AI cloud provider's net loss widened to $709 million as interest and depreciation costs rose. Those figures came in the company's earnings presentation.

The company credited strong execution, favorable pricing and customer demand for its AI cloud platform for the growth. Backlog rose 138% from $55.6 billion a year earlier, with AI labs, hyperscaler customers, enterprises and AI-native companies all adding to it. Backlog represents committed future revenue under contracts rather than revenue already earned. CoreWeave expects 36% of it to be recognized within 24 months, 38% in months 25 through 48 and 26% after 48 months. Active power exceeded 1.7 gigawatts after more than 200 megawatts were added during the quarter.

Operating income improved to $207 million from $52 million, lifting operating margin to 6% from 4%. Net interest expense rose to $846 million from $310 million, and depreciation and amortization climbed to $1.889 billion from $630 million. Those increases explain why the net loss widened from $110 million despite the stronger operating result. Company-defined capital expenditures reached $14.5 billion, compared with $1.85 billion a year earlier.

CoreWeave raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion from the previous $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion. Full-year capital expenditures are now expected at $37 billion to $39 billion, with the low end raised from $35 billion because the company expects to deploy infrastructure sooner than planned. During the quarter it raised about $4.2 billion in convertible notes and closed a $2.6 billion term-loan facility. CEO Michael Intrator said about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits is expected over the next three months.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave AI Cloud Revenue Climbs 168% as Backlog More Than Doubles - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: A vision for harnessing AI for humanity
stories.Summary:
China's "AI Plus" action plan, adopted by the State Council in August 2025, positions artificial intelligence as a foundational element across science, industry, agriculture, public administration and healthcare rather than only a tool for the tech sector. An opinion piece in China Daily, written by the chairman of the Turkish-Chinese Business Development and Friendship Association, argues that the most significant change from AI is taking place in factories, farms and hospitals rather than on consumer screens. The author asks who will benefit from the productivity gains and whether technology will serve people or the profit motives of a few corporations. The article presents China's approach as a model, though it notes Turkiye cannot simply copy it.

According to the piece, AI in manufacturing is being built into every stage of production, from design and pilot testing to mass production and operations. Digital twins simulate production lines before factories are built, machine vision supports quality control, and predictive algorithms flag machine failures before they happen. The author says China's advantage rests on four pillars: a comprehensive industrial supply chain, large volumes of real-world production data, engineering capacity to scale lab innovations, and close alignment among government, academia and industry. The stated aim is higher-quality goods using less energy and fewer raw materials, with workers freed from heavy, dangerous and repetitive jobs.

The author credits the "Education Power Construction Plan 2024-35" with linking educational outcomes to national modernization goals, and says barriers between universities and factories are being removed through joint research platforms. Vocational education is described as being elevated to a cornerstone of technological modernization, with companies helping design curricula and students training in real production settings. The article also says that practical human expertise must be captured in digital systems for the real economy to be transformed. On global governance, it cites the Global AI Governance Action Plan published in July 2025, which calls for safe, controllable and inclusive AI, and the founding in Shanghai in July 2026 of the World AI Cooperation Organization by 29 nations, which aims to support cooperation on policy, technology and governance.

For Turkiye, the author recommends tying AI policy to industrial strategy, measuring academic success by the translation of research into production as well as citation counts, and making AI infrastructure accessible to small and medium-sized enterprises. The author suggests focusing on strengths such as automotive, textiles, agriculture and defense through joint AI production centers linking universities, vocational schools and manufacturers. The piece concludes that the countries that integrate AI most effectively into factories, schools and everyday production will lead, and that success should be judged by whether AI brings shared prosperity. The article reflects the author's views rather than those of China Daily.

Articles.Title: A vision for harnessing AI for humanity - China Daily

stories.Headline: CoreWeave beats quarterly revenue estimates as AI demand defies growing doubts
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, the AI cloud company backed by Nvidia, reported third-quarter results that beat analyst expectations, and executives said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that they expect the company to become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028. The company's revenue surged nearly 170% to $3.66 billion, above the $3.55 billion estimate, and its per-share loss of 95 cents was smaller than the $1.16 loss analysts expected. Shares were up about 5% in volatile extended trading after falling more than 40% over the past month. The stock had become the focal point of fears about an AI bubble, with investors worried about heavy borrowing to build data centers as interest rates rise.

CoreWeave said its contracted revenue backlog reached $132.5 billion at the end of September, up from $104 billion at the end of June. Quarterly capital spending rose to $14.5 billion from $9.4 billion in the prior quarter. The company now expects 2026 revenue of $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion, compared with its earlier range of $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion, and it raised the low end of its annual spending target by $2 billion to a projected $37 billion to $39 billion. CEO Mike Intrator said in a statement that customer contracts come first and that investment follows, and he disclosed $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected to flow in over the next three months. The company also said it would not tap unsecured debt markets at current yields and would rely on cash flow from customer commitments to repay debt.

Intrator is responsible for the company's public explanation of its strategy, and he argued that lenders have concrete collateral because the spending is tied to committed demand. CoreWeave has never turned a profit, according to data compiled by LSEG, and carried about $46.9 billion in total debt as of the end of September. Its customers include Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic. The results came as the broader AI trade faced a crisis of confidence, which was amplified by Democrats' sweeping win in the US midterm elections that has raised expectations of tighter regulation of the data-center build-out. Recent earnings reports from hyperscalers also hinted at delays in data-center projects and a slower ramp in spending.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave beats quarterly revenue estimates as AI demand defies growing doubts - WTVB

stories.Headline: Indonesia to promote regional cooperation, AI innovation at APEC meeting - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
Indonesia plans to push for stronger regional economic cooperation, more inclusive trade and new opportunities in artificial intelligence at the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. The announcement was made on Wednesday, November 11, by a senior official, according to Xinhua. The Director General for Asia-Pacific and African Affairs at Indonesia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Santo Darmosumarto, spoke at a press briefing in Jakarta. He said APEC remains a strategic platform for economic growth and for tackling challenges shared across the region.

Darmosumarto said Indonesia's priorities include better regional connectivity, stronger supply chains and more inclusive trade and investment. He noted that a particular focus would be expanding opportunities for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. On technology, he described AI as an important area for collaboration among APEC economies, especially to ensure emerging technologies benefit developing countries. He also stressed the importance of cooperation in building a more open, equitable and resilient Asia-Pacific region.

Darmosumarto said Indonesia would promote the safe, responsible and human-centered use of AI. He added that Indonesia is seeking closer cooperation in agriculture, energy, women's empowerment, transportation and natural resources. The articles provided do not give the exact dates of the Shenzhen summit or describe any specific agreements or commitments. They also do not report reactions from other APEC members.

Articles.Title: Indonesia to promote regional cooperation, AI innovation at APEC meeting - Xinhua

stories.Headline: [Field Report] AI technology leaves the lab and sets sail for the market with Kakao
stories.Summary:
On the morning of November 10, 2026, AI startup teams from four Korean science and technology institutes presented their technologies to investors at Kakao AI Campus in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province. The teams came from KAIST, GIST, DGIST and UNIST, and the event was Kakao AI Sail: Set Sail, Season 2, an AI startup competition run by Kakao Investment Co., Ltd. and kakao AI sail. The program aims to find promising AI technologies and link them with investment and proof-of-concept projects at Kakao affiliates. A total of 122 teams applied this year, about 85% more than the 66 in the first edition, and 12 of them reached the finals.

Kakao affiliates, including Kakao, KakaoBank, Kakao Mobility, Kakao Entertainment and Kakao Pay, set 18 challenges tied to business needs, and teams proposed technologies and business models to meet them. Rokon, which won the top prize, presented a way for AI to learn knowledge spread across a company, automating a task that once required specialist engineers and took three to six months, now done in an average of two to three hours at about 90% of the existing method's performance. Its work agent, Puzzle, could be paired with Kakao's AI service Kanana to serve 10.2 million employees at small and medium-sized businesses. Millitrack and Space AI won excellence awards, and five teams received honorable mentions. The competition carries 75 million won in prize money, along with investment consideration and PoC opportunities with Kakao affiliates.

Kim Do-young, CEO of Kakao Investment Co., Ltd., spoke at the event about the need to invest in research achievements from regional institutes. He noted that about 73% of last year's venture investment funds were concentrated in companies in the Seoul metropolitan area. He compared a ship's safety in port with its purpose to sail, and encouraged the teams to pursue bigger goals. Kakao Investment's own framing of the event is that unlike ordinary startup competitions, the program can lead to investment and PoCs even after the awards are presented.

The first edition produced results that the article describes as successful. AniBridge AI, with roots at KAIST, received follow-on investment after an investment from Kakao Investment and reached a company valuation of 20 billion won. Blackbox, a UNIST team, carried out a paid PoC with Kakao Entertainment, while Broz, with roots at DGIST, raised investment and was discussing technical integration with Kakao Map. The article presents these outcomes as evidence that research-stage AI can move toward commercial use through the program.

Articles.Title: [Field Report] AI technology leaves the lab and sets sail for the market with Kakao - 파이낸셜뉴스

stories.Headline: CoreWeave's backlog quality tested by AI bears, says Jefferies' Brent Thill
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave's backlog quality is under scrutiny after skeptics questioned the health of the AI cloud company's future revenue, according to a CNBC interview with Brent Thill, a senior software analyst at Jefferies, published on November 10, 2026. The segment appeared on "Closing Bell: Overtime," where Thill discussed the company's quarterly results and what they signal about its outlook. The video description frames the discussion around bears who are testing whether the backlog, the contracted revenue the company has yet to recognize, is as solid as it appears. The article itself is a short video summary and does not give figures for the backlog, revenue or contract terms. Nothing in the material says what changed in the company's operations or obligations.

The available text names Thill as the analyst who joined the program and frames his comments as a check on the company's health going forward. It does not include his specific assessment, any price targets, or the reasoning behind any view. The page also lists unrelated segments from the same network about utilities and data center demand, including a Entergy executive saying the election did not change power demand expectations and an Oracle executive citing five large U.S. data centers under construction. Those items are context on the data center boom but are not about CoreWeave.

The article does not say whether CoreWeave or its management responded to the questions raised. The story is a brief, unverified item built on a video description rather than a full report, so the specifics of the backlog dispute and the company's results remain unknown. The articles do not say what comes next for the company or its stock. More to follow.
