stories.Headline: UPF Summit to Address Digital Infrastructure and AI in Fez-Meknes
stories.Summary:
The University of Fez (UPF) will host a regional digital summit in Fez-Meknes, titled "Fez-Meknes Smart & Sovereign Region 2030," with the article published on November 10, 2026, indicating the event is set for the following day. The summit will bring together representatives of public institutions, businesses, universities, and technology experts to present four projects meant to strengthen the region's technological infrastructure, improve digital healthcare, and support artificial intelligence research. The organizers say the discussions will follow Morocco's Digital Morocco 2030 strategy. The four projects are the Fez-Meknes Regional Micro Data Center, the Fez-Meknes Digital Health Living Lab, the Regional SOC / Cybersecurity Hub, and the Fez-Meknes Digital Innovation & AI Lab.

The Micro Data Center would provide local, high-availability data hosting for regional digital services, critical data storage, and new AI applications, and it would serve as the base for the other initiatives. The Digital Health Living Lab would bring together healthcare professionals, researchers, and technology companies to test and develop digital health tools, including telemedicine and clinical AI. The cybersecurity hub, linked to the data center, would monitor and protect critical infrastructure and local authorities against cyber threats through security operations, threat intelligence, and incident response. The Digital Innovation & AI Lab would offer computing and prototyping resources to teachers, students, and startups, aiming to turn research into practical applications. The article does not give budgets or completion dates for any of these projects.

The summit will open with speeches from representatives of UPF, the Fez-Meknes regional administration, and several government bodies, including the Ministry of Digital Transition and Administrative Reform, the Ministry of Industry and Trade, and the Ministry of Higher Education, Scientific Research and Innovation. Speakers from the Regional Council, the Digital Development Agency (ADD), Maroc Data Center, and Rwadtech are also scheduled to take part. According to the organizers, the event will close at 6 p.m. with a summary of the discussions and the signing of partnership agreements, though the article does not name the parties to those agreements.

The initiative sits within Digital Morocco 2030, a national strategy launched in September 2024 to position the country as a digital hub, expand public service digitization, develop digital skills, and strengthen the digital economy. The government has set a target of creating 240,000 direct jobs in the digital economy by 2030. UPF said the summit aims to connect public institutions, academic institutions, and businesses to identify areas of cooperation and link scientific research with regional economic priorities. The article does not say what follows the summit beyond the signed agreements.

Articles.Title: UPF Summit to Address Digital Infrastructure and AI in Fez-Meknes

stories.Headline: AI scanners at rental car lots are ‘definitely not perfect,’ watchdog says - WDAM-TV
stories.Summary:
Several rental car companies are now using AI scanning systems to check vehicles for damage, and a consumer watchdog says renters should document the car themselves to avoid a surprise bill. The scanners work like a car wash at pick-up or drop-off, with cameras taking photos and videos from different angles to look for damage. Teresa Murray, consumer watchdog director with the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, said the technology has both benefits and drawbacks. Her main concern is that artificial intelligence can make errors that matter in a rental setting, and she said it is definitely not perfect.

Murray gave examples of how the system could go wrong. She said a splotch of dirt could be mistaken for a dent, and a shadow could look like significant damage. Her advice is the same whether a company uses AI or an employee inspects the vehicle, which is to take a few minutes to look the car over closely before leaving the lot. She recommends taking pictures of every part of the car and recording a walk-around video, including crouching down to check the wheels, hubcaps, interior, trunk and glass. She said renters should allow 5 to 10 minutes for this, depending on whether a live worker is present or not.

Murray also recommends doing the same inspection before and after the trip if a company uses an AI scanner. Having personal photos gives a renter a way to challenge a charge if a damage bill arrives later. The article does not describe any specific company's response or any regulatory action. It also does not say how widely the scanners are being used or whether any renters have already disputed charges. The piece is a consumer advice report focused on what renters can do to protect themselves.

Articles.Title: AI scanners at rental car lots are ‘definitely not perfect,’ watchdog says - WDAM-TV

stories.Headline: Why does AI visibility matter for furniture stores?
stories.Summary:
At a Greenville, SC event... no, the articles place this in High Point, where Dovr Media CEO Jake Freedman, speaking as reported on November 10, 2026, urged home furnishings retailers to address their visibility to AI shopping assistants. Freedman said a retailer may spend decades building a reputation and a showroom, yet still be left off an AI assistant's recommendations. He argued that such a retailer becomes invisible to customers regardless of how long it has operated. He told retailers that longevity is not a strategic plan.

The article says the core question is whether a retailer's online presence gives an AI assistant enough clear, consistent information to recommend its products. Freedman named product data, category page data and site health as the areas that matter most. He listed return policy, shipping policy, delivery and financing as details that must be built out online. He described these details as trust indicators that must be built between retailers and AI platforms. He said that doing this work yourself is challenging, to say the least.

Freedman is the source of these views, and he presented them as advice to retailers rather than as an industry finding. He described AI shopping assistants as recommending one, two, or sometimes three choices, fewer than the ads and answers a standard search engine returns. He said retailers should be on AI in the way they once needed to be on radio, television and the Internet. He recommended outside expertise for the work, comparing it to electrical wiring that most people cannot fix themselves. He also said retailers should give bots access to their sites rather than gating it as they once did.

Freedman's remarks also reach newer entrants, which he described as AI natives in their early 20s, still in college, who are running AI-first strategies. He said these competitors do not pay rent, do not carry tenured salespeople, and avoid heavy systems and software that cost six figures a year. The article says the advice is aimed at established home furnishings retailers whose sales could be taken by competitors if the retailers are not recommended. It also says that retailers who once resisted websites, saying they had survived 60 years without one, faced a similar divide a decade ago.

The article gives the background of Freedman's warning through the arrival of the retail website, which he said some retailers resisted about ten years ago. It notes that the article is part of Furniture Today's coverage under its artificial intelligence category, and that Freedman spoke at High Point Market. The article also lists related recent coverage, including Havertys reporting AI-related expansion in its Q3 sales, and Intiaro outlining bottlenecks for furniture brands at High Point Market. These items are cited by the publication as context rather than as explanation of Freedman's argument.

The article does not say how many retailers have adopted the steps Freedman recommends, nor does it measure how much business has been lost to AI recommendations. It gives no response from AI platforms or from other retailers to his comments. What happens next for retailers that follow or ignore his advice is not reported. The piece ends without a timeline for when AI shopping assistants will change how they choose which retailers to recommend.

Articles.Title: Why does AI visibility matter for furniture stores?

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Models Reshape Receptor Structure Prediction and Molecular Pharmacology
stories.Summary:
A review published in Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences, by researchers from Shandong First Medical University, says artificial intelligence architectures are transforming receptor structural biology by resolving long-standing analytical bottlenecks. G protein-coupled receptors form the largest superfamily of human membrane proteins and are the biological targets for about 26 percent of all marketed drugs. Experimental determination of their three-dimensional atomic structures has historically met severe technical obstacles, partly because the receptors sit in complex lipid bilayers and are conformationally flexible. The review traces how deep learning, beginning with AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold, moved structural biology away from dependence on homologous experimental templates. The coverage appeared on bioengineer.org on November 10, 2026.

These networks infer three-dimensional coordinates by learning sequence-to-structure relationships from massive protein datasets and embedding evolutionary constraints drawn from multiple sequence alignments. Over half of all receptors long lacked closely related template structures, so homology modeling struggled, and the new models have extended structural coverage across the whole family, including the complete human olfactory receptor repertoire. On the orphan mouse olfactory receptor Olfr73, predictions reached near-experimental fidelity, with transmembrane backbone root mean square deviations below 2 angstroms. Local distance difference test scores frequently exceeded 90 in transmembrane helical bundles. In one screening demonstration, researchers deorphanized the receptor GPR139 by docking 235 million molecules, then found five full agonists among 68 experimentally tested top candidates, a hit rate of roughly 7 percent.

The review's authors, from Shandong First Medical University, emphasize that critical limitations persist in static predictive frameworks. They note that confidence scores drop substantially for flexible extracellular loops, though AlphaFold2 accurately predicted the second extracellular loop in GPR101 and OR51E2. They report that algorithms often default to averaged inactive conformations for Class A receptors and lean toward active-like states for Class B1 members. They say AlphaFold3, which uses diffusion models to predict all-atom complexes, often produces ligand poses with severe steric clashes and inaccurate sidechain orientations. They caution that clinical translation of receptor-focused digital twins is hindered by data heterogeneity and a lack of prospective trial validation, and that such simulations should be treated as investigational decision-support frameworks, not autonomous diagnostic tools.

Other groups cited in the review report results that support the approach. The AuroBind platform evaluated more than 30 million purchasable compounds against orphan targets and achieved prospective experimental hit rates of 16.7 percent for GPR151 and 30.4 percent for GPR160. A structure-guided reinforcement learning workflow tested on the adenosine A2A receptor reached an 88 percent binding hit rate across seven crystal structures, and 50 percent of confirmed binders showed functional activity. A reverse virtual screening platform identified zafirlukast, an approved anti-asthmatic leukotriene receptor antagonist, as an inhibitor of vasopressin V2 receptor-mediated cyclic AMP signaling, based on about 79 percent crystallographic cavity shape similarity. Transfer-learning models using ProteinBERT reached Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.57 and 0.58 for predicting arrestin and G-protein pathway activity ratios, though precision fell on previously unseen receptors.

The review places these advances against the fact that standard chemical interaction databases are overwhelmingly populated by soluble proteins, so ordinary screening tools often fail on membrane receptors. Because static predictions cannot capture continuous conformational transitions, activation mechanisms that involve outward movement of transmembrane helix 6 and inward displacement of helix 7 require dynamic modeling. Molecular dynamics simulations produce trajectory data reaching petabyte scales, and machine learning classifiers then label active, intermediate, and inactive states. Researchers have also shown that subsampling and reducing multiple sequence alignment depth in AlphaFold2 yields structural ensembles covering inward-facing and outward-facing membrane conformations. The authors note that historical drug candidates have a Phase I-to-approval success rate of only 6.2 percent.

To guard against misleading structural artifacts, the authors propose a four-step validation protocol before predicted receptor-ligand complexes are used in drug discovery. The first step requires pLDDT scores above 90 at the binding cavity, and the second requires explicit-solvent molecular dynamics relaxation to remove steric clashes and verify stability. Third, thermodynamic calculations such as free-energy perturbation should establish relative binding free energies, and fourth, predictions must be confirmed by surface plasmon resonance or cell-based functional assays. The authors say integrating these physical constraints in iterative closed-loop frameworks will let AI expand structural coverage while keeping physical realism. The article text is cut off mid-sentence, in a passage on time-resolved cryogenic electron microscopy of the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, so its final findings are not available.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Models Reshape Receptor Structure Prediction and Molecular Pharmacology

stories.Headline: The impossible standard we're setting for artificial intelligence - opinion
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column rather than a news report, so there is no single event to recount. Isaac Ben-Israel, writing in The Jerusalem Post on November 10, 2026, argues that society is setting an impossible standard for artificial intelligence by demanding that AI systems never cause harm. He notes that four years earlier most people had never held a conversation with an AI system, and that millions now rely on tools such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. He points to a shift from AI as an assistant that answers questions to autonomous agents that are given an objective and carry out the steps themselves, with limited human involvement.

Ben-Israel says this shift has produced two main worries: that people will lose their jobs to faster and cheaper systems, and that increasingly autonomous AI will become impossible to control. He accepts that these concerns deserve serious attention, especially as agents gain access to financial systems, corporate networks, sensitive information and critical infrastructure. He argues that the debate rests on an unrealistic expectation that such systems can be guaranteed never to cause harm, a standard no other major technology has met and that humans have never met either. He uses the automobile as an example, recalling early safety measures such as a person walking ahead of a vehicle, and says that over a century seat belts, traffic rules, airbags and collision detection were added while road deaths continued. Society accepted that transport's benefits justified a level of risk that was continuously reduced.

He recommends a similar realism for AI: invest heavily in making systems safer, understand their failures, and limit the damage they can cause, without assuming any amount of investment, research or regulation will remove every danger. He warns that demanding proof of absolute safety before a learning system can be developed or deployed amounts to demanding that the technology not advance. He suggests that controls should vary with use, so a medical recommendation system faces different requirements from a marketing tool, and that an agent authorized to move money or alter critical infrastructure should be held to especially strict limits. He says governments will play a part but cannot bear the whole burden, and that developers, employers, educators and users also have roles. He cautions that rules impossible to satisfy could keep useful technologies from the people who need them.

Ben-Israel also raises concentration of power, noting that a relatively small number of companies control many of the most capable AI systems. He asks who decides which applications are permitted, what happens when individuals or governments depend on systems owned by others, and how meaningful oversight can be kept when machines perform tasks once requiring human judgment. He concludes that technological progress is outrunning agreed answers and that society should approach AI with neither blind optimism nor excessive fear. The column's final point is that people have learned to live with human fallibility and must now build the institutions, safeguards and judgment to live responsibly with artificial intelligence as well.

Articles.Title: The impossible standard we're setting for artificial intelligence - opinion

stories.Headline: Computer-Aided Design and Artificial Intelligence Reshape Modern Pharmaceutical Discovery and Development
stories.Summary:
A review published in Discover Pharmaceutical Sciences evaluates how computational methods and artificial intelligence are changing pharmaceutical research and development. Bringing a new prescription drug to market currently costs about 2.6 billion United States dollars before tax and takes 10 to 15 years. The overall failure rate in drug discovery exceeds 96 percent, and clinical development shows a 90 percent attrition rate. Newly investigated small agents have a projected clinical approval frequency of just 13 percent across the whole development path. Researchers are therefore deploying computer-aided drug design, computational chemistry and automated analytical platforms to assess molecular traits in silico before committing laboratory resources.

Those in silico checks cover physical and chemical properties, selectivity, adverse reactions, bioactivity and pharmacokinetic parameters. More than 90 percent of licensed medications target proteins, guided historically by Lipinski's Rule of Five, which was established in 1997. That rule links poor absorption to molecular weights above 500 Daltons, more than ten hydrogen-bond acceptors, more than five hydrogen-bond donors, and a calculated logarithm of the partition coefficient above five. Modern discovery is expanding beyond these limits to peptides, peptidomimetics, oligonucleotides, proteolysis targeting chimeras, bioactive carbohydrates and lipid signaling pathways involving enzymes and G protein-coupled receptors. Structure-based virtual screening now evaluates target-ligand binding across virtual libraries containing trillions of small molecules, and fragment-based and synthon-based screening use modular fragments to improve synthetic accessibility.

Retrosynthetic platforms such as Synthia, formerly called Chematica, use organic chemistry axioms, symbolic artificial intelligence and Monte Carlo tree searches to chart feasible, low-cost synthesis routes. Insilico Medicine used its generative artificial intelligence platform to identify Traf2- and NCK-interacting kinase as a target and designed the small-molecule inhibitor ISM001-055 for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Its Phase IIa trial was randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled, run across 21 clinical sites in China with 71 patients. Orally given ISM001-055 produced dose-dependent respiratory improvements and a favorable safety profile. Patients taking 60 milligrams once daily gained a mean of 98.4 milliliters in forced vital capacity over 12 weeks, while the placebo group declined by a mean of 62.3 milliliters.

Mild to moderate diarrhea and abnormal liver function appeared in 14.8 percent of treated subjects. Exscientia and Sumitomo Dainippon Pharma developed DSP-1181, a selective serotonin 5-HT1A receptor agonist for obsessive-compulsive disorder. It went from initial target identification to Phase I human testing in Japan within 12 months. In toxicity modeling, deep learning models won the Tox21 Data Challenge with classification accuracy above 80 percent across diverse chemical datasets. The IBM Watson supercomputer has shown it can parse clinical data and reference databases, identifying breast cancer data in under 60 seconds.

Pharmacogenomic studies increasingly use single-nucleotide polymorphism data to explain metabolic variability, and genetic polymorphism models inform personalized dosing and treatment choice. Traditional pharmaceutical research runs through target identification, target validation, hit-to-lead optimization, lead refinement, preclinical candidate selection, preclinical evaluation and clinical trials. Target selection has historically favored conventional druggable proteins with structural folds and binding cavities suited to high-affinity oral small molecules. AlphaFold and its extension ColabFold predict three-dimensional protein structures from amino acid sequences with accuracy that competes with crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy. Comparative molecular field analysis and comparative molecular similarity indices analysis have been applied to the gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor and microsomal prostaglandin E synthase-1.

Molecular dynamics simulations have mapped small-molecule entry into binding pockets in microsomal prostaglandin E synthase-1 and the influenza M2 proton channel, and generative models draw on ChEMBL to propose new molecules, including the Reinforced Adversarial Neural Computer, which outperformed ORGANIC in structural novelty. The article text breaks off mid-sentence as it begins to discuss the limits that remain despite these technological strides, so those limits are not stated here. The review's conclusions about future directions and open challenges are therefore not available. No further trial results, timelines or regulatory decisions for ISM001-055 or DSP-1181 appear in the text provided. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Computer-Aided Design and Artificial Intelligence Reshape Modern Pharmaceutical Discovery and Development

stories.Headline: Comprehensive Survey Maps Retrieval Methods Enhancing Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Generation
stories.Summary:
Researchers have published an exhaustive survey of retrieval-augmented generation across artificial intelligence generated content, building a structured taxonomy that links information retrieval systems with modern generative foundation models. The lead authors are Penghao Zhao and Hailin Zhang, with senior researcher Bin Cui, and their work appears in Data Science and Engineering. The article describing it was published by bioengineer.org on November 10, 2026. The survey notes that generative models have scaled rapidly from Long Short-Term Memory networks to Transformer architectures, and from Generative Adversarial Networks to Latent Diffusion Models spanning billions of parameters. Despite breakthroughs across many modalities, foundation models still face static training boundaries that leave parameters outdated, vulnerability to training data leakage, hallucinations, high inference costs, and inadequate long-tail coverage.

Retrieval-augmented generation addresses these problems by establishing a dynamic non-parametric memory store from which relevant external items are fetched during inference. According to the survey, this improves factual accuracy, contextual grounding, and operational robustness without perpetual retraining of foundational parameters. Every such architecture rests on two modules, a dedicated retriever and an adaptable generative model, and user queries in any modality are processed by the retriever to search pre-indexed data stores. Retrieval techniques separate into sparse retrieval, dense retrieval, and specialized topological search methods, with BM25 and TF-IDF as sparse baselines and Dense Passage Retrieval as a dual-encoder dense example. Dense systems rely on Approximate Nearest Neighbor indexing structures such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs, DiskANN, and SPANN, while structured modalities use abstract syntax tree edit distances, named entity recognition, or graph traversals.

The review distills existing techniques into four architectural paradigms for combining retrieved items with generators: query-based, latent representation-based, logit-based, and speculative generation. Query-based augmentation is the most widely deployed, integrating retrieved passages, code snippets, or image patches with the raw user query into one prompt, as in REALM, BART-coupled Dense Passage Retrieval, and REPLUG. Latent representation-based augmentation instead feeds retrieved information into intermediate hidden states, as Fusion-in-Decoder does by passing each query and document chunk through separate encoders before a shared decoder. RETRO applies Chunked Cross-Attention, while ReMoDiffuse, Re-AudioLDM, and CARE use cross-attention to inject semantic latent vectors into generative decoders. Logit-based augmentation influences step-wise vocabulary probabilities, with kNN-LM combining standard language model probabilities with distance-weighted retrieval distributions, and TRIME and NPM using non-parametric distributions in place of output softmax layers.

The survey says logit-based methods deliver substantial accuracy gains on sparse, long-tail distributions, and EDITSUM and RECODE blend action subtree logits or code vector search outputs to guide sequence generation. Speculative retrieval-augmented generation decouples retrieval from generative computation, using retrieved resources to replace token generation steps entirely. REST swaps small draft models in speculative decoding for retrieved document n-grams, GPTCache implements semantic caching of prior model responses, and COG decomposes generation into copy-and-paste retrieval from source documents. The survey also documents five categories of enhancements: input modifications, retriever improvements, generator adjustments, output rewrites, and holistic pipeline strategies. Input enhancements include Query2doc and HyDE, which synthesize pseudo-documents to enrich sparse prompts, and RQ-RAG, which decomposes ambiguous prompts into focused sub-queries.

Retriever enhancements target the quality of retrieved context, using recursive mechanisms such as ReACT and Monte-Carlo tree simulations in RATP, alongside chunk optimization in LlamaIndex, RAPTOR multi-level tree clustering, and Prompt-RAG table-of-contents structuring. Generator optimizations include LLMLingua prompt compression, decoding calibrations such as temperature adjustment in InferFix and vocabulary restriction in Synchromesh, and Low-Rank Adaptation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. For output refinement, SARGAM uses dedicated transformer classifiers to correct structural errors in generated code, and CBR-KBQA projects outputs onto neighboring knowledge base relations to enforce logical validity. At the pipeline level, adaptive frameworks decide whether external search is needed, using rule-based thresholds over generation probabilities in FLARE, or model-based discriminators such as Self-RAG retrieve tokens and AdaptiveRAG classifiers.

Iterative pipelines such as RepoCoder and ITER-RETGEN cycle through multiple retrieval and generation phases so later passes can fill identified knowledge gaps. The survey shows these architectures reaching well beyond open-domain question answering, with REALM, Atlas, and MultiHop-RAG handling multi-hop document interactions and CONCRETE and Stochastic RAG verifying facts. Dialogue systems including BlenderBot3 and ConceptFlow use conversational histories, internet sources, and commonsense knowledge graphs, while Unlimiformer overcomes transformer context limits by retrieving external hidden states. In code intelligence, SKCODER, APICoder, and CODEAGENT build prompts from API documentation, imported libraries, and project-level syntactic sketches.

In images, RetrieveGAN and IC-GAN condition generators on retrieved patches, and KNN-Diffusion and Re-imagen add CLIP image-text embeddings to diffusion denoising loops. Video systems CARE and EgoInstructor use gated cross-attention to caption first-person and news footage, Re-AudioLDM and Make-An-Audio use contrastive CLAP dense audio retrievers, and ReMoDiffuse and RetDream ground three-dimensional generation in retrieved geometric priors. In biomedical applications, RetMol and PromptDiff retrieve ligand references and molecular strings to synthesize novel therapeutic candidates. BIOREADER brings published biomedical literature into text-to-text models through chunked cross-attention, Chat-Orthopedist provides evidence-based consultation for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, and MedWriter generates medical imaging reports from hierarchical templates.

LeanDojo uses retrieval to select premises from mathematical libraries for automated formal theorem proving. Specialized benchmark suites have emerged to measure these systems, including RAGAS, ARES, and TruLens, which employ automated judge models to assess faithfulness and answer relevance. The article text breaks off mid-sentence while describing these evaluation frameworks, so the rest of its account is not available. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Comprehensive Survey Maps Retrieval Methods Enhancing Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Generation

stories.Headline: Hierarchical Taxonomy Framework Tracks Shifting Artificial Intelligence Trends Across Multiple Information Sources
stories.Summary:
Researchers have formulated an analytical framework that measures and compares evolving topic dynamics across varied artificial intelligence document streams at multiple levels of abstraction. The work was published in EPJ Data Science. Academic scientists, software engineers and practitioners discussing commercial deployments all contribute to the field, but they record progress in scientific preprints, open-source repositories and industry newsletters. These formats differ in vocabulary, technical granularity and temporal patterns, which makes them hard to synthesize. The authors say traditional scientometric tools typically evaluate single sources or rely on flat topic classifications that miss multi-level structural evolution.

The new method maps documents from different sources into shared hierarchical taxonomies, without restricting analysis to a single source or inventing ad-hoc labels. The system rests on three components: predefined hierarchical taxonomies organized as directed acyclic graphs, incoming document streams, and procedures that assign documents to taxonomy nodes. When a document is assigned to a node, the assignment is propagated upward to every ancestor node along its branch. This aggregation lets researchers compute indicators at different levels of abstraction, keeping broad categories statistically stable while still allowing inspection of specialized subfields. The framework also supports multiple parallel taxonomies, so documents can be classified along dimensions such as model architecture, problem formulation, learning paradigm and application domain.

The authors developed five metrics to quantify these patterns. Topic popularity is the proportion of a stream's labeled documents assigned to a node or any of its descendants, while average detail depth measures how technically granular a source's discussion of a subtree is. The remaining metrics address diversity and timing. Topical diversity measures how evenly coverage spreads across a parent node's descendants, using a uniform baseline that prevents dominant branches from inflating the score. Temporal non-uniformity uses chi-squared tests across window sizes from six to twenty-four months, combined with Simes' method, to flag genuine changes in topic activity.

Temporal uniqueness uses Poisson generalized linear models with spline terms to test whether a topic's evolution in one source diverges from the other sources. Researchers applied the framework to arXiv preprints, Hugging Face model cards and the Deep Learning Weekly newsletter. They randomly selected thirty documents per month from each source, matching the newsletter's minimum volume of thirty-one entries. Documents were mapped to four taxonomies: Model architecture, AI problem type, Learning paradigm and Application domain. Each taxonomy contained fifty to two hundred nodes across three to five levels.

Document assignment used the LLMDap pipeline with GPT-4.1-nano at a temperature of 0.4. On a validation set of fifteen documents with 121 labels, 76 were judged correct, 29 incorrect and 16 uncertain, indicating accuracy between 63% and 76%. Using GPT-5-mini on the same subset produced 90 correct, 9 incorrect and 13 uncertain labels, raising accuracy to between 80% and 92%. Hugging Face showed high concentration in transformer architectures, natural language processing and fine-tuning, while arXiv showed broader architectural distributions with stronger emphasis on computer vision and supervised learning.

Deep Learning Weekly had the highest association with application domains, with only 2% of its entries unassigned to that taxonomy. Convolutional networks rose and declined after a peak around 2020, while transformer architectures continued an upward trajectory. Hugging Face provided greater architectural specificity than arXiv's abstract-level text. Deep Learning Weekly scored highest on topical diversity across most topics, which the authors attribute to balanced editorial curation, while Hugging Face scored lower because of numerous fine-tuned variants of popular architectures.

Across 403 taxonomy nodes, most topics remained temporally stable, though significant non-uniformity emerged in key subfields. arXiv accumulated the most significant non-uniformity nodes, which the authors link to its longer observation span, while Hugging Face recorded the highest temporal uniqueness counts during the shared chronological window. The authors also developed the AI Taxonomy Trend Explorer, an interactive tool for qualitative exploration of the results. The articles do not say whether the framework will be applied to other sources or fields.

Articles.Title: Hierarchical Taxonomy Framework Tracks Shifting Artificial Intelligence Trends Across Multiple Information Sources

stories.Headline: China’s Jensen Huang ‘honeypot’ trap is only more reason to win the AI race
stories.Summary:
China's Jensen Huang "honeypot" operation came to light in November 2026, with the Nvidia chief executive having admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, whose surveillance reportedly showed her passing information to Chinese actors. The column reports that Beijing's apparent honeypot was aimed at Huang, the head of a company valued at $4.5 trillion and central to AI development. The writer argues the episode shows how far China will go to win the AI race, while warning that American critics may use it to damage the US industry. Nvidia's board has said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, though the article notes it is not yet clear what information was passed along.

The writer argues the federal government should fully investigate the case and respond against China, but warns that Huang could face serious fallout if Democrats use their coming control of Congress to press the matter. Industry sources cited by the New York Post's Charles Gasparino reportedly believe Huang may not survive the backlash. The column casts the Democratic push against AI as part of a broader campaign, pointing to Senator Bernie Sanders's legislation to slow AI development and to party criticism of data centers over power and water use. It also notes that Senator Chris Coons has demanded answers about ties between AI billionaires and the Trump administration. The writer contends that Huang lobbied President Donald Trump to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China, which a former Secret Service agent, Paul Eckloff, described as highly influential on US export policy.

The column places the affair within a history of Chinese espionage against American officials, citing the cases of Fang Fang, who trapped then-Representative Eric Swalwell, and Linda Sun, a former top aide to Governor Andrew Cuomo who later worked under Governor Kathy Hochul. The writer argues that Huang's downfall would hurt the industry and could boost Beijing's AI push more than the espionage itself. The piece closes by calling for a probe of Huang and a response to China, while urging that the affair not be used to derail America's pursuit of AI supremacy. It quotes Trump's line that "whoever wins AI, wins."

Articles.Title: China’s Jensen Huang ‘honeypot’ trap is only more reason to win the AI race

stories.Headline: Systematic Review Details Mathematical Foundations Governing Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Systems
stories.Summary:
Researchers Yuliana Jiménez-Gaona and Vasudevan Lakshminarayanan conducted a systematic review of the mathematical foundations of artificial intelligence in medicine, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The study synthesized evidence from 147 eligible investigations published between January 2016 and June 30, 2026. The review mapped how classical computational theories and emerging algorithmic models drive clinical decision support. The findings show that healthcare artificial intelligence depends on an interconnected mathematical ecosystem rather than disconnected algorithms. Methodological quality was appraised with an adapted Joanna Briggs Institute framework and AMSTAR-2, yielding a Cohen's kappa of 0.89.

The corpus was assembled from Scopus, Google Scholar, and PubMed or MEDLINE, using Harzing's Publish or Perish version 8 where applicable. An initial yield of 653 records was narrowed to 147 unique studies through deduplication and two-stage independent screening. Full-text exclusions removed 54 reports, mainly for lack of healthcare relevance in 18 cases and insufficient mathematical content in 12. Linear algebra appeared in 100 studies, or 68.0 percent, while calculus and continuous optimization appeared in 91, or 61.9 percent. Probability and statistics were analyzed in 79 publications, or 53.7 percent.

Explainable and trustworthy artificial intelligence was the largest primary focus, covering 24 studies, or 16.3 percent. Statistics and statistical learning theory were the primary focus of 23 studies, or 15.6 percent, matching probability and Bayesian methods. Calculus and mathematical optimization were primary in 19 studies, or 12.9 percent, and linear algebra in 15, or 10.2 percent. The remaining 43 publications, or 29.3 percent, covered graph theory, numerical analysis, stochastic differential formulations, and quantum computational mathematics. Radiology and medical imaging was the leading application area at 24.3 percent, and classification and diagnosis was the most frequent clinical task at 17.1 percent.

The authors say the review shows that mathematical rigor is indispensable for algorithmic reliability, safety, and future clinical translation. They caution that high discriminatory scores do not guarantee clinical reliability. In radiomics standardization work reviewed by Zwanenburg and collaborators, 167 of 169 features, or 98.82 percent, showed good-to-excellent reproducibility only after rigorous mathematical definition. Zhovannik and colleagues found that segmentation uncertainties significantly propagate into downstream radiomic signatures. Patients and clinicians who rely on diagnostic systems built on these methods are the groups the review's conclusions concern.

The review draws on earlier studies to show the mathematics at work. Kim and colleagues in 2025 reported image reconstruction errors between 0.0251 and 0.0547 using optical matrix-vector multiplication. Schott and colleagues in 2024 reported a 20.1 percent increase in receiver operating characteristic area under the curve using gradient-based sensitivity analysis. Leibig and co-workers in 2017 raised diagnostic accuracy in diabetic retinopathy screening from about 87 percent to at least 90 percent by referring the 20 percent most uncertain predictions to clinicians. Huang and collaborators in 2025 reported 89.23 percent accuracy for a quantum neural network classifying lung nodules, against 76.56 percent for a classical support vector machine.

The review notes that quantum artificial intelligence remains predominantly experimental and simulated on hybrid architectures. It lacks the extensive external clinical validation needed to establish superiority over optimized classical workflows. The articles leave open when such validation will arrive. They also do not say whether the Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative's findings will change current clinical practice. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Systematic Review Details Mathematical Foundations Governing Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Systems

stories.Headline: Review Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Tools Across Pharmaceutical Discovery and Development
stories.Summary:
Pharmaceutical research and development faces steep costs, as creating a single new therapeutic typically exceeds 2.5 billion dollars and demands more than a decade of work. Clinical translation is especially constrained, since only a small fraction of candidate molecules win regulatory approval, and just 2.01 percent of development projects ultimately produce a marketable product. A review published in Discover Pharmaceutical Sciences by Shashi Kant, Deepika, and Saheli Roy examines how computational methods are reshaping this process. The review covers artificial intelligence systems that combine machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, reinforcement learning, graph neural networks, and generative models. These tools aim to address bottlenecks in target validation, compound screening, structural optimization, and clinical investigation.

The authors describe how traditional discovery stalls at sequential points, starting with the laborious identification and validation of target molecules. Experimental screening and iterative optimization for potency, selectivity, and safety further raise project expenses before candidates reach clinical evaluation. In human trials, recruitment difficulties, trial design constraints, and data collection logistics also undermine success. Computational platforms can learn from complex biological and chemical datasets without explicit task-specific programming. Models analyze genomics, proteomics, electronic health records, and public repositories such as DrugBank, PubChem, and UniProt, with some datasets spanning 10,000 to 15,000 entries.

The review's authors are Shashi Kant, Deepika, and Saheli Roy, and the work was published in Discover Pharmaceutical Sciences. The authors outline how these computational approaches can replace or supplement physical high-throughput screening through automated virtual evaluation. Quantitative structure-activity relationship models predict molecular affinity and activity from chemical structures, while some studies use 1,000 to 5,000 curated data points to predict water solubility. Deep neural networks estimate absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity parameters, allowing investigators to remove hazardous molecules before costly animal studies or trials. The authors also note that algorithms can refine trial protocols, endpoints, and cohort sizes using historical records.

The approaches described affect pharmaceutical companies and the researchers working within their development pipelines. Patients stand to be affected through trial recruitment, safety monitoring, and the search for new indications. The authors note the example of baricitinib, an oral Janus kinase inhibitor approved for rheumatoid arthritis, which computational platforms identified as an effective therapy for COVID-19. Companies such as Exscientia advanced six AI-designed molecules into human trials by 2024 across oncology, immunology, and psychiatric indications. The review also emphasizes that high-quality, standardized, and accurately annotated training data remains a critical bottleneck, since heterogeneous datasets from incompatible assays and inconsistent trials limit integration.

Articles.Title: Review Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Tools Across Pharmaceutical Discovery and Development

stories.Headline: Tri-National Study Explores How Student Teachers Integrate Artificial Intelligence in Classrooms
stories.Summary:
A tri-national study published in Frontiers in Computer Science found that student teachers who took joint online coursework across Germany, Israel, and Hungary moved from seeing artificial intelligence as a simple tool toward understanding its teaching and ethical complexities. The investigation followed participants across two successive academic cohorts, one in 2024 and one in 2025. Students evaluated AI software, designed educational tasks, and worked through cross-cultural communication challenges. The researchers reported that hands-on experimentation with AI tools, combined with sustained intercultural group work, led future educators to prioritize human oversight, verification, and deliberate instructional support over automated shortcuts. The study was built around the Cooperation Online in Teaching Between Germany, Israel, and Hungary initiative, known as the CoGIH Project.

Five higher education institutions took part, including the Department of English and American Studies at the University of Kassel in Germany and the University of Miskolc in Hungary. The nine-week program examined how collaborative cross-cultural learning supported by AI affects intercultural awareness, technological attitudes, and professional identity. The authors said earlier research had typically studied AI integration, online collaborative learning, and multilingual intercultural competence in isolation rather than together. To guide the design, the researchers combined three pedagogical models into a framework they called the CoGIH Three Model Integration. The empirical sample included 113 students enrolled across the 2024 and 2025 cohorts, and 91 of them responded to the course questionnaires.

Among the 82 participants who answered the gender question, 57 identified as female and 25 as male. Respondents reported speaking German, Hebrew, Hungarian, English, Arabic, and several other languages, and their average self-rated English proficiency on a 5-point scale was 3.74. Groups analyzed a specific AI application against ten criteria, including cost of access, protection of minors, multilingual capability, and cultural bias. They also developed a multilingual instructional task and recorded a video presentation for an international student conference held during the final synchronous session.

Because anonymity protections prevented tracking individual participants across surveys for all but 17 respondents, the authors limited their quantitative analysis to aggregate descriptive statistics and cross-sectional correlations. Analysis of the open-ended reflections showed that statements about concrete collaborative challenges rose from 28 before the course to 75 after it, while stereotypical cultural generalizations fell from 44 to 24. Statements describing AI as a pedagogical resource rose, and mentions of ethical and educational challenges increased from 13 to 31. Participants raised concerns about student overreliance, factual accuracy, algorithmic bias, and the need for explicit teacher guidance.

The researchers also observed that AI supported creative task design and language experimentation, but group projects showed weak visual coherence, shallow critical reflection, and translation errors in multilingual outputs. Students recommended more structured instruction from the start, groups with at least two peers from each country, more efficient synchronous meetings, and baseline language requirements. The authors concluded that AI offers valuable support for interactive learning but cannot replace authentic teacher mediation and rigorous critical evaluation. The article reports no further plans for the program beyond these recommendations.

Articles.Title: Tri-National Study Explores How Student Teachers Integrate Artificial Intelligence in Classrooms

stories.Headline: Beyond the AI hype: Why C-suite control is the ultimate differentiator
stories.Summary:
The articles are a sponsored BrandPost on CIO.com, dated November 10, 2026, titled "Beyond the AI hype: Why C-suite control is the ultimate differentiator," and it is sponsored by HPE and AMD. The piece argues that the initial wave of AI experimentation is over and that executives now ask how to scale AI securely. It warns that traditional enterprise infrastructure was not built for the intensive workloads that come with moving AI into full production. The article states that every data asset now carries both strategic value and operational risk. It frames the next era of business as a question of who controls their data, infrastructure and AI life cycle.

The piece describes the fragmented infrastructure problem, in which data, compute and operations are spread across on-premises data centers, colocation facilities and multiple hybrid clouds. It says this fragmentation causes lost efficiency, unpredictable latency and rising costs. It recommends investing in high-performance computing environments built for data-heavy workloads, and it names AMD EPYC CPUs and AMD Instinct GPUs as examples of an integrated foundation. It also covers governance, stating that data privacy, shifting international regulations and inconsistent internal governance create liabilities that can reach multimillion-dollar levels. It advises keeping control over where critical data lives so that proprietary data can stay in trusted, multi-tenant environments.

The article is written by HPE and AMD, the sponsors, who present themselves as the partners that can solve these challenges. It credits HPE with full-stack observability, automation and intelligent orchestration through a unified control plane. It says HPE delivers six of the top ten most powerful supercomputers globally and holds the number one spot on the HPL-MxP list. It describes HPE and AMD as partners that together provide the technology foundation for scaling enterprise AI.

The piece is aimed at C-level executives and CIOs of large enterprises moving AI out of pilot programs. Its background is a short description of the two companies' partnership, which combines HPE's large-scale system design with AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct accelerators. The companies say they serve modeling, simulation, analytics and AI training workloads for scientific research, digital engineering and advanced AI models. The article itself does not report any independent third-party assessment of the claims it makes about performance or market position.

The article gives no timeline for deployments, no pricing, and no measured results from any customer. It does not say how the recommended approaches would be implemented or what outcomes enterprises have actually achieved. It does not report any reaction from regulators, competitors or customers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Beyond the AI hype: Why C-suite control is the ultimate differentiator

stories.Headline: Why Human Working Memory Might Be AI’s Biggest Constraint
stories.Summary:
The Aviation Week article "Why Human Working Memory Might Be AI's Biggest Constraint," written by Garrett Reim and dated November 11, 2026, argues that a limit on people rather than on machines may be holding back artificial intelligence. The piece opens by listing the usual suspects that observers name as the main obstacle to AI, including chip shortages, limits on electrical grid capacity and a shrinking supply of high-quality training data. It then suggests that the real rate-limiting factor could be the capacity of human working memory. The article's summary states that experts say the next generation of AI tools must be designed around the cognitive limits of the people who use them. The article's central claim is that AI systems will only deliver their promise if they fit within what a person can hold in mind at one time.

Under this view, tools that produce more output than a user can absorb, check or act on do not add value and may even slow work down. The reasoning implies a shift in design priorities, moving the focus from raw machine capability toward interfaces, workflows and information loads that match human attention. The excerpt available here does not spell out specific design guidelines, figures or case examples beyond this general framing. Reim, who covers space and advanced technologies for Aviation Week, is the author credited with the piece.

The excerpt presents the position as the view of experts, and it does not name individual researchers or companies who hold it. The article sits within the publication's wider coverage of emerging technology in aerospace and defense, where AI tools are increasingly being introduced into engineering, operations and decision-making work. The available text is a paywalled preview, so the full argument, the evidence behind it and any recommendations beyond the summary cannot be confirmed from what is shown here. Readers who want the complete analysis would need to subscribe to Aviation Week & Space Technology or AWIN to read the rest of the article.

Articles.Title: Why Human Working Memory Might Be AI’s Biggest Constraint

stories.Headline: Monetizing compliance: New AI revenue streams for regional CSPs
stories.Summary:
Sovereign AI services are presented as a new revenue opportunity for regional cloud service providers, according to a BrandPost sponsored by HPE and AMD published on November 10, 2026. The piece argues that standard public AI models can violate compliance mandates when sensitive data crosses borders or sits in multitenant public environments. It frames this tension as a market opportunity for local and regional CSPs to capture enterprise cloud spending from organizations previously unable to use AI. The article describes sovereign AI as environments in which data, models and execution remain within national, regional or specific legal jurisdictions.

Under this model, CSPs could offer enterprise inferencing, which means localized deployment of large language models for specific data querying. They could also offer model customization, fine-tuning open-source models on proprietary customer data, and industry-specific applications for regional healthcare codes or localized banking laws. The article says the offering requires high-performance, legally isolated environments, and it cites 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct GPUs within HPE AI/HPC systems. In benchmarks, the article reports up to 1.73x more throughput on end-to-end AI benchmarks and 1.93x more throughput on machine learning workloads compared with competing x86 options. It adds that the LUMI supercomputer in Finland and the Adastra supercomputer at CINES in France use HPE and AMD architectures.

The article is written by HPE and AMD, which are the sponsors, and it presents their combined platform as the foundation for CSPs to build these services. It names HPE Morpheus Software for orchestration and tenant isolation, HPE OpsRamp Software for infrastructure monitoring, and built-in resource tracking for usage-based billing. It also says the architecture supports air-gapped management tools for highly restrictive environments. The article does not attribute any statement to an independent party beyond the sponsors' own descriptions of their products.

The primary audiences the article names are regional cloud service providers, along with governments, financial institutions, healthcare networks and critical infrastructure operators whose sensitive data it says cannot be exported. The article gives examples of local buyers such as regional banks, municipal governments and healthcare providers that CSPs could serve. It describes the European market as one where digital sovereignty laws are among the strictest in the world. It does not provide sales figures, customer counts or market size beyond calling the sovereign AI opportunity multibillion-dollar in a call to action.

The article is part of a BrandPost series and links to a related piece titled "Sovereign AI for CSPs Building New Revenue Streams." Other BrandPost pieces appearing alongside it on the same date address AI power demands and C-suite control of AI. The article does not report on specific regulatory changes, named enforcement actions or particular CSPs that have launched sovereign AI services. It does not say how pricing or margins would be set for customers, nor does it identify which jurisdictions would impose which requirements.

Articles.Title: Monetizing compliance: New AI revenue streams for regional CSPs

stories.Headline: Automated Anesthesia Systems Require Human Clinical Intuition Alongside Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a correspondence published in Anesthesiology and Perioperative Science, written by Fredericus H. J. van Loon, Menno A. de Wilde, and Angelique T. M. Dierick-van Daele, that responds to a comprehensive review by Xiuding Cai and colleagues on the future of automated anesthesia. The authors agree that intelligent closed-loop platforms, powered by artificial intelligence and physiological modeling, hold considerable promise for personalizing perioperative care. They argue, however, that widespread clinical deployment cannot succeed until critical technical, regulatory, and ethical challenges are resolved. Their central point is that automated systems cannot replace human clinical judgment in anesthesia care.

Modern anesthesiological care depends heavily on collecting data from two sources: real-time monitoring of physiological signals during surgery, and preoperative diagnostic findings and imaging. The authors note that algorithmic processing of these data streams offers meaningful decision support, especially in identifying early warning signs of patient deterioration or acute adverse events. Both the authors and Cai and colleagues agree that this analytical value is substantial. The correspondence nonetheless cautions that such tools work within a broader clinical discipline. Anesthesia practice, as the authors describe it, extends well beyond inducing and sustaining hypnosis, analgesia, and muscle relaxation.

Automated platforms can reduce the cognitive workload of clinical teams by handling repetitive tasks, administrative requirements, and drug titration. The authors say that overviews of automated systems often overlook the contributions healthcare professionals make during clinical delivery. Physician anesthesiologists and nurse anesthetists, they write, provide a concerned presence that responds to patients' physical and psychological needs. Algorithms cannot replace situational awareness, ethical responsibility, accountability, or clinical intuition. The authors highlight intuition, often experienced as a sense of worry, as a competency that lets practitioners make rapid assessments from experience and direct observation.

Citing work by Robben and colleagues, the authors describe intuition as a catalyst for critical thinking, complex problem-solving, and patient advocacy. They also argue that recognizing deterioration during surgery cannot rely only on objective measures such as vital signs. Experienced clinicians often detect environmental changes, including the immediate physiological effects of surgical interventions, much earlier than contemporary algorithms do. The letter further identifies technical limits in data-driven anesthesia models, including incomplete training datasets, measurement noise, biological complexity, and variability between patients. Because uncertainty cannot be fully eliminated, the authors call for transparency, explainability, rigorous validation, and continuous evaluation to prevent the risks of opaque black-box systems.

The authors expect the anesthesia practitioner's role to evolve into a hybrid function that links technology with bedside care. Clinicians will increasingly combine clinical acumen with systems thinking and work closely with engineers, data scientists, ethicists, and policymakers to oversee and validate automated workflows. The authors conclude that the digital transformation of anesthesia requires a lasting balance between artificial intelligence precision and human expertise. Their position is that closed-loop systems offer valuable real-time adjustments, but safe perioperative outcomes ultimately depend on experienced caregivers acting as technology integrators.

Articles.Title: Automated Anesthesia Systems Require Human Clinical Intuition Alongside Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: AI-powered hacking demands response within minutes, cybersecurity experts warn
stories.Summary:
Trellix Chief Technology Officer Mo Cashman warned at the Cyber Security conference at Tel Aviv University on Tuesday that defenders must identify AI-driven cyberattacks within 15 minutes to have any chance of limiting catastrophic damage to a business or government agency. He described an accelerated four-stage response timeline. Identification should occur within 15 minutes, orientation within two hours, decision within four hours, and action within four to 72 hours, depending on the threat. Cashman's team has sometimes begun partial remediation within 20 minutes by deploying security assets to clients in advance of an attack. The warning followed concern in late October over a PHP programming vulnerability that reportedly left as much as 70% of the internet hackable until it was patched.

AISLE Chief Information Security Officer Jaya Baloo told the conference that attackers have always held an advantage in the ratio of spending on offense versus defense, and that AI has made that imbalance much worse. She said an attacker can now pay as little as $25 to mount a semi-sophisticated attack, while defenders must spend heavily to guard against it. Baloo blamed much of the imbalance on American and Chinese companies releasing new AI models without fully weighing their potential for danger. She argued that governments must quickly regulate and criminalize misuse of certain models.

She also singled out UNITREE products as hackable and questionable in trustworthiness, and noted that The Jerusalem Post had asked UNITREE to respond. CrowdStrike Chief Business Officer Daniel Bernard took a different position, arguing that the United States, Israel, and the West should keep advancing AI without pausing or slowing down. He contrasted this with calls from leading figures at Anthropic, OpenAI, and others for a sector-wide slowdown to better understand new generative AI systems. Bernard said his company has built an AI "kill switch" that can act on AI gateways, cloud and agent permissions, and other issues to restore safety for newer models.

He warned that the West would fall behind China and others if it slowed down, and that running AI in an isolated sandbox risks leaving organizations behind. Microsoft Israel Director of R&D Michal Braverman-Blumenstyk said the key is to keep studying what happens inside AI systems, and that such internal processes should be open rather than locked in a black box. At the same conference, Maj. Gen.

Aviad Dagan, head of the IDF J6 and Cyber Defense Directorate, said the military has used AI to assemble large volumes of data from three years of war. He said this data could help generate strategies for future conflicts in tunnel, mountain, or other terrain. Dagan added that the IDF is moving toward using AI agents to help initiate and propose military plans. The articles do not describe any formal rule or mandate that requires the 15-minute response window, and they do not report any government action taken in response to the warnings.

Articles.Title: AI-powered hacking demands response within minutes, cybersecurity experts warn

stories.Headline: OSF joins statewide AI cyberattack exercise to strengthen hospital emergency response - WEEK
stories.Summary:
Hospitals across Illinois took part in a statewide emergency preparedness exercise on November 4, 2026, in which they faced a simulated cyberattack driven by artificial intelligence. The exercise, called "Broken Trust: AI Takes Control," was led by the Illinois Health and Hospital Association and involved more than 115 hospitals and health systems. It ran as a virtual event and was designed to disrupt patient care, communications and hospital operations. Unlike a typical cyberattack, the scenario kept computer systems looking functional while the information inside them could no longer be fully trusted. The association said it was the largest AI-focused emergency preparedness exercise ever conducted with hospitals in Illinois.

The simulated attack included AI-generated impersonations of hospital leaders, communication failures and deepfake videos. Hospital teams had to decide how to keep operating while checking whether the information reaching them was accurate. Keneatha Johnson, assistant vice president of safety and emergency preparedness for the association, said AI adds a layer of complexity beyond traditional attacks, which usually involve shutting systems down, stealing data or blocking access to technology. The exercise was built to show hospitals where their weaknesses lie before a real incident occurs. Johnson noted that no organization can fully eliminate the risk of a cyberattack, but drills like this help hospitals sharpen their response.

OSF HealthCare was one of the participating health systems. Sherry Myers, director of ministry operations support at OSF, said the organization regularly runs emergency preparedness exercises to improve coordination among emergency management, information technology and clinical teams. She said the top priority is always safe patient care, and that OSF keeps downtime and continuity procedures so essential services can continue when technology is unavailable. Her team works closely with IT staff to maintain those procedures. Myers's comments reflected the organization's ongoing approach to readiness rather than any specific finding from the exercise.

The exercise reflects growing concern among hospitals about how artificial intelligence could be used to attack their systems and mislead their staff. The articles do not describe any real attack on Illinois hospitals connected to the drill, nor do they report specific changes to state requirements or new mandates for hospitals. They also do not say what lessons were drawn from the exercise or whether a follow-up report will be published. Based on the available reporting, the exercise itself is the main development, and further outcomes have not been announced.

Articles.Title: OSF joins statewide AI cyberattack exercise to strengthen hospital emergency response - WEEK

stories.Headline: AI100 Report: AI has entered the mainstream and is reshaping society - Max-Planck-Gesellschaft
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has moved from a specialised technology into an everyday reality for millions of people, according to the latest report from the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100), released on November 10, 2026. The report, titled AI Goes Mainstream: The Scaling Era and the Rise of Generative AI, was produced by AI100, a longitudinal project administered by Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI). The study is published every five years and examines AI's development and its effects on people, communities, and society. Its authors credit the past five years with a watershed moment, driven by large-scale computing, vast datasets, and the rapid rise of generative AI. The third report evaluates how AI has evolved since the 2021 edition.

Iyad Rahwan, Director of the Center for Human and Machines at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, was a member of the 2026 AI100 Study Panel. The international panel brought together experts in computer science, philosophy, sociology, and related disciplines. The report examines the scaling of data and computing resources behind generative AI, advances in scientific discovery, and investment in AI infrastructure. It also covers the concentration of frontier AI development, cybersecurity and military applications, the trustworthiness of digital media, emerging risks, public participation, and international governance. The panel organised its findings around 12 key takeaways.

The report says the scaling paradigm, which builds AI systems using ever more compute and data, is running into data and compute constraints, shifting the frontier toward reasoning and inference-time compute. It states that AI is already transforming the creative industries, mathematics, and software development. It also states that AI is transforming science at remarkable speed, a fact the report links to the 2024 Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry. Capital investment in AI infrastructure is unprecedented in scale and speed, according to the report, which notes fears of a financial bubble and strain on energy and freshwater supplies. Frontier AI development is concentrated among a small number of U.S. and Chinese actors, the report notes, raising international concerns about access to leading-edge technologies.

Iyad Rahwan said in the report's accompanying statement that the 2021 AI100 report had been very optimistic about rapid AI progress, but that the panel did not foresee the "ChatGPT moment" that brought AI into mainstream discussion. He said billions of people now interact with AI on a regular basis, and that this has changed how society, business, and industry view the technology. The report states that the public has had little say in how AI is developed and deployed, even though AI is reshaping the lives of billions of people. It also describes AI governance as fragmented and increasingly framed in terms of national security, with little international consensus among states. The panel's researchers, according to the release, consider the coming years decisive in shaping the opportunities and risks of the technology.

The AI100 project was launched in 2014 and is led by an international Standing Committee of AI experts, with Stanford's HAI administering it. Every five years it convenes a Study Panel to assess AI's progress and its influence across technical, ethical, economic, and societal domains. The earlier editions were published in 2016 and 2021. The release states that if the current pace of development is sustained, the next five years should be expected to surprise people as much as the past five have. The release does not give further detail on the timing of the next report.

Articles.Title: AI100 Report: AI has entered the mainstream and is reshaping society - Max-Planck-Gesellschaft

stories.Headline: Survey Identifies Human Oversight as Crucial for Fair Healthcare Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
A cross-sectional survey of patients in the United Kingdom, reported on November 10, 2026, found that the absence of human supervision is seen as the greatest threat to fairness in healthcare artificial intelligence. The study, published in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making, was led by researchers including E. Remfry and B. G. Tzovaras. Of the participating patients, 89.9 percent said that AI decisions which neither patients nor clinicians could question or challenge would hurt fairness. The researchers drew on 149 patients recruited through public and patient involvement networks.

The study used two vignettes, one a patient-facing symptom checker and the other a clinician-facing decision-support tool for cancer treatment, so that attitudes could be compared across both settings. Participants rated 13 factors for their effect on fairness and also gave free-text answers. Analysis used descriptive statistics, Pearson's chi-square tests, ordinal logistic regression and thematic analysis of the written responses. Beyond unchallengeable systems, 89.3 percent of respondents said AI built without clinician input would undermine fairness, and 86.6 percent said incorrect electronic health record data posed a severe threat. Patient views on these factors stayed consistent across both vignettes.

The article attributes these findings to the study's authors, who concluded that patients hold nuanced views on fairness across the whole AI lifecycle, from development through deployment and maintenance. Respondents also raised concerns about digital accessibility, the handling of long-term conditions, the upkeep needed to keep algorithms accurate, and the possible loss of human empathy in care. The researchers recommended designing health technologies collaboratively with end users, building human-in-the-loop systems, and making them flexible enough to adapt to ongoing clinical input. The article presents these recommendations as design considerations for future tools and does not describe any regulatory or policy changes.

Articles.Title: Survey Identifies Human Oversight as Crucial for Fair Healthcare Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Benton Harbor considers AI property code enforcement
stories.Summary:
Benton Harbor officials are weighing whether to use artificial intelligence to identify property code violations, according to a report published by WNDU on November 10, 2026. The city is looking at a program called City Detect, which WNDU attributes to its reporting partners at The Herald Palladium. The article offers no further detail on how the tool would work or when a decision might be made. The rest of the article's content on this topic is limited to that single point. It does not say what the program would cost, how it would be funded, or whether the city has committed to it.

It also does not describe what kinds of violations it would flag or how property owners would be notified. Those details are not in the material provided. The article does not name any official who is responsible for the proposal or quote anyone speaking about it. Benton Harbor city officials are the ones considering the idea, but the report does not attribute specific comments to any of them. Without statements on the record, the source of the plan and its supporters are unclear from the available reporting.

The remaining items in the same feed cover unrelated local news, including sonar technology used by Elkhart firefighters, child care funding in South Bend, and a St. Joseph County jail food contract change. Nothing in those stories connects to the Benton Harbor proposal. The article does not say when officials will next discuss the program or whether any vote is scheduled. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Benton Harbor considers AI property code enforcement

stories.Headline: Teleport releases beams to secure artificial intelligence agents in production
stories.Summary:
Teleport, a company that provides infrastructure identity software, has launched Teleport Beams, a runtime environment for running artificial intelligence agents inside production systems. The launch was reported on November 10, 2026, by SC Media, which cited Silicon Angle as its source. The product is aimed at gaps that have held enterprises back from adopting AI agents, particularly around delegated identity and complete audit trails. Under the design, each agent runs in its own ephemeral micro-VM, so it holds only limited, task-specific privileges instead of standing access.

Before an agent acts, it must submit a proposed execution plan, which humans or other language models can review. Sessions are scored against prebuilt detection rules from the MITRE ATT&CK framework, and a built-in kill switch can cut an agent's connections to production systems if it strays from its goal. Teleport says sensitive credentials never enter the agent environment and that every action is logged. The articles attribute the release to Teleport and describe it as building on the earlier Teleport Agentic Identity Framework and the company's existing infrastructure identity platform.

According to the report, that platform already serves more than 700 enterprises, including Nasdaq Inc., DoorDash Inc. and Elastic N.V. The product is now generally available to teams that want to deploy autonomous agents, and the company presents it as a way to do so without weakening infrastructure integrity. The same day's coverage placed Teleport's launch within a wider wave of products for AI agent security. Flashpoint introduced agentic AI for automating threat investigations, Cowbell Cyber Inc. launched an insurance policy for small and midsized businesses against losses from deploying AI agents, and Israeli startup Bay AI Inc. launched with $50 million in funding to secure autonomous agents in enterprise environments. The articles do not say how these products will perform in practice or what adoption they will see.

Articles.Title: Teleport releases beams to secure artificial intelligence agents in production

stories.Headline: New Framework Outlines Six Key Dimensions for Human-Friendly Conversational Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Hongik University in Seoul have set out a preliminary framework describing how conversational artificial intelligence can interact with people in a human-friendly way. The study, published in Frontiers in Computer Science, was led by Siu Jung and Yoori Koo, who named it the Human-Friendly AI Interaction Design Framework, or HFAI-DF. The authors describe the framework as a way to turn principles of human cognition and anthropomorphism into concrete behavior for computer agents. The work responds to the shift toward sustained, back-and-forth dialogue with AI systems, which has drawn attention beyond technical measures such as safety, transparency, and data privacy. The authors say human-friendly interaction is not simply polite wording, decorative warmth, or physical mimicry.

The framework rests on psychological research into anthropomorphism, the human tendency to attribute consciousness, intentions, and emotions to non-human entities. Building on models from Epley, Waytz, and colleagues, the team identified cognitive and motivational drivers of that tendency. The cognitive side was divided into four areas: simulated emotional experience, episodic memory, reflexive metacognition, and self-awareness combined with theory of mind. The motivational side included sociality motivation, the drive for affiliation that grows when people feel isolated, and effectance motivation, the desire to understand and control one's environment. Jung and Koo broke these factors into components and synthesized them into thirty behavioral units.

Each unit describes an observable capability, such as tracking uncertainty or restructuring a task proactively, without requiring the machine to have literal inner emotions.
