To test how users perceived the thirty behaviors, the authors surveyed 208 adults from Generation MZ, defined as people born from 1981 through 2012. The group included 109 participants aged 20 to 29, 83 aged 30 to 39, and 16 aged 40 to 44. Participants rated each behavior on a seven-point scale using three adjective pairs: machine-like versus human-like, unnatural versus natural, and artificial versus lifelike. Each item was shown with a realistic interaction scenario written by the researchers.

The authors analyzed the responses with exploratory factor analysis in SPSS Version 31.0, and sampling adequacy was strong, with a Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of 0.93. The analysis produced six dimensions that the authors arranged from the agent's internal self-regulation outward to collaborative contribution. The first dimension, Self-Aware Interaction, has five items and an internal consistency of 0.823, and its strongest element is identity and role awareness at 0.738. It also includes learning history representation, explanation of reasoning grounds, self-monitoring, and recognition of uncertainty. The second dimension, User-Adaptive Responsiveness Interaction, has three items with an alpha of 0.825, led by detection of verbal and non-verbal cues at 0.658.

The third, Context-Aware Reasoning Interaction, has five items with an alpha of 0.870, and its leading element is user error recognition and guidance at 0.733. The fourth, Socio-Emotional Interaction, has six items with an alpha of 0.872 and was identified by the authors as the central relational hub, with moderate correlations of 0.403 to 0.476 with all five other dimensions. The fifth, Creative Collaboration Interaction, has seven items with an alpha of 0.907, and the sixth, Proactive Assistance Interaction, has four items with an alpha of 0.865. Jung and Koo present the framework as a research model and urge caution about applying it.

They state that AI does not have genuine feelings, subjective experience, or consciousness, and they warn that poorly calibrated friendliness could produce deceptive attachment, emotional dependency, or discomfort when a system's imitation of human behavior breaks down. The authors also note that socio-emotional features that help in counseling settings may distract from or undermine analytical decision-support tools and high-stakes work. They acknowledge empirical limitations as well, including that the exploratory factor analysis relied on third-person evaluations of written scenarios. The articles provided do not describe any planned follow-up studies or deployment timelines.

Articles.Title: New Framework Outlines Six Key Dimensions for Human-Friendly Conversational Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Air Force previews AI training as it prepares to deploy new tools
stories.Summary:
The Department of the Air Force is expanding its use of artificial intelligence and preparing the training its personnel will need to work with fast-changing tools. According to Federal News Network, the Air Force and Space Force first spent their time building the strategy and policy that would govern AI use. Susan Davenport, the department's chief data and AI officer, said that foundation is now ready to be tested. She spoke on November 6, 2026, at an AI event in Washington, and the report was published on November 10.

The services plan to launch AI tools tailored to 15 missions, ranging from intelligence to nuclear operations, with a civilian or officer overseeing progress in each area. At the same time, the department is rolling out courses that teach airmen and guardians how to develop and apply AI, along with its limitations. Davenport said the department intends to introduce a three-level training approach by the end of November. The 100-level course covers general AI principles for everyday work, the 200-level course covers building AI-powered workflows with lessons on topics such as legal guardrails, and the 300-level course targets developers. Completion will be logged in service members' permanent training records, which can count toward promotion and job selection.

Davenport described the approach as part of a broader push to shorten the time needed to attack targets, save commanders time, and speed decisions compared with America's adversaries. The department will track progress through quarterly showcases where officials overseeing each AI mission area, called domain principals, report their achievements and seek help on persistent problems. Two showcases have been held so far, and a third is planned for December or January. That meeting is meant to bring Air Force and Space Force units together with research organizations and private companies that could supply solutions. Davenport said the first showcase made clear that research and development partners were missing from the room where the department's campaign goals were discussed.

Davenport also said the department wants to move away from a single central team that cleans and tags the large volumes of data processed each day. Instead, organizations would gain more control over their own data, which would clarify which information is reliable and make it easier to share. She described AI as a gift that lets the department reimagine its mission and do things it has never done before. The article does not say when the decentralized data approach will take effect or what the total cost of the training and tools will be.

Articles.Title: Air Force previews AI training as it prepares to deploy new tools

stories.Headline: Hybrid Swarm AI Framework Detects Synthetic Interior Renders With 97.5 Percent Accuracy
stories.Summary:
Researcher Zhengfang Wu has published a study in Discover Artificial Intelligence describing a computational framework that distinguishes real interior photographs from synthetic computer-generated renderings with 97.5 percent accuracy. The framework is called the Glowworm Swarm-Optimized Attention-enriched Variational Autoencoder, abbreviated as GSO-Att-VAE. The article was published on November 12, 2026, on bioengineer.org. The study targets a growing problem, since generative systems can now produce detailed interior spaces that standard inspection tools often fail to flag. The authors say existing automated design tools lack a way to separate authentic photographs from synthetic outputs while also optimizing spatial parameters.

The framework combines statistical filtering, sparse spatial encoding, hierarchical visual extraction, attention-guided probabilistic modeling, and swarm intelligence in one pipeline. It is designed to run on edge devices rather than requiring centralized server infrastructure. The study used the publicly accessible Edge AI Interior Spatial Design Dataset hosted on Kaggle, which contains 4,000 synthetic interior scene records and 69 tabular columns. The target attribute, Image_Authenticity, labels each record as either Real_Interior or AI_Generated. Of the 68 predictor variables, the framework uses 58 pre-computed structured spatial metadata attributes supplied with the dataset rather than deriving them from raw pixels.

Images pass through two-dimensional Gaussian filtering, and the numerical attributes are standardized using Z-score normalization. Wu formulated the GSO-Att-VAE framework to address these deficiencies through a unified architecture that couples visual features with structured spatial attributes. The article attributes the design to Wu alone, as the study's sole named researcher. According to the article, the framework's authors frame their purpose as resolving the operational silos that separate image generation, aesthetic scoring, layout planning, and authenticity detection. The article quotes Wu's aim only in paraphrase, stating that the work is meant to close these gaps in a single edge-compatible system.

The article does not report any further statement from Wu beyond the study itself. The article does not report reactions from other researchers, companies, designers, or users of interior visualization tools. It identifies the groups most affected as those relying on automated interior design and architectural visualization, where synthetic or physically flawed renderings can feed into layout analyses and produce implausible recommendations. It also notes that interactive smart interior installations depend on low-latency local processing, which centralized cloud systems cannot easily provide. The article gives no figures on how widely such tools are currently used.

It does not describe any deployment of the framework outside the reported experiments. The article explains that generative pipelines such as StyleGAN variants, diffusion frameworks, and vision-language systems have sped up interior concept creation but typically separate rendering from geometric verification. It notes that classical classifiers for visual authenticity rely almost exclusively on two-dimensional pixels and ignore structured parameters such as room dimensions and illumination vectors. It also states that centralized cloud architectures introduce latency and bandwidth demands that limit real-time responsiveness. The study's own evaluation reported an F1-score of 96.9 percent, precision of 97.3 percent, recall of 97.4 percent, and an area under the ROC curve of 97.2 percent.

On an 800-instance test set, the model correctly identified 392 of 400 AI-generated images and 388 of 400 real photographs. The article's account ends at the reported results and the comparison against classical classifiers and deep learning backbones, which it begins to describe but does not complete in the portion provided. It does not state whether the results have been independently replicated, whether the framework will be released or deployed, or how it performs on data beyond the Kaggle dataset. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Hybrid Swarm AI Framework Detects Synthetic Interior Renders With 97.5 Percent Accuracy

stories.Headline: Fewer hours and higher wages – or more burnout and surveillance: employers told to prepare for AI
stories.Summary:
The Australian government has issued a best practice guide on how employers should adopt artificial intelligence at work, and it warns that the technology could either improve or worsen conditions for ordinary workers. Workplace relations minister Amanda Rishworth launched the guide on Thursday 12 November 2026, as large firms cut staff in restructures linked partly to AI. Qantas announced 850 job cuts targeting finance, human resources and marketing roles, National Australian Bank announced 2,500 job losses, and Canva announced 1,200 layoffs. The guide says entry-level work may be the first to be automated.

The guide paints an optimistic picture, suggesting wider AI use could raise productivity, boost wages, offer shorter and more flexible hours, or provide more meaningful work. It also concedes "potential hazards," including intrusive worker surveillance, poor rostering, unrealistic performance standards and possible discrimination. It warns that if basic tasks are automated, the remaining work may become more intense and complex. It also flags that some employers could use expanded monitoring for performance management.

Rishworth said employers must give workers a clear plan about how automation could affect their jobs and the chance to move into new roles. In a speech in Sydney, she said adding AI without consulting workers could increase workloads, because people must navigate an extra step. The guide cautions that younger, older and First Nations workers, along with women and people with a disability, face disproportionate impacts. Labor MP Ed Husic, the former industry minister, asked at a parliamentary hearing on the big four banks who would receive the benefits of higher productivity.

Greens leader David Shoebridge accused the government of watching from the sidelines and said the guidance was too weak. He argued that a worker who loses a job to an algorithm would have no legal recourse under the current approach, and he called for the protections to be written into law. The Reserve Bank this week reported "little evidence to date" of AI disrupting the labour market, while saying future effects were highly uncertain. It noted "tentative signs" of impact on roles such as clerks, computer programmers and call centre workers.

Articles.Title: Fewer hours and higher wages – or more burnout and surveillance: employers told to prepare for AI

stories.Headline: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Platform Connects Architectural Concepts to Physical Fabrication
stories.Summary:
Researchers have introduced FUGenerator, an integrated multimodal artificial intelligence platform intended to link architectural design concepts with physical fabrication. The platform was developed by Xinhui Xu, Tinghao Feng, Yulu Zhang, Zhengcheng He, and Philip F. Yuan, and the article describes it as open access. It was reported on November 11, 2026, by bioengineer.org. The system is aimed at gaps in domain knowledge, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and software interoperability across the building design lifecycle. The authors say existing tools suffer from format incompatibilities, irreversible data loss, version inconsistencies, and opaque generative processes.

FUGenerator is built around three components: a dual-subgraph architectural knowledge graph, a multimodal algorithm library, and a node-based traceable workflow editor. The knowledge graph's semantic subgraph includes more than 13,200 building regulation clauses and 283 peer-reviewed academic papers. Regulatory coverage centers on structural integrity, building fire prevention, general safety, and sustainable construction. The text module relies on ChatGLM-6B, fine-tuned on about 20,000 regulatory question-and-answer pairs, with training completed on an NVIDIA A100 in about two hours. Visual synthesis uses Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models with ControlNet, whose layers were tuned on roughly 4,500 architectural images.

Resolution is upgraded with ESRGAN, and single-image three-dimensional reconstruction uses TripoSR. The article attributes the work to the research team led by Xinhui Xu, Tinghao Feng, Yulu Zhang, Zhengcheng He, and Philip F. Yuan. It says the team structured the platform to resolve interoperability and specialization deficits found in commercial tools such as DALL-E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, and Runway Gen-2. The authors describe those tools as performing isolated single-modality conversions or lacking architectural depth.

The team states that natural language serves as the semantic channel connecting text, two-dimensional imagery, parametric formats, and fabrication data. The article does not give any statement from the researchers beyond these descriptions of their aims. The platform was tested in a university design curriculum with 21 fourth-year undergraduate architecture students over eight weeks. The students designed chairs across four fabrication groups: timber tectonics with five students, bamboo weaving with six, three-dimensional printing with four, and mixed reality construction with six.

Telemetry showed peak generation bursts above 180 design iterations in one hour, with initial furniture schemes completed within the first 20 days. A later eight-week phase scaled the workflows to a multi-story timber tower and an undulating bamboo footbridge. The timber team drew structural logic from the Yingxian Wooden Pagoda and fine-tuned two custom LoRA models. The article is a feature-style summary of the research and does not describe commercial availability or results beyond the testing it reports.

It does not say how many students completed the later phase or how the scaled prototypes performed. Usage data showed low adoption of direct image-to-3D generation because of mesh quality limitations, a limitation the article notes without resolving. The source does not state whether the platform will be further developed, deployed beyond the university curriculum, or evaluated by independent parties. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Platform Connects Architectural Concepts to Physical Fabrication

stories.Headline: Survey: Patient comfort with AI varies by level of provider involvement - American Hospital Association
stories.Summary:
A Gallup survey published November 9, 2026, examined how comfortable U.S. patients are with artificial intelligence in their care. The survey found that 56% of U.S. adults who visited a primary care provider in the past year are comfortable with AI making diagnosis or treatment decisions, provided those decisions can be changed or overridden by their provider. Another 38% said they are comfortable when AI assists and their provider makes the final decision. Only 9% said they are comfortable with AI making treatment decisions without any provider review. The results show that patient comfort depends heavily on how much a clinician stays involved in the decision.

Most patients who were surveyed want a human provider to keep the final say, even when AI is helping with the analysis. The findings suggest that the level of provider oversight matters more to patients than the mere presence of AI in care. The articles do not describe any new rule or requirement that follows from the survey. The survey was published by Gallup, and the American Hospital Association reported on it in its AHA News coverage. The articles do not identify any individual officials or researchers who commented on the findings beyond the survey results themselves.

The AHA's own recent activity on AI includes a new policy webpage launched November 3 and recommendations to the Food and Drug Administration sent October 19 on regulatory frameworks for generative AI-enabled medical devices. The survey is part of a wider debate among hospitals, regulators and patients about how AI should be used in clinical settings. The AHA has also covered related topics such as AI governance in hospitals and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's October 7 launch of an AI initiative on medical evidence reviews. The articles do not say what steps, if any, will follow from the Gallup findings.

Articles.Title: Survey: Patient comfort with AI varies by level of provider involvement - American Hospital Association

stories.Headline: Siemens Q4 profit jumps 32% on AI infrastructure demand; raises growth targets
stories.Summary:
Siemens AG shares climbed to an 11-week high on Thursday, 12 November 2026, after the German industrial group reported quarterly results that beat expectations and raised its medium-term growth targets. Strong demand for AI-related data centre equipment and rail contracts pushed orders to a record for the quarter. The stock rose 4.44% to €289.30 after touching an intraday high of €291.45, its highest level since August 28. It also outperformed Germany's DAX, which gained around 0.9% during the session.

For the quarter ended September 30, net income rose to €2.43 billion from €1.84 billion a year earlier. Revenue increased 11% to €23.68 billion, while profit at the Industrial Business climbed 22% to a record €3.90 billion. The industrial profit margin improved to 16.8% from 15.3%. Orders surged 58% to a quarterly record €34.77 billion, lifting the book-to-bill ratio to 1.47 and the order backlog to €143 billion.

Growth was led by Smart Infrastructure and Mobility, with Smart Infrastructure's revenue rising 16% to €7.24 billion and its order intake jumping 40% on large data centre contract wins in the U.S. and Europe. Digital Industries revenue rose 11% and profit increased 50%, driven mainly by operational improvements in automation. Mobility's orders more than quadrupled, supported by major German rail contracts including a €2.4 billion high-speed train order. Siemens attributed these gains to continued investment in electrification, digital infrastructure and rail transportation.

Looking ahead, Siemens expects comparable revenue growth of 9% to 11% in fiscal 2027 and earnings per share before purchase price allocation accounting of €10.20 to €10.80. The company pointed to investment in AI and digital infrastructure, public investment programmes and a recovery in industrial activity as key growth drivers. For the full fiscal year, net income fell 9% to €9.47 billion, reflecting a €2.1 billion gain from the sale of Innomotics in the prior year. Revenue rose 6% to €83.37 billion, Industrial Business profit increased 13% to a record €13.29 billion, and the proposed dividend rises to €5.50 per share from €5.35.

Articles.Title: Siemens Q4 profit jumps 32% on AI infrastructure demand; raises growth targets

stories.Headline: Corporate AI Training in Australia: Paloren Trains Whole Departments on Approved AI Tools and Real Tasks
stories.Summary:
Paloren, an AI strategy, implementation, automation and training company, is offering Australian organizations corporate AI training that covers whole departments, according to a press release dated November 12, 2026, republished on FinancialContent. The offer is aimed at organizations planning training for 2027, and it is built around the AI tools each company has already approved and the tasks its teams repeat every week. Paloren delivers half-day and full-day workshops, four-to-six-week department programs and executive coaching. The company is co-founded by Aaron Agius and Alex Agius.

Before any session, Paloren records which tools each team is approved to use, such as Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and which functions are switched on. Cohorts contain six to 16 people, with multiple cohorts for larger groups, and role-specific practice lets finance, operations and customer service teams each work on their own material. Each format includes a baseline exercise, safe practice materials, reusable task instructions, a later independent attempt and a workplace trial with a named reviewer. The article says managers receive work they can inspect rather than just an attendance list. Remote sessions run in Australian working hours, and onsite delivery is available by arrangement.

The training is delivered by founders and senior practitioners at Paloren. The company says organizations can start a discussion by sharing team sizes, approved tools and two or three priority tasks. The article describes Paloren as a business that builds AI into the systems companies already run and trains their people to own it. It notes that course selection for Microsoft 365 users can start from the Word, Teams and Outlook work staff already do.

Paloren's Australian AI Training Price Index, checked on November 10, 2026, found a median published starting price of A$4,900 per group for private team sessions. The index covered 13 offers from eight providers, and session lengths ranged from about one hour to a full day. Because of that spread, the index advises comparing duration and group size before comparing price. The article also notes that it is third-party content and that the publisher makes no guarantees about its accuracy or completeness.

Articles.Title: Corporate AI Training in Australia: Paloren Trains Whole Departments on Approved AI Tools and Real Tasks

stories.Headline: PARTNER CONTENT: Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data
stories.Summary:
PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was disclosed in 2026 after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, and PHP shipped fixes the following day. The article reports that frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and that the flaw reportedly went undetected for more than a decade. Several security firms saw exploitation attempts before the fixes were released, and Cloudflare reported early attacks hours ahead of the patch. The article frames these events as a sign of how quickly the threat landscape is now shifting for IT and security teams. The piece argues that autonomous IT operations need a governed loop in which software finds risks, ranks them, proposes fixes and carries them out within limits people define.

Routine, low-risk actions can run automatically, higher-impact ones wait for human approval, and some actions are never delegated at all. Every step leaves a reviewable and reversible record. The article says that three problems make this difficult: incomplete visibility into every copy of PHP, the need to hop between separate asset, scanning and attack-surface tools, and the shrinking gap between disclosure and exploitation. It adds that putting an AI agent on top of stale, fragmented data scales these problems rather than solving them. The article is written as partner content, and it presents Tanium's real-time endpoint data as the foundation for trustworthy automation.

It names four qualities such data should have: accuracy, speed, control, and shared truth across IT, security and the system of record. Matt Psencik, a threat research engineer at Tanium, is quoted saying that the installations he worries about most are those a security team does not know it owns. The article also says World Wide Technology, a Tanium partner, hosts a Tanium lab where customers can test approaches before production, and it promotes Tanium Atlas as the product intended to reduce tool-hopping. The article gives practical first steps: find every copy of software, including bundled copies, by comparing the CMDB with what is actually on the network; rank systems by internet exposure and decide in advance which actions are automatic, which need approval and which are never delegated; and pilot one contained, low-risk workflow with approvals and a reviewed audit trail before widening scope.

Articles.Title: PARTNER CONTENT: Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data

stories.Headline: AI reshaping infrastructure, energy and connecting networks
stories.Summary:
A survey of 2,000 adults across 11 markets, conducted in September 2026 by RETN, an independent global network service provider, found that AI is reshaping digital infrastructure, energy use and the networks that connect them. The findings were published by Computer Weekly on 12 November 2026. The survey polled 600 people in the US, 800 in the UK, Germany, the Netherlands and Spain, and 600 in China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines. RETN supplemented the results with views from its senior network experts.

The survey found that 53% of respondents named AI tools as the biggest driver of new datacentre construction, and that half of respondents did not want such facilities built near them. Growing power and cooling demands are pushing datacentres toward remote sites where land and energy are available but fibre may be scarce, so RETN warned that developers now need to involve network carriers two to five years before a site goes live, up from one to two years previously. The research also found that AI traffic makes up only a small share of open internet growth, with 80 to 90% of RETN's AI-related requests being for private point-to-point links, dark fibre and dedicated interconnects. Real-time AI processing, fed by connected devices, is expected to reverse the download-heavy pattern of the current internet and push computing toward the network edge.

RETN chief executive Tony O'Sullivan said the industry is only at the start of the changes AI will bring to networks. He argued that the networks best placed for the future will be those able to adapt when geopolitics shifts and to keep running when individual parts fail, rather than simply those that build the most capacity. The article also says that 84% of those surveyed use AI and that 54% said losing access would disrupt their lives within days. Three-quarters had experienced problems with their preferred AI service in the past year, and 18% had begun regularly using an alternative provider. The article's accompanying links describe carriers introducing AI-based network management tools and expanding capacity, but the survey itself does not set out any binding requirement or regulatory change.

Articles.Title: AI reshaping infrastructure, energy and connecting networks

stories.Headline: Orange walks AI tightrope to capture 'hundreds of mil' in value
stories.Summary:
Orange Business Services, the enterprise unit of French operator Orange, is using AI to pursue value in the hundreds of millions of euros, according to an article by Iain Morris published on November 12, 2026, on Light Reading. The piece profiles Miguel Alvarez, Orange Business Services' chief data and AI officer, who was interviewed on the sidelines of the Techritory event held in Latvia the previous month. The article frames Alvarez's position against warnings from critic Cory Doctorow about AI's effects on workers. Alvarez describes his approach as treating AI as another tool rather than letting the machine direct people.

The article describes how Orange is meeting its AI value targets. Orange's group-level value creation target is in the hundreds of millions of euros, and Orange Business Services had a 2025 target of €50 million (US$55.5 million), which was achieved. This year that target has reportedly been raised to €70 million ($77.7 million). Orange is exploring several hundred AI-based use cases, with thirty already in production at Orange Business Services and twenty being industrialized in a subsequent AI expansion. Orange has also reduced its global workforce by roughly 10,000 employees since the end of 2022, to around 126,000 in September.

Alvarez says the value is measured across cost savings, cost avoidance, revenue protection and additional revenue generated. He attributes much of the gain to shorter development times and faster activity rather than headcount reduction. He gave a product example in which a working version was reached in a couple of months, a process he estimates would otherwise have taken four to five times longer. Software development has also changed, with some teams now automating most steps of the development lifecycle through requirement-driven development. Alvarez also expects agentic systems, not humans, to write most future code, while people will still learn core coding concepts.

Alvarez stresses that Orange must maintain control over AI, particularly because the technology is non-deterministic. He says he must balance guardrails against giving agents enough freedom to find better solutions, which could also lead to more errors. Orange uses a mix of commercially available frontier models and open-weight alternatives, deployed on its own infrastructure including on-premises, so it does not depend on public cloud from the start. Agents are built on an open-source framework from LangChain, a San Francisco-based nonprofit, so they can be moved between environments. Alvarez notes that open-weight models are about six months behind the frontier models, though they have improved enough to handle more sophisticated use cases.

Doctorow, a former guest on the Telecoms.com podcast, has warned of AI's "reverse centaur" dynamic, in which humans are steered by AI, and fears companies will use AI to cut jobs. The article notes that little evidence links AI to mass layoffs in any sector. It cites the US unemployment rate of 4.2% in October, down from 4.5% in November last year, and a Bank of England Monetary Policy Report for November finding AI's contribution to UK productivity growth at just 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points annually since 2024. Alvarez's own children, he says, are not learning rudimentary math by hand because they will not need to in the future. Adoption within Orange has grown well beyond expectations, with more than 100,000 active users, against an original hope of 10,000 to 20,000 within a couple of years of ChatGPT's launch.

The article does not state how the €70 million target for this year is progressing or whether it will be met. It also does not detail how many of the several hundred use cases will reach production, or how Orange will address the tension between agent freedom and the risk of errors. Alvarez's remarks on the future balance between human and machine roles in coding remain expectations rather than established outcomes. The article also leaves open how Orange's reliance on open-weight models will develop as frontier models continue to advance.

Articles.Title: Orange walks AI tightrope to capture 'hundreds of mil' in value

stories.Headline: AI needs accountability. Veterans can help provide it
stories.Summary:
This article is an opinion commentary, not a news report, so the story it carries is an argument rather than an event. Shlomo Engelson Argamon, associate provost for artificial intelligence and dean of the Graduate School of Technology at Touro University, published it on November 10, 2026, in Federal News Network. He argues that as artificial intelligence spreads into health care, benefits decisions, finance, cybersecurity and critical infrastructure, the country needs workers who can judge AI's risks and take responsibility for its use, not only workers who know how to operate it. He points to a concrete case, an AI tool that might recommend denying a disability claim, to show why someone must answer for errors. He says Washington has so far focused on AI literacy and guidelines for responsible use, which he calls necessary but insufficient.

He proposes that veterans fill this gap, since military service can build disciplined judgment, accountability and calm decision-making. He cites RAND Corporation findings that leadership, decision-making, dependability and attention to detail are skills veterans bring to civilian work. He notes that veterans still need specialized technical, legal and professional training in AI. He backs this with data that more than half of job postings seeking AI skills are outside IT and computer science, that such postings more than doubled from a year earlier by August 2026, and that employers seek more than 100,000 professionals a year with AI ethics and governance expertise. His core proposal is that Congress create a Veterans AI Workforce Partnership Program within the Labor Department's Veterans' Employment and Training Service, which would administer grants and remain accountable for employment outcomes.

He argues that the program would need a Labor-chaired board including the VA and NIST, with the VA overseeing eligibility and veteran support and NIST setting competencies, risk standards and evaluation protocols. He says existing efforts, including VET TEC 2.0, Registered Apprenticeships, DoD SkillBridge and NSF education programs, each address part of the problem but none integrates AI accountability, so coordination alone would leave no one answerable for the full pathway. He recommends funding stackable credentials, paid experience through SkillBridge and apprenticeships, and regional partnerships, and he proposes $120 million for an initial two-year phase serving at least 10,000 veterans, about $60 million a year. He also proposes tracking completion, placement, wage gains and retention with reviews at six and twelve months, and an independent evaluation after two years. The article does not report any government response to these proposals, and it offers no timeline for Congress to act on them.

Articles.Title: AI needs accountability. Veterans can help provide it - Federal News Network

stories.Headline: Data Center Backlash Is Bipartisan, and That Changes the Math for AI Investors
stories.Summary:
Voters in the November 2026 midterm elections delivered a sharp rebuke to artificial intelligence development, according to a Motley Fool article by Ben Gran published November 12, 2026. Americans across both parties appear to agree that they do not want AI data centers built near their homes. Data tracked by Ballotpedia showed that as of November 4, voters had decided 47 local ballot initiatives on whether to support or limit AI data center development. Of those, 46 initiatives, or 98%, produced outcomes against the development of AI data centers. The article calls this a sign that the AI industry faces a public relations problem.

A CNBC poll found that 56% of voters ranked data centers as a "crucial or major" factor in how they voted on Election Day. Many voters fear AI data centers will raise utility costs and do not want to give up local land and resources without economic benefits for their communities. Newly elected Democratic governors in Ohio and Texas have proposed moratoriums on new AI data center construction. The article notes that the proposals would halt new construction in those two states. Voters also support candidates who are skeptical of AI data centers, according to the article.

Ben Gran, the article's author, frames the backlash as a risk for investors rather than assigning blame to any one party. The article attributes the sell-off to the shifting political mood after the November 3 election. Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote a research note on November 4, as reported by CNBC, saying the midterms would likely slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 data centers across the US. Ives also wrote that his firm now expects Big Tech capex growth to peak in 2027, rather than in 2028 or 2029 as previously expected. Dominique Toublan, head of U.S. credit strategy at Barclays Investment Bank, wrote in a November 4 note that the pushback is bipartisan but local, making the buildout pricier rather than stalling it.

The sell-off hit AI-related stocks in the days after the election, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 falling 5.5% between November 3 and November 5. The iShares Semiconductor ETF plummeted about 15% over the same period, and Caterpillar lost about 11.3%. The article reports that these names have since recouped some of their post-election losses. Toublan's view that scarce power favors the biggest balance sheets is cited as a reason large cash-rich companies could benefit. The article names Alphabet as an example of such a company, and contrasts it with neocloud CoreWeave, which has drawn investor concern about its high debt and rising interest expenses.

The article gives no timeline for when the proposed moratoriums in Ohio and Texas will take effect or whether they will pass. It does not say whether the 800 to 1,000 planned data centers will be delayed or cancelled. The article's author does not say whether the AI boom is over, only that it could be heading for a slowdown. Gran suggests investors could hold the Invesco Nasdaq 100 ETF, which returned about 13.1% annually over five years. The article does not state how the broader AI build-out will fare after the 2027 peak Ives forecasts.

Articles.Title: Data Center Backlash Is Bipartisan, and That Changes the Math for AI Investors

stories.Headline: The sketch Qwen refused to write: How abliteration restores local AI control
stories.Summary:
The InfoWorld article by Oleg Mikheev, published 12 November 2026, describes how he used a technique called abliteration to remove refusal behavior from the Qwen 3.8 27B open-weight model. He began after noticing that the model would write political satire mocking American politics but gave a canned refusal when asked for the same kind of sketch criticizing the Chinese government. The article explains that abliteration, popularized by a developer known as FailSpy through an open-source library, removes hard refusals without retraining the model. Soft refusals, where a model answers but deflects or biases its response, are harder to remove because they are embedded in the model's semantic understanding and require fine-tuning. The method works by isolating a "refusal vector" inside the model's activation space and then orthogonalizing the weight matrices to neutralize that vector.

Mikheev built a custom five-stage harness, run in a Docker container on an NVIDIA GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory, that extracts the language model from the roughly 56 GB, 18-shard checkpoint. The pipeline probes the baseline, mines the refusal direction at layer 60 of 64, sweeps configurations in memory, bakes the change into the weights, and then accepts or rejects the result. The baseline runs use temperature set to 0 and thinking set to 0 so that responses are deterministic. The bake step modifies the residual-writing modules across layers 1 to 63, and the vision tower is left unchanged. Mikheev says he is a senior technology leader and software architect, with two decades of experience at firms including Capital One, Barclays, Actuate, Zuora and Personal Capital/Empower, and that he has consulted for the DTCC, the NYSE, Morgan Stanley and regional government agencies.

He argues that open-weight models carry risks, including the need to trust producers that no backdoors are embedded and the bias imposed by Chinese government regulations. He also notes that deploying an unknown pre-abliterated model from a repository such as HuggingFace is bad practice, which is why he built his own harness. The article's author notes that the custom framework was created with Qwen's help. The technique matters to developers and enterprises who host AI locally on consumer-grade hardware and want control over the models they run. Mikheev notes that the safety mechanisms used to prevent harmful output can be co-opted for state-level censorship.

He also cautions that a globally abliterated model, stripped of all safety rails, could produce genuinely harmful answers, which is why he limited the changes to specific political satire prompts. Mikheev says the abliterated model produced the requested sketch, titled "The Ministry of Mandatory Joy," with comedic timing comparable to its earlier American satire. He acknowledges the result is far from perfect, since responses to most political questions remain heavily biased. The article does not say how many prompts the final refusal vector required beyond the two prompts he found effective, and it does not describe the results of formal evaluation. It also leaves open whether techniques for removing soft refusals will be addressed in a future article, which Mikheev only says exist.

Articles.Title: The sketch Qwen refused to write: How abliteration restores local AI control

stories.Headline: How On-Page AI Assistants Are Transforming Digital Reading and Deep Research
stories.Summary:
This is not a news event but a sponsored opinion and overview piece published on vocal.media on November 12, 2026, by Qeemah Cloud, the creator of the Vezz me on-page AI reading assistant. The article argues that people who research dense digital text lose focus when they copy passages into separate AI chatbots in other tabs. It describes a shift toward small floating assistants that appear inside the browser page, triggered by a keyboard shortcut or a text selection, so the source text stays visible. The piece also presents this approach as a more ergonomic alternative to persistent sidebars that compress page layouts.

The article says these in-page tools are built around several features, including customizable hotkeys, adjustable panel size and opacity, and follow-up questions that do not create new browser history entries. It sets out security expectations as well, saying that responsible tools should send only the text a user selects, keep queries apart from browsing histories, and use secure backend proxies to protect API keys. It also states that such extensions should act only on user-initiated triggers rather than continuously reading background page content. The article gives no specific figures, dates for product releases, or measured results from studies.

Responsibility for the content rests with Qeemah Cloud, which the article describes as an accounting, ERP and POS platform with ZATCA Phase 2 compliance, and which also created Vezz me. The article notes that it was drafted with the help of an AI tool and reviewed against usability research, cognitive ergonomics and browser extension security standards, and it describes itself as an objective informational overview rather than formal commercial advice. The piece itself names no independent researchers or studies beyond general references to human-computer interaction findings. The article does not describe any next steps or planned changes beyond its general conclusion that in-page intelligence is a step toward more sustainable information use on the web.

Articles.Title: How On-Page AI Assistants Are Transforming Digital Reading and Deep Research

stories.Headline: Department of Justice forms AI task force
stories.Summary:
The Justice Department announced on Thursday that it has formed a new unit called the Super Intelligence Task Force, or DOJ-SITF, to deal with the misuse of artificial intelligence. Attorney General Todd Blanche set it up in an Oct. 13 memo, and the department made the formation public this week. The name follows a late September executive order from President Donald Trump telling federal agencies to call AI "super intelligence." The group is meant to protect American leadership in the technology from being compromised by bad actors. Those include foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individuals or companies engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct.

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss will co-chair the task force. It will coordinate the department's criminal and civil enforcement work involving AI, recommend enforcement priorities, and develop guidance on prosecuting unlawful AI-related conduct. It will also absorb the AI Litigation Task Force, which the department created in January under then Attorney General Pam Bondi to challenge state AI laws. The new group will serve as the department's main point of contact with the Super Intelligence Force, a White House body Trump announced last month and put under National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton. That body coordinates the government's engagement with various organizations and AI companies.

Blanche said the Justice Department will keep identifying and prosecuting people whose use of the technology breaks the law, including by targeting American taxpayers, critical U.S. infrastructure, or other national security interests. He added that the task force will take affirmative steps, as appropriate, to promote American dominance in the field, and that it will help the department work with Clayton to make sure critical technologies serve the American people. Weiss said the department has a responsibility to use its law enforcement tools to deter improper use. The department also said it will push companies deploying AI to keep strong internal controls so the technology behaves as intended.

The announcement did not say how many staff the task force will have, what it will cost, or when it will report. The name change adds a wrinkle, since super intelligence already has an established meaning, a term philosopher Nick Bostrom defined as any intellect that greatly exceeds human cognitive performance in virtually all areas of interest, separate from AI generally. Some coverage gave the announcement date as Nov. 5, while one report dated it to Thursday of this week. The Super Intelligence Force that the new unit will work alongside was created in early October, according to one report.

Articles.Title: U.S. Justice Department launches task force to counter AI-enabled fraud and cybercrime - 디지털투데이
