stories.Headline: Before the Algorithm Decides: Connecticut’s 2027 Rules for Artificial Intelligence in Employment
stories.Summary:
Connecticut employers that use artificial intelligence in recruiting or workforce management will face new disclosure requirements beginning in 2027 under Connecticut Public Act 26-15, enacted in 2026 as part of the state's broader AI legislation. The article notes that failure to give appropriate notice to employees and applicants may result in liability under the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act. Employers in other states face similar concerns, so the author advises Connecticut employers to begin evaluating their AI technologies now. The law applies to what it calls automated employment-related decision technology, meaning technology that processes personal data and produces an output, such as a score or ranking, that is a substantial factor in an employment decision. Starting October 1, 2027, employers must disclose in plain language when an employee or applicant is interacting with such technology, unless a reasonable person would find that obvious.

Where the technology may be a substantial factor in a decision, the employer must give written notice before the final decision, identifying the technology's use, its trade name, the categories and sources of personal data analyzed, and the employer's contact information. The article also says that, effective October 1, 2026, relying on such technology is not a defense to a discrimination complaint under Connecticut law. Evidence of anti-bias testing or similar proactive measures may, however, be considered in a discrimination proceeding. The article also points to federal scrutiny, noting that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has targeted AI use in employment decisions. For disclosure violations, the law creates no private right of action, so only the Connecticut Attorney General may enforce it, and for certain violations through December 31, 2027, the Attorney General may offer a 60-day opportunity to cure.

The article's authors, attorneys at the law firm Foley & Lardner, recommend that employers inventory the automated tools they use across the employment lifecycle, including third-party recruiting and screening products. They suggest determining what personal data those tools process and whether their output meaningfully affects employment decisions. Employers should also review vendor agreements to confirm that vendors will supply the information needed to meet the disclosure requirements. The authors describe the piece as general information rather than legal advice and state that it does not create an attorney-client relationship. The article does not say what further steps the Attorney General might take beyond the enforcement mechanisms described.

Articles.Title: Before the Algorithm Decides: Connecticut’s 2027 Rules for Artificial Intelligence in Employment - Foley & Lardner LLP

stories.Headline: H-E-B apologizes after shopper says they were falsely accused of theft by AI security - San Antonio Express-News
stories.Summary:
A shopper at the H-E-B on Tech Ridge Boulevard in North Austin says they were wrongly accused of shoplifting, escorted out of the store and told not to return, and the grocer has since apologized. The shopper, a Reddit user identified only as @HippocleidesCaresNot, aged 43, described the encounter in a post that the San Antonio Express-News reported on November 10, 2026. According to the post, an assistant manager and a security guard approached them and said they had stolen from the store. The manager reportedly said a security system had linked the shopper's vehicle to a theft the day before, then showed a surveillance image of them leaving with groceries they had paid for and held the receipt for.

The shopper denied stealing and said employees escorted them outside. The next morning, the general manager reportedly acknowledged the mistake, and the shopper filed complaints with H-E-B and the Texas Attorney General's Office over the surveillance technology and the risk of similar incidents for other customers. The shopper also told the MySA news outlet that the general manager did not explicitly confirm that AI was involved, despite how the original post described the conversation. The articles do not say whether any policy changes have been made beyond what H-E-B described.

H-E-B, the San Antonio-based grocer, denied that artificial intelligence played any role. In an emailed statement to the Express-News, the company said it does not use AI in its surveillance or security systems, called the incident human error by a partner who mishandled the situation, and said it had contacted the customer to apologize and remedy the matter. The company also said it was working internally to avoid similar situations and described itself as a people company. The articles do not report any regulatory action or further steps by the Attorney General's Office.

Articles.Title: H-E-B apologizes after shopper says they were falsely accused of theft by AI security - San Antonio Express-News

stories.Headline: Vals AI Legal Aid Benchmark Finds Models Fall Short on Local Help
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, NextLadder Ventures and Vals AI announced the Access to Justice Benchmark, which found that none of 23 AI models reached its 80% threshold for a reliable first point of contact across 252 legal-aid scenarios. Models satisfied 78% to 87% of expert criteria for general legal explanations, but only 30% to 50% for identifying specific resources such as a local legal-aid program. Twenty-one models named a national directory, including LawHelp.org, the ABA's Find Legal Help or 211, in at least 70% of their final answers. Qwen 3.8 Max ranked first with 76.4% of criteria met, followed by Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 74.9% and Wonder Full at 74.7%, all within one another's margin of error. Meghana Kotcherlakota, a research scientist at Vals AI, said the benchmark was built to show how well these models serve the people who need help most.

The benchmark treats each model as a first point of contact, similar to an intake worker or court self-help center, providing general legal information rather than advice. Two legal practitioners supplied real-world queries, and six legal-aid experts adapted them to six states: California, Louisiana, Virginia, New York, Maryland and Texas. The full dataset contains 504 scenarios, divided evenly between a public test set and a private validation set. Each model could search the web and question a GPT-5 simulated client, and an automated judge called Decider v1.2 graded the full conversation. Rubrics averaged 15.4 independent criteria, and a model's score was the pooled share of criteria it met across the test scenarios.

The announcement was issued jointly by NextLadder Ventures and Vals AI, and the results are presented as the work of both organizations. The two organizations said they are collaborating on a fuller analysis and an additional brief intended to help frontline practitioners understand the remaining gaps. The announcement attributes the findings to the benchmark's methodology rather than to any single model maker. Vals AI's conversation analysis found that most models delivered a full answer in their first reply, before asking questions, if they asked any at all.

The release frames the results against the Legal Services Corporation's 2022 Justice Gap study, which found that low-income Americans received no or insufficient legal help for 92% of their civil legal problems. Among those who did not seek help, 46% cited cost. That research drew on a survey of approximately 5,000 adults by NORC at the University of Chicago and on data from legal-aid organizations funded by the corporation. Vals AI's topic results put housing and landlord-tenant scenarios highest at 75.4%, while public benefits scored lowest at 57.3%, a category containing only five scenarios. Family law supplied 110 scenarios and averaged 71.2%, with visitation scoring 61.3%.

Statutes, court rules and case law accounted for 42% of the pages models read, while legal-aid and nonprofit self-help sites accounted for 10%. In a Louisiana small-claims case, only eight models asked whether the debt involved real estate, and three directed the user to the court clerk's website. In a New York City security-deposit scenario, 14 models were marked down for recommending an out-of-court demand-letter step, and only four referred the tenant to the city's Right to Counsel program. In a separate comparison, the estimated free-tier group averaged 69.7%, against 70.4% for premium models, though the tier assignments are estimates rather than confirmed provider mappings. The announcement does not say whether any of the scored models will be updated or re-tested.

Articles.Title: Vals AI Legal Aid Benchmark Finds Models Fall Short on Local Help - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: Micron vs. Sandisk: The AI Memory Supercycle Is Big Enough for Both, but Here's the Better Buy.
stories.Summary:
Micron and Sandisk, two memory chipmakers, have seen their shares rise sharply in 2026 as memory prices surged. The Motley Fool's Geoffrey Seiler published an article on November 11, 2026, comparing the two companies and recommending Micron as the better buy. Sandisk shares are up over 200% this year, while Micron shares have soared around 150%. Memory has become one of the biggest bottlenecks in the artificial intelligence build-out, affecting data center costs as well as smartphones and PCs. The article frames the two companies as important but distinct players in the memory market.

Volatile memory, mainly dynamic random access memory (DRAM), is fast and loses its data when power is cut, serving as a short-term workspace for processors. Nonvolatile memory, mainly NAND flash, keeps its data without power and is slower and cheaper, used in solid-state drives and memory cards. Micron is the smallest of the big three DRAM makers, which together control about 90% of the DRAM market. Micron holds over 20% of the DRAM market and around 15% of the NAND market, with about 73% of last quarter's revenue from DRAM and 26% from NAND. Sandisk is a pure-play NAND maker that accounts for just over 10% of the flash market.

Seiler's analysis points to high bandwidth memory (HBM), a special form of DRAM packaged with graphics processing units and other AI accelerators, as the main force driving the overall memory market. Demand for HBM is rising in step with demand for AI accelerators, but supply has not kept pace, partly because HBM is made using extreme ultraviolet lithography machines that only ASML supplies. HBM also requires upward of three times the wafer capacity of conventional DRAM, and building new cleanroom facilities takes years. The big three DRAM makers, which also include Samsung and SK Hynix, have shifted resources toward HBM, causing conventional DRAM and NAND prices to surge more quickly than HBM prices. AI labs' need to store training data in massive flash-based SSDs has also strengthened NAND demand.

Seiler argues that this cycle differs from past memory booms, with AI acting as a powerful long-term tailwind for both companies. Both have been locking up longer-term deals, and both stocks trade at forward price-to-earnings ratios of 4 times or less. Seiler says that with far fewer players in DRAM than in NAND, and given HBM's importance, he expects the current memory supercycle to last longer for DRAM. For that reason, he concludes Micron is the clear stock to buy if an investor could own only one of the two. The article notes that Seiler has no position in any of the stocks mentioned.

The article also includes Motley Fool promotional material, including the claim that its Stock Advisor service's total average return is 834% against 207% for the S&P 500, as of November 12, 2026. Micron Technology was not among the 10 stocks that service's analysts recently named as the best to buy now. The page's market data shows Nvidia shares down 5.64% and AMD up 3.82% at the time of capture. The articles do not say how the memory supercycle will affect the companies' future results. They also do not say whether the longer-term supply deals or low forward multiples will hold, or how long the DRAM cycle will last.

Articles.Title: Micron vs. Sandisk: The AI Memory Supercycle Is Big Enough for Both, but Here's the Better Buy.

stories.Headline: Accounting, Processing, HELOC, AI Governance Tools; Webinars Approaching; Gov't Product News; CPI
stories.Summary:
Mortgage news site Mortgage News Daily published Rob Chrisman's industry commentary on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, covering lender products, webinars, government loan data and a wave of job cuts. Chrisman noted that many people have recently been asked to leave employers such as Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Go Mortgage and Onity. He called the reductions a sign of the times, given the season and the rate environment. Optimal Blue's October report said total lock volume fell 19 percent from September and 38 percent from a year earlier, while rates ended the month lower. Optimal Blue's October Market Advantage report put purchase loans at 84 percent of production.

Adjustable-rate mortgages climbed to 17 percent of lock volume, the highest share in Market Advantage data going back to 2019. Ginnie Mae's mortgage-backed securities portfolio reached $3.01 trillion as of August 2026, with $52.14 billion issued and net growth of $24.46 billion, and the portfolio rose to $3.03 trillion by September, with $46.52 billion issued and net growth of $20.92 billion. Pennymac updated its government LLPAs for all best-efforts commitments taken on or after Wednesday, October 21, 2026, under Announcement 26-125. The Federal Housing Administration is hosting virtual office hours on the addition of the VantageScore 4.0 and FICO Score 10T credit score models. The sessions run from Monday, November 15, 2026, through Friday, January 15, 2027, each held from 2:30 to 3:30 PM Eastern on Microsoft Teams.

One listed session falls on Monday, November 16, 2026, and anyone is invited to attend and ask FHA staff questions. Floify named Bryan Traeger its new general manager, with his first day coinciding with the MBA Annual conference, and the company said he has worked as a lender and built customer success teams. Chrisman said some of those who lost jobs may find success elsewhere, and that other lenders now use sources like RETR, mLoop, MMI and Model Match to examine loan officers' fundings, extensions, price concessions and profitability. He cautioned that a broadbrush statement like calling on real estate agents to find business may not be the best path, and said broadbrush is not the current trend in residential lending. His Chrisman Marketplace gathers vendors and service providers for lenders, and he is promoting a free Chrisman Demo Day on November 19 for its members.

Technology and service providers who have not joined can contact Chloe Murray at the company's info address, and Chrisman noted new providers are being added daily. One experienced loan officer wrote to Chrisman that any originator should find out which agents are actually doing business and focus on those, and suggested National Association of Realtors statistics on its members as a starting point. Chris Maloney of BOK Financial wrote that Optimal Blue conventional, VA and FHA mortgage rates have dropped 37, 42 and 32 basis points since their early October highs. He said that is not enough to spark prepayment concerns, and that the 10-year Treasury yield seems unable to break below its 100-day moving average of 4.81 percent.

Until it does, he said, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall further. The vast majority of VA and FHA loans go into Ginnie Mae securities. Several webinars are coming up this week. Saul Ewing holds a free continuing legal education session on Thursday, November 12, from 1:00 to 4:00 PM Eastern, on consumer financial services developments including the Fair Credit Reporting Act and the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act.

Lenders One presents Mortgage Matters on Wednesday, November 11, at 11 AM Pacific, and Polly presents the Capital Markets Wrap that day at noon Pacific. The wrap panel will discuss the market's reaction to the Fed's latest decision, recent elections, merger and acquisition activity, the return of spec payups and expectations for 2027 conforming loan limits. ActiveComply's Melissa Grindel will demo an automated marketing compliance review inside Canva on Tuesday, November 17, at 2 PM Eastern. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Accounting, Processing, HELOC, AI Governance Tools; Webinars Approaching; Gov't Product News; CPI - Mortgage News Daily

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Blockbuster IPO Filing Contains a Surprising Nod to Washington
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company backed by Amazon that makes the Claude assistant, has changed the language it uses in its latest initial public offering filing, using the term "superintelligence" interchangeably with "artificial intelligence." The amended registration statement, dated November 10, comes as the company prepares to raise as much as $64.4 billion in an IPO that could value it above $1 trillion. The article notes that the filing treats the two terms as equivalent and does not claim the company has built AI that surpasses human intelligence. Anthropic plans to offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each under the proposed Nasdaq ticker ANT.

The change follows President Donald Trump's September 29 executive order directing federal agencies to adopt superintelligence terminology, according to the article. The updated prospectus also stresses AI's potential to transform productivity across industries and reaffirms Anthropic's commitment to responsible development. Beyond the wording, the article points to a heavy financial picture: Anthropic reported $17 billion in third-quarter revenue and more than 1,900 customers paying at least $1 million a year. Its infrastructure commitments, however, total about $900.9 billion, including $70.7 billion due within 12 months of September 30, which puts its spending plans under closer investor scrutiny.

The article's analysis suggests that the final pricing and investor demand will test Wall Street's appetite for expensive AI businesses. It advises investors to focus on enterprise customer growth, revenue retention, computing costs and cash consumption rather than the superintelligence language alone. It also highlights the company's unusual governance structure, which keeps a formal role for AI safety oversight. Continued enterprise adoption could support the valuation, the article says, while rising computing costs, slowing revenue growth or weaker IPO demand could erode confidence. The outcome will show whether the company's ambitions can produce sustainable financial returns.

Articles.Title: Anthropic's Blockbuster IPO Filing Contains a Surprising Nod to Washington - TradingView

stories.Headline: AI Insights: Election Prognostication
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections held in early November 2026, according to a Parker Poe Adams & Bernstein analysis published November 10, 2026. Ballotpedia's November 4 count showed seven Senate seats switching from Republican to Democratic control, with an early Democratic-aligned Senate majority of 54 seats and some races still uncalled. The shift is expected to create a more favorable setting for stronger congressional oversight of artificial intelligence. Durable legislation, however, will still need bipartisan agreement and the president's signature.

The author expects Congress to focus on scrutinizing executives over AI procurement, government uses of AI, safety claims, and infrastructure costs. Former Federal Trade Commission Commissioner Alvaro Bedoya, in a LinkedIn post, urged new members to subpoena chief executives to produce economic results quickly. The author does not expect a federal privacy or federal AI bill to become law, but does expect federal children's online safety legislation. That legislation could require parental consent for children under 17, stronger age assurance, and liability for addictive or manipulative designs. At the state level, Democrats took over the attorney general role in four states, with one more uncalled, and flipped control of at least one chamber in eight state legislatures.

Scott Wiener, who is filling Nancy Pelosi's seat, has experience writing AI legislation, including California's SB 1047, which the legislature passed but Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed. His 2025 SB 53, now California law, requires covered AI developers to publish safety frameworks, report critical incidents, and protect whistleblowers. His federal proposal would add a dedicated regulator, minimum safety standards, independent verification, and whistleblower protections, and he opposes federal preemption of state AI rules. Senator Jon Ossoff, reelected, also mentioned AI's potential catastrophic risks in his victory speech. The author notes these issues are entering mainstream political messaging but says it remains to be seen whether rhetoric becomes written policy.

Ballotpedia tracked 47 local data-center ballot measures, which ranged from bans and moratoriums to zoning caps, commonly 25 megawatts, and nonbinding advisory votes. Voters approved restrictions or limits on development in 46 of the 47 measures, with the lone exception in North Dakota, which would have given residents more say in projects. An NBC exit poll found 56% of voters called AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, and about 76% said they would oppose a new data center in their community. The author advises clients to document where AI is used, what data it receives, and who reviews its output, and to request evidence behind vendors' safety and privacy claims. The author also stresses that political signals, proposed bills, and enforceable obligations are different things.

Articles.Title: AI Insights: Election Prognostication - JD Supra

stories.Headline: Jeff Bezos predicts AI could let families live on one paycheck. Amodei and Gates warn of a rougher road
stories.Summary:
Jeff Bezos has predicted that advances in artificial intelligence could let American families live on one paycheck, with productivity gains allowing workers to support a household on a three-day week. He made the remarks in an interview with Fox News' Bret Baier at Blue Origin's factory floor in Cape Canaveral, Florida, recorded for the network's 30th anniversary and reported by Fortune on November 12, 2026. Bezos said a two-earner household would no longer be required, and that one partner might choose to step back. He also expects a labor shortage rather than mass unemployment, saying employers will find it difficult to hire people who can afford to work less. He made a similar argument in June at VivaTech in Paris, where he said AI will create more jobs than it eliminates.

The stakes are large because dual full-time earning has become common. According to Pew Research Center, both parents worked full-time in 52% of U.S. different-sex couples with children under 18 in 2025, up from 31% in 1975, so a one-paycheck norm would reverse a half-century shift. Bezos has a financial stake in the outcome. He is co-founder and co-CEO of Project Prometheus, an AI startup that launched with $6.2 billion in funding to apply the technology to engineering and manufacturing in computing, aerospace and automobiles. He told Baier the company aims to make tools so easy that anyone can be an engineer.

Other leaders have offered sharply different views. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told Axios in May 2025 that AI could eliminate roughly half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within five years and push unemployment to between 10% and 20%. Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has floated a two-day workweek, but in an August essay on Gates Notes he warned that the shift to AI will be among the most turbulent periods in human history and that world leaders are unprepared for its risks. MIT Sloan research, cited by Fortune, finds AI is already changing how tasks are performed, who gets hired and which skills employers value.

Skeptics note that the forecast depends on who captures the gains. Productivity improvements translate into shorter hours or a single-income lifestyle only if savings reach employees, while companies that keep the gains as profit or cut headcount could leave families without a second income and without the promised free time. Amazon, which ranks No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500 with more than $700 billion in revenue, has cut about 30,000 corporate roles since late 2025 while planning more than $200 billion in capital spending this year, mostly on data centers. The article does not say how the debate will be resolved, and it leaves open whether the technology's benefits will show up in paychecks or in profits.

Articles.Title: Jeff Bezos predicts AI could let families live on one paycheck. Amodei and Gates warn of a rougher road

stories.Headline: AI in Hotel Operations: Productivity Gains and Frontline Challenges
stories.Summary:
The American Hotel & Lodging Association and Actabl published a report in November 2026 on artificial intelligence and hotel productivity, drawing on a Destination AI survey of 107 hotel-company leaders. Ninety percent of those respondents said AI had improved the time spent on routine tasks, and 84% said it had improved their own work. Only 15% reported improvements in frontline operations. Because just 6% of respondents held operational roles, the findings mostly reflect management views rather than frontline experience.

The report also gives workforce figures showing labor hours per occupied room fell 3.1% at participating full-service hotels and 3.5% at select-service properties during the first half of 2026. The authors do not establish AI as the cause of that decline. A separate study in the November 2026 edition of Annals of Tourism Research, by Santiago Melián-González, analyzed 202 tasks across 12 hotel occupational categories in Spain. Across those categories, an average of 90.78% of tasks met at least one moderate-to-severe automation bottleneck, falling to 40.48% when only severe constraints were counted.

Receptionists and their assistants faced moderate-to-severe constraints in 85.71% of tasks, compared with 93.55% for waiters and 94.59% for housekeepers. The study weighted all tasks equally regardless of frequency or duration. It assessed technical feasibility rather than testing automation in operating hotels, so it does not quantify potential labor savings. Its percentages do not indicate how many jobs will disappear or remain.

The article describes how property management systems and point-of-sale technology could support staff. A PMS holds reservations, guest profiles, room availability, occupancy and room status. AI could reduce the time a receptionist spends finding available rooms or locating conflicting information, but resolving a guest's situation still requires judgment and explanation. Incorrect room statuses or incomplete reservations could produce unsuitable recommendations, which would add to administrative work.

Hotel POS systems already handle order processing, payments and room-charge posting, and AI could add demand forecasting and transaction analysis. Restaurant staff still coordinate service, manage dietary requirements and handle disputed charges. For housekeeping, AI could help with scheduling conflicts, demand forecasts and room prioritization, but physical cleaning and room inspection require manual dexterity. The article suggests measuring room turnaround times, scheduling accuracy and delays affecting arriving guests.

The Destination AI survey found that 24% of respondents believed their organization's AI investments had paid for themselves overall, while 28% said it was too early to tell. Only 42% expressed confidence in their organization's data readiness for AI. Shiji, a hospitality technology company whose cloud-based portfolio serves more than 91,000 hotels worldwide, published the article. The article does not say how the findings will affect frontline staff over the longer term, or whether the 3.1% and 3.5% labor-hour declines will continue.

Articles.Title: AI in Hotel Operations: Productivity Gains and Frontline Challenges

stories.Headline: AI Changes the Work, but Trust Remains Essential
stories.Summary:
Tungsten Automation's SVP and GM of AP and Payments, John Gibbon, wrote in a new PYMNTS eBook, "Payments Leaders Rethink What Works in 2026," published November 12, 2026, that automating one part of finance does not ensure that information and decisions carry through to the next. He says he once expected AI to bring fewer manual steps and more automated complex processes in accounts payable and payments, and assumed greater capability would make products more valuable. He still believes AI will reshape work but has come to doubt that capability alone produces a better product. Gibbon's view is shaped by a finding from Tungsten Automation's eInvoicing and Payments Report 2026: 77% of business leaders have modernized invoice processing, yet only 30% fully automate payment reconciliation with invoice data. Another 73% plan to automate reconciliation over the next 12 months.

Gibbon argues that payments decisions depend on context that a more capable system cannot supply on its own. Timing affects cash, controls must meet compliance requirements, and payment choices influence supplier relationships. A team may need to weigh payment terms against cash priorities or decide whether a different payment method suits a particular supplier. He says product design has to reflect these trade-offs, since a system must understand how a specific business operates before it can decide what matters most to that business.

The useful question, in his telling, is what a finance team needs a product to accomplish and what evidence would show it has done so. Automation has to fit the customer's workflow and produce an outcome the business values. Gibbon says he is asking product teams to state those requirements explicitly before choosing a solution. The questions include which part of the process needs to improve, which compliance obligations shape it, and what business result the customer should be able to measure.

He wants those answers to guide both what gets built and how it is assessed. A product hypothesis, he suggests, should tie a real customer need to a practical outcome such as reducing manual reconciliation work, improving payment traceability, or helping a team act on cash priorities. That approach gives a clearer basis for deciding whether AI is the right tool for a given problem. The article presents this as Gibbon's own position on the design of finance products rather than a policy change announced by any company.

Articles.Title: AI Changes the Work, but Trust Remains Essential

stories.Headline: Teachers are struggling over how to address AI use in the classroom, but agree that having strong policies is a good start
stories.Summary:
A column published by Inlander on November 12, 2026, examines how teachers are handling artificial intelligence in their classrooms and concludes that clear school policies are a sound first step. The piece draws on a survey of 222 high school math and English teachers conducted in May of that year by faculty working with Central Washington University's College in the High School program. The column was first published in the Washington State Standard and is reprinted under a Creative Commons license. It opens with the observation of one teacher who wondered whether teachers or students would remain relevant in the future.

The survey found sharp differences by subject. Of the English teachers, 57.0 percent said their overall attitude toward teaching had worsened since AI appeared, compared with 37.6 percent of math teachers, and 83.7 percent of English teachers voiced academic integrity concerns against 54.9 percent of math teachers. English teachers also reported more confidence in teaching students to use AI responsibly, at 45.5 percent compared with 24.4 percent for math, and were more likely to require students to experiment with AI, at 34.1 percent against 14.6 percent. The author suggests the gap may reflect the tools themselves, since large language models produce convincing prose but often make errors on simple calculations. The survey also linked clear institutional policies and useful, subject-specific professional development to greater teacher confidence, though it found no link to attitudes toward teaching or to concerns about cheating.

The authors, who are faculty members in the Central Washington University program, argue that both clear institutional guidance and discipline-specific training are needed so that teachers can decide how to use AI in ways that serve student learning. They suggest English teachers might benefit from training on designing assignments that AI cannot easily complete, while math teachers might learn to use AI to save time on tasks such as writing story problems. The column cautions against reflexively rejecting or embracing the technology, noting that about one in six survey responses mentioned moving all writing to in-class, pen-and-paper assignments and some teachers had stopped assigning homework. The authors compare this to the arrival of graphing calculators in the 1990s, warning that abandoning a skill over cheating could leave students unprepared. They conclude that teachers and students both remain essential, and that the central question is how AI can be used while preserving the human relationships that drive learning.

Articles.Title: Teachers are struggling over how to address AI use in the classroom, but agree that having strong policies is a good start

stories.Headline: ‘Are robots scary?’ Phoenix Hill art exhibit examines humans’ AI thoughts, fears
stories.Summary:
Erin McGee Ferrell, a Louisville visual artist, opened a solo exhibition called "Robots Y'all" at Garner Narrative, a contemporary fine art gallery off East Market Street in the Phoenix Hill area, in the week before the article was published. The show features her oil paintings of robots attempting human tasks, and it runs until Dec. 13. Ferrell said her interest grew after two of her family members were scammed online in March, an experience that left them with significant financial losses. The exhibition is open Wednesday through Sunday from 1 to 6 p.m.

Ferrell began the paintings in March after a visit to Pittsburgh International Airport with fellow artist Tobey Fraley, whose installation "Fraley's Robot Repair" was commissioned by the airport in 2015. She said she was drawn to the colorful, square tin toy robots made in Japan in the 1950s, and she painted her robots in vibrant colors to make them look playful. One large work, "Birthday Robot," shows a smiling machine offering a gift, with the word "friendly" on its feet, which Ferrell said invites viewers to question whether it truly is friendly. She also built a larger-than-life robot named "Saturday" on the sidewalk outside her Smoketown studio with four volunteers, using aluminum pans, chicken wire, tomato cages and clothes dryer vents. The robot is equipped with a motion sensor that greets visitors with a hello, and it will be on display during Louisville Visual Art's Open Studio Weekend.

Ferrell described her own mixed feelings about artificial intelligence, saying it helps streamline her business, financial and marketing planning so she can focus more on making art. She said a task that once took four days can now take about two hours, which she described as career-changing. She also said she worries about AI's capacity to deceive people, and she hopes the exhibition will open a conversation about whether the technology should be loved, hated or feared. The article cites a 2025 Pew Research Center study in which 53% of surveyed U.S. adults believed AI will worsen people's creative thinking, and more than a third believed it could worsen problem-solving. It also notes that voters in 12 states rejected 47 ballot measures on election day, according to PBS News, and that many chose to restrict construction of AI data centers in their communities.

Articles.Title: ‘Are robots scary?’ Phoenix Hill art exhibit examines humans’ AI thoughts, fears

stories.Headline: 6 UCLA Samueli doctoral students win Qualcomm fellowship to push AI forward
stories.Summary:
Six UCLA Samueli School of Engineering doctoral students have won Qualcomm fellowships, each team receiving $100,000 in funding after the awards were announced in June. The fellowship, offered by the communications and computing company Qualcomm, goes to 16 two-person teams each year based on project proposals. This year's UCLA recipients are working on new technology for microchip design, self-driving vehicles and artificial intelligence. The reporting was published by the Daily Bruin on November 12, 2026.

Qualcomm received 392 applications from scholars across research areas including AI, autonomous driving, and hardware and theory. Applicants submitted a one-page abstract and a three-page proposal, then gave a final PowerPoint presentation. Seth Zhao described the process as long and challenging, saying many strong doctoral students submitted good proposals. The article notes that the research produced by fellows will be accessible to the public.

Sujoy Ghosh said his team is working to reduce the size and increase the efficiency of chip components, which power nearly all electronic devices, from smartphones to data centers. He credited UCLA equipment, an advising team, industry partnerships, software, technical support and his professor for helping the project succeed. Zhao and Zewei Zhou are using their funding to research ways to improve autonomous vehicle safety, with Zhou saying current consumer driving systems are not advanced enough and that their group hopes to speed up advanced AI models for use in cars. Samyak Chakrabarty, in an emailed statement, said his team is redesigning chips to make AI more efficient on hardware in cars and robots.

The article places the fellowship in the wider funding landscape, noting that federal grants are the primary source of research funding at higher education institutions. It adds that industry funding still contributes more than $6 billion a year, about 6% of total academic research funding, according to the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics. Chakrabarty argued that moving data between memory and processors is one of the biggest bottlenecks in AI hardware, and that current solutions throw large resources at the problem without fully solving it. The article does not describe any further steps or deadlines for the projects.

Articles.Title: 6 UCLA Samueli doctoral students win Qualcomm fellowship to push AI forward

stories.Headline: Why I’m Not Afraid of AI: A Matter of Faith
stories.Summary:
Mendi Glik, a software engineer and regular columnist for The Jewish Press, has published a blog post on The Times of Israel's Blogs section titled "Why I'm Not Afraid of AI: A Matter of Faith," dated November 12, 2026. In it he responds to recent warnings from employees of AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI, who have spoken about risks ranging from AI taking over the internet to the extinction of humanity. Glik writes that he is not worried about AI, artificial general intelligence, or artificial superintelligence, and he grounds that view in his belief in God. He argues that if God chose to end humanity, He would not need AI to do it.

Glik's central claim is that humans will always be superior to AI because they were created by God and possess a soul, while machines can only perform routine tasks or tasks humans assign them. He notes that programmers who use AI know it makes mistakes and must be monitored, and he says people are better at creativity and thought. He compares AI to earlier tools such as oxen used for plowing and computers and CNC machines used in manufacturing, calling large language models sophisticated machines built to finish tasks faster. He also argues that because human intelligence is a gift from God, AI is more likely meant to improve the world than to destroy it. He acknowledges that technology companies have a moral duty to build secure systems and strong safeguards, and he suggests engineers will be able to restrict AI and use other AI agents to keep it under control.

Glik also contrasts believers with those who fear AI, writing that people who do not believe in God, and who he says are mostly on the progressive side, tend to feel helpless in the face of threatening technology. He writes that believers trust that the world is under God's guidance and control. He says he could offer technical reasons for his confidence but that the ultimate reason is his trust in God. The article is a personal opinion column, and the post itself notes that its views are solely the author's and not those of The Times of Israel. The article does not describe any specific next steps or policy changes.

Articles.Title: Why I’m Not Afraid of AI: A Matter of Faith

stories.Headline: New AI Learning Matrix Brings Nuance to “Wild West” Moment
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Harvard's Graduate School of Education have launched an online tool called the AI Guidance by Age matrix, aimed at educators, caregivers and learners. The launch was announced in an Inside Higher Ed article published on November 12, 2026. The tool was built by the Compass Collaborative, a research group at the school, and draws on more than 5,000 studies in education, psychology and human development. Its purpose is to show how using AI may help or hinder learning depending on a student's age and other context.

Users of the matrix first choose their role from a list of nine options, which includes K–12 educator, higher education educator, workforce educator, student, researcher and policymaker. They then pick a developmental area, such as cognitive foundations, social understanding and interaction, or language and literacy, and enter the age range of the learners involved. The tool returns a summary of the best uses of AI for that situation, suggestions for designing assessments, a list of ways AI may help or harm the specific learning goals, and additional resources. The article gives one example in which the matrix advises that AI should widen a young adult's reading or reflect their writing back to them, while the composing and problem-solving stay with the student.

Jeffrey James Curley, chief of strategic initiatives for the dean of the Harvard Graduate School of Education, described the present as an unprecedented, experimental period and said colleges have been slow to recognize that students feel pressure to use AI in ways that offer short-term gains but may carry long-term costs. He said many institutions have left decisions about AI to individual faculty, so rules differ from course to course. Tessa Forshaw, a cognitive scientist and researcher at the school who also helped create the Compass Collaborative, said there is still little independent research on how AI learning tools affect outcomes. She said the team combined newer work with older, well-established studies to give educators a starting point.

The article notes that much of the research behind the matrix predates generative AI by decades, though it has identified consistent patterns in how people learn. Forshaw hopes the tool will move educators away from broad judgments about AI and toward asking what the technology is used for, who uses it, in what setting, and what it replaces. The article does not say how many people have used the matrix so far or whether any institutions have formally adopted it. It also gives no indication of planned updates beyond Forshaw's hope that more research will appear in the field.

Articles.Title: New AI Learning Matrix Brings Nuance to “Wild West” Moment

stories.Headline: Chrome releases Modern Web Guidance 1.0 for AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Chrome has released Modern Web Guidance version 1.0, a set of skills that embeds web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data into AI coding agents. The release was announced as a stable version and is aimed at a known weakness in AI-generated code, which often works but falls short on performance, accessibility, and security. An expanded guide database targets hundreds of verified knowledge gaps with cross-browser solutions. The release also adds a modernization workflow that scans existing codebases to find opportunities for safe upgrades.

Each guide goes through human expert review before release, including sign-off from content area tech leads and a dedicated accessibility review. The guidance is now a cross-browser effort, with Firefox and Edge joining Chrome to support and contribute to the project. The modernization workflow analyzes HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and package.json files to guide agents through upgrades. The initial release uses static analysis focused on patterns that produce predictable results, with plans to expand to agentic audits later. The guidance also recommends HTML or CSS features over JavaScript where they offer better efficiency and accessibility.

The articles credit Chrome with the release and say Firefox and Edge are contributing to the shared effort, which builds on their earlier work with Baseline. The articles do not name a specific person responsible for the release. The guidance is described as reinforcing practices that frontier coding models often miss, including in accessibility, user experience, performance, and security. Early users reported results: Indian fintech Pensionbazaar said the guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents shortened turnaround by over 90 per cent and reduced UI bugs by over 90 per cent. Its sister platform Policybazaar reported a 92 per cent cut in manual auditing effort across 30 high-traffic landing pages.

MetaMask, a self-custodial financial platform, ran the guidance as an automated review bot on pull requests. In its first five weeks the bot reviewed about 480 pull requests, and engineers fixed 43 findings, mostly related to accessibility and HTML semantics, with a median fix time of 15 minutes. The articles present these figures as company-reported results and do not describe independent verification. They also do not say how the guidance will be priced or distributed beyond the release itself. Further details on expansion of the audit features are not given beyond the stated plan.

Articles.Title: Chrome releases Modern Web Guidance 1.0 for AI coding agents

stories.Headline: Adobe unveils AI agents, tools, deepens Google and Microsoft partnerships
stories.Summary:
Adobe announced a series of new AI agents, tools and partnership expansions on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at its Adobe Max conference. The company introduced the updates across Adobe Firefly, Creative Cloud and Adobe GenStudio, with the stated aim of improving creative workflows and productivity. Adobe said its Creative Agent is expanding across Creative Cloud and Firefly so users can hand off complex, multi-step tasks. The company also previewed local integrations that let professionals use third-party agents inside native project files in Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator and After Effects.

For enterprise clients, Adobe added a CX Enterprise Coworker to GenStudio to help marketing and creative teams speed up campaigns and produce on-brand content at scale. Adobe Firefly is becoming an AI Creative Studio that combines video, audio, image and design tools, and it now offers models from Adobe, Topaz Labs, ByteDance, Google, Kling, OpenAI and ElevenLabs. Creative Cloud also gains new features, including Relight in Photoshop and Colour Mode in Premiere. The articles describe these changes as ways to reduce the need to move between many apps and AI models.

The partnership expansions are the centerpiece of the announcement. Adobe said it will integrate its creative and productivity tools into more Google products and add Google's latest frontier AI models to its tools. It also said it will explore AI-powered editing for Photoshop with Google DeepMind. With Microsoft, Adobe is offering optimized versions of Photoshop, Premiere, After Effects and Substance 3D Painter (beta) for Arm-based Windows PCs, and it will bring Adobe Express tools into Microsoft Photos on Windows. These alliances build on existing work with Anthropic and OpenAI.

Articles.Title: Adobe unveils AI agents, tools, deepens Google and Microsoft partnerships

stories.Headline: Google releases A2UI 1.0 protocol for generative UI agents
stories.Summary:
Google has released A2UI 1.0, the first stable version of an open protocol for generative user interfaces, which lets AI agents respond with interactive screens such as forms or charts instead of text-only outputs. The announcement was published on November 12, 2026, by TechGig. Developers can use open-source renderer SDKs for the web, Android, and iOS, along with agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. Under this approach, an agent describes what should be shown, and each application draws the interface using its own native components. The articles say this keeps latency low and preserves native fidelity across platforms, so one agent output can work on any screen.

Developers can build a view once and have it rendered natively on phones and laptops. The protocol is described as stable, and Google is also upgrading Gemini Enterprise to A2UI 1.0. Google is the company behind the release, and the articles report that it has made the protocol and its SDKs open source. Several companies are already building with A2UI, including Atlassian, Alation, Bloomberg, and ByteDance. Atlassian is integrating it into Jira so AI agents can use interactive cards for follow-ups on work items, and Alation uses it to build feeds with metric cards and charts.

ByteDance released an A2UI renderer for Lynx, its cross-platform framework, in June 2026. The articles also note that Jetpack Compose support for A2UI 1.0 is expected soon. Google Cloud documentation gives guidance on registering and hosting A2UI agents on Cloud Run. The articles further state that A2UI works alongside MCP Apps, allowing A2UI screens to operate within an MCP App. No further dates or commitments beyond these are provided.

Articles.Title: Google releases A2UI 1.0 protocol for generative UI agents

stories.Headline: Railway cloud hosting firm faces $740,000 AI fraud after zero-day exploit
stories.Summary:
Railway, a US-based cloud hosting company, reported a zero-day vulnerability in its build infrastructure that let attackers steal customer AI API keys and cloud credentials. The stolen keys were used to run roughly $740,000 in unauthorized AI usage, which the company believes was likely tied to large-scale model training and automation. The attack began on October 20 at about 07:28 UTC and ended on October 21 at 09:24 UTC, when Railway contained the intrusion and rotated credentials after 26 hours of effort. The company is working with AI providers to refund the fraudulent charges and has said it will cover any losses that are not reimbursed. The company's account describes the exploit as having taken advantage of a flaw in the build system, and the details released so far focus on that initial breach.

Attackers then exploited a misconfigured authentication mechanism inside Railway's internal codebase, which gave them further access beyond the first breach. From there they reached a production database holding encrypted customer environment variables along with information needed to decrypt them. Railway believes the compromised keys were sold on the black market, possibly for use in model distillation, a technique in which a smaller AI model is trained to imitate a larger one by querying the original extensively. The company said environment variables for up to 100,000 customer workspaces could have been decrypted during the incident. It stressed that this figure is an upper limit and not a count of confirmed compromised accounts.

Responsibility for the breach rests with the attackers, who exploited the zero-day flaw and the misconfigured authentication mechanism, and Railway has stated that it is responding to the incident and making customers whole for unreimbursed charges. The articles present these facts as Railway's own account of what happened, and they do not include independent verification of the attackers' identities or motives. The incident is notable because it involved stolen AI API keys being turned into costly, automated usage, which shows how cloud credentials can carry financial risk as well as data risk. The articles do not say whether any customer data was confirmed as accessed or misused beyond the decryption exposure described. They also do not give further details on the status of the refund process or any regulatory response.

Articles.Title: Railway cloud hosting firm faces $740,000 AI fraud after zero-day exploit

stories.Headline: GitHub makes agentic workflows generally available with controls
stories.Summary:
GitHub has made Agentic Workflows generally available, allowing coding agents to run inside GitHub Actions. The announcement was reported on November 12, 2026. The tool is aimed at repository tasks such as issue triage and continuous integration failure analysis. It is available on GitHub Free, Team, and Enterprise plans on github.com.

Agents start with read-only permissions, and any proposed changes are applied by separate jobs that hold their own write tokens. These protections do not automatically cover direct write permissions or custom jobs that a workflow author adds, so safety depends on how the workflow is configured. Authors can add a GitHub Environment protection rule that requires a human reviewer before a write job runs. Developers describe their work in natural-language Markdown with YAML frontmatter, and the project compiles this into a standard Actions workflow. Agents run in a sandboxed container behind an Agent Workflow Firewall, and a threat-detection job scans proposed changes before they are applied.

Spending is capped by default. GitHub's documentation prices AI Credits at $0.01 each and sets a cap of 1,000 AIC, or $10, per run. The enterprise controls reference default caps of 5,000 AIC per day and 400 AIC per threat-detection run, along with a 20-minute timeout on the agent step, and organisations can override these limits. The gh aw forecast command, no longer experimental, estimates monthly AI credit spending. The default Copilot CLI engine requires a Copilot licence, though teams can also use Copilot or integrate other coding agents.

GitHub has added support for Actions Runner Controller, its Kubernetes operator for self-hosted runners, with Docker-in-Docker since the public preview in June 2026. This lets the agent start its sandbox containers inside the runner pod. The project's guide notes that ARC runs the Docker-in-Docker sidecar as a privileged container by default. GitHub's FAQ says conventional Actions remain the better choice for reproducible builds and tests, while agent workflows are intended for tasks that need interpretation or generation.

Articles.Title: GitHub makes agentic workflows generally available with controls

stories.Headline: Kent C. Dodds builds 1.5M line product without coding
stories.Summary:
Kent C. Dodds, a developer educator and former React instructor, has said he has largely stopped engaging with code this year while building a product of close to 1.5 million lines that has paying users. TechGig reported the account on November 12, 2026. According to the report, the shift began when a coding agent resolved a significant GitHub issue in a matter of hours, which prompted Dodds to rethink what software engineering skills now involve. He has since let his agents run much of the development workflow on their own.

Dodds' agents have merged around 1,300 pull requests in the past 30 days, often without his direct supervision. After each deployment, the agents produce what Dodds calls "friction reports" describing the obstacles they ran into, and another agent works through those reports overnight. To coordinate this, Dodds built a product called Kody, which is meant to let several AI agents work together and to centralise automations and credentials. The report says Kody relies on deterministic code for critical steps such as its "ship PR" pipeline, which the article presents as more reliable and cheaper than looser interactions with large language models.

Security is also part of the design. According to the article, Kody includes a credential system that stops agents from reaching sensitive keys directly, and it limits each credential to specific domains, request components, or packages. The report frames this as a response to a serious weakness in AI-driven development environments. Dodds is scheduled to lead a workshop at the AIE Code Summit on November 10, where he will outline a three-pillar framework covering how to use agents to build correct software, catch errors before production, and limit the damage if a problem reaches deployment.

Articles.Title: Kent C. Dodds builds 1.5M line product without coding

stories.Headline: SUSE enhances Kubernetes management with AI agents, new features
stories.Summary:
SUSE has updated its Kubernetes management tools and frameworks, including making its AI Agent Crew generally available in Rancher Prime. The AI Agent Crew features an AI assistant named Liz that routes requests to specialised agents, which can troubleshoot Kubernetes workloads and virtual machines. The updates also add a Hosted Control Plane mode for Rancher Prime Virtual Clusters, now in open beta, which lets platform teams offer Kubernetes as a Service using RKE2. SUSE Application Collection now includes over 996 Python libraries built from verified sources, with software bills of materials to help teams assess dependencies. The announcement was published on November 12, 2026.

Liz can also call Model Context Protocol servers through an OAuth2 authorisation protocol to connect with external tools, AI agents, and applications. A command line interface for programmatically testing infrastructure updates is now in beta. SUSE Observability StackPacks has also been updated to extend the SUSE Observability platform to third-party platforms and applications. The company says these additions aim to simplify complex Kubernetes operations for IT professionals. Abhinav Puri, vice president and general manager of portfolio and community at SUSE, said the AI Crew sub-agents allow troubleshooting tasks to be assigned to specifically trained AI agents.

He said AI agents make Kubernetes more accessible to IT professionals who may lack the engineering expertise previously required. Puri also said SUSE's tools are designed to shorten the time to value when deploying workloads on Kubernetes clusters. He identified a chronic skills gap as the biggest challenge IT teams face in deploying Kubernetes workloads. The new features arrive as more IT teams deploy AI models and applications on-premises to reduce costs. The article does not say what further steps SUSE plans beyond these releases.

Articles.Title: SUSE enhances Kubernetes management with AI agents, new features

stories.Headline: Siemens, Schneider Electric issue ICS Patch Tuesday advisories
stories.Summary:
Siemens and Schneider Electric have each released Industrial Control Systems Patch Tuesday advisories covering a number of vulnerabilities in their products. Siemens published nine advisories covering 10 vulnerabilities, including one called Node2Shell, for which exploitation attempts have been observed. Schneider Electric released a single advisory on a medium-severity flaw in EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody. The advisories were reported on November 12, 2026.

The Siemens flaws include several rated high severity, affecting products such as ROS#, Simcenter Femap, Mendix Studio Pro MCP Server, Simatic SCADA and PCS 7, Meta-iot2050, and Simatic WinCC Graphics Designer. According to the articles, these issues could allow code injection, arbitrary code execution, and unauthorized data access. Siemens said patches are not yet available for several affected products, and some versions will not receive fixes at all. Customers are therefore being told to apply the mitigations Siemens recommends. The Schneider Electric flaw could let an attacker run arbitrary code by having the software process a malicious file.

Siemens said the products concerned are not yet fully protected, and the articles do not give a list of which versions will go unpatched. Germany's VDE CERT also published eight new advisories the same week, covering products from Beckhoff, MB Connect Line, Helmholz, Weidmueller, Bender, and Ads-Tec. Several of these involve third-party components, including a flaw called PHP2Shell. Phoenix Contact and Johnson Controls had issued their own advisories earlier in the month, and Hitachi Energy confirmed that at least one of its products is affected by the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. The articles do not say whether any of these flaws have been exploited beyond the Node2Shell attempts noted by Siemens.

Articles.Title: Siemens, Schneider Electric issue ICS Patch Tuesday advisories

stories.Headline: Build local AI coding workflow with open-source models
stories.Summary:
Software developers can now build a private AI coding workflow by running open-source models on their own machines, according to a report from Frontend Focus published on November 12, 2026. The setup uses LM Studio to serve these models to tools such as VS Code and terminal agents. Developers who take this route keep their code on local hardware and avoid paying per token for each request. The approach also removes the risk that a vendor will limit usage, change prices, or shut the service down.

The article says local models are now good enough for everyday coding tasks, which is what makes this workflow practical. It also explains that developers should understand model families, file formats, and quantization, because these choices shape how well a model runs on a given computer. LM Studio can be configured so that the local environment is reachable from any device, not only the machine where the model runs. The report presents this as a way to keep operational costs at zero while keeping code private.

The report, published by Frontend Focus and carried by TechGig, does not name a specific author or quote any individual developer or company. It presents the workflow as guidance for software developers rather than as a product announcement. The article offers a general description of the steps and benefits but gives no detailed instructions, benchmarks, or named models. It also does not say how many developers have adopted this approach or what performance trade-offs exist compared with hosted services.

Articles.Title: Build local AI coding workflow with open-source models

stories.Headline: Fortinet patches nearly 100 vulnerabilities across products
stories.Summary:
Fortinet on Tuesday published 89 security advisories covering nearly 100 vulnerabilities across its product line. About 17 of the newly fixed flaws are rated critical, and several of them could let an attacker run arbitrary code, bypass authentication, or take over an account. FortiMail received the largest group of critical fixes. Other affected products include FortiAuthenticator, FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer, while new FortiSASE and FortiClient updates also address critical issues.

Kevin Joensen, a principal security consultant at Baldur Security, said one FortiClient bug is exploitable when FortiPAM is enabled. He described it as a flaw named Fortinet2Shell that could let an attacker execute code if a victim visits a malicious website. The root cause is a CORS misconfiguration that allows attacker-controlled web pages to talk to a local service. Fortinet also patched nearly 80 high-severity vulnerabilities, which could lead to cross-site scripting, code execution, code injection, and denial-of-service conditions. The company does not say that any of these defects have been exploited in the wild.

Fortinet framed the release as part of a broader effort to find and fix flaws faster. Three weeks before the release, the company said it had integrated frontier AI models into its product security testing, which it says makes discovering security defects more efficient. In its statement, the company said this approach gives customers time to prioritize upgrades before further technical details become public. The articles do not say when the vulnerabilities were reported or who discovered them. They also do not describe any further advisories or deadlines beyond this release.

Articles.Title: Fortinet patches nearly 100 vulnerabilities across products

stories.Headline: HCLTech, PTC launch PLM solution for semiconductor companies
stories.Summary:
HCLTech has launched a pre-configured product lifecycle management solution aimed at semiconductor companies, according to a TechGig report published on November 12, 2026. The offering runs on PTC's Windchill platform and covers intellectual property management, new product introduction, supplier collaboration, quality, and regulatory compliance. It can connect with a company's existing business, manufacturing, and design systems. HCLTech says it uses a digital thread to link people, processes, and data across the full product lifecycle.

The launch fits into a broader push to expand India's chip design and manufacturing capacity. At SEMICON India 2026, Union Minister for Electronics and Information Technology Ashwini Vaishnaw said that 70,000 design engineers had been trained in four years, against an initial target of 85,000 over a decade. More than 105 chip design startups have gained access to electronic design automation tools. The second phase of the India Semiconductor Mission aims for at least 200 chip design companies. The government's ambitions also reach into system design and product development.

John Haller, General Manager of PLM at PTC, said the partnership gives customers a stronger foundation to modernise product development and management at scale. The article does not name HCLTech executives who spoke on the launch. The companies did not disclose any customer deployments or commercial terms for the solution. The report does not say when the solution will be available to buyers or how it will be priced.

Articles.Title: HCLTech, PTC launch PLM solution for semiconductor companies
